====================================================================================================

News Analysis: Poland's strong growth masks mounting fiscal risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:25:38 CST
06:25:38 KST

WARSAW, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Poland's economy has maintained relatively strong growth, but rising public debt, elevated borrowing costs and growing banks' exposure to government securities are raising concerns about the country's ability to sustain investment and long-term development.
A report released Friday by SGH Warsaw School of Economics (SGH) and the Polish Bank Association (ZBP) highlights a growing dilemma: how to bring public finances under control without undermining the investment needed to support future growth.
GROWTH WITHOUT FISCAL RELIEF
Poland has shown robust economic activity in recent years. According to the European Commission's spring forecast, its gross domestic product (GDP) grew 3.6 percent in 2025, and is projected to grow 3.25 percent in 2026 and 2.7 percent in 2027.
However, this relatively strong performance has not translated into a corresponding improvement in public finances. The European Commission expects its debt-to-GDP ratio to rise from 59.7 percent of GDP in 2025 to 64.5 percent in 2026 and 68.3 percent in 2027.
The divergence between economic growth and fiscal performance reflects structural pressures on government spending.
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Poland's widening fiscal deficit since 2021 reflects a substantial increase in expenditure. Public spending is now close to levels in advanced European economies, while government revenues remain closer to the average for Central and Eastern Europe (CEE).
The SGH-ZBP report reaches a similar conclusion. It estimates that around 76 to 78 percent of state-budget expenditure is effectively rigid, including pensions and transfers, healthcare, defense, public-sector wages and debt service.
Such spending commitments leave limited room for fiscal adjustments. Higher borrowing costs are adding to the pressure. The yield on Poland's 10-year government bonds reached 6.55 percent on Sept. 15, its highest level since early 2023.
The report estimates that annual debt-service costs could rise from 66.5 billion zlotys (about 17 billion U.S. dollars) in 2024 to nearly 130 billion zlotys (about 33 billion dollars) in 2029.
As a growing share of public resources is devoted to servicing existing debt, the government's flexibility to finance new development projects could become increasingly constrained.
BANKS' GROWING EXPOSURE TO PUBLIC DEBT
Beyond the direct fiscal burden, the report identifies another potential risk: the growing concentration of government debt on Polish banks' balance sheets.
Between 2017 and the first quarter of 2026, Treasury debt and liabilities of government-related funds covered by the SGH-ZBP study increased by about 1.5 trillion zlotys (about 380 billion dollars). Banks increased their holdings of government and state-guaranteed securities by 561 billion zlotys (about 143 billion dollars), absorbing about 37 percent of that increase.
A strong domestic investor base can help stabilize government financing by reducing dependence on foreign investors. But it also ties the government's fiscal position closer to the banking system.
Government debt instruments account for roughly a quarter of Polish bank assets, the highest share among the EU countries compared in the study.
This exposure could become problematic if rising sovereign risk premiums reduce the market value of government securities or limit banks' capacity to expand lending.
The report's simulation suggests that a three-percentage-point increase in Poland's sovereign risk premium could reduce banks' additional lending capacity by about 204 billion zlotys (about 52 billion dollars).
INVESTMENT NEEDS COMPLICATE FISCAL CHOICES
The challenge is particularly significant given Poland's substantial long-term investment requirements.
The SGH-ZBP report estimates that investment demand in energy, infrastructure, digitalisation and defense could total around 4 trillion zlotys (about 1.02 trillion dollars) by 2040. At present, Polish companies finance about 74 percent of investment from internal funds.
Meeting future investment needs on this scale will require broader access to financing, including bank credit, capital markets and public investment support.
This creates a difficult policy trade-off. Cutting investment may improve the fiscal numbers but weaken productivity and future revenues. Continued heavy reliance on public borrowing, however, would raise debt-service costs and deepen banks' exposure to sovereign debt.
The economic impact will also depend on how borrowed funds are used. The SGH-ZBP report therefore advocates a gradual, multi-year consolidation that protects productive investment rather than simple austerity policy.
It also recommends shifting toward a financing model in which public and EU resources are used to mobilize private capital through guarantees, equity investment and risk-sharing arrangements.
For Poland, the central challenge is not simply to reduce public borrowing, but to ensure that fiscal consolidation and investment financing reinforce rather than undermine each other. ■

PANAMA CITY, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- A 7.2-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday, with its epicenter 39 kilometers northwest of Tonosi, a town in Los Santos province, according to a revised report from the University of Panama's Institute of Geosciences.
Strong shaking was felt locally. Videos shared on social media showed the roof of the Albrook bus terminal swaying and windows shaking violently in several buildings.

The tsunami warning department of the Chilean Navy's Hydrographic and Oceanographic Service also issued an alert, saying the earthquake could trigger a tsunami affecting the country's Easter Island. ■

Hurricane Isaias barrels toward Gulf coast as category 3 storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:22:04 UTC
06:22:04 KST

Isaias strengthened into a category 3 hurricane on Friday as it barreled toward the US Gulf coast, where states of emergency have been declared in Alabama, Florida and Mississippi.
The hurricane, the first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late 2026 season, is expected to cause a “life-threatening storm surge”, officials said. Isaias is forecast to make landfall on Friday night, somewhere along the western Florida Panhandle, with surging seas up to about 7ft (2.1 meters) and waves as high as 30ft (9.1 meters).
“Damaging hurricane-force winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, where a hurricane warning is in effect. Residents in these areas should prepare for the possibility of long-duration power outages,” the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) said.
Noaa said a storm surge was expected from south-east Louisiana to Suwannee, in north-east Florida. Isaias could also dump up to 15in (380mm) of rain on coastal areas and even spawn tornadoes overnight on Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and south-western Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore.
Heavy rain began falling along the coast on Friday morning and winds were picking up sharply, with tropical storm conditions expected by early afternoon.
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 115mph on early Friday evening, down from 120mph at mid-morning, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC). The NHC at that time said increasing wind shear was weakening the storm’s intensity.
The center also said that Isaias was about 90 miles south of Pensacola, Florida, and headed north at nearly 17mph.
The NHC said Dauphin Island, a barrier island off the Alabama coast, could see a 7ft (2.1-meter) storm surge, while Indian Pass, 200 miles to the east on the Florida coast, could see a 6ft surge.
“Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today,” the NHC said. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast.”
Alabama’s governor, Kay Ivey, ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Dauphin Island, Gulf Shores and Orange Beach on Thursday, while officials encouraged voluntary evacuations for residents. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double red flags signaled that beaches were closed.
Ivey has declared a state of emergency for 40 counties in Alabama, while Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida, has declared a state of emergency in 27 counties. Several cities and counties in south Mississippi have done the same. DeSantis said 5,000 national guard troops were expected to mobilize in Florida, where at least four school districts cancelled late-week classes.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which predates the satellite era of the 1960s for tracking hurricanes.
Before the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.
As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3m barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf’s 371 crewed oil platforms had been evacuated.
The storm could be the first major test of the ability of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to deploy a large workforce after the Trump administration’s sweeping cuts and restructuring of the agency, emergency management experts say.
The Trump administration has said it wants to eliminate, or drastically downsize, Fema, putting more burden on states. More than 4,300 employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, about 17% of the workforce, according to a recent US Government Accountability Office (GAO) report.
The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

US lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:14:37 UTC
06:14:37 KST

US lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 - The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist.
The move comes after Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration had opened talks with Myanmar's military-installed government, reversing US policy that sought to isolate the generals who overthrew elected leaders in 2021.
It was unclear if the decision to remove Myanmar national Theint Win Htet from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) was a result of the talks.
After the 2021 coup, former President Joe Biden's administration imposed sanctions on senior Myanmar military officers and companies it accused of providing support for the military junta, which triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
The Treasury in January 2024 targeted the Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies, its founder Thein Win Zaw and his family, saying the company imported and distributed petroleum on behalf of the military and that the family owned at least 20 companies closely associated with the regime.
Thein Win Zaw's adult daughter, Theint Win Htet, sued the Biden administration seeking her removal from the SDN List, but her case was dismissed in February 2025. The sanctions freeze any US assets of those targeted and generally bar Americans from dealing with them.
The US in July 2025 lifted sanctions on several other Myanmar nationals and a firm under sanctions for aiding the military.
Theint Win Htet filed a new complaint in July this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father's business affairs, adding that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the US, where she completed a bachelor's degree at New York University and was enrolled in a master's program at Columbia University.
"Plaintiff’s US credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been unable to complete her university studies in the United States," said the complaint by Theint Win Htet, who said in the complaint she now lives with her mother in Bangkok. Her mother remains under US sanctions.
Campaign group Justice For Myanmar denounced the US move at a time when it said the Myanmar military was escalating attacks on civilians. "It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta's terror," the group said.
Theint Win Htet's lawyer, Washington-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday voluntarily dismissing the lawsuit after her delisting. Ferrari declined to comment. REUTERS

The Western Bulldogs have brought a ruthless mentality to Pride Round in thrashing Essendon by 43 points.
Friday night's 10.5 (65) to 2.10 (22) result was the Bulldogs' seventh win for the season and sent a warning to the top eight sides on the cusp of finals.
It came despite their shaky start in front of a home crowd at Whitten Oval.
Essendon came out firing and Emily Gough kicked the first goal inside the first two minutes, spurring the Dons, who played with high pressure and repeatedly locked the ball in their forward half.
The Bulldogs responded with five unanswered goals with the help of an unstoppable Isabelle Pritchard, who had 30 disposals and 10 clearances.
"We weren't playing the style of game that we came to play," Dogs midfielder Jess Fitzgerald said after quarter time.
"We wanted to come into the game with a bit of a ruthless mentality, and we felt like we didn't bring that in the first.
"So, yeah, we turned that on."
Essendon were down by 25 points at half-time but hopes of repeating last week's win over the Giants, a comeback from 24 points down at half-time, were cut short by their inability to find the goals.
After Gough's early major, the Bombers kicked nine points until Sophie Alexander found their second just before three-quarter time.
The Bombers managed one more point in the final term, while the Dogs slotted another three goals.
Star forward Sarah Hartwig had a career-high four goals and helped the Western Bulldogs surpass the 60-point mark for the fifth time since 2025.
"Honestly, it's just that work rate and the pressure that we bring, especially in the forward line. That's what we pride ourselves on," she said.
Despite the win, the Bulldogs still have work to do in the season's run home, Hartwig said.
"We're not looking to finals yet. We've got three tough games coming up, so we're going to focus on that first," she said.
The Dogs will face Carlton, Melbourne and Geelong — all premiership contenders — in the final three games of the season.
Essendon will play North Melbourne, before facing Hawthorn and Collingwood.

Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare. Ukrainian forces combined assaults with drones and ground robots to reclaim territory in Donetsk Oblast while limiting their exposure to Russian fire.
More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit. Russian officials confirmed the fires but named none of the targets.
Ukraine reruns its Vivaldi playbook outside Kramatorsk and pushes Russia back across the Siverskyi Donets, ISW says. Even Russian milbloggers now concede Ukrainian gains east of Sloviansk, including a river crossing toward a key height.
Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant. In Bashkortostan, Ukraine’s General Staff says its forces hit a Gazprom refinery. Salavat’s mayor says an unnamed enterprise there keeps working.
Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says. The faster drones break through Ukraine’s air defenses more reliably, and ISW expects the same strike pattern in Russia’s winter campaign against Ukraine’s energy.
Intelligence and technology
Air-raid sirens cost Kyiv’s weapons makers 61.8 working hours in month, nearly eight days, yet their contract deadlines stay fixed, two groups say. Ukraine’s gunmakers want the government to count real siren downtime against contract deadlines.
Ukrainian producer that neutralized more than 7,000 drones over 100 square kilometers in year, plays enemy in Pentagon contest, and gets invitation to continue. Ukraine’s Phantom Defense built the counter-drone environment for the Pentagon’s Gauntlet II.
Ukraine uses up Europe’s yearly supply of thermal sensors in about five months, so two Ukrainian firms will build their own plants in the West. Their new venture wants to give Western armies their own supply of the chip that lets thermal cameras see body heat in the dark.
Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites. Substations near Ukraine’s western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe, could be among the first targets.

Trump says Russia agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel to US and global markets as he blames Ukraine for fuel price hikes driven by Iran war. The announcement comes as Trump pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, which Ukraine targets to weaken Moscow’s war economy.

Ukrainian journalists say Austria detained them “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated. Tkach says armed people smashed the car windows, forced the journalists onto the road, and put a knee on his neck during the detention.
Russia sells cheaper fuel abroad and pays to keep its own pumps running amid Ukraine’s refinery strikes, but crude money still flows. After Ukraine’s drone strikes on refineries, Russia’s diesel exports, once its biggest fuel export, fell to a decade low.
Fought against Ukraine, now claimed to be victims: Kenya’s plea for five men held by Ukraine. Kenya says the men took Russian army contracts under false job promises.
Moldova pulls its border officers off Ukrainian soil again as Russian drones keep hitting crossings. “They will work on the territory of Moldova.” Moldovan Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin, on withdrawing border personnel from Ukraine.
Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization. The move comes as Moscow rejects reports of a new call-up while Ukrainian officials warn Russia is preparing to expand its forces.

Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast. Residents are being warned that, in addition to constant Russian attacks, there is a risk of encountering explosive devices.
Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk. Hours after the strike, the head of Donetsk Oblast ordered public transport in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk halted, saying Russia had made the buses a target.
A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle. Zlatoslava is in hospital in Chernihiv. Her aunt, a police officer, was wounded in the strike.

Investigators say prosecutors shielded scam call centers. Their office has now fired eight people and is checking how its ex-chief left Ukraine. The acting chief also ordered out a deputy at the regional office he ran until September and dropped no-contest hiring of outsiders.

Macron’s nuclear throwdown, Mossad’s man in Germany, Ukraine in flames: RT stories that shaped the week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:04:53 UTC
06:04:53 KST

Macron’s nuclear throwdown, Mossad’s man in Germany, Ukraine in flames: RT stories that shaped the week
Macron sends a nuclear message
When France’s military test-fired its latest nuclear-capable ballistic missile, the submarine-launched M51.3, on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron chose to milk the spectacle for every last drop of propaganda value. “To be free, we must be feared,” he said. “And to be feared, we must be powerful.”
The launch, Macron said, was intended as “a clear message… for wherever it must be received.”
The missile may have splashed down in the north Atlantic, but the message was received “loud and clear” in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the following day. “Problems should be resolved through dialogue, not demonstrative missile launches,” but Russia will take “all necessary measures” to protect its strategic security, Peskov added.
France is currently modernizing and expanding its nuclear arsenal amid a broader rearmament push, but it remains unclear how Paris intends to pay for its remilitarization. This week, RT looked at France’s looming sovereign debt crisis and the violent riots tearing the country apart from within.
This domestic turmoil isn’t unique to France, nor is it something that can be fixed with minor policy tweaks. As RT examined on Friday, mass migration has already pushed European housing, security, and welfare systems to the breaking point. With native Europeans set to become minorities in their own countries in the coming decades, the social and political consequences could be deadly.
Germany’s enemies within
France is not the only European power gearing up for conflict abroad while its political and economic foundations disintegrate at home. Germanys’ foreign intelligence chief opened the week with a warning to lawmakers: Moscow is waging “a shadow war” against Europe, and “Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia.”
The Kremlin views accusations of “shadow war” and “hybrid war” – which are unprovable by nature – as “hastily cobbled-together provocations,” designed to serve “Kiev and the militaristic wing of the European political class.”
They’re provocations that Berlin is looking less and less able to follow through on. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is going from one electoral humiliation by the right-wing AfD to another, anti-war protests are spreading, and conscientious objections to a proposed military draft have tripled.
However, the German government can’t trust the loyalty of its own intelligence agents. Former spymaster August Hanning was charged with treason and espionage this week, in what appears to be the country’s worst spy scandal since the Guillaume affair of the 1970s.
German prosecutors aren’t revealing which foreign services Hanning allegedly collaborated with, but as RT explored in the latest installment in our ‘Wired for War’ series, all the signs point to Israel’s Mossad.
Russia reminds Zelensky what it’s capable of
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky is also on shaky ground this week. “Disappointment” and “shame” are now the most common feelings Ukrainians associate with him. US President Donald Trump blamed him for the worldwide diesel fuel shortage while Zelensky doubled down on silencing his critics, stepping up his long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.
He soon learned that Russia always responds. Russian forces pounded data centers, logistics hubs, weapons depots, and missile factories across Ukraine this week, including production plants of Ukraine’s flagship ‘Flamingo’ cruise missiles. “People in Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kiev regime for this. It is Zelensky who bears full personal and political responsibility for it,” the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
The strikes continued all week, as Zelensky prepared to fly to Miami for a meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Friday. Witkoff and Kushner were bringing “new ideas and proposals” aimed at resolving the conflict. The two could travel to Moscow later this month for another round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Although Zelensky’s situation at home may be deteriorating, he can still count on the support of his backers in Europe. Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk, who has been sanctioned by Ukraine and the EU over his war reporting, was detained in Montenegro on Friday. Zvinchuk founded the ‘Rybar’ Telegram channel, and was reportedly preparing to film a report on Montenegro’s plans to align its visa policy with EU standards. To the country’s pro-EU government, that now counts as “hybrid activity.”
‘Muslim NATO’ triggers article 5: Saudi Arabia calls for backup
Saudi Arabia’s renewed conflict with Yemen’s Houthis is not going well for Riyadh. After conquering a swathe of new territory along the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Houthis declared Saudi airspace a “theater for military operations” this week, and struck Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport multiple times to make their point.
After an emergency meeting on Monday, Pakistan and Türkiye decided to deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia – the first deployment of the newly-formed “Muslim NATO.” Britain has also agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes; France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems; and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former jihadist, is reportedly considering entering the conflict on the Saudi side.
RT examined why the long-dormant Saudi/Houthi conflict is flaring up again, and compared the manpower, resources, and weaponry that Yemen’s Saudi-backed government and the Houthis bring to the table, as the government prepares for a ground offensive against the militants.
India hits a wall with Washington
Russia and the Soviet Union “stood by us in many ways when our security, when our territorial integrity were under threat,” Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar told a gathering of foreign policy experts last weekend. These ties are “not easily forgotten,” he said, adding that India is not going to sever its relations with Russia under Western pressure. That pressure looms in the shape of the so-called “sanctions from hell” Washington is threatening to unleash upon Russia’s trading partners.
A spat over work permits has driven another wedge between New Delhi and Washington. After US Vice President JD Vance lashed out at eight US and Indian tech giants for using H-1B visas to hire “indentured servants” from India over American workers, India’s Foreign Ministry slammed Vance for his “deeply offensive” comments.
“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the ministry said.
At the same time, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Indian “oligarchs” of wielding undue influence over the country’s telecoms regulators, as his bid to introduce Starlink internet access to the Indian market remains stalled. India’s Communications Ministry called his allegations “baseless and misconceived,” but Musk doubled down on Thursday, asking whether telecoms and media tycoon Mukesh Ambani was “the real boss of India?”
And finally…
India has chosen to play a central role in the emergence of a new, multipolar world order. Last month’s BRICS summit in New Delhi showed just how seriously India takes this role, ending with a joint declaration – drafted despite sharp differences between BRICS nations – on the Middle East, global governance, and opposition to unilateral sanctions.
BRICS could face its biggest political test yet, however, if Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva loses his upcoming runoff election against Flavio Bolsonaro, son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro. Should Bolsonaro win, he is likely to pull Brazil into the orbit of the US, where Trump has made no effort to conceal his hostility toward BRICS.
Russian analyst Fyodor Lukyanov broke down what a Bolsonaro victory would mean for the multipolar project, and with two weeks to go until the runoff election, we’ll be keeping a close eye on Brazil.

Baykar chief warns unchecked technology race could lead to ‘terrible extinction’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:02:32 UTC
06:02:32 KST

Selcuk Bayraktar, chairman of the board of trustees of the Turkish Technology Team Foundation (T3 Foundation) and chair of the defense firm Bayar, warned Friday that unchecked technological ambition could lead to “a terrible extinction” for humanity, its children, and future generations, urging the world to rethink the purpose of technological development.
“We aim to build a fairer, more beautiful and better world that serves the good of humanity along the path we are pursuing together with the TEKNOFEST generation,” Bayraktar said, referring to Turkiye’s premier aerospace, space, and technology festival, recently held in the country’s southeast.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026), organized by the International Astronautical Federation, was held this week at the NEST Congress Center in the southern Turkish city of Antalya, co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency and SAHA Istanbul under the coordination of the Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu Agency is the event’s global communications partner.
A panel titled “The Future Starts Here: Technology, Space and the Next Generation” was held during the congress, featuring Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir and Bayraktar, with Anadolu CEO Serdar Karagoz serving as moderator.
Speaking at the panel, Bayraktar said 1.6 million students had applied to competitions at the recent TEKNOFEST in Sanliurfa, southeastern Türkiye.
He said 55,000 students had applied to space-related competitions at TEKNOFEST to date, compared with 20,000 applicants across all competitions in the festival’s first year.
This year, 10,000 participants applied to the rocket competition, which he called a key technology for space access, while 796 applied to the vertical-landing rocket competition and 1,190 to the model satellite competition.
“These figures paint a truly hopeful picture for our journey into the skies and beyond, into space,” he said.
Bayraktar said the term “Kizilelma” (red apple) represents an ideal of civilization and a sacred goal to strive for. He said they had pledged to fly the Bayraktar KIZILELMA unmanned combat aircraft in the centenary of the Turkish Republic and achieved that goal a year ago.
He said their ambitions have since expanded, pointing to Fergani Space, a venture established to advance Türkiye’s independence and sovereignty in space.
Bayraktar said Fergani was established to develop the Ulugh Beg global positioning system, with funding in part from Baykar, which earns more than 90% of its revenue from high-tech exports. He said the initiative was intended to support independence in space for Türkiye and friendly and brotherly regions.
Also speaking at the panel, Anadolu CEO Karagoz said Türkiye has made remarkable strides in developing its own technology, pointing to its satellite production capabilities and plans for a mission to the Moon.
“We are no longer just a country that uses space technologies; we also develop it. We have an important goal ahead of us: the mission to the Moon. We are one of 11 countries worldwide capable of producing communications satellites,” he said.
Karagoz stressed the importance of developing skilled young people to compete internationally in technology.
“To compete in technology, you need strong human resources. That is why we have the TEKNOFEST generation,” he said.
“Against technology giants that develop technology for power and control, the TEKNOFEST generation, which develops technology for the benefit of humanity, gives us all hope.”
Karagoz also highlighted the progress Türkiye has made in the field. “Thirty years ago, Türkiye’s ambitions in space were something of a dream,” he said.
“But today, we see ideas turning into projects, and projects into tangible products.”
Bayraktar said Baykar had achieved the fastest transformation in the large-class unmanned aerial vehicle sector over 20 years, becoming the world’s largest manufacturer and a leading global exporter in the field.
He reiterated that more than 90% of Baykar’s revenues come from exports, saying this success had been made possible by sharing technology with friendly and brotherly countries.
“Our rapid pace of innovation enabled us to develop the most effective solutions on the battlefield. Wherever it has been used, this technology has brought independence. It has also enabled us to advance across different technological fields, including space, using entirely our own resources,” he said.
Bayraktar said the most valuable element in developing technology is people, emphasizing that the purposes technology is developed for matter more than the technology itself.
He noted that technologies widely believed to be civilian, including smartwatches and cellphones, can also be used as intelligence-gathering tools.
He said the next generation of technology developers is crucial, adding that this was one of the main reasons behind the establishment of TEKNOFEST.
“Success in unmanned combat aerial vehicles alone is not enough for a country to achieve full independence and prosperity. It must advance alongside all other fields. Developing a single unmanned combat aircraft cannot, on its own, guarantee sovereignty and independence,” he said.
Bayraktar said major monopolies had emerged in existing technologies around the world, adding: “Rather than focusing on today’s race, focusing on races that have yet to begin seems to be a more effective strategy for countries like ours — countries that are only beginning to build their technological ecosystems.”
He said countries need to strive to establish a presence across all technological fields while also developing strategies suited to their own scale and civilizational sphere.
Bayraktar described rapidly advancing high technology as the driving force behind the world’s most significant transformation. He said social media is an extraordinary technology that enables people to communicate by video and messages with others on the other side of the world.
However, he said humanity has become trapped in a web, with every step people take and even their heart rates being turned into data in the hands of global monopolies.
He argued that these companies can influence what people think, say, and do, adding that artificial intelligence is increasingly doing the thinking for people.
Bayraktar said the global order is pursuing a strategy of “make people addicted, create dependence, and leave them without alternatives.”
He said another path remains possible for humanity, emphasizing the need to recognize human dignity and reflect on the consequences of technological progress.
“We can see this in the wars that have recently begun and never seem to end. If we continue at this pace, driven by this ambition, a terrible extinction awaits us all — humanity, our children, and future generations,” he said.
Bayraktar said similar concerns had emerged after World War II, when global powers recognized the danger posed by the enormous accumulation of weapons and technological capabilities.
“If we play this game the same way once again, humanity itself will cease to exist,” he said.
He argued that the international order, rules, and institutions established to protect life and maintain global balance have been repeatedly violated and undermined.
Bayraktar said the TEKNOFEST generation, as well as intellectuals and elites involved in the space ecosystem, has an important responsibility.
“In a world where even the killing of babies can be rationalized, no one can truly be innocent, and such a world cannot continue to exist,” he said.
He reiterated that the goal of the path pursued with the TEKNOFEST generation is to build a fairer, better world that serves humanity.

US V-P Vance does not know if Pentagon will proceed with live-stream of Fort Hood gunman’s execution
WASHINGTON - Vice-President J.D. Vance said on Oct 9 he does not know whether the Pentagon will proceed with a livestream of the execution by firing squad of the former US Army psychiatrist convicted in the deadly 2009 Fort Hood shooting, a plan that has drawn broad condemnation.
Several Republican lawmakers criticised the move championed by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, while a top US Catholic bishop called the plan “barbaric” and former US officials said a live-stream of the execution would hand terrorists a recruiting tool.
“I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to a live-stream.
Vance added that if a livestream of the execution scheduled for Dec 3 occurs, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
The No. 2 US official’s comments raise questions about the extent of opposition within President Donald Trump’s administration to the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was found guilty in a US military trial of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas.
Trump said at a White House event that Hasan deserves the death penalty by firing squad, calling him “a maniac.”
The Republican president has not said whether he thinks the event should be shown on a live-stream.
A senior White House official familiar with the matter said that Trump “doesn’t oppose the idea” of a live-stream of the execution, but that his position is not yet final and he could change his mind.
The White House is hearing concerns from lawmakers, allies and religious leaders who are urging the administration to not live-stream the execution, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or live-stream of a lawful execution.
‘For all to see’
Hegseth, a Trump appointee, said on Oct 8 the public nature of the execution would demonstrate “there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
Hegseth reposted a comment Trump made in 2013, possibly about the Boston Marathon bombers, saying: “Should be public execution for all to see – you will end this bull**** fast!”
The Pentagon on Oct 9 declined to say whether families of those killed in Hasan’s attack would be invited to attend the execution, as is common practice in civilian executions.
It remains unclear how the Army would select the shooters and what protocols might be followed during the execution itself. The Pentagon said it would release details later.
A top US Catholic official condemned the plan.
“This decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” said Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops.
The Catholic Church opposes capital punishment. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has written a book about his faith.
Hegseth, a member of a conservative evangelical denomination, has invoked Christian language when discussing the Iran war and has led prayer services at the Pentagon. Hegseth has brushed off Pope Leo’s criticism of the war.
Hasan is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945. Hasan, an American-born Muslim, said during his 2013 trial that he carried out the shootings to try to stop what he called a US war on Islam.
“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance told reporters.
‘Free propaganda’
Joe Kent, who resigned this year as Trump’s head of the National Counterterrorism Centre, said the effort to deter extremism could backfire.
“Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality – it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists,” Kent wrote on social media.
Several Republican lawmakers urged the administration not to live-stream the execution.
Senator John Curtis wrote on social media that “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”
Representative Austin Scott wrote live-streaming executions “is what jihadists do.”
Representative Rob Bresnahan said the pain felt by victims and family members “deserves respect, not a public show.”
Brendan Carr, chair of the Federal Communications Commission, told CNBC it is his understanding that the execution would not air on broadcast TV but said he would defer to Hegseth on whether US networks could air it.
US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. Military regulations have not applied that same prohibition. Courts have rejected lawsuits brought by media organisations seeking broader public access to executions.
The UN human rights office said public executions violate prohibitions against torture.
“Public executions constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment,” Shabia Mantoo, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told a news briefing in Geneva.
Decision and debate
The decision to livestream the execution comes at a time of heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the botched lethal injection last week of a Tennessee woman who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder. The controversy has flared in the run-up to the Nov 3 US midterm elections in which Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The execution is scheduled to be held at the same sprawling military base where Hasan opened fire with a handgun in a medical facility. A military jury sentenced Hasan to death after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed with US forces to Afghanistan. Hasan was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.
The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. REUTERS

How Hurricane Isaias got so dangerously strong so fast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:01:33 UTC
06:01:33 KST

Just one day ago Hurricane Isaias was a Category 1 hurricane. Overnight, it ballooned into a major Category 3 storm with 120-mile-per-hour winds and is set to slam into the U.S. Gulf Coast Friday evening with “life-threatening storm surge,” “devastating winds” and the potential for tornadoes, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
So how did this storm get so dangerous so quickly?
For one, Isaias’s presence alone is something of an anomaly. As Scientific American previously reported, Isaias is the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic region this season, setting a record for the latest first arrival of any hurricane since satellite monitoring began.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meteorologists say Isaias’s late formation is largely because of the presence of El Niño, a pattern of unusually warm ocean waters in the eastern Pacific Ocean that can alter weather patterns across the planet. During El Niño years, hurricane activity in the Atlantic typically drops thanks to choppy wind conditions in the atmosphere, or increased vertical wind shear.
But when that wind shear happens to weaken, any burgeoning storm can quickly grow wherever there’s abundant warm ocean water. And there is plenty of that in the Gulf right now.
And the storm may have particularly gotten a boost from a large, deep warm-water eddy in the Gulf of Mexico, hurricane specialist Michael Lowry wrote on Substack. This blob of exceptionally warm water formed by spinning off of the Gulf’s Loop Current that is notorious for boosting hurricane strength. The eddy is giving Isaias a “second wind” as it nears landfall, Lowry wrote.
Warm ocean water fuels tropical cyclones, explains Kim Wood, an associate professor of hydrology and atmospheric sciences at the University of Arizona. “The warmer ocean waters are, the more energy is available, especially if those waters are warm through a deep layer,” Wood says. As a storm’s wind pushes the ocean’s surface water, water deeper down swells up to replace it, they add. If that water is warm—as it would be in this eddy—it can serve as “a longer-lasting energy source” for the storm.
A hurricane warning—meaning hurricane conditions are expected—is in effect for parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida, with wind, rain and flooding risks expected throughout the wider Gulf Coast region, including in Louisiana and Georgia, and well inland, NOAA predicts. Isaias isn’t expected to weaken until after it makes landfall.
Gulf Coasters in Isaias’s path should look out for local guidance on how to prepare for the storm’s arrival, including any potential evacuation orders, according to NOAA.

Major earthquake strikes Panama—damage and injuries are expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:01:31 UTC
06:01:31 KST

A major earthquake struck Panama on Friday afternoon, but how many people have been affected remains unclear.
The quake struck at 12:56 P.M. local time and was initially measured as an 8.0 magnitude by the U.S. Geological Survey, but that was later downgraded slightly to a 7.7. The quake struck around nine miles (14 kilometers) southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a small village in Panama’s Herrera Province. Around 4.6 million people experienced moderate to severe shaking, according to the USGS, and potentially strong aftershocks could follow.
On social media, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino said he had given instructions to mobilize personnel, resources and aid to the area.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
No statistics on injuries or deaths have yet been released. The affected area has a relatively low population density.
While the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Tsunami Warning System had initially warned that the quake could pose a tsunami threat in Costa Rica, El Salvador, Peru, Mexico, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Colombia and Ecuador as well as Panama, as of Friday afternoon the alert was no longer in effect.
The threat of tsunami has likely largely receded, says USGS seismologist Susan Hough, as the quake occurred on land and happened at a relatively shallow depth.
“Because this was on land and shallow, you’re not on the seafloor, so it didn’t move the seafloor underneath the water column, and that’s what you need to generate a tsunami,” she says.
Shallow earthquakes do lead to more shaking being felt at the surface, though. USGS modeling put the likely casualties in the range of dozens to hundreds of fatalities and damages in the hundreds of millions dollars.
The U.S. embassy in Panama did warn U.S. citizens in the area to avoid damaged structures, as well as the coast, and to monitor local emergency broadcasts for updates.
Panama is located near the intersection of several major tectonic plates. To the south are the Cocos and Nazca plates, with the Caribbean plate to the north and the South American plate to the east.
“It was a shallow lateral fault, what we call strike-slip, so similar to the San Andreas,” Hough says.
While the meeting place of tectonic plates can lead to the formation of subduction zones, areas where the denser plate is forced underneath the light plate into Earth’s mantle, which can lead to powerful earthquakes as pressure builds, Hough said the subduction zones near Panama don’t meet, which is why the country usually experiences less powerful quakes.
“There’s a complicated zone of faulting that’s at that juncture, and so this earthquake was on one of those faults,” she says. “It was quite large compared to other earthquakes that have been seen in that area.”

Selcuk Bayraktar warns unchecked technology race could lead to 'terrible extinction'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:00:18 UTC
06:00:18 KST

Selcuk Bayraktar, chairman of the board of trustees of the Turkish Technology Team Foundation (T3 Foundation) and chairman of Baykar, has warned that unchecked technological ambition could lead to "a terrible extinction" for humanity, its children and future generations, urging the world to rethink the purpose of technological development.
"We aim to build a fairer, more beautiful and better world that serves the good of humanity along the path we are pursuing together with the TEKNOFEST generation," Bayraktar said on Friday.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026), organised by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), was held at the NEST Congress Center in Antalya, co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency and SAHA Istanbul under the coordination of the Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry.
A panel titled "The Future Starts Here: Technology, Space and the Next Generation" was held during the congress, featuring Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir and Bayraktar, with Anadolu CEO Serdar Karagoz serving as moderator.
He said 55,000 students had applied to space-related competitions at TEKNOFEST to date, compared with 20,000 applicants across all competitions in the festival’s first year.
This year, 10,000 participants applied to the rocket competition, which he described as a key technology for space access, while 796 applied to the vertical-landing rocket competition and 1,190 to the model satellite competition.
"These figures paint a truly hopeful picture for our journey into the skies and beyond, into space," he said.
Bayraktar said the term "Kizilelma" represents an ideal of civilisation and a sacred goal to strive for. He recalled that they had pledged to fly the Bayraktar KIZILELMA unmanned combat aircraft in the centenary year of the Turkish Republic and achieved that goal a year ago.
He said their objectives had since expanded, pointing to Fergani Space, a venture established to advance Türkiye’s independence and sovereignty in space.
Bayraktar said Fergani was established to develop the Ulugh Beg global positioning system, with funding in part from Baykar, which earns more than 90 percent of its revenue from high-tech exports. He said the initiative was intended to support independence in space for Türkiye and friendly and brotherly regions.
UAV success
Bayraktar said Baykar had achieved the fastest transformation in the large-class unmanned aerial vehicle sector over 20 years, becoming the world’s largest manufacturer and a leading global exporter in the field.
He reiterated that more than 90 percent of Baykar’s revenue comes from exports, saying this success had been made possible by sharing technology with friendly and brotherly countries.
Bayraktar said the most valuable element in developing technology was people, emphasising that the purpose for which technology is developed matters more than the technology itself.
He noted that technologies widely believed to be civilian, including smartwatches and mobile phones, could be used as intelligence-gathering tools.
He said the next generation of technology developers was crucial, adding that this was one of the main reasons behind the establishment of TEKNOFEST.
"Success in unmanned combat aerial vehicles alone is not enough for a country to achieve full independence and prosperity. It must advance alongside all other fields. Developing a single unmanned combat aircraft cannot, on its own, guarantee sovereignty and independence," he said.
Races that have yet to begin
Bayraktar said major monopolies had emerged in existing technologies around the world, arguing that countries should focus not only on current technological competition but also on races that had yet to begin.
"Rather than focusing on today’s race, focusing on races that have yet to begin seems to be a more effective strategy for countries like ours — countries that are only beginning to build their technological ecosystems."
He said countries needed to strive to establish a presence across all technological fields while also developing strategies suited to their own scale and civilisational sphere.
Bayraktar described rapidly advancing high technology as the driving force behind the world’s most significant transformation. He said social media was an extraordinary technology that enabled people to communicate by video and messages with others on the other side of the world.
However, he said humanity had become trapped in a web, with every step people took and even their heart rates being turned into data in the hands of global monopolies.
He argued that these companies could influence what people thought, said and did, adding that artificial intelligence was increasingly doing the thinking for people.
Bayraktar said the global order was pursuing a strategy of "make people addicted, create dependence and leave them without alternatives."
He said another path remained possible for humanity, emphasising the need to recognise human dignity and reflect on the consequences of technological progress.
"We can see this in the wars that have recently begun and never seem to end. If we continue at this pace, driven by this ambition, a terrible extinction awaits us all — humanity, our children and future generations," he said.
Bayraktar recalled that similar concerns had emerged after World War 2, when global powers recognised the danger posed by the enormous accumulation of weapons and technological capabilities.
He argued that the international order, rules and institutions established to protect life and maintain global balance had been repeatedly violated and undermined.
"In a world where even the killing of babies can be rationalised, no one can truly be innocent, and such a world cannot continue to exist," he said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The Northern Ireland secretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists.
Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked.
He said he took the decision after advice from Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of the Northern Ireland Police Service, that the parade “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect” across Northern Ireland.
The Parades Commission ruled two weeks ago that a small, circumscribed march could pass along Garvaghy Road – a reversal of 28 years of successive bans. But police prevented the Orangemen from marching after thousands of residents and supporters, including Sinn Féin leaders, blocked the road.
Garvaghy Road residents welcomed the secretary of state’s decision, saying it brought relief and certainty after a tense standoff that revived memories of the 1990s, when Orangemen fought pitched battles with police in an attempt to march the route.
It was the only “sensible, reasonable and logical outcome”, said Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.
The Sinn Féin leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the party’s Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said in a statement that residents had endured fear and anxiety. “There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening.”
The Irish government welcomed the decision and appealed to both sides to seek common ground. “This isn’t a time for triumphalism or claiming victories or anything like that,” said the taoiseach, Micheál Martin. “Those on the unionist, loyalist side will look at this through a different prism. We need to be conscious of that. We need to acknowledge that.”
Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, accused Boutcher and Bryant of bowing to republican agitation and threats of potential violence. “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest. The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters, and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”
Robinson asked the secretary to state to explain what the government will do to “restore confidence in the rule of law”.
Earlier on Friday the chief constable asked Bryant to review the Parade Commission’s determination, made last month, that conditions in Portadown enabled the parade to go ahead.
“I’ve looked at the changing situation in Portadown, the fact that it’s very difficult for that procession to proceed, and I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” said Bryant.
He thanked Portadown’s Orange Lodge for its “peaceful and law-abiding approach” and regretted that both sides could not reach a compromise, leading to a standoff. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”
Boutcher said the dispute had affected relationships within and between communities and the police. “It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long-term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”
The dispute has fuelled angry exchanges at the Stormont assembly and destabilised the executive, with unionists demanding O’Neill step down as first minister for allegedly breaking the law at a Garvaghy Road protest.
Earlier on Friday, the PSNI sent the Sinn Féin deputy leader a letter probing alleged criminal offences relating to her involvement in the protest. O’Neill said she will cooperate with the investigation.

The two elections that revolve around Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:56:16 UTC
05:56:16 KST

The two elections that revolve around Iran
Israel is now formally in campaign mode. The Knesset dissolved on July 17, and voters go to the polls on October 27, 2026. A week later, on November 3, American voters decide the composition of Congress.
The overlap is almost exact, and it has turned the relationship between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump into something closer to a competition than an alliance. What helps one man survive politically threatens to sink the other.
Netanyahu needs Iran to dominate the Israeli campaign. His best path back to power runs through a public that feels an immediate security threat and a prime minister positioned as the only leader capable of ordering military action at scale. Trump needs the opposite: proof to American voters that a long war is over, that gasoline prices are falling, and that no more Americans are dying for someone else’s fight. The result is a near-perfect zero-sum bind. A new round of escalation could hand Netanyahu a path to victory while costing Republicans their House majority. A negotiated end to the conflict could hand Trump a signature achievement while leaving Netanyahu exposed to hostile polling and an unresolved domestic reckoning.
An opposition advantage that doesn’t guarantee a government
On paper, Netanyahu’s position looks weak. The Knesset has 120 seats, a governing coalition needs 61, and any party must clear a 3.25% threshold to enter parliament at all – meaning the real battle isn’t just for vote share but for keeping allied parties above the line.
As of October 8, 2026, Israeli polling presents a mixed picture, with neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Zionist opposition securing a parliamentary majority in the latest surveys. A Channel 13 poll published on October 7 put Netanyahu’s bloc at 55 seats, the Zionist opposition at 50, and Arab parties at 15. The Yashar party of former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s Likud were tied at 20 seats each, although Eisenkot retained a personal lead as the preferred prime minister, with 44% support against Netanyahu’s 40%.
A Channel 12 poll published on October 5 showed a different balance: 49 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, 54 for the Zionist opposition and 13 for Arab parties. Yashar led Likud by 23 seats to 21, while Eisenkot led Netanyahu by 41% to 38% on suitability for prime minister.
A summer survey on whether Netanyahu should even run again found that 61% of Israelis opposed his participation in the upcoming election, while 35% supported it. Among Jewish respondents, 57% opposed another candidacy and 39.5% supported it.
None of this makes his defeat inevitable, because the opposition’s real problem is forming a coalition. Eisenkot, the Bennett-Lapid alignment, Avigdor Liberman’s party, and the left could plausibly out-poll Netanyahu’s bloc and still lack a workable majority without leaning on Arab parties, an arrangement much of the Jewish opposition leadership is unwilling to commit to publicly. A Netanyahu bloc stuck around 50 seats doesn’t automatically mean a change of government; it leaves room for him to peel off defectors, split rivals, or force a repeat election.
His current partners – the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism, along with the far-right Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism – are disciplined blocs, but keeping them requires continuing to push yeshiva exemptions from military conscription, expanding executive influence over the judiciary and media, and holding a hard line on the Palestinians. Those same moves alienate the center, military reservists, and secular Israelis. The conscription fight in particular has repeatedly brought the coalition to the brink of collapse, and in its final weeks before dissolution the outgoing Knesset pushed through several contested measures on conscription, judicial authority, and media regulation.
War helps Netanyahu
Security remains the one lever capable of reshaping the campaign overnight. On the normal political agenda, Netanyahu has to answer for the October 7, 2023 intelligence and defense failure, the strain of prolonged reserve-duty mobilization, a difficult economy, and years of domestic polarization. A fresh war pushes all of that into the background and reframes the election as a referendum on wartime leadership.
The pattern has already played out once. After what Israelis broadly regarded as a successful twelve-day war with Iran in summer 2025, Likud’s support hit its highest point since the 2022 election. But by July 2026 the party had slid back down to roughly 21-24 seats.
Israeli public opinion is a genuine paradox here: war-weary, yet unwilling to accept a settlement seen as premature. Only 38% of respondents believe Israel’s security position has actually improved since the war with Iran. Polling from the Institute for National Security Studies finds 43% believe the war ended without a clear result, 37% consider Iran the winner, and just 15% consider Israel the winner. Separately, 66% viewed the US-Iran memorandum signed in June as unfavorable to Israel, and a majority of Jewish respondents have said ending the war on its current terms is incompatible with the country’s security interests.
This paradox gives Netanyahu an opening to argue the war produced nothing decisive because Washington called off the pressure too early. New war with Iran, in this framing, is finishing an unfinished job: dismantling nuclear infrastructure, ballistic missile production, IRGC command targets, and the logistics networks supporting Iran-aligned militias.
Such an escalation could pull wavering right-of-center voters back from Eisenkot and Bennett toward Likud. But Eisenkot himself is a former chief of staff with his own security credentials, which means a strike alone won’t be enough – Netanyahu needs a fast, unambiguous result he can credibly claim as his own achievement.
A drawn-out or inconclusive operation would do the opposite. Israelis are already skeptical of what has been achieved so far; further destruction, extended mobilization, and strikes on the home front risk changing the question from “is Netanyahu decisive enough” to “why, after years of fighting, has this government still not delivered lasting security.”
There’s an economic constraint layered on top. The Bank of Israel’s forecast projects 4% GDP growth in 2026, a budget deficit of 4.9% of GDP, and public debt near 69% of GDP – but that assumes no new war with Iran and a cooling of hostilities in Lebanon. The central bank has warned that a proposed defense-spending increase of up to 25 billion shekels (about $8.1 billion) would push up the deficit, debt, and inflation simultaneously. A new war could therefore improve Netanyahu’s electoral standing while it undermines the macroeconomic recovery his government depends on.
What Netanyahu wants from Trump
Netanyahu needs to persuade Trump of three things: that any diplomatic pause gives Tehran time to rebuild its missile and nuclear capacity; that limited strikes around the Strait of Hormuz don’t resolve the underlying strategic problem; and that any agreement must include dismantling enrichment capacity, removing stockpiled material, capping the ballistic missile program, and weakening Iran’s regional proxies.
Israel’s regional strategy much more than just Iran, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, Iran-backed militias in Iraq and Yemen, strategic competition with Türkiye, and preserving military superiority amid the possible sale of F-35s to Ankara. Trump’s agenda is even wider: freedom of navigation, energy prices, the relationship with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, expanding the Abraham Accords, and casting himself as the president who ended the war. Israel remains a central ally in that picture, but no longer the only crucial player.
A new war is dangerous for Trump
At home, however, election math is pulling Trump in the opposite direction. Republicans are defending an extremely narrow majority in the November 3 midterms. The House currently stands at 218 Republicans to 214 Democrats, one independent, and two vacancies. The Senate split is 53 Republicans to 45 Democrats and two independents caucusing with Democrats – and of the seats up for election, 22 are held by Republicans against just 13 held by Democrats, which is obviously structurally unfavorable for the Republicans.
A war with Iran is itself an electoral liability. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found only about a third of Americans support it, against 62% opposed. Roughly 69% of respondents, including 40% of Republicans, say Trump has failed to explain the operation’s objectives. Earlier Pew and Quinnipiac surveys told a similar story, with 59% to 60% calling the use of force a mistake or not worth the cost.
For American voters, the war’s most tangible effect is the price at the gas pump. Disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and volatile oil prices pushed the average gasoline price above four dollars a gallon; EIA data puts the national average at $4.35 as of October 5, after peaking near $4.56 in the spring. The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index slipped from 88.6 in August to 81.9 in September, the lowest since 2014.
The link between the war and household costs is especially damaging for a president who campaigned on lowering prices and ending open-ended foreign wars. Even many voters who favor a hard line on Iran don’t see defending Israel as sufficient justification for prolonged US involvement – AP-NORC polling found 67% of Americans call preventing higher fuel prices an important priority, compared with just 39% who say the same about preventing threats to Israel.
Congress has already registered the discontent. On July 23, the Republican-controlled House passed a resolution demanding an end to military action against Iran without congressional authorization, 214 to 208, with four Republicans crossing party lines. The measure is largely symbolic, but it demonstrates how easily the Iran question could split a majority that already has no margin for error.
Two paths forward
The immediate choice facing both leaders has changed from whether to start a fresh offensive or pursue a peace deal, to whether the current pause can survive the election season. On October 8, Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms, while keeping the blockade in place and describing talks with Tehran as productive. That in turn puts a publicly declared American timetable around Netanyahu’s room for maneuver before Israel’s October 27 vote. It does not amount to a peace agreement, guarantee Israeli restraint, or rule out a response to a new attack.
Escalation remains a risk, but it can no longer be presented as an equally likely, openly US-backed campaign strategy before the elections. Axios reported on October 7 that the Pentagon had ordered preparations for possible renewed combat. If fighting resumes, Netanyahu could try to rally voters around wartime leadership, but the electoral benefit would depend on the outcome. A brief operation with demonstrable gains might help Likud; missile retaliation, civilian losses, and renewed mobilization could instead reinforce doubts about his government’s ability to deliver lasting security.
For Trump, the more immediate objective is to keep the conflict from producing another economic shock before Americans vote. His announcement leaves coercive pressure intact. Shipping through Hormuz also remains vulnerable: Iranian attacks on tankers have resumed even as Washington describes progress in getting Gulf oil to market. Avoiding a new bombing campaign may reduce the risk of a sudden price surge, but it cannot by itself restore normal navigation or ensure cheaper gasoline within weeks.
A diplomatic breakthrough could still improve Trump’s position, especially if it makes shipping safer and brings sustained relief at the pump. Its effect on Netanyahu would depend on the terms. An agreement seen in Israel as leaving Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities insufficiently constrained could expose him to criticism from both rivals and his own right-wing partners. A settlement with credible restrictions and verification could give him an achievement to defend. In either case, a quieter security environment would leave more room for the domestic issues already shaping the campaign: accountability for October 7, ultra-Orthodox conscription, and the confrontation over the judiciary.
The shared-success option rests on sustained pressure producing enforceable concessions without another regional escalation. Both leaders could claim credit for such an outcome. But negotiations, implementation, and verification are unlikely to fit within the remaining days before the election, and neither Washington nor Jerusalem has control over Tehran’s response. A pause that holds through the votes may still leave the central disputes unresolved and renewed fighting possible afterward.

United Nations Special Envoy to Yemen Hans Grundberg says that the country has slid back into “full-scale war” as fighting between the Houthis and internationally recognised government forces continues.
During a meeting at the UN Security Council on Friday to discuss the situation in Yemen, Grundberg said civilians, including women and children, were bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.
“Ongoing instability in the Middle East continues to impact dynamics in Yemen, while developments in Yemen, in turn, reverberate across the region,” he said.
“Regional security, freedom of navigation and the protection of international trade are legitimate concerns that must be addressed. International engagement on Yemen must also be grounded in the realities of Yemen and the needs and aspirations of its people,” Grundberg added.
The envoy stressed that “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now.”
“Ultimately, gains on the battlefield cannot substitute for the negotiations that will be required to settle the conflict,” he said, urging Security Council members to collectively support mediation efforts.
According to the UN, at least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others have been injured since August, with children bearing a disproportionate toll during the ongoing clashes.
‘Dangerous escalation’
The UN representative for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi, told the Security Council that the threat from the Houthis was no longer an “internal Yemeni affair”.
Al-Saadi called on the council to take “decisive, practical measures” to reduce the flow of funding, weapons and technology to the Iranian-backed group and also strengthen cooperation with the Yemeni government.
He thanked Riyadh, which supports the government, for “standing beside the Yemeni people and their government, and for their continued support to state institutions and our economy”.
This comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue, with the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority reporting on Friday that the King Khalid International Airport, north of Riyadh, was subjected to two attacks on Thursday, in which three Saudi citizens were killed.
Gulf states and European countries have condemned the attack on the airport, with Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs calling it “unacceptable”.
During the council meeting, Saudi Arabia’s UN representative, Abdulaziz al-Wasil, said the UN body must address the “dangerous escalation” ongoing in Yemen.
“These rapid developments in Yemen and the continued escalation by the terrorist Houthi militias must be addressed by the Council,” al-Wasil said.
Al-Wasil added that Riyadh will “not allow Yemen to be turned into a staging ground for threats to its security or to the freedom of navigation”.

Kachka served as deputy prime minister from July 17, 2025, to July 14, 2026. His move to Brussels was announced during a July government reshuffle, when Zelensky said Kachka would swap roles with Ukraine’s then-ambassador to the EU, Vsevolod Chentsov.
During Kachka’s tenure overseeing EU integration, Ukraine opened its first two accession negotiation clusters — groups of policy areas in which candidates must meet EU requirements. These covered fundamental reforms, including the rule of law, and external relations.
In December 2025, Kachka and EU enlargement chief Marta Kos co-signed a letter identifying the 10 most pressing rule-of-law reforms Ukraine should complete by the end of 2026.
read also
He also worked with the European Commission to agree on the timing and content of reforms tied to installments of the EU’s 90-billion-euro loan for Ukraine, finalized in April.
Speaking at the Bruegel think tank’s annual conference in Brussels on Sept. 2, Kachka sought to reassure European partners that Ukraine would maintain its reform efforts despite the war.
“The voices and questions of member states and different stakeholders are not ‘blah, blah, blah,’” he said when asked by the Kyiv Independent how he would reassure Brussels. “The scale of this mutual undertaking on deterring Russia is so huge that it requires enormous trust between all of us.”
“Rule of law, anti-corruption, is really the cornerstone of this trust,” he added.
His appointment comes amid parliamentary delays in passing EU-backed legislation, which have put installments worth 2.1 billion euros and 3.7 billion euros at risk.
Zelensky has called on the EU to bring forward some loan installments scheduled for 2027. Kachka said the request reflected unfulfilled promises of additional financing from other allies.
He praised the EU’s decision to borrow jointly to support Ukraine’s wartime needs, calling it “a really revolutionary thing,” and said he remained optimistic that partners including the U.K., Canada, and Japan would provide further support.

No information about fatalities or injuries has been reported so far.
