Turkey jails 2 journalists pending trial for fund crisis 'misinformation'
A Turkish court on Friday jailed two journalists pending trial for allegedly spreading misinformation over a sprawling investment fund scandal, while another two were granted conditional release, media reports said.
Turkey has been grappling with the fallout from an investment fund scandal which erupted in mid-September, prompting an investigation into allegations of widespread market manipulation.
The scandal has put pressure on President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AKP, with one senior party official resigning after allegations about her investment activities.
The main opposition Yeni Parti on Thursday questioned whether two ministers had profited from investing in the suspect funds.
Trade Minister Omer Bolat and Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas have denied any wrongdoing.
All four journalists were hauled in on Friday over content that also raised questions about the involvement of senior AKP figures.
The court ordered Mustafa Balci of the pro-opposition Sozcu daily, and Saban Sevinc of the online news channel Bizim TV, to be jailed pending trial for posting an image on X suggesting a link between AKP spokesman Omer Celik and one of the key investment fund suspects.
But the court granted conditional release to two other journalists -- Ismail Saymaz and Murat Agirel from Sozcu TV who were named in a suit filed by the trade minister over a report questioning his links to the scandal.
Earlier, a top AKP official accused the opposition and the media of targeting the party with a "web of lies".
"We will absolutely not let our party and government be targeted, whether by Yeni or the journalists they paid to act as their mouthpiece," AKP secretary general Eyyup Kadir Inan told the private NTV.
"Legally, we will hold them accountable for all attacks on our party."
'Record profits'
The crisis erupted when several funds were unable to satisfy investor redemption demands.
Regulators quickly placed seven companies that manage 131 investment funds with assets reportedly worth some $17 billion into liquidation.
More than 455,000 individual investors have been affected, regulators say.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigators found 214 individuals and legal entities had earned a total of 187.6 billion lira ($3.8 billion) through funds managed by three firms: Tera, Pusula and Hedef.
Those who had invested in funds managed by Tera had earned record profits over 90 billion lira, he told Sabah newspaper.
He said investigators were looking into those who sold shares in the days before the crisis hit the headlines, who had "exited the funds with prior knowledge and based on information provided to them".
Prosecutors sent a list of names to the TMSF deposit insurance fund "which has started officially notifying the individuals about the return of the money" to a voluntary restitution account run by the regulator, he said.
It was not clear whether they would face prosecution.
Meanwhile, AKP on Friday submitted a bill to parliament about fund liquidation and investor repayments, but there was no immediate word on when lawmakers would vote on it.
The two ministers whose investments were questioned hit back with legal action, with Bolat suing the two Sozcu journalists and Goktas filing suit against three Yeni lawmakers for slander.
She also vowed to pursue "media outlets that spread these allegations".
"Ozgur Ozel and his colleagues will pay the price for these lies and slanders," AKP's Inan warned, referring to the main opposition leader who heads the Yeni Parti.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The legislation was introduced by a group of deputies, including Edmunds Jurevics, head of the New Unity parliamentary faction. Most lawmakers from the Stability! party abstained from the vote.
The new rules update Article 2 of the Law on Restrictions on Actions Threatening National Security. Similar travel bans previously applied to state officials, civil servants, and members of the Saeima.
Authors of the legislation noted that local representatives have detailed knowledge of critical infrastructure, civil defense plans, transport hubs, and municipal assets.
Lawmakers determined that uniform travel restrictions must apply to elected officials at both the national and local government levels, Delfi reported.
Starting September 1, 2026, Latvia enforced a broad ban on the import of a wide range of industrial products from Russia and Belarus, applying the restrictions to both direct shipments and deliveries arriving through third-party countries.
The Latvian government officially confirmed the start date during a cabinet meeting on August 25, following earlier parliamentary support at the end of July.
Under the regulations, the restricted list covered a large selection of consumer items and finished products, including printed books, newspapers, and other printed matter.

Zelensky argued that easing sanctions on Russia without a clear and durable de-escalation agreement would be a sign of weakness that benefits Moscow. “In my view, this is a weak decision,” he said.
The Ukrainian president appeared to respond directly to Trump’s announcement. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he said.
Zelensky also pointed to the EU’s decision to delist two Russian oligarchs – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – both closely connected to Putin and the Kremlin’s war effort.
Since that move, he said, Russian strikes and terror of civilians have only intensified.
When the US lawmakers asked what it would take to end the war, Zelensky listed three conditions:
- enforcement of sanctions under the law championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham
- support for Ukraine in protecting lives
- and sustained pressure on Russia over the war.
De-escalation offered – again
Zelensky reiterated that Kyiv is prepared to take de-escalation steps that match Russia’s own, and that the American negotiating team is aware of this position.
Zelensky framed Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries and other oil facilities as a response to Moscow’s years-long campaign against Ukraine’s power grid. Halting them, he said, would depend on Russia ending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Moscow, however, has repeatedly rejected such arrangements. In the very few times it had agreed to a ceasefire, it failed to honor it, with attacks resuming immediately.
The president stressed that any easing of the conflict must be reciprocal rather than one-sided, and pointed to Russia’s results on the battlefield. In his view, Russia is relying on strikes against civilians to make up for its failure to reach its military goals.
This year, he said, Russian forces are weaker on the front line than at any earlier point in the war.
“That is exactly why Putin relies on terror. That is exactly why he relies on attempts at backroom deals on one or another easing of pressure on Russia, to buy more time and more opportunities for war.”

The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.
Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.
Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.
Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.
The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.
“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”
Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree.
New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.
There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.
Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.
“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.
Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.
The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

playfool’s game installation at V&A puts you in the role of data center cleaner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:35:09 UTC
05:35:09 KST

playfool’s game installation at V&A puts you in the role of data center cleaner
the server interactive game installation uses a playful cleaning routine to highlight the often-overlooked labor of maintaining digital infrastructure and cultural collections.
real data center vacuum turns server maintenance into a game
The Server is an interactive game installation by art-design duo Playfool that invites visitors to take on the role of a data center cleaner. Commissioned by the V&A Museum through its Emerging Designer Commission, the work uses a real data center vacuum as a controller, allowing players to remove digital dust from a sculptural server.
The installation draws parallels between the maintenance of data centers and the conservation of museum collections. Although data centers are highly automated, cleaning remains a manual task essential to their operation. Similarly, museum objects require ongoing care long after their creation. Through a playful sequence of movements, The Server makes this often-overlooked labor visible and examines the human work that sustains digital infrastructure.
An interactive game reframes cleaning as an ongoing act of care
Referencing Mierle Laderman Ukeles’ practice of maintenance art, the project frames cleaning as an ongoing process shaped by changing conditions and repeated actions. It invites visitors to consider the physical labor behind technological progress, as well as the relationship between people, machines, and their environments.
Developed by creative duo Playfool, Daniel Coppen (UK/SG) and Saki Maruyama (JP), for the V&A Museum Emerging Designer Commission, The Server is on view at the V&A in South Kensington, London, through October 18th, 2026.
project info:
name: The Server
designer: Playfool | @studioplayfool
lead designers: Daniel Coppen, Saki Maruyama
sound designer: Matteo Bandi
fabrication: Art & Assembly
videographer: Nico Lejtreger
commission: V&A Museum, Emerging Designer Commission
curator: Carrie Chan
producer: Katya Spiers
special thanks: Ella-Marie Maude and Johanna Puisto from the V&A Conservation Department

Washington suspends sanctions on Russian fuel trade, including import to US
The US Treasury Department has announced a temporary sanctions waiver on the Russian fuel trade amid skyrocketing global prices. The move allows the sale, delivery, offloading, and import of Russian diesel, including to the United States, until at least April 7, 2027.
The announcement came after President Donald Trump announced a major agreement with Moscow, following a Friday phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump stated in a Truth Social Post, adding that Moscow could provide up to 3,000,000 tons of additional diesel “within a short period of time” depending on the state of its refineries, which have recently been under constant threat of long-range Ukrainian strikes.
Russia is ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets, the Kremlin said in a statement following the phone calls between the two presidents. Moscow is “sure that it would have a positive effect on the entire global economy,” the statement added.
Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak also confirmed that Moscow would be lifting diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule. The process will be started “immediately,” the official told TASS.
“Russia welcomes US steps aimed at stabilizing the global energy market and gradually restoring normal energy trade, and stands ready to coordinate future actions to create a more predictable and healthy market,” the deputy prime minister stated.
The Russian government had previously extended a ban on the export of diesel and ship fuel, as well as gas oils until October 31 to stabilize the domestic market which had been suffering from increased seasonal demand linked to harvesting time.
Under the existing restrictions, fuel producers have been barred from exporting fuel until the end of October and non-producers were banned from doing it until January 31, 2027. A total ban on gasoline exports is in place until the end of January as well.
The development comes as the global markets are still reeling from the supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran. Russell Hardy, the CEO of Vitol – one of the world’s largest oil trading companies – warned earlier this week that the market had burned through much of the stock that previously helped absorb disruptions. There aren’t any more inventories to drain in the West,” he stated on Wednesday.
Last week, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude and refined products from emergency stocks, beginning with diesel to curb the soaring prices as the Trump administration demanded Europe do more to deal with the issue.

Prosecutors oppose Luigi Mangione’s push for dismissal of state charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:18:18 UTC
05:18:18 KST

Manhattan prosecutors filed paperwork on Friday opposing Luigi Mangione’s arguments for dismissing his state-level case in the killing of the UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson.
Mangione on 14 August pleaded guilty to federal charges in Thompson’s 4 December 2024 killing outside a Midtown hotel – weeks before his scheduled 8 September New York state murder and weapons trial. The killing prompted an intense manhunt but also sparked an outpouring of rage against the practices of the for-profit US healthcare industry.
Shortly after he entered his guilty plea to two federal stalking charges, Mangione’s legal team filed a motion to dismiss the state-level murder case against him.
Judge Gregory Carro, who is overseeing Mangione’s state case, subsequently postponed these proceedings, scheduling the next court date for 10 December, according to a 17 August letter. Carro told prosecutors to respond to Mangione’s push for dismissal by 9 October and gave his defense a 30 October deadline to reply.
Mangione’s defense has argued that New York state’s double jeopardy law prohibits him from being prosecuted by the Manhattan district attorney’s office.
New York state law holds that “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”.
Manhattan prosecutors argued in their papers that Mangione’s murder case can proceed “under an exception” to the state double jeopardy law. They insist that elements of the federal stalking and state murder charges do not overlap in a way that would trigger double jeopardy protections.
Mangione has claimed that Manhattan prosecutors cannot pursue weapons charges against him because he had previously faced federal weapons counts. But the federal court dismissed these counts, Manhattan state prosecutors noted.
“Statutory double jeopardy applies only when a defendant has been ‘separately prosecuted’ for the same misconduct, and dismissed federal charges do not constitute a separate prosecution,” they argued.
As for the murder charge, Manhattan prosecutors insist that the federal stalking charges Mangione pleaded guilty to are dramatically different from his state murder case.

Tesla’s ‘Full Self-Driving’ Becomes ‘Assisted Driving’ in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:18:15 UTC
05:18:15 KST

Tesla’s most advanced driver-assistance feature is named Full Self-Driving (Supervised), but it can’t actually drive itself. While the feature can handle tasks like accelerating, braking, steering, and parking, the automaker requires drivers to stay alert and intervene at all times. Now, the company has officially renamed it to Tesla Assisted Driving (TAD) in Europe as it works to convince regulators to allow its use on public roads.
Tesla offered to change the name, according to a statement by the German Transport Ministry. The statement says that German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger found the “FSD” name “somewhat misleading.” After discussions with Tesla last month, Bilger said he would now advocate for European regulators to approve the feature “as quickly as possible.” The EU will likely vote on its approval by the end of the year.
On Friday, Tesla began using the Tesla Assisted Driving language on its European sales website. The automaker didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tesla has resisted changing the feature’s name for years, even defending it in court. Last year, California’s Department of Motor Vehicles concluded that Tesla’s use of the terms “Full Self-Driving” and “Autopilot” (an older and less advanced driver-assistance feature) was misleading and violated state law. After the agency threatened to suspend Tesla’s manufacturing and dealer licenses in the state, the automaker stopped using the term “Autopilot.” It has also continued to append “(Supervised)” to the official name of its Full Self-Driving tech.
Tesla drivers say FSD has improved tremendously since its introduction in 2020, and fans online say they’ve been able to take entire trips without intervening in their Tesla’s driving. But FSD has faced plenty of scrutiny. In March, the US federal government opened a probe into the system after nine incidents in which FSD allegedly failed to respond because of reduced visibility and didn’t warn its drivers to take over. Tesla recalled an older version of the software in 2023, after the US government found that it didn’t follow some traffic laws.
Tesla and CEO Elon Musk have pushed for other global markets to approve its driver assistance technology for years. That would likely create a lucrative, software-based funding stream for the world’s most valuable automaker. (Currently, Tesla charges $99 per month for a Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription in the US.) Australia and New Zealand approved it last year. The Netherlands became the first European government to give Tesla provisional permission to launch FSD this past spring. A version of the feature became available to Chinese customers in May.
This week, Reuters reported that Tesla presented misleading safety data to European regulators as it lobbied for FSD approval. Safety researchers have accused the automaker of also using misleading statistics to promote its tech in the US.

Rising fuel costs slashed Delta’s profit outlook despite strong demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:17:15 UTC
05:17:15 KST

Rising fuel costs slashed Delta’s profit outlook despite strong demand
Rising fuel prices push Delta’s annual fuel expenses up by $6bn, affecting its profit outlook for 2026.
Delta Air Lines cut its profit forecast despite heightened demand as fuel costs surge across the air travel sector.
The Atlanta-based air carrier said in its third-quarter earnings report released on Friday that it expects its annual fuel costs to jump by $6bn, as ongoing tensions between the United States and Iran have sent fuel prices surging across the global aviation sector.
Overall, US airlines spent nearly $43bn on fuel in the first eight months of the year, a $13.2bn increase from the same period a year earlier.
On Wall Street, Delta cut its earnings outlook for the year to adjusted earnings per share of $5.10 to $5.60, down from its July forecast of $6.50 to $7.50. The midpoint of the new range is below analysts’ average estimate of $5.46, according to LSEG data.
Delta’s stock tumbled in midday trading as the trading week came to a close. It was down 1.1 percent from Friday’s opening price. While the stock has fallen 4.4 percent over the past five days, it has performed well in 2026, gaining nearly 18 percent since the beginning of the year.
CEO Ed Bastian said the airline had raised prices by roughly 20 percent this year and said those prices could be sustained even if fuel prices decline.
Delta Air Lines is the first of the major US airlines to report earnings and is generally more protected from price fluctuations than its competitors because it owns a refinery in Pennsylvania, which it acquired in 2012.
Despite higher prices, demand remains elevated, with 60 percent of flights in the fourth quarter already booked. Delta also announced several new international routes, including Seattle–Tokyo, Japan and Boston–Venice, Italy, as well as Austin-Paris, France, all beginning next year.
Bastian told the Wall Street Journal that holiday bookings also remain strong and that premium travel is growing, with premium seat revenue jumping 18 percent for the quarter compared with the same period last year.
Broadly speaking, premium flights can be a boon for major airlines, and prices in the segment are rising. Average ticket prices for premium seats across major airlines were up 11 percent compared with the same period last year, according to the Airline Reporting Corporation’s monthly report, which tracks airline ticket transactions.
But lower-income consumers are pulling back. US consumer sentiment is slumping, according to the University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers, which released its Consumer Sentiment Index on Friday.
“Overall, sentiment for lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock portfolios dropped steeply this month, groups that have fewer resources to weather increases in prices,” Joanne Hsu, director of the Surveys of Consumers, said in the release.
Delta’s report comes as the US summer travel season draws to a close, following reports that lower-income travellers would pull back amid rising prices. In May, 51 percent of Americans earning less than $100,000 annually said travel would be one of the first expenses they would cut, according to a report from consulting firm Deloitte.
United Airlines is the next major carrier expected to report earnings, with results slated for after the market close on October 20. Like Delta, United’s stock was down on Wall Street, falling 0.8 percent from Friday’s opening price.

Flydubai co-pilot plotted ‘suicide’ attack on Israel, UAE says

Flydubai co-pilot plotted ‘suicide’ attack on Israel, UAE says
Attorney General says suspect admitted he acted alone after preparing psychologically and physically for the attack.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates say the co-pilot who tried to seize control of a Flydubai aircraft on September 30 was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.
Emirati public prosecutors believe the plan “drew inspiration from the 9/11 attack”, Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said in a statement carried by state news agency WAM on Friday, referring to the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
WAM reported al-Shamsi’s comments as well as updates on what Emirati investigators had discovered about the alleged plot after launching an inquiry into the incident on October 1.
They found that the 29-year-old suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport”, WAM reported.
The attorney general said the suspect had worked for several airlines in different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining Flydubai in January.
Investigators examined Flydubai’s recruiting procedures and found the suspect had met all professional and security requirements, including holding a pilot’s licence and providing a certificate of good conduct.
“However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot,” the statement said.
Al-Shamsi’s statement did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing, and contained the most detailed account yet from prosecutors about what they believe to have happened.
UAE officials have not identified the suspect, who is accused of attacking his co-pilot, the captain of the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight that was carrying 174 people on board. But people with direct knowledge of the matter have identified him as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, both the Reuters and Associated Press news agencies reported.
Al-Shamsi said the suspect had told investigators he had prepared psychologically and physically for the attack by viewing material promoting “terrorism” and taking boxing lessons.
The findings indicated that “signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia”, the statement said.
It added that the suspect “admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others”, and that he “provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution” in the presence of his lawyer.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
At 7:05am (03:05 GMT) on September 30, Flight FZ1073 departed Dubai for Tel Aviv, climbing to 34,000ft (more than 10,300 metres), according to Flightradar24. A little more than two hours later, it suddenly began a steep descent.
Flight-tracking data showed the plane plunging more than 17,000 feet in about two minutes, before climbing and descending again.
A fight had begun in the cockpit between the two pilots after the co-pilot stabbed the Indian captain of the plane, Smit Machchhar.
Machchhar later described finding himself seriously wounded on the cockpit floor as the aircraft descended.
Passengers and crew members reportedly entered the cabin and overpowered the co-pilot. The aircraft eventually levelled out at about 15,000 feet. Its transponder was subsequently switched to code 7500, signalling unlawful interference.
Two reserve pilots who were on board took control of the jet and landed it in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia. The plane landed safely at 9:45am local time (06:45 GMT).
Saudi authorities said both pilots were taken to hospital and were later transferred to Abu Dhabi after being medically cleared.

China denies report of reciprocal nuclear site visits with US

Faisal Mahmud
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
China on Friday denied a report that Beijing and Washington had discussed reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, with further talks reportedly planned in the coming months.
"The relevant report is not true," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular news conference in Beijing, according to an official transcript of the briefing.
The denial came after CNN reported, citing sources familiar with the matter, that China and the US had discussed possible reciprocal visits to nuclear sites.
According to an earlier CNN report, preliminary discussions covered possible visits to US Department of Energy laboratories and corresponding Chinese research centers, alongside potential access to nuclear test sites.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), in its June report, estimated that China possessed 620 nuclear warheads as of January 2026, compared with more than 5,000 held by the US, including retired warheads.
According to SIPRI, the world's nine nuclear-armed nations possessed an estimated 12,187 warheads, including 190 held by India, 170 by Pakistan, 90 by Israel and 60 by North Korea. Russia and the US together accounted for nearly 86% of the global inventory.
SIPRI said China was expanding its nuclear arsenal faster than any other country, while Washington and Moscow continued extensive nuclear modernization programs.
The developments follow the expiration of the New START nuclear arms reduction treaty between Washington and Moscow in February.

Ukraine’s prosecution service has dismissed eight people named in connection with an anti-corruption probe into the alleged protection of scam call centers, acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalskyi reported. His office is also running internal checks on several officials linked to the case. A separate probe covers the trip abroad of his predecessor, who left Ukraine in September.
Ukraine’s main prosecution service is auditing itself while the country’s anti-corruption agencies investigate an alleged scheme run from inside it. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) allege that a PGO official set up a criminal organization in mid-2025. They say it drew in serving prosecution employees and unofficial associates, took bribes for leaving scam call centers alone, and laundered the proceeds. The investigation is called Operation Carthage.
A probe from the outside, an audit from the inside
Ukraine’s main prosecution service is auditing itself while the country’s anti-corruption agencies investigate an alleged scheme run from inside it. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) allege that an official of the Prosecutor General’s Office (PGO) set up a criminal organization in mid-2025. They say it drew in serving prosecution employees and unofficial associates. The group allegedly took bribes for leaving scam call centers alone and then laundered the proceeds. The case is known as Operation Carthage, Espreso reported.
Dismissals and polygraph tests
Seven of the eight dismissed people worked at the PGO, Kovalskyi said. Separately, four people were removed from administrative posts, including the heads of the IT department and the cybercrime directorate. Kovalskyi said 24 prosecutors took polygraph tests. The results went to a commission running an internal investigation. He wrote that trust in the prosecution service would be restored not through announcements of change but through consistent, balanced decisions and concrete results.
The internal probe concerning former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko covers his trip abroad. Investigators are checking whether he followed established procedure and how the business trip was organized. Kravchenko left Ukraine in an official car on the night of 13–14 September, Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing law enforcement sources. He explained his departure as an official trip to Lithuania.
On 14 September, Kravchenko announced he had signed a notice of suspicion against NABU director Semen Kryvonos. That evening, his own office said Kryvonos had never been properly served and that the register entries were cancelled.
On 15 September, lawmakers backed Kravchenko’s resignation 317–0. Two days later, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy assigned Kovalskyi the duties of prosecutor general by decree. Before that, Kovalskyi headed the Khmelnytskyi Oblast Prosecutor’s Office.
Two Carthage figures under internal review
The PGO completed an internal investigation into Aidyn Khudiiev, a former deputy department head, Kovalskyi said. Its findings will go to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of Prosecutors, and the PGO abolished his post. SAPO prosecutor Mykola Karas told a court hearing that detectives seized $50,000 at Khudiiev’s workplace during the Carthage searches.
Ukraine’s chief prosecutor fled. Politicians still choose the man who can prosecute them.
The PGO is also investigating Serhii Kropyva, former deputy head of its international cooperation department. NABU detained him on 4 September, the first day of the operation. The internal probe looks at whether he used his powers for private interests and interfered in other prosecutors’ work. The PGO’s General Inspectorate has filed a disciplinary complaint against him with the same commission, and his post was also abolished.

Trump strikes deal for over 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel despite sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:08:19 UTC
05:08:19 KST

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel, a dramatic shift in U.S. policy toward Moscow as Washington seeks to ease soaring fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections.
The announcement came just weeks after Trump signed sweeping sanctions legislation targeting Russia's energy sector over its war in Ukraine, raising questions about Washington's commitment to maintaining economic pressure on the Kremlin.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward. An additional 3 million tons would be delivered within a relatively short period, he said.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote on social media.
Shortly after the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The authorization allows Russian diesel loaded onto tankers as of Friday to be supplied to global markets without triggering U.S. sanctions until April 2027.
The White House did not immediately clarify who would pay for the shipments, when the fuel would become available or whether deliveries scheduled for November would arrive before the November 3 elections.
The agreement comes as the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets. According to AAA, the average price of diesel in the United States reached $6.23 per gallon Friday, after hitting a record $6.52 on September 22.
Zelensky: ‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky sharply condemned the agreement, warning that increased Russian energy revenues would help Moscow finance its continued war against Ukraine.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," Zelensky wrote on X.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," he added.
The Kremlin said the Trump-Putin phone call focused on prospects for resolving the war in Ukraine and also addressed developments in Iran.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev welcomed the agreement, saying cooperation between Moscow and Washington on diesel and energy would benefit the world.
The announcement also drew criticism from Democrats. Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called the decision "infuriating" and accused Trump of undermining sanctions intended to weaken Russia's war economy.
The latest Treasury authorization follows several temporary exemptions granted to Russian energy shipments since the outbreak of the Iran war. However, it marks a more substantial relaxation of restrictions, extending beyond the shorter waivers previously issued.
For Moscow, the agreement offers an opportunity to expand energy revenues despite Western sanctions. For Kyiv, it represents a potentially damaging reversal of efforts to constrain Russia's ability to finance its invasion.

The 3rd Italian-Estonian Space Conference, titled “Italy and Estonia After Artemis II: Driving the Next Lunar Renaissance,” will take place on October 29 at the Estonian Business School in Tallinn.
The event, organized as part of the Software Defined Space Conference 2026 in collaboration with the Italian Embassy in Tallinn and the ICE office in Stockholm, will bring together experts, researchers, and representatives from the Italian and Estonian space industries and will focus on lunar exploration.
Two panel discussions will address, in particular, the construction of infrastructure and robotic systems for a permanent presence on the Moon, as well as “Digital Moon” technologies such as small satellites, imaging, cybersecurity, and New Space.

Trump says Russia to supply diesel to US and global market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:04:13 UTC
05:04:13 KST

Trump says Russia to supply diesel to US and global market
- Trump says Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets, with more to follow, as he tries to cut record fuel prices before the midterm elections.
- The deal came after US sanctions on Russian energy companies and drew criticism from Ukraine’s Zelensky, who said “gifts to Putin will not bring peace”.
- Analysts said the move is unlikely to lower prices much, while the White House is also considering using the Defence Production Act to boost US diesel output.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump said on Oct 9 that Russia had agreed to immediately supply diesel to US and global markets, in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, although analysts said the amounts would likely not reduce prices greatly.
The move comes as the price of diesel, used in agriculture, heating homes and trucking, is near a record high. The Nov 3 congressional elections will determine control of Congress.
Trump said on social media he had a “highly successful” discussion with President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets.
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised cooperation between Russia and the United States on diesel and energy in a post on X shortly after the call.
The unusual move comes after the US imposed sanctions on Russian energy companies over Russia’s full-scale war with Ukraine that began in 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticised Trump’s move.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” he said on X.
The US Treasury Department issued a general licence on Oct 9 allowing importation of Russian diesel until April 7.
Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million tonnes “immediately thereafter.”
Even more would follow, Trump said, “based on the condition of their diesel refineries,” which have been damaged by Ukrainian attacks.
‘Nothing burger’
Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices.
“I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is,” Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, said on X, adding that Russia usually exports much more diesel when its refinery fleet is not under attack.
The 300,000 tonnes to be immediately delivered is equal to about 2.25 million barrels of diesel.
The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.
“It’s clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market,” said Jim Mitchell, an analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie.
Diesel prices, which can drive inflation, are up 70% since the US and Israel launched the war with Iran on Feb 28. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing average US diesel prices to US$6.28 a gallon on Oct 8, according to the AAA motorist group.
The price climb is despite two recent moves by Trump to boost supplies of the fuel: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is normally used for farm equipment.
US diesel futures fell sharply following news of the deal and were trading at US$4.64 a gallon, down more than 4.8%.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump said.
Defense Production Act
Three industry sources said earlier on Oct 9 that Trump will issue a directive in the coming days to some US department heads to find ways to control diesel prices.
The directive, which they said could take the form of a presidential memo, will push officials to find ways to bypass local and state regulations blocking energy production and use the Cold War-era Defence Production Act to increase output of oil and fuel.
Under the DPA, the president can authorise US-backed loans or loan guarantees to expand domestic manufacturing of critical materials and to require companies to prioritise government contracts for essential goods.
The White House has been weighing how to use the DPA to expand refining capacity as the war with Iran exposes US vulnerability to supply disruptions and price spikes.
Refining executives told administration officials last month that federal money would be better directed towards making refineries more efficient or expanding plants rather than financing a new refinery, which would be more costly and take years to complete. REUTERS

Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
US President Donald Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in an effort to cut fuel prices before November's midterm elections. The move marks a stunning change of policy after the US and its allies hit Russia with waves of sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver another 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Trump’s shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia’s energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.
Read moreTrump says Ukraine, Russia agree not to hit energy targets
His move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.”
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on November 3.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reposted the Treasury Department’s announcement on X Friday and said that “Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world”.
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new US investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The US has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the US was $6.23 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on September 22.

Following Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury said its Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) was temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports to global markets.
The move comes amid a worsening global fuel supply crunch, as conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have disrupted oil shipments and refinery operations, driving up diesel prices worldwide.
In the US, diesel prices have surged by around 70% since the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February and remain at record highs, according to data from the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The export ban is due to expire at the end of October. It was not immediately clear whether the Putin-Trump agreement would affect the restrictions.

Women more drawn to hypothetical jobs where most employees were women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:00:16 UTC
05:00:16 KST

Learning that a workplace employs mostly women made women more interested in hypothetical jobs and more likely to expect that they would belong there, according to four studies published in PLOS One. The findings suggest that existing representation may encourage future representation, and the gender makeup of a workplace sometimes mattered more to women than whether a job ad stressed exceptional brilliance.
Women remain underrepresented in fields such as science, technology, politics and academia. One explanation is that some professions are associated with “brilliance” or natural intellectual ability, qualities that people often stereotype as more masculine. Previous research has found that messages emphasizing brilliance can reduce women’s interest in certain educational and professional opportunities.
Stella F. Lourenco of Emory University and colleagues examined another possible influence: how many people of one’s own gender already work in a field. Because fields seen as requiring brilliance also tend to have fewer women, it has been difficult to tell which of the two is driving women’s choices. The researchers conducted four studies involving 1,680 U.S.-based participants recruited through the online research platform Prolific.
The first study included 96 participants (average age 30.7 years; 60 women). Each participant estimated the proportion of men and women in 30 occupations drawn from a list of 60 and rated how much they felt they would belong in each one. They also rated how much each occupation required innate talent, how competitive and cutthroat its culture seemed, and how similar they felt to the people who work in it.
The second study included 194 participants (average age 36.3 years; 95 women). They read a fictional job advertisement that emphasized either brilliance or dedication. The participants then estimated the gender balance of the workplace and rated their interest in applying and their expected sense of belonging.
The third study included 399 participants (average age 33.5 years; 200 women). This time, the advertisements explicitly stated that either 75% of employees were men or 75% were women. The advertisements also emphasized either brilliance or dedication.
The final study, the only one whose design and analyses were registered in advance, included 991 participants (average age 39.5 years; 496 women). It varied both which gender formed the majority and how large that majority was, using ratios of 60% to 40%, 75% to 25% and 90% to 10%.
In the first study, participants’ average estimates closely matched actual occupational gender distributions, suggesting that people are generally aware of which occupations are more male- or female-dominated. Women reported a stronger sense of belonging in occupations they expected to have more women, even after accounting for beliefs about brilliance, perceived workplace culture and perceived similarity to workers. Men’s sense of belonging was not linked to their estimates.
In the second study, participants assumed both jobs employed more men than women, estimating about 40% women on average. Those who expected more women in the workplace reported more interest and belonging, and once their estimates were taken into account, the type of ad no longer predicted either outcome. Expected representation still predicted interest after accounting for perceived workplace culture and similarity, but no longer predicted belonging.
The third study provided stronger evidence because gender representation was directly manipulated. Women showed more interest in female-dominated jobs than in male-dominated ones, and when a job was female-dominated, their interest matched men’s. They also reported greater belonging in female-dominated workplaces, even when the job advertisement emphasized brilliance. Men’s interest and belonging did not depend on whether the workplace was mostly men or mostly women.
Women even reported greater belonging in a female-dominated job that emphasized brilliance than in a male-dominated job that emphasized dedication, suggesting that representation could outweigh the wording used to describe the qualities needed for success. Messaging still mattered within female-dominated jobs, where women anticipated more belonging when the ad stressed dedication. In male-dominated jobs, the type of ad made no difference to women’s sense of belonging.
The fourth study showed that women’s responses generally grew stronger as the gender imbalance became larger. Women reported more interest and belonging when women formed a 75% or 90% majority than when men did, but showed little difference at 60% to 40%. When men were in the majority, women anticipated less belonging than men did, a gap that widened with the imbalance, while women’s interest and belonging in female-majority jobs matched men’s in male-majority jobs. Men showed some preference for workplaces in which men were the majority, although this pattern was less consistent.
Messages about dedication still mattered. In the fourth study, women, but not men, were more interested in jobs that stressed effort and commitment rather than natural brilliance. However, once perceived workplace culture and similarity were taken into account, the type of ad no longer predicted belonging, while the effects of gender representation held.
Across the studies, perceptions of a competitive, cutthroat workplace culture and of how similar participants felt to the employees were also strong predictors of interest and belonging. The researchers suggest that gender ratios may serve as a signal of what a workplace’s climate will be like, including how supportive or competitive it is. They argued that improving representation and changing workplace messages may be most effective when pursued together.
“Altering beliefs about brilliance for success in specific professions, though important, may be insufficient for increasing female representation in fields where women are underrepresented,” the authors concluded.
There are a few things to keep in mind. The studies used hypothetical job advertisements, so participants’ ratings may not predict real applications or career decisions. Only the fourth study was preregistered, and the effects, while consistent, were generally small to moderate in size.
The study, “Gender representation begets gender representation,” was authored by Stella F. Lourenco, Kylee Novick, Ryno Kruger and Arber Tasimi.

Peruvian candidate named Hitler Mussolini wins mayoral election

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
A Peruvian candidate named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores emerged as the virtual winner of Sunday's mayoral election in the Andean district of Queropalca, drawing attention because his name coincides with those of two of the 20th century's most notorious dictators.
Flores, 45, ran for the Ahora Nacion party and received 229 votes, equivalent to 34.54% of valid ballots, local media reported Friday.
His closest rival, Gaspar Benilde Osorio Zambrano of Renovacion Popular Peru, secured 204 votes, or 30.77%, while Itala Yovana Santillan Vara of Pais para Todos came third with 187 votes, accounting for 28.21% of valid ballots, according to local media reports.
Two other candidates received considerably fewer votes. Alianza para el Progreso secured 35 votes, or 5.28%, while the Partido Democratico Somos Peru received eight votes, representing 1.21%.
A total of 707 ballots were cast in the district, including 663 valid votes, 30 blank ballots and 14 invalid ballots.
Flores led his closest rival by 25 votes, while the difference between the first- and third-place candidates was 42 votes.
Local outlet Ahora Regional reported Friday that Flores had emerged as the virtual winner. Peru's electoral authorities had counted all three tally sheets from the district, although formal proclamation of the winner was still pending, according to Peruvian media reports.
The candidate's name recalls Adolf Hitler, leader of Nazi Germany, and Benito Mussolini, Italy's Fascist dictator during World War II.
Peru has previously had another local politician named Hitler. Hitler Alba served as mayor of the Andean town of Yungar from 2011 to 2014 and returned to office after winning another local election in 2018, according to media reports.
The vote was part of Peru's 2026 regional and municipal elections, held on Oct. 4 to choose local authorities across the country.

Erik Prince's forces suffer battlefield loss in Congo, former UFC fighter among wounded, sources say
DAKAR, Oct 9 - Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said.
The frontline clash shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously helped Congo’s army secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east.
A veteran special operator reported on his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported.
The attack in South Kivu on September 17 left about 20 dead and wounded, two sources working with Congo's government said. The dead included at least seven Congolese and a former member of New Zealand's Special Forces, while the wounded included Kennedy and another foreign contractor, the sources said.
A Vectus Global representative declined to comment. The company has not previously suffered casualties in Congo, a source with direct knowledge of the operation said.
One of the sources who works for Congo's government said that Rwandan forces backing the M23 rebels may have surprised them by tracking a drone used for surveillance operations to their location.
Spokespeople for the Congolese and Rwandan governments and for the M23 did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Kennedy, the former mixed martial arts fighter, survived the attack with three gunshot wounds to the leg, three sources said, and is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in the suburbs of Washington.
Kennedy has a popular podcast channel and millions of followers on social media. Trump is a fan of UFC, hosting fights at the White House this year.
The US State Department and Walter Reed declined to comment. Kennedy's parents did not respond to requests for comment.
A Congolese security source, who said some 20 people were wounded and killed in the attack, added that villagers were likely among the casualties as well. Reuters spoke to at least 10 sources either with direct knowledge of the attack or briefed on the outcome.
PRINCE TOOK EXPANDED ROLE IN CONGO'S CONFLICT
Prince's initial mandate in Congo was to secure and improve revenue collection from the country's vast mineral reserves, which have been plundered for decades, fuelling relentless conflict in the east.
But in January and early February, his forces deployed to Uvira after Washington helped broker a deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from the strategic town.
The size of Prince's forces in Congo is unclear.
One of the sources with direct knowledge of the attack said the Vectus team was travelling between locations when the ambush took place and its sophistication suggested Rwandan forces were involved.
"It reinforces the need for DRC sovereignty to be restored. It's an incredibly dangerous place right now," the source said.
Two other sources said the ambush was carried out by the Rwandan military.
Prince is the founder of now-defunct private military firm Blackwater, some of whose members were pardoned in 2020 for killing Iraqi civilians.
The State Department has said it does not have any contracts with Prince in Congo, though US officials have said they plan to work more closely with Vectus Global in Haiti.
The deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from Uvira was part of wider agreements brokered by the Trump administration to try to end the conflict in eastern Congo.
POPULAR PODCASTER
Kennedy, a father of four, has posted his views on politics, culture, fitness and more on social media. He also runs a popular YouTube podcast in which he interviews UFC fighters, veterans, cultural disruptors and others.
He has often posted about his family, including four young children. In late August, he posted about having "incredible conversations about what being a man means and what sacrifice really looks like" with his son. He did not disclose details about his upcoming trip to Congo.
The United Nations and Western powers say Rwanda backs M23, even exercising command and control over the group. Rwanda denies this. Fighting in the decades-long conflict flared early last year, with M23 fighters making rapid gains in the east, which is rich in tantalum, gold, lithium and other minerals. REUTERS

Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands
Saudi Arabia said on Friday that three people including a pilot were killed in attacks on Riyadh international airport the day before when Yemen's Houthis claimed hits on the facility.
Houthi media reported on Friday that Saudi attacks on Sanaa airport killed two people, while the civil defence agency in the Yemeni capital reported extinguishing fires caused by Saudi strikes, including one that it said destroyed a factory.
The conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised government -- supported by Saudi Arabia -- surged in July, and has since spilled over into the neighbouring kingdom.
In addition to seizing territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have attacked transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter with drones and missiles.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said two attacks on Thursday on Riyadh airport and a Saudia airlines plane had "resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens".
The national carrier confirmed the death of the aircraft's captain.
The attacks on the Saudi capital forced diplomats stationed there to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city on Thursday.
Numerous flights at Riyadh airport were delayed or cancelled, and the civil defence agency said missile "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Friday appeared to suggest that planes would need to seek the group's permission to fly in or out of Riyadh.
"Humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh Airport will be permitted for all flights authorised" by a Houthi coordinating body in Sanaa, he wrote on X.
'Advances are limited'
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it supports have struggled to reverse the Houthis' advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, which is crucial to global shipping.
While a Saudi diplomat said on Friday that Saudi-backed forces had retaken the area, a military source on the ground gave a conflicting account, saying fighting was ongoing.
The Yemeni military source told AFP that government forces had launched a "major operation" in the strait region, supported by Saudi air power, but added that "fighting is fierce and advances are limited".
Houthi-affiliated media, meanwhile, said an attack by government forces south of the strait had been repelled.
A regional source told AFP on Friday that Saudi Arabia would not bow to the Houthis' "military blackmail" and would not agree to a truce until the Yemeni government regained all the territory it lost in recent weeks.
The Houthis' Al-Massirah TV channel reported fresh Saudi strikes on Sanaa, shortly after a large demonstration in support of the group in the city.
The raids targeted military positions far from residential neighbourhoods, according to an AFP correspondent.
The Houthis, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014.
Riyadh's military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.
Evacuation warning
After declaring the start of their counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The Houthis have warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.

BAE Lands Contract for F-35 Block 4 Electronic Warfare Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:57:55 UTC
04:57:55 KST

BAE Systems has received a contract from Lockheed Martin to install an upgraded Block 4 electronic warfare system into new F-35 Joint Strike Fighters, as well as to retrofit some older jets.
BAE’s AN/ASQ-239 EW systems will be installed on lots 20 to 22 of the F-35, the company said in an Oct. 6 statement, and some older F-35s with previous versions of the EW system will be retrofitted to have the latest version installed.
“BAE Systems has been the EW supplier for the F-35 program for the past 21 years, successfully designing and developing the Block 1, Block 2, and Block 3 configurations” of the AN/ASQ-239, Amber Dolan, BAE’s vice president of F-35 solutions, said in a follow-up statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “We are currently developing Block 4 systems that can accelerate the delivery of advanced EW capabilities via adaptable hardware and incremental software updates.”
The updated EW suite is part of a broader program of upgrades to the Lockheed Martin-made F-35, collectively referred to as Block 4. Lockheed previously awarded BAE a $491 million contract for the F-35 EW systems in 2023, and another $493 million contract in 2021.
The Block 4 EW systems that will be in F-35 lots 20 and beyond “offer improvements in threat detection, situational awareness, and capabilities to counter modern threats,” Dolan said.
BAE declined to say how much the contract is worth and how many EW systems it will deliver for new jets and retrofits. The company said it has delivered more than 1,500 EW systems for the F-35 so far.
BAE said the AN/ASQ-239 system provides both offensive and defensive EW capabilities, which give pilots a 360-degree view of the battlefield and allow the F-35 to operate in environments protected by enemy fighters, missiles, drones, or integrated air defense systems. Its passive long-range sensing capabilities combine with high-speed signal processing and advanced algorithms to allow pilots to detect and counter threats before an enemy can act, the company said. The system’s software can also be quickly updated to account for new threats.
A previous upgrade to the AN/ASQ-239 EW system—called the Digital Channelized Receiver/Techniques Generator and Tuner Insertion Program, or DTIP—was launched in 2018. Those DTIP improvements allowed for previous versions of the EW system to be condensed into a smaller footprint that required less power, which created space for the new Block 4 modernization.
BAE said it has made investments in facilities—including the 2022 opening of a new 200,000-square-foot engineering and production facility in Manchester, N.H.—to help design and develop new EW systems. BAE also designs and manufactures EW systems at facilities in Merrimack, N.H., Nashua, N.H., and Austin, Texas.
