‘They're testing us’: suspicious incursions in Syria revive fears of another Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:57:02 UTC
04:57:02 KST

Brig. Gen. Sivan Bloch, the new commander of the IDF's Bashan Division, had barely a week to settle into his position before facing a series of incidents along the Syrian border that soldiers and local officials fear may be more than a coincidence.
The first occurred Sunday night, when a 22-year-old Palestinian living in Damascus attempted to infiltrate an IDF outpost near the Syrian village of al-Hamidiyah. A soldier from the Carmeli Reserve Brigade shot and killed him. Only a mobile phone and cash were found in his pockets. Hours later, on Monday afternoon, two Syrians riding a motorcycle approached a police outpost in the Quneitra area. Neither was armed, but both ignored calls to stop under the military's suspect-arrest procedure, prompting soldiers to open fire. One was wounded and taken to Israel for medical treatment, while the other was detained for questioning.
"They're testing the terrain," a reserve officer serving in the sector said this week, stressing that these were not the first incidents involving people approaching Israeli military positions in recent weeks. Several weeks earlier, a Syrian civilian armed with a knife climbed onto an IDF position at the Nahal Golan outpost. He was captured and taken for questioning. The military said the suspect had mental health problems, but along Israel's northern border, incidents involving seemingly erratic individuals sometimes raise suspicions of organized reconnaissance, similar to patterns soldiers recall from Lebanon and Gaza before October 7, 2023.
"They send individuals and cells, doing all kinds of things to see where we're operating and how we respond," the officer said. "It reminds me of the period before October 7. Disturbances, one person here, another there. They're checking how long it takes you to respond, how you respond and from where you detect them." He is not alone. Many soldiers serving in the area suspect that the Syrians who entered the buffer zone, where unauthorized entry is prohibited, were attempting to gauge the military's response at positions located just a few kilometers apart.
The working assumption: someone is testing Israel
So far, the IDF can point to its successful responses to the incidents. But the willingness of individuals to approach military positions remains troubling. Investigators hope questioning the suspects will clarify what prompted the incidents and whether any connection exists between them. For now, the military says that despite the concerning circumstances, no common link has been established. Officials say they need several more days to determine whether a particular organization or other actor was behind the incidents and whether they signal a change in the security situation.
The IDF acknowledges that it cannot conclusively rule out the possibility that the latest infiltration attempts were intended to harm soldiers. Regardless of their motives, the suspects entered areas where they were not permitted to be, leading troops to open fire. Another detail raising concern is that all three suspects in the latest incidents came from the Damascus area, relatively far from the border. So far, however, investigators have found no connection between them and previous terrorist activity or specific organizations.
The military insists it is not complacent. Its working assumption is that Israeli positions are being tested, and commanders acknowledge that no amount of preparation can guarantee complete protection against an attack. Military officials say there is no shortage of organizations interested in attacking Israeli forces and potentially civilians. Iran-linked groups, Palestinian organizations, ISIS, Hamas, Hezbollah and other actors operate in Syria and could seek opportunities along the border.
Accordingly, operational procedures have been tightened, and troops have been briefed on possible attack scenarios. The military is preparing on the assumption that further attacks will eventually be attempted. That, according to the IDF, is also the rationale for maintaining soldiers inside Syrian territory: any attempted infiltration would first encounter military forces rather than Israeli civilians. In recent months, Israeli troops have identified individuals gathering intelligence and documenting military activity in southern Syria. Some were civilians, while others were believed to have been operating on behalf of organizations seeking vulnerabilities in Israel's defenses.
The latest encounters are part of a broader pattern that has characterized the sector since the beginning of 2026. The buffer zone east of the Golan Heights has become an area of persistent, low-intensity military activity. Since the collapse of Bashar Assad's regime, the IDF has established approximately 10 company-sized outposts inside Syrian territory. Soldiers patrol open terrain and villages populated by Sunni Muslim civilians. Particularly in the southern Golan sector, military officials describe local attitudes toward Israel as deeply hostile, more so than among some Druze, Christian and Circassian communities. "Ultimately, there is no real, effective control over this area by any Syrian authority," a reserve officer said.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government has sought to demonstrate that it is taking steps to distance potential threats from Israel. In late September, for example, Syrian authorities announced the arrest of three Hezbollah-affiliated terrorists accused of attempting to position missile launchers near the Israeli border. At the same time, Syrian local media have increasingly carried hostile messages toward Israel, while negotiations over a security agreement between the two countries remain stalled.
‘The army is preparing for 500 pickup trucks, but 1,500 will come’
While the IDF investigates the incidents, civilian leaders on the Israeli side of the border are unconvinced by suggestions that the incursions could be unrelated. They are demanding that the military treat them as potential elements of an organized hostile operation. "It's exactly like the kites," said Golan Regional Council head Uri Kelner, referring to incendiary kites used along the Gaza border before the October 7 attack. "When one thing happens, you say it's a drop. When several things happen, it's already rain."
Kelner believes the incidents amount to organized testing of Israel's defensive readiness. "In my understanding and assessment, someone is pushing this. Someone is learning from it, someone is watching it. That is clear to us," he said. "On the other side, they are watching. They don't like the fact that the IDF is in the buffer zone, and they're preparing for days when they will begin harassing our forces over this."
Despite the danger of explosives and close-range confrontations, Kelner views the buffer zone itself as a crucial protective barrier for Israeli communities. "These are good incidents," said Kelner, a reserve lieutenant colonel and former deputy commander of the IDF's 55th Reserve Brigade. "An attacker arrives, encounters the IDF's forward security line and doesn't get near the fence. That's our lesson from October 7. We don't wait for them to reach us. We're ahead of them."
For Kelner and other regional leaders, the greatest danger is that international pressure could eventually force Israel to withdraw from the buffer zone. U.S. President Donald Trump recently addressed the issue, saying the Syrians did not want Israeli forces in their territory and that Israel should redeploy its troops. He also spoke about Israeli deployments in Lebanon. After Israel's upcoming elections, any new government could face comparable or even greater pressure.
Kelner is therefore demanding a commitment from candidates across the political spectrum that the IDF will remain on the Mount Hermon ridgeline and deep inside the buffer zone "forever." Katzrin Local Council head Yehuda Dua also opposes withdrawal, warning that such a move would endanger not only the Golan Heights but Israel's security as a whole. "Leaving here would simply be security madness," a reserve officer serving in the area added.
Kelner is proposing a three-stage strategy designed to institutionalize Israel's existing deployment. The first stage involves strengthening ties with Syria's Druze population. "The IDF operates there and, according to foreign reports, arms them, while also taking care of quite a few civilian needs," Kelner said. He argued that allowing Syrian Druze to work in Israel would serve both economic and security interests. "We need those Druze to come work in Israel, because if they don't work for us, someone from Hezbollah or Iran will pay them $100 a month. With us, they earn that in two days of work."
The second stage would make Israel's physical presence in the buffer zone permanent, with no withdrawal permitted. The third would designate Israeli communities along the border fence as a forward defensive line, providing them with substantial weapons and ammunition so they could withstand an attack without allowing it to spread farther into Israel.
For Kelner, the lessons of October 7 leave no room for complacency. "We're not preparing for the previous war, but for the next one," he warned. "There are 21 divisions in the Syrian army that are training and growing stronger. The IDF is preparing to stop an assault by 500 pickup trucks, but 1,500 pickup trucks will come. And then we could find ourselves back on October 7, big time."
The military, however, offers a more restrained assessment. Although the IDF acknowledges that a large-scale attack from Syrian territory is technically possible, it currently assesses the probability of such an assault as relatively low. Military officials say the capability to launch an attack involving 1,500 pickup trucks may exist, but they do not believe such an operation would serve the interests of the actors on the other side of the border at present. The possibility cannot be dismissed, they stress, but it is not considered a highly likely scenario.
Where are the motorcycles heading?
Katzrin council head Yehuda Dua remains deeply concerned. He says the explanations offered by the military following the latest incidents have done little to reassure him. "The army doesn't view this as something major, and senior officials in the National Security Council say these attempts to approach our forces do not become a strategic threat to the State of Israel," Dua said, describing the assessments he has heard in closed discussions.
He believes the relatively limited concern over motorcycles approaching Israeli positions echoes the attitudes that prevailed near Gaza before October 7. "I think we're starting to become a little like the Gaza Strip 20 years ago," he said. "It started there, too, with a trickle of stones, Molotov cocktails and infiltration attempts. Where do these motorcycles want to go? They're probably not coming to have coffee in Ein Zivan. They apparently want to reach a soldier or carry out an attack, and learn our responses and how we operate in the area."
Dua suspects that individuals approaching Israeli positions may be paid by larger organizations to test the military's defenses. He suggested that such networks could be associated with al-Sharaa's government, Hezbollah or Iranian-backed militias, although no evidence has yet established such connections in the latest incidents. "There are murderous terrorist cells here that send these attackers, paying them to test Israel's borders and understand how far they can get," he claimed. "There could be a much bigger plot taking shape here."
Dua is demanding that Israel impose a cost on Syria if the incidents continue. "Today, the State of Israel needs to be the side that initiates, not the side that reacts," he said. "We need to send a very clear message that if these incidents continue and escalate, Israel will also escalate its responses against Syria as a sovereign state, against government institutions, public institutions and gas, water, electricity and oil infrastructure."

“God said no tonight. My life for a watch.”
The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department said in a separate statement on Friday it is investigating the robbery reported by Allen, without naming him.
The sheriff’s department’s statement said the robbers demanded a watch and bracelet from the victim at knifepoint and gunpoint. One of the robbers then pistol-whipped the victim, “causing a laceration to his forehead”, before the attackers fled in a car with “the victim’s watch”, according to the statement.
First responders medically evacuated the victim but did not take him to a hospital, according to the sheriff’s office.
The agency said its major crimes bureau was investigating the case and asked anyone with information about possible suspects to call the sheriff’s office’s West Hollywood station.
Allen’s Instagram post on Thursday expressed a desire for West Hollywood authorities to use Flock Safety license plate cameras to capture the pair who robbed him.
While many cities of late have canceled the use of such cameras amid misuse and privacy concerns, West Hollywood’s city council voted narrowly to keep using Flock cameras, albeit with new safeguards, as the Beverly Press & Park Labrea News reported in July.
Allen also wrote in a reply to his video on Thursday that he was “def concussed and at hospital”.
Among those who replied to Allen’s video on Thursday was singer Gavin DeGraw, who was hospitalized after being beaten up in New York City in 2011, according to various media reports. “That’s so fucked up,” DeGraw wrote.
A reply from the West Hollywood city council candidate Kyle Brazeal said in part: “This is insane, unacceptable and I’m sorry this happened.”
Allen portrayed the character Toby Cavanaugh on Pretty Little Liars during its seven-season run from 2010 to 2017. He also had a role in Walker from 2021 to 2024 and guest starred in February in an episode of the Nathan Fillion show The Rookie.

With anti-Zionist motion, Britain's Green Party shifts the Overton window on antisemitism - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:52:15 UTC
04:52:15 KST

Anybody with half a brain can see that the motion passed by the Green Party of England and Wales is disgraceful.
By 1,022 votes to 813, a British political party decided that Zionism – the national liberation movement of the Jewish people – should be “treated as any other form of racism.” It also endorsed one Palestinian state across all the territory on which Israel now stands.
Others far more erudite than I have dismantled the motion’s ignorance and malice. Jonathan Freedland, writing in The Guardian, exposed its central conceit: yet again, non-Jews have decided to tell Jews what Zionism means and which parts of our identity are permissible.
Almost every synagogue movement in Britain has some connection with Zionism. The Greens are therefore placing much of organized Jewish life under suspicion.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry called the decision “a stain on the history of the United Kingdom.” It is. But I want to focus on something even more ominous: a shift of the Overton window.
The Overton window, named after the American policy analyst Joseph Overton, describes the range of ideas considered politically acceptable at any given time. Inside “the window” are opinions that respectable politicians and institutions can advocate without being dismissed as extremists. Outside “the window” are the ideas regarded as beyond the pale – too offensive, absurd, or dangerous to merit serious consideration.
The window moves through argument, crisis, repetition, and institutional endorsement. An idea that begins as unthinkable is aired as radical, discussed as controversial, then accepted as one legitimate view among others.
The public need not embrace it. The crucial change occurs when a mainstream institution says the unsayable and everyone else is required to debate it.
That is what happened in Brighton. “Zionism is racism” did not remain on a placard at the edge of a demonstration or in an anonymous social media post.
A party with elected MPs and serious electoral ambitions debated it, voted on it, and adopted it as official policy. The unthinkable became a conference motion, and the conference motion became party policy. The genie is out of the bottle.
Thankfully, there has been wide condemnation. Four of the Greens’ five MPs opposed the motion. Liberal Democrats condemned it. Labour MPs referred it to the police and the Equality and Human Rights Commission. The co-leader of the German Greens called it “intolerable and unacceptable.” A society protects its moral boundaries only when decent people defend them loudly.
But condemnation does not put the genie back in the bottle. From now on, another activist, councilor, or party will not introduce a wholly unthinkable idea. They will be citing an existing British party policy.
The next proposal will seem less shocking because the first boundary has already been crossed. That is how the window moves, and why British Jews will feel less secure even if the Greens never come near government.
The political climate has been brewing for a considerable time. Last year, then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer recognized a Palestinian state whose borders, capital, government and security arrangements had not been agreed with Israel.
Last month, Foreign Secretary Edward Miliband banned trade in goods from Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria and accused “settler terrorists” of ethnic cleansing.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham apologized for Labour’s earlier approach to Gaza, as though the principal moral failure after October 7 was excessive sympathy for Israel.
Words and policies do not cause every act of violence. Individuals remain responsible for their crimes. But public language creates an atmosphere.
Giving permission to antisemites
When Israel alone is turned into a pariah, when Zionism is declared racist, and when Jewish attachment to Israel is treated as evidence of moral corruption, antisemites hear permission even if politicians insist they never gave it.
Look at Britain, where this motion was passed. Two worshippers were killed in the terrorist attack on Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation in Manchester on Yom Kippur last year.
In April, two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green in an attack declared to be terrorism, after Jewish ambulances in the area had been set ablaze. Counterterrorism police foiled an Islamic State-inspired plan to attack a march against antisemitism and then Jewish neighborhoods in Manchester with automatic weapons. The plotters wanted to kill hundreds.
Just days ago, a court heard allegations that two Iranian men had watched Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue as part of a chlorine-bomb plot. Thank God for the police and security services who foiled these plans.
Then there is the BBC. Journalist Patrick Christys recently highlighted again the evidence concerning BBC Arabic, which is supported by the license fee and government money.
A leaked dossier by former BBC standards adviser Michael Prescott described contributors with documented antisemitic or pro-Hamas views presented repeatedly as neutral witnesses. One appeared 522 times; another, who had written that Jews should be burned “as Hitler did,” appeared 244 times. This is institutional failure on a grotesque scale.
For many months after October 7, I resisted comparisons with pre-war Germany. Britain is not Nazi Germany, and careless historical analogies weaken the argument. There are still democratic institutions, courageous police officers, and political leaders willing to condemn antisemitism.
But institutional antisemitism does not arrive one morning in a familiar uniform. It advances when institutions mark Jews out, when a national broadcaster platforms hatred, when governments apply standards to the Jewish state that they apply to no other, and when violence becomes part of the security calculation of Jewish life.
Britain is not there yet. But it is no longer moving safely away from there either.
On October 24, 2023, less than three weeks after the Hamas massacre, I wrote in this newspaper that it was time for the Jews of Britain to leave. I wrote with a heavy heart and, perhaps, with a hope that events would prove me wrong.
They have not. What I did not foresee was how quickly the deterioration would come.
The Green motion has done something politically very consequential: it has made an antisemitic proposition respectable enough to become party policy. The Overton window has shifted. British Jews can feel the cold air coming through it.
The writer is a rabbi and physician who lives in Netanya. He is a co-founder of Techelet-Inspiring Judaism. For more of his work, go to: rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com

Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:52:00 UTC
04:52:00 KST

French students decry failures of education system
October 9, 2026
Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.
At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.
Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.
The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end.
Problems of centralization
Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.
The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.
Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.
Dilapidated infrastructure
Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).
According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.
Macron tried in vain to address problem
Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.
The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created.
Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.
These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.
Increasing deficiencies
The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.
Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.
The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.
Cancelled lessons
Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.
The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.
Broken promises of equality
France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.
The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.
Protests in the run-up to the presidential election
It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.
Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.
With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.
This article was originally published in German.

Hanukkah Barbie is here, and she actually got the Jewish holiday right - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:51:40 UTC
04:51:40 KST

The miracle of Hanukkah came early this year: Hanukkah Barbie is here.
Mattel would like us to call her “Holiday Sweater Barbie.” Respectfully, no. This is Hanukkah Barbie.
She is dressed in the blue-and-yellow color palette that retailers have apparently decided belongs exclusively to Hanukkah. Her sweater is covered in Jewish stars and dreidels, with a light-up hanukkiyah built right into the front.
As if the sweater isn’t Hanukkah enough, she also dons blue-and-white gingham pants. And then there are the tiny tan shearling boots, because Hanukkah Barbie understands comfort.
Naturally, I bought her immediately.
Unboxing her involved approximately 613 tiny plastic ties, but once I finally freed her, I was even more delighted than I expected to be. I have spent an unreasonable amount of my adult life thinking about Hanukkah merchandise, and holding an actual Hanukkah Barbie feels slightly surreal.
This story also has a wonderfully Jewish twist: Barbie was created by Ruth Handler, the daughter of Jewish immigrants, who co-founded Mattel and introduced Barbie in 1959.
It feels almost bashert that a doll created by the daughter of Jewish immigrants, which became woven into American childhood, is finally celebrating a Jewish holiday — more than six decades after her debut!
I’m not sure Handler ever imagined this particular outfit, but I like to think she would have loved it.
And judging by the frenzy around her, plenty of people seem to agree.
She has repeatedly sold out at major retailers, sometimes within hours of appearing online. Clearly, I wasn’t the only one determined to bring her home.
I understand the impulse.
There are few shopping instincts stronger than a Jewish person unexpectedly encountering genuinely good Hanukkah merchandise. You see it. You buy it.
Which is why I was particularly disappointed when some other outlets decided that the big Hanukkah Barbie story was apparently her nose.
Questions arise regarding Barbie's nose size
The articles drew on a handful of Reddit comments questioning whether Mattel had intentionally given its Jewish Barbie a larger nose. Hanukkah Barbie had barely arrived, and somehow the conversation had already turned to one of the most tired stereotypes about Jewish appearance.
So, for reasons I absolutely did not anticipate when I ordered this doll, I have now become familiar with Barbie face sculpts.
The Barbie face many of us probably picture is known in collector circles as the Millie sculpt. Another existing Mattel face sculpt, known as Violet, dates to 2018 and has appeared on other Barbies for years. It has pronounced dimples, fuller cheeks, and a somewhat more prominent nose.
To my eye, Hanukkah Barbie’s face looks like an iteration of Violet, but it does not appear to be the exact same sculpt. When I put her next to a Barbie with the Violet sculpt, Hanukkah Barbie’s face looks more petite. And while Violet dolls are marked “2018” on the backs of their heads, the back of Hanukkah Barbie’s keppe reads “2026.”
That doesn’t tell us exactly what changed, or why. Mattel has not identified Hanukkah Barbie’s face sculpt publicly, as far as I can tell. But based on my own side-by-side comparison, I see similarities to a face already used on other Barbies, not evidence that Hanukkah Barbie was designed around a stereotypically Jewish nose.
Focusing on what Mattel got right
If we’re going to scrutinize the choices Mattel made with Hanukkah Barbie, I’d rather focus on the ones the company actually got right.
The Hebrew letters on the dreidels are accurate. Her hanukkiyah has the correct number of branches. The sweater lights up. Technically, the illumination reads more like three glowing sections than nine individually blazing candles, but I’m willing to give Barbie a pass for imperfect light-up-sweater technology.
Those details may seem small, but Mattel itself knows how quickly one mistake can become the story. In 2023, packaging for its Barbie honoring the Cherokee Nation’s first woman principal chief famously contained an error in the Cherokee text that turned “Cherokee Nation” into “Chicken Nation.”
This time, Mattel did its homework. And maybe that’s part of why the response from the Jewish community has been so extraordinary. There’s something pretty powerful about finally feeling seen.
I just have one more pressing question for Mattel: When are we getting the Hanukkah Dreamhouse?

For this Jewish rock fan, ‘Free Palestine’ no longer feels like freedom - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:51:36 UTC
04:51:36 KST

I remember going to see Bruce Springsteen in the late 1970s, when, at the end of his exhausting three-hour marathons dedicated to embracing life, he would shout out before the encore, “Remember, nobody wins unless everybody wins.”
To me, that albeit naive sentiment embodied the spirit of rock & roll, the invitation inside Big Star’s “Thirteen” of “Rock and roll is here to stay, come inside, well, it’s okay.”
I bought the No Nukes album in 1980, paid to see the film, and campaigned against nuclear power plants at Seabrook, New Hampshire. I chanted “Sandinista” along with The Clash, even though I had barely a smidgen of an idea of what the whole Nicaragua conflict was about. Rock & roll and social justice went hand in hand, and I found a loving home.
That promise of inclusion, safety, and community has become increasingly shattered for this Jewish, Israeli Zionist amid the baffling intersection of ‘Free Palestine’ with the liberal values I cherished growing up with in the US.
Last week, at the impressive and impassioned Power to the People concert in Maryland organized by longtime progressive Tom Morello, a Springsteen insider and onetime leader of agit-rockers Rage Against the Machine, performers rightfully railed against the destructive policies of US President Donald Trump, the brutality of ICE, and the threat of fascism making inroads in America.
However, Macklemore – already the recipient of a significant career boost when booted off of the Ed Sheeran tour for turning his opening set into a political pro-Hamas rally – delivered a prerecorded video message that defined “power to the people” as combating humanitarian crises around the world, including “And lastly, Free Palestine.”
During Public Enemy’s incendiary performance, frontman Chuck D called out “Free Palestine, Free Haiti, and please free a closed mind.”
'Voted to remove Ed Sheeran from the lineup'
And Morello himself, while not spouting “Free Palestine” directly, entered the fray when he announced to the cheering crowd that the festival’s artists had “voted to remove Ed Sheeran from the lineup” – an indirect reference to Macklemore’s dismissal from the Sheeran tour.
The same week, country superstar Zach Bryan, apparently in a big middle finger to New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who pressured promoters to drop Macklemore from the Sheeran tour, sported a black “Free Palestine” T-shirt (along with a curious far-right “Appeal to Heaven” insignia) on both nights of his sold-out shows at the stadium.
His drummer wore a shirt bearing the name Hind Rajab, a Palestinian girl killed by the IDF in Gaza in 2024, along with a big “5,” her age.
It appears that “Free Palestine” and its equally simplistic and sinister sister slogan “Genocide” have become a prerequisite for entertainers, if they are as far left as Morello or as far right as Bryan.
Anyone who invokes sympathy for Israel – whether Sheeran or Pink, who said that Jewish families at Sheeran’s shows should not have to be uncomfortable – or attempts to explain that there are two sides to the Israel-Palestinian story, that maybe there was no genocide, a factoid invented by the Qatari propaganda machine, is immediately ridiculed and ostracized by the hip fashion plate keffiyeh wearers.
Let’s face it – a well-placed keffiyeh scarf looks much cooler than a yarmulke. And “Free Palestine,” like “Sandinista” some 45 years ago, is an easy, guilt-free way to feel like you’re politically active without having to make an effort.
But if anyone would take a minute and look for a second beyond the slogan, there’s no way to interpret it as anything but a call to dismantle the State of Israel. And for a Jewish concertgoer to hear it chanted with gusto, it’s not only uncomfortable; it’s scary... and dangerous.
That simplistic but loaded phrase being chanted only days before October 7, the third anniversary of the brutal assault by Palestinian Hamas terrorists, was a grotesque distortion of history and what is right and wrong.
This week, Israelis have mourned their indescribable losses of October 7 and since, as freshly as if it took place yesterday. Tales of unbelievable heroism contrasted with recollections of unbelievable Hamas savagery.
The “Free Palestine” advocates ignore that narrative and treat Israelis not as victims but as arrogant aggressors intentionally wiping out Palestinian children for sport. As we know here, but apparently few others do, nothing could be further from the truth.
A few artists – a motley crew, to be sure – get it. They have stood up on Israel’s side, ranging from A-lister Jerry Seinfeld and established star David Draiman of Disturbed to ’80s pop star Boy George (who just sold out the Menorah Mivtachim Arena in Tel Aviv in November and added another show), 2000s-era singer/songwriter Five for Fighting, folk rocker (and Bob Dylan’s son-in-law) Peter Himmelman, and actor/comedian Michael Rappaport.
But most everyone else, whether fearful of shrinking their fan base and income or simply hesitant to wade into the lethal waters of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, has remained silent.
However, silence is no longer an option. Gaza is in ruins, and thousands of people are wallowing in tents as the winter approaches.
Every Gazan death, like every Israeli death, in this conflict can be placed at the feet of Hamas. Gaza must be freed from its deadly clutches and its refusal to disarm and relinquish control of the land it destroyed, to enable its rebuilding.
That’s what “Free Palestine” should mean, not the profane falsification, currently proliferating on concert stages, at film festivals, and on awards show daises around the world, that places the blame only on Israel and blindly encourages the alarming global rise of antisemitic attacks against Jews.
That’s when I would feel like it’s a safe environment to go to concerts again in the US or Europe – when Zach Bryan’s drummer can also wear a T-shirt with the names of Ariel and Kfir Bibas, murdered intentionally by Hamas, and with their ages, four and nine months, and be embraced by the crowd as vociferously as when he splashed Hind Rajab, killed inadvertently by the IDF in a war attempting to free hostages.
That’s when I’ll feel heard and included – when the audience and the performer chant together, in a righteous call for liberty and justice that the best rock & roll has always championed: “Free Palestine... from Hamas!”
Springsteen and Joan Baez expressed it best when they performed a powerful acoustic duet, at the Power to the People concert last week, of Dylan’s iconic “Chimes of Freedom.”
“Tolling for the aching ones whose wounds cannot be nursed
For the countless confused, accused, misused, strung-out ones and worse
And for every hung-up person in the whole wide universe
And we gazed upon the chimes of freedom flashing”
When the aching ones and their wounds refer to both the Gazans and the Israelis who have lost so much, that’s when everybody can start winning again.

Australia's Test start no disaster, but order issues hint at troubles ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:51:32 UTC
04:51:32 KST

It was Steve Waugh — Mr Mental Disintegration himself — who once said the most emotionally taxing aspect of his time as the most important man in Australian cricket was not the burden of captaincy, nor the concurrent need to keep making big runs, but his role as a national selector.
How long to wait for a treasured teammate's form to come right, when the axe might end his career? Should he be replaced with fresh blood or someone on a second or third chance, as Waugh himself had once been? What was the right balance of talent and personalities?
Overnight in Durban, Waugh's man-management issues seemed trifling compared to the self-inflicted problems of Australia's current selectors. But you'd need a very specific combination of tarot cards and crystals to work out which question of George Bailey's led to the answer "Nic Maddinson".
The final analysis on day one was not entirely disastrous. Australia stumbled to 6-187 before bad light stopped play and there were at least positive signs in a few problematic areas.
One was a solid start from Marnus Labuschagne, whose momentary lapse on the brink of lunch ended a sparkling partnership with Steve Smith. The other was a steady hand from Matt Renshaw, who was undefeated on 46 at the day's premature end.
There were deeper currents, though. Troubling ones. What stood out was not just the sense of a well-drilled bowling attack reminding the world why South Africa was the reigning world champion, but of Australia, with its makeshift batting order and selection on the fly, presenting as an increasingly confused rabble.
Maddinson's mere selection was contentious enough; he had not played a first-class match in 19 months. The corollary was throwing him to the wolves as opener on a pitch offering lateral movement. That second part was so surprising to most onlookers that the host broadcaster initially had him down as batting at five.
But then, how else could it have played out? Had Cooper Connolly got the nod instead, he probably would have slotted in at five and Renshaw would have moved up to open with Travis Head, himself a world-class number five whose impact in Tests is now being blunted by his ongoing hostage ordeal at the top of the order. Further problems flow from there.
You had to feel for Maddinson. Mark Waugh, who was among the selectors who picked the left-hander for his first three Tests in 2016, has since admitted he had been discarded too quickly. Now he's been brought back almost at random and given this thankless task.
Maddinson's 33-ball duck was awful to watch, but one would hope he's backed to make a slightly better fist of whatever follows.
Another thing Steve Waugh used to do was make it clear to each player in his team what was expected of them in their specific role. It's hard to imagine things being phrased so plainly now. Aside from Labuschagne and Smith, could any current Australian batsman say he's in the right spot for the right reason?
At 32, Head's identity crisis should, on current evidence, be considered a serious matter for the future of this team.
Right now, we are being asked to accept that Renshaw — an undoubtedly tough and capable player whose Test record is nevertheless modest — needs to bat where he is most comfortable, and that as a result, Head, now in his prime years, needs to play an essentially experimental role that is clearly not suited to him.
It is true that Bailey's job has been made harder by injuries to Cameron Green and Josh Inglis, and a dearth of irresistible opening candidates in the Sheffield Shield. But the strangest aspect of all the pre-tour kvetching over selection was how much of it centered on Labuschagne, who was and remains the logical choice at three.
Far more baffling, in hindsight, was the lack of focus on Bailey's claim that the number-three slot could be just as easily filled by Connolly, who has never made a first-class century, or the since-injured Inglis, neither of whom have batted higher than five for their state.
Even in this era of "false threes" and result pitches, the linchpin positions in the top order should surely not be devalued so casually. Australia is now approaching double digits for opening combinations of the post-Warner era.
Anyway, that is what Australia could have controlled. What it still can't, it seems, is the sideways movement of medium pacers. When this tour was merely on the horizon, Kagiso Rabada and Lungi Ngidi loomed as the destroyers.
Both are missing in Durban, yet Marco Jansen and Wiaan Mulder caused Australia just as many problems without Jansen ever really hitting their stride.
It made for an absorbing battle, but for Australia things could actually have been far worse. We must now accept a world order in which the combination of the words "Ollie Robinson" and "Ashes hero" are not just plausible but a distinct possibility.
The consolation is that a Test series is never decided on its opening day and can therefore often be taken with a grain of salt, per Merv Hughes's tinder-dry diary entry following the first day of another Test series, three decades ago:
"Back to hotel. Few beers downstairs, then up to room … Have room service. Watch Cape Fear. Quiet night." Thus ended the day Shane Warne bowled the ball of the century.
Nothing so dramatic transpired this time around but, for Australia, you sense the road ahead will be trying.

Paris court jails Indian man for leading sadist neo-Nazi cult that tortured girls
A 29-year-old Indian man was sentenced to 20 years in prison Friday in a Paris trial over his alleged involvement in an international criminal network that targeted vulnerable children in the US, Britain and Canada and coerced them into producing violent and sexual videos.
A Paris court on Friday sentenced a young Indian man to 20 years in prison for leading a masculinist group that forced young girls, many of them minors, to perform sexual acts and in some cases tortured them.
Prosecutors had sought a 30-year jail term for Rohan Rane, a 29-year-old who they described as a neo-Nazi lover of sadism and macabre ultra-violence.
Most of the dozens of victims of the group led by Rane were American girls, the court was told. Many were aged under 15. Other young male members of the masculinist group were from the United States, India, Germany and New Zealand.
Six of the girls, now aged between 18 and 21, made official complaints. About 20 victims were identified but others could not be contacted, prosecutors said.
After five days of hearings, mainly behind closed doors, the court found Rane guilty of offences, notably extortion committed as part of an organised gang, with the aggravating circumstances of acts of torture and barbarity perpetrated on the victims.
Prosecutors said all of the girls were lured by the "CVLT" group that was driven by nihilism, racism, anti-Semitism, Nazi aesthetics and values, and the hatred of feminists and the LGBTQ+ community.
Read moreThe rise of masculinism: Violence and misogyny online (1/3)
The group became active ahead of the Covid-19 pandemic on the Discord platform with Rane as its leader.
The Indian went to France to study at a commercial school in the southern town of Antibes before becoming a sports coach.
Vulnerable victims were picked out in online forums and persuaded to send nude images. The men threatened to tell their families and school friends if they did not give in to their demands.
According to investigators, many of the girls were black or Jewish and they were forced to engage in sexual acts or to self-harm with knives, including scoring the names of their tormentors or a Nazi swastika into their skin.
The scenes were accompanied by insults and jeers from the men, who called themselves "war lords". One 26-year-old American group member has been jailed in the United States for the 2021 rape of a 12-year-old.
Rane was first arrested in 2021 in France. US authorities passed on information about his leadership in the "CVLT" group and how he had vaunted his desire to fullfil his "sadism".
A US group, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, first rang alarm bells over "CVLT" in 2020 after discovering disturbing images of a 12-year-old online with the name "Rohan" scored into her skin.
The French hearings remained closed following a US request, despite requests from some of the American victims who came forward that a public example be made of Rane's case.
The court was told that threats had been made to the victims, witnesses and even some US prosecutors.
US authorities have indicated that they will seek Rane's extradition once his sentence in France is served.

What happens when house prices fall? Canada and New Zealand offer some clues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:42:08 UTC
04:42:08 KST

Australia's housing downturn is gathering pace, with prices now more than 5 per cent below their peak and forecasts pointing to further falls.
While that may seem like good news for first homebuyers, higher interest rates have done little to improve housing affordability so far. Four rate hikes this year have cut borrowing capacity by about 9 per cent, or $90,000, for a median-income household, according to data analytics company Cotality.
Homeowners and renters are also under pressure. According to Roy Morgan research, more than 32 per cent of borrowers are now at risk of mortgage stress — up 8.4 per cent since January — while the rental market remains tight.
The major banks and analysts are predicting a decline of between 7 and 15 per cent, while United States investment bank Morgan Stanley has forecast the biggest price correction in 40 years.
The broader economic backdrop is also weighing on households. Interest rates are at their highest level in 15 years, while the cost of living crisis and growing fears of recession have kept consumer confidence near historic lows.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But looking across the Tasman to New Zealand and across the Pacific to Canada could provide insight into what lies ahead for Australia's property market.
All three countries have experienced housing crises, marked by unprecedented price booms during the COVID-19 pandemic, housing shortages and affordability pressures.
Since then, Australia has taken a different path. While home values in New Zealand and Canada began falling several years ago, Australia's downturn is only just beginning.
As of the first quarter of 2026, house prices relative–to–incomes had fallen substantially from their COVID-era peak in New Zealand and Canada, while Australia's remained above its pandemic-era high, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.
Australia's ratio, by contrast, is now 4.7 per cent above its COVID-era peak.
Could Australia follow a similar trajectory? And what lessons can be learned from their housing corrections?
New Zealand's housing correction
Across the ditch, average property prices rose 85 per cent between 2010 and 2020, then surged another 44 per cent during the pandemic, peaking at NZ$1.06 million ($1 million) in 2022.
Nick Goodall, head of research at Cotality New Zealand, says the property boom was fuelled by ultra-low interest rates, pandemic support measures and looser lending rules.
He describes the peak as "very artificial", with the market reversing once interest rates started to rise.
To curb post-pandemic inflation, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand lifted its cash rate 12 times in a row to 5.5 per cent by May 2023.
By comparison, Australia's cash rate peaked at 4.35 per cent in November 2023.
New Zealand then entered recession in 2023, as higher interest rates weighed on demand and the labour market weakened, contributing to about an 18 per cent decline in property values from their peak over 18 months.
Prices have remained broadly flat since.
But affordability has begun improving as interest rates have fallen, following nine consecutive rate cuts from mid-2024.
Cotality data shows the national value-to-income ratio, which measures how many years of household income are needed to buy a median-priced home, fell from a peak of 9.8 in late 2021 to 6.7 in the second quarter of 2026.
Goodall says a more useful measure is the median gross household income needed to service a mortgage, with now sits at 40 per cent, down from a peak of above 50 per cent in late 2021 and below the long-term average of 42 per cent.
Supply and planning reforms have also played a role, particularly in Auckland, where changes allowed greater housing density.
"Enabling more properties to be built on the same area of land that was available previously for only one property, certainly has led to less growth or maybe a greater decline [in prices]," Goodall tells SBS News.
First homebuyers accounted for 29 per cent of sales in the most recent quarter, the highest proportion since Cotality started tracking the data in 2003.
Rental affordability has also improved, with rents 1.8 per cent lower in 2025 than a year earlier — the first annual decline in a decade, according to Realestate.co.nz.
[Renters have] got less competition out there, so they can take their time. They know they've got the power in their hands because there's high supply.
Meanwhile, investors have been squeezed by higher ownership costs, weaker expectations of capital gains, and softer rental returns as housing supply increased and population growth slowed.
"[Property investors] can make it work, but it's definitely not the easy game it used to be when interest rates were really low," Goodall says.
Canada's housing correction
In Canada, home prices surged more than 50 per cent during the COVID-19 pandemic, before falling about 20 per cent from their early-2022 peak.
The boom was fuelled by very low interest rates and a shift towards larger suburban homes as lockdowns and remote work changed where people wanted to live.
The Bank of Canada lifted the cash rate from 0.25 per cent in March 2022 to 5 per cent in July 2023, with prices starting to fall sharply later that year before declining more gradually.
Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada, says while the correction offered some relief, prices remained far higher than before the pandemic and housing remained particularly unaffordable in cities such as Toronto and Vancouver.
"If you ask ordinary Canadians, it's still unaffordable in many parts of Canada … it's just that it's less unaffordable than it was just a couple years ago," he tells SBS News.
He says Canada's cash rate, which has been at 2.25 per cent since October last year, which he expected to rise in the year ahead, while slower economic growth could weigh on wage growth, meaning affordability is unlikely to improve anytime soon.
A surge in post-pandemic migration added significantly to housing demand, with Canada adding more than 1.2 million people through permanent and temporary migration in 2023 alone.
The Canadian government subsequently moved to reduce migration pressure, cutting temporary resident arrivals by about 43 per cent.
It also aimed to slash permanent migration from a previous target of 500,000 to 395,000 last year, with further reductions in the years to follow.
Hogue says curbing temporary immigration had cooled the rental market.
Data from rentals.ca this month show asking rents across Canada were down 4.2 per cent year-over-year, marking the 24th consecutive month of decline.
But Hogue says the drop in demand had a spillover effect, with condo developers launching fewer projects because of lower returns and higher building costs.
He says that could be a problem when migration picks up again.
"This is a big concern for those like me thinking ahead in three or four-or five-years' time."
What Australia can learn
New Zealand has seen housing affordability improve, while Canada continues to face significant affordability pressures.
To understand what that means for Australia, it's worth first examining why its housing market took a different path from Canada and New Zealand.
Australia's pandemic housing boom was less pronounced than those of New Zealand and Canada, with prices rising about 25 per cent between April 2020 and February 2022, according to Cotality.
After an initial fall, however, Australian property prices recovered and continued rising until reaching a new peak in March 2026. They have since fallen for six consecutive months, leaving prices 5.2 per cent below their peak.
Despite the decline, housing affordability has reached a record low on realestate.com.au's measure, with a typical-income household able to afford just 12 per cent of homes across Australia.
Independent economist Saul Eslake says Australia's downturn is only beginning this year partly because governments have until recently supported the housing market through cash grants and other schemes.
He points out Canada and New Zealand did not intervene in the same way.
Eslake also notes Australia's unemployment rate, currently 4.6 per cent, is lower than Canada's 6.4 per cent and New Zealand's 5.6 per cent, reducing pressure on households to sell and, in turn, on property prices.
While Australia's cash rate of 4.6 per cent is currently higher than New Zealand's 2.75 per cent and Canada's 2.25 per cent, Eslake notes that differences in cash rates do not necessarily translate into an equivalent difference in mortgage rates.
Canadian mortgages are often fixed for five years, with many rates until recently higher than Australian variable mortgage rates. New Zealand floating variable rates have also often sat around Australian rates, despite the country have a lower cash rate.
Eslake points out New Zealand's population growth had been slower than Australia's, partly because many New Zealanders moved across the Tasman in search of better economic opportunities, while Canada introduced measures to curb temporary migration several years ago.
The federal government only announced tightened temporary migration rules last month, while the Coalition and One Nation have promised deeper cuts.
"Cuts in the immigration intake, depending on how large they are, and depending on what categories of migrants they fall on, could reduce the demand for housing," Eslake says.
Eslake estimates a 10 to 15 per cent decline in house prices over two years could improve affordability, while warning a sharper fall would harm the economy.
But for affordability to become the priority, he says there needs to be a fundamental shift in how housing is treated.
Australians have increasingly come to think about housing as a vehicle for, to use the common politician's phrase that I hate, ‘a means of getting ahead', without, of course, ever asking the question ahead of whom?
"To which the answer is your own children and grandchildren. In other words, we've come to think of housing as a vehicle for wealth accumulation, rather than a vehicle for providing basic human needs."
Even now, Eslake says governments have been reluctant to frame policy, such as changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax which have cooled investor demand, as an effort to make housing more affordable.
"We have consciously sought to reduce investor demand for established housing, in order to make housing cheaper for first-home buyers, in other words, to make housing more affordable," Eslake says.
"But they haven't said that. They have run away from it … they are still captured by the idea that the main purpose of housing is a vehicle for accumulating wealth rather than meeting basic human needs."
New Zealand economist Shamubeel Eaqub argues that changing this mindset may be just as difficult as changing housing policy.
New Zealand's experience, he says, has shown that people can become so accustomed to rising house prices that accepting a different path becomes a major psychological barrier.
"When house prices are rising, I think it's very easy to kind of focus on the fact that we're just wealthier and it's just easy," he tells SBS News.
But the real work of an economy is actually much harder in terms of how we create good businesses, good jobs, good quality of life, and those wider competitive and policy settings that are good for society.

Ukraine’s prices experienced a sharp increase compared to last month, as the economy faced pressure from higher logistics, water supply and food costs, the State Statistics Service reported Oct. 9.
Ukraine’s consumer inflation rose 2.1% in September compared with August, by far the sharpest monthly increase this year, pushing annual consumer inflation to double digits at 10.0% from 8.1%.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and administratively regulated prices, also jumped 2.0% on the month, accelerating to 8.8% year-on-year from 8.1% in August. The figures broke a three-month stretch in which the core rate had held flat. This stickiness had previously worried Ukraine’s central bank, but now prices are spiking instead of falling toward the central bank’s target.
The State Statistics Service published its latest report on Oct. 9.
Graph by Olena Hrazhdan/Flourish
War in the Middle East puts additional pressure on prices in Ukraine
The war in the Middle East is still making logistics prices spike, affecting inflation, and creating additional pressure on the war-battered Ukrainian economy.
The annual rate of fuel and lubricants climbed to 46.2% from 38.7% year-on-year in August. Transport services cost 36% more than a year earlier, up from 35.9% in August. Road passenger transport prices rose 39% annually, while rail passenger fares increased 19.2%.
Sybiha Presses WTO Chief on Black Sea Shipping, Remote Audits
Ukraine’s Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport implemented a 30% increase in Ukrzaliznytsia freight tariffs effective Aug. 1, but the state-owned company still keeps consumer tariffs low despite heavy losses caused by Russia destroying locomotives.
Food prices reverse course
Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose 1.9% in September from August, reversing the 1.3% decline the month before, and their annual rate accelerated to 8.9% from 6.0%. This marks the seasonal trend of prices rising slightly, when the new harvest arrives in summer and Ukraine heads toward autumn and winter.
Eggs stood out in the food basket, jumping 43.6% on the month after a 4.0% rise in August. Their annual trajectory flipped due to a base effect, swinging to a 12.2% increase from an annual decline a month earlier. Sugar also accelerated sharply, up 8.3% in September compared with 2.2% in August. Milk, meat and fish rose no more that 3% in September.
Fruit and vegetables slowed their price fall after the summer harvest, falling 5.7% and 2.3% respectively, though both declines were less sharp than August’s seasonal plunge of 12.0% and 18.3%.
Education increases by 20% while local authorities keep pushing water tariffs up
This year’s water tariff revisions are pushing up utility prices: water supply is now up 87.6% year-on-year and sewerage 83.1%, both accelerating from August’s already elevated annual rates of 77.6% and 73.6%.
Education costs rose 17.4% on the month, by far the largest increase in any category, driven by a 23.3% jump in higher education costs and a 14.3% rise in secondary education. The category’s annual rate climbed to 19.6% from 14.6% in August.
Alcohol and tobacco prices rose 17.2% in September, roughly matching August’s pace.

EU vows to protect ICC as Europe condemns US sanctions plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:34:47 UTC
04:34:47 KST

The EU has called the US announcement of imposing sanctions on the International Criminal Court "deeply regrettable," reaffirming its commitment to protecting the court's independence and operations.
"The European Union has been a constant supporter of the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is deeply regrettable that the United States has announced intentions to impose sanctions," the European Commission said in a statement on Friday.
The bloc pledged to work closely with the court to ensure it could continue operating effectively.
It also said it would cooperate with all 125 states party to the Rome Statute, the court's founding treaty, to safeguard its independence and "vital mission."
Noting that the sanctions would not take effect for another six months, the EU said there was still an opportunity for dialogue with Washington.
Backlash from Europe
Several European countries condemned the move, reaffirming their support for the court's independence and its role in prosecuting serious international crimes.
Denmark, Sweden, Austria and Portugal joined the EU, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands in criticising Washington's decision.
"Denmark profoundly disagrees with the USA's decision to impose sanctions against the ICC, which will have enormous consequences for the court's work and for the investigation of the most serious international crimes," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said on X.
"Denmark confirms its unwavering support for the ICC," he added.
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said Stockholm regretted the US decision, stressing that Sweden and the EU stood firmly behind the court's role in ensuring accountability and justice for victims.
"Multilateralism and international institutions for ensuring accountability are needed more than ever at a time when violations of international law continue to cause immense suffering," she said.
Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger described the sanctions as "another stage of escalation," saying they also called into question the sovereignty of states that established the court.
"We condemn these sanctions in the strongest possible terms," she said, pledging continued efforts by Austria and its partners to protect the court and its staff.
"Especially small states like Austria rely on international law applying to everyone, regardless of how large or powerful a state may be," she added.
Portugal also condemned the sanctions, saying they undermined the independent exercise of international justice and efforts to combat impunity for serious crimes.
It stressed that institutions defending international law must be able to fulfil their mandates without pressure or interference.
ICC rejects sanctions as 'assault on rule of law'
The ICC strongly rejected the sanctions, describing them as an attempt to obstruct justice and an "assault on the rule of law."
Court President Tomoko Akane said the institution would continue its work "with independence and impartiality."
The EU described Washington's announcement as "deeply regrettable" and said it was prepared to take measures to protect the court's operations.
The bloc also said the six-month period before the sanctions take effect offered an opportunity for dialogue.
European Council President Antonio Costa stressed that international justice must be defended, saying lasting peace required accountability.
Costa said the EU would take appropriate steps to protect the ICC and continue supporting the court and the Rome Statute system through political, diplomatic, financial and practical means.
Belgium called for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court and those supporting its work.
Switzerland said it opposed "sanctions, threats or other measures" aimed at undermining the ICC's independence.
The Netherlands described the sanctions as an "undesirable new escalation" and pledged continued support for the court as its host country.
The reactions followed an announcement of sanctions against the ICC by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Rubio said President Donald Trump would not allow the court to prosecute Americans and threatened to "end the ICC" unless it stopped what he described as its "threats."

Thieves steal 30,000 bottles of wine in Italy's largest-ever heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

04:33:46 KST

Thieves steal 30,000 bottles of Italy's most prized wines in $5.8 million heist
Thieves stole about 30,000 bottles of some of Italy's most prized wines worth an estimated $5.8 million from a winery in Tuscany, in what the producer described Friday as the country's largest wine theft on record.
The theft targeted Marchesi Antinori's facility near Cortona, in the province of Arezzo, where a group of at least seven thieves on Saturday night made off with bottles of some of Italy's most sought-after wines.
Chief Executive Renzo Cotarella said the thieves disabled the winery's alarm system and surveillance cameras before entering with two large trucks. Using the company's forklifts, they loaded the vehicles with wine and fled during the night.
"It is certainly a very well-prepared gang," Cotarella said, adding that it may be the same group that has targeted other Italian wineries in recent months. "A theft of this size and value has never occurred in Italy."
Wine Spectator reported that in July, 3,300 bottles were stolen from the renowned Italian producer Castello Banfi.
Cotarella received the 2026 Winemakers' Winemaker Award from the Institute of Masters of Wine, and the winery is well known for producing Italy's most renowned vintages.
Thieves made off with wines, including bottles of Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. The theft was discovered Monday, but the company made it public on Friday to avoid interfering with the investigation.
The stolen bottles were all from the 2023 vintage and are typically sold at a retail price of between 150 euros (approximately $168) and 500 euros each ($560). They included about 10,000 bottles of Solaia, one of Antinori's flagship wines, from what Cotarella described as an exceptional year.
The company, founded in 1385 and run by the Antinori family for 26 generations, said it was alerting customers worldwide to be wary of offers outside official sales channels.
"We are informing our clients around the world and asking them to pay attention to any offers outside the official channels," Cotarella said.
Authorities are investigating how the stolen wine may be sold. Police and Carabinieri officers are examining surveillance footage and other evidence. Cotarella said he remained confident investigators could trace the shipment, noting that two truckloads of wine would be difficult to move without attracting attention.
The theft eclipses previous high-profile wine robberies in Italy. In 2017, thieves stole about 2,000 bottles of rare wines valued at 750,000 euros — about $840,045 — from a warehouse near the Adriatic resort town of Cervia.

European states, Canada, Japan and UN back ICC against US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:32:13 UTC
04:32:13 KST

European states, Canada, Japan and UN back ICC against US sanctions
Several US allies call to ‘defend’ and ‘protect’ the ICC following Washington’s decision to sanction the judiciary body.
The United States has imposed a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), prompting several countries – including US allies – to condemn the move and reiterate their support for the world’s war crimes tribunal.
On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington would be banning transactions with the “rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate”, adding that President Donald Trump would “never allow” the Hague to prosecute Americans.
The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.
The US Treasury Department announced the penalties with a six-month initial grace period and other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecommunications, software, pension payments and transactions related to detainees.
Rubio said the sanctions would give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns and would be adjusted if they did not meet those demands.
The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members, such as Israel. The United States and Israel have never joined the court.
In response to the sanctions, the ICC said that the move was an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order”. It called on its 125 member states to defend the institution.
“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC said in a statement. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment.”
The Trump administration sanctioned more than a dozen judges and prosecutors before issuing sanctions on the court itself Friday.
Allies ‘regret and disagree’ with US move
Soon after the US announcement, top United Nations officials condemned the move.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed” by the expected impact of the sanctions on the court as a whole, particularly its ability to carry out its mandate, a statement from his spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.
“Today’s decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar,” the statement added.
UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk called for immediate measures to protect the ICC. “These sanctions – the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel for the work they do every day to advance accountability for the very worst violations of human rights – are unacceptable,” he said.
ICC member states that are US allies also expressed dismay at the decision.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, whose country hosts the ICC, said the US’s decision was “deeply regrettable”.
“We will stand firm in defence of the court. At the same time, it’s important to note that the sanctions will not take effect immediately and that service providers can continue to work for the ICC. The six-month period before the sanctions take effect creates scope for dialogue,” he said.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan said they “regret and strongly disagree” with the sanctions.
“If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families … We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties,” they said.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot also said Brussels would discuss support for the ICC with European Union foreign affairs colleagues on Monday and at the upcoming European Council.
“We will press for concrete protection. The court’s independence cannot depend on whom it investigates. Europe must act. Belgium is calling for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court,” Prevot said.
US aims to ‘ultimately destroy’ ICC
Similarly, organisations and rights groups sounded the alarm over the implications of the US decision.
Philippe Bolopion, executive director of US-based Human Rights Watch, said the Trump administration had made clear its aim to “destroy” the ICC and “shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court”.
“The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, is above the law. Governments that value human rights and accountability should condemn this outrageous move and take swift action to protect the ICC, its staff, and all those who cooperate with it, starting with the European Union using its laws to mitigate the sanctions’ impact in the region,” he said.
The Executive Director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, James Goldston, said the sanctions were a “calculated attack on the rule of law and the principles of judicial independence and equality that underpin it.”
“This is the latest move in a campaign of coercion intended to destroy the system of international justice,” he said.
Amnesty International called on countries to “resist”. Trump’s “sanctions are designed to isolate and ultimately destroy the International Criminal Court”, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty’s senior director for research, policy, advocacy and campaigns, said in a statement. “This existential attack must fail. States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures.”
Amid widespread criticism, Israel commended the US move.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed the sanctions and praised Trump and Rubio for taking this “critical decision”.
“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” Netanyahu wrote on X.
In 2024 the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on war crimes and crimes against humanity charges for the war on Gaza.

The Defense Department, which President Donald Trump calls the War Department, is barred from providing research funding to any entity that works with Chinese universities on the list. It calls collaboration with listed schools "a compliance risk" that puts US federal funding at risk.
The department in August said it would investigate 30 US schools around whether they collaborate with Chinese institutions on the 1286 list.
Among the schools Moolenaar asked the Defense Department to include is Tsinghua University, a top Chinese school that has educated many of the country's business and political elite.
Some US business leaders, including the chief executives of Nvidia, Apple and Advanced Micro Devices, serve on the advisory board at Tsinghua's business school, postings that are meant to foster ties between US and Chinese companies.
Nvidia declined to comment, and Tsinghua, Apple and AMD did not respond to a request for comment. REUTERS
