Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russian attacks on civilian vessels, sailors, and Ukrainian ports in the Black Sea pose a threat to global food supply chains. The security of shipping must be restored without delay,” Sybiha said, adding that Kyiv is counting on WTO’s support to achieve a just peace.
Ports under constant pressure
While the Black Sea ports and their maritime corridor technically remain open, reciprocal strikes between Russia and Ukraine have increased in recent months, making food shipping severely dangerous and effectively functioning as a blockade.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, at least 274 civilian vessels and 1,173 port infrastructure facilities have been damaged or partially destroyed, Ukraine’s Ministry for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport reported on Sept. 14.
US Congress Delegation Backs Expanded Starlink Access for Ukraine
Since then, the escalation has continued and increased, with Russia consistently targeting foreign-flagged civilian vessels heading towards Ukrainian ports. Drone incursions and violation of EU members have also increased, particularly in Romania and Turkey.

With sea routes under attack, Sybiha said, opening new markets for Ukrainian agricultural products has become especially important, and remote audits could be key to that effort.
According to the Foreign Minister, Ukraine had developed unique experience with the tool during the war and has agreed with the EU, UK and Canada to apply it in practice.
This could “make global agricultural trade more resilient,” he said. In remote audits, foreign regulators can review a country’s food safety controls without having to travel there for an on-site inspection.
Sybiha reiterated that Ukraine is ready to advance and promote, within the WTO, “an international standard for conducting remote audits and inspections and for recognizing their results.”
He appealed to Okonjo-Iweala for help towards building support for the initiative among other WTO members, subsequently expressing gratitude to the WTO chief for “an open and constructive exchange of views.”

Training workshop helps Kermanshah artisans explore Iraq’s handicrafts market

Training workshop helps Kermanshah artisans explore Iraq’s handicrafts market
TEHRAN- Nearly 50 handicraft artists and practitioners in Iran’s western Kermanshah province have attended a training session on exporting their products to Iraq, as part of efforts to expand international markets for locally made traditional crafts.
The workshop, titled “Handicraft Exports to Iraq,” was organized by the Handicrafts Department of the Kermanshah Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Office in cooperation with Madaen International, an export accelerator company, CHTN reported on Friday.
Amin Kogani, deputy head of handicrafts in Kermanshah province, said the development of new markets and sales channels for handicrafts was among the department’s main priorities.
He noted that Iraq, due to its geographical proximity and existing market potential, offers promising opportunities for Kermanshah’s artisans to introduce their products to international customers.
During the session, participants learned about the characteristics and potential of Iraq’s handicrafts market, marketing and sales strategies, requirements for entering foreign markets, and practical procedures for exporting their products to the neighboring country.
Kogani emphasized that producing high-quality handicrafts alone was not sufficient to ensure success in international markets. Artisans also need to understand their target markets, consumer preferences, marketing techniques, packaging standards, sales channels and export regulations.
He added that specialized training sessions could strengthen the commercial knowledge of artisans and producers while helping bridge the gap between production and access to markets.
The provincial handicrafts official said the department sought to support both the production of traditional crafts and the preservation of their authenticity, while creating more opportunities for local artisans to promote and sell their work in domestic and international markets.
He described Iraq not merely as a nearby destination for Kermanshah’s handicrafts, but also as a potential gateway for expanding exports and introducing the province’s artistic and cultural capabilities to a wider audience.
The workshop also focused on practical ways for artisans to enter the Iraqi market, enabling participants to pursue marketing, sales and export opportunities with a better understanding of the requirements involved.
The initiative reflects broader efforts to strengthen the commercial capacity of Iran’s handicrafts sector by combining traditional production skills with professional marketing and export training.
Iran is home to a rich variety of handicrafts shaped by its diverse regional cultures, centuries-old artistic traditions and locally available materials. Persian carpets and kilims, pottery and ceramics, metalwork, woodcarving, traditional textiles, enamelwork, miniature painting and inlaid woodwork are among the country’s best-known crafts. These products represent not only artistic skills passed down through generations but also an important part of Iran’s cultural heritage and creative economy.
The handicrafts sector has considerable potential to generate employment, support small businesses and create income opportunities, particularly for women and rural communities. Unlike many industrial products, traditional crafts often rely on specialized skills and distinctive regional designs, giving them cultural and artistic value in international markets. Expanding their commercial reach can therefore contribute both to economic development and to the preservation of traditional knowledge.
Export development, however, requires more than producing distinctive and high-quality goods. Access to international markets depends on identifying customer preferences, adapting product presentation to different markets, ensuring suitable packaging and shipping, developing recognizable brands and establishing reliable distribution channels. Digital marketing and e-commerce can also help artisans reach overseas customers directly, reducing their dependence on traditional intermediaries.
Neighboring countries, including Iraq, offer potential opportunities for Iranian handicrafts because of geographical proximity and longstanding cultural and commercial connections. For provinces such as Kermanshah, these links can provide a starting point for developing cross-border trade, establishing business partnerships and introducing local products to new customers. Training artisans in export procedures, pricing, market research and international sales can help turn this potential into sustainable business opportunities.
Strengthening cooperation between handicraft producers, export companies, trade organizations and cultural institutions could further improve the sector’s competitiveness. By combining the authenticity of traditional Iranian craftsmanship with modern business practices, Iran can broaden the international reach of its handicrafts while supporting artisans, preserving cultural heritage and creating new sources of income.

The illusion of control in Washington’s Iran gamble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:50:03 UTC
03:50:03 KST

The illusion of control in Washington’s Iran gamble
TEHRAN — Gore Vidal’s famous observation that the United States is a nation of amnesia, learning nothing because it remembers nothing, was never merely a witty aside. It was a prophecy dressed as satire. Washington has spent decades proving him right.
Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya each arrived with their own vocabulary of justification, carefully packaged as liberation, security or necessity. Now American power may move toward Iran again, while Yemen may become another front in a conflict Washington claims it can manage.
The pattern is familiar: military superiority creates confidence at the beginning, while political control proves far more elusive afterward.
The same script, a different stage
Washington speaks of “pressure” and “diplomacy” in the same breath, as though sanctions, military threats and economic coercion constitute genuine negotiation.
Iran, however, is not Iraq. After decades of sanctions, pressure and confrontation, Tehran has built a strategy designed for endurance rather than surrender.
Its military capabilities are dispersed and hardened, while its geography is vast, mountainous, and strategically difficult.
Yemen: The warning Washington should not ignore
Yemen provides a powerful warning. Saudi Arabia, supported by Western arms and assistance, entered the war in 2015 expecting military pressure to produce a decisive outcome.
Years later, the conflict had become a prolonged catastrophe, while Ansarallah demonstrated resilience and retained the ability to challenge their opponents.
For Washington, the lesson should be obvious. Opening another front against an adversary such as Iran would create consequences that cannot be neatly contained.
Where regional war becomes global crisis
The Strait of Hormuz turns the confrontation into an international economic problem. Any serious disruption immediately affects oil markets, shipping costs, insurance rates, and supply chains far beyond the Persian Gulf.
Recent reductions in commercial traffic demonstrate how quickly geopolitical confrontation can become an economic shock. Iran’s ability to influence access to Hormuz gives Tehran leverage that cannot simply be neutralized by deploying more military hardware.
This is the contradiction Washington repeatedly overlooks. Governments make strategic decisions inside secure rooms, but the economic consequences escape those rooms almost immediately.
A military confrontation in Iran means higher fuel prices in America, rising transport costs in Europe, and increased inflation across Asian markets.
The trap of coercive pressure
Washington’s strategy appears to rest on the belief that enough pressure will eventually force Iran to abandon its strategic position and accept terms dictated by its adversaries. Yet decades of sanctions have produced a different response: adaptation.
Iran has expanded alternative trade relationships and strengthened its position within emerging Eurasian transport and economic networks. The International North-South Transport Corridor, connecting India, Iran and Russia, has gained greater strategic importance as states seek alternatives to Western-dominated routes.
Iran’s geography, energy resources and transport infrastructure also make it significant to China’s wider Eurasian connectivity.
This does not mean Beijing, Moscow and Tehran constitute a formal military alliance. They do not. But sustained pressure has encouraged greater cooperation among countries seeking to reduce dependence on Western systems.
That is the paradox of coercion. Pressure intended to isolate an adversary can encourage it to build new partnerships, new routes and new forms of resilience.
Diplomacy is not surrender
The most dangerous assumption is that another application of military force will somehow produce a different political result from previous wars.
A wider confrontation with Iran would be difficult to contain. Strikes on Iranian military facilities provoke retaliation against American and allied interests across the region.
Attacks affecting energy infrastructure damage the very economic networks on which global markets depend.
Disruption in Hormuz, combined with instability around the Red Sea, intensifies pressure on energy and shipping markets and deepens an already fragile global economy.
Diplomacy is not weakness. Negotiation is not surrender. They are recognition that some conflicts cannot be solved by destroying enough infrastructure, and that military superiority does not guarantee political control.
The human cost of the gamble
Behind every military calculation are people who never made the decisions that put them at risk. Families in Tehran and Sanaa do not write speeches in Washington, yet they absorb the consequences.
Washington can launch the first missile, but it cannot dictate everything that follows. It cannot guarantee that escalation will remain limited, that retaliation will stop at a chosen point, or that economic blowback will stay overseas.
That is the illusion at the heart of modern interventionism: believing that superior firepower is equivalent to control. It is not.
Iran is not Iraq, and the Persian Gulf is not a battlefield that can be entered, dominated, and forgotten.
Washington may think it is gambling with Iran, but Iran is not a wager that can be settled by overwhelming firepower. Tehran has spent decades preparing to endure pressure, adapt to isolation, and resist attempts at coercion.
The real danger is not simply what America can destroy. It is what America cannot control once the destruction begins.
The choice is not between war and surrender. It is between diplomacy and hubris. Washington should understand the difference before another gamble turns into a catastrophe no power can contain.
Washington may think it is gambling with Iran, but Iran is not the kind of opponent a superpower can threaten into submission; it is the kind that can turn America’s gamble into its greatest strategic reckoning.
The article does not necessarily represent the views of the Tehran Times.

Air-raid sirens cost Kyiv’s weapons makers 61.8 working hours in month, nearly eight days, yet their contract deadlines stay fixed, two groups say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:49:16 UTC
03:49:16 KST

Air-raid sirens are quietly stealing the hours Ukraine needs to build its weapons. The alerts ate up 61.8 hours of the standard work schedule in Kyiv between 27 August and 29 September, almost eight working days in a little over a month, yet weapons makers still face unchanged contract deadlines, the Ukrainian Gunmakers Council and the League of Defense Enterprises of Ukraine say.
In September 2026, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said that every hour of air-raid alerts costs Ukraine’s economy about $45 million as businesses halt and workers shelter. For arms makers, those lost hours collide with fixed delivery dates and the penalties that follow if they slip.
The council’s figure covers Kyiv alone, and each plant loses more depending on its location, schedule, and processes, the groups said. On top of the siren time comes the wait to shut equipment down safely, move workers to shelter, and restart once the all-clear sounds.
A missed deadline carries a daily fine, and after 30 days, an extra 7 percent penalty. Money meant for components and the next orders goes instead to penalties and court disputes.
A rule that ignores the sirens
The contract date stays fixed unless the customer agrees to move it, the groups said. That leaves producers paying for stoppages they do not control, while the weapons still have to ship.
The Gunmakers Council has drafted changes to Cabinet Resolution No. 1275 to establish a single method for confirming real downtime from alerts and its effect on each contract’s deadline, it said. A customer could check alert times against official data and verify stoppages and restarts against a plant’s own production records, with each request judged on a case-by-case basis.
Waiting on the ministry
The groups say they have repeatedly raised the issue with the Defense Ministry and sent official letters proposing changes, and they are urging the ministry and the Defense Procurement Agency to act without delay.
They want a defined list of supporting documents, a deadline for reviewing requests, and rules for applying the mechanism to contracts that have already been signed. Until a decision comes, enterprises keep losing production time, and the risk of delay grows, the groups say.

Why Afghanistan’s Neighbors Have Not Backed Pakistan’s Strikes on the Taliban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:48:00 UTC
03:48:00 KST

On October 5, Moscow hosted the eighth meeting of the special representatives and senior officials from regional countries for the Moscow Format to discuss political and economic relations with Afghanistan and counterterrorism and counter-narcotics cooperation. The Moscow Format includes Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
But the meeting failed to adopt a joint statement because the Pakistani and Afghan delegates disagreed over the language on terrorism. The Taliban objected to the frequent mention of terrorism in reference to Afghanistan.
Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said the Afghan delegates accepted similar language last year. He believed that the changed relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan might have caused Kabul’s objection this time.
The meeting was held only a week after the most recent confrontation between Islamabad and Kabul. On September 18 and 26, Pakistan suffered deadly terrorist attacks in its northwestern province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, that together killed about 44 people and injured about 138. Pakistan responded with airstrikes on different targets in Afghanistan that it believes were the training camps and hideouts of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its associated factions responsible for the cross-border attacks.
At the Moscow summit, Pakistan’s delegation said the Taliban were complicit in those attacks in Pakistan because the terrorist groups were operating on Afghan soil with impunity. The Taliban said Pakistan was using military aggression in violation of international law for an issue that could be resolved through political negotiations.
The Moscow Format meeting failed to bridge these differences enough to allow for a joint communique. What’s noteworthy is that other countries that share borders with Afghanistan – such as China, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – did not use their diplomatic capital to reach an understanding on language that included everyone’s concerns.
Afghanistan’s neighbors have different levels of concern about militancy there. Their strategies, especially on counterterrorism, are a function of the nature of their border with Afghanistan, the extent of the threat from militant groups on Afghan soil, and the Taliban’s scale of cooperation regarding those groups. From their perspective, military force is not the most effective solution to address the issue.
China shares a border of only about 92 kilometers with Afghanistan, high in the Wakhan Corridor, marked by rough terrain and the nearly 5,000-meter high Wakhjir Pass. In terms of a terrorist presence in Afghanistan, Beijing considers the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) its main concern and has pressed the Taliban to act against the group. The Taliban have reportedly relocated ETIM fighters away from the border, and they now have a dispersed presence. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat to China is smaller, and any movement across the pass is easy to detect.
Uzbekistan similarly shares a short border of 144 kilometers with Afghanistan, almost entirely along the Amu Darya. Regular cross-border movement is concentrated at the closely guarded Termez-Hairatan road and rail crossing. But the militant groups in Afghanistan that concern Tashkent have shown only a limited capacity for cross-border attacks. There was one incident in 2022 of rockets being fired toward Termez, which didn’t cause any casualties. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat is relatively small and easier to contain.
Tajikistan’s case is closer to Pakistan’s in terms of the long border and threat. Dushanbe shares about 1,374 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, much of which runs along the Panj River and passes through remote and mountainous territory and is difficult to monitor consistently. The cross-border threat therefore needs more immediate attention. In November 2025, two cross-border attacks from Afghanistan’s Badakhshan province killed five Chinese workers in Tajikistan.
As for Taliban cooperation, Kabul has offered these countries help in investigations and has arrested suspects after cross-border attacks.
Pakistan’s case is of a different magnitude on all these counts.
Pakistan shares 2,640 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, where Pashtun and Baloch communities live on both sides. Afghanistan has never recognized the border since Pakistan’s founding. Islamabad has been fencing it since 2017, but militants continue to cross it. A disputed frontier with kinship networks on both sides gives militants far more routes and tricks to enter Pakistan than Afghanistan’s northern borders offer.
Pakistan also faces a much larger threat. Its key concerns are the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), and the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). Islamabad charges that all three groups have a presence in Afghanistan, especially the TTP. U.N. monitors estimate the TTP, which has carried out the most frequent and lethal attacks in Pakistan, has about 6,000 fighters in Afghanistan.
By September 2026, Pakistan’s terrorism situation had worsened sharply, with 1,232 militant attacks in nine months, already 169 attacks above those recorded in all of 2025. Consistent attacks on this scale raise domestic pressure to take firm action.
Moreover, the Taliban have shown limited willingness to cooperate with Pakistan on the issue of militant groups. The Taliban leadership describes TTP members as Pakistani refugees and refuses to classify them as militants. U.N. monitors report that the group enjoys greater liberty and support from Taliban authorities. Kabul has offered to relocate the TTP fighters away from the Pakistani border, but that step cannot stop the militant movement through the long and porous border with Pakistan.
Pakistan has, therefore, asked for written guarantees that the militants would not use Afghan soil as a base for attacks in Pakistan. The Taliban have rejected this demand, which was why the Istanbul talks failed in November 2025.
Pakistan has said its operations will continue until the Taliban take verifiable action against militant groups on Afghan soil. Yet none of Afghanistan’s neighbors has publicly supported Pakistan’s airstrikes. China, Russia, and Iran have called for restraint and offered to mediate, and Uzbekistan urged a diplomatic resolution. China hosted informal talks in Urumqi in April but those ended without agreement.
Whether in Urumqi or more recently in Moscow, repeated efforts at finding common ground have fallen flat. While none of Afghanistan’s neighbors is comfortable with the idea of cross-border terrorism, none of them has sanctioned Pakistan’s military retaliation, either.

Only 2 other countries hold public executions as U.S. plans first in 90 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:47:45 UTC
03:47:45 KST

Only 2 countries held known public executions last year. The U.S. is preparing for its first in 90 years.
When Nidal Hasan is put to death by firing squad during a public livestream, he will become the first person to be publicly executed in the United States in nearly a century.
The Defense Department announced Thursday the execution of Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted in the 2009 killings of 13 people at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed on Dec. 3. Hasan is paralyzed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair after being shot in the back by police who responded to the mass shooting.
"He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Jack Posobiec on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
The decision has generated widespread, bipartisan criticism.
The list of countries that still carry out public executions, whether on video or in a public place, is very short and almost entirely countries accused of human rights violations.
Afghanistan and Iran are the only two known countries to execute anyone publicly in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, according to Amnesty International. Yemen publicly executed multiple people in 2021, according to the group.
"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Republican Sen. Thom Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."
History of public executions in U.S.
Two public executions in the mid-1930s are considered to be the last public uses of the death penalty in the United States.
The last large-scale example of a public execution in the United States was Rainey Bethea in 1936. The crowd on hand to watch the hanging was estimated at 20,000 people, according to a local newspaper at the time.
Bethea was accused of raping and murdering a 70-year-old woman in her home in Owensboro, Kentucky, in June 1936. He accidentally left his recognizable prison ring at the scene, and confessed to the crime several times, though he did recant during a failed appeal.
He was never convicted of murder, only rape, which still carried the death penalty. Bethea, who was 26 years old, was hanged on Aug. 14, 1936.
A year later, Roscoe "Red" Jackson was executed in Galena, Missouri, also by hanging. He was convicted of killing a traveling salesman and stealing his car after being picked up by the victim as a hitchhiker.
The crowd for Jackson's execution was much smaller, since it was not held in the public streets of the city like Bethea's hanging.
"Just how many were inside is not known, though it is thought the space would accommodate at least 400 people," wrote the authors of an article on the execution from the local Stone County News-Oracle.
"Executions shouldn't be public spectacle," Human Rights Watch interim U.S. Program Director Michael Bochenek told CBS News in a statement. "The death penalty is a relic of an inhumane past and should be abolished once and for all."
Public executions in Iran
Iran, which the United States has accused of gross human rights violations, is one of the most prolific users of public executions in the world currently. The U.S. and Iran are also locked in a war, and President Trump has routinely cited Iran's executions of protesters as a reason the regime deserved to be deposed.
At least 24 people were publicly executed in Iran from 2022 to 2025, according to Amnesty International.
Fifty-nine people were executed this year in Iran between March 18 and Aug. 31, including dozens who took part in anti-government protests earlier this year, according to Human Rights Watch. Five of those executions have been public, the organization said.
While not capital punishment, thousands of protesters were also killed by government troops opening fire on those demonstrations.
In late February, eight days before launching strikes against Iran, Mr. Trump said he had threatened military action against Iran if they publicly executed hundreds of people.
"They were going to hang 837 people, and I gave them the word, if you hang one person, even one person, that you're going to be hit right then and there," Mr. Trump said. "I wasn't waiting two weeks and negotiating. And they gave up the hanging. They didn't hang 837, supposedly they didn't hang anybody."
Public executions in Afghanistan
Afghanistan has publicly executed at least 12 people since 2022, according to Amnesty International, though its reports note there were possibly more.
Public executions in Afghanistan have spiked since the Taliban swept back into power in August 2021. Executions have even been carried out in front of thousands of onlookers in sports stadiums, including one in November 2024 that earned worldwide condemnation.
"I condemn today's horrific public execution," Richard Bennett, who monitors human rights violations in Afghanistan for the United Nations, said in a statement at the time. "These atrocious punishments are clear violations of human rights and must be immediately halted."
Another person, reportedly convicted of murder, was publicly executed in a sports stadium in October 2025, according to the U.N.
The Taliban regularly carried out public executions during their first period of rule in the 1990s, until the U.S. invasion in 2001 forced them out of power.
Public executions elsewhere in the world
North Korea is also believed to carry out public executions, though reporting is difficult from the extremely isolated country.
In February, Amnesty International put out a report that included interviews with North Korean defectors who said they had been forced to watch public executions as a way of warning them against committing similar supposed crimes — sometimes for as little as watching foreign television programs.
"Authorities told everyone to go, and tens of thousands of people from Sinuiju city gathered to watch," one female defector interviewed by the human rights group said. "They execute people to brainwash and educate us."
Saudi Arabia, which was widely criticized for its public executions for decades, has apparently ended its use entirely in recent years. The infamous Deera Square, where many beheadings took place in the capital, Riyadh, has not hosted an execution since 2019, according to Reuters.
The death penalty is still used frequently in Saudi Arabia, even if not public. There were a record 347 people executed in 2025, according to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights. The year prior 345 people were executed. By comparison, 47 people were executed in the United States last year.
The Iran-backed Houthi militant group, which controls large areas of western Yemen, also sometimes carries out public executions. Though not recognized as the controlling government, they do hold enormous power in the country. Nine people were executed at once in public in 2021 for the killing of a Houthi general, according to the Geneva International Centre for Justice.
"International human rights bodies have long found public executions as incompatible with the prohibition on cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement to CBS News. "The claim that the death penalty serves as a greater deterrent is simply unfounded: there is no evidence that it has a unique deterrent effect. The death penalty does not make us safer."
"Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end," he added.

U.S. plan to livestream execution by firing squad draws bipartisan, international outrage

U.S. plan to livestream execution by firing squad draws bipartisan, international outrage
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Pentagon plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Ft. Hood, Texas, in 2009.
- Republicans and Democrats, human rights officials, religious leaders and legal experts condemned the broadcast plan.
In confirming his plans to livestream Ft. Hood mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan’s military execution by firing squad on Dec. 3, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called it a “no brainer” punishment for a “radical Islamist terror attack” on U.S. service members.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand [that] there are serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said in an interview with Real America’s Voice network.
Others across the country and around the world — Democrats and Republicans, human rights experts, legal scholars and military and religious leaders — condemned it as a barbaric throwback to an era when executions were cast as entertainment, and as the world’s leading democracy adopting a form of punishment carried out in modern times only by authoritarian regimes and terrorist organizations.
“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) wrote on X. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
“I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that,” Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) wrote.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights said that “the livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.” The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops said it would “further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people.”
The suspect, stable after being shot himself, is accused of killing 13 and wounding 30 at the Texas Army base. It’s not clear whether he is the author of inflammatory comments on the Web.
Matthew Robinson, a criminal justice professor at Appalachian State University and author of a book on U.S. capital punishment titled “Death Nation,” said he was “appalled” by the plans. “It strikes me as meant to be entertaining.” He said the last military execution was in 1961, and the last by firing squad was in 1945.
Hasan was an Army psychiatrist and major who in 2009 entered a medical building on the Texas military base with a laser-sighted handgun, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others. He has since spoken of being a “martyr” if executed.
President Trump, an outspoken proponent of the death penalty for years but also a past critic of public executions in places like Iran, has signed off on Hasan’s execution but not addressed Hegseth’s plans. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, said Friday that people should remember that Hasan “brutally murdered a lot of innocent people.” But he also said he would not watch a livestream of the execution, and expressed doubt that it is “actually going to happen.”
On his first day in office this term, Trump issued an executive order requiring federal agencies to restore the death penalty to prominence. In April, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that it had taken steps to do so, including by “expanding the protocol” to include firing squads.
Five states allow execution by firing squad: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. The U.S. Supreme Court has repeatedly turned down appeals contending such executions amount to “cruel and unusual punishment,” which is barred under the 8th Amendment. South Carolina executed three men by firing squad last year.
When the Supreme Court last year rejected an Alabama inmate’s request to be killed by firing squad rather than with nitrogen hypoxia, liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor — joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson — dissented, writing, “Boyd asks for the barest form of mercy: to die by firing squad, which would kill him in seconds, rather than by a torturous suffocation lasting up to four minutes. The Constitution would grant him that grace.”
Last week, Tennessee inmate Christa Pike survived what was meant to be a lethal injection of the barbiturate pentobarbital. Other states have also struggled with executions by lethal injection in recent years.
Much of the criticism of Hegseth’s plan for Hasan has centered not on the method of killing, but on the livestreaming of it.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said the center has “no record of any execution being livestreamed” and is “not aware of any regulation or precedent for a military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public.”
Fox News commentator Howard Kurtz wrote: “I’m sensing revulsion on the left and right, not so much for killing a death row prisoner — although firing squad seems extreme in the modern age — but for the Pentagon to live-stream it, turning this into a horrifying TV show to entertain the masses. Is this America?”
Daniel LaChance, an associate history professor at Emory University and author of the book “Executing Freedom: The Cultural Life of Capital Punishment in the United States,” said the last public execution in the U.S. occurred in 1936, when a Black man convicted of rape was hanged in Kentucky — which still allowed public executions after most states had abandoned the practice.
That execution was “by all accounts a grotesque carnival” and “sort of like a gladiatorial contest brought to life in the 20th century, where the crowd was surly, shouting,” LaChance said. “It was a debacle.”
That the Trump administration is seeking to turn capital punishment into a public spectacle once more, LaChance said, is out of line with decades of thinking on the issue, but in line with Trump’s own ethos about crime and punishment.
“His whole brand is this kind of populist, anti-elitism. And when executions moved into the bowels of prisons in the early 20th century, they were really becoming bureaucratic affairs, run by experts, carried out in front of a small group of professionals and clergy,” LaChance said. “It was a denial of the public’s right to see a punishment that was carried out in their name, in part because there were elites who thought that the public couldn’t handle this kind of spectacle, that they were misbehaving, that it would generate more disorder when an execution is designed to do the exact opposite: to generate order.”
Trump clearly thinks he is pushing back against elitism and expertise and giving people what they want, LaChance said, though the question many scholars have is whether doing so will “increase people’s bloodthirst” or force them to recoil — and ultimately decrease support for such punishments.
Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.
Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School, said Trump has publicly mused about killing people by firing squad for years, so Hegseth’s plans to use that method should not be surprising. However, the decision to livestream the killing is clearly a source of “dismay” for many. “Even people who are resigned to the death penalty, who don’t have religious or other scruples about the death penalty, have real heartburn over this,” he said.
Fidell said “brutality” has become an “operating principle” for the Trump administration broadly, with its decision to host an Ultimate Fighting tournament at the White House, its immigration tactics across the country and now its plans to livestream an execution — which Fidell said has “nothing to do” with deterring future crime.
“There’s a pathology going on here that is so out of keeping with the dignity that ought to characterize the taking of a life as a result of a legal process,” he said.
Robinson, of Appalachian State, said a student of his asked Friday morning what would happen when children tune in to watch the execution, which Robinson said he believes they will do, as if it’s a video game. He said the idea was appalling — and not just to him.
“I imagine the rest of the world, the civilized world, will see this and have the same response that I did,” he said. “They’ll respond with shock.”
Times staff writer David G. Savage contributed to this report.

President Donald Trump has selected conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to serve as the next White House press secretary, he announced Friday.
Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August, in the position.
Zacharia currently works as a communications adviser at Trump Media and Technology Group, the company that runs Trump’s social media platform Truth Social. She previously worked at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as a spokesperson for former Secretary Kristi Noem, and appears frequently on conservative media including Fox News and Newsmax.
Zacharia wrote on X that being selected as White House press secretary was “the honor of a lifetime” and vowed to “[communicate] to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day.”
It is not clear when Zacharia will start her new role. The Trump Administration, which often refers to itself as the “most transparent” in history, has not held a formal press briefing in 36 days, since Vice President J.D. Vance took to the briefing room in early September.
In a post on Truth Social announcing his selection, Trump praised Zacharia for “an unblemished record of support” and being “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.”
“She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump continued. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration.”
The New York Times first reported that Zacharia had been tapped by the White House.
Zacharia, who currently lives in California and graduated from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, has also worked as a general counsel for almost three years at Fix California, a conservative non-profit founded by Ric Grenell, who served as Acting Director of National Intelligence during Trump’s first Administration. The organization works to promote a conservative agenda around the state.
In June, Zacharia was appointed to the advisory board of NovaRed Mining Inc, a Canadian mining company based in Vancouver, according to a company announcement. Just a week before Zacharia’s appointment, Noem also joined the advisory board.
Leavitt, who became the youngest White House press secretary in history at the age of 27, this week joined Fox News as an on-air contributor, the network announced on Monday. She is the third of Trump’s former press secretaries to join the network. She begins on Nov. 1.
Trump announced Leavitt’s departure through a Truth Social post in which he said that she “will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”
Leavitt responded with a lengthy post on X in which she thanked the President and the White House and said that she would remain “a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party. ”
Leavitt gave birth to her second child, Viviana, in May. She went on maternity leave that month and later announced that she would be stepping down from her role to spend more time with her family.
Trump’s time in office has been characterized by a contentious relationship with the media, which he has repeatedly attacked and derided while serving as President. Leavitt echoed that attitude during her time behind the podium, becoming known for her acerbic remarks and quick deflections during press briefings.
Zacharia will enter the White House during a fight over the media’s access to the President. Trump on Sept. 18 banned POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House grounds, sparking an ongoing legal battle. Though the outlets’ access to the White House has been restored after a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, Trump has since restricted POLITICO and CNN from boarding Air Force One, preventing them from carrying out their White House pool duties and drawing further blowback.
Zacharia would also be entering the White House at a time when Trump is facing record-low approval ratings over his handling of the war in Iran, which has contributed to rising inflation in the U.S., and as the fast-approaching November midterms threaten Republicans’ control over both chambers of Congress.

Panama struck by 2 powerful earthquakes, U.S. Geological Survey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Panama struck by 2 powerful earthquakes, U.S. Geological Survey says
A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck near Panama's southern tip on Friday morning, shaking buildings more than 100 miles away in the capital and prompting evacuations, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. A second powerful 6.6 magnitude earthquake struck the country later in the day following a series of aftershocks.
The initial quake was centered about 7 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba and struck at a depth of about 7 miles, the USGS said. The 6.6 magnitude quake came about two and a half hours later, with its epicenter about 8 miles west of Río Grande on Panama's Pacific coast and a depth of about 6 miles.
The U.S. Pacific Tsunami Warning Center had initially warned about the possibility of tsunami waves hitting Panama's coast, but later said the threat had passed.
Tremors were felt in Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news.
"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're OK, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. "Everyone is outside, scared."
Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, including several measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months.
Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela's La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people.
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino called for calm on Friday, writing on social media: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. He said there were no reports of damage in the capital, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers.
Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé, around 93 miles from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district's main square, as well as damage in the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. No casualties were immediately reported.
Local news outlets also reported that the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama's Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday afternoon that it was reopening.
The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the key global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.
The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake centered in nearby Costa Rica killed 23 people, injured 559, and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region.
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 25,000-mile arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur.
Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called "difficult times."
"Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia's support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed," he wrote on social media.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was "closely monitoring" the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.

&quot;Examples of how a city should and should not be managed during wartime&quot; — expert compares the chaos in Klitschko&apos;s Kyiv with the order in Terekhov&apos;s Kharkiv

"Examples of how a city should and should not be managed during wartime" — expert compares the chaos in Klitschko's Kyiv with the order in Terekhov's Kharkiv
Kyiv • UNN
An expert compared Klitschko's and Terekhov's performance during the war. In Kharkiv, transport, underground schools, and social support are operating.
While Vitali Klitschko is declaring a “survival mode” in Kyiv and urging residents to leave, in frontline Kharkiv Ihor Terekhov’s team is ensuring the operation of free public transport, underground schools, and a social support system. Political analyst Yevhenii Prokopyshyn drew attention to this contrast in the work of the two mayors, UNN reports.
“Kyiv and Kharkiv are excellent examples of how a city should and should not be managed during wartime,” Prokopyshyn wrote. According to him, Kyiv’s authorities spent the year reporting on preparations for winter and allocating substantial funds for this purpose. However, at the beginning of October, the city encountered disruptions in electric transport, electricity, and water supplies. “The city’s electric transport has effectively stopped, there is no electricity, problems have begun with water and sewage, and Klitschko himself, throwing up his hands, declared a survival mode in the city and urged residents to leave. Is this the same ‘effective management’ that his supporters have repeatedly spoken about?” the analyst noted.
Meanwhile, Prokopyshyn emphasized, Kharkiv is located approximately 25 km from the front line and is constantly under Russian shelling. Despite this, free public transport continues to operate in the city, underground schools are functioning, and socially vulnerable residents and those affected by the war receive free meals. The analyst separately highlighted the difference in the positions of the two mayors. While Klitschko urges residents to leave the capital, Terekhov, according to him, invites people to return to Kharkiv.
“Terekhov is not urging citizens and businesses to leave the city; on the contrary, he says: come back. And he is inviting not only residents who have left, but also internally displaced persons, refugees, and relocated businesses to Kharkiv. About 200,000 citizens have already moved to Kharkiv to live, mostly from Donbas,” he stated.
Prokopyshyn also compared the cities’ financial capabilities: according to the data he cited, Kharkiv’s annual budget, with a population of approximately 1.3 million, is about UAH 20 billion, while Kyiv’s budget, with a population of approximately 2.6 million, is about UAH 120 billion.
“In Kharkiv, they do not promise to prepare somehow or do something someday — Terekhov and his team simply get things done,” the blogger stressed.
He acknowledged that Kyiv and Kharkiv differ in scale, resources, and problems, and that the consequences of Russian attacks cannot be blamed solely on the mayors. At the same time, in the analyst’s view, it is precisely during crises that the quality of management decisions, preparedness for emergencies, and the authorities’ attitude toward people become most apparent.
“Kyiv’s authorities must be held accountable for their failed work, acknowledge this, and resign so that other people can correct the mistakes and save the city. As for Kharkiv’s authorities, they can only be praised — Terekhov is truly a capable manager, the kind so sorely lacking even at the higher, national level,” Yevhenii Prokopyshyn concluded.

Too useful to die: Russia’s post-Soviet project gets an Iranian boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:45:13 UTC
03:45:13 KST

Too useful to die: Russia’s post-Soviet project gets an Iranian boost
The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit held in Turkmenistan on October 9, 2026 delivered a forceful answer to those who have spent years predicting its demise. As it marks its 35th anniversary, the organization brings together countries with different priorities and is drawing interest even beyond the former Soviet Union. The biggest surprise at this year’s summit was not simply the Iranian president’s attendance at a gathering traditionally reserved for Commonwealth leaders, but Masoud Pezeshkian’s proposal to establish a ‘CIS+1’ format. Tehran signaled its readiness for sustained cooperation with an organization whose work had been confined to relations among former Soviet republics. In doing so, Iran gave the Commonwealth fresh momentum, proposing to broaden its agenda beyond the post-Soviet region.
Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov had good reason to describe the CIS’s 35th anniversary as an important historical milestone. The summit in Turkmenistan bore out that assessment.
More than a Soviet afterthought
The Commonwealth began as an integration project, although its achievements have differed from the expectations of the early 1990s. It helped preserve the agreements underpinning trade, transportation links, and cultural and social ties after the breakup of a shared state. New borders cut across economic networks built over decades. The CIS enabled many of those connections to adapt to the realities of national sovereignty. Businesses retained access to customers and suppliers, while people could continue working, studying, and staying in touch with loved ones in neighboring countries. It is in these everyday arrangements that the value of the CIS becomes clear.
Competing visions of the Commonwealth’s future emerged in its earliest years. Ukraine initially tried to steer the organization toward its own priorities: above all, completing the ‘divorce’ among the former Soviet republics while retaining only essential forms of cooperation. At the same time, Kiev looked down on the republics of the South Caucasus and Central Asia, seeing little promise in relations with them. Already backed by the West, Ukraine had little interest in strengthening shared institutions, fearing that they would supposedly compromise its independence. Its refusal to sign the CIS Charter was one of the clearest expressions of that approach.
Russia pursued a different course, seeking to preserve ties among the newly independent states and give them an opportunity to draw closer on a new footing. Russia’s 1995 strategic policy explicitly set the goal of building an economically and politically integrated association. Europe’s experience showed that sovereignty was entirely compatible with common markets and institutions for cooperation. Moscow therefore saw long-term potential in relations with the republics of Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Independence should not have meant that neighbors had to learn all over again how to trade, negotiate, and work together.
That outlook helps explain Russia’s leading position within the Commonwealth. Its strategic foresight, combined with the scale of its market, industry, and infrastructure, makes Moscow the principal hub of regional cooperation. Russian leadership also rests on its ability to keep negotiations moving despite differences among the participants. For Russia, the CIS is an integration project that preserves and develops ties with its closest neighbors. Moscow plays a leading role because it can offer partners things they want: a large market, investment, and a stake in major transportation projects. Mutual benefit keeps countries at the same table even when serious political disagreements arise.
The economic ties that keep the CIS together
Economics remains the most compelling argument for the Commonwealth. At the summit, Vladimir Putin announced that Russia’s trade with CIS countries exceeded $110 billion in 2025. Behind that figure are export earnings, factories kept busy, and deliveries of essential goods. A change in rhetoric cannot erase the importance of the Russian market to its partners. Russia, in turn, has an interest in stable neighbors and cooperation across production networks. Amid external restrictions, trade among these countries helps sustain economic activity and gives businesses a wider choice of suppliers.
One of the most important achievements of the CIS has been its network of free trade agreements. This should not, however, be portrayed as a single set of rules applied uniformly across the former Soviet Union. Participation varies from one agreement to another, and exemptions and restrictions remain. That is what gives practical significance to Moscow’s call in Turkmenistan to remove trade barriers. The next phase of integration should make it easier for businesses to operate by reducing border delays, making payments more predictable, and aligning product requirements. Designating 2029 the Year of Transport Connectivity sets a direction for that work.
The Commonwealth’s history also contains an almost comical legal paradox: Ukraine formally remains part of the CIS. At least, that was how the organization’s secretary-general, Sergey Lebedev, described its position in May 2026. Kiev has long stopped participating in CIS bodies and has been terminating agreements. Ukraine also declined to sign the CIS Charter in 1991, so its status as a founding and participating state must be distinguished from membership under the Charter. The irony is that Kiev has spent years declaring a break with the Commonwealth without formally completing a full withdrawal. Refusing to take part in the organization’s work and withdrawing from individual agreements do not, by themselves, sever every remaining tie.
Iran opens a new chapter
Against that backdrop, Iran’s arrival is especially striking. For the first time, an Iranian president attended a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State as a special guest and proposed a mechanism for cooperation. An organization repeatedly dismissed as having outlived its purpose has attracted the interest of a major power outside its traditional geographic reach. That is what makes Iran’s move so significant. The relationships built within the Commonwealth have value in their own right for an outside partner. The CIS’s further development can therefore draw on new areas of cooperation that enhance its international standing.
The CIS+1 proposal fits within the CIS Plus framework established in Dushanbe on October 10, 2025. Pezeshkian proposed putting Iran’s relations with Commonwealth countries on a lasting, practical footing. For now, the initiative still needs an organizational structure. But its political significance is already clear: Tehran sees the CIS as a suitable forum for coordinating shared interests. The Commonwealth gains an opportunity to expand cooperation without requiring an outside partner to join the organization. Iran gains a channel for working with several countries at once whose decisions affect its trade and transit routes.
Iran’s interest rests on solid economic foundations. The country connects the Caspian region to the Persian Gulf and provides access to maritime trade routes through its southern ports. For Tehran, cooperation with Russia and Central Asia broadens its choice of routes and reduces dependence on particular stretches of its transport network. For CIS countries, it offers additional access to the Iranian market and beyond it, the markets of South Asia. The North-South transport corridor, Caspian shipping, and rail links through Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan all converge here. Amid military risks and sanctions, the ability to choose among shipping routes becomes an economic asset in its own right.
A foundation for closer economic ties is already in place. A comprehensive free trade agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union and Iran took effect on May 15, 2025. CIS+1 would allow cooperation to be discussed with a broader group of countries. For Russia, it offers a way to connect different strands of its Eurasian policy. For Tehran, it would complement preferential trade terms with transportation and investment agreements. The format would not automatically extend free trade to every partner, but it could help coordinate projects among countries with different integration commitments.
The political significance of Iran’s participation was evident in the October 8 meeting between Vladimir Putin and Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of events in Turkmenistan. Taken together, Tehran’s participation in the broader gathering and its talks with the Russian president offered a public demonstration that Iran is not internationally isolated. It still has partners and opportunities to discuss the development of those relationships at the highest level. That matters for a country facing military, sanctions, and diplomatic pressure.
Putin reaffirmed Russia’s willingness to help resolve the situation in the Middle East and spoke positively about bilateral relations. According to him, Russian-Iranian trade grew by more than 21% in 2025. Pezeshkian thanked Moscow for its stance, including at the UN, and emphasized his interest in speeding up joint projects. The talks showed that discussion of the regional crisis had not pushed economic cooperation off the agenda. They also demonstrated Russia’s ability to bring partners together and address the most pressing international problems with them. Iran, for its part, showed that attempts to isolate it had deprived Tehran of neither political support nor opportunities for economic cooperation.
Shared challenges, wider horizons
The choice of Turkmenistan as the summit’s host is also telling. Ashgabat’s policy of permanent neutrality has not prevented it from working actively within the CIS or welcoming Commonwealth leaders. Participation allows the country to develop cooperation with its neighbors while maintaining its own foreign policy course.
In the Turkmen resort of Avaza, participants also discussed a problem whose consequences are already being felt by the Caspian’s coastal states: falling sea levels. The retreating shoreline is creating difficulties for ports and shipping while threatening fisheries and tourism. For Avaza itself, where substantial sums have been invested in hotels and resort infrastructure, the issue concerns the future of the entire coast. The Caspian environmental summit held alongside the CIS gathering therefore deserves attention in its own right. Addressing this problem will require a joint effort. No single country can solve it alone, and the decisions made will affect the preservation of the sea, port operations, and the future development of coastal cities.
The results of the summit in Turkmenistan give grounds to speak of a new stage in the Commonwealth’s development. The CIS endures because its participants need economic ties and a forum for reaching agreements, while Iran’s arrival confirms the organization’s appeal beyond its existing membership. Russia retains its leading role in bringing countries together and gains an opportunity to broaden the reach of our integration efforts through cooperation with outside partners. Iran’s initiative still has to move from proposal to concrete decisions. But the central shift has already taken place: the anniversary summit discussed not only how to preserve the Commonwealth, but how to expand its possibilities. Many in the West expected the CIS to fall apart. The summit in Turkmenistan showed the opposite: the organization is alive, functioning, and extending its reach.

Former ICC judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:40:03 UTC
03:40:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Navi Pillay, judge behind UN inquiry into Israeli occupation, wins Nobel Peace Prize
Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge who oversaw a UN report that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law".
This year's Nobel Peace Prize underlined the importance of maintaining an organised international order, the committee said in its citation.
"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack," it said.
"We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence."
Born in Durban, in South Africa's Natal province, in a family of Indian Tamil origin, Navi Pillay, 85, has been a judge on several international courts, including the International Criminal Court and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.
She was also chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous".
She has also served as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.
In 1967 she became the first woman to start a law practice in Natal and the first non-white woman to serve on South Africa's High Court.
Pillay held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict, and demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career, said the committee.
"A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," said the citation.
The Hague-based ICC has been the target of an escalating campaign by US President Donald Trump, who last month urged countries to leave it.
Washington has already imposed targeted sanctions on several prosecutors and judges at the court and, according to sources, is considering wider sanctions in retaliation for the targeting of Israeli leaders.
The Palestinian foreign ministry on Friday welcomed the awarding of the Nobel Peace Price to Pillay, saying the recognition honoured "all those who stand firm in defending international law and justice".
"Throughout her distinguished career, she has pursued the truth and defended the rights of the oppressed in South Africa and around the world, including Palestine, with integrity, courage, and honour," the ministry said in a statement.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a fugitive of the ICC wanted on war crimes charges, slammed the award, accusing Pillay of being a "bigot" against Jews for concluding that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

The US Tsunami Warning System showed potential tsunami threats across much of Central America's Pacific coast.
A magnitude-7.7 earthquake jolted Panama on Friday, setting off panic in the capital city and warnings of dangerous tsunami waves.
USGS said the quake was detected at 1756 GMT with an epicenter 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in the south-center of Panama. It initially measured at magnitude 8.
The quake was registered at a shallow depth of 12 kilometers, meaning its impact was likely to be more severe.
It was felt across the country of around 4.5 million people, according to the USGS.
Several large aftershocks, one a magnitude-6 tremor, were recorded.
There were no reports yet of casualties but extensive damage was expected, particularly in the center of the Central American nation.
Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200 kilometers from the epicenter, AFP witnessed.
Tsunami waves up to three meters high could hit the Panama coastline in the coming hours, the US Tsunami Warning System said.
Earthquakes are rare in Panama and when they do occur usually strike in western Chiriqui province.

Ukrainian producer that neutralized more than 7,000 drones over 100 square kilometers in year, plays enemy in Pentagon contest, and gets invitation to continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:38:37 UTC
03:38:37 KST

A Ukrainian company has played the enemy in a Pentagon drone contest, and the US liked what it saw. Phantom Defense, a Ukrainian defense-tech firm, was one of three companies whose systems built the counter-drone environment for Gauntlet II, the second stage of the US military’s Drone Dominance program, and has been invited to take part further, Defender Media reports.
Drone Dominance is the Pentagon’s four-phase effort to field cheap attack drones fast, a roughly $1 billion program to buy more than 200,000 low-cost attack drones by 2027. Phantom Defense brought a system that was already proven at home, where in one city it neutralized more than 7,000 enemy drones over an area of more than 100 square kilometers in a year, the company says.
Rather than enter a drone of its own, Phantom Defense supplied the resistance that the American drones had to fly through. Its setup paired the Specter PRO, L, X, and XL jammers with the Streamhunter video-interception tool and a command-and-control layer that detected and classified targets, coordinated the countermeasures, and confirmed the kills. The jammers suppressed drones and held up in heat and rain, it adds.
The arrangement lets American developers fly their drones under live electronic attack rather than calm conditions, recreating a battlefield where a drone’s performance swings with the jamming around it, according to the company.
One map to run the whole fight
At the center sits Phantom Defense’s C2 system, Kupol, which integrates separate tools into a single ecosystem on a shared map. It lets crews run electronic warfare remotely, without driving out to a position, and ties in sensors, interceptor drones, and turrets, the company says.
Kupol reads the terrain and a drone database to propose the best way to take down a target, then logs each mission automatically so its recommendations sharpen over time.
The high-power Specter PRO station, built to shield positions, critical infrastructure, and cities, serves as the hardware anchor.
An invitation, not yet a contract
Previously, Ukraine’s battle-tested drone makers also took part in Drone Dominance. However, they didn’t succeed in it, though some of their technology competed under Western partners. The program bars direct purchases from Ukrainian firms, which must set up a US legal entity to bid.

European countries condemn US sanctions against ICC

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:37:28 UTC
03:37:28 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Several European countries condemned US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, reaffirming their support for the court's independence and its role in prosecuting serious international crimes.
Denmark, Sweden, Austria and Portugal joined the EU, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands in criticizing Washington's decision.
"Denmark profoundly disagrees with the USA's decision to impose sanctions against the ICC, which will have enormous consequences for the court's work and for the investigation of the most serious international crimes," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said on US social media platform X.
"Denmark confirms its unwavering support for the ICC," he added.
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said Stockholm regretted the US decision, stressing that Sweden and the EU stood firmly behind the court's role in ensuring accountability and justice for victims.
"Multilateralism and international institutions for ensuring accountability are needed more than ever at a time when violations of international law continue to cause immense suffering," she said.
Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger described the sanctions as "another stage of escalation," saying they also called into question the sovereignty of states that established the court.
"We condemn these sanctions in the strongest possible terms," she said, pledging continued efforts by Austria and its partners to protect the court and its staff.
"Especially small states like Austria rely on international law applying to everyone, regardless of how large or powerful a state may be," she added.
Portugal also condemned the sanctions, saying they undermined the independent exercise of international justice and efforts to combat impunity for serious crimes.
It stressed that institutions defending international law must be able to fulfill their mandates without pressure or interference. 
ICC rejects sanctions as 'assault on rule of law'
The ICC strongly rejected the sanctions, describing them as an attempt to obstruct justice and an "assault on the rule of law."
Court President Tomoko Akane said the institution would continue its work "with independence and impartiality."
The EU described Washington's announcement as "deeply regrettable" and said it was prepared to take measures to protect the court's operations.
The bloc also said the six-month period before the sanctions take effect offered an opportunity for dialogue.
European Council President Antonio Costa stressed that international justice must be defended, saying lasting peace required accountability.
Costa said the EU would take appropriate steps to protect the ICC and continue supporting the court and the Rome Statute system through political, diplomatic, financial and practical means.
Belgium called for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court and those supporting its work.
Switzerland said it opposed "sanctions, threats or other measures" aimed at undermining the ICC's independence.
The Netherlands described the sanctions as an "undesirable new escalation" and pledged continued support for the court as its host country.
The reactions followed an announcement of sanctions against the ICC by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Rubio said President Donald Trump would not allow the court to prosecute Americans and threatened to "end the ICC" unless it stopped what he described as its "threats."

Explainer: Trump administration tightens rules on US green card programme for skilled tech workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:37:00 UTC
03:37:00 KST

The US government said on Thursday it is suspending some of the world's biggest tech and IT firms, including Microsoft, Cognizant and Capgemini, from a key green card programme that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment.
Senior US officials cited alleged fraud as the reason behind the move, saying companies have been using the programme to replace American workers with cheaper foreign workers. The decision is part of the Trump administration's broader efforts to tighten oversight of employment-based immigration programmes.
What has been suspended?
The suspension targets a key employer-sponsorship mechanism called the Permanent Labour Certification, or PERM, used by major technology companies and outsourcing firms.
The US government said it would not accept new PERM applications or process any pending ones for certain companies.
PERM took effect in 2005 to speed up the long processing times under the previous paper-based "Alien Employment Certification" program.
Under the programme, the US Department of Labour (DOL) allows an employer to sponsor a foreign worker for permanent residency. Qualified US employers initiate the process, not individual workers.
The Labour Department must certify to US Citizenship and Immigration Services that there are not enough qualified, available US workers for a given job opportunity and that employing the foreign worker will not affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans.
Outside of PERM and family-based routes to permanent residency, individuals can also self-petition for green cards through processes such as the EB-1A application for individuals with extraordinary ability or the EB-2 National Interest Waiver.
Why does the programme matter?
The PERM programme serves as a critical bridge between temporary work status and a green card for many foreign skilled workers.
Many IT firms employ hundreds of thousands of workers who typically start on temporary work visas such as the H-1B, and later seek permanent residency.
Without the option to be sponsored by their employer under PERM, foreign workers could lose a key route to permanent residency and would have to stay on temporary visas for longer.
For companies, recruiting foreign talent could become harder, as many workers overseas view the path to permanent US residency as a key reason for taking a job.
Which companies are affected by the suspension?
The US said it is suspending Microsoft and Adobe along with some of the largest IT firms in the world, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
Other companies such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet's Google remain free to participate in the programme.
Why is the US putting applications on hold?
The Trump administration says the restrictions are intended to strengthen oversight of employment-based immigration and protect job opportunities for American workers.
Vice President JD Vance said companies are using the PERM programme to replace American employees with foreign workers and undercut their wages.
Vance said on Thursday: "Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers."
The suspensions follow President Trump's move to impose a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions for highly skilled foreign workers, which federal courts have blocked.
How does PERM differ from H-1B?
An H-1B is a temporary work visa that lets skilled foreign workers work in the US, generally for up to six years.
PERM, meanwhile, is a permanent labour-certification process.
The freeze does not appear to affect current H-1B visa holders directly.
What could restricting PERM do?
The restrictions have prompted differing assessments of their potential impact on the US labour market and technology sector.
The Trump administration argues that tighter controls on employer-sponsored immigration can help prevent misuse of the system and prioritise American workers.
Some experts said that while PERM suspensions might target specific companies, such policies risk making the US less globally competitive by deterring highly skilled foreign talent.
"It is a fallacy to think that you can protect American workers by keeping skilled foreign workers out of the country.
You think that foreign talent competes with Americans within our borders, they'll certainly compete with Americans by working abroad," said Chad Sparber, Director of the Lampert Institute for Civic and Global Affairs at Colgate University.
