Breaking Down the Electric Ending of Take Charge of My Heart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:35:05 UTC
03:35:05 KST

Korean dramas are famously chaste compared to Western TV series. Though there are some exceptions, most K-dramas shy away from featuring even passionate kissing, let alone full-on sex scenes. But Take Charge of My Heart, Netflix’s latest Korean-language romance, adds a jolt, making “skinship,” or the physical intimacy between two people, a central part of its premise. In the supernatural series, TV scriptwriter Na Bo-bae (When the Phone Rings’ Chae Soo-bin) has electrical currents coursing through her body, making it so she will zap anyone she touches with bare hands. Because of the condition, Bo-bae has never dated. The lack of real-world experience is hindering her latest TV drama script—a romance about a chaebol heiress and her bodyguard.
Meanwhile, chaebol heir Baek Ho-rang (Trigger’s Kim Young-kwang) has an artificial heart that is failing. When Ho-rang and Bo-bae happen to be in the hospital at the same time, Ho-rang’s doctor discovers that physical proximity to Bo-bae charges Ho-rang’s artificial heart. Even more shocking to Bo-bae, she can touch Ho-rang without anything happening to him. As Ho-rang waits for a surgery for a new artificial heart in three months, the two strike a deal: Bo-bae will move into Ho-rang’s massive house, and act as his portable charger, and Ho-rang will go out on dates with Bo-bae as research for her script. Of course, what begins as a mutually beneficial arrangement becomes something deeper when the two fall in love.
Will corporate machinations from Ho-rang’s aunt and cousin, Choi Do-yoon (Idol I’s Jung Jae-kwang), or an unexpected change in Bo-bae’s powers keep them apart? Here’s everything that happens in the Take Charge of My Heart’s finale.
The Ho-rang exception
Take Charge of My Heart plays fast and loose with its plot logic, which is to say that the series is not overly concerned with consistency or science when it comes to characterizing Na Bo-bae’s powers. Our protagonist was hit by lightning as a child. She survived the incident, but hasn’t been able to touch others without electrocuting them ever since—until Ho-rang. While Ho-rang’s resistance to Bo-bae’s powers could be artificial heart-related, the series also implies that it has more to do with fate. The two are meant to be together.
Much of Bo-bae and Ho-rang’s relationship is encouraged by the necessity of their skin-to-skin contact. While Bo-bae can charge Ho-rang’s artificial heart by being within 10 meters of him, her charge-up is even more effective when the two hold hands, hug, or kiss. Though they don’t kiss as part of their contract, their hand-holding and embraces help both Bo-bae and Ho-rang realize that they have feelings for one another.
What happened to Ho-rang’s parents?
As is often the case with leading male characters in K-dramas, Ho-rang is an orphan. His loving parents died in a car accident when he was a child. While we learn early on in the series that they were on their way to see Ho-rang, the full context of the tragedy doesn’t become clear until the finale.. At the time, Ho-rang was in the hospital because of his heart condition, and was being visited by his grandmother, aunt, uncle, and cousin. Upset at constantly being overshadowed by his cousin, Choi Do-yoon called Ho-rang’s parents and lied to them, saying something was wrong with their son and that they needed to come quickly. In their rush, Ho-rang’s parents got into a fatal car crash. Years later, Do-yoon is still traumatized by this accident, and is still sick of being treated as the screw-up of the family.
Bo-bae is kidnapped by Ho-rang’s cousin
Do-yoon has not given up on being the successor to the TS Group, the family chaebol. But he knows he needs to get rid of the much more competent Ho-rang to do so. Knowing that Bo-bae is Ho-rang’s priority, Do-yoon kidnaps her on the night of the TS Group’s 30th anniversary celebration. When Bo-bae doesn’t arrive, Ho-rang is anxious but continues on with his speech. However, because Do-yoon also spiked his drink, Ho-rang’s artificial heart battery is losing power fast. He collapses on stage, his heart no longer functioning.
Meanwhile, Bo-bae uses her electric powers to escape from the temple Do-yoon’s hired goons have locked her in. She and Jae-ho rush to the party and arrive shortly after Ho-rang has collapsed. A desperate Bo-bae gives Ho-rang CPR, and sends a massive electrical current into his body. Ho-rang’s heart starts beating again, but Bo-bae collapses in the effort. When she wakes up again, Ho-rang’s doctor tells Bo-bae that she can’t touch Ho-rang again without endangering his life. He had surgery to get a new artificial heart, and Bo-bae’s electrical touch could stop it.
Take Charge of My Heart ending, explained
A heartbroken Bo-bae flees the city to go to her parents’ house in Dae-jeon, leaving a still-recovering Ho-rang alone. She soon discovers that her touch no longer shocks people. Her powers have temporarily short-circuited before, after large discharges of energy, but they always come back. Though she is able to touch others without hurting them, she worries that her electricity could return at any time.
Meanwhile, Ho-rang’s medical emergency has shaken confidence in his role as TS Group successor. His grandmother gives the role to Do-yoon. However, Ho-rang cares about getting Bo-bae back then securing his future at TS Group. He goes to Dae-jeon in an attempt to convince Bo-bae that they still belong together. Bo-bae, who is worried about Ho-rang’s health, is hesitant at first. But Ho-rang quickly wins over her parents by helping them with their muscat grape jam business. He convinces Bo-bae to take a chance on them, and they return to Seoul to oust Do-yoon from the TS Group.
The ousting doesn’t take much effort, as Do-yoon soon sabotages his own role in the company. He drives drunk and crashes his car. With Do-yoon embroiled in yet another scandal, Ho-rang’s grandmother re-instates Ho-rang as the chaebol heir. She meets Bo-bae, who quickly wins her over with her kind heart. Bo-bae’s career also gets back on track. Her new drama, The Bodyguard in My Heart, begins filming. Bo-bae’s best friend, Cho Seo-jeong (Kim Ah-young), is the director. Ji Eun-ho (Study Group’s Cha Woo-min), Bo-bae’s actor friend who confessed his unrequited feelings to Bo-bae earlier in the season, films a cameo in the series.
Ever the supportive boyfriend, Ho-rang comes to the filming. At the time of the series’ ending, Bo-bae’s powers have not returned. She and Ho-rang are able to cuddle up together to watch the first episode of The Bodyguard in My Heart. Ho-rang cries when Na Bo-bae’s name appears on the screen. In many ways, the drama is the story of their own love.

‘Barbaric’: US lawmakers condemn plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution

‘Barbaric’: US lawmakers condemn plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution
Republican and Democratic lawmakers condemn Pentagon plan to livestream the Fort Hood shooter’s execution by firing squad.
United States Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has received widespread condemnation over his announcement to livestream the execution of a man who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas.
Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle in the US Congress were quick to react in the hours after the Pentagon chief told a conservative news outlet on Thursday that former US Army Major Nidal Hasan’s death by firing squad would be made public.
“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting”, Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who recently expressed regret for his 2025 vote to confirm Hegseth to lead the Department of Defense, said on social media. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
Republican Congressman Austin Scott, who serves on the US House Armed Services Committee, also opposed the announcement.
“I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that,” the Georgia lawmaker said on X.
Scott’s Republican colleague in the US House, Congressman Rob Bresnahan, said, “The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families.”
“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” Bresnahan said.
Al Jazeera has not heard back from the three Republican senators – Susan Collins, Mitch McConnell and Lisa Murkowski – who opposed Hegseth’s confirmation.
Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for the shooting at Fort Hood.
On Monday, US President Donald Trump authorised the use of a firing squad in Hasan’s execution. Hegseth said Thursday that it would take place at the military base on December 3 at 1pm local time (19:00 GMT), the same time the 2009 shooting took place.
Later on Friday, Trump confirmed he “absolutely” approved of the execution of the Fort Hood shooter but said he had not made a determination on showing the death via livestream.
US Senator Jack Reed, who serves as the top Democrat on the US Senate Armed Services Committee, called on the Trump administration on Friday to “reconsider” the decision, saying it is a “gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters”.
“Live-streaming an execution is a barbaric spectacle,” the Rhode Island lawmaker told Al Jazeera in a statement. “This is yet another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure’s repeated failings which have only weakened our national security and standing in the world”.
Reed added, “It is absolutely shameful and damaging to America’s interests and core values.”
His fellow Democrat, Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut, rolled his eyes and appeared visibly shocked during a CNN interview on Thursday when asked about Hegseth’s decision.
“That’s disgusting”, Murphy told CNN’s Erin Burnett. “Is he mimicking ISIS [ISIL] executions? I understand that, in this country, we have the death penalty, but public executions [are] medieval”.
But not every lawmaker is opposed to the idea.
Republican Congressman Andy Ogles of Tennessee said on social media that “public execution is what this terrorist deserves”, calling Hegseth’s decision “excellent”.
Army policy
US Vice President JD Vance, during a trip to his home state of Ohio on Friday, told reporters he won’t “be watching” the livestream of Hasan’s death.
“I see these announcements. I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen”, Vance, who served in the US Marine Corps, said. “Let’s sort of see … when he’s executed.”
US Army policy limits who may witness military executions. According to regulation issued by the military branch, no person under the age of 18 may witness an execution. Victims, their family members, the prisoner’s lawyer and at least two members of the news media are among the limited number of people who are allowed to view.
For Hasan’s execution to be “public”, Reed said Trump would have to approve a waiver.
When asked whether Trump would grant that permission, the White House referred Al Jazeera to the Pentagon.
The head of the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which regulates broadcast communications in the country, said on Friday he would defer to the Pentagon on whether US networks could air the execution.
“Ultimately, we’re going to defer to Secretary Hegseth and, you know, his decisions on how to move forward with this,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a CNBC interview.
An official at the Defense Department told Al Jazeera that the agency has “nothing additional to provide”.
The United Nations has strongly condemned the livestreaming of Hasan’s execution, stating that it would breach international law.
A spokesperson for the UN human rights office told the news agency AFP that broadcasting the execution would be “tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.
The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.
In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.
Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.
For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.
For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.
Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.
The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Judith Lucy's cancer journey will reveal resilience she didn't know she had
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:30:00 UTC

perspective
Judith Lucy's cancer journey will reveal resilience she didn't know she had
Welcome, Judith Lucy, to the After Cancer Diagnosis Club.
It's a club no-one wants to join. There are a host of peculiar requirements. And the club remains a mystery to anyone who is not already a member.
Based on her post on Tuesday, Judith has already enjoyed the induction. The shock of diagnosis is all the more shocking because no-one can tell you precisely what the diagnosis is. Surprise!
For many, an initial finding turns out to be the tip of the cancer iceberg, with each step potentially cascading into more possibilities and medical pathways.
As a lovely breast care nurse explained to me down the phone as I waited for the biopsy result that ensured my entry to the After Cancer Diagnosis Club, you never really get one diagnosis.
But the upside is, that means even the worst news can change!
Judith spoke highly of her delightfully named surgeon, Dr Fun. You will rely on them like no-one you've ever relied on before to meticulously work their way through microscopic layers of skin and tissue and extract the stuff that will kill you.
All journeys are different
There are so many decisions to make in those first few days and there is so much information. Who knew there were so many types of cancer? What's the difference between a stage and a grade?
The medical professionals who work in this field are brilliant and in Australia we have remarkable survival rates.
But it's an extraordinary journey, and it's different for everyone.
Loading...
A few years back, my mammogram and my dental check-up were both due in the same week, but I only had time for one: I picked the scan foolishly thinking it would be the least problematic!
Good choice. That led to a repeat mammogram, which led to a guided biopsy, which led to a complete mastectomy, resulting in an even worse diagnosis.
At that point my oncologist arrived and explained that in a year it would most likely be largely behind me. A year!
She was right, of course. A year of chemo, radiation and then mostly it was done. But, of course, it wasn't really done.
Just because you're not hooked up to an infusion every week doesn't really signal "the end" of cancer treatment.
Stretching out for years ahead – for me at least – is the Tamoxifen treatment, daily oral hormone therapy medication that rattles your bones. Then I opted for the reconstruction and a second mastectomy. Judith plans the same. No regrets here, but these are exhausting procedures.
And after the treatment there is the constant vigilance. Too many headaches? Scan for brain metastases! Strange rash that won't quit? Biopsy for a recurrence!
Finding a path
My gorgeous kids were my anchor. The sound of my eldest tapping away at her homework next to my hospital bed made me feel safe enough to sleep, but it's a cruel thing asking to borrow your children's strength.
And you'll do most of this alone, sorry to say. Even the most willing families and friends will struggle to understand the fear, the aches, the change.
As one of my friends once described it, "done or dead" is what most people can deal with. Best to project positivity at all times. Emphasising the bright side and gags about a free boob job is the safe way to go. But it can make the experience all the lonelier.
Loading...
"I'm fine" is so much easier an answer for others to hear than "I hurt all the time" or "God, the tiredness!".
Bits of my body will never feel the same. You know how amputees talk about phantom pains? I have a phantom itch where my breast tissue used to be, but no amount of scratching can get to it because there is no sensation in the skin.
It's constant reminder of what was there. As if you needed one.
Listen to Judith and get your boobs checked.
And Judith, you're about to be amazed by the people you meet and what you're capable of.
Annie White is an ABC journalist.

Family turns bare island into reef oasis after guano mining destroys it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Guano mining left Lady Elliot Island a barren wasteland. Now it's a tropical oasis
For thousands of years the tiny island at the southernmost tip of the Great Barrier Reef was alive with cacophonous birdsong.
But within a decade of guano miners arriving in force with their picks and shovels in the 1860s, Lady Elliot Island was silent, denuded of all foliage and bereft of the seabirds that once lived there.
It remained a barren wasteland for more than 100 years before one family decided to revive it and started planting trees.
The cotton-wool clouds separate to reveal the first glimpse of Lady Elliot Island.
A ring of waves crashes on the outer edge of the reef, and the island's airstrip is a prominent ribbon of jade encased in forest green.
From the sky, the coral cay 80 kilometres off the coast of Bundaberg is a picture of pristine natural beauty.
On land, birdcalls fill the air.
Humans now have a permanent presence here, but for millennia, this island belonged solely to seabirds.
That's what made it such a prize to guano miners in the mid-19th century.
"The thing that seabirds do really well is poo," says Christine Dudgeon, who manages the island's research and rehabilitation program, Leaf to Reef.
"It was covered in about two metres of guano, and this was a really valuable substance at the time for fertilisers."
Guano, the accumulated waste from birds or bats, is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium.
This nutrient powerhouse fuelled the new world of modern, input-intensive farming that emerged in the early 1800s.
After German explorer Alexander von Humboldt took samples of guano back to Europe, farmers' demands for the fertiliser soared.
Commercial guano mining started in Peru in 1840, but the profitable global trade quickly expanded to hundreds of Pacific and Caribbean islands that were uninhabited by humans.
Seabird colonies along Australia's east and west coasts were displaced as miners moved in, destroying entire island ecosystems to meet agriculture's insatiable demand for fertiliser.
With hundreds of thousands of seabirds nesting, feeding and pooing on the 45-hectare Lady Elliot Island, settlers quickly identified the coral cay as a guano goldmine.
However, initial attempts to remove guano from Lady Elliot Island in the early 1850s were thwarted when two ships, the Bolton Abbey and The Countess of Minto, came to grief. One was wrecked on the reef encircling the island and the other was driven out to sea.
Ten years later, in 1863, the Queensland government granted Jack Askunas the first official mining lease for the island for £300 a year.
He cleared trees, shrubs and grasses to reach the guano, destroying habitat that had supported birdlife for thousands of years.
An estimated 20,000 tonnes of guano, with a raw market value equating to about $30 million today, was removed from the island over the next decade.
In his wake, Askunas left a demolition site, uninhabitable even by the seabirds that used to nest there.
"This became like a moonscape, absolutely barren," Dr Dudgeon says.
"Then after that, they [the miners] put some goats onto it just in case there were shipwrecks, so that there was some food [for survivors]."
Any plants that sprouted were eaten by the goats.
Then came the lighthouse keepers, who arrived with very pretty but very invasive plants, which the island's environmental staff are still trying to eradicate.
It took the bird's eye view of an entrepreneurial aviator to change the island's fortunes.
A man with a plan, a woman with a green thumb
Aviator Don Adams saw the potential for tourism opportunities when he flew over Lady Elliot Island in the 1960s and was immediately attracted to its coral reef.
But with almost no vegetation, he knew substantial rehabilitation of the island would be essential.
All that remained were eight Pisonia trees that the miners had left behind. Those trees still stand today, making them at least 160 years old.
Mr Adams and his wife Moya reached an arrangement with the Commonwealth Department of Transport to build an airstrip on the island in return for a lease on a portion of land for recreational purposes.
Their son, Peter Adams, remembers many weekends and holidays sharing the island with daytrippers, who his father would take snorkelling and scuba diving on the reef.
At that time, it was far from a luxurious resort.
"The accommodation was pretty basic. We had an A-frame house, we had kerosene fridges and gas lights. We only had tank water," Mr Adams recalls now.
"Before the airstrip, the lighthouse keepers used to refer to it as the Alcatraz of the Barrier Reef because … you got sent there and that was it.
"But [with] the aeroplanes, you could be in Bundaberg within half an hour."
Mr Adams spent the last half of his childhood, from ages nine to 18, on the island and recalls flying model aeroplanes, go-karting and riding motorbikes around its two-kilometre circumference.
He distinctly remembers that the vegetation was so sparse at the time that you could see from one side of the island to the other.
Wanting to rehabilitate the coral cay correctly, Don and Moya started by surveying native species growing on similar islands in the Great Barrier Reef.
Coconuts collected from Dunk Island were used to grow coconut palms on Lady Elliot that are still standing.
But the real engine room of the revegetation project was a nursery created in the backyard of the Adams family home in Hervey Bay, where Moya propagated casuarina, pandanus and umbrella trees.
The family flew hundreds of saplings to the island.
Then the hardest part started; planting and watering by hand.
"I distinctly remember digging holes in the coral with a crowbar," Mr Adams says.
"I remember … walking around with a bucket of water trying to keep these things alive for a long time."
He says "it was a start" to the rehabilitation program that won Don and Moya a conservation award from the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland in 1974.
"I remember somebody saying, 'Why did you cut down the trees to make the airstrip?' And, well, the airstrip was there before the trees grew," Mr Adams says.
The island became Don's happy place.
"It was a bit of a sanctuary for Dad out there," he says.
"Out of all the things Dad did in his life, I remember him once saying his small involvement with Lady Elliot was the thing he was most proud of."
'They will be seen, they will be heard'
Now known as the Home of the Manta Ray, Lady Elliot Island's menagerie of marine creatures and its spectacular coral reefs are marketed as its main tourism drawcards.
But it is the ubiquitous birdlife, which has triumphantly reclaimed this island in recent decades, that provides the holiday soundtrack for visitors to its eco-resort.
The view of the Sun setting over the horizon is crisscrossed by thousands of dark streaks as white-capped black noddies return to nest after a day of fishing, swooping between guests on their way to dinner.
They are among a diverse range of seabirds now nesting and roosting on the coral cay once again.
By day, wedge-tailed shearwaters, or mutton birds, along with brown boobies and crested terns soar over the breaking waves, looking for their next meal.
On land, red-tailed tropicbirds can be found hunkering under shrubbery as they keep their newly hatched chicks warm.
It is perhaps not so surprising then to find that earplugs are supplied in the resort's rooms to help guests block out the birds' night-time calls.
It's a professional hazard that brings much joy to University of the Sunshine Coast seabird researcher Zerra Egerton.
"We are in their territory. I always think of us as guests here," she says.
"So when I hear the babies crying all night long, I am just stoked. They can wake me up as much as they like.
"It's true that maybe not a lot of people necessarily come here to experience the bird life. But once they're here, and especially in summer, you cannot avoid the birds.
"They will be seen. They will be heard. They will be felt, occasionally."
The birds have an intricate and symbiotic relationship with the island's vegetation.
The trees and foliage once again provide protection and nesting materials, while the birds bring nutrients from the sea to the land, which supports vegetation growth.
"There was no-one here [in the 1800s] except the birds," Ms Egerton said.
"To [the miners], it just looked like a resource that they could take without any moral implications … it was just an opportunity.
"But now we see that system so differently."
Solar panels fuel 'beating heart' nursery
The care and preservation baton has been passed on to the Gash family.
Husband and wife duo Peter and Julie first visited the island in the 1980s and became involved in its tourism activities in 1997 when their company, Seair Pacific, began flights to and from the island.
Once their daughters Amy and Chloe arrived, the family's attachment to Lady Elliot's unique beauty deepened, and the Gashes became the island's custodians (leaseholders) in 2005.
Determined to continue the rehabilitation work started by the Adams family, and maintained by the intervening leaseholders, the Gashes investigated ways to create an even more eco-friendly resort.
Two decades on, 33-year-old Amy Gash is now the resort's executive general manager, and often scoots around the island on a battery-powered buggy.
"We believe it's our responsibility to keep this place as pristine and as beautiful as it is for today, and also [for] the future," she says.
"We really wanted to … minimise our footprint and basically transition from that traditional reliance on fossil fuels."
In 2008, the family built a "first-of-its-kind hybrid solar power station", and has now installed more than 1,000 solar panels and 250 batteries on the island.
"We can almost confidently run 100 per cent of the time on solar power," Ms Gash says.
Over the past two decades, more than 20,000 trees have been planted on the island.
"We carry on that program that was started in the 70s by Don Adams," Ms Gash says.
"We're really proud to have partnered with the Great Barrier Reef Foundation in about 2017, which really helped us accelerate the planting of trees here at Lady Elliot.
"Everything you see … has been planted by hand on Lady Elliot Island, or it's been introduced by a bird species bringing out its seeds along the way."
Liam Turner, the ecosystem manager of the revegetation program, said that in the 10 years since the island's nursery was established, staff had propagated 22 species of native trees, shrubs and grasses.
"The nursery is the beating heart of the whole program," he says, adding that revegetation has been completed across about 70 per cent of the island.
However, taking care of the environment is a never-ending job, as 120 species of introduced weeds compete with native grasses and ground covers.
"You can't just remove weeds and expect everything to return to some sort of semblance of what it was prior to guano mining," Mr Turner says.
"In place of those weeds, we've got to put in all the native [plants] … And on top of that, we've got to continue doing maintenance in those areas to keep the weeds away and allow that native vegetation to establish.
"They do suppress and naturally compete with the weeds once they start getting established, but you've got to get them to that point."
This is where the eco-resort plays a role, with all food scraps providing an essential ingredient for the nursery's potting mix.
"It gets mixed in with cardboard and woodchips, goes through a big auger and then that gets turned into a pretty nasty putrefied substance [that comes] out … after about two weeks," Mr Turner explains.
The substance is then mixed with green waste and isolated for two years.
"We get this beautiful black soil at the other side of it, which we use for all our potting mixes that we have in the nursery," he says.
"It's good that we can produce it here so we're not importing soil to the island and … [potentially] introducing all sorts of pests and diseases.
"My big dream is that eventually we'll get to a point where none of that's necessary and the ecosystem's kind of self-sustaining and can sort itself out, which we are seeing signs of, which is fantastic."
'We never want it to go quiet again'
The thriving seabird population on Lady Elliot Island is testament to the success of Don Adams's vision to rehabilitate the barren wasteland left by guano miners in the mid-1800s.
Dr Dudgeon says the birdlife has made "an extraordinary recovery".
The primary species responsible for the nutrient flow is the black noddy, about 100,000 of which nest on the island each year, up from just a few thousand in the 1960s.
Another of the island's notable species is the red-tailed tropicbird, which is only found in two locations in Queensland.
"Tropicbirds started nesting here in the 1980s and it certainly seems that their nests are increasing over time, which is parallel with increasing vegetation that's available for them," Dr Dudgeon says.
She says seeing the changes to the island's ecosystem is encouraging.
"A lot of us work in places where you're seeing the more negative impacts all the time," she says.
"It's a great privilege to get to work out here and see … what a healthy environment is, what a biodiverse environment is. It's a very inspirational place."
Like Dr Dudgeon, Ms Egerton is astounded by the transformation from desolate island to subtropical paradise.
"It was quite bleak, just a bare white rock and quite a gruelling place to exist on for months on end," she says.
"It's incredible what's been achieved in such a short period of time in terms of the seabirds returning and the vegetation."
While the birdlife can be noisy, sleep-disruptive and a tad smelly, Ms Egerton wouldn't have it any other way.
"It's very, very special to have seabirds that breed [here] because that means that this island is literally sustaining their populations," she says.
"We love this island and we love the animals here, and we don't ever want it to go quiet again."

ICC an instrument of ‘neocolonialism’ – Liberian politician (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is an instrument of neocolonialism designed to exploit Africa, Liberian politician Emmanuel Gonquoi has said.
Speaking to RT on Thursday, Gonquoi, a commander from the Economic Freedom Fighters of Liberia, urged African nations and developing countries to abandon The Hague-based court, accusing it of serving Western interests rather than delivering impartial justice.
“It is about time for African nations and developing countries to withdraw from the ICC because the ICC has been controlled as an instrument for neocolonialism,” he said.
Established in 2002 under the Rome Statute, the ICC is tasked with prosecuting genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression, and relies heavily on the cooperation of its 125 members. However, some of the world’s most powerful states, including the US, China, India, and Russia, reject its authority.
The court has long faced accusations of disproportionately targeting Africa and selective justice. Five countries – Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad, and Venezuela – have initiated withdrawal proceedings, raising concerns about its future.
Gonquoi argued that African leaders face prejudice at the court, claiming they are effectively presumed guilty before their cases are heard. He also accused Western powers of influencing judicial outcomes to advance their political interests.
He called for an “international justice system with African characteristics,” saying that regional tribunals should reflect the cultures and values of the people they serve.
“What we see in the Netherlands is not a globalized justice forum,” he said, describing the ICC as a system set up to “exploit Africa” and prevent African leaders from making decisions that benefit their own countries.

Powerful 7.6-magnitude earthquake hits Panama and triggers tsunami warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:29:26 UTC
03:29:26 KST

A powerful 7.6 magnitude earthquake has struck Panama and triggered tsunami warnings along the west coast of Central and South America, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).
The quake hit along the southern coast of the country, the USGS said. It was centered near the southern tip of the Central American country, about 14km (9 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, the USGS said.
The Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama said the quake struck at just before 1pm local time near the southern town of Tonosí. The Panamanian institute said that a second 6.0 magnitude earthquake struck soon after, at 1.22pm.
By 1.3opm there had reportedly been 13 aftershocks.
The president, José Raúl Mulino, said he had asked a key minister to call for calm. “What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” Mulino wrote on X.
Local newspaper La Prensa said that across the Central American country, buildings, schools and homes were evacuated as a result of the “powerful movement of the earth”.
Footage published by La Prensa showed severe damage to several buildings in the city of Penonomé, including the St John Baptist Cathedral. Other photos showed a highway to the west of the capital that had been completely sheared in half by the earthquake.
Tremors were felt strongly in the capital of Panama City, according to witnesses who spoke to Reuters. The Associated Press reported that buildings shook and visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.
The USGS said hazardous waves were possible along the coasts of Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico, although the tsunami warning for Chile was cancelled at 4.18pm local time.
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. He said there were no reports of damage in the capital, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers.
Smith said several injuries had been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé, about 93 miles (150km) from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage in the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. No casualties were immediately reported.
Local news outlets also reported that the church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama’s Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways.
Tocumen international airport in Panama City, one of the region’s busiest airports with more than 20 million travelers in 2025, said it would temporarily suspend operations and activated evacuation plans. It said operations would resume once security conditions had been checked.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, wrote on social media that he was “closely monitoring reports of the earthquake in southern Panama. The United States stands with the people of Panama. At the request of the Panamanian government, the State Department is rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist.”
The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the key global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.

Powerful quake hits Panama, damages homes; canal operations normal

- The US Tsunami Warning System warned of possible hazardous waves for Panama and several Pacific countries, and said Hawaii also faced a tsunami threat.
AI generated
PANAMA CITY - A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Oct 9, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
The US Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6km, with an epicentre in a sparsely populated area about 200km from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.
In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights.
The Panama Canal, about 203km from the epicentre, was operating normally.
About 90 vessels including bulk carriers, tankers and container ships were waiting at both ends of the key waterway to transit or dock at berths serving storage terminals and trans-shipment services, according to monitoring data from LSEG’s Workspace.
Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old economy ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive.
“They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?,” he said.
President Raul Mulino travelled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicentre and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged.
Despite the force of the Oct 9 tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the destruction of other recent powerful quakes in the region, with no deaths or injuries immediately reported.
Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300.
An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake. This compares to nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia.
Prolonged vibrations
Nestor Luque, director of Panama’s geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive build-up of pressure that is occasionally released.
“The seismic signals have travelled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere.”
In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old US military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged.
“The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I’ve felt in years,” Rios said.
Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. 
“It’s a miracle they didn’t get killed,” he said. “They looked like they were swinging in a hammock.”
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets.
“We’re scared. It’s just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it could fall on us,” said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes.
Omar Smith, who heads Panama’s civil protection agency, told local outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.
Videos shared by newspaper La Prensa showed the tower of a historic building had collapsed along with several balconies of a residential building in Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicentre and Panama City.
In the capital, the service on two lines of the Panama City Metro was temporarily suspended for safety reasons, the operator said. Nationwide, Panama’s ministry of education ordered the closure of schools.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama’s gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Oct 12 to test the country’s emergency response capabilities against earthquakes. REUTERS

AI deepfake ads grow more popular in US midterm campaigns, blurring truth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:23:43 UTC
03:23:43 KST

AI deepfake ads grow more popular in US midterm campaigns, blurring truth
The US midterm election campaign has been filled with political ads featuring AI deep fakes that can mislead voters.
San Francisco, USA: Bruce Blakeman, a Republican who is running for governor of New York, released campaign ads featuring Zohran Mamdani, New York City mayor, and Kathy Hochul, the state’s governor, gardening together and collaborating to raise prices for residents.
Another ad features Hochul talking about hiking tolls and fares so people cannot afford to drive or take the subway.
Neither Hochul nor Mamdani was actually in the ads, which were made using artificial intelligence (AI). A spate of AI-generated ads that are obviously fake but grab voter attention have been a feature of campaigns in the lead up to the pivotal United States midterm elections on November 3.
While regulation has focused on labelling AI deepfakes that could mislead voters, it is “slopaganda” – or identifiably fake ads – that mark this campaign season, says Scott Babwah Brennen, director of New York University’s Center on Technology Policy and co-author of a recent report, Political Slopaganda.
Political candidates and their supporters have spent more than $80m to make more than 164 AI-based ads this election season, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, a non-partisan election advertising tracker. Republican candidates and their backers were behind 80 percent of these ads, the group found.
Blakeman defended his ads, saying they were clearly labelled as AI-generated – a disclaimer the ads do carry for a few seconds at the start – and follow a long tradition of satire and parody in American politics.
But slopaganda – a mix of low-quality AI “slop” and propaganda – is being used to “communicate deeper truths rather than factual truths”, said Brennan, meaning it could shape perceptions of a candidate’s character or ideology and could “impact voter trust”.
Other such ads showed Sherrod Brown, a Senate Democratic candidate from the state of Ohio, as the last guest at a party, having overstayed his welcome.
James Talarico, a Senate Democratic candidate from the state of Texas, was shown in a blue dress similar to the character Maria from the movie The Sound of Music, while Mike Rogers, a Senate Republican candidate from Michigan, appeared as a superhero.
In San Francisco, when Democratic California state Senator Scott Wiener released an AI chatbot in the high-profile race to succeed House Speaker Emeritus Nancy Pelosi, who represents the tech-industry city in Congress, it drew an immediate backlash.
The chatbot answered around 5,000 questions about his opponent, Connie Chan, parodying her record of ostensibly blocking real estate development in the city, her accent as well as her naturalized citizenship. The move sparked criticism for being bigoted and Wiener withdrew the chatbot, saying that while it was innovative, “it missed the mark”.
No federal law
Deepfake ads have emerged in a landscape that aims to protect political speech, including when done through parody. While there is no federal law regulating ads made with AI deepfakes, 31 states have passed their own laws calling for ads made using AI to be labelled.
“State laws do what they can without encroaching on the First Amendment,” said Ilana Beller, director of State AI Governance and Policy at Public Citizen, a Washington, DC, based consumer rights advocacy group. “There is still a need for a federal law,” she said.
Adam Rose, chief operating officer of Starling Lab, a research centre on technology and human rights co-founded by Stanford University and the University of Southern California, said some changes made by AI could just be colour or voice correction that the government does not need to label. AI-generated ads should not be banned, he said.
Instead, Rose said, candidates are always involved in making “judgement calls” on the ads and these calls reflect on them. For Wiener, Rose said, releasing the chatbot “showed bad judgement. It showed voters something about him”.
Wiener is running to represent San Francisco in the US Congress, a city that is the global epicentre of the AI industry with two of the biggest AI companies, Open AI and Anthropic, based there. The city’s representative will play an important role as legislation around AI emerges, especially as polls show a majority of Americans are more concerned than excited about the technology.
“This is a transition moment as AI is reshaping our society,” says Ian Krager, a spokesperson for Connie Chan. “This race is a harbinger for the country. It is a moment where we can show the world America can lead the world on AI development without asking working people to bear the cost.
“And it is clear Connie Chan is with working families while Scott Wiener is with the AI companies,” he said, citing the AI chatbot.
As a state senator, Wiener drafted a California law last year requiring AI companies to disclose security incidents where autonomous systems created by extremely large AI models are involved in dangerous or harmful incidents. A less stringent version became law last year. His office did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Labels as clear as food labels
Looking at the final stretch of the November midterms and beyond, Public Citizen’s Beller said there is a need to make labelling of ads that use AI as clear and easily understood as food labels so voters can evaluate them accordingly.
“People need to know to look for labels,” she said, as it’s important to create awareness about AI deepfake ads, especially among younger voters and seniors.
In New York, the Democratic Party has filed a complaint with the state board of elections saying the ads violate disclosure requirements and are “misleading to the voters”. But Blakeman has said that “people find it humorous. They like satire”.
The ads are “trying to get attention when candidates know there is political power to be gained by getting attention”, said NYU’s Brennen.
With AI deepfake ads only growing, some candidates have publicly said they will not use them. “People seem to like [the candidates] for it,” said Beller.

UAE: Omani Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack
October 9, 2026
The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, according to the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor.
The statement released on Friday by Attorney General Hamad Saif al Shamsi and published by the state media did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing.
What has the investigation revealed so far?
According to the statement, UAE public prosecutors believe that the co-pilot's plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US and aimed at "causing the greatest possible loss of life."
The investigation found that the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the flight route and airport. He had worked for several airlines in different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining Flydubai in January 2026.
The prosecutor's findings also showed that he met the professional and security requirements for employment.
These requirements included holding a pilot's license, providing a certificate of good conduct, and completing the necessary background checks.
"None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," according to the statement.
What happened on Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?
On September 30, the Indian captain of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was injured when the co-pilot attacked him with an ax.
The captain opened the cockpit door, enabling passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit and fighting for control after the plane suddenly descended around 5,000 meters (17,000 feet).
Most of the passengers on board were Israeli. They have been hailed as heroes in Israel.

Ukraine's companies The Fourth Law, Odd Systems launch Project Foundation to manufacture thermal imaging sensors in Europe, USA
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:20:15 EEST
03:20:15 KST

Ukrainian companies The Fourth Law and Odd Systems announced the launch of a joint project, Project Foundation, which will involve the production of uncooled thermal imaging sensors in Europe and the United States, the companies said in a joint press release on Thursday.
"It is imperative that we provide sensor sovereignty for the EU and US on the shortest timeline possible. After building cameras for 14 years we know exactly what the future robotics, defense, and automotive industries need," CEO of The Fourth Law and co-founder of Odd Systems Yaroslav Azhnyuk said on Facebook.
According to the press release from the companies, the project aims to quadruple the production of thermal imaging sensors in Europe and double it in the United States within three years.
The planned financing for the project will include not only investments from The Fourth Law and Odd Systems but also external equity capital, debt financing, grants, and pre-sales to customers. Currently, the companies are noting interest from investors and partners in participating in the project; however, financial agreements will be announced after they are finalized.
According to Azhnyuk, the initiative will encompass the development of LWIR sensors, as well as the deployment of a network of partner and in-house manufacturing facilities. This project will create a new industrial base for defense and civilian needs and provide drone, automotive, and robotics manufacturers with affordable sensors.
"Building thermal cameras has shown us what manufacturers need from the sensor inside: performance, a reliable supply and a price that works at scale. We are building Project Foundation around those requirements," Director of Strategic Programs and Funding at The Fourth Law and Odd Systems Ihor Nakonechny said, who will lead the project team.
According to the companies, Project Foundation's headquarters is located in Eindhoven (the Netherlands), while the first factories – First Foundation and Second Foundation – will open in Europe and the United States, respectively.
The project's network will have a shared technological base and its own sensor designs. Technological partnerships have now been established with a number of global laboratories in the field of semiconductors and microbolometers, as well as with thermal imaging camera users around the world. The first sensors under this initiative are expected in 2027.
The Ukrainian companies The Fourth Law and Odd Systems were founded in Kyiv in 2023 by entrepreneur Azhnyuk. They operate both in Ukraine and in other European countries and the United States.
The Fourth Law specializes in developing scalable autonomy for robotic systems, with a primary focus on the defense sector.
Odd Systems, in turn, develops and manufactures thermal imaging and daytime cameras for drones and other robotic systems.

Detectives of the Bureau of Economic Security (BES) have uncovered the illegal large-scale industrial production of alcoholic beverages and alcohol distillates without excise tax stamps in Cherkasy region, the agency's press service reported.
According to the investigation, the suspects organized the illegal production of goods at a facility in Uman that held a license to produce alcohol, but the license was used as a cover for unlawful activities. The director of the private enterprise and his accomplice were served with notices of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 28, Part 1 of Article 204 and Part 2 of Article 28, Part 2 of Article 204 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine in connection with the illegal production and sale of alcoholic beverages by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy. The enterprise's license to produce alcohol was revoked, while procedural guidance in the case is being provided by prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General, with operational support from the National Police. The pretrial investigation is ongoing.

Russian Oil Refinery Recruits Anti-Aircraft Gun Crews to Defend Against Ukrainian Drones

- Category

Russian Oil Refinery Recruits Anti-Aircraft Gun Crews to Defend Against Ukrainian Drones
Russia’s Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara posted vacancies for crews to operate anti-aircraft and armored vehicles protecting the facility from drone attacks, according to Verstka on October 9.
The outlet reported that the Rosneft-owned refinery listed the positions on HeadHunter on October 8. The vacancies sought personnel for a ZSU-23-4 Shilka self-propelled anti-aircraft gun and a BMP-2 Berezhok infantry fighting vehicle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Applicants were required to sign contracts with Russia’s Ministry of Defense to join the mobilization manpower reserve, complete specialist training, and undergo combat coordination. One vacancy required recruits to "serve as part of a BMP crew in barracks mode during training periods."
The duties included protecting defense-industrial facilities in the Samara region, destroying aerial targets, maintaining weapons readiness, and keeping the combat vehicle operational. The listed workplace was 25 Groznenskaya Street, the address of the Kuibyshev refinery.
Both listings have since been removed from HeadHunter search results and moved to the archive. Direct links indicate that the employer may have already selected candidates and is no longer accepting applications.
The ZSU-23-4 Shilka is a Soviet-designed tracked air-defense system armed with four 23 mm automatic cannons. Originally developed to engage low-flying aircraft and helicopters, such systems can also be used against drones operating within their engagement envelope.
The BMP-2 Berezhok is an upgraded infantry fighting vehicle fitted with a modernized combat module. In the refinery role described by the vacancy, its weapons would form part of a local defensive force protecting the industrial site.
The vacancies follow a recent strike on the same facility, which was hit in an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on September 22 that sparked a fire at the site.
Analysis of eyewitness footage preliminarily identified the refinery's AVT-5 processing unit as one of the targets, with several other fires observed across its territory. Part of Rosneft's Samara refining group alongside the Novokuibyshevsk and Syzran plants, the facility processed 4.7 million tons of crude in 2024, roughly 94,400 barrels per day.
That attack came a day after Ukrainian drones struck the Bashneft refinery complex in Ufa, about 1,600 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.

Gaza ceasefire ‘exists in name only’, more than 100 NGOs say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:15:06 UTC
03:15:06 KST

Gaza ceasefire ‘exists in name only’, more than 100 NGOs say
Humanitarian and human rights groups call out Israel’s continued killings and restrictions across the enclave.
One year after the so-called ceasefire in Gaza was reached with United States backing, it exists only on paper, according to more than 100 humanitarian, human rights and civil society organisations.
“The ceasefire exists in name only, with Israeli forces continuing to kill and injure Palestinians daily, and restrictions on aid, equipment and rebuilding materials preventing families from recovering,” a joint statement by the NGOs said on Friday.
Amnesty International, the Norwegian Refugee Council, Save the Children, Oxfam, Greenpeace and dozens of other international groups said Israeli attacks in the enclave have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians, including at least 327 children, in the year since US President Trump announced a deal to end hostilities as part of the Gaza Board of Peace framework.
“It is utterly shameful that a full year after the ceasefire was signed, so little has improved for Palestinians in Gaza,” Jan Egeland, secretary-general of the Norwegian Refugee Council, said in the joint statement.
Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save the Children, said, “A ceasefire is meaningless if children are still being killed and families are still unable to rebuild their lives.”
He noted that since the October 10, 2025 ceasefire was announced, “nearly one child has been killed every day.”
In the three years since Israel’s October 2023 genocidal war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and 175,000 others wounded – about one in every 13 people in Gaza – according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
A conservative World Health Organization (WHO) estimate suggests roughly 24 percent of the wounded have life-changing injuries requiring long-term rehabilitation, a quarter of them children.
Gaza’s few remaining health facilities are overwhelmed and have dwindling supplies, and none of its 36 hospitals is operating at full capacity, with widespread shortages of medicine, equipment and fuel, Friday’s ministry statement said.
It said that more than 18,500 patients, including at least 4,000 children, need medical evacuation, and more than 1,000 have died while waiting.
Almost 2 million Palestinians in the enclave are also in desperate need of shelter, where 80 percent of structures are damaged, the statement said.
Norwegian Refugee Council’s Egeland warned that restrictions on equipment and construction materials continue to prevent recovery.
“Israeli restrictions are still preventing the required equipment or materials, which are the only ways for communities to begin rebuilding their lives,” he said.
At the same time, 1.4 million people in Gaza are “facing crisis-level hunger or worse through the end of the year”, the statement added.
On Friday in Gaza, Israeli forces shot dead at least one Palestinian after firing live ammunition at civilians in the al-Musaddar, Maghazi and Bureij refugee camp areas in the centre of the Strip, which also came under heavy Israeli artillery shelling.
In Khan Younis in the south, Israeli tanks directed heavy fire towards the Bani Suheila roundabout, where a number of injuries were reported.
On Thursday, at least eight Palestinians were killed and dozens injured in Israeli air strikes and shelling across Gaza.
Friday’s statement noted that Israeli forces had further squeezed the Palestinian population into an even more crowded environment by arbitrarily moving the so-called “Yellow Line”, established as a buffer to separate Israeli-controlled areas and the Palestinians as part of last year’s ceasefire framework.
The “ceasefire” took effect on October 10, 2025. Since then, Israel has killed at least 1,471 Palestinians and injured 5,189.
Three years of Israeli attacks have killed at least 74,254 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. That is about one in every 30 people, or 3 percent of the pre-war population.
The Palestinian Ministry of Health counts only deaths recorded at hospitals or officially registered. The true toll is likely much higher, as it excludes the thousands still buried in destroyed buildings or missing.
“Accountability cannot be buried under the rubble,” Agnes Callamard, the secretary-general of Amnesty International, said in the joint statement. “The persistent failure to hold Israel accountable and press Israel to comply with the International Court of Justice’s binding orders continues to fuel the atrocity crimes on a mass scale against Palestinians.”

Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:14:02 UTC
03:14:02 KST

Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami
Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s Kaluga region overnight into October 9, Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He said Ukrainian forces struck infrastructure in Kaluga but gave no further details. Nine people were injured, five of whom were hospitalized.
Yandex later said its data center in Kaluga had come under drone attack. No employees were injured, but “several data center modules have been completely disabled.” The company warned that some Yandex services could experience disruptions.
This was the second attack on the Russian tech giant’s data centers in two days. Overnight into October 8, drones struck a data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region. A fire broke out, and the data center was shut down completely. Soon after the attack, users began reporting disruptions to Yandex services, media websites, and other services, including Avito, Ivi, Megafon, Russian Railways, and T-Bank.
Responding to the attacks, Yandex said its data centers were the company’s “iron heart” and that keeping them operational was “critical to services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
“We understand that for our users, clients, and partners, every outage disrupts plans and prevents them from doing things they normally do in their daily lives or at work. Yandex teams are doing everything they can, day and night, to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. This is our most important task right now, but unfortunately, it isn’t easy,” Yandex said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky briefly addressed the attack on Yandex on the evening of October 8: “You all know they [Russian forces] have struck our data centers and are still striking them. We responded. I can’t share all the details.”
Russia has regularly struck data centers in Ukraine in recent weeks. Since late September, Russian forces have damaged or destroyed data centers belonging to at least eight companies. Russia’s Defense Ministry has called these strikes a “forced digital detox.”
The peace process
Ukrainian representatives will meet with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the United States on October 9 and 10. The Ukrainian delegation has traveled to Miami, where the talks will take place. Its members include presidential chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, Davyd Arakhamia, who leads the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, and Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov. Reuters reported that Washington had invited national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO and the EU.
According to Axios, Kushner and Witkoff plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” for ending the Russia–Ukraine war. No details were given. The two presented the proposals to President Donald Trump at a meeting on October 8.
An Axios source said Witkoff and Kushner could travel to Moscow in October for further talks with Vladimir Putin.
Shortly before the Miami talks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there were currently no prospects for a peaceful settlement of the Russia–Ukraine conflict. He said the war had reached a “strategic stalemate”: Russia continues to insist on full control of the Donbas, a condition Ukraine finds completely unacceptable.
Rubio said the situation could be resolved in only two ways: through a negotiated settlement or escalation by one or both sides.
In response, Zelensky said breaking the stalemate would require increasing economic pressure on Russia, allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and refusing to reach agreements with Moscow on any future projects:
It would cost them nothing, absolutely nothing, to help Ukraine. And I’ve said frankly: Give us that. Help us defend our airspace and dominate it. Then Putin will come to the negotiating table. Why? Because he’ll lose everything. He’ll lose everything. Three months, two months — he’ll lose everything.
But instead, we’re waiting for the Chinese to develop their equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where’s the truth in that? Where’s the honesty? Where is any of it? What dead end? What dead end? This isn’t a dead end. It’s called unwillingness. It’s not a dead end.
In mid-September, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. In practice, however, that did not happen. Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Kremlin called an energy ceasefire “a very good idea.” Sources told The Kyiv Independent that Russia had demanded U.S. sanctions relief during talks on a possible energy ceasefire. It is unclear which sanctions were involved.
The war in photographs: the aftermath of a Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia
On the morning of October 9, Russian forces struck Zaporizhzhia with aerial bombs. Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, said six aerial bombs had been dropped on the city. Homes and cars were damaged. According to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service, a 50-year-old man was killed and 14 people were injured.

After the Gaza genocide, Palestine is humanity's litmus test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:12:23 UTC
03:12:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Three years after October 7, is supporting Palestine humanity's litmus test?
Three years after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led offensive into southern Israel, the motivations and objectives of the attack remain unclear.
It is now a matter of record that negotiations between Hamas and Israel, mediated primarily by Egypt and Qatar, were ongoing throughout 2023 and had reached an advanced stage. The negotiators had agreed on a text and were on the cusp of producing an agreement, but at the last moment Israel’s leadership got cold feet.
The various warnings Israel received during the Autumn of 2023 were primarily intended to persuade the Israeli government to accept what its negotiators had agreed to, because the alternative would be renewed hostilities. The Israeli security establishment responded with a proposal to conduct a wave of assassinations against the Palestinian leadership in the Gaza Strip, but this was rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the grounds that the status quo had served Israel well for many years and should therefore be indefinitely prolonged.
Were the Palestinians seeking to compel Israel to stop dithering and consummate the agreement on the table? Was the Hamas leadership abandoning a process in which it lost faith, instead seeking leverage in the form of captured Israeli soldiers to force Israel into an exchange of prisoners? Or was it determined to shatter the status quo irrevocably?
It is difficult to answer this question with confidence because the October attacks succeeded beyond Hamas’s expectations. Israel was caught completely unprepared, its forces collapsed like a house of cards, and the resulting carnage eliminated the prospect of a renewal of the negotiations.
Hamas acted unilaterally, and it appears doubtful that it anchored its initiative in an expectation that its regional partners, with whom it had not coordinated, would join its campaign. More likely, it anticipated a furious Israeli response that, albeit on a larger scale than previous Israeli assaults on the Gaza Strip, would, like them, eventually run its course.
This also shaped Hamas’s strategic approach, and there is little evidence it seriously prepared for alternative scenarios.
Israel’s calculations were of course entirely different. If in October 1973 it could at least ascribe its failures to a coordinated operation by two powerful regular armies supplied by the Soviet superpower, in 2023 it faced a more severe crisis. The unprecedented attacks were conducted within its own boundaries, and were administered by a modestly armed militia operating from a besieged, postage-stamp-sized territory Israel had dominated since the 1960s.
Consumed by maniacal bloodlust and a determination to exact revenge on an unprecedented scale in order to restore its power of deterrence, that same day Israel responded with a self-consciously genocidal campaign that continues to this day.
Within the Gaza Strip, Israel’s objectives have graduated from indiscriminate mass slaughter, to making the territory unfit for human habitation, to physically erasing it from the map.
Remaking the region
With its security doctrine in tatters, yet fortified with the unconditional assistance of the United States, and the active complicity or passive acquiescence of most Western states, Israel, beginning in 2024, also set out to remake the entire region. Henceforth, Israel would work not only to eliminate the capabilities of its enemies but also to ensure that they lacked the means to develop capabilities that could threaten the Zionist state.
This mission would not be complete without dismantling the Islamic Republic of Iran, and in Donald Trump, Israel finally found its mark.
Yet Israel’s greatest success also proved to be a turning point. What was intended as the final act in a campaign to impose unchallenged regional hegemony instead exposed the limits of Israeli power, and more importantly precipitated the decline of US power in the Middle East and arguably the beginning of the end of the US global empire.
Closer to home, the Gaza Genocide has for the majority of humanity transformed Israel into an irredeemably toxic entity.
Since at least 1967, the Zionist state has been exempt from the rules and standards every other member of the international community is expected to observe and respect. Any and every effort to hold Israel to account for its expanding crimes and savagery was discredited, denounced, delegitimised, and demonised as an illegitimate initiative, motivated by Jew hatred, to hold the survivors of the Holocaust, the only democracy in the Middle East, and the most moral army in the solar system to an impossibly high double standard.
Decades of such impunity set the stage for the Gaza Genocide, and arguably made it inevitable. Yet two years of live-streamed slaughter, and the shameless pride and glee its perpetrators took in their barbarity, have decisively turned the tables. So much so that candidates for political office in the United States who heretofore lived in terror of AIPAC and would sell their mothers to obtain its endorsement, today derive political advantage from publicly renouncing it.
Confronted with this definitive and irreversible loss of the public square, Israel and its apologists have resorted to measures generally associated with totalitarian states to enforce compliance. Yet this methodology too has failed, even as Israel and the US seek to dismantle international institutions that refuse to do their bidding.
As the genocide enters its fourth year, two clocks are ticking. The first is Israel’s race against time to eradicate the Palestine question and establish its sovereignty over the entirety of the country before the end of the Trump administration. The second, slower one, is translating Israel’s pariah status in world opinion into policy changes by governments. Slowly, but surely, the second clock is advancing, and when it strikes midnight, Israel’s game will be up.
In 2026, the struggle for justice in Palestine has become a litmus test, not only for basic morality and decency, but also for a politician’s integrity on other issues.
The tragedy is that the Palestinian national movement remains in disarray, unable to arrest and reverse its advanced state of disintegration. A credible leadership, with a coherent strategy, capable of mobilising its own people and inspiring the confidence of the multitudes who support them, is vital if the second clock is to have a winning chance of overtaking the first.
Mouin Rabbani is Managing Editor of Jadaliyya and author of Gaza Apocalypse (OR Books 2026).

Ukraine war latest: Drones strike another Yandex data center in Russia

Key developments on October 09:
- Second Russian Yandex data center damaged by drone attack in two days, company says
- Twenty Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on Donetsk, independent monitors claim
- Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
- Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
- Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
A drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, disabling several modules at the facility and threatening further disruptions to the company's services.
Several modules of the data center were completely disabled, Yandex said in a statement carried by pro-government Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
"Some Yandex services may experience disruptions as a result," the company said, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Yandex reported no injuries at the facility.
The attack came as drones struck other parts of Kaluga Oblast overnight, injuring nine people, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He also reported damage to houses in two districts of the oblast. Russian authorities claimed to have shot down 26 drones over the region.
Ukraine has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the attack on the Kaluga data center.
The strike marks the second reported attack on a Yandex data center in Russia in two days.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing the facility to suspend operations and disrupting parts of Yandex's cloud infrastructure.
The Sasovo facility houses tens of thousands of servers and two of the company's three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence models. Yandex said it was still assessing whether damaged equipment could be restored.
The attack coincided with reports of widespread internet disruptions across Russia, affecting banking services, transport websites, and online platforms.
Responding to questions about the Sasovo strike on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would continue retaliating against Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
"We responded to them," he added. "I cannot share all the details."
Russian forces struck several Ukrainian internet providers and data centers in Kyiv in late September, disrupting internet access for approximately 100,000 households, according to Ukrainian officials.
