Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
Ukrainian missile strikes on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war, independent monitors claim.
Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet that tracks Russian military deaths in collaboration with the BBC Russian Service, identified 20 officers killed in the attack.
Each of the dead Russian officers was identified by name, age, and rank by Mediazona. Seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain, and one senior lieutenant were killed in the strikes, which hit the headquarters of the Central Military District and the 41st Combined Arms Army in occupied Donetsk.
According to Mediazona, 18 of the Russian officers died immediately in the missile strike, while two succumbed to their injuries.
Denis Pushilin, the head of the Russian illegal occupation administration in Donetsk Oblast, confirmed in a post on Telegram that Ukraine had launched an attack on targets in Donetsk on Aug. 26, claiming that Anglo-French "Storm Shadow" air-launched cruise missiles were used, and that eight civilians were injured.
Mediazona also identified two other instances of "mass casualties" amongst staff officers of the 41st Combined Arms Army, according to their research, eight officers were killed on Aug. 4, with an additional four killed on Sept 8, 2025.
At least 276,113 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine since 2022, according to Mediazona, which tracks individuals killed by searching through obituaries, posts on Russian social media networks, and leaked Russian databases.

Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
Russian forces forcibly removed 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown destination, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 9.
The civilians, including children, young people, and elderly residents, were taken from an area of the oblast where active fighting continues. Their current whereabouts and the conditions in which they are being held remain unknown, Lubinets said.
"Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman did not specify which settlement the civilians were taken from or where they had been transported.
According to Lubinets, Russian forces published footage of what they described as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. He said the footage showed signs of intimidation and pressure on civilians who had not consented to being relocated.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the circumstances of the reported removals.
Lubinets also warned that Russian occupation authorities had created a Telegram bot to collect personal information under the pretext of evacuation, potentially putting civilians and their relatives at risk.
Forcible transfers and deportations of civilians from occupied territory are prohibited under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Lubinets said he had appealed to Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding information about the 25 civilians, their whereabouts and conditions, and measures to secure their return to Ukraine.
He also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the United Nations, and other international organizations for assistance.
Russia has repeatedly forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territories since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In March 2026, a United Nations commission concluded that Russia's deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children amounted to crimes against humanity.

Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
Several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports all halted operations during the alleged Ukrainian raid, disrupting flights and causing long delays.
According to FlightRadar24, an open-source air traffic monitoring website, multiple Russian government aircraft from the Rossiya Special Flight Detachment, which transports top-level Russian government officials, were scheduled to fly into Moscow's airports on Oct. 9.
At least one of the aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-96-300PU flying from Türkmenbaşy in Turkmenistan to Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, was reportedly forced to divert to St. Petersburg, according to FlightRadar24.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed "the Ministry of Defense's air defense forces repelled an attack by 15 UAVs" on the Russian government's messaging app, MAX.
A number of unknown balloons, which both Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels claimed were launched by the Ukrainian military, were also seen in the Russian skies.
Local Russian Telegram channels showed mysterious balloons in the skies near Moscow, and air defense activity.
Russian outlet BAZA claimed that, "reconnaissance balloons launched from Ukraine," were shot down over Yaroslavl Oblast, a region of Russia north of Moscow.
By 5:42 p.m. Moscow time, Russian wire service RIA Novosti reported that Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports had reopened.
On Sept. 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced a plan to close Russia's skies.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said, as he warned "every airline that uses Russian airspace" against flying over the country.
"The Russian sky will be de facto closed," he added.
In the weeks following the announcement, Ukrainian drone raids have caused severe disruption to Russian air travel, but the result has fallen short of the complete closure Zelensky promised.

Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said.
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+, citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said.
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

Summer travel demand in Ukraine shifts to safer, countryside locations – Ribas Hotels Group
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:11:03 EEST
03:11:03 KST

The summer season of 2026 showed that Ukrainians had become significantly more selective, with demand shifting away from popular resorts toward safer locations and countryside accommodation formats, Ribas Hotels Group told Interfax-Ukraine.
In May, the company forecast a record season for domestic tourism. However, actual occupancy in the Odesa cluster reached 63%. In the Carpathians, some hotels recorded record occupancy, while others failed to achieve the expected growth. The network's average occupancy rate for the summer season was 61.6%, while its average daily rate (ADR) increased by 22% year over year.
"This summer, we observed not so much uniform growth as a redistribution of demand. The performance of an individual hotel depended to a significant extent on its location and format. Guests still want to take vacations, but they have become much more careful in assessing the conditions under which they are willing to do so," said Rehina Shapovalova, head of sales at Ribas Management.
One of the season's main behavioral findings was a change in booking lead times. In May, the average booking window was 62 days, compared with 44 days a year earlier. However, this trend did not persist: as the season approached, guests once again began making decisions closer to their departure dates, indicating that demand remained highly dependent on the current situation in individual regions. As forecast, the average length of stay remained above three nights.
The largest discrepancy between forecasts and actual results was recorded in Odesa. Ribas Hotels Group had expected occupancy of at least 75% across the city and 85% across the region, but the actual seasonal rate reached only 63%. At the same time, the average room rate in the Odesa cluster increased by approximately 21% compared with the summer of 2025, while the actual average nightly rate in May-August was UAH 3,688.
"The main factor this summer was not so much purchasing power as location," Shapovalova said.
According to her, even guests who had the means and were willing to pay more declined to stay at hotels in the city center or near critical infrastructure facilities.
Another distinctive feature of Odesa was that the highest room rates and the largest tourist flows did not coincide in time. Hotels managed to maintain strong results in June and July, whereas in August, traditionally one of the busiest and most expensive months, visitor numbers fell short of expectations.
Expectations of a 19% increase in demand in the Carpathians also failed to materialize, although a number of hotels in Bukovel operated at high occupancy during peak periods. Depending on the property, average hotel occupancy was 56%, reaching 100% on peak days and exceeding 80% in July and August. The average seasonal ADR was UAH 5,235.
"The flow of guests who did not travel to Odesa did not automatically shift to Bukovel. The same transportation problems affected their choices, while in Bukovel itself, guests also experienced discomfort because of active construction. As a result, demand was redistributed to surrounding areas, particularly cottages and countryside resorts. Overall, the desire to take vacations has not disappeared, but the security situation, transport accessibility and expectations about the near future had a significant impact on guests' choices," the expert said.
An unusual result was the distribution of occupancy in Zakarpattia: demand for vacations throughout the week was more evenly spread than anticipated in the May forecast. During most of the season, there was virtually no significant difference between weekdays and weekends, with occupancy fluctuating between 56% and 58%. In August, which is usually the peak month, the gap became somewhat more pronounced: occupancy was approximately 67% on weekdays and 72% on weekends. Seasonal ADR reached UAH 7,254.34.
In Lviv region, the May forecast was confirmed: average occupancy in August was approximately 79%, with no significant declines on weekdays. The seasonal ADR for hotels in Lviv region reached UAH 2,738.23, up 10% from last year.
Shapovalova noted that this summer, alongside large resort complexes that remained popular with families because of their swimming pools, spas and infrastructure, demand for cottages increased noticeably in both the Carpathians and Kyiv region. The average ADR in this segment was UAH 6,662, up 8% year over year. In particular, Mandra Morion in Mykulychyn, Ivano-Frankivsk region, recorded average occupancy of 73%, up 5%. At Mandra Petrichor in Kyiv region, average occupancy was 58%, including 51% on weekdays and 78% on weekends.
Safety was a key factor, and its influence only intensified toward the end of the season. Guests increasingly asked whether hotels had shelters, particularly when booking in Odesa and other potentially dangerous regions. They assessed not only whether a shelter was available at the hotel itself but also the property's location in relation to potentially dangerous facilities.
"This summer, there were no cases of hotels in the Ribas Hotels network canceling confirmed bookings. At the same time, changes in the security and transportation situation affected guests' own choices: they could decide against particular locations and instead choose other regions or vacation formats," Shapovalova said.
According to the expert, the main positive signal of the summer was that Ukrainians continued to find opportunities to take vacations despite difficult security and transportation conditions. For the hotel industry, this means a need to adapt quickly to changing demand and offer a range of formats tailored to different audiences. On the negative side, the season once again highlighted how fragile even the most carefully prepared forecasts can be, Shapovalova noted.
"When we see positive trends and use them as the basis for our plans and strategy, external factors beyond our control can very quickly change the picture. That is why it remains important for us not only to forecast demand accurately but also to be flexible enough to respond promptly to changes. And, of course, guest safety remains one of our top priorities," she concluded.
Ribas Hotels Group is an international full-cycle hotel management company and hospitality business ecosystem established in Odesa in 2014. Its portfolio includes more than 50 projects under construction, in the launch phase or under management in Ukraine, Poland, Türkiye and Bali. The company develops urban and resort hotels under the Ribas Hotels, Ribas Rooms, WOL home + hotel and Mandra Moments brands.

US Senate Armed Services Committee chair sees no end to war through Ukraine relinquishing sovereign territories
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:05:20 EEST
03:05:20 KST

U.S. Republican Senator Roger Wicker, who chairs the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee, stated that he does not see an end to the war in Ukraine coming at the cost of Ukraine giving up its sovereign territories.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, he made these remarks at a press conference in Kyiv on Friday.
Wicker said Russian President Vladimir Putin would not be able to defeat the Ukrainian people either this year or next. He added that, if allowed to do so, Putin could make life unbearable for Ukrainians and said he believed this was precisely what the Russian leader was seeking to achieve.
He noted that winter was approaching and recalled that the previous winter had been very difficult for Ukrainians because of Russian attacks.
Wicker said it was not yet clear how difficult conditions would be, but argued that the Russian leader intended to make people's lives unbearable. He added that, beyond power outages and the lack of heating and light, Putin also intended to target the water supply system in order to intensify the suffering of civilians.
According to Wicker, Ukrainians did not want such conditions but were prepared to endure them.
He concluded that, given the events of recent years and the current circumstances, he did not see an end to the war that would involve Ukrainians relinquishing sovereign territory seized as a result of what he described as an invasion in violation of international law.

US sanctions on ICC 'brash attempt' to dismantle international legal system: UN experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:04:59 UTC
03:04:59 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
- Experts urge governments to defend court's independence and call on EU to activate Blocking Statute to shield ICC from sanctions
- UN human rights chief warns against chilling effect, urging all 125 states party to Rome Statute to take urgent steps to safeguard court's operations
UN experts warned Friday that US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) amounted to a "brash attempt" to dismantle the international justice system, urging governments to protect the court's independence.
"Sanctioning the institution entrusted with delivering justice for the gravest international crimes is an assault on the foundations of international accountability and rule of law," the experts said in a statement.
The warning followed Washington's imposition of sanctions on the ICC as an institution, after earlier measures targeting more than 10 current or former ICC judges and personnel, as well as a UN special rapporteur.
The experts said the sanctions directly harmed victims of atrocities who relied on the court for justice, accountability and reparations.
"The sanctions are aimed at bringing the ICC to its knees; and ensuring US allies are not held accountable for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity," they said.
The experts urged the EU to immediately activate its Blocking Statute to prevent European operators, including banks and service providers, from complying with third-country sanctions that violate international law.
They also called on governments to protect ICC personnel and individuals working with the court.
The experts urged states to use existing international agreements to mitigate the impact of the sanctions and safeguard the court's operations.
"Silence and inaction will only embolden further attacks. States must act collectively now to protect this Court," they warned.   
UN rights chief calls US sanctions 'unacceptable'
Separately, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk described the US sanctions as "unacceptable," calling for immediate measures to protect the court and those cooperating with it.
"These sanctions – the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel for the work they do every day to advance accountability for the very worst violations of human rights – are unacceptable," Turk said in a statement Friday.
He warned against allowing the measures to have a chilling effect on individuals and organizations working with the court, urging all 125 states party to the Rome Statute to take urgent steps to safeguard its operations.
"They have a particular obligation to protect the institution they have created," he stressed.
Calling for the withdrawal of all sanctions against the ICC and its personnel, Turk said: "We need to be investing more in ensuring justice and accountability – rather than penalizing those who are documenting, investigating and prosecuting serious violations."

Spain and Greece refuse to transfer Patriot systems to Ukraine whose service life is nearing its end - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:04:14 EEST
03:04:14 KST

Spain and Greece refuse to transfer Patriot systems to Ukraine whose service life is nearing its end - media
Kyiv • UNN
Greece and Spain have Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose service life is expiring. NATO and the EU are calling on them to transfer them to Ukraine.
Greece and Spain possess stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems whose expiration dates are approaching. These missiles could be transferred to Ukraine, but the countries have so far refused, reports UNN, citing The Telegraph.
The publication notes that Greece and Spain— two NATO countries—have some of the largest stocks of such missiles in Europe, while Kyiv is persistently asking for additional means of protection against Russia's plans to carry out the most severe long-range mass strikes of the war.
Ukrainian officials have disclosed information about intercepted Russian plans for a new campaign aimed at destroying the country's energy system, with the goal of plunging cities into darkness and testing the population's resilience during the winter period.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly called on allies to provide more interceptor missiles for the American Patriot systems currently in Ukraine—the most effective systems for shooting down enemy warheads.
Kyiv fears that Russian forces could use a thousand missiles, drones, and aerial bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, as well as the infrastructure of Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine needs between 300 and 360 Patriot interceptor missiles to withstand Russia's winter campaign.
Given the urgent need to provide Ukraine with the necessary means, efforts have focused on encouraging Greece and Spain to transfer part of their stocks.
NATO and EU representatives have tried to persuade Greece and Spain to transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles to Ukraine whose expiration dates are approaching.
Greece is believed to have at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles, whose service life—calculated at 23 years—will soon expire.
The exact number of missiles in Spain's reserve is unknown, although last month the country's foreign minister announced that Madrid would transfer five interceptors to Kyiv.
Participants in the talks are reluctant to name the two countries publicly, fearing that this could damage relations with them.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas raised the issue during talks in Ireland last month, stating: "We know that some countries have interceptor missiles whose expiration dates will soon pass. So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine."
As a diplomatic source told The Telegraph, the approach chosen is to ask Greece and Spain: "How can we help you make this decision?"
"It would be logical if at least those interceptor missiles whose expiration dates are approaching were sent to Ukraine," the interlocutor added.
Interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, like other missiles, have a specified storage life during which the manufacturer guarantees their effectiveness.
Fabian Hoffmann, a missile-weapons expert from the University of Oslo, said: "The manufacturer guarantees that the missile will function properly for a certain period of time. After this period ends, the missiles must undergo recertification.
During recertification, components whose expiration dates have passed—such as batteries or rocket engines—are replaced, and the operability of the remaining systems is also checked.
Of course, missiles may function even after their expiration date, but if they fail, the manufacturer bears no responsibility for this."
Ukraine receives 95% of its Patriot missiles through a NATO-led initiative that involves using European funds to directly purchase these interceptors from the United States.
However, the war with Iran has caused a global shortage that even Washington is finding difficult to overcome.
According to some estimates, the United States and its allies used at least 800 Patriot interceptor missiles in the first days of the conflict that erupted in February.
At the time, senior Ukrainian officials said that Kyiv had received only 600 such missiles over four years.
Earlier this year, the Ukrainian Air Force stopped publishing daily data on the number of intercepted ballistic missiles amid an increasingly acute shortage of ammunition.
Anonymous sources cited by The New York Times suggest that the U.S. stockpile of Patriot missiles may total fewer than 1,700 units.
This raised questions about the Pentagon's readiness to replenish Ukraine's supplies at a time when the United States itself is engaged in hostilities against Iran.
The Telegraph approached the defense ministries of Greece and Spain for comment.

Commercial operations can begin once the companies meet the prescribed requirements.The government has also said security clearances remain pending for all three licensed operators, rejecting the suggestion that Starlink alone is facing regulatory hurdles.

Boluda Towage eyeing acquisition of Ukraine's LBS Towage from TIS co-owners
Ukraine

2026-10-09
21:02:11 EEST
03:02:11 KST

The Antimonopoly Committee of Ukraine (AMCU) has authorized BT Black Sea S.a.r.l. (Luxembourg), owned by global port towage operator Boluda Towage S.L. (Spain), to acquire control of Ukrainian tugboat operator LLC LBSH, whose beneficiaries are co-owners of TIS, Ukraine's largest privately owned stevedoring company.
According to a statement published on the AMCU website, the relevant decision was adopted Thursday. The committee also authorized BT Black Sea S.a.r.l. and Cornlex Impex Limited (Nicosia, Cyprus) to engage in coordinated actions involving a five-year noncompete commitment stipulated in the July 1, 2026, Shareholders' Agreement concerning LBSH between Cornlex Impex Limited, ConTerm UKR SARL (the former name of BT Black Sea) and LBSH.
According to the Luxembourg registry, BT Black Sea S.a.r.l. was registered in June this year under the name ConTerm UKR SARL, with share capital of EUR 12,000. Later that month, Boluda Towage became its owner, and in September the company adopted its current name.
According to its website, Boluda Towage is one of the world's leading maritime services providers. The company operates worldwide and manages a fleet of more than 400 vessels in 100 ports across 18 countries on four continents: Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America.
In 2025, shipping group Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), also one of the world's largest ocean container carriers, acquired a 49% stake in Boluda Towage.
In June this year, it was reported that MSC had acquired a 51% stake in the TIS container terminal at the Pivdenny Port.
According to YouControl, the other owners and beneficiaries of the TIS container terminal are Oleksiy Fedorychev and his Fedcom Invest SAM, with an 18.375% stake; Oleh Kutateladze, with a 9.19% stake; and brothers Yehor Hrebennikov and Andriy Stavnitser, with stakes of 11.72% and 9.72%, respectively.
LBSH LLC is registered in Odesa region and specializes in activities related to water transport services, including providing tugboat services at Ukraine's seaports.
According to YouControl, the company's ultimate beneficial owners through BPSh LLC are Hrebennikov (29.7%), Stavnitser (30.35%) and Kutateladze (39.6%).
LBSH's revenue rose by 15.9% in the first half of this year, to UAH 460.3 million, while its net profit increased by 58.9%, to UAH 106.8 million.

Carbon Accounting May Be the Most Important Climate Fight You've Never Heard About
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:01:32 UTC
03:01:32 KST

I’ve found a surefire way to mess with the good vibes during my on-the-record conversations with CEOs and senior executives: bring up carbon accounting. In an instant, a conversation that felt open and transparent moments prior can turn into guarded talking points or simply go quiet.
Carbon accounting may be the wonkiest topic in the already wonky world of climate change and emissions reduction. And few areas inspire more passionate debate and infighting than the rules for measuring and attributing them. But underneath the jargon lies a high-stakes question: who is responsible for each ton of carbon emissions? How that question is answered over the coming months and years will shape everything from climate regulations to corporate energy purchasing decisions.
A report by the Aspen Institute and shared exclusively with me ahead of its Oct. 9 release offers a rare window into that fight. It draws on a multi-day summit this February that brought together the field’s key players—including academics, NGOs, and industry voices—to debate the path forward on how best to account for carbon emissions. I attended the closed-door summit having agreed to report on the discussion without identifying individual participants. It concluded in a ceasefire of sorts with promises to work together even as the core debates remain unresolved.
Future Proof
Weekly
Making sense of the climate and energy economy.
To understand the carbon accounting landscape, you need to understand the system at the center of the debate. For more than two decades, one approach, known as the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHGP), has flourished and become the de facto global standard. Under GHGP’s approach, emissions are divided into scopes: Scope 1 for direct emissions from a company’s operations, Scope 2 from a company’s purchased electricity, heat, and cooling, and Scope 3 for value chain emissions. The GHGP approach has driven a variety of guidance documents and informed regulation and certifications issued by other entities.
But, as with any such initiative, GHGP is not perfect. And a growing number of stakeholders—particularly businesses—have called for changes of varying scope and scale.
The resulting fault lines in the carbon accounting debate are many. There are technical questions like over what time scale (hourly vs. annual) companies must match their electricity use with their clean energy purchases. And there are questions about the degree to which carbon accounting relies on estimates rather than true measurements. But, perhaps more than anything else, there is a debate about responsibility: in accounting for emissions, who should really be held responsible?
The technical matters are divisive on their own. The philosophical questions cut to the core of the climate challenge.
The weather in Aspen was unseasonably warm. That didn’t keep the seminar room from turning chilly at times. While no one in Aspen said that the GHGP approach is perfect, perspectives on what to change and by how much varied widely.
Defenders of the current system say that Scope 2 and Scope 3 reporting has motivated voluntary corporate action. Scope 2 rules, in particular, give companies a clear way to claim credit for the clean electricity they buy, and that predictability has helped fuel a boom in long-term renewable power contracts, known as power purchase agreements. And predictability matters. While in theory it may be possible to design a better system, the GHGP approach is entrenched, and it could take decades for a new system to earn such widespread adoption.
The critiques are multifold. The GHGP approach allows for “double-counting.” In other words, multiple companies end up accounting for the same emissions under different scopes. Think of steel in a building. The steel producer, the construction firm, and the building owner are all technically responsible for the steel emissions.
A primary alternative approach, which originated in academia and now has a coalition of industry players advocating for it, accounts for emissions using “e-ledgers.” Every unit of emissions is accounted for once, placed on a ledger, and then transferred as a product moves through the world. It’s an elegant approach with real advantages. It would incentivize companies to focus on decarbonizing their own operations and give them high-quality emissions data to use in procurement. But some in the room in Aspen noted that it would be difficult to implement. It only really works if every single player on the value chain participates.
The sharpest divide, however, concerns emissions from using a product. Under GHGP’s Scope 3, an oil company counts the emissions from every gallon of gasoline its customers burn. That is the primary driver of its enormous carbon footprint. An e-ledger works differently, with emissions traveling with a product and responsibility belonging to whoever does the burning. That leaves consumers with greater accountability even if they have little influence over the broader system.
The e-ledger approach emerged from the corners of academia in a series of highly publicized articles beginning in 2021. And, in 2025, a coalition of companies including ExxonMobil, BlackRock, and others backed the launch of a business coalition to advocate for an e-ledger approach.
At the same time, the call for change comes amid the retrenchment of climate from its front and center position in the public zeitgeist, making some companies less willing to commit the resources necessary to fully embrace the work required by GHGP. GHGP has responded, hiring a new CEO and instituting a string of reforms.
Given the stakes and the players involved, it’s no surprise that the conversations in Aspen were heated at times. And yet the summit ended with a detente of sorts, as participants agreed to work together to find common ground. Indeed, some participants noted that e-ledgers can help with tracking a product’s carbon footprint, while the broader GHGP rules should apply for a whole company.
What happens next in this wonky corner of the climate community concerns more people than you might expect. It will shape regulations—including climate disclosure rules in California and the European Union—and affect where businesses target their climate initiatives. Perhaps most importantly, it will affect how we answer the question of who is responsible for future emissions.

Emotional blunting is common in depression and bipolar disorder, even after symptoms ease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:00:15 UTC
03:00:15 KST

A study of Thai outpatients receiving treatment for depression found that more than half reported emotional blunting, a dulling of emotional responses. Rates did not differ significantly among people with major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, and bipolar disorder, and emotional blunting was less common among patients whose depression was in remission, though it remained common in that group as well. The paper was published in BMC Psychiatry.
Major depressive disorder is one of the most common mental health conditions worldwide, affecting hundreds of millions of people. Estimates suggest that its global prevalence rose by roughly 27% in 2020 alone, as the COVID-19 pandemic brought stress, isolation, and economic disruption.
Major depression does not have a single cause but instead develops through a combination of biological, genetic, physical, behavioral, and environmental influences. Adverse childhood experiences such as abuse, neglect, bullying, and domestic violence are particularly important risk factors and are also associated with poorer treatment response and a greater chance of depression recurrence.
One common feature of depression is emotional blunting, in which people experience reduced emotional responsiveness. The term covers experiences such as apathy, loss of motivation, anhedonia (a reduced ability to feel pleasure), emotional numbness, and diminished empathy. Emotional blunting appears to be especially common during acute episodes of depression and may persist after treatment.
Emotional blunting is also a known side effect of some antidepressants, particularly selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, which can leave people feeling emotionally indifferent or unable to cry. It can impair daily functioning, and in one recent study, up to 40% of patients said they had considered stopping their antidepressant because of it.
Study author Narak Chadbunchachai and colleagues at Khon Kaen University in Thailand set out to measure how common emotional blunting is among patients whose depression was mild to moderate or in remission, and to examine its links to childhood adversity. They expected emotional blunting to be more intense among remitted patients who had experienced more adversity in childhood.
Participants were 106 outpatients at a university hospital in Thailand who had major depressive disorder (61 of them), persistent depressive disorder (19), or bipolar I disorder (26). Persistent depressive disorder is a long-lasting form of depression in which a person has a depressed mood for most of the day, on more days than not, for at least two years, often with additional symptoms such as low energy, poor self-esteem, and hopelessness. Participants’ average age was 29 years, and 73% were women.
To take part, patients had to have mild to moderate symptoms, could not be at risk of suicide, and had to have been on the same antidepressant treatment for at least a month. Half of the participants met the criteria for remission, meaning they had few remaining symptoms on a clinician-rated depression scale.
Participants were first asked a single screening question from the Oxford Depression Questionnaire about whether, in the past six weeks, they had felt emotionally numbed or blunted, detached from the world around them, or as if they no longer cared about things they used to care about. They then completed the full 26-item questionnaire, which measures the intensity of emotional blunting across several dimensions, along with a questionnaire on adverse childhood experiences and two measures of depression severity.
Based on the screening question, 56% of participants reported emotional blunting. The rate was 51% among those with major depressive disorder, 63% among those with persistent depressive disorder, and 62% among those with bipolar disorder, differences that were not statistically significant. On the full questionnaire, most participants scored in the “minimal” range, 36% scored in the “mild” range, and one person scored in the “severe” range.
Emotional blunting was less common among participants whose depression had remitted (45%) than among those whose depression had not (66%). Across the whole sample, people with more severe depressive symptoms and more past mood episodes tended to report more intense emotional blunting, though these associations were modest. Among remitted patients, blunting was not linked to symptom severity.
The links with childhood adversity were limited to specific parts of the questionnaire and were weak. One aspect of emotional blunting, not caring about things, tended to be stronger among participants who reported more frequent emotional or physical abuse in childhood and among those who reported less emotional support from their families. Overall emotional blunting scores were not significantly linked to any type of childhood adversity.
Among remitted patients, the links between not caring and both emotional abuse and low emotional support held, and a second aspect, feeling emotionally detached, was associated with more frequent domestic violence in childhood. When the researchers accounted for how much participants attributed their blunting to their antidepressants, only the link between not caring and low emotional support remained statistically significant.
“Remission was associated with a lower prevalence of EB [emotional blunting]; however, the prevalence remained high even among remitters,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about depression. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Additionally, the assessment of adverse childhood experiences was based on participants’ current memories of their childhood events, leaving room for recall bias to have affected the results.
All participants were taking antidepressants, and more than 90% attributed at least some of their emotional blunting to their medication. Because the study had no comparison group of remitted patients who were not taking antidepressants, it cannot separate emotional blunting as a lingering symptom of depression from emotional blunting as a side effect of treatment.
The paper, “Prevalence of emotional blunting and its association with childhood adverse experiences in depressive episodes,” was authored by Narak Chadbunchachai, Papan Vadhanavikkit, Sirinapa Aphisitphinyo, Pattharee Paholpak, Nawanant Piyavhatkul, Parinda Pienroj, and Pongsatorn Paholpak.

Labor's surcharge headache exposes a government on the back foot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Labor reverses credit card surcharge call after backlash, but businesses are still angry
Australia's fastest drivers are descending on Bathurst this weekend, but it's Treasurer Jim Chalmers setting records for reversing at speed.
Fresh from a trip to Japan, where he met with investors to sell Australia as an economic partner, Chalmers announced two spectacular government backdowns.
First, he revealed Labor would temporarily cover the cost of surcharges so the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) ban on credit card payments could be delayed by six months.
Then he confirmed the government would scrap proposed changes to disaster recovery funding that would have resulted in the Commonwealth reducing its contribution from 75 to 50 per cent.
The treasurer remained composed throughout the hastily arranged press conference on Friday — every government's favoured day for "taking out the trash" — but he was plainly spinning his wheels.
Chalmers argued the two decisions showed the Albanese government took feedback "very seriously".
By feedback he presumably meant 10 days of Labor getting absolutely rinsed on social media, talkback radio and any other platform the small business community could find.
Messaging a mess from the start
The surcharge debacle has been a source of political pain both in terms of public backlash toward the government and internal Labor grumbling about Chalmers.
Yesterday's announcement somewhat addressed the former, but the treasurer's attempt to assert the ATO had made its own decisions was viewed by many colleagues as farcical.
By Chalmers' own admission, the government knew the ATO was preparing to make a tough call and even asked for the initial two-month transition period.
Nothing screams "independent decision" like a government being actively involved in discussions and then intervening to change the outcome when the backlash became too intense.
It also might have been easier for the ATO to make the case it could not justify foisting $200 million in surcharge costs onto the taxpayer, had the government not decided to take responsibility for what was a regulatory decision by the Reserve Bank.
The messaging around the entire issue was a mess from the start, though Chalmers's ill-timed trip to Japan did not help.
All week, senior government members variously defended the call to ban credit card payments on tax bills, urged the ATO to consult further or, by Thursday, outright raised "concern" with the decision.
There was nowhere else to go but reverse if Labor wanted to avoid an unnecessarily bruising parliamentary sitting next week.
Transparency measure gets co-opted
The confusion around the tax issue wasn't the only comms misstep.
On the day the surcharge ban took effect, Labor MPs and ministers — including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese — cheerily posted to social media promoting the change as a cost-of-living measure.
But the accumulated fee charged by banks, card networks and terminal providers was always going to be passed onto the consumer.
The ban on surcharges was about making the cost of accepting cards visible and more competitive, rather than a "surprise" at the end of a transaction.
It was a transparency measure.
That's why the prime minister's Instagram video telling Australians they would save $1.6 billion a year in fees fell so flat.
It garnered about 250,000 views this week — along with a barrage of negative comments — while videos and memes shared by influencers and small businesses criticising the move racked up as many as 2 million or even 6 million views apiece.
The satirical content suggested customers were in fact the big losers, because a cup of coffee had gone from $5 plus an 8 cent surcharge to $5.50 following the ban.
It was a mark of how much the government was on the backfoot that not one Labor MP managed to argue that removing such a surcharge did not, by itself, justify a 50 cent price hike.
Sure, small businesses maintained there had been rising costs across the board that warranted the level of price increases, but that still doesn't negate the very basic maths.
The electorate is angry
Labor has been able to draw this nuanced distinction before.
The government has ended temporary cuts to the fuel excise twice, making clear that any price rises beyond the restored tax would be unacceptable for consumers.
Chalmers was notably effective in 2022 when he also framed the end of the excise as a moment for an honest, adult conversation with Australians about budget pressures.
Aside from the treasurer's absence this week, the other factor now making it harder for the government to launch this kind of argument is the broader economic and political environment.
The electorate is angry. They are getting poorer and feeling under strain, and are no longer predisposed to give this government the benefit of the doubt.
If a voter sees a social media post about Labor making their coffee cost 50 cents more, they are far more likely to accept the assertion and look for no further evidence.
On multiple occasions this year the government has been slow to react to backlash percolating on meme pages.
The prevailing view inside Labor is that the small business community — and particularly those currently racking up millions of views on pithy Instagram reels — are not their core voters.
But the mistake is assuming the audience for those complaints is confined to the people making them.
Discontent spreads quickly, explanations struggle to keep up, and Labor has increasingly been on the defensive over decisions of its own making.
Like a driver at Mount Panorama who brakes too late at Conrod Straight, Chalmers has found himself in the gravel trap, having badly misjudged the conditions.

How Firmus, the biggest IPO in three decades, fell over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

How Firmus's plans for the biggest IPO in three decades fell over
It was supposed to be the second-biggest stock float in Australian history.
Sydney-based AI startup Firmus Technologies was close to listing on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) at a $43.7 billion market capitalisation.
It would have been the biggest IPO since Telstra listed in 1997.
The company, founded in 2019 by Oliver Curtis, Tim Rosenfield and Jonathan Levee, had planned to raise about $7 billion by going public.
The intention was to list and then borrow more to build data centres across Australia, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
Investors grow anxious
By Wednesday night, the IPO plans began to unravel and reports emerged that bankers were considering lowering the share price and valuation towards $30 billion.
On Thursday morning, as Firmus scrambled to save the IPO, it withdrew from appearing at a federal parliamentary inquiry into AI.
By Friday, the founders's grand plans had fallen apart and the float was pulled.
Despite being backed by global AI giant Nvidia, investors had grown anxious.
Firmus had previously said it secured $US2 billion ($2.86 billion) in commitments from investors, including Nvidia and Blackstone.
Other potential investors felt the company's share price offer was overpriced, some felt there was not enough detailed information in the IPO prospectus, and many were spooked that the rapid growth of AI and data centres would soon stop.
The founders are now hoping to pursue further private funding and Firmus will attempt to list on the Nasdaq next year.
What caused the Firmus float to fail?
A mixture of factors led to the float's demise, including the high per-share price offer, which by Thursday had reportedly fallen from $11 to $8.25.
The company was being given a similar valuation to Woolworths, according to Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway.
"The economics look good now and the growth is very fast now, but what that looks like again in five or 10 years is the big question mark," he said.
The timing of the IPO was also wrong.
Commentators say fears of an AI bubble, set against a backdrop of mounting concerns from politicians and the community about the rapid rise of data centres, also played a part.
"Firmus ran into a wall of AI anxiety right at the time that they had planned to list," Philip Wohl from Reliance Investment Research said.
And then there was some angst over Mr Curtis's colourful past. He served a year in jail in 2016-17 for insider trading before co-founding Firmus as a bitcoin mining company in 2019.
Mr Wohl said Firmus's assertion that it was market volatility that prevented it listing at its desired price was "a euphemistic way of describing exactly what happened".
"The market is more uncertain now when it comes to AI hardware and, given the perhaps aggressive pricing that they were targeting, they really didn't see the demand," he said.
'They do have to come back to the market'
Ten Cap Investment co-founder and lead portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said the IPO was overpriced, but thought a second attempt was on the cards.
"The valuation for the company was way too high to start with," she said.
"It is almost three times what the valuation was when they raised money just a few months ago.
"At some stage they do have to come back to the market simply because it's a very capital-intensive business. It requires listed shares."
Floodline Research founder Anna Wu said the founders should have tried to list in the United States because the Nasdaq was a bigger and more accepting market than the ASX for emerging tech.
"The downside is much tougher competition and, as an Australian company, Firmus may struggle to attract the same attention and valuation as its US peers," she said.
The Nasdaq has recently hit record highs and is up 43 per cent in the past year, but Australia's tech sector has faltered by comparison.
The ASX All Technology Index, which tracks the share prices of 42 tech-linked stocks on the ASX, has dropped almost 18 per cent this year, including 9 per cent in September alone.
In part that is because Australian technology listings are more heavily skewed towards software companies, which have been sold off in the so-called SaaSpocalypse as investors have worried that AI will undercut their business models.
Investors were also questioning whether Australia had the energy infrastructure energy to support data centres.
"We're in a slightly different regime now for AI, in terms of its life cycle," Ms Wu said.
"It's no longer 2023, where everything's about big ideas and anything with AI in the name would go past any valuation test."
She said the lack of details on the Firmus IPO and concerns about Mr Curtis's criminal past also weighed on some investors.
"That creates more ambiguity," she said.
"So when the market gets hit by oil anxiety every second day, and when investors are facing a much higher capital cost, that would actually drive the question on the valuation.
"It probably sends the sentiment signal to the broader community that right now an IPO is not a free lunch anymore."
Nvidia's play in an Aussie startup
Nvidia was contacted for comment about its position on Firmus after the IPO flop.
Ms Wu said Firmus was likely tap the AI giant for a greater investment.
Nvidia already has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus and has reportedly been providing funding as well as selling Firmus its chips.
"Nvidia … is going around the world buying anything that it thinks is going to take over in the local market," Ms Wu said.
Mr Holloway said the investment made sense because Firmus data centres got "their chips out there".
For customers such as Meta and OpenAi, partnering with companies such as Firmus can be the only option to access these chips.
"There is a very, very short supply of Nvidia's high-quality chips and a lot of demand for AI model training," Mr Holloway said.
"If you had access to those chips, which Firmus did with its partnership with Nvidia, you can basically name your price."
Ms Wu said the backing of Nvidia was still on the cards.
"Nvidia's long-term partnership with Firmus is an endorsement … but also, it's a move towards expanding in the Australia-Pacific region and trying to integrate with the local infrastructure provider," she said.
'Too many unknowns' about IPO
Mr Curtis and his publicist wife Roxy Jacenko opened up a Singapore office two years ago, sparking intrigue from the Australian expat population.
But IPOs in Australia are notoriously challenging to get right.
Mr Holloway said the IPO uncertainty had led more companies in Australia to put off listing.
"We've seen the number of IPOs on the ASX fall considerably in the last few years," he said.
Rather than "floating in public markets, remaining in private hands is becoming much easier" because a surplus of private cash.
But analysts say IPOs being delayed or pulled is likely to become more common.
Firmus's website said it had two sites operational in Australia and Singapore, and that five were "under development".
"There were just too many unknowns here and it required too much optimism for investors to take that leap of faith with Firmus," Mr Wohl said.

Breadcrumb
Flight cancellations hit Saudi capital Riyadh amid Houthi attacks
Airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and countries have issued warnings against travel to the country as Houthi ballistic missile attacks continue to target the kingdom's airports, leading to numerous casualties.
Among the airlines that have suspended flights are Lufthansa, which said that flights to Riyadh were suspended through to 16 October due to "current developments in the Middle East".
India's Indigo has also cancelled its flights to the city until 9 October, while Air India and Alaska Air have suspended flights until 10 October, according to Reuters.
Alongside airlines, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) announced on Friday that it has expanded the airspace within Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks.
"These recurrent missile and drone attacks, together with the activation of air defence systems, create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft, as well as risks associated with missile and drone overflights, interception activity and falling debris," the agency warned.
EASA warned that while southern and south-western parts of Saudi airspace "remain particularly exposed," Riyadh, Tabuk, Medina and Yanbu were also flagged as risks for airlines.
The membership-based organisation OPSGROUP also issued its own warning against flying to Saudi Arabia on Friday.
The warnings against flying to Saudi Arabia come as the war in Yemen continues to escalate following a Houthi offensive launched in Taiz province in September.
On Sunday, Yemen's government announced a general offensive nationwide aimed at retaking the capital Sanaa, with Saudi Arabia providing airpower to support the campaign.
As part of the escalation, the Houthis have launched drone and ballistic missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, initially against energy installations, though this has escalated to the targeting of airports in the country.
This includes Riyadh airport, where Houthi attacks killed three people on Thursday, and a Saudia Airlines plane was also destroyed.
Saudia Airlines issued an obituary for one of their employees, a pilot, who was killed in an attack on Thursday.
The Houthis launched follow-up attacks on Friday, with their spokesperson posting on X that "humanitarian flights to/from Riyadh Airport will be permitted for all flights authorised by the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center based in the capital Sana'a."
Flights to the airport continued throughout the day, despite strikes and Houthi threats.
Alongside flight cancellations, several countries warned their citizens to exercise caution when travelling to the country, including the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Development Office, which issued advice against all but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province, and Taif City and Taif International Airport.
Alongside the UK, both Japan and the US also issued travel warnings to Saudi Arabia amid the escalation.

US sanctions court that seeks to arrest Putin, prompts backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:57:08 UTC
02:57:08 KST

The U.S. on Oct. 9 imposed severe financial sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), which issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2023.
The new sanctions would prohibit transactions with the court after a grace period of six months. Any companies doing business with the court afterward can be punished by the U.S. government.
The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. issued a joint statement in support of the ICC on Oct. 9.
"We... reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," they said. "As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the court by the United States."
The ministers said that they appreciate "the work undertaken by the court to prepare for such measures so that the Court can continue to fulfil its mandate under the Rome Statute and we underline our unwavering support in enabling the court in doing so."
"Nevertheless, if put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families," they said. ".... We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties as we prepare for the Assembly of States Parties in December 2026. We will continue to work together to support the court’s vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability."
In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and another Russian official, Maria Lvova-Belova, for "unlawful transfer of population (children) from occupied areas of Ukraine to the Russian Federation."
Previously, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had also sanctioned many of the court's judges individually.
Trump has criticized the ICC's attempts to investigate alleged crimes committed by U.S. military personnel and its actions against Israel.
In 2024, the court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, then Israel's defense minister, as part of an investigation into alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The court, set up in 2002 and based at The Hague in the Netherlands, investigates genocide, war crimes, and other offenses.

Nigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion.

Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one.
The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed.
In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place.
The investigation into Farage’s gift began after the Guardian revealed in May that the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.
The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.
Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members.
They would then have further discussions and call a further hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty. That process can take weeks. The MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more.
If parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, a recall petition could be held, requiring signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over a period of six weeks.
In the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats, and Conservatives are hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister.
But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the byelection against independent candidates including Count Binface by more than 11,000 votes.
He has also recently embarked on a tour of the country, in an attempt to shore up his core support, and a reorganisation of his party HQ. This includes launching a new Reform TV channel to pump out the party’s message direct to voters, hiring a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations.
Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, when he beat the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling. The Conservative had previously won the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate in the seat.

"Another issue is that most of these buses are school buses purchased by territorial communities using partial funding from the state budget. This made it possible to deliver nearly 200 new buses in September alone, 64% more than last year," the group said in a statement on its website.
The new bus market grew by 2.6% over the first nine months of the year.
Experts believe that the unusual pattern of bus deliveries observed in September this year was related to the financing of these purchases. As a result, a significant volume of deliveries took place not at the beginning of the school year, but during its first month.

Four families, four stories of separation. The authors of ‘Stolen Youth,’ a new book from Meduza about how Russia abducted thousands of Ukrainian children, explain why they wrote it.

17:51:58 UTC
02:51:58 KST

Four families, four stories of separation. The authors of ‘Stolen Youth,’ a new book from Meduza about how Russia abducted thousands of Ukrainian children, explain why they wrote it.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, thousands of Ukrainian children have ended up in Russia. The scenarios varied: some fled the combat zone, and the only way out led through the Russian border; others were taken from occupied territories deeper into the occupying country, often under false pretenses, such as a school trip; still others were sent by their own parents to Russian children’s camps to escape the danger, only for the parents to later find they couldn’t get them back. The Russian state made active use of this: it placed the children with new families and even issued them new passports on an expedited basis. In 2023, the International Criminal Court in The Hague ruled that the removal of children from Ukraine was a war crime. Journalists Nina Nazarova (Russia) and Sviatoslav Khomenko (Ukraine) have collected in their book ”Stolen Youth: How Russia Kidnaps Ukrainian Children — And How Ukrainians Get Them Back” four different stories of families who fell victim to this crime, and have also described in detail those who organized the removal of children, and those who are still helping bring them home.
We published this book together with the StraightForward Foundation, which helps create uncensored nonfiction about Russia.
Nina Nazarova, coauthor of ‘Stolen Youth’
This book began in April 2022. I was watching a conference of Russian officials live on YouTube for work — usually a dreary spectacle. But this video stunned me: For the first time, I heard officials openly acknowledge that they had brought thousands of Ukrainian children into Russia, including from Ukrainian cities that the Russian army had just destroyed.
At that moment, a year before the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova on suspicion of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children, some journalistic instinct told me that these children would become a central issue in this war.
Our book puts a human face on the legal term “unlawful deportation.” It tells the stories of four families, the four very different ways their children were separated from their loved ones, and how difficult, sometimes impossible, it was for them to get home. These are stories of human resilience — children’s resilience, too — that even the most unpredictable circumstances couldn’t break.
Whatever happens on the battlefield and in negotiations, thousands of Ukrainian children are already living as Russians, their identities altered, their citizenship changed. In any event, the consequences will be felt for years and decades to come — simply because people live a long time, and traumas like these rarely heal without leaving a mark. Our book is a first attempt to show and make sense of what happened through the lives, experiences, and suffering of individual people. It’s important to remember that behind every figure officials cite are real children, each of whom deserves to be with their loved ones and grow up in peace in their home country.
Sviatoslav Khomenko, coauthor of ‘Stolen Youth’
By the time Nina called and suggested we write a book together about how Russia steals Ukrainian children and how Ukrainians try to bring them back, I had already written or co-written several articles on the subject. It’s probably what most sharply distinguishes the war Russia unleashed from other wars of our time. An investigator from the International Criminal Court and staff from the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights had already contacted us with questions about it.
From the first days of the full-scale invasion, it was clear that Russia’s goals went beyond parading its troops down Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s main street, removing Ukraine’s defiant president, and forcing the neighboring country into the “Russian fold.” Ukrainian children were a separate target.
Russian officials were positively proud that their state was bringing thousands of Ukrainian children into Russia, giving them new names, finding them new families, and then turning little Ukrainians into little Russians using manuals written specifically for that purpose.
Realizing the scale of what was happening sent a chill down my spine. Russia claimed it was rescuing the children — children it had stolen itself — from the hardships and horrors of war and all but expected gratitude for its actions. This was pure gaslighting, and it made me question my own grasp of reality.
Still, for me, writing this book felt like putting together a puzzle. The tears of a woman from Balakliia whose teenage son didn’t come home from a children’s camp; Vladimir Medinsky’s boorish remarks about the children Russia had stolen; new school curricula for Ukrainian children in occupied territories; the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin — as we wrote the book, these and many other details came together into one big picture. A picture that simply cannot be ignored or overshadowed by the other, perhaps more obvious, consequences of the war Russia unleashed.
Sometimes I imagine that someday I’ll tell my daughter a fairy tale about an evil sorcerer who fancied himself ruler of the world, stole children, and wanted to turn them into his servants. In the fairy tale, though, the children’s moms and dads and the many good people who helped them managed to free them all and bring them home.
But the story told in this book has no happy ending. Russia has taken the lives of hundreds of Ukrainian boys and girls and stolen the childhoods of thousands. And now, as I write these words, it continues to hold thousands of Ukrainian children on its territory.
If this book helps bring the world’s attention back to the children who can still be helped, then we won’t have written it in vain.

Just one day after the attempted downing of a Flydubai flight bound for Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said investigators had determined that the Omani co-pilot had undergone "Islamist jihadist brainwashing." But only now, following a statement by the United Arab Emirates' attorney general, has it become clear that the suspect's radicalization began long before his visits to Syria, nearly a decade ago in Australia.
According to the Emirati statement, the suspected attacker, Hamam al-Hammami, confessed that while studying in Melbourne, he regularly attended a mosque affiliated with the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT). During his visits, he became acquainted with people associated with an Islamic center known as MyCentre. Al-Hammami lived in Australia between 2015 and 2017, and the center was headed then, as it is today, by Samir Mohtadi, a preacher known as Abu Hamza.
Mohtadi, whose family is of Lebanese descent but who grew up in Australia, came under scrutiny last year over a sermon and a social media post containing inflammatory anti-Zionist rhetoric. His remarks offer a glimpse into the views promoted by the preacher who leads the organization identified in the suspect's account. However, investigators have not established that Mohtadi or MyCentre played any role in the attempted attack or in al-Hammami's radicalization.
In the statements reported last year, Mohtadi described Zionists as "scavengers" and "bloodsuckers" and declared that Australia was waging a war against Islam. At the same time, he was pursuing plans to establish a multimillion-dollar Islamic complex known as a "sanctuary" through his registered charitable organization.
During a sermon at an Islamic center in Melbourne, attended by a reporter from The Australian, the imam called on Allah to "cast terror into the hearts of the Zionists."
"O Allah, grant victory to our mujahideen in Palestine, strengthen their footing and grant them a clear victory," he said in Arabic. "O Allah, shake the ground beneath the feet of the Zionists. O Allah, deprive them of the blessing of security, scatter their gatherings and tear their unity apart."
Mohtadi also told worshippers that they were not obliged to adopt the values of Australia, despite the country having welcomed them, granted them citizenship and provided them with full political, social and economic rights, including freedom of religion.
"The war being waged here is far more dangerous than the war in Gaza," he preached. "They want to implant in our minds the idea that God does not exist. That is why this is a war over the mind. They want us to doubt Allah, to doubt the Day of Judgment and to doubt the Prophet."
Speaking to the Australian newspaper, Mohtadi defended his right to express his views about Zionism. In a post published on the official Facebook page of the Islamic Information and Services Network of Australasia (IISNA), he declared his absolute opposition to the State of Israel and described Zionists in dehumanizing terms.
"We do not believe in a country called Israel. Every righteous person believes that there is Palestine and that there is no Israel," he said. "I have always said, and I have always believed, that Zionists are not normal. They are bloodsucking human beings, they are scavengers. They are not human, I swear by Allah."
"God willing, may they all return to Russia, Ukraine, America and Britain, and may Palestine be cleansed of these filthy Zionist terrorists," he continued.
Despite the controversy surrounding those statements, IISNA has remained a registered charity in Australia. The organization has also previously received government support for community events and educational initiatives.
The revelations have drawn renewed attention to al-Hammami's years in Melbourne after UAE Attorney General Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi announced Friday that the suspect had intended to seize control of the Flydubai aircraft and crash it into the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport, with the aim of causing the greatest possible number of casualties.
According to the investigation, the first signs of al-Hammami's extremist beliefs emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia. Investigators said he was exposed to radical literature and online material glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide attacks, and eventually became inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.
The suspect has confessed to acting alone, but Emirati authorities are continuing to investigate his connections and the possible involvement of accomplices. His account of contacts in Melbourne has opened another line of scrutiny into his ideological development, although the extent to which individuals he encountered in Australia influenced his plans remains unclear.

British nuclear subs have only fire hoses as drone defense – media
British sailors are drilling to fend off potential drone attacks against £4 billion ($5.3 billion) Vanguard-class subs using fire hoses as the only onboard “air defense weapon,” The Sun has reported.
The hoses, known as “center fed reels” are placed on submarine decks as a precaution when the vessels are moored at the British naval base Clyde in Scotland, the UK’s most sensitive military site, the tabloid reported on Thursday, citing anonymous sources. The equipment has pistol-grip nozzles that would allow sailors to direct water at approaching drones.
“You have to use what you’ve got,” the tabloid cited one of its sources as saying.
The Royal Navy’s four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines are the only British platforms equipped to carry and launch Trident II nuclear missiles, which deliver the UK’s only operational nuclear weapons. According to The Sun, the Navy insists that layered defenses, including “physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities,” protect the subs.
The report comes as the Royal Navy is facing what a former senior commander has described as its worst crisis in 350 years.
The UK’s entire fleet of nuclear-powered Astute-class attack submarines are not fit for combat duty, retired chief of the Naval Staff, Lord Alan West, told The Sun earlier this year. Five of the vessels are facing maintenance and availability delays, while the sixth, according to the Royal Navy, is still undergoing sea trials ahead of returning to service.
West described the number of ships the Navy has as “pathetic.” The fleet has just five operational frigates and no amphibious assault ships, while former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government retired four frigates, two assault ships, two tankers, and a nuclear-powered submarine during his time in office, The Sun reported in July.
This year, the UK has pledged an additional £15 billion in military funding, citing alleged threats from Russia. London has also seized and aided in seizing ships it has accused of being part of the so-called Russian ‘shadow fleet’ – a practice Moscow has denounced as “piracy.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Moscow wants to attack NATO and has accused Western European leaders of escalating tensions with Moscow, pointing to their statements about preparing for a possible war with Russia in 2029 or 2030, repeated military exercises in the Baltic Sea, and attempts to detain Russian vessels. “This is all escalation,” he said last week.

Over 100 groups condemn Israeli actions during so-called 'truce'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
