The Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than words | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:52:10 UTC
01:52:10 KST

By holding Holborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. The seat has substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average 19.3-point fall in four byelections under Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance.
The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of a motion declaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski now says he would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend?
He intends to remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But with calls for his resignation growing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March, YouGov put the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling 10% nationally.
As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating has fallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats.
In an interview with the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, who said she wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion.
Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing the controversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order.

A prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), based on an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), has sent an indictment to court in a case involving the alleged embezzlement of UAH 129 million allocated for the restoration of critical infrastructure in Kamianske district, Dnipropetrovsk region.
Seven people have been charged, including a local businessman alleged to have organized the scheme, the head of the municipal enterprise that commissioned the reconstruction, the director and deputy director of the company that won the tender, the head of an intermediary company used for procurement, a deputy head of the design organization and an employee of a company controlled by the alleged organizer, SAPO said in a Telegram post on Friday.
According to the investigation, members of an organized group helped a company controlled by the alleged organizer win a 2022–2023 tender for reconstruction of a water pipeline in Kamianske district.
Under the contract, the winning company was required to purchase pipes. Investigators found that the pipes were bought from the manufacturer at market prices and then resold to the municipal enterprise at prices more than three times higher, SAPO said.
The alleged scheme caused losses of more than UAH 129 million to the municipal enterprise. The suspects allegedly took control of the funds and disposed of them at their own discretion, the anti-corruption prosecutor's office said.
The alleged organizer and people under his control subsequently laundered the funds by transferring them to accounts of other related companies, SAPO said.
The beneficial owner of the company that won the tender was a prominent local businessman who was wanted by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation for property crimes, SAPO added.

Iran Guards say struck tanker transiting Hormuz via 'illegal route'
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that they had struck a tanker attempting to take an "illegal route" through the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has sought to blockade since the outset of the Middle East war.
Maritime trackers also reported on Friday that an unknown projectile sparked a fire aboard a ship off the UAE coast, but named a different vessel.
In a statement carried by official media, the Guards said Iranian forces "have taken control of the administration of the strait".
"In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck," they added.
Iran has attempted to impose its control over the Hormuz over the course of the war, insisting that vessels seek its permission to cross via its preferred routes.
However, ships have increasingly been willing to risk transiting via an alternative route hugging the strait's southern coast.
Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said on Friday that a ship 13 nautical miles (24 kilometres) off the UAE's Al Jazeera Al Hamra, southwest of the strait, was struck by a projectile, which caused a fire on board.
"Status of the crew, damage assessment and environmental impact are unknown at present. Authorities are investigating," UKMTO said in a statement.
British security firm Vanguard also reported the incident, and identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged crude tanker GEM NO.2.
The incident comes days after a tanker was hit off Qatar, around 500 kilometres (300 miles) west of the vital strait.
Ships in the Gulf and those attempting to transit the strait -- the only maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region -- have come under repeated attack since the US and Israel sparked the Middle East war in late February.
Iran has blockaded the strait ever since, though some vessels do manage to cross, and US media has reported on American military efforts to protect ships on the southern route.
The United States has set up its own counter-blockade of Iranian ports and occasionally fires on vessels linked to Tehran.
Hormuz is vital to the world economy, with around a fifth of the planet's oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the strait before the war began.

US sanctions on ICC spark global backlash, European calls for action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:50:00 UTC
01:50:00 KST

The U.S. faced mounting international criticism Friday over its sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), as European governments, Canada and Japan rallied behind the tribunal and warned that Washington's move threatened international justice and judicial independence.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the U.K., alongside their counterparts from Canada and Japan, expressed strong opposition to the sanctions, warning of serious consequences for the court's operations and personnel.
"We, the undersigned States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the ministers said.
They cautioned that the restrictions, if implemented, would significantly affect the tribunal's work, its employees and their families, while welcoming preparations aimed at maintaining its operations.
The eight countries pledged to maintain dialogue with nations outside the Rome Statute, the treaty establishing the ICC, ahead of the Assembly of States Parties in December.
"We will continue to work together to support the Court's vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability," they said.
The ICC itself denounced the measures as an attempt to obstruct justice and intimidate those cooperating with the tribunal.
The sanctions represent "an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," the court said, warning that they undermine the principle that no individual is above the law.
The tribunal vowed to continue its work despite the restrictions but urged its member states to defend its independence.
"The Court, for its part, will not be deterred," it said, adding that its future also depended on the governments that established it.
The European Commission similarly criticized Washington's decision and pledged to consider measures to protect the tribunal and European businesses affected by the sanctions.
"The EU stands ready to take any necessary measures to enable the Court to carry out its work," the commission said, referring to investigations and prosecutions involving war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen described the sanctions as deeply regrettable but emphasized that a six-month period before their implementation would allow time for negotiations.
"We will stand firm in defence of the Court," he said, adding that service providers could continue working with the tribunal during the transition period.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot called for more decisive European action, urging the EU to activate its Blocking Statute to shield the court from the effects of U.S. sanctions.
"Europe must act," Prevot said, announcing plans to raise the issue with EU foreign ministers and at the upcoming European Council meeting.
German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig also condemned the decision, highlighting Washington's historic role in establishing international criminal accountability following World War II.
She recalled that the United States had championed the Nuremberg trials against senior Nazi officials, helping lay the foundations of modern international criminal law.
"It is utterly staggering that the US, of all countries, is now setting out to destroy this idea once and for all," Hubig said.
In Washington, Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called the sanctions "unfortunate and short-sighted," accusing the Trump administration of further isolating the United States and undermining efforts to prosecute atrocities in Ukraine and Darfur.
Human rights organizations also criticized the measures, linking them to Washington's opposition to ICC proceedings involving U.S. and Israeli officials.
Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch, accused the Trump administration of seeking to dismantle the tribunal to protect American and Israeli officials from potential prosecution.
He urged governments, particularly the EU, to take immediate steps to protect the ICC, its employees and those cooperating with its investigations.
James A. Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, similarly described the sanctions as a deliberate challenge to judicial independence and equality before the law.
He characterized the move as part of a broader effort to weaken the international justice system.
The sanctions have intensified tensions between Washington and its European allies over the ICC, which has faced U.S. criticism over its investigations involving American personnel and arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

====================================================================================================

Watchdog Urges Better Alignment Across Pentagon’s Planned GPS Backups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:47:39 UTC
01:47:39 KST

All of the U.S. military services are pursuing capabilities to complement GPS amid concerns that the constellation is increasingly vulnerable to interference, but a new government watchdog report calls for better coordination and prioritization among those efforts to avoid delays and duplication.
Today’s GPS constellation is a mix of new and legacy satellites, the oldest of which are nearly 30 years old. The system has become essential to the entire global economy, affecting industries like agriculture, banking, and transportation, which are dependent on the system for timing and positioning. It’s also a fundamental military capability, particularly important for navigating in remote areas and helping guide missiles and drones.
In recent years, U.S. leaders have sounded the alarm about GPS vulnerabilities, especially jamming and spoofing. Because the Pentagon is dependent on space for precision targeting and communications, signal disruption poses a growing threat. Efforts to modernize GPS satellite, ground, and user equipment have faced repeated delays, exacerbating those concerns.
The Air Force, Space Force, Army, Navy, and Marine Corps have all pursued programs to either augment GPS capabilities or serve as a backup should the constellation be unavailable. For example, the Space Development Agency and the Army are fielding positioning, navigation, and timing, or PNT, satellites in low-Earth orbit, and the Navy is developing a PNT receiver that can calculate a ship’s position without the use of GPS using celestial bodies like stars, planets, and satellites on predictable orbits.
While these efforts have seen various degrees of success, an Oct. 7 report from the Government Accountability Office highlights risks within the current GPS modernization plans and the services’ various alternative PNT pursuits.
“Ineffective coordination of the fragmented interdependent PNT efforts among multiple military services—sometimes across more than one—hampers efficient alignment of those efforts,” GAO says in its report. “Pursuing modernized GPS and complementary PNT technologies to augment GPS requires foresight and planning. Integration timelines for weapon systems are often lengthy, and schedules must be properly aligned for the development of such modernized PNT technologies and their integration into weapon systems.”
As an example, GAO points to efforts to upgrade munitions to use M-code, a specialized, secure GPS signal. If the munitions have an integrated M-code capability before the aircraft, ships and ground platforms that fire them—which GAO says is likely to occur—that could cause synchronization issues before and after launch since positions are usually passed from a platform to a munition.
The report notes that officials has made some steps to consolidate PNT development efforts into joint program offices but argues more is needed. The agency recommends the Army, Navy, and Department of the Air Force identify opportunities to consolidate complementary programs to “ensure better strategic alignment with DOD and the other services” and drive efficiency.
“These efficiencies may improve schedule alignments between interdependent programs and ease the realignment of resources for higher priority programs within the portfolio to ensure that warfighters obtain these necessary capabilities to address current and future threats,” GAO writes.

Drone attack on Erbil camp renews Kurdish fears over Iran War fallout
Two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil on Thursday night, raising fresh concerns about security in Iraq's Kurdistan Region following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces and their air defence systems.
The Kurdistan Region's Counter-Terrorism Service said the attack took place at 22:19 local time in the Kawergosk area of Khabat district, west of Erbil, the regional capital. No casualties were reported.
Local reports said the drones caused material damage near the site, although other accounts suggested they had crashed in an uninhabited area. The extent of the damage remains unclear, and no group has claimed responsibility.
The attack follows more than a month of relative calm in Erbil and has renewed concerns over the region's vulnerability to drone strikes, particularly after US-led coalition forces withdrew their air defence systems at the end of September.
Kurdish officials have repeatedly called for stronger air defences and greater coordination with the federal government in Baghdad, which holds primary responsibility for protecting Iraqi airspace.
A captain in the Kurdish Peshmerga forces told The New Arab that the latest attack highlighted the urgent need for air defence systems capable of intercepting drones, a role previously carried out by the international coalition.
"The renewed attacks make it necessary to accelerate the provision of air defence systems capable of dealing with drones," the officer said, speaking on condition of anonymity. He added that surveillance and interception measures alone could not provide sufficient protection without dedicated defensive capabilities.
The officer suggested the attack could be linked to Iran, citing the nature of targets struck in previous incidents. However, there has been no official confirmation of responsibility for Thursday's attack.
The Kurdistan Region has faced repeated drone and missile attacks in recent months amid escalating tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and associated refugee camps have been among the targets.
Earlier attacks have also affected areas of Erbil and Sulaimaniyah provinces, with Kurdish security authorities reporting the interception of drones targeting civilian and military sites. Some strikes blamed on Iran have killed members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq.
The latest incident comes shortly after the US-led coalition completed its military withdrawal from Iraq under an agreement reached between Baghdad and Washington in 2024.
Coalition forces previously operated air defence systems in the Kurdistan Region that intercepted incoming drones and missiles. Kurdish political and military leaders had warned before the withdrawal that removing those systems without providing replacements would leave the region exposed to further attacks.
The Kurdistan Regional Government has argued that its airspace forms part of Iraq's national airspace and that the federal government must take responsibility for its protection.
Ali al-Harki, a member of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), told The New Arab that the renewed attacks threatened civilians and placed further pressure on the region's security arrangements.
"There is an urgent need for Baghdad to assert its authority over Iraqi airspace and take security measures to prevent further attacks," he said.
"Kurdistan's security is part of Iraq's security, and the Baghdad government cannot distance itself from the responsibility it must assume for protecting the country's airspace."
The attack has also raised concerns about the safety of refugee families living in camps across the region, particularly those associated with Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have previously been targeted.
Those concerns have grown following the departure of US forces and their defensive equipment from Erbil, which has left regional authorities seeking alternative arrangements to protect civilian areas and critical infrastructure.
With the perpetrators of Thursday's attack still unidentified, Kurdish officials are pressing Baghdad to strengthen air defence capabilities and improve coordination between the Iraqi military and the Peshmerga to prevent further strikes.

Happy birthday to the ROC
Today marks the 115th birthday of the Republic of China (ROC), while on Oct. 1, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) celebrated its 77th birthday.
From a historical and logical perspective, a 115-year-old nation could never be the “descendant” of a 77-year-old nation, let alone recognize a regime that is 38 years younger as its “motherland.”
If we insist on considering age and historical origins, it is actually the ROC that, historically, represents the shared memory of the people of the PRC over 77 years old.
We must not, simply because the word “motherland” easily evokes associations with bloodlines, ancestral origins or cultural roots, blindly accept this country, with a political system opposed to ours, as our motherland.
This year, I happen to be wishing my country a happy birthday as a soldier in military training.
This country can be called in many ways: It can be the ROC (Taiwan), the ROC, or simply Taiwan. Regardless of the name changes, the core fact remains: The ROC has been firmly rooted in Taiwan for 77 years. During this time, the values of democracy and freedom have become inextricably linked to the people of this land, perfectly integrated with their lives.
Through 115 years of democratic trials and tribulations, and 77 years of deep-rooted commitment, our nation has always been here.
Huang Yi-sheng
Taichung

OpenAI is expecting to reach or exceed US$70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, according to people familiar with the matter, driven largely by growth in its enterprise business.
The ChatGPT maker’s annualized revenue was roughly US$50 billion at the end of last month, the people said. The figure represents a projection of OpenAI’s yearly sales based on a shorter period.
The company shared the numbers with investors as part of discussions for its latest fundraising effort, said the people, requesting anonymity to discuss private information.
Photo: Reuters
The company is in talks to raise US$30 billion or more at a US$1.4 trillion valuation before the new money, Bloomberg first reported last month.
OpenAI declined to comment.

Some outlets reported last month that OpenAI was already projecting nearly US$70 billion in annualized revenue, based on investor estimates.
The Financial Times reported on Thursday that the discrepancy came from OpenAI’s investors attempting to calculate OpenAI’s annualized revenue using the same methods as rival Anthropic PBC, which accounts for sales from cloud providers differently.
On Thursday, tech shares led losses in the S&P 500 after reports that OpenAI’s annualized revenue would be lower than some previous estimates. The NASDAQ 100 fell 1.4 percent. A gauge of chip giants sank 3.4 percent.
While OpenAI has pushed back plans for an initial public offering until at least next year, citing its focus on AI safety efforts, Anthropic is expected to sell shares in an IPO as soon as next month.
OpenAI is in talks with multiple investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi-based MGX, to help anchor its new financing round, Bloomberg has reported.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

Firmus Grid Ltd abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, after the Nvidia Corp-backed data center company failed to lure global investors who have grown increasingly skittish over frothy AI valuations.
It was a dramatic about-face for a company that just days ago was signaling healthy demand for a deal that would have valued it at US$30 billion, up from US$10.5 billion less than three months ago. The canceled deal is a stark example of investor pushback against AI financing terms that some worry have become too generous as global borrowing costs climb and the long-term payoff from the technology remains uncertain.
Firmus, whose business model hinges on a steady influx of fresh capital, will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange and consider other funding options, according to a statement yesterday.
Photo: AFP
“Having considered recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions, the board determined that the terms on which the offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the company’s business and long-term growth outlook,” it said.
The IPO showed signs of stress soon after books opened for institutional investors this week. The struggles underscored investors’ polarized views on the deal. Some saw the business as well placed to benefit from the artificial intelligence boom, while others are worried about the valuation and existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the debut. Part of the difficulty was convincing potential investors of the steep increase in market value for a company without a proven track record that had revenue of US$51 million in the 2026 financial year.
AI FACTORIES
Firmus, which was looking to raise as much as US$5.5 billion including a greenshoe option, must now find other ways to raise funds to keep its ambitious expansion plans on track. The company aims to build data centers it calls AI factories using hardware from backer Nvidia. It has a pipeline of 912 megawatts, of which only 46MW has been built, according to investor documents seen by Bloomberg.
“Investors just weren’t prepared to pay a sky-high price up front for capacity that’s still largely on the drawing board,” eToro lead analyst for APAC and Middle East Josh Gilbert said. “The timing hasn’t helped either, with higher yields lifting borrowing costs and shrinking what investors will pay today for earnings that sit years down the track.”
Firmus will also explore a potential listing in the US in the longer term, people familiar with the matter have said.
DATA CENTER PIPELINE
The failed deal underscores growing concern over how much capital AI infrastructure companies are demanding from public markets at a time when borrowing costs are rising. Much of Firmus’ valuation was based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centers across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms Inc and OpenAI.
The strain is spreading across credit markets in the US, where a record wave of AI-related borrowing is forcing investors to reassess the risks around some of the biggest technology companies. Nearly US$500 billion of new debt has been priced this year to fund AI infrastructure, while rising financing needs and interest rates have driven up credit-insurance costs and weakened tech debt performance.
“There’s no question investors feel more anxiety recently, as the tech sector rallies despite mounting risk on every other front,” Rayliant Global Advisors head of portfolio management Phillip Wool wrote in a LinkedIn post. “Everything at this point hinges on the virtuous cycle of AI infrastructure spending boosting hardware and hyperscalers’ AI investment exciting shareholders about their own future earnings growth.”

Every day, Shanti Dangol stares down at Nepal’s Trishuli River from her makeshift shelter, searching for traces of the home she lost and wondering when she will have a roof over her head again.
Dangol is among hundreds of people living in tent shelters following a catastrophic Himalayan flood triggered by a mountain and glacier collapse near Nepal’s border with China on Aug. 26.
More than 1,400 people died and over 5,000 remain missing after tsunami-like waves swept through northern mountainous areas, destroying homes, roads, bridges and settlements.
Dangol, a former hotel owner, now lives in a tent in a forest clearing in Betrawati, Rasuwa district.
She shares the plot with 25 other families who also lost their homes.
“Where are we supposed to go? What are we supposed to do? The river now flows where our house once stood,” Dangol said.
Photo: AFP
“Where will the government settle us?”
Dangol lost 18 relatives in the disaster, as well as two four-story houses. Four employees from her hotel are still missing. “We just want somewhere to live, we don’t need anything more,” she said. “That is what worries us more than anything else.”
Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the UN last month that the flooding “was a warning to the world” about the rising dangers of climate change.
Government report shows that more than 7,500 private houses were damaged in the floods.
‘NO PROPER PLACE’
In Rasuwa district alone, more than 1,000 people are in temporary shelters, said Kamal Prasad Pandey, the district’s chief administrative officer.
“We are also equally concerned about their permanent settlement, their hygiene and mental health issues,” he said.
Aarati Magar, 26, who lost her newly opened hotel in the disaster, lives in the same plot in a tent with her daughters, aged eight and three, worrying about their safety and education.
“It is tough to stay here. There is no bathing place and no proper place to live,” she said. For 58-year-old Narayan Man Dangol, the prospect of spending months in a tent is particularly worrying as winter approaches. “I don’t see a situation where we can stay in the tent for a long time,” he said.
“The wind will carry it away, and then it will rain again. This is just cloth. Living inside a cloth house is very difficult,” he said.
He said he had lost his life’s earnings. “Life will never be the same for us, we can no longer work in the fields and earn at this age,” he said.
‘RESTORE THEIR LIVELIHOODS’
Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of Nepal’s disaster agency, said authorities were “moving to the search and recovery phase”, and were working on “transitional shelters and identifying resettlement areas.” Families have also lost businesses, jobs and access to essential services, leaving many uncertain about how they will rebuild their lives.
“Recovery is about much more than rebuilding damaged infrastructure,” said Kyoko Yokosuka, the UN Development Program head in Nepal.
“It is about helping people restore their livelihoods, reopening local economies, restoring essential services and ensuring communities can move forward with dignity and hope,” she said.
For Dangol, the former hotel owner, the immediate concern is finding somewhere safe to live.
“We were victims of this flood, but we don’t want the next generation to be homeless like us,” she said.

Jurist Navi Pillay receives this year’s Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former UN human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, yesterday won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.
Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have rejected the findings of the UN commission she led on Gaza. The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court; Pillay has worked at both.
Pillay’s work “is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world,” Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jorgen Watne Frydnes said in announcing her win.
Photo: AFP
The committee said it sought to bolster international law at a time of conflict, and Watne Frydnes said Pillay’s award was a message to those seeking to undermine “the international rules-based system and the institutions.”
Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, the location of the trials of Nazi war criminals that helped lay the foundations of international law.
“Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me,” she said. “You don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this.”
Pillay dedicated her award to “survivors of international crimes,” and called on world leaders to respect international legal institutions.
“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. “My message to leaders, political leaders, is that ... you have a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war.”
Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
The commission also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former minister of defense “have incited the commission of genocide.”
Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations.
Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of antisemitism or allegedly turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel.
Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

Climate hopes shift from politics to the courts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

The political fight against global warming may be losing steam, but the legal battle is heating up. Over the past decade, legal activists have successfully taken a number of national governments to court, triggering the adoption of more climate-friendly policies in countries including the Netherlands, Pakistan, Switzerland, South Korea and others.
“There is momentum for climate litigation in the courts,” said Dennis van Berkel of the Climate Litigation Network, which supports legal action against states and corporations.
In one such victory earlier this week, Australia’s highest court blocked the expansion of a coal mine in New South Wales, citing its climate impact.
Photo: AFP
“Climate change litigation is growing domestically and internationally,” said Margaret Young, a law professor at the University of Melbourne.
On the political front, from Europe to the US, governments have been scaling back climate ambitions and policies, and global climate negotiations at the upcoming COP next month are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels that drive global warming.
But over the past two years, three international courts have affirmed in advisory opinions that countries have legal obligations to address climate change: the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, and the International Court of Justice (ICJ). A fourth opinion is expected from the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights.
“A lot has been achieved in a short period of time,” said Margaretha Wewerinke-Singh, a law professor at the University of Amsterdam who served as a legal expert in proceedings before all three courts.
While an advisory opinion issued by such a court is not legally binding in the same way as a judgment in a contentious case, van Berkel said the legal principles set out in those opinions are already being used in national courts.
“That norm is now flowing back to being picked up by the plaintiffs in different countries (and) used in their litigation,” he explained.
A Paris court cited the ICJ opinion in a ruling in June last year that ordered TotalEnergies to include emissions linked to the use of its products in its corporate vigilance plan. In January, a Dutch court also cited the opinion when it ordered the Netherlands to strengthen its climate plan in a case brought by residents of the Dutch Caribbean island of Bonaire. Both rulings are being appealed.
“Despite what politicians say about the international legal system, judges still respect and apply international law in many countries around the world,” said Sophie Marjanac, legal director at the Redwater Insights think tank.
‘TIGHTENING NET’ FOR OIL FIRMS
When it comes to corporations, the legal precedent is less established than for states, but there is a “tightening net” for oil companies, said Jasper Teulings, who also works for the Climate Litigation Network.
In some cases, years of litigation have led to permits for oil, gas and coal projects being overturned, including in the UK. Norway’s Supreme Court is expected to rule soon on licenses for projects in the North Sea.
And the Supreme Court of the Netherlands is next year expected to rule in a closely watched case brought by the environmental group Milieudefensie against Shell, deciding whether to impose a specific emissions-reduction target on the energy giant.
MAKING POLLUTERS PAY
Another potential breakthrough would be a ruling requiring a major polluter to compensate people harmed or threatened by climate change, wherever they live, in proportion to the company’s greenhouse gas emissions.
German courts moved toward that principle last year in a case brought by Peruvian farmer Saul Luciano Lliuya against energy company RWE. Although they rejected his claim for compensation, the courts left the door open to holding major emitters liable for climate-related payments.
Similar lawsuits are now pending in several countries, including cases brought by Philippine victims of Typhoon Odette against Shell in the UK, residents of Indonesia’s Pari island against cement maker Holcim in Switzerland, and Pakistani farmers affected by 2022 floods against RWE and Heidelberg Materials in Germany.
There have also been setbacks.
Climate groups have lost lawsuits against oil companies in the US. And in New Zealand, the government changed the law to block a lawsuit brought by Maori activist Mike Smith against six domestic companies, but he has vowed to continue the fight.
There was a time when Chinese master Yuan Shimao thought martial arts were all about punching and kicking. As a young practitioner, he focused on speed and strength. “I trained that way for many years without becoming still enough to search within myself,” said Yuan, who founded a kung fu academy in central China in 2004. “But as you gradually settle into stillness, you begin to understand what the scriptures mean by spirit,” he added. “You can begin to rediscover yourself.” That process is known as “entering the Dao” in martial arts. Photo: John Jones / Imagn Images

Taiwan offers much more than tech, Tsai Ing-wen says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

Taiwan offers the global democratic community much more than just semiconductors, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) told an audience at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution in San Francisco on Thursday, while defending her “boring” leadership style as a necessary asset to find common ground.
Tsai spoke about how Taiwan has managed differences, responded to crises and built societal resilience.
Discussions about Taiwan often focus on semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), cross-strait relations, the risk of conflict and occasionally touch on its popular food and drinks, she said.
Photo: CNA
However, those topics are only part of the story, Tsai said, pointing to the nation’s 23 million people and their experience of building a democracy under challenging circumstances.
“That experience has shaped who we are and continues to shape how we approach the future,” she said.
Democracies face growing challenges from outside and within, as increasingly sophisticated authoritarian influence campaigns coincide with domestic populism and political polarization, she said.
The domestic divisions make it harder to reach a consensus on how to respond to outside threats, she added.
Tsai also warned that advances in AI have lowered language barriers, making it easier to spread disinformation across borders.
“Ill-intentioned actors, especially from outside, use social media platforms to spread false and misleading information to drive a wedge between fellow citizens, between societies and their governments, and even between countries,” she said.
However, decades of external pressure and intense domestic political competition have taught Taiwan how to safeguard democracy while keeping its institutions open and its society resilient, Tsai said.
Taiwan has moved from authoritarian rule to its first direct presidential election in 1996 to become the vibrant democracy it is today, she said.
“That transition taught us how to confront deep political differences without allowing those differences to make democratic progress impossible,” she said.
Managing relations with China has required preparedness and restraint, Tsai said, adding that decades of pressure from Beijing have made Taiwan more resilient and pragmatic.
Although Taiwanese hold differing views on what form relations with China should take, there is a consensus on maintaining the cross-strait “status quo,” avoiding unnecessary provocation, and protecting Taiwan’s democracy and security, she said.
“Democracy, resilience and partnership are the foundation of our collective future,” Tsai said, adding that no amount of threats or coercion would shake Taiwan’s determination to engage with and contribute to the world.
While some people described her as “boring” during her time as president, Tsai said that “being boring can be useful” in an era of increasing political polarization in which provocation attracts more attention than restraint.
This is especially true when needing to ensure Taiwan’s security while finding enough common ground to keep democracy moving forward, she added.
Tsai arrived in the US on Monday and is scheduled to return to Taiwan tomorrow.
Additional reporting by Su Yung-yao

Giant Taiwan flag flies freely on National Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:23 UTC
01:43:23 KST

Largely banned from display internationally due to Beijing’s objections, a giant Taiwanese flag suspended under a US-made Chinook helicopter and flown over Taipei is one of the most eye-catching moments of Double Ten National Day.
Since 2019, as a way to boost unity amid rising Chinese pressure, the military has every year flown a massive flag beneath one of its tandem-rotor Chinook CH-47SD helicopters over the Presidential Office Building in Taipei while the national anthem is sung during Oct. 10 National Day celebrations.
President William Lai (賴清德) is to give a keynote address mid-morning today, laying out policy objectives and addressing relations with China.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
China has ratcheted up efforts to stop countries engaging with Taipei, including preventing Taiwan’s flag from being displayed at sports events such as the Olympics.
One of the helicopter pilots taking part in rehearsals this week, 40-year-old Lin Chang-cheng (林昶成), said that the flag is a “concrete symbol of national sovereignty.”
“This is especially true given that we have actually suffered a lot of suppression in the international community, so when we see the national flag being displayed, it’s an extremely moving moment,” Lin said at Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport).
National Day is held on the anniversary of a 1911 uprising that led to the overthrow of China’s last imperial dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China (ROC).
The ROC government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s (毛澤東) communists, who proclaimed the People’s Republic of China.
Suspended from a long, weighted cable beneath the helicopter, the 12m-by-18m ROC flag is made out of the same tough, lightweight material used for parachutes.
While the flag is a contested symbol even within Taiwan, especially for those who champion an entirely separate identity from China, catching sight of it flying over Taipei is exciting for those watching from the city’s hills.
“When I see the Taiwan flag, I feel that it represents freedom, democracy and freedom of speech,” said Hsiao Shao-chun, 44, watching rehearsals on Taipei’s outskirts.
During the Cold War, National Day celebrations in Taiwan were heavily military focused, with speeches about “retaking the mainland.”
These days, the event is more about showcasing Taiwan’s soft power and global visibility.

Fort Hood shooter’s execution to be livestreamed: US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:19 UTC
01:43:19 KST

The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said on Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years.
The US army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said.
Photo: Reuters
Pentagon officials said the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the US, especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” said Eugene Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails.
Those are benefits that would be useful at a time when Pike’s botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes, she said.
As many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are being seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, codirector of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions.
Although there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, “I don’t recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government,” she said.
Semel said she was skeptical that the administration of US President Donald Trump had given a second thought to the legal and social questions presented by the decision.
Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment.
He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of fleeing soldiers.
It was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims, Hasan said.
A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial.
Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement.
He could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, but given his behavior at trial, he might not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan told jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence.

Shark attack survivor Mel Ismail recounts his ordeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:19 UTC
01:43:19 KST

As shark attack survivor Mel Ismail fought the predator that severed his leg, he noticed something odd.
“I saw its eye ... a big black eye,” Ismail said. “But it was winking back at me — I was trying to get my fingers in its eye and just pushing its eye as I was being dragged.”
When the shark swam off, he managed to struggle back to shore, the surfer and professional firefighter said in an Australian Broadcasting Corp interview broadcast on Thursday.
Photo: Australian Broadcasting Corp via AP
He was surfing at Glenfield Beach near Geraldton on Australia’s west coast when he was attacked on Sept. 14. He lost his right leg below the knee.
Ismail said he was resting when he spotted a pod of about 20 dolphins before being hit by something big. It was the first time he has spoken publicly about the attack.
“I thought I got hit by a dolphin, initially,” Ismail said. “And suddenly — bang — something grabbed me and dragged me down into the water. And I knew it was a shark.”
Ismail said it looked like the shark winked at him before it bit his leg.
Many sharks, including the white shark and mako shark, do not have eyelids, but when attacking prey, they roll their eyeballs backward into their sockets as a protective measure, exposing a tough layer of white cartilage.
Authorities have yet to determine the species of shark that attacked Ismail.
Alone and bleeding at the back of the surf break, Ismail caught a wave that took him about 20m closer to shore.
Ismail said he was out of breath and losing strength when he spotted surfer Shannan Dunn coming down the dunes on to the beach.
Dunn went to Ismail’s rescue, helping the shark victim on to his board.
Ismail described Dunn as having “eyes like saucers.”
“The first thing he [Dunn] said to me is, ‘Where’s the shark?’” Ismail said. “I said, ‘I don’t know. I’ve got a bit going on here.’”
Once they returned to the beach, an onlooker crafted a tourniquet for Ismail using a leg rope and another onlooker phoned for an ambulance.
A pair of teenagers helped Ismail climb into Dunn’s car and they drove along the beach to meet an ambulance.
“I had a heap of people laughing, keeping me alive, keeping me positive in the back,” Ismail said.
“I gave a few knuckles to the people there, because I was feeling good,” he added. “I started to feel like I [was] going to make it.”
Four days after Ismail was attacked, 63-year-old swimmer Greg O’Neill was fatally mauled by a large white shark. O’Neill was attacked off Sorrento Beach in Perth’s northern suburbs.
Ismail said he intends to return to the surf as a bodyboarder.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.
Three spearfishing divers were killed by sharks off the Australian coast in four weeks over May and June. In January, a 12-year-old boy died in a hospital days after he was mauled by a bull shark in Sydney Harbor.
Australia has averaged between two and three fatal shark attacks a year since 2000, the Australian Shark Incident Database showed.

Putin says Caspian Sea shoreline in Russia receded by 20,000 sq km in 20 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:19 UTC
01:43:19 KST

Kanyshai Butun
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Friday that the Caspian Sea’s shoreline in Russia had receded by an estimated 20,000 square kilometers (7,722 square miles) over the past 20 years, warning of serious environmental and economic consequences.
Speaking at the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, Putin said the sea’s water level was falling by an average of nine centimeters (3.5 inches) annually, threatening biodiversity, fisheries and coastal soil stability.
“Falling water levels have a negative impact on the socio-economic situation in the Caspian region, reduce the investment attractiveness of trans-Caspian logistics corridors, and threaten a decline in the population's quality of life, job losses, and other acute crises,” he said, attributing the decline primarily to climate change.
Putin said Russia was working with regional partners to protect the Caspian ecosystem and supported developing an action plan on fluctuations in the sea’s water level through 2036.
He also backed establishing a special commission to investigate the causes of the decline and develop measures to address its consequences, adding that Russia was preparing a comprehensive research program on changes in the Caspian Sea’s water level through 2030.
Moscow has also proposed creating a digital twin of the sea using artificial intelligence to model water-level changes and improve navigation safety.
He stressed the need for coordinated action among Caspian littoral states to preserve the sea’s ecosystem and ensure sustainable regional development.
“In conclusion, I would like to reiterate that Russia has always advocated—and will continue to advocate—for strengthening and developing cooperation among our states in the interests of preserving the Caspian region’s ecosystem, ensuring its sustainable growth, and improving people's quality of life,” he said.
The meeting was attended by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

Taiwan’s Double Ten reckoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:17 UTC
01:43:17 KST

On Oct. 10, 1911, gunfire in Wuchang (武昌) shattered the stillness of late-Qing China. What began as a regional uprising quickly ignited a chain reaction across the empire, toppling a dynastic order that had endured for more than two millennia and ushering in one of Asia’s first republics — the Republic of China (ROC). From that moment, the 10th day of the 10th month became a date of epochal significance, not merely in Chinese history, but in the broader arc of Asia’s encounter with modernity.
Yet today, as Taiwan marks Double Ten National Day, the holiday’s meaning has undergone a transformation as profound as the revolution it commemorates. No longer a ritual of nostalgic irredentism or a symbolic claim to a lost mainland, Oct. 10 has become, for many in Taiwan, a celebration of something far more tangible: the nation’s hard-won democracy.
The linguistic footprint of this shift is subtle, but telling. Merriam-Webster, the only major English dictionary to include the term “Double Ten,” defines it as a holiday observed by the ROC to commemorate the 1911 uprising. First recorded in 1940, the term is a calque from the Chinese shuang shi (雙十) — “double tenth,” marking the 10th day of the 10th month. But language, like history, is never static. In Taiwan, the word now carries connotations its early 20th-century coiners could scarcely have imagined.
By the 1960s, the holiday had hardened into a spectacle of revanchist theater. On the 50th anniversary in 1961, Time magazine described the scene in Taipei: 11,000 troops marched past the reviewing stand while 160 jet fighters roared overhead, and Nationalist frogmen swam ashore on an uninhabited island to plant their flags. Then-president Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) declared that conditions on the mainland resembled those of 1911, predicting imminent uprisings and promising a massive counteroffensive. For Chiang, Double Ten was a rallying cry; for then-Chinese premier Zhou Enlai (周恩來), it was a footnote to what he dismissed as an old-fashioned bourgeois revolution.
However, Taiwan’s own political evolution has rewritten the script. The lifting of martial law in 1987, the first direct presidential election in 1996, and nearly four decades of vibrant democratic practice have gradually stripped Double Ten of its revanchist overtones. The parade names tell the story: from “Chinese Unification” in 1991, criticized as excessively sinocentric, to “National Defense Performance” under former president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁), “Defense Exhibition” under former president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), and, in 2023, the English designation used that year: “Taiwan National Day.” Each renaming reflects a society negotiating its identity, shedding the baggage of a continental past in favor of an island-centered present.
This is not mere semantic gamesmanship. It is the linguistic expression of a deeper truth: Taiwan has become something the 1911 revolutionaries dreamed of, but never saw realized, a functioning liberal democracy in Asia. Its legislature features robust opposition voices. Its press criticizes the government without fear. Its citizens take to the streets not as subversives, but as participants in their own governance. These are not abstract ideals; they are the daily texture of life in a society that completed a peaceful transition from authoritarianism, rare in the region.
To be sure, the holiday remains politically contested. Beijing views any invocation of “Taiwan National Day” as a provocation. Some still mourn the loss of a broader Chinese identity, but for a growing number of Taiwanese, Oct. 10 is less about remembering a revolution on a distant mainland than about honoring their own journey, from martial law to free elections, from isolation to global relevance.
In an era when authoritarianism is resurgent and democratic norms are fraying, Taiwan’s story carries weight beyond its shores. Double Ten, once a symbol of republican aspiration, has become something more urgent: a testament to democratic resilience. The revolution of 1911 opened a door. Taiwan, against all odds, walked through it, and kept walking, all the way to a future its founders could hardly have envisioned. That is the true legacy of Double Ten. Not the restoration of a vanished empire, but the preservation of a living democracy.
Hugo Tseng has a doctorate in linguistics, and is a lexicographer and former chair of the Soochow University English Department.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:14 UTC
01:43:14 KST

US President Donald Trump’s administration accused Microsoft Corp, Adobe Inc and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a US worker visa program and suspended them indefinitely from a longstanding immigration initiative that has served as a crucial talent pipeline for Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
The suspensions, announced on Thursday by US Vice President J.D. Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, also target information technology services giants Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp, Infosys Ltd, Tata, Wipro Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd and Capgemini SE. Those firms, either based in India or with large operations there, are often called outsourcers for their role offering contract IT work to other businesses.
At a briefing in Washington, Sonderling said there were multiple federal investigations under way into the use of a system that allows US employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.
Photo: Bloomberg
“We are cutting off the head of the snake — the companies that enabled this abuse for decades,” Sonderling told reporters at Thursday’s briefing.
Vance singled out Microsoft, the world’s third-most valuable company, for what he characterized as exploitation of the program.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” he said.
In a statement, Microsoft defended its use of visa programs and said that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information. Adobe and the Indian companies named by Vance and Sonderling did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Vance’s comments assailing Microsoft came hours before Trump honored the company’s chief executive officer, Satya Nadella, with a National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to spotlight US scientific leadership. Just last week, Nadella joined other tech industry leaders at a White House luncheon to discuss safeguards for artificial intelligence.
“Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them, they do a lot of important things,” Vance said. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company. It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.”
The moves announced by Vance and Sonderling take aim at the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, which allows companies to sponsor a foreigner who has been working in the US under the H-1B and other visa holders to become a legal permanent resident, the first step to becoming a US citizen.
Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers.
As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent, targeting a major source of workers for the industry. The changes have included proposals for $100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries.
Vance urged the US-based companies to shift their policies to employ more US workers.
“Stop defrauding the American worker. Stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do,” the vice president said.

01:43:11 KST

What animal looks like a bird, acts like a mouse, and sounds like the name of a fruit? Meet the kiwi. Native to New Zealand, the kiwi has tiny wings, furry-looking feathers and a long beak, making it strangely cute. Still, it has become one of the nation’s best-known symbols.
Evolution had a hand in shaping the kiwi’s unique look. Millions of years ago, when New Zealand lacked land predators, the kiwi lived in an environment where flight was unnecessary for survival. Gradually, it adapted to a ground-dwelling lifestyle. Its wings shrank into small stubs hidden beneath its feathers, while its flight muscles were replaced by strong legs built for walking and fast running. Its feathers also transformed into hair-like structures that provide perfect camouflage in the forest.
Even its sense of smell evolved in a surprising way. Unlike most birds, which rely mainly on sight to find food, the kiwi depends on an exceptional sense of smell. It developed a long beak with nostrils located at the very tip. While foraging for food, it repeatedly taps its beak against the ground to sniff out insects and worms hidden beneath the soil.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
By the time humans arrived in New Zealand, the kiwi had settled into its own way of life. Its sharp call, which sounds like “kee-wee,” earned the bird its name. Interestingly, the fuzzy fruit we eat was later named “kiwi fruit” because its brown, fuzzy skin reminded people of the bird, not the other way around. Today, the word kiwi still confuses people. Is it a fruit, a nickname for New Zealanders, or a bird? In New Zealand, the answer begins with the bird, a national icon and one of the country’s most recognizable identities.
什麼動物看起來像鳥、行為像老鼠，名字聽起來像水果呢？來見見奇異鳥吧。奇異鳥原生於紐西蘭，牠們有迷你翅膀、看起來毛茸茸的羽毛，還有長長的鳥喙，怪可愛的。不過，牠們成為了紐西蘭最知名的象徵之一。
演化在形塑奇異鳥的獨特外觀上插了一腳。數百萬年前的紐西蘭缺乏陸地掠食者，奇異鳥住在不需要靠飛行生存的環境中。牠們逐漸適應了地棲的生活方式。牠們的翅膀縮小成隱藏在羽毛下的小殘翼，用來飛行的肌肉則被適合步行和快跑的強壯雙腿取代。牠們的羽毛也轉變成毛髮般的結構，能在森林裡提供完美的偽裝。
甚至連牠們的嗅覺也有驚人的演化。與大多數主要仰賴視力來找食物的鳥類不同，奇異鳥依靠的是絕佳的嗅覺。牠們發展出長長的鳥喙，鼻孔位於尖端。在覓食的時候，牠們會反覆用鳥喙敲打地面，以嗅出藏在泥土下的昆蟲和蟲蟲。
等人類抵達紐西蘭時，奇異鳥已經適應了自己的生活方式。牠們宏亮的叫聲聽起來像kee-wee，使其獲得kiwi這個名稱。有趣的是，我們吃的那種毛毛水果後來會被稱為「奇異果」，是因為其棕色的毛毛外皮讓人們聯想到奇異鳥，而非反過來。如今，kiwi這個字仍讓人們感到困惑。是一種水果、紐西蘭人的綽號，或是一隻鳥呢？在紐西蘭，答案始於奇異鳥，牠們是國家象徵，也是紐西蘭最具辨識度的形象之一。

Shorter season pitched as salary cap battle looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:10 UTC
01:43:10 KST

MLB proposed cutting its regular season to 154 games from 162 starting in 2029 during bargaining on Thursday, a plan that the MLB Players’ Association said was tied to a salary cap it firmly opposes.
The proposal, which comes as the league and the union negotiate a new collective bargaining agreement before the current one expires in December, would also expand the Division Series of the playoffs to a best-of-seven from a best-of-five affair.
Shortening the regular season would create a standard weekly off day benefiting player health, the MLB said.
Under its proposal, the higher-seeded clubs in the Wild Card and Division Series would select their opponents beginning in 2027.
The players’ association said it is reviewing the proposed changes.
“Players will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table,” it said in a statement. “Unfortunately, the league once again made clear that all of its proposals are contingent on players’ agreement to a salary cap, a system that guts player rights and compensation, as well as its other anti-player proposals.”
Other North American leagues have lengthened their schedules in the past few years.
The NHL went to 84 games from 82 this season, and the NFL, which added a 17th game in 2021, wants an 18th.
The NFL players’ union has pushed back.
However, the bigger fight is expected to be over a salary cap, which could lead to a lockout or strike.
In their first proposal in May, MLB owners asked for a hard cap of US$245.3 million, including player benefits, and a payroll floor of US$171.2 million, starting in 2027.
The MLB union has long opposed any form of salary cap.
The collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
The last time owners pushed for a cap, players went on strike in 1994.
The 232-day stoppage forced the cancelation of that year’s MLB World Series.

EDITORIAL: Inclusivity is not a token gesture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:08 UTC
01:43:08 KST

A police raid on a gay bar in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area one week ago prompted a protest by civil groups and members of the LGBTQ community, who characterized the raid as excessively forceful and demanded that police apologize and stop stigmatizing LGBTQ culture.
Police from the Wanhua Precinct raided the bar, Commander D, after obtaining a search warrant following complaints that the venue might be contravening public decency laws. Police said they found people without clothing and seized used condoms, taking 51 people to the police station for questioning and referring the bar’s owner to prosecutors.
The legality of the raid itself is not the issue. Police had obtained a warrant, and authorities have a legitimate responsibility to investigate suspected contraventions of the law. What is far more difficult to justify is how the raid was carried out.
People at the scene said officers ordered them to squat or kneel, prevented them from using their phones and initially refused to let some people put their clothes back on. One person taken in for questioning said they were held for more than six hours after being accused of breaking public decency laws, having removed their shirt shortly before police arrived because the bar was crowded and hot.
There were also allegations that police searched personal belongings and treated large numbers of patrons as suspects. One officer was recorded asking a disabled customer in a restroom how disabled people “manage to have sex in there.”
Police have disputed some of these allegations and said the orders were necessary to secure the premises, prevent interference with the investigation and preserve evidence. However, after reviewing body camera footage, the Taipei City Police Department found that four officers had used inappropriate or discriminatory language.
The lead investigator was disciplined for failing to stop the remarks, while the Wanhua Precinct chief was disciplined for inadequate supervision. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) apologized to those affected and said police discipline would be bolstered, while emphasizing that everyone, regardless of gender, sexual orientation or identity, should be treated equally.
Those measures are necessary, but they do not answer the deeper concerns raised by the operation.
A search warrant gives police legal authority to enter and search a specified premises. It should not, by itself, give officers unlimited discretion over how they treat the people inside and their property.
The alleged offenses were not violent crimes or an immediate threat to public safety. If the bar or its customers contravened public decency laws, they should be dealt with according to the law. However, law enforcement must still be proportionate to the conduct being investigated.
There is also the broader question about how such operations are planned and supervised. The government should review what circumstances warrant a forceful raid and how officers are expected to execute search warrants under a variety of circumstances. Sensitivity and diversity training should also be improved, particularly when officers are dealing with communities that have historically faced discrimination and stigma.
The Taiwan Alliance to Promote Civil Partnership Rights and other groups said the incident was not simply a matter of individual officers misspeaking or a single instance of excessive enforcement. They described it as the “resurfacing of long-standing homophobia, discrimination and abuse of power” within the police system.
Taiwan became the first in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019 and has developed a reputation as one of the region’s most LGBTQ-friendly societies. Taipei is preparing to host its annual Pride event on Oct. 31, the largest in East Asia and one that attracts visitors from across the region.
For a community that has long been a target of discrimination and oppression, an aggressive police operation at an LGBTQ venue carries much deeper implications than a few inappropriate remarks. It can reinforce the perception that LGBTQ spaces are inherently suspicious or depraved, and that people who enter them need not be treated with dignity when the state exercises its authority.
Penalizing the officers involved is not enough. Beyond providing the public with a clear account of what happened and explaining the legal basis for the treatment of those detained, the government and police department should outline concrete measures to ensure that misconduct like this does not happen again — and they should do so before the Pride event, rather than simply waiting for the controversy to fade.
The government should ensure that all residents, regardless of their identity, feel safe, respected and equally protected under the law — that is what defines an inclusive city.

China’s targets for growth have become a trap for Xi Jinping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:07 UTC
01:43:07 KST

China’s latest effort to prop up its battered housing market and spur the economy is getting a poor reception. The measures are underwhelming and unlikely to achieve much beyond improving Beijing’s chances of meeting its already restrained growth ambitions.
That is damning the initiative with faint praise. The deeper problem lies in how China measures economic success. The government itself deserves some blame: It does not aspire to beat expectations, merely to meet them. And those expectations are set at the start of each year with the much-heralded unveiling of an economic growth target. China should jettison it.
The negative reception for the real estate package, which includes subsidized loans and support for favored sectors, helps explain why a change of approach would be beneficial. Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has been trying to nurse the property market back to health for years, with limited success. There is nothing wrong with experimenting when existing remedies are not working. Washington tried repeatedly to contain the subprime crisis in 2007-2009. Several measures proved inadequate before policymakers eventually restored confidence.
However, the criticism also misses a more fundamental point. Investors and businesses still have not fully adjusted to the reality that this is not the China of old. Growth will be slower, more modest and likely to drift lower over time. Beijing’s annual GDP targets can help manage that transition by signaling what policymakers consider an acceptable pace of expansion, but they can also become a trap. By turning that number into a test of economic success or failure, the government encourages policies aimed at hitting the target rather than confronting the deeper problems holding back growth.
There is no sign that major stimulus along the lines of 2008 is in the works. That does not mean a fresh policy push is not needed. What is required, though, is a new narrative. Each batch of data produces much the same picture — and a similar disappointed response: Domestic demand is weak while exports power ahead. Last month’s numbers and third-quarter GDP, due in two weeks, are unlikely to alter that story.
The report card can almost be written in advance. The figures will be judged largely by whether they leave China on course to meet its growth aspirations. Fall too far behind, and calls for another dose of stimulus will intensify; stay on target, and policymakers can afford to wait. In the preceding quarter, the economy expanded 4.3 percent from a year earlier, slightly below the bottom of the 4.5 percent-5 percent range articulated by Xi. The near-universal prescription was for more public spending. But monetary easing looked a distant prospect then, and still does. People’s Bank of China officials have repeatedly stressed that they are in no hurry.
The stated goals get in the way of a dispassionate assessment of China’s economic performance. They establish useful parameters and offer some insight into the expectations of top decision-makers, but they also create an artificial benchmark for what is not merely achievable, but desirable. If the goal looks comfortably within reach, everyone can relax. If it appears distant — or attainable only with considerable effort — the case for stimulus strengthens. Either way, the target ends up driving the interpretation. The numbers rarely get to stand on their own.
Targets do have a useful signaling role. They allow Beijing to indicate the pace of economic growth it wants, and the degree of weakness it is prepared to tolerate. For much of the post-COVID period, the goal has hovered around 5 percent. Moving to a range acknowledges that growth might undershoot that pace and, more broadly, that tougher times lie ahead.
However, Beijing is not solely to blame. Some of the problem lies with those of us assessing China. If the economy is performing poorly, we should say so; that judgement should not depend on whether an official target is met. And there is plenty to criticize. For years, hopes have rested on a rebalancing of growth away from exports and toward domestic demand. It has yet to happen. That is hardly a new critique, but it remains a valid one.
The narrative surrounding China’s economy is stuck. The numbers are not great, but nor are they terrible, assuming they can be believed. Some slowing is only natural: The bigger the economy becomes, the harder it is to keep delivering outsize gains. Government support increasingly seems designed to stabilize the expansion, not accelerate it. As Bloomberg Economics points out, this is not a sprint. A gradual deceleration toward annual growth of around 2 percent over the next decade is increasingly in the cards.
What is needed is a new way of thinking about the world’s second-largest economy, one that does not depend on crystal-ball gazing by cadres. Only then can we judge whether China is doing well, doing poorly or simply muddling through. Don’t expect that breakthrough any time soon. Whether 4.5 percent is comfortably in the bag or tantalizingly out of reach, expect it to dominate discussion of the third-quarter report.
Xi would be well advised to dispense with numerical growth targets. Once the current one has been met, of course.
Daniel Moss is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian economies. Previously, he was executive editor for economics at Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
