‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:32:38 UTC
01:32:38 KST

The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.
The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.
The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.
The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”
Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”
Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.
Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”
Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.
JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision.
When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen.
“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.
Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.
The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.
The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.
Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.
Media have sought to televise US executions in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.
Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.
In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.
Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.
The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.
The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.
Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.
Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.
“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”
Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press.
Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.
“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”
Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.
It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.

Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St Pancras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:32:30 UTC
01:32:30 KST

When Zack Polanski addressed his campaigners flush with victory after the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, he declared: “Labour’s electoral stranglehold is over.” The election of Hannah Spencer as the new Green MP for the Greater Manchester seat was a seismic victory, he continued: “I said we were here to replace Labour and this is what replacing looks like.”
But in the wake of Polanski’s defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on Thursday, and a calamitous row over the party’s stance on Zionism, the debate around what, or who, could be replaced has shifted to Polanski himself.
On Friday the leader of the Green party in England and Wales was defiant after losing to Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, who took 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 33%. Asked what was going wrong in his party, which has fallen from highs of 21% in some polls after the victory in Gorton and Denton to around 10-11%, Polanski, responded: “If things are going wrong by the fact that we just tripled our vote share and had our second best byelection result in Green party history, you know what? I’ll take that.” While emphasising that Green members would ultimately decide who they wanted as leader, he said: “Of course I can carry on.”.
That the last few months have been difficult for the Greens – and Polanski in particular – is beyond doubt. Polanski himself is, according to new polling from More in Common, now less popular with voters than Nigel Farage, and is the least popular major UK party leader, falling by four points to a -28 net approval.
His standing, bruised by a series of controversies over a failure to pay council tax and the sharing of a post criticising police, has been further damaged by a controversial motion that was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton last weekend, equating Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. Polanski’s decision to abstain from the debate and the vote to instead campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, was condemned by his detractors, but also, more significantly, criticised by senior figures in his own party.
The former Green leader Caroline Lucas told BBC Newsnight on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”. Asked if he should stand down, she said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection.” Following his defeat she appeared to temper her position, saying Polanski had “transformed the party” and she hoped he would now “help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures”.
On Friday, pressure mounted, as the leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, called for Polanski to step down, saying it was a “big mistake” for him not to have spoken and voted for amendments stating that any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians, rather than impose a one-state system.
But there was bullishness among the Polanski faithful, with Greens Organise, the leftwing faction that backed his leadership bid, saying he should stay on. A statement from the group said that “not all growth and success is linear, there will be ups and downs; the real test for a political organisation is how we deal with failure”. It added: “We have reshaped the British political landscape. The Green party can still become the ecosocialist party we need. Zack is still the leader who can get us there.”
Green party supporters pointed out that the party achieved a 13-point swing from Labour in Holborn and St Pancras, traditionally a safe Labour seat. The Camden councillor Hamza Chowdhury – who was overlooked as the candidate in the constituency in favour of Polanski – went as far as saying the result was “a huge win for the Green party and the wider movement”.
Polanski supporters point out that since he was elected leader in September 2025, the party has quadrupled its membership to more than 230,000. As well as the winning of its first ever seat in the north of England, he presided over the Greens’ best-ever performance in May’s local and mayoral elections, including gaining their first-ever directly elected mayoralty, in Hackney, east London.
Nonetheless, the result in north London exposed the dual challenge Polanski now faced, said Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. At the same time as the replacement of Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham had brought disillusioned progressives back to Labour, Polanski had become a more polarising figure.
A series of missteps, starting when he shared a social media post critical of police after the Golders Green stabbings, had damaged his popularity with the wider UK public, added Tryl. “It was just one of those moments which gave soft Green supporters pause for thought. Similarly, many people don’t vote directly on something like the Zionism is racism motion, but it adds to that sense of ‘oh, I thought these were nice guys who were focused on the environment’.”
The result in north London was a “good one” for Labour, he added, despite the drop in its majority. While governing parties usually get hit hard in byelections, the drop in Holborn was below the average for defending a seat at byelections in any postwar parliament, he noted.
But Labour hopes of the death of the Green party were likely to have been exaggerated. “I think writing off the Greens is premature,” he said. “Burnham has managed, for now, to unite the left, but a lot of big decisions, including on North Sea oil drilling and, more importantly, the budget, are coming down the line.”
As for Polanski, the path towards rebuilding the popularity that saw him win the support of young voters desperate for hope and change would lie in a return to his original economic messaging around “rip-off Britain” and generational fairness, rather than divisive internal battles, said James Baggaley from UCL’s Policy Lab. “The question for the Greens and Polanski now is: do they want to reassure voters on questions of antisemitism and also get back to what they were actually winning on, which was the economy?”

Lina Altawell
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
 Israeli occupiers carried out 19 attacks against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank from early Friday until around noon, targeting olive farmers, trees, crops, livestock and vehicles, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The commission said its preliminary monitoring, based on field reports, showed a surge in attacks during the olive harvest season, including assaults on farmers and the burning and uprooting of olive trees.
“The attacks included torching a vehicle during an assault on farmers in Tell, uprooting more than 50 olive trees in Qusra and targeting olive pickers in Jurish, Beita, Naqoura, Birzeit, Deir Ibzi and Far'ata,” according to the commission.
“Occupiers also opened fire in Deir Ballut, while a farmer was injured in Kafr ad-Dik,” the commission said.
“An elderly Palestinian woman was injured in Birin, east of Hebron, after occupiers unleashed dogs at farmers, while sheep were stolen in Ein Qiniya,” according to the commission.
A Palestinian man and his child were also assaulted and their vehicle stolen in Yabroud, while vehicles came under attack in Sarda and Al-Rayhan.

Occupiers also set fire to olive trees in Wadi al-Shaer, between Salfit and the village of Al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya, according to local sources.
Near Ramallah, Israeli forces fired tear gas at olive pickers in the Wadi al-Lubban and Gharaba areas east of Abwein and prevented farmers from reaching their land, Wafa reported.
Dozens of occupiers also stormed an area between Sarda and Al-Rayhan north of Ramallah, threw stones at Palestinian vehicles and fired live ammunition into the air, damaging a memorial at the site.
In Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, occupiers released their livestock onto Palestinian land in Khirbet Umm al-Khair, threatening grazing areas and crops, Wafa said.
The Palestinian olive harvest season began on Sept. 20. The Agriculture Ministry expects about 21,000 tons of olive oil to be produced during the current season.
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said more than 45,000 trees were cut down or damaged across the West Bank during the first half of 2026, including more than 26,000 olive trees.
Since October 2023, Israeli forces and occupiers have intensified attacks against Palestinians and their property across the occupied West Bank. Palestinian figures say 1,210 people have been killed, 13,350 injured and 26,000 arrested during that period.

French unions block Israel Elbit arms shipment but El Al step in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:32:13 UTC
01:32:13 KST

Breadcrumb
French unions block Israel arms shipment to Elbit, warn of Israeli airline El Al's role
French trade unions and pro-Palestinian groups say they have prevented a shipment of military components from being flown to Israel by Air France, but warn the same cargo has now been booked onto an Israeli airline's flight scheduled for Saturday.
A source at activist group Urgence Palestine told The New Arab on Friday that the shipment, destined for Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems Land, remained in France after workers and campaigners intervened to stop its transport on an Air France flight from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport on Thursday morning.
"The shipment did not leave and is still in France," the source said, adding that Air France had cancelled the transport contract despite publicly denying that the cargo had ever been booked onto its flights. The organisation said it had evidence of the original booking, as well as the new flight number and air waybill.
According to a statement issued by the unions on Thursday, French manufacturer Mijno, based in Saint-Étienne, and freight company DSV have rebooked the shipment onto Israeli airline El Al's flight LY220, scheduled to depart Charles de Gaulle Airport on Saturday, 10 October.
The unions, including branches of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) and SUD Aérien, have called on French authorities and airport management to prevent the cargo from leaving the country. They said France's obligations under international law remained unchanged regardless of which airline transported the goods.
The shipment reportedly contains mechanical components used in systems fitted to military vehicles and intended for Elbit Systems Land, part of Israeli defence manufacturer Elbit Systems.
The unions credited the mobilisation of freight handlers, loading crews and airport workers, following an alert from Urgence Palestine and the Palestinian Youth Movement, with preventing the shipment from leaving on Thursday's Air France flight AF966 to Tel Aviv, scheduled for 09:35.
Air France denied on Thursday that the cargo had been booked onto its flights, saying it did not transport weapons or ammunition to Israel. The Stop Arming Israel campaign disputed the airline's account, claiming that the shipment's details had been removed from its booking system on Wednesday evening. The New Arab has not independently verified the booking records or the contents of the shipment.
Two associations, NIDAL and Action Sécurité Éthique Républicaines (ASER), have also taken legal steps to challenge the shipment, asking the French prime minister's office to establish whether an export licence had been issued, identify the intended end user and examine any guarantees governing its use.
Through their lawyers, the groups also asked customs authorities at Charles de Gaulle Airport and in Lyon, through which the cargo was reportedly due to pass, to locate and inspect the shipment. They called for any export authorisation to be suspended if necessary.
The associations argue that exporting components intended for military vehicles to Israel could breach France's obligations under the Arms Trade Treaty and the Genocide Convention. They also raised concerns about possible French government complicity in alleged crimes committed by Israeli forces in Gaza.
France's foreign ministry defended its export policy on Thursday. Spokesman Pascal Confavreux said military components could be exported to Israel only if they were intended exclusively for defensive purposes or incorporated into equipment subsequently re-exported to third countries.
He said France fully complied with its international commitments and that exports were subject to strict parliamentary oversight and guarantees concerning their use. However, he did not explain how authorities verified the final use of components once delivered to Israeli companies.
French military exports to Israel have faced growing scrutiny amid the war in Gaza. An investigation published in June 2025 documented continued shipments of French-made military components to Israel, while French dockworkers previously refused to load weapons components reportedly destined for Israeli manufacturers.
The latest mobilisation is part of a broader campaign launched in early October by around 60 organisations seeking to end military cooperation with Israel and prevent the transport of weapons and military components through French companies, ports and airports. Similar actions by port workers in Italy have also disrupted suspected arms shipments to Israel.
The unions have urged airport workers to remain vigilant ahead of Saturday's planned departure and called on Air France to make a public commitment not to transport any equipment destined for Israeli military use.

"The live streaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," UN human rights office spokesperson Shabia Mantoo told reporters in Geneva.

The planned broadcast would reportedly mark the first public execution in the US in nearly a century.

As Trump mulls new strikes on Iran, what options does he have?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:29:19 UTC
01:29:19 KST

Breadcrumb
As Trump mulls new strikes on Iran, what options does he have?
Following renewed US troop movements into the Middle East, the US is reportedly gearing up for a new round of strikes on Iran after weeks of deliberations by President Donald Trump.
Trump has on several occasions stated that he would not launch new strikes until after the midterm elections, the latest being on Thursday, saying on Truth Social that discussions with Iran were "productive."
Yet, according to both The New York Times and Axios, Trump mulled the possibility of further strikes following a meeting with his national security staff in Camp David on 2 October. A final decision is set to occur within the next seven to 10 days, Israel's Channel 12 reported.
The New Arab explores if and how the US military will escalate tensions, and if Iran will retaliate.
What is now in the region?
As it stands, the US has around 50,000 troops and a host of assets in the region, including the 82nd Airborne Division, air defence systems, surveillance, refuelling and strike aircraft that it built up before and during the start of the Iran war.
This includes the USS George Washington aircraft carrier, involved in blockading Iran and escorting shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, and the USS Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, housing the 11th Marine Expeditionary Group.
In recent weeks, reports have shed light on new deployments, with some stating there will be between 9,000 and 10,000 troops, including the 13th Marine Expeditionary Group aboard the USS Makin Island, stationed alongside the USS Theodor Roosevelt, according to The Wall Street Journal.
This would maintain US carrier deployments to the region at two, following the withdrawal of the USS George H.W. Bush, which has since arrived in Thailand. It is unknown if the George Washington is also set to withdraw.
The US has also sent two additional Patriot missile batteries, used to shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, to prop up the dense web of systems already deployed and further protect Saudi and Qatari energy sites, according to Axios.
What are Trump's options?
According to Dr Andreas Krieg, Senior Lecturer in Defence Studies at King's College London, the deployments signal that the US "wants to restore escalation dominance without yet committing to another major war", with the troop and carrier deployments acting as both deterrence and preparation.
"The US is reinforcing air and missile defence, force protection, ISR [Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance], logistics and command capacity around Israel and the Gulf, while simultaneously giving Trump a much larger menu of strike options," he told The New Arab.
That menu has been reported on by The New York Times, with five plans drawn up focusing on a short, three-day campaign of intense strikes focusing on the drone and missile arsenal of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, their command posts and headquarters, alongside energy facilities.
Strikes on infrastructure are also expected to occur in the event of a US bombardment, and Israel is also expected to take part in an escalation, with Israeli media reporting that Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir is being briefed on US preparations.
The deployment of two carriers is a key aspect of this, with Krieg noting that it gives US military flexibility in any strike campaign against Iran, increasing sortie rates, allowing the US to enforce a blockade and protect shipping, and giving the US options to escalate the campaign targets.
"Trump wants Tehran to believe that rejecting American terms could now carry a much higher military cost," Krieg said, adding "but these deployments also expose the central weakness of the US position: every additional American asset placed in the Gulf creates another target Iran can threaten".
How could Iran respond?
Like in previous rounds of attacks on Iran by the US or Israel, Tehran is likely to retaliate.
Krieg told The New Arab that Iran would likely respond in two stages, the first being a focus on survivability, with the IRGC and military dispersing assets into hardened facilities, using decoys and decentralising command, to survive the initial strikes.
The second would see a horizontal escalation, targeting US bases and logistics hubs, pressuring Gulf infrastructure, and disrupting maritime traffic around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb through its Houthi allies.
"I think Tehran's calculation remains that the Gulf is America's vulnerability. Iran would aim to make any renewed US campaign immediately costly for Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and global energy markets," he said.
"Iran is likely to answer by making clear that such an escalation cannot be geographically contained inside Iran."
This was echoed by Ali Vaez, Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, who told The New Arab that "Iran cannot match the US militarily, so its strategy is to make escalation costly and geographically expansive."
"Its leverage lies in convincing Washington that any attack on Iran will reverberate across the region," he added.
"I fear that a high US casualty event might compel Trump to throw caution to the wind and go after Iran's infrastructure, which will result in Iran scorching the region," Vaez said.
Is this the same as the February attack?
Much of what is being debated is similar to what played out in February when the war began, with Andreas Kreig telling The New Arab, "There is a striking degree of repetition. The United States still essentially has the same coercive menu it had at the beginning of the war."
Those same escalation plans are part of the same "strategic calculus" employed by both sides, Kreig added, noting that the US is continuing to attempt to use military power to shorten the conflict, despite not being able to translate military power into political leverage, while Iran is playing for time.
"Unless one side changes that underlying logic, we are likely to keep seeing variations of the same escalation pattern rather than a genuinely new strategy," Krieg said.

Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Ben Gurion terminal after two scouting flights, UAE says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:28:39 UTC
01:28:39 KST

The United Arab Emirates' attorney general confirmed Friday that the Omani co-pilot who attempted to seize control of a Flydubai passenger jet intended to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion Airport, revealing that his Islamist radicalization had begun years earlier while he was studying in Australia.
UAE Attorney General Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said the suspect, Hamam al-Hammami, had planned a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel's main international airport. The co-pilot confessed to acting alone, but the attorney general emphasized that the investigation into his connections and possible accomplices was continuing.
According to the official statement, al-Hammami "intended to seize control of the aircraft and use it to carry out a suicide attack against the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport, with the aim of causing the greatest possible number of casualties."
Investigators found that the first signs of his radicalization and inclination toward terrorism emerged in 2017, when he was studying in Australia. During that period, the suspect was influenced by takfiri ideology, an extremist interpretation of Islam, through radical literature and online content glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide attacks.
The statement added that the co-pilot "drew inspiration from the September 11 attacks in the United States, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his mind. According to his confession, this was connected to his decision to pursue a career in aviation."
Radicalization in Melbourne and preparations for the attack
According to the UAE statement, al-Hammami confessed that while studying in Melbourne, Australia, he regularly attended a mosque affiliated with the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT). During his visits, he became acquainted with individuals associated with a center called My Centre.
He claimed the center was managed by a Lebanese man known as Abu Hamza and allegedly received support from an organization linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. These claims were made by the suspect and have not been independently established.
Al-Hammami also told investigators that he had prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by increasing his exposure to material encouraging terrorism and undergoing boxing training with a private instructor.
The investigation found that the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the flight route and Ben Gurion Airport as part of his preparations for the alleged terrorist plot. He decided to carry out the attack during his third flight to Israel, on September 30.
Investigators also examined how the suspect had been recruited by Flydubai. According to the statement, he met the airline's professional and security requirements, including holding a valid pilot's license, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required background checks.
However, none of those procedures revealed indications of his extremist beliefs or his intention to carry out a terrorist attack.
Cockpit struggle and emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
The Emirati statement also detailed the events aboard the flight. According to investigators, the suspect surprised the aircraft's captain inside the cockpit and attacked him with an emergency axe. The captain, Smit Machchhar, resisted the assault and attempted to summon help.
A pilot assigned to operate the aircraft's return flight was also on board and happened to be near the cockpit when the attack took place.
"He noticed the cockpit door repeatedly opening and closing in an unusual manner, which aroused his suspicions," the statement said.
The pilot approached the cockpit and attempted to enter using the access code. After gaining entry, he saw the suspect attacking the captain and immediately intervened.
The Emirati account gave limited attention to the role of Israeli passengers in stopping the attack, stating that the pilot intervened with the assistance of a crew member and several passengers.
Together, they rescued the injured captain and subdued the suspect.
Meanwhile, the captain assigned to the return flight and his co-pilot regained control of the aircraft, diverted it from its original route and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Suspect confesses to acting alone, investigation continues
According to the UAE authorities, al-Hammami provided a detailed confession in the presence of his lawyer, after all legally required safeguards and guarantees had been ensured.
The suspect described his motives and the various stages of planning and carrying out the attempted attack.
He admitted to acting alone, without the involvement of others, although investigators are continuing to examine evidence to verify that claim.
The UAE Public Prosecution also collected testimony from the aircraft's captain, the pilot assigned to the return flight, his co-pilot and members of the cabin crew.
The attorney general emphasized that the investigation remains ongoing, particularly regarding the suspect's connections and the possibility that others may have been involved in planning or facilitating the attempted attack.

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç

The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday strongly rejected US sanctions imposed on the institution, calling them an attempt to obstruct justice and vowing to continue its work independently.
“This measure targets an independent judicial institution, created by treaty and entrusted by 125 States Parties with investigating and prosecuting genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression,” the court said in a statement.
The ICC described the sanctions as “an assault on the rule of law” and the foundations of the international legal order.
It said the measures aimed to disrupt the court’s operations and intimidate those working for or cooperating with it.
“The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
The court said the sanctions followed US designations against 13 independent judges and prosecutors, adding that it would not be deterred from carrying out its mandate.
The ICC called on member states to take concrete steps to ensure it had the resources needed to continue its work.
“This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law,” the statement said.
The court also said that “no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice.”
It added that future generations and victims of mass atrocities would judge how the international community responded to the sanctions.
The statement followed an announcement by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio of sanctions against the court.
It also emphasized the court's role in ensuring accountability for serious international crimes.
"As a court of last resort, the ICC plays an important role in combating impunity for the most serious international crimes," it said.
Announcing the sanctions, Rubio said: "President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans. That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court."
He also threatened to "end the ICC" unless it stopped what he described as its "threats."

Yemen's humanitarian crisis worsens as fighting displaces 200,000: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:25:32 UTC
01:25:32 KST

Yemen’s humanitarian crisis has sharply deteriorated amid renewed fighting that has displaced more than 200,000 people since early August, a senior United Nations official warned, calling for urgent international action to prevent further suffering.
Mohamed Yahya, assistant secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and deputy emergency relief coordinator, delivered the warning on Friday during a UN Security Council briefing on behalf of humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher.
“Today, I must warn the Council that Yemen’s humanitarian crisis has sharply worsened. Further inaction will cost lives,” Yahya said.
He said escalating hostilities over the past two months had forced families already worn down by more than a decade of conflict to flee their homes, often after exhausting their savings and losing their livelihoods.
The latest displacement represents the highest number of newly displaced people since the 2022 truce, according to Yahya.
Nearly 4,000 others have crossed the Bab al Mandab Strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia.
Civilian casualties mount as health services come under pressure
Women and children were bearing the heaviest burden as violence intensified, Yahya warned, citing figures from the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights showing that at least 46 civilians had been killed and more than 130 injured since early August.
The influx of conflict-related casualties is pushing Yemen’s already overstretched health system closer to collapse, he said, warning that inadequate funding and resources would deepen the emergency, hinder recovery and leave vulnerable families less able to withstand future shocks.
Yahya stressed that a political solution was essential to preventing further suffering, cautioning that continued fighting would displace more people and further restrict humanitarian access.
“The people of Yemen need more than our concern and our outrage. They need our collective action, our concrete support, and our unwavering commitment to deliver,” he said.
Children face growing threats to safety and education
Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save the Children International, told the Security Council that the escalation was threatening children’s safety, education and well-being.
For many children, she said, schools and education had increasingly become a refuge from danger rather than a pathway to opportunity.
“Yemen is a country of tremendous vibrance and hope. This latest escalation risks reversing its fragile recovery,” Ashing said.
She warned that the country faced a “deadly convergence” of conflict, displacement, economic decline and a rise in infectious and waterborne diseases.
Children were also at “disproportionate risk” from explosive weapons, she said, urging urgent action to prevent further harm.
“Without urgent action, more children will be pushed deeper into hardship, with lasting consequences for their survival, learning, and protection,” Ashing said.

Latvia’s border guard seeks greater powers amid increasingly violent border crossings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:25:20 UTC
01:25:20 KST

As “armed, masked escorts” lead migrants from Belarus into Latvia, the Latvian Border Guard is seeking greater powers to “protect Latvia’s security.” The interior minister supports the proposal.
On 5 October, a group used makeshift stairs to enter Latvia. While the Baltic country of two million has faced irregular migration from Belarus since 2021, the latest incident was particularly aggressive.
The group of 20 migrants was led by “armed, masked escorts openly threatening Latvian soldiers,” Latvia’s Interior Minister, Jānis Dombrava, told Euronews. In the following hours, border surveillance equipment was damaged, reducing Latvia’s “ability to detect and respond to further incursions.”
“The combination of armed intimidation and targeted sabotage raises the risk of a violent confrontation and tests both our defences and our willingness to respond,” Dombrava said, adding that it’s “a security threat, not simply a migration-management problem.”
Latvia completed the fencing of its 173-kilometre border with Belarus this year and installed advanced surveillance systems, making crossings harder. The obstacles are making facilitators increasingly aggressive, according to Guntis Pujāts, head of Latvia’s State Border Guard.
“That’s why they are trying to be more aggressive and so to throw stones as well, to show what looks like a weapon and so on,” Pujāts told Euronews, adding that the incident “shows that the situation is not going to decrease but in the opposite way”.
More powers to Border Guard
The State Border Guard is now seeking greater powers to protect its personnel and secure the country’s border, as Latvia enters its fifth year of dealing with irregular migration from Belarus. The interior minister supports the move.
Currently, border guards already have the right to use firearms in circumstances prescribed by law, including when responding to serious threats and attempted acts of sabotage.
Pujāts wants to broaden their powers, as well as those of police and military personnel supporting border operations, to enable them to “protect the security of Latvia”.
On Thursday, the Border Guard submitted a proposal to the Interior Ministry seeking changes to the rules.
Under the proposed changes, border guards would no longer have to issue a warning before using force in certain circumstances, Pujāts said. They would also be able to use the tools at their disposal to stop and “neutralise” people damaging border infrastructure.
“We will not be obliged to warn before, and we will be allowed all tools that we have to stop and so to neutralise persons who are damaging our border infrastructure,” he said.
The interior minister confirmed to Euronews that he will propose amendments “to give those protecting our country clearer powers and greater discretion when facing threats of this kind.”
“Those who protect Latvia's state border – border guards, soldiers and other officials – must be confident that they will not be unjustifiably subjected to criminal prosecution for the lawful use of firearms or special means,” he said.
Pujāts said he did not know how long it would take for the proposal to become law. Asked when he would like the changes to take effect, he replied: “Yesterday, or the day before yesterday.”

Businesses and industry can provide substantial support to Ukraine's energy sector during periods of massive Russian attacks, Vitaliy Zaichenko, CEO of NPC Ukrenergo, said during an online meeting with representatives of the European Business Association (EBA) on Friday.
"As a result of Russian strikes on power generation facilities, electricity transmission networks and distribution grids in several regions, which occur almost daily, we are already being forced to introduce scheduled power outages," he said.
At the same time, according to the CEO, many large enterprises, office buildings and shopping centers have their own backup power sources that are not connected to the main grid. If all these installations operated continuously, rather than only during power outages, the need to impose restrictions could be significantly reduced.
"We are also asking industry to reconsider its production schedules. Reducing electricity consumption by large enterprises during peak load periods on the power system would also shorten the periods when forced outages have to be implemented," Zaichenko emphasized.
During the discussion between business representatives and Ukrenergo management, participants also addressed ways to simplify the procedure for connecting generating installations to the main grid, as well as the repayment of outstanding debts to renewable energy producers and on the balancing market. The parties agreed to continue the dialogue and examine the proposals they had presented to each other in detail.
As reported, official industry statistics currently account only for backup generating capacity owned by industry and businesses that is connected to the networks of transmission system operators. However, the capacity of generating installations operating in fully autonomous mode is not included in official data, meaning that the actual volume of this generation remains unknown.

UAE: flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israel's Ben-Gurion Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:24:18 UTC
01:24:18 KST

The United Arab Emirates' attorney general said Friday that the co-pilot who seized a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv planned to crash the plane into Israel's main Ben-Gurion Airport.
According to the UAE's state news agency WAM, the suspect admitted attempting to hijack the flight and said he had visited Tel Aviv at least twice beforehand to "familiarize himself with the flight route and the airport." The UAE prosecutor general said the plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.
The Omani co-pilot, identified as Hamam al-Hammami, allegedly attacked the captain in the cockpit with an emergency crash axe and attempted to take control of Flight 1073 last Wednesday, as it carried 174 people from Dubai to Israel. The incident caused the aircraft to plunge 16,000 feet in 30 seconds.
The prosecutor general said the investigation, launched on October 1, found that the co-pilot told investigators he had acted alone, but authorities are still examining whether he received assistance. According to the UAE prosecutor general's statement, his radicalization began in 2017, when he started taking an interest in extremist ideologies and terrorist acts.
The captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to open the cockpit door despite his injuries, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene. Al-Hammami reportedly stabbed the captain several times. Two other pilots aboard the plane helped subdue the co-pilot and land the aircraft in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where al-Hammami was detained before being transferred to the UAE. After waiting in Saudi Arabia for several hours, the passengers returned to Ben-Gurion Airport.
According to two Israeli officials familiar with the Emirati investigation, al-Hammami told interrogators that he had applied to fly for an airline operating routes to Tel Aviv. A third source briefed on the probe said he had planned to crash the plane into Ben-Gurion Airport and had previously intended to hijack and crash an earlier flight to Israel, but abandoned that attempt. It was unclear why he changed his mind, though the source said he was believed to have known someone aboard the earlier flight.
Israeli officials have said al-Hammami planned the attack before joining flydubai. He had previously been removed from flight training at Oman Air over concerns about extremist views, according to sources familiar with the matter. ABC News reported that he had been suspended in 2024 after extremist materials were found in his possession while he was a trainee co-pilot.
The UAE prosecutor general said al-Hammami had met flydubai's professional and security requirements, and that the airline's checks before hiring him had not uncovered extremist views or links to terrorist activity. The attorney general said al-Hammami had worked for several airlines in different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining flydubai in January 2026.
A social media account linked to al-Hammami also drew scrutiny after the incident. CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing his name posted footage of Israeli aircraft and images of Al-Qaida figures about nine hours after the attempted hijacking. The posts' author was unclear, as was whether they had been scheduled in advance. The profile said al-Hammami had worked for Oman Air for seven years before leaving in February 2025, then spent about seven months at Royal Air Maroc before joining flydubai.
The Emirati prosecutor general has described the incident as a terrorist attack. Anwar Mohammed Gargash, a senior diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, also publicly called it a "terrorist act." Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said al-Hammami had "undergone Islamist radicalization" and "came to crash the plane with its passengers." Netanyahu said Israel was investigating whether the co-pilot had acted on someone else's orders.
The UAE has not announced formal charges against al-Hammami, and it is not known whether he has appointed a lawyer. Oman has not commented on the incident. UAE and Israeli authorities, as well as flydubai, did not immediately respond to requests for comment when Reuters reported on the investigation.
The incident prompted Netanyahu to order a review of foreign airlines flying to Israel, after he said pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel, including Oman, were not permitted to operate flights to the country. It remains unclear how al-Hammami was assigned to the Tel Aviv route. An Australian counterterrorism unit is also investigating his ties to Australia; a source said he studied at RMIT University in Melbourne around a decade ago.
Flydubai suspended its flights to Israel until further notice after the incident. Israeli carriers Arkia and Israir have since operated repatriation flights from Dubai for Israelis stranded by the suspension.

26 women, 4 children killed in Sudan RSF drone strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:23:29 UTC
01:23:29 KST

Breadcrumb
26 women, 4 children killed in Sudan RSF drone strike: official, witnesses
A drone strike launched by Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces killed 26 women and four children on Friday near the southeastern border with Ethiopia, an official and eyewitnesses told AFP.
The latest front line in Sudan's war between the regular army and the RSF is the border region with Ethiopia, which is facing its own internal conflict that threatens to escalate into a regional war.
Since Sudan's war broke out in April 2023, it has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and created the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
This year alone, nearly 100,000 people have been displaced across Blue Nile state, according to UN figures.
In a displacement camp in Blue Nile's Abu Shendi, survivors "buried 26 women and four children" from Friday's strike, one person involved in the burial told AFP.
The drone hit just outside the camp, near an informal gold mining site, where women earn a daily wage using chemicals and their bare hands to clear gold nuggets from clumps of earth men have extracted.
The victims included "young girls who work with their families in refining the gold", another eyewitness said.
The country's multi-billion-dollar gold trade, built mostly on makeshift operations like Abu Shendi's, fuels the war efforts of both sides.
Mahgoub al-Sheikh, the governor of Wad al-Mahi where the attack took place, said the drone was launched from "inside Ethiopia".
Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of harbouring RSF fighters and bases within its territory.
Ethiopia has denied the accusations, though local sources say the porous border is a key supply line for the paramilitary and its allies.
'War of atrocities'
Throughout this year, the RSF has pushed an offensive approaching state capital El-Damazin.
The advance could put the army in a bind, forcing it to defend territory on both the Blue Nile front and in the Kordofan region, where a year of deadly drone strikes has left the two sides in a stalemate.
The Sudan war, now in its fourth year, has evolved into an ever more sophisticated conflict using armed drones, enabling both sides to launch far-reaching attacks without sacrificing their fighters.
More than 1,100 people were killed by drone strikes during the first five months of this year alone, according to UN figures.
The conflict, which the UN calls a "war of atrocities", has visited a litany of horrors on civilians including ethnic massacres, famine and indiscriminate attacks on residential areas.
The RSF has specifically been accused of genocide and systematic sexual violence.
Attempts to bring the warring parties to the table have failed, as former allies army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Daglo jostle for the upper hand.
Both continue to receive robust support from external powers, according to the UN, who fuel the conflict with weapons and mercenaries.
The UAE denies widespread reports it backs the RSF through Sudan's neighbours, while the army has received support from Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

Zionism, racism and the Green party in turmoil | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:22:50 UTC
01:22:50 KST

As ever, Jonathan Freedland is on the money in his article (The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think, 3 October). As a non-religious Jew-ish Londoner, I am appalled at the passing of the motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism, and I am seriously considering leaving the Green party as a result.
While I condemn the Israeli government’s actions against the Palestinian people, and I am not a Zionist myself, Zionism as defined by the motion is only one political interpretation and completely ignores ancient religious and cultural definitions held by many Jews who also condemn the current Israeli government.
I have worked with Palestinians and Israelis on the West Bank and in Jerusalem in the cause of peace and reconciliation, and firmly believe in equal rights for everyone in Israel and the occupied territories. That cause will be set back by this decision, which will give fuel to antisemites who hide their racism under an anti-Zionist guise.
This decision is a shot in the foot for the Green party, risking the alienation of British Jews and others who, like me, support peace and reconciliation, believe in equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians, and strongly oppose the actions of the current Israeli government.
Simon Lawson
London
Jonathan Freedland is right that Zionism means different things to different people, and that Jewish historical attachment to Israel cannot simply be dismissed. But that complexity can also become a way of avoiding the more important question: what has Zionism produced in practice?
“Fire is destructive” does not mean every use of fire is destructive. It means fire has destructive potential, which is why we recognise boundaries around its use. The same applies to Zionism. Jewish self-determination is not inherently racist; but when a political project pursued in its name produces permanent occupation, settlement, displacement, unequal rights and Palestinian subordination, it is legitimate to ask whether the project has crossed those boundaries. Therefore, “Zionism is racist” can be a true description of the manifestation of Zionism embodied in the current Israeli state.
The issue, therefore, isn’t whether a benign definition of Zionism can be imagined. It plainly can. The issue is whether the political reality created in its name conforms to that definition. We should be able to examine Zionism as we examine any other political ideology: by its effects, its institutions, and the boundaries it recognises. Criticising a political ideology or the actions of a state is not the same thing as attacking Jews or Judaism.
Raymond O’Brien
London
Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Green party success in the EU elections in 1989 saw a huge increase in membership and a wave of entryism. By 1991 it was fragmented and irrelevant. Zack Polanski’s election as leader of the Green party also saw a wave of entryism.
It was never tenable to allow a gathering composed of those who can afford, or choose, to turn up to be the party’s policymaking body. But for many Greens it is an article of faith; proof of the party’s commitment to “democracy”. They were called “fundis” (fundamentalists) in my day. A group of us (“realos”) tried to change things in 1990 with a motion arguing that a “leadership” structure was necessary in a world where we were under the media microscope. The motion passed, but the party split.
It is tragic to see a party that has pulled itself up by its bootstraps since the early 1990s, that has worked hard to win representation locally, and that has won seats in Westminster under a voting system that disadvantages newcomers, being stopped in its tracks by its lack of internal democracy.
Here’s a suggestion from an oldie. Organise an internal referendum on the motion and let the whole membership decide. And put an end to the travesty of democracy that saw it adopted in the first place.
Lyn Dade
Twickenham, London
As a member of the Green party, I was dismayed by the profoundly counterproductive “Zionism is racism” motion passed at conference on Sunday. Since his election as leader and his success in broadening the party’s appeal, opponents of Zack Polanski and the Greens have repeatedly sought to portray the party as antisemitic. This motion hands them the ammunition they have been looking for.
Until now, the Greens have stood out among UK political parties in their willingness to describe Israel as an apartheid state and to condemn its actions in Gaza as genocidal. That argument risks being obscured by an entirely avoidable debate over accusations of antisemitism.
The motion is also historically and politically flawed. While the form of Zionism represented by the Israeli state today is exclusionary and discriminatory, it does not follow that all forms of Zionism are racist.
Zionism emerged, in large part, as a response to the persecution of Jews in Europe. To erase that history from our understanding of Zionism is to overlook the reality of anti-Jewish racism that helped give rise to the movement.
I hope the Green party leadership can find a way to distance itself from this damaging motion and refocus attention on holding the Israeli government accountable for its treatment of the Palestinians.
Prof Benjamin Selwyn
University of Sussex

Ukrainian journalist Tkach says he was detained in Vienna “like a terrorist”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:21:00 UTC
01:21:00 KST

Ukrainian journalist Tkach says he was detained in Vienna “like a terrorist”
As reported by Ukrinform, this was stated by Mykhailo Tkach, head of the investigative journalism department at Ukrainska Pravda, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda.
“From the way I experienced it, we were detained like terrorists. They did not communicate with us at all. There were these shocking screams, they were all shouting and pointing weapons at us, and there was simply no communication,” the journalist said.
According to Tkach, he and Bondarenko were traveling from one filming location to another. About 3–5 kilometers from central Vienna, their car stopped at a traffic light. At that moment, seven armed masked men ran up to the vehicle. They smashed the windows and pointed their weapons at the journalists.
Tkach added that he immediately raised his hand and said in English that he was a journalist. He and Bondarenko were pulled out of the car, thrown face down onto the road, searched and had their hands restrained behind their backs with tape.
“I kept repeating that I was a journalist. Instead, one of these men put his knee on my neck and shouted at me to be quiet. Then they dragged me away. There was an archway nearby, and they pulled me under it, made me face the wall again and told me to keep quiet,” he said.
According to Tkach, he was detained by masked men who did not identify themselves or explain their actions. The journalist did not see any identification and did not notice the word “police,” so for the first 30–40 minutes he believed that he and Bondarenko were being abducted.
The journalist realized that they were police only after he was taken out from under the archway and saw police vehicles. He was placed in a separate compartment of a van and driven for about 20 minutes with the sirens on.
Tkach said that he had not seen Bondarenko since the moment of his detention. At the same time, the journalist saw the shattered glass from the car window fly into the cameraman’s face.
At the police facility, Tkach had all his belongings taken away, was ordered to remove his shoes and was placed in a solitary cell. According to him, he waited there for about two hours without any explanation, although he repeatedly asked police officers why he had been detained. During that time, a doctor examined him and asked about his condition.
Later, Tkach was taken to another room and ordered to strip completely, after which his clothes were taken away. His belongings were later returned, and the journalist was weighed and measured.
The journalist was also asked to sign a document in German. He refused, explaining that he did not understand what was written. According to Tkach, the police officer became angry and started shouting in response.
He was then taken to two people whom he believed to be investigators. Only then, according to the journalist, did a substantive conversation begin.
Ukrainska Pravda added that Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said Tkach had been released after being detained in Vienna, while cameraman Bondarenko remained in custody. The minister said the Ukrainians had been detained on suspicion of espionage.
The journalist was released at 4:00 on Friday after spending 12 hours in custody. The cameraman, who was detained together with Tkach, was injured during the detention and “was in hospital.” Bondarenko’s questioning only began overnight.
As reported by the media, Mykhailo Tkach, head of the investigative journalism department at Ukrainska Pravda, was detained in Vienna while carrying out an editorial assignment related to locating fugitive Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.

Explainer-Is it legal for the US to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's execution?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:19:59 UTC
01:19:59 KST

Explainer: Is it legal for the US to live-stream the Fort Hood shooter’s execution?
- The Pentagon plans to live-stream Nidal Hasan’s firing squad execution, raising legal and human rights questions after President Donald Trump approved it on Oct 5.
- US law allows firing squad executions, but a federal ban blocks broadcasting in prison cases; military rules do not clearly do the same, and courts have limited public access.
- Hasan may still challenge his sentence in federal court, which could delay the Dec 3 execution, while the UN says livestreaming would be “cruel and inhumane” and breach torture rules.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Pentagon said on Oct 8 that it would live-stream the firing squad execution of the man who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, raising questions about the legality of the unprecedented announcement.
Here’s what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad.
Is death by firing squad legal in the US?
Yes. The US Supreme Court said in a unanimous 1879 decision that execution by firing squad is not “cruel and unusual punishment” prohibited by the Constitution.
The justices in 2025 cleared the way for South Carolina to carry out its first execution by firing squad in decades.
Five states currently allow executions by firing squad: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. The Trump administration earlier this year said it would allow execution by firing squad in the federal prison system.
The US Army also once regularly carried out executions by firing squad of US soldiers found guilty of desertion or other offences. Hundreds of US soldiers were sentenced to death during the Civil War from 1861 to 1865.
Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the president is the only person who can approve a death sentence for a member of the US armed services. President Donald Trump on Oct 5 signed off on the Pentagon’s plan to execute the Fort Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist.
Can executions be broadcast?
Executions in the US were once public spectacles, but in the last century have been carried out in correctional facilities away from the public eye.
In 1936, a man convicted of rape was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a public hanging in Missouri.
A US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. But military regulations have not applied that same prohibition to military executions. Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder by a military jury in 2013, following a court-martial trial.
State laws regulate who can witness executions, generally limiting access to authorised officials, family members, legal counsel, and a handful of media representatives.
Courts have long rejected lawsuits brought by media organisations seeking broader public access to executions.
In 2001, a judge denied a request by an internet company to live-stream the lethal injection execution of Timothy McVeigh, an anti-government militant who bombed a federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995, killing 168 people. The Justice Department did provide a restricted, closed-circuit television broadcast exclusively for survivors of the bombing and victims’ families.
Could Hasan challenge his execution in court?
While Hasan has exhausted his direct appeals within the military justice system, he can still challenge his underlying conviction and sentence in the federal civilian court system.
Such a challenge, known as a federal habeas corpus proceeding, provides another layer of review before a death sentence is carried out.
Even if unsuccessful, that move could stall the execution, potentially for years. Hasan’s execution is currently set for Dec 3.
Hasan could also file a civil rights lawsuit seeking to challenge the method of his execution, legal experts said.
Hasan told a panel of military mental health experts in 2010 that he wished he had been killed during the attack because it would have meant God had chosen him for martyrdom, an indication that he may not exercise all his legal options. Hasan acted as his own attorney during his 2013 military trial and offered almost no defence.
What about international law?
The United Nations has condemned the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution, saying it is a cruel and inhumane form of punishment that violates an international human rights treaty adopted in 1984 known as the Convention Against Torture. But that treaty, like many other international legal frameworks, is not judicially enforceable within the US court system.
“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” said the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. REUTERS

Explainer: Is it legal for the US to live-stream the Fort Hood shooter’s execution?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Explainer: Is it legal for the US to live-stream the Fort Hood shooter’s execution?
- The Pentagon plans to live-stream Nidal Hasan’s firing squad execution, raising legal and human rights questions after President Donald Trump approved it on Oct 5.
- US law allows firing squad executions, but a federal ban blocks broadcasting in prison cases; military rules do not clearly do the same, and courts have limited public access.
- Hasan may still challenge his sentence in federal court, which could delay the Dec 3 execution, while the UN says livestreaming would be “cruel and inhumane” and breach torture rules.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Pentagon said on Oct 8 that it would live-stream the firing squad execution of the man who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, raising questions about the legality of the unprecedented announcement.
Here’s what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad.
Is death by firing squad legal in the US?
Yes. The US Supreme Court said in a unanimous 1879 decision that execution by firing squad is not “cruel and unusual punishment” prohibited by the Constitution.
The justices in 2025 cleared the way for South Carolina to carry out its first execution by firing squad in decades.
Five states currently allow executions by firing squad: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. The Trump administration earlier this year said it would allow execution by firing squad in the federal prison system.
The US Army also once regularly carried out executions by firing squad of US soldiers found guilty of desertion or other offences. Hundreds of US soldiers were sentenced to death during the Civil War from 1861 to 1865.
Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the president is the only person who can approve a death sentence for a member of the US armed services. President Donald Trump on Oct 5 signed off on the Pentagon’s plan to execute the Fort Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist.
Can executions be broadcast?
Executions in the US were once public spectacles, but in the last century have been carried out in correctional facilities away from the public eye.
In 1936, a man convicted of rape was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a public hanging in Missouri.
A US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. But military regulations have not applied that same prohibition to military executions. Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder by a military jury in 2013, following a court-martial trial.
State laws regulate who can witness executions, generally limiting access to authorised officials, family members, legal counsel, and a handful of media representatives.
Courts have long rejected lawsuits brought by media organisations seeking broader public access to executions.
In 2001, a judge denied a request by an internet company to live-stream the lethal injection execution of Timothy McVeigh, an anti-government militant who bombed a federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995, killing 168 people. The Justice Department did provide a restricted, closed-circuit television broadcast exclusively for survivors of the bombing and victims’ families.
Could Hasan challenge his execution in court?
While Hasan has exhausted his direct appeals within the military justice system, he can still challenge his underlying conviction and sentence in the federal civilian court system.
Such a challenge, known as a federal habeas corpus proceeding, provides another layer of review before a death sentence is carried out.
Even if unsuccessful, that move could stall the execution, potentially for years. Hasan’s execution is currently set for Dec 3.
Hasan could also file a civil rights lawsuit seeking to challenge the method of his execution, legal experts said.
Hasan told a panel of military mental health experts in 2010 that he wished he had been killed during the attack because it would have meant God had chosen him for martyrdom, an indication that he may not exercise all his legal options. Hasan acted as his own attorney during his 2013 military trial and offered almost no defence.
What about international law?
The United Nations has condemned the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution, saying it is a cruel and inhumane form of punishment that violates an international human rights treaty adopted in 1984 known as the Convention Against Torture. But that treaty, like many other international legal frameworks, is not judicially enforceable within the US court system.
“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” said the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. REUTERS

AMSTERDAM, Oct 9 - The Trump administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
Below are some reactions to the move:
THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT:
The sanctions are "an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.
"The designation is aimed at disrupting the Court’s operations and at intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the Court. The Court, for its part, will not be deterred. ... Yet the Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the States that created it."
ISRAELI PRIME MINISTER BENJAMIN NETANYAHU:

Why the UK Greens’ Zionism is racism motion matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:17:51 UTC
01:17:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Why the UK Greens’ Zionism is racism motion matters
Since the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the “Zionism is racism” motion following a membership vote of 1022-813 at its party conference last weekend, it has provoked intense opposition. Backlash has come not only from the right and much of the mainstream press but also from sections of liberal and left media.
Opponents inside and outside the party are even trying to attribute the motion to Party leader Zack Polanski’s loss in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
The motion itself defines Zionism as an ethnonationalist political project and asserts the Party’s commitment to Palestinian liberation, the right of return, BDS, and a full arms embargo against Israel. Moreover, it calls for establishing a single, democratic State across historic Palestine.
Whatever one thinks of every clause of the motion, its political significance extends beyond the text itself. A proposition long confined to Palestinian liberation movements and the anti-imperialist left has become the formal policy of a British parliamentary party. That represents a significant shift in the terrain on which Palestine is debated in electoral politics.
Fifty years of ‘Zionism is racism’
The assertion that Zionism is a form of racism is hardly new to the Palestinian national movement. In November 1975, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 3379, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism and racial discrimination. Despite this being revoked in 1991, the political argument it embodied did not disappear with it.
In the decades that followed, Palestinian organisations have been joined by major international and human rights bodies in documenting systems of domination and discrimination against the Palestinian people. During the Second Intifada, the world witnessed Israeli tanks storm Palestinian refugee camps. We saw 12-year-old Mohammed Al-Durrah murdered in his father’s arms by the Israeli military in Gaza. In 2021, a global uprising erupted in response to the theft of the El-Kurd family home in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of Jerusalem. In 2022, we watched the footage of the murder of Palestinian journalist Shireen Abu Akleh.
We have spent the last three years dumbfounded in horror at the genocidal violence waged in Gaza, livestreamed by brave young journalists on the ground.
At the level of international law, Al-Haq has been defending Palestinian human rights since 1979, conducting research, preparing reports, and intervening on breaches of international human rights – work that has seen them sanctioned by the United States.
International NGOs have also documented the grave human rights abuses against the Palestinian people. In 2021, Human Rights Watch concluded that Israeli authorities were committing crimes against humanity. In 2022, Amnesty International concluded that Israeli authorities impose a system of apartheid against Palestinians.
This evidence makes it increasingly difficult to treat Palestinian descriptions of their oppression as illegitimate or unfounded. This is why 50 years after Resolution 3379, Palestinians and their allies are still advancing a fundamental challenge: that a political order that privileges one national group while dispossessing, displacing or subordinating another cannot be genuinely reconciled with equality.
Reversing the burden
The significance of the motion passing becomes clearer when placed alongside another definition that has shaped British politics over the last decade. In May 2016, the IHRA adopted a non-legally binding working definition of antisemitism. In the aftermath, political parties, universities, councils, and other public bodies adopted it, sparking intense political struggle.
Significant segments of the Palestine movement organised against the adoption of the IHRA definition of antisemitism, arguing that it conflates antisemitism with anti-Zionism and with genuine critique of the Zionist entity of Israel. The University and Colleges Union (UCU) and the British Medical Association (BMA) both passed motions rejecting the IHRA definition as a result of grassroots organising from their members.
The widespread adoption of the IHRA definition, or even the prospect of its adoption, meant much of the Palestine movement spent the following decade fighting on defensive terrain. Organisers and campaigners repeatedly found themselves required to establish that anti-Zionism did not equate antisemitism. They prefaced their responses and arguments with a rejection of antisemitism, explaining that advocacy for Palestinian liberation remained legitimate political speech and a valid aspiration.
The controversy surrounding Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership of the Labour Party brought these debates into the centre of British electoral politics. Accusations of antisemitism, disputes over the IHRA definition, and arguments over the boundary between antisemitism and anti-Zionism became inseparable from the wider political struggle surrounding Corbynism. Against that history, the Green Party vote gains its greatest significance.
For years, the political question directed towards supporters of Palestine has effectively been: can you prove that your anti-Zionism is not antisemitic? The Green Party motion reverses that presumption so the question, instead, is: can a political ideology premised on maintaining Jewish supremacy through the displacement and discrimination of the native Palestinian population really be reconciled with principles of anti-racism?
For perhaps the first time in contemporary British parliamentary politics, proponents of Zionism are being asked to defend Zionism itself against an explicitly anti-racist framework. This is the paradigm shift the Green Party vote represents.
The motion's impact extends beyond its wording. It marks a change in the terms on which Palestine can be discussed within British electoral politics. For decades, Palestinians and our allies have been forced onto the defensive, required repeatedly to justify our opposition to Zionism and to prove the legitimacy of our struggle. Passing this motion brings a position long articulated within the Palestinian national movement into mainstream party politics.
Whether the Green Party caves to the backlash or other political institutions follow remains to be seen. Polanski holding the line on the motion's argument, despite his defeat in the by-election last night, is a good sign. Nevertheless, regardless of what happens in the coming weeks and months, the proposition that Zionism should be subjected to an anti-racist critique is no longer a discussion taking place solely at the political margins, and that is a win worth celebrating.
Jeanine Hourani is a London-based writer and community organiser. She’s a PhD candidate in Middle East Politics at the University of Exeter and a member of the Palestinian Youth Movement.
