‘The real deal’: Sagal Abdi-Wali’s journey from child refugee to Labour MP in former PM’s seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:17:24 UTC
01:17:24 KST

For Sagal Abdi-Wali, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras, being elected to replace Keir Starmer in the north London constituency is “deeply personal”, she said in her acceptance speech.
The 43-year-old has lived in the area since the 1990s when, as a seven-year-old, she fled war-torn Somalia with her mother and four brothers, eventually settling in Gospel Oak in Camden, which largely falls within the constituency. Her journey from refugee to member of parliament was one which she hoped would inspire “people who look like me”, she said. “This is Camden and this is Britain.”
If she represents many in the diverse and youthful neighbourhood, however, Abdi-Wali is also very much a Labour party insider. Decades of volunteering in the community dovetailed with many years of active local party politics, even before she was elected to the borough council in 2022. She became the Labour cabinet member responsible for housing two years later, and in May was elected the first Black female leader of Camden council. She also chaired the local constituency party for four years.
Those deep party and community roots help explain how Abdi-Wali was selected from a long list of more than 100 to fight the seat for Labour after Starmer’s resignation last month, say friends – and were also key in seeing off the challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski.
“She genuinely is deeply rooted in so many different parts of the constituency,” says a close friend who was involved in her campaign. “I suppose all MPs like to think they are, but with Sagal it is the real deal.
“There’s a real community connection there, [and] I think the Green party and Zack Polanski underestimated how energetic and big the Labour campaign was going be. I don’t think they knew that those very deep roots in the constituency existed.
“That’s the thing about a byelection, you only have four weeks. So if those roots are already there, you’ve got a huge, huge head start.”
Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for neighbouring Hampstead and Highgate, agrees: “Her love of Camden is so obvious, and people really value that. She’s very caring, very local, and she genuinely seems to have a passion for politics and public service.”
After “lots of flat candidates” in the past, Siddiq says, “people like a bit of passion.”
It was walking past increasing numbers of homeless people in King’s Cross in the austerity years of the 2010s that encouraged Abdi-Wali to become more active in party politics, perhaps unsurprisingly given her own background. “It was only when I was old enough to look back and think about it in a philosophical way,” she has said, that she noticed “my mum was always looking after us and made our lives nice, serene … whether we were in a refugee camp or temporary housing.”
Homelessness and housing would be one of her priorities as an MP, she said in her acceptance speech on Friday morning, as would calling for Thames Water to be brought into public ownership and working to increase access to jobs and apprenticeships for young people – all causes that chime with Andy Burnham, too.
Abdi-Wali has long been involved in community groups working with young people, including being a governor of several schools and founding football clubs where she still plays regularly and is “pretty aggressive on the pitch”, according to her close friend. (She is also an “ardent” Spurs fan, the friend says, “which may count against her in the [Arsenal-dominated] constituency”.)
Housing is one issue where she has faced some criticism; Abdi-Wali was the cabinet member in charge of the borough’s housing when in November 2024 the housing ombudsman published a damning report calling the council’s service rude, defensive and inadequate. Friends point out that she had been in the post for only six months and defend her record in the period she was in charge of the brief.
Abdi-Wali also shrugged off a tweet when she was selected by Reform’s Zia Yusuf , which Labour representatives swiftly called “clearly racist” and was condemned even by other senior Reform figures.
“I rang her and said: ‘Are you OK?’” says Sidiq. “I wanted to reassure her that we were there for her. But she said: “‘No, I feel very resilient about it. It’s made me even more determined to get on and do it.’”

Montenegro to deport Russian pro-Kremlin war blogger and founder of Rybar propaganda project Mikhail Zvinchuk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:16:11 UTC
01:16:11 KST

Montenegrin authorities are set to deport Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Russian pro-war propaganda project Rybar. Zvinchuk’s wife, Valeria, and three of the project’s employees, are also on the deportation list, local outlet Vijesti reported, citing Montenegro’s Police Directorate. Bosnian investigative journalists found that Zvinchuk entered Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina after flying there from Germany.
News of the detention of Zvinchuk, his wife, and other Rybar staff emerged earlier in the day on Oct. 9. Vijesti identified the other detainees as Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko. All five individuals have now been ordered to leave Montenegro, with law enforcement authorities saying the decision was made on the basis of national and internal security grounds.
According to Montenegrin police, Zvinchuk, his wife, and Rybar employees entered the country two days earlier. They stayed in the town of Risan on the Bay of Kotor, where they were ultimately detained. Officers seized cameras, a GoPro, a filming drone, and mobile phones from the group.
Bosnian investigative outlet Detektor found that Zvinchuk and his team entered Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They arrived in Sarajevo on Oct. 2 on a flight from Germany. While Zvinchuk, his wife, and Rybar employees were in the country, elections were taking place in Bosnia. Bosnia’s Security Ministry has not yet commented on the information.
On Oct. 6, Rybar published a video roundup for the Solovyov Live program that was filmed in Bosnia. The following day, Oct. 7, the Rybar team entered Montenegro by land.
Zvinchuk later boasted that he had entered Montenegro despite the sanctions and travel ban levied against him. In a post on social media, Zvinchuk said Montenegro was the 26th country he had visited and described how he entered the country:
“Remember: even if you are under sanctions, like me, even if you have a travel ban, like me, even if you are traveling to a country that has pledged, out of solidarity, to enforce that travel ban, as in my case ... THERE IS A WAY!”
Zvinchuk added that travelers like him could always run into “an idiot border guard who turns out all your pockets but forgets to check the database.”
On Oct. 8, prior to his arrest, Zvinchuk again appeared on the Russian propaganda channel Solovyov Live, where he claimed that “Montenegro is in tears because visas are being introduced for Russian tourists.”
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X earlier today:
“The message following today's successful action in which the head of the information network ‘Rybar’ was apprehended is clear: out institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future.”
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk, a former employee of the Russian Defense Ministry’s press service, is under EU and UK sanctions. The EU’s sanctions justification says he is part of a working group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts in support of the ongoing war against Ukraine. Rybar’s main Telegram channel has more than 1.5 million subscribers.
In 2024, the United States offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about people working on the project, which it said used social media to "sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence in the United States.” The U.S. State Department also listed Zvinchuk as being involved in attempts to influence the U.S. electoral process.
In February 2026, OpenAI blocked a network of accounts linked to Rybar. The project’s team had used ChatGPT as a content farm to generate social media and blog posts in Russian, English, and Spanish.
In September, Czech police detained and questioned Russian nationals Vitaly Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov, whom journalists from local outlet Seznam Zprávy had earlier lured to a meeting in Prague and secretly recorded discussing their work for the Rybar project. After questioning, both were ordered to leave the Czech Republic within three days as undesirable persons.
Chashchukhin and Dolmatov are known to live in Germany, where Chashchukhin performs work for sanctioned Russian media outlets Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV. In his reports, he portrays Germany as a country in economic decline, claiming its only hope for prosperity requires a halt to arms supplies for Ukraine and a return to the purchase of cheap energy from Russia.
Zvinchuk’s detention drew reactions from Russian government officials including Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov and ex-president Dmitry Medvedev, and also from media outlets, bloggers, and pro-war channels. Ivan Filippov, a propaganda researcher and author of the Telegram channel “All Quiet on the Zzzzzestern Front,” told the independent outlet Vot Tak that many commentators — regardless of their views — were asking why a sanctioned Russian propagandist who was aware of the risks had traveled to a NATO country that is seeking EU membership:
“Some people are expressing sympathy, but looking at the reactions now, the dominant question is why he went there in the first place. The pro-war “Z”-community is genuinely stunned. [Head of RT] Margarita Simonyan believed he would be extradited to Ukraine,” Filippov said.
Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and is seeking to join the EU after adopting the euro in 2002 and applying for membership in the bloc in 2008. It imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The government recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens starting from Nov. 1, as Montenegro aligns its visa policy with the European Union ahead of a possible accession by 2028. Local media reported this spring that around 14,000 of the 21,000 Russians registered in Montenegro had left after the government announced plans to introduce visa requirements.
“Montenegro’s accession as the 28th member state by 2028 is within reach,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at an EU-Western Balkans summit in June.

Ukraine's Anti-Corruption Court hands down 8-year sentence in UAH 800 mln NBU loan fraud
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:15:15 EEST
01:15:15 KST

The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) has sentenced the director of a private company used in a scheme to misappropriate approximately UAH 800 million in loan funds from the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and launder the proceeds to eight years in prison, the press service of the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) said on Telegram.
According to SAPO, the convicted individual agreed, in exchange for monetary compensation, to head a company controlled by a criminal organization and took actions to conceal its illegal activities and facilitate the scheme.
According to the statement, in 2013, members of the criminal organization conducted a series of transactions involving several companies through the organization's controlled bank, PJSC Real Bank. These transactions artificially weakened the bank's liquidity and created grounds for obtaining a stabilization loan from the NBU.
The National Bank provided Real Bank with a loan of approximately UAH 800 million secured by property whose value had been overstated sevenfold.
"After obtaining the funds, the management of PJSC Real Bank, in collusion with other members of the criminal organization, arranged a series of fictitious financial transactions involving the accounts of controlled enterprises displaying signs of being fictitious. The funds were then laundered by withdrawing part of the money in cash, converting another part into foreign currency and transferring it outside Ukraine for the benefit of foreign companies that were nonresidents," the agency said.
The court found the defendant guilty under Part 1 of Article 255, Part 4 of Article 28, Part 5 of Article 191, as well as Part 4 of Article 28 and Part 2 of Article 366 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. He was sentenced to eight years in prison, with confiscation of property, a fine and a three-year ban on holding the relevant positions. The court also partially upheld the NBU's civil claim and ordered the defendant to pay more than UAH 503 million in damages.
According to SAPO, the convicted individual has been hiding in temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine since 2014.

Unknown

2026-10-09
16:14:17 UTC

The ICC was established to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity that might otherwise go unpunished.
The European Union on Friday described US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) as "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work".
"The EU will work closely with the ICC to ensure it continues to operate effectively," the European Commission said, adding it hoped that the six-month delay before the sanctions applied meant "there is room for dialogue"
One possible EU response would be to activate a legal instrument known as the "blocking mechanism", which prohibits European firms from obeying the US sanctions "actively or by deliberate omission", giving the European Union a potential means of cushioning some of the impact.
European Council President Antonio Costa and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten responded to the sanctions on Friday during a joint press conference in The Hague.
"The justice, international justice, is the only alternative to revenge. Then we don't have lasting peace without accountability," Costa said.
"We urge United States to engage in the next, in the upcoming six months in order to overcome this, but our commitment is, we have a full commitment to support and continue to support ICC, the independence of the international justice, and to protect the members of the ICC and their staff."
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten on Friday reaffirmed the Netherlands' commitment to defending the ICC against proposed US sanctions.
"We will do whatever we need to defend the ICC," Jetten said.
US sanctions on the ICC: What happened?
The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC, accusing the tribunal of political bias and unfairly targeting Americans and Israelis over alleged war crimes.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the measures on Friday, shortly after South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. However, the decision to impose sanctions had been made well before the Nobel announcement.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”
The sanctions freeze any ICC assets held in the United States and give US companies and individuals six months to end their business dealings with the court.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday welcomed US sanctions against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged crimes committed in Gaza.
"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," Netanyahu's office posted on X.
How has the ICC reacted to the US sanctions?
The ICC condemned the sanctions, describing them as an attack on the rule of law and the international legal order.
“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.”
ICC President Tomoko Akane said the court would “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.”

“Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare”: Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September, and winter will make it worse, analyst says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:13:48 UTC
01:13:48 KST

- Ukraine's "middle strikes" on Russian logistics haven't let up
- Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September
- A shift to protected convoys hasn't reduced the truck losses
Ukraine's campaign of so-called "middle strikes" targeting Russian supply lines isn't generating the same headlines it did back in the spring, when the campaign was intensifying.
But that doesn't mean Ukrainian units aren't launching thousands of drones a month and blowing up a lot of Russian trucks. Indeed, the pace of Ukrainian strikes, concentrated along the main supply routes threading through occupied southern Ukraine into occupied Crimea, has leveled off without ever really decreasing since an early summer surge.
It's evident Ukraine's middle-strike campaign "didn't stop and wasn't slowed down," noted French mapper Clément Molin, one of the most important observers of the counterlogistics campaign.
For September, Molin tallied 770 confirmed drone strikes on Russian trucks in the logistical zone 10 km beyond the line of contact. That's up from 630 strikes in August, 656 in July, and 586 in June, the month the campaign really got underway. There were just 214 strikes in May and at most a few dozen in each of the previous three months.
Whether Ukrainian troops can take advantage of the Russians' weakening logistics anytime soon is less evident.
Since June, the Ukrainians have hit around 700 Russian trucks a month that analysts can confirm with video and photographic evidence. There are undoubtedly many more damaged and destroyed trucks that left no digital evidence.
There are thousands of Russian trucks on the road in Ukraine every day, so hitting 700 of them in a month won't immediately strangle Russian logistics. But that accumulating destruction does strain Russian logistics—and terrify the truck drivers who are in the drone crosshairs. "Russian drivers post videos on a daily basis, showing how dangerous a ride in southern Ukraine is getting," Molin wrote.
What's remarkable is that the counterlogistics campaign hasn't faltered even as the Russians have adapted. Early on, Russian trucks mostly traveled alone and without protection, making them fairly easy picking for a bevy of Ukrainian middle-strike drone types including the Hornet, the B-2, the RAM 2X, the Chaklun, and various high-endurance first-person-view quadcopters.
The drones ride along Ukraine's overlapping command and control systems, which include Starlink satellite terminals (some dangling from balloons) as well as mesh radio networks. Many of the drones have built-in AI for autonomously detecting and homing in on trucks in the final seconds of flight.
Convoy operations
Reeling from the truck strikes, the Russians adapted this spring. Commanders began requiring all trucks to travel in convoys including mobile fire support groups, analysis group Tochnyi reported in May, citing Dmytro Putiata, a retired command post battle captain from the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces 20th Brigade "K2."
Trending Now
Today the Russian convoys have a standard structure, according to Molin. "Convoys usually gather three to five trucks and two to three air-defense trucks." Combined with radio jamming gear that's increasingly common on both the supply trucks and the gun trucks, that's seemingly a lot of protection.
But the drones target the gun trucks, too, peeling back the protection in order to expose the supply trucks to follow-on attacks. In that way, the Ukrainians have sustained their attacks on the supply trucks despite the increase in mobile air defense activity along the most important supply routes.
And it's going to get worse for the Russians as fall wears into winter. "Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare and the arrival of winter and more difficult conditions will not help," Molin wrote.
There will be less foliage on the trees lining the roads, and thus less cover from Ukrainian surveillance. Moreover, Molin pointed out, "it will be more difficult to go off-road" and avoid the big paved roads that are the main drone kill zones.
Russian logistics are under pressure, and that pressure is only increasing. Ultimately, the Ukrainians aim to starve Russian forces in Crimea. Strikes on cargo ships plying the Black Sea prevent the Russians from simply shifting the logistics off the coast. Meanwhile, strikes on overland logistics "may lead to substantial softening of front-line positions," Tochnyi noted in May.
Softening those front-line positions to the point of melting away could facilitate what Tochnyi described as "eventual breakthrough operations" in occupied southern Ukraine.
It's not inconceivable. Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps recently proved, by way of its successful Operation Vivaldi, that local Ukrainian counteroffensives are possible.
But that doesn't mean they're easy. To win, the 3rd Army Corps had to carefully husband its forces and meticulously prepare the battlefield under conditions of strict secrecy before attacking. That same kind of preparation is underway along the supply lines into Crimea, but it's unclear whether local Ukrainian forces have enough combat power in reserve to shift from defense to offense and exploit Russia's deepening supply woes.
At least not yet.

Insurance model is no substitute for the NHS | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:13:09 UTC
01:13:09 KST

In Dining across the divide (4 October), the young participant, Ted, is quoted as expressing his “desire to abolish the NHS and replace it with a social insurance model. This would still have provision for free treatment at the point of need, but people would pay through insurance systems, and they would choose the level of cover they’ve got. Those models deliver far better outcomes for patients.”
As a retired insurance underwriter, I must disagree profoundly with Ted’s assertion. Let’s concentrate on business fundamentals. Insurance comes in two “flavours”: first, events that become likelier as time goes on – eg, life assurance. The older you get, the more likely you are to die and the more premium is needed to cover the risk; and second, events whose likelihood stays essentially the same over time, eg home insurance – the likelihood of a house burning down is much the same for everyone and the cost is spread evenly between policyholders.
Clearly, medical insurance is flavour one. Premiums need to rise with age. To reduce premiums and keep customers, insurance companies apply ever-increasing “excesses” and “co-pays” and can refuse to cover pre-existing conditions. The more you need medical insurance, the more expensive and difficult it is to get.
There is also the business case. When you buy an insurance policy, premiums are calculated to include the cost of claims (about 60%); administration (about 10%); sales (about 20%); shareholder profits (about 15%); less investment returns (about 5%).
In contrast, an NHS-style system does not require either sales costs or shareholder profits. Of course, there would be no investment return – but nevertheless, it is still about 30% cheaper to operate than an insured healthcare system. Like most sound business ideas, it’s simple arithmetic.
Susan Jones
Biggin Hill, London

Responding to the announcement that the Trump administration has set the first military execution since 1961, and that the execution will be carried out by firing squad and livestreamed to the public, Justin Mazzola, Deputy Director of Research at Amnesty International USA, said:

Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:10:50 UTC
01:10:50 KST

Ukrainian assault troops suffered more than 10 times fewer casualties than Russian forces during Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian military veteran said on 9 October, describing the ratio as unprecedented and highlighting Ukraine’s improved ability to protect its soldiers during offensive operations.
The counteroffensive has been a significant Ukrainian success, reclaiming territory in northern Donetsk Oblast and disrupting Russia’s plans to advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. The reported casualty ratio points shows Ukraine’s ability to make offensive gains while reducing the human cost of assaulting fortified positions.
Yevhen Dykyi made the remarks in an interview with Radio NV, saying the results showed how Ukrainian forces had learned to limit losses while attacking defended Russian positions.
Protecting troops during offensive operations
Dykyi said the casualty ratio was one of the operation’s most important outcomes.
He said that Ukrainian assault troops suffered more than 10 times fewer casualties than Russian forces during the counteroffensive.
“That speaks volumes. We have learned how to protect our people, and that is extraordinarily vital,” he added.
Operation Vivaldi disrupted Russia’s advance in Donetsk
The Third Army Corps launched Vivaldi in mid-September in northern Donetsk Oblast, near Lyman, where Russian forces had spent months trying to advance toward Ukraine’s fortified cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
The operation aimed to clear Russian troops from positions north of Lyman and disrupt Moscow’s plans to encircle the remaining Ukrainian-held parts of Donetsk Oblast. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps announced the counteroffensive on 15 September, initially reporting that its forces had cleared Russian infiltrators from several settlements and liberated Serednie.
By 30 September, Ukraine had regained 176 square kilometers of territory during the operation, according to figures cited by the Ukrainian presidential office. Ukrainian authorities also reported that their forces had captured around 250 Russian soldiers and inflicted more than 5,000 Russian casualties, including killed and wounded.
The counteroffensive also disrupted Russia’s effort to advance behind Ukraine’s fortified defensive line. By threatening Russian positions north of Lyman, Ukrainian forces complicated Moscow’s plans to encircle the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk area rather than attack its defenses head-on.
Unmanned systems help limit casualties
A key feature of Vivaldi has been the use of unmanned systems to attack fortified Russian positions before Ukrainian infantry moves in. Ukrainian forces deployed ground robots carrying grenade launchers to fire into Russian shelters, while explosive ground vehicles were used to destroy bunkers and strongpoints.
In one reported tactic, heavy drones delivered kamikaze ground robots more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines, allowing Ukrainian operators to attack positions without exposing infantry to direct fire.

Americans' debt problems are flashing a warning not seen since the Great Recession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:10:41 UTC
01:10:41 KST

The ability of U.S. families to stay current on their debts worsened over the past three years, hitting levels not seen since the aftermath of the global financial crisis, the Federal Reserve reported Friday.
In the central bank's Survey of Consumer Finances, researchers found that while wealth disparities narrowed somewhat, the ability to meet debt payments deteriorated significantly.
"Families were more likely to be behind on their financial obligations than at any point since the 2010 survey," stated the survey, a data-rich document the Fed releases every three years to chronicle the nation's financial health.
The country in 2010 was just emerging from what became known as the Great Recession, a period that ran from December 2007 to June 2009. A collapse in the subprime mortgage market resulted in contagion across the largest financial institutions in the U.S. and the world, sending unemployment at one point to 10%.
According to the new findings, the portion of families behind on loan payments at the end of 2025 soared from about 12% in the prior survey to nearly 20%, a gain of some 67%. Those behind by two months or more also accelerated considerably, moving to more than 8% from 5% in 2022.
While the report covered the period through 2025, Americans' concerns over their finances have persisted. A New York Fed survey released earlier this week showed that households reported their financial situations had worsened from a year ago and were likely to be weaker in the year ahead.
Friday's Fed report showed the share of debt to income also posted a large gain. Families with payment-to-income ratios of greater than 40% jumped to 8.6%, up from 6.5% in 2022 and the highest level since 2013.
At the same time, the net worth of higher earners soared, with those in the top income group seeing their median net worth rise 31%.
The report covers a period where the economy continued to grow but with inflation rates not seen since the early 1980s.
Amid that climate, the Fed found that real median, or midpoint, family income increased 7% but average income dropped 6%.
"Families in the lower ends of the income and net worth distributions saw modest increases in median and mean income, while families in the upper ends saw declines," the report stated. "These patterns indicate that income inequality decreased slightly between surveys."
The report noted that income gains were particularly strong with families aged 75 or older while tumbling 25% for those aged 35 to 44, which the Fed attributed to declines in capital gains income for that group.
"The exceptions to the general pattern of a rise in median income were for Black non-Hispanic families, Asian families, and families toward the top of the usual income and net worth distributions," the report stated. "For these families, both median and mean income fell."
Overall, net worth generally increased.
Inflation-adjusted average net worth rose 7% to $1.24 million, though median net worth climbed just 2% to $215,900, reflecting gains among those at the higher end. The report noted that net worth was "much slower" than the prior report that covered the 2019-22 period.
There were considerable disparities among education groups. Those with a college degree had 1.9 times the median income level than those with "some college" and nearly three times the median net worth. Lower-income families "saw some declines" in wealth while those with higher incomes saw gains. Families in the bottom one-fourth of income median net worth declined 6% while average net worth fell 4%.

US Sanctions International Criminal Court; Rubio: ‘Either the ICC Will End Its Threats, or We Will End the ICC’

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:10:21 UTC
01:10:21 KST

The US imposed fresh sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution on Friday, Oct. 9, widening its campaign against the Hague-based tribunal.
The move came only hours after the former ICC judge, Navi Pillay, won the Nobel Peace Prize. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the measure in a statement, first published by Reuters, designating the court under Executive Order 14203.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“[US] President [Donald] Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said. “This is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
What the sanctions really mean
Established in 2002, the ICC is a Netherlands-based court that prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest international crimes, including war crimes, genocide and other crimes against humanity.
While most European and NATO countries are members, the US has never formally joined, and neither has Turkey.
Washington has previously sanctioned several ICC prosecutors and judges. However, the new step goes further, sanctioning the court itself and possibly penalizing companies that provide services to it.
The Trump administration maintains that the US never accepted the authority to prosecute Americans. It has also objected to the court’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and to its investigation into the conduct of US soldiers in Afghanistan.
Montenegro Detains Russian Z-Blogger Targeted by US
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also been placed under an ICC arrest warrant a year into the full-scale invasion, for the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children from occupied territories of Ukraine to Russia.
According to Reuters, the US Treasury issued four general licenses that allow some transactions linked to ICC telecommunications, software, pension payments and the court’s detainees shortly after the announcement was published.
ICC officials had reportedly spent months preparing for sanctions, by replacing Microsoft software on office computers with open-source alternatives and setting up new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
Rubio: ‘We don’t need it’
In his official statement, Rubio argued that both Republicans and Democrats have long rejected the idea that the ICC could prosecute US citizens, troops or political leaders. “America never joined the court,” he said, reiterating that “we don’t need it. And we don’t want it.”
The Trump administration, according to Rubio, had spent more than a year signaling what it expected from the court. It postponed the designation out of respect for its partners, hoping the ICC would change direction or that its member states would restrain it.
“However, neither the ICC nor States Parties have yet taken meaningful steps to address our concerns,” he claimed, accusing those he described as globalist “experts” of wanting to target American servicemembers, Border Patrol agents and elected officials as possible targets via the court.
While the sanctions were reportedly designed to leave the door open for diplomacy, giving member states a chance to negotiate a solution, Rubio also used the statement to issue a direct warning to US allies.
“We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court,” he said, adding that otherwise Washington would continue dismantling the court “brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”
ICC vows to continue work despite sanctions, EU condemns the move
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told Reuters the sanctions “must be condemned,” adding that the court will continue working “across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions.”
Shortly after the announcement of the sanctions, the ICC issued an official statement on its website, condemning the designation as an attempt to obstruct justice and intimidate those who work or cooperate with the court.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the statement read.
It also described the designation as an unprecedented step that follows US sanctions against 13 of its judges and prosecutors.
“The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas reaffirmed EU’s support for the Court, noting that the six-month period before the measures take effect could possibly offer a window for dialogue. “Protecting the ICC remains an EU priority,” she said.
However, the Trump administration has openly opposed the court for years and is widely expected to continue doing so. During his first term, Trump imposed targeted sanctions on court officials, which President Joe Biden later lifted.
Reuters reported that the ICC Registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler urged the EU to be ready to use its so-called “blocking mechanism” earlier this week – a tool that can protect European countries from sanctions applied beyond US borders.
“No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice. History will judge this moment,” the ICC concluded in its statement.

The DOJ Is Weighing Perjury Charges Against Cassidy Hutchinson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:09:08 UTC
01:09:08 KST

Federal prosecutors have been weighing a perjury and obstruction-of-justice case against Cassidy Hutchinson, who implicated President Donald Trump in the January 6 Capitol riot in testimony four years ago, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
The efforts mark the Justice Department’s intent to proceed against Hutchinson, a former aide to ex-Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, though prosecutors are not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment until at least after the midterm elections, the sources say.
Hutchinson testified as a star witness to the committee that investigated the riot, recounting that Trump encouraged his supporters to march to the Capitol even though he knew many were armed. She sat for several interviews in addition to her public testimony, where she recalled hearing that Trump had lunged at one of his Secret Service agents after being told he could not join his supporters at the Capitol.
In recent months, prosecutors at the Justice Department have focused on the fact that the former special counsel, Jack Smith, did not corroborate much of Hutchinson’s account to the committee, and the Secret Service’s denial of any altercation in the presidential limo, the sources say.
By comparing the transcripts of Hutchinson’s interviews with the committee and against her testimony to Smith’s team, prosecutors have been trying to construct a case based on how her testimony has changed, the sources say.
Prosecutors have also taken a special interest in Hutchinson’s claim that she had penned a statement on a notecard for Trump to release during the Capitol riot—a claim disputed by former Trump White House counsel Eric Herschmann, who said he had written the note.
It was not immediately clear whether prosecutors intend to ultimately proceed with both perjury and obstruction charges, which have been under consideration for several months. The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Hutchinson and her lawyer did not respond to texts and calls seeking comment. Hutchinson, now 29, has kept a low profile since publishing a memoir of her time in Trump’s first administration in 2023 titled Enough.
Punchbowl News first reported the Justice Department’s interest in charging Hutchinson.
The grand jury investigation is the latest example of the Justice Department pursuing criminal cases against Trump’s perceived political enemies. Trump fired former US attorney general Pam Bondi in April partly for moving too slowly to bring such cases, sources familiar with the matter said.
Some Justice officials have been skeptical about whether there is a viable criminal case against Hutchinson, in part due to the high bar for successfully prosecuting perjury charges, the sources say. To prove that Hutchinson lied to Congress, prosecutors would need to show beyond a reasonable doubt that Hutchinson lied, that she did so knowingly, and that it materially impacted the investigation, former US attorney Joyce Vance tells WIRED.
The investigation into Hutchinson became a priority for the DOJ after a criminal referral by Representative Barry Loudermilk, a Georgia Republican who for years has been deeply critical of the January 6 committee investigation. Loudermilk had separately sought to depose Hutchinson until he was blocked by House speaker Mike Johnson, who was concerned it could surface damaging texts of a sexual nature between lawmakers and Hutchinson.
In an unorthodox move, the referral ended up getting assigned to the Civil Rights Division at the DOJ, as opposed to the US Attorney for the District of Columbia or the Criminal Division, which would usually handle public corruption cases.
Under Justice Department guidelines, the Civil Rights Division is only supposed to take cases with a nexus to a civil rights violation. The division is led by Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump loyalist who has been a reliable advocate for the Trump administration's prosecutorial agenda.

GFCN chief proposes expert cooperation between CIS states to sniff out transborder fakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:08:06 UTC
01:08:06 KST

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. President of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) Vladimir Tabak proposed establishing direct cooperation between expert teams from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) for streamlining information checks to expose transborder fakes and methodology exchanges.
"The next practical step will be to coordinate direct contacts between national expert teams for on-the-spot exposure of fakes and establish regular methodology exchanges. The GFCN is ready to provide CIS countries with its technological and educational resources in order to establish a direct network of cooperation between experts. Our goal is not to impose ready-to-use solutions but rather give our counterparts tools for safely protecting the sovereignty of their media space," the GFCN chief said, addressing the second Global Digital Forum.
According to Tabak, the common cultural and language context makes former Soviet republics vulnerable to transborder manipulations. These threats include bogus stories about elections, fraudulent deep fakes involving country leaders and fake coverage of migration issues, he explained. So far this year, more than 93 original fakes fueling interethnic tensions have been reported in Russia, he noted.
Tabak said potential fields of cooperation with CIS countries could include the use of the anti-deep fake system Zephyr developed by ANO Dialog Regions, joint site verification and the introduction of educational modules on fact-checking taking the countries’ national features into account.
The demand for fact-checking expertise across the globe has transformed the Network into a global hub that unites more than 130 experts from 55 countries, including Western economies which Tabak said have reported a shortage of applied techniques in fact-checking.
Since news pegs can affect the course of hot conflicts, the international community needs clear rules for regulating media similar to international conventions on the prohibition of cluster munitions of chemical weapons, Tabak argued.
TASS is the media partner of the forum.

No Drone Debris Found on Damaged Black Sea Ship, Bulgarian Officials Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

No Drone Debris Found on Damaged Black Sea Ship, Bulgarian Officials Say
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov and Navy Commander Rear Adm. Kiril Mihailov said an inspection of the merchant ship Able, damaged in a drone attack in the Black Sea on the night of October 6, found no drone debris that could establish the origin of the unmanned vehicle.
The vessel remains stable but has suffered a breach in its stern and taken on water. Military personnel found extensive fire damage inside the ship, whose cargo is wheat. Signs also indicated that the crew had used the available emergency rescue craft to evacuate.
“Unfortunately, we were unable to identify drone debris so that we could identify it,” Defense Minister Stoyanov said, stressing that without concrete evidence, it was impossible to determine whether the drone was Russian or Ukrainian.
Mihailov said it was too early to determine whether Able would sink. The vessel is tilted toward the stern because of the breach that allowed water to enter, while its engine room is believed to be partially flooded.
Inspectors detected no pollution or spillage during the examination.
The Navy is monitoring Able and a second merchant vessel abandoned by its crew, located about 40 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian coast. Both ships are in international waters.
“Our coast along the territorial lines is sufficiently protected, but the war is being fought in the Black Sea and is close to us,” Mihailov said. He added that drones would continue falling into the sea as Russia and Ukraine exchange attacks using such weapons, while winds and currents could carry some of them toward Bulgaria’s coastline.
Mihailov also reported that the Navy had destroyed a drone about 15 nautical miles east of Sinemorets that day.
Stoyanov said Bulgaria has anti-drone systems, including equipment manufactured by Bulgarian companies, and is expecting further deliveries. However, he noted that drone technology is advancing faster than the capabilities available to counter it.
“There is no one to guarantee 100% protection,” the defense minister said. He added that Bulgaria is involved in joint projects with NATO allies, EU member states, the United States and Turkey to obtain various systems.
Commenting on the visit to Sofia by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, Stoyanov said he had not met with the Ukrainian official. As far as he knew, Budanov had met only with Prime Minister Rumen Radev.
Radev confirmed that he had held talks with Budanov, explaining that the meeting had been requested by the Ukrainian official. The Council of Ministers had announced that the visit was arranged at Budanov’s request and kept confidential for security reasons.
During the October 8 meeting, Budanov presented the Ukrainian side’s views on the prospects for reaching a peaceful settlement to the war in Ukraine.
Radev said that various theories had been circulating about the drone attack on the merchant ships, but none had been substantiated by evidence.
The prime minister praised the military personnel who inspected the damaged vessel, commending their courage and professionalism in conducting a thorough search for drone remains. Since none had been found, he said, no definitive conclusions about the attack could yet be made.
Radev also called for support for efforts to restore peace in Ukraine, saying an end to hostilities was vital not only for the countries at war but for Europe as a whole, which continues to bear a heavy social and economic cost.
“Efforts to establish peace in Ukraine deserve our support. The cessation of hostilities is in the interest of the whole of Europe, because we continue to pay an extremely high social and economic price. It is high time to give way to the full potential of diplomacy and to use all possible channels of communication and dialogue,” Radev said.
The prime minister reiterated that the origin of the drones involved in the attacks on the ships in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea remained unknown.

UK coastguard agency chief faces calls to resign over use of unverified data to back up pay plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:07:29 UTC
01:07:29 KST

The head of the UK coastguard agency is facing calls to resign after she was found to have used unverified data to back up her controversial plan to strip rescue officers of their pay.
Virginia McVea, the chief executive of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), claimed more than 90% of coastguard rescue officers supported the proposal, citing an official survey. Now, after an Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) investigation, the agency has admitted its poll did not sufficiently back up the claim.
Nicola Savage, a national officer for the GMB union, which represents coastguard rescue officers (CROs), said: “If Ms McVea is unable to produce the reports she refers to, we would consider this as a deliberate attempt to mislead. If this is the case, she should resign – as hundreds of coastguards have already asked her to do.”
Joe Robertson, one of several MPs who have campaigned on CROs’ behalf, accused McVea of misleading MPs and coastguards during three separate meetings at which he said she cited the figure.
He called on her to “do the right thing and apologise for misleading MPs, CROs and the public”, adding: “Please also give a written account of how you came to repeat this false line over and over again and why you still have not published the surveys which you promised to MPs in our meeting on 24 June.”
The MCA’s plan to strip coastguards of their pay was a reaction to a court defeat. A judge affirmed that while CROs volunteered for service, they were classed as workers with the right to minimum wage and holiday pay because they were paid for their time, among other factors. Rather than respect this status, the MCA tried to stop remunerating CROs in an attempt to reclassify them as volunteers.
This led to heavy criticism from MPs, CROs and coastal communities, with the GMB union saying nearly 600 CROs had backed its vote of no confidence in McVea.
Seeking to defend the plan, McVea cited the 90% figure, but MPs told the Guardian in July they felt misled by her.
In a letter to McVea this week, the OSR’s director general, Ed Humpherson, said: “Neither of the surveys [cited] asked CROs directly about their support for the proposed volunteer model, so do not provide evidence relating to the reported claims. [The] MCA has been unable to provide any further evidence to underpin the reported claims.”
Leaked results of an MCA survey, revealed by the Guardian in July, showed CROs had actually been asked how volunteer and worker models would affect their availability.
The results suggested the MCA had included people who said they would become less able to respond to calls if they were volunteers, as well as those who replied “other”, among those in support of the volunteer model.
The agency said at the time: “Survey findings were considered alongside a range of operational, legal and practical factors.” But it refused to say how.
The plan was ultimately scrapped by the maritime minister, Keir Mather, as he responded to near universal criticism. CROs are still waiting to find out what system will be adopted, but it is understood the option of not paying coastguards is no longer on the table.
The MCA has been approached for comment.

Thousands rally for anti-austerity protest in Brussels amid clashes
Belgian police respond to ‘troublemakers’ on sidelines of main rally with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges.
Clashes have erupted near Brussels Central station on the sidelines of a demonstration organised by the country’s socialist trade union against the federal government’s austerity plans.
As thousands of protesters gathered at the station on Friday, a smaller group clashed with the police and threw wooden beams, glass bottles and rubbish bins, The Belgian Times reported.
Police were deployed in large numbers around the stations as officers checked groups of young people not wearing trade union colours.
Police said the main trade union rally went ahead peacefully but “groups of troublemakers were responsible for serious incidents before and after the march.”
Riot police responded to those protesters with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges. Police said those who “cause the problems of public order are not linked” to the rally.
Reporting from Brussels, Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard said damage was caused during Friday morning’s protests with an “acrid smell of burning in the air”, due to fires that were set and the tear gas.
“Police [and] emergency services have been arriving, starting to disperse or clean up and then the protests flare up again. So the day is still early; often these things get worse in the evening in terms of the street violence,” Birchard explained.
“There were some young people who came out, they say they were inspired by what they had seen in France in terms of school protests, and they also wanted to talk about the education environment they’re learning in,” she said, adding that the students felt that they were “not being listened to”.
The clashes came after a week of tension in the city of Liege after authorities banned gatherings as students clashed with police and vandalised shops. More than 200 people were arrested in Liege, and dozens of police were injured.
The ABVV trade union and the Christian ACV, the country’s two biggest unions, organised protests on Friday morning, with protesters marching from Brussels Central station to Brussels South Station under the slogan “stay out of our pockets”.
Police said about 30,000 people attended the demonstrations, while ABVV had earlier estimated attendance at 50,000.
The anger stems from the government’s austerity measures, as officials consider a new budget that opposes potential measures that affect purchasing power, the wage indexation system and value-added tax (VAT), as well as plans to introduce annualised working time.
At the same time, the ACV organised a separate protest involving hundreds of activists at the capital’s headquarters of the governing coalition parties.

Paramount-Warner Bros. merger puts Ellison’s Israel ties, political pressure in spotlight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:07:23 UTC
01:07:23 KST

Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has brought CNN and CBS News under common ownership, with financial backer Larry Ellison’s support for Israel and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair’s appointment as an adviser adding political dimensions to the media merger.
The transaction closed on Oct. 6 following the required regulatory approvals, according to the company’s completion announcement.
The combined company, named Skydance, brings together Paramount and Warner Bros. studios, HBO, Paramount+, CNN, CBS News and major sports broadcasting assets.
The agreement announced in February valued Warner Bros. Discovery’s equity at approximately $81 billion and its enterprise value, including debt, at $110 billion.
The financing plan included $47 billion in new shares backed by committed investment from the Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners, according to a company filing. 
Trump’s pressure on Netflix
The bidding contest unfolded alongside public pressure from US President Donald Trump on rival bidder Netflix.
In a February Truth Social post, preserved in an online archive, Trump demanded that Netflix dismiss board member Susan Rice, a former senior official in Democratic administrations, or “pay the consequences.”
The post also shared criticism from activist Laura Loomer urging Trump to block Netflix’s proposed Warner Bros. transaction.
Netflix subsequently announced on Feb. 26 that it would not match Paramount’s higher offer.
Co-chief executives Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said the price required made the acquisition “no longer financially attractive.” The company attributed its withdrawal to the terms of the deal, without citing Trump’s pressure. 
Ellison’s support for Israeli soldiers
Larry Ellison, the Jewish-American co-founder of Oracle and father of Skydance chairman and chief executive David Ellison, has made substantial financial contributions supporting Israeli soldiers. His family background is documented by the Jewish Virtual Library.
At a November 2017 gala, he gave $16.6 million to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, which was the organization’s largest single gift at the time, according to Jewish Telegraphic Agency reporting citing the organizers.
The donation was designated for welfare facilities at a training campus for mixed-gender infantry units.
“We should do all we can to show these heroic soldiers that they are not alone,” Ellison said at the event. 
Blair’s Gaza role and controversies
Skydance’s Oct. 6 board announcement named Blair as a board adviser acting in a personal capacity, with a role in shaping strategic priorities. The announcement did not assign him an editorial position.
Blair also holds responsibilities concerning Gaza. A Jan. 16 White House statement named him to the founding Executive Board of Trump’s Board of Peace and the Gaza Executive Board, whose responsibilities include governance, reconstruction and financing.
His involvement in Gaza planning has previously prompted Palestinian objections.
On Jan. 1, 2024, the Palestinian presidency rejected reported efforts to assign Blair a role in relocating Palestinians from Gaza and declared him unwelcome in Palestinian territories, according to an official statement carried by Palestine News and Information Agency (WAFA).
In July 2025, the Financial Times reported that two institute staff members participated in discussions on a Gaza redevelopment project involving Boston Consulting Group consultants and Israeli businessmen.
The institute said it had never authored, developed or endorsed a proposal to relocate Gazans, according to the report.
Blair subsequently endorsed Trump’s September 2025 Gaza plan in a public statement, describing it as “bold and intelligent.”
In an April 28 Security Council briefing, he advocated a transitional period of international support and disarmament arrangements acceptable to Israel, alongside reconstruction and eventual Palestinian self-government.
His institute’s relationship with Larry Ellison predates the media appointment. Its 2021 financial review described a philanthropic partnership with the Larry Ellison Foundation supporting digital infrastructure initiatives.  
Binding editorial safeguards
The merger includes specific obligations concerning CNN and CBS News.
Under a settlement with 12 state attorneys general, the company must establish a five-member News Editorial Independence Board within 180 days of closing, according to its Sept. 30 regulatory filing.
The board will comprise established journalists, set guiding editorial principles and resolve specified disputes concerning bias, fairness and compliance with those principles.
David Ellison has also pledged noninterference.
“We believe in editorial independence and we will never interfere,” he said, according to CNN’s Oct. 6 broadcast transcript.
CNN also reported that Ellison supported its legal challenge against the Trump administration over press access.

Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has slammed Kiev city authorities for an “almost complete failure” to protect the capital’s critical infrastructure from Russian attacks, escalating his longstanding feud with Mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who blames central government corruption.

Speaking to AFP, Klitschko again blamed some of the shortcomings in Kiev’s winter preparations on Zelensky’s government. Rejecting accusations that city officials had fallen behind, he argued that “finding scapegoats won’t make people warmer.”

Klitschko warned that even extensive preparations might prove insufficient if the capital’s air defenses failed to repel further strikes.
Zelensky acknowledged a “big deficit” in air defenses on Thursday, appealing to Western backers for more interceptor missiles ahead of winter. Multiple media reports have linked shortages of Patriot interceptors in US and allied stockpiles to the US-Israeli war with Iran.

NEW DELHI: INDIA bloc leaders on Friday met President Droupadi Murmu and submitted a memorandum outlining four demands, as the opposition intensified its campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.In the memorandum submitted to the President, the opposition demanded: CEC’s resignation, scrapping of assembly elections held over the last two years, suspension of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and a return to paper ballots.“We urge you to take cognisance of this grave situation and use your good offices to ensure that the following demands are addressed without delay,” the memorandum read, listing four demands, including the restoration of 13.30 crore voters allegedly deleted from electoral rolls.The memorandum added: “We approach you because, in moments when every other door has been closed, the people of India look to the Office of the President as the final guardian of that covenant...”
After meeting Murmu, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said he had expected the President to deny that vote theft was taking place but was surprised by her response.

In Russia, they want to raise the upper age limit for military service for women: details of the bill
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:06:17 EEST
01:06:17 KST

In Russia, they want to raise the upper age limit for military service for women: details of the bill
Kyiv • UNN
The bill proposes raising the upper age limit for women’s service from 45 to 50. The changes also concern the period of time spent in the reserve.
The Russian authorities have proposed raising the maximum age for women’s military service. The relevant draft law has been published in the State Duma’s database, reports UNN.
Details
The draft law proposes raising the maximum age for women to remain in military service from 45 to 50, as well as extending the reserve service age limits for female officers and women with other ranks: from 50 to 55 and from 45 to 50, respectively.
The authors of the draft law state in its explanatory note that amid the Russian-Ukrainian war, the majority of personnel in medical units are female service members, "including those who have reached (are reaching) the maximum age for remaining in military service."
The draft law also states that the current maximum age for remaining in military service does not always allow individuals to complete the required period of service to qualify for a pension and other support measures.
Recall
In Russia, conscripts are increasingly facing a ban on traveling abroad, with restrictions in some cases appearing directly during border control.

AI sector gathers at Ai Everything event in Abu Dhabi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:05:23 UTC
01:05:23 KST

Ömer Arıkan
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The Ai Everythng event in the capital of the UAE brought together technology companies, academics, and investors from more than 60 countries. 
The Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Center hosted the event featuring more than 400 artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure providers and startups. 
Amazon, Intel, Microsoft, and many other companies showcased their AI solutions to more than 200 investors during the organization. 
Marc Raibert, co-founder of Boston Dynamics and executive director of the Robotics and AI Institute, told Anadolu at the event. 
"You know, it's a great time to be in the AI and especially the physical AI part of robotics, which is what I do," Raibert said.
He noted the sector experienced significant developments recently.
"And I think there's just so much going on this year, the last year, there's been huge investment," Raibert stated.
Looking ahead to future years, he added, "It's going to be amazing to see all the things to get it accomplished."
"At the Robotics and AI Institute, we develop physical systems, mobility systems that are a little bit unusual," Raibert explained.
"We develop manual dexterity systems that will make robots able to do more things with their hands," he highlighted.
"But one of the ideas is not to work on immediate products, but to work on the longer range solutions that are going to make the next generation of robots much more capable than how they are today," Raibert noted.
During his speech at a panel titled The Rise of Physical AI, he mentioned AI language models easily access massive internet data, but gathering data for physical robots poses significant difficulties.
He explained they utilize large language models to teach robots what to do in their project named Watch, Understand, Do.
Applying human learning processes in factories to robots creates a difficult problem requiring developers to build skills from the ground up and focus on perception, according to Raibert.
He described developing humanoid robots as climbing the Mount Everest of robotics.
Raibert stated humans remain unique in manual dexterity and perceiving the world.
He added robot technology advances every day but currently lacks the level to truly compete with humans.
Touching upon Tesla CEO Elon Musk's goal to produce billions of humanoid robots in five years, Raibert pointed out overly optimistic expectations in the field.
He expressed admiration for Musk's achievements with SpaceX, Starlink, and Tesla.
Raibert stated Musk will probably not produce the stated number of robots in five years but successfully became a fundamental force drawing public interest to the sector.
More than 180 experts evaluated the latest developments in AI during various panels at the event.

Friend of suspected FBI data thief says he warned 'crazy' teen not to hack bureau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:04:43 UTC
01:04:43 KST

‘Crazy’: Friend of suspected FBI data thief warned him not to hack bureau
- A friend of suspected FBI hack suspect Saif al-Din Khader said he warned the teen many times not to attack the bureau, calling him “crazy” and “suicidal”.
- Reuters says the ShinyHunters-linked breach may affect all FBI staff, while the bureau says it is “aggressively investigating” the hack and Khader is now in custody in Jordan.
- Former hacker Adem El Adeb, known as “Pryx”, says he has quit cybercrime and is starting a cybersecurity firm, but he still says he is “proud” of his hacking past.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - A friend of the suspected thief of a massive cache of personal data from the FBI says he begged the teenager not to do it.
Adem El Adeb, 19, told Reuters that he tried to convince Saif al-Din Khader in September that breaking into the FBI would bring the weight of the US government down on his shoulders but that Khader would not be swayed.
“You’re suicidal,” El Adeb recalled telling Khader in an early September message exchange.
He said he told the teen he was “crazy” and that he should drop the idea.
“Not only once. Multiple times. I tried to advise him.”
The hack claimed by the ShinyHunters hacking group, which Khader is alleged to have played a key role in, has rocked the bureau.
El Adeb, alias ‘Pryx’, says he has gone clean
Reuters has not independently verified the scope of the breach, but the FBI has told staffers it is operating under the assumption the stolen data pertains to all its employees, a person briefed on the matter told Reuters in September.
The FBI did not return a message seeking comment on El Adeb’s account. It has said it is aggressively investigating the ShinyHunters hack.
Khader, whom El Adeb says is 17, was taken into custody in Jordan on Sept 29 and is cooperating with the bureau’s investigation, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters. Attempts by Reuters to reach Khader, members of his family or representatives for him have been unsuccessful.
Reuters has spoken to a handful of former associates of Khader - whose alleged hacker nickname was Rey - including El Adeb, who is better known under his old hacker nickname, Pryx.
The two were publicly known members of the cybercrime group Hellcat, which emerged in 2024 and took responsibility for several attention-grabbing hacks, including a break-in at France’s Schneider Electric, where the hackers demanded US$125,000 (S$160,000) worth of baguettes as ransom.
Rey and Pryx were identified as Khader and El Adeb by the Israeli cybersecurity research firm Kela in a report circulated in March 2025 and reviewed by Reuters. The report tied Pryx to El Adeb in part by showing that Pryx’s criminal ventures shared infrastructure, software tools and communication channels with a security-focused website called Pato, whose guide once listed El Adeb as its author.
Reuters reached El Adeb through an email address listed in Kela’s report. In a video interview from the Gulf emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, El Adeb acknowledged being Pryx and identified Khader as Rey, but he said that, unlike his friend, he had put his cybercrime days behind him.
El Adeb, who chain-smoked the Emirati cigarette brand Manchester Red through the hour-long interview, said he quit cybercrime before he turned 18 and is now setting up a cybersecurity business called VulOne with a cofounder.
“I’m clean now,” he said.
El Adeb said he was born in Tunisia and that his parents moved to the United Arab Emirates for work. He said he and Rey met online when they were 11 or 12 and beginning to experiment with hacking. He said they bonded over their shared support for the Palestinian cause and that they vandalised websites to act out their preteen political sensibilities.
“We thought it was cool when we were kids,” El Adeb said. “But then we grew out of it. We started to think that hacktivism is cringe.”
El Adeb ‘proud’ of cybercriminal background
Less cringe, he said, was making money.
El Adeb said Khader and other young cybercriminals formed Hellcat and went on a digital rampage, breaking into organisations around the world. Analysts say the group was noteworthy for publicly humiliating victims, something El Adeb described as “trolling.” He declined to say how much he earned from Hellcat’s cybercrime spree.
Reuters could not fully corroborate El Adeb’s account of his past or his exchanges with Khader. El Adeb said he “nuked” most of their messages after Khader was detained. But his recollections of their relationship line up with published research from security professionals, interviews El Adeb has conducted as Pryx and a podcast featuring Pryx released earlier this year, in which he said he had left cybercrime.
Other young hackers have publicly claimed to have gone straight while allegedly continuing to hack and steal. In an interview in 2025, Khader said he had quit hacking. Pepijn van der Stap, another suspected ShinyHunters hacker, repeatedly told journalists he had put his days of theft and extortion behind him. He was arrested by Dutch police on Sept 15 and is being investigated over allegations that he tried to organise murders abroad.
Attempts to reach representatives for Van der Stap were unsuccessful.
El Adeb insisted he was out of the game, describing himself as a “retired threat actor.” But between drags of his cigarette, El Adeb said he felt no shame or regret over his hacking.
“I’m proud that I had this experience,” he said. “I’m actually very happy and proud that I had actual cybercrime experience in a field that is filled with people that claim they know stuff but they never actually experienced real hacking.” REUTERS

A tornado in Sicily overturned cars and seriously injured people
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:04:25 EEST
01:04:25 KST

A tornado in Sicily overturned cars and seriously injured people
Kyiv • UNN
A tornado destroyed a house and damaged a school in Marsala and neighboring towns. A married couple were hospitalized in serious condition; the authorities will allocate funds.
On Friday, vehicles were overturned and two people sustained serious injuries as a tornado swept through the Sicilian city of Marsala and neighboring settlements. Experts called the event almost unprecedented for the Mediterranean island, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The storm caused panic among local residents: the tornado destroyed a house and also damaged a school and other buildings in Marsala and the neighboring towns of Petrosino and Mazara del Vallo.
"It was almost like an American tornado; nothing so destructive has been seen here in the memory of the current generation," Salvatore Cocina, head of Sicily's Civil Protection Service, told Reuters.
As early as the beginning of September, the agency warned that the hot summer had caused a great deal of heat to accumulate, which could trigger extreme weather events in the autumn.
"This once again highlights the problem of extreme weather events that have become characteristic of recent years due to the climate crisis," Cocina said.
Video released by local media shows a school in Marsala with shattered windows and a partially collapsed roof, as well as passenger cars and trucks overturned onto their sides and power-line poles blown down by the wind.
A couple caught at the epicenter of the storm while traveling by car was hospitalized in serious condition.
The president of the Sicily region, Renato Schifani, promised to allocate special funds to address the consequences of the emergency; a warning about possible extreme weather events also remains in effect for Saturday, as rains and storms continue to hit the island.

India: Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:04:03 UTC
01:04:03 KST

Responding to the sweeping and disproportionate restrictions imposed by the Delhi Police and the Government of India ahead of planned protests in the capital on Saturday 10 October, Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India, said:
“Peaceful protesters must be able to demand accountability from those in power without facing intimidation, arbitrary detention, or sweeping restrictions on their freedoms.
“From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law. Demonstrations should not depend on obtaining prior permission from the police. At most, organizers may be expected to notify the authorities of their plans.
Peaceful protesters must be able to demand accountability from those in power without facing intimidation, arbitrary detention, or sweeping restrictions on their freedoms
Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India
“With more than 30,000 security personnel reportedly being deployed in the city, it is critical that police protect the public, not punish people for exercising their rights. Security measures are there to protect people, not punish them for exercising their fundamental rights. We urge the authorities to exercise the utmost restraint and take all necessary steps to protect and facilitate the right of peaceful assembly.”
Background
The protesters, led by the Cockroach Janta Party, student unions and opposition parties, have been protesting since 2 October to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation amid controversy over the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. More than 130 million people have been deleted from electoral rolls since 2025.
The Delhi Police stated that permission to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar on 10 October had not been granted.
Student union members and activists associated with the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) have been detained, placed under house arrest outside Delhi or intercepted and detained while travelling to the capital by road and rail.
Restrictions on travel into Delhi will reportedly be put in place from the night of 9 October to the early hours of 11 October, with Delhi Metro stations scheduled to close, bus services set to be suspended, and the capital’s borders to be sealed to buses, trucks, tractors and other large transport vehicles.
A 24-hour mobile internet shutdown has been ordered in central Delhi from Friday night. The suspension will cover a 4km radius around the protest sites, according to a notification issued by the Deputy Commissioner of Delhi Police’s Special Cell.
Meanwhile, the Supreme Court on Friday provided partial relief by directing the Government of India not to completely suspend train services to Delhi or shut down Delhi Metro stations. The court directed the government to regulate these services in accordance with the principle of proportionality, ensuring that public transport remains accessible, and commuters are not inconvenienced. The Supreme Court has asked the Centre to consider designating an alternative venue to Jantar Mantar for peaceful protests, emphasizing the need for a location equipped with adequate facilities and amenities for protesters.
Approximately 22,000-armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi Police officers expected to be deployed.
