Which European countries are winning the tech funding race?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:06:01 UTC
00:06:01 KST

Investment in European tech startups is rebounding after a slow summer, but remains unevenly spread with the UK capturing almost half of all funding, according to figures from tech.eu.
European tech funding surged to €15.8 billion across 300 funding deals in September, bringing the total for 2026 to almost €60 billion, according to the latest figures from online publication tech.eu, although half was made up by UK investments.
The spike in activity represents a quarter of the year’s investment so far, a strong rebound on August’s activity which saw just €3.2 billion raised across 165 deals.
The activity also shows that European companies are attracting significant investment in technology, raising the prospect that they could one day scale up and help ease the continent’s reliance on US Big Tech.
However, investment still falls way behind the US, which attracted $50 billion in the same period and $800 billion in annual cloud/AI infrastructure.
Of September’s 300 deals, 25 companies raised more than €100 million each, including three rounds exceeding €1 billion secured by AI platform company Mistral and AI infrastructure firm Nscale. 34 deals were made with undisclosed values.
September’s largest deal came from French AI company Mistral, raising €3 billion in a series D round at a post-money valuation of more than €21 billion.
Cloud computing and artificial intelligence secured the most investment by sector, with €5.541 billion invested in cloud across 44 deals and €4.194 billion in AI.
Fintech (€847.7 million), health tech (€826.3 million), space (€725.8 million), robotics (€508.3 million), software (€421.1 million), security (€319.8 million), telecoms (€315 million) and deep tech (€274.5 million) made up the rest of the top 10 invested tech industries.
The UK remains Europe’s top fundraising market in September, securing €7.3 billion, half of the month’s total, in over 65 transactions.
Trailing the UK are France (€3.478 billion), Germany (€1.155 billion), the Netherlands (€1.119 billion), Spain (€615.8 million), Portugal (€524.1 million), Sweden (€399.9 million), Italy (€373.1 million), Bulgaria (€177.7 million) and Finland (€175.8 million).
September’s investments were made by more than 11,700 investors, with French public sector investment bank BPI France taking part in the most deals (8).
German public-private venture capital firm High-Tech Gründerfonds came in second with 7, followed by Italian venture capital firm Vento with 6, the UK’s national innovation agency Innovate UK with 6, UK venture capital firm Balderton Capital with 5, and the European Investment Bank with 5.
The EU has a number of funding instruments targeting tech, as the bloc aims to not only end its reliance on America’s Big Tech but also secure its own technology sovereignty.
In July, the European Commission launched a €10 billion public-private initiative to support the building of seven AI gigafactories across Europe. It also aims to unlock €20 billion in private funding to power trillion-parameter models to rival leaders such as Claude and ChatGPT.
The European Investment Bank also runs the TechEU Programme, which pools €70 billion in debt and equity to mobilise €250 billion by 2027 to take European startups from seed to IPO.
The European Commission has also made available €8.1 billion worth of funding through its Digital Europe Programme to support supercomputing, cybersecurity, advanced digital skills and semiconductors via the Chips Act.
And finally, there’s the Scaleup Europe Fund, a €5 billion initiative managed by Swedish private equity firm EQT to invest in AI, quantum computing, clean tech and biotech.

Why Kim Jong Un Should Want a 4th Summit With Donald Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:06:00 UTC
00:06:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump’s push for a fourth summit with Kim Jong Un has so far been rejected by the North Korean leader, who may be playing hard to get. However, based on our decades analyzing North Korea, participation in countless face-to-face meetings with North Koreans – official and unofficial – and numerous visits to North Korea, we think that some in Pyongyang may believe their country could benefit greatly from a fourth summit, though not in terms of what Washington may think.
In view of North Korea and Kim’s experience, especially his three summits during Trump’s first term in office, and Pyongyang’s analysis of the president’s current foreign policy, the North Korean Foreign Ministry would emphasize the following points that lay out a strong case with Kim Jong Un for a fourth summit.
First, it would point out that because of Kim’s policies in the military and economic fields, taking advantage of shifts in international geopolitics, especially Pyongyang’s close relationship with Russia and China, North Korea is in a position of strength for a summit, should the chairman choose to proceed.
The United States and Trump, on the other hand, are in a much weaker position than before. The president’s overconfidence and erratic personality will almost certainly result in missteps that further weaken the U.S. position. And he doesn’t grasp that another summit will greatly benefit North Korea, which is now working in opposition to Washington.
The ministry would add that, as Kim has said many times, the past – the previous summits in Singapore, Hanoi, and at the Demilitarized Zone – is gone. Back then, the chairman focused on improving relations with Washington in return for putting his nuclear program on the table and creating space for North Korea to modernize its economy.
But today, another summit would improve North Korea’s global position by supporting its friends – China and especially Russia – undermining Washington’s influence abroad, and, hopefully, nudging Trump to accept Pyongyang’s growing nuclear arsenal. The ministry would also observe that, more than ever, Trump’s missteps have made the situation ripe for creating tensions in the already fraying South Korea-U.S. alliance.
Time Is on Pyongyang’s Side
Just as in the past, should Kim decide to proceed, the timing and venue of a new summit will be the subject of considerable back and forth with the Americans. In this instance, the North Koreans may believe the result of a summit could be more consequential because of Trump’s personality and his growing domestic political weakness.
The ministry would applaud Kim Jong Un’s policy of delaying a summit decision to take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to meet and extract unilateral concessions has already resulted in victories. The president has shortened one South Korea-U.S. exercise and left a cloud hanging over the rest.
Trump has also inched away from Washington’s long-standing pursuit of denuclearization and toward accepting North Korea as a nuclear power. That appears to have had the added benefit of setting off an internal debate. The State Department continues to back denuclearization, contradicting Trump’s position and sending confusing signals to U.S. allies.
Looking ahead, the North Korean Foreign Ministry would predict that if the Republicans lose the upcoming November congressional elections, as expected, nothing will save Trump from a greatly weakened situation. As a result, he may be anxious to make even more concessions to paint any outcome – even simply holding a meeting with Kim – as a personal victory.
North Korea’s Real Assessment of President Trump
While North Korea’s media have avoided direct criticism of Trump and continued to note Kim’s personal relationship with him, in private, foreign ministry analysts probably believe that his worst personality traits, evident in 2018 and 2019, have only become worse. These, in turn, will provide openings to reach agreements that further support Pyongyang’s strategy.
They would emphasize seven traits that will affect Trump’s performance at a North Korea-U.S. summit. First, at 80, he is seven years older than when the last summit was held and has declined physically and mentally. As the aged typically do, he has good days and bad days. Second, he reacts well to flattery, more so than ever. Third, Trump has a higher opinion of himself and his negotiating ability than in the past, even in the face of repeated failures. Fourth since he is more likely to rely on his gut feelings rather than expert advice, Trump will act impulsively. Fifth, he is losing his grip on reality. American media often laugh at many of his claims. Sixth, Trump has rolled out the red carpet at summits with presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia and Xi Jinping of China, despite their opposition to Washington’s global interests. He mistakenly believes that flattery can overcome policy differences.
Perhaps even more important, Kim’s advisors will point out that Trump does not understand strategic thinking. Past summits with North Korea have demonstrated that he has no grasp of the wider picture; the U.S. war with Iran again underlined his short sightedness. It is doubtful he will understand that the North’s new objectives are different from the past and inimical to U.S. interests.
The American Negotiating Position
Given this analysis of Trump, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry would conclude that he will either repeat standard U.S. positions or come up with his own on the spur of the moment without expert advice from his staff.
Trump knows denuclearization is not in the cards. Instead, he may float the idea of a nuclear freeze. If he does bring it up, the chairman could simply repeat his insistence that Pyongyang needs a strong deterrent. From his perspective, that deterrent is not just to maintain North Korea’s security but an absolute requirement for regional balance, especially given the growing danger of Japanese militarism.
The president may also repeat his proposal made at the 2019 Hanoi summit for a moratorium on further testing of intercontinental-range ballistic missiles (ICBMs) that can reach the United States. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung advanced the same idea at the recent United Nations General Assembly session. The proposal wouldn’t include the shorter-range missiles that target Seoul and Tokyo. As a result, it will prove controversial in South Korea and could create new tensions in U.S. relations with Japan.
The ministry would suggest that Kim could easily parry such a proposal by insisting that any moratorium on ICBM launches must include other countries with those missiles. That would be consistent his position that North Korea is now a global power and cannot be expected to make concessions other nuclear powers will not. And, of course, neither the United States nor the others will be open to that idea,
Trump is likely to dangle sanctions relief for North Korea – a centerpiece of past summits – in return for concessions. The ministry would note, however, Pyongyang’s success in avoiding those restrictions with assistance from Moscow and Beijing, as well as the billions of dollars North Korea earns from illicit cyber activities. As a result, Kim should not see sanctions as the card that Washington once imagined them to be. Still, lifting them could have some secondary political value for North Korea, enhancing its international standing and further normalizing its status.
Moreover, a proposal to lift sanctions could backfire and cause problems for the United States. It could stir up trouble in the Western bloc in the United Nations Security Council since lifting restrictions would face stiff resistance from Britain and France. On the domestic front, fiddling with sanctions would spark criticism from both Trump’s own party and political opponents. While he will not care, such policy turmoil further weakens the United States.
Just as in the past, the president will probably showcase grandiose, even far-fetched, and unachievable schemes to modernize North Korea’s economy. He has done that more recently with a proposal to turn Gaza into a modern coastal metropolis. Pyongyang’s position is quite clear – foreign aid is poisoned candy and should be rejected out of hand unless the chairman decides otherwise.
Finally, Trump can be expected to try to interfere with North Korea’s strong support for Russia in its war with Ukraine. However, the ministry’s America watchers would note that Washington has consistently underestimated the chairman’s commitment to the new relationship with Moscow. Presumably, few if any in the White House read Kim’s last letter to Putin expressing continued full support for Russian operations in Ukraine. Just how hard Trump will push is an open question given his zigzagging approach to the war and his hopes for a better relationship with Putin.
A Potential North Korean Strategy
The Foreign Ministry will argue that a Trump-Kim meeting represents a golden opportunity to secure important objectives while only taking tactical steps that appear to be concessions. It will also open doors to significant strategic gains. It would recommend the following steps.
Kim’s overall summit approach should showcase his statements over the past year that North Korea is seeking “peaceful coexistence.” That theme has mesmerized the Americans. However, meaningless formulations used before by nuclear weapons states, such as “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” would cloak the North’s real objectives. So would any pledge to “work for peaceful resolution of outstanding differences.”
All of this will appeal to Trump who is determined to declare peace in his time and secure the Nobel Prize. In reality, highlighting “peaceful coexistence” would put North Korea in a position to protest virtually any steps the United States takes in the region as contradicting Washington’s assertions of a desire for peace.
While Trump’s aides are sure to warn him ahead of time, the ministry would recommend that Kim press the president to go beyond his random public statements on the North’s nuclear capabilities to put it in writing, perhaps in a summit declaration. Any acknowledgment of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal coming out of the meeting, even only verbal, will create turmoil in Seoul and Tokyo.
The chairman should certainly encourage Trump to reduce the U.S. military commitment to South Korea. He will be pushing on an open door. Trump has made it clear in the past that he is willing to further limit U.S. military activity in and around the Korean Peninsula. One possibility is ending joint South Korea-U.S. military exercises. The ministry would caution that it is unclear how far the president will go. But its experts would point out that he has also been consistently looking to draw down U.S. forces in the South for years.
Finally, North Korea’s diplomats would recommend that Kim seriously consider accepting any offer Trump makes to recognize the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a sovereign state. Embassies in each capital could serve as a formal line of communication after decades of hostility. In theory, they can be framed as a step to reduce tensions and avoid accidental war. In practice, they will do neither.
If diplomatic recognition occurs, Trump will claim credit for taking another step to build peace. However, this measure will reinforce North Korea’s goal of demonstrating that it is a global player to be reckoned with and further its objective of gaining international acceptance as a nuclear power.
The Bottom Line
The Foreign Ministry is likely to conclude that a fourth summit will advance Kim Jong Un’s goals, especially in view of Trump’s poor foreign policy performance and personality flaws.
Even if there is no concrete outcome, the ministry would argue that the optics will be important in positioning North Korea for the future. Just having a summit will strengthen Kim’s standing abroad. Should an impatient Trump walk out again as he did in Hanoi, rather than an embarrassment to the chairman, it will emphasize Washington’s negative image and cause problems with Seoul and Tokyo.
No matter the outcome, it will also be possible to exploit Trump’s post-summit behavior to advance Pyongyang’s objectives. He will continue to insist he has a good personal relationship with Kim. That will be useful as a shield providing time for North Korea to continue to build up militarily for the remainder of the president’s term in office.
Finally, if the past is any guide, the Foreign Ministry will conclude that the chances are an erratic Trump will never stick to what he says. As a result, any agreement may not survive more than a few months. Then North Korea will be able to take tougher steps. For example, after the 2019 Panmunjom summit, Trump went back on his promise to cancel an upcoming joint South Korea-U.S. military exercise. As a result, Pyongyang stonewalled the U.S. in subsequent negotiations and ended its missile test moratorium.

China agrees to curb hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:05:57 UTC
00:05:57 KST

The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.
The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.
“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.
China has been flooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.
Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.
“This is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold talks with his Chinese counterpart.
Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.
China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.
It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

EU commissioner: Turkey moving further away from membership goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:05:27 UTC
00:05:27 KST

Breadcrumb
EU commissioner says recent Turkish actions widen gap with its EU membership goal
Turkey is moving further away from its objective of joining the European Union because of its recent efforts to crack down on the LGBTQ+ community and limit media freedoms, the EU commissioner for enlargement said on Friday.
Turkey has been an official candidate to join the EU since 1999, but its accession has long been frozen over issues ranging from its human rights record to democratic backsliding.
Last week, a Turkish court ordered access to independent news outlet T24's website and social media accounts blocked after authorities said it had published 118 pieces of content over the past year deemed to constitute "LGBT propaganda".
The decision was taken as part of the "My Family is Safe" investigation, a widening crackdown targeting LGBTQ+ groups which the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and the EU.
Speaking to reporters in the northwestern province of Edirne where she attended the opening of an EU-funded railway project, Commissioner Marta Kos said the bloc had a strong interest in developing a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with Turkey in light of "new realities" in Europe, but that concerns over democratic standards remained.
"The latest developments affecting media freedom, the rights of the LGBTQI+ people and local democracy are widening the gap with Turkey's objective of joining the EU," Kos said.
The EU's annual enlargement report, due on October 28, will reflect "our serious concerns in these areas", Kos said, adding that she would "not shy away from stating the facts publicly and clearly".
There was no immediate Turkish government reaction to Kos' remarks.
NEED FOR EU-TURKEY COOPERATION HAS GROWN, KOS SAYS
Despite the lack of progress on its membership aspirations, Turkey has been looking to increase cooperation with the EU. It has repeatedly called for the updating of its customs union with the bloc, and has asked to join various EU programmes.
These include the Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, which helps member states to make defence investments, the Single Euro Payments Area initiative, or SEPA, which facilitates cashless euro bank transfers, and its "Made in Europe" rules, which are aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing.
Kos said conflicts in the region, especially the expansion of the Russia-Ukraine war to the Black Sea, showed the importance and necessity of cooperation with Turkey.
"The relevance of Turkey today is significantly higher than it was four or five years back," she said.
Kos said the EU had two tracks of work currently ongoing with Turkey, focused on a "targeted update" of the customs union that would require legislative alignment from Ankara. The other focuses on public procurement, which she said was important for Ankara's aim of joining the "Made in Europe" rules.

THE HAGUE – The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Oct 9 strongly rejected the sanctions imposed on it by the US government and called on its member states to make sure it can continue to function.
“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order,” the court said in a statement.
The war crimes court said it would continue to “fully discharge its mandate” – which is to prosecute individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression when member states are unwilling or unable to do so.
But it said it would not be able to do so on its own, and called on its members, which do not include the United States, to make sure it has the means necessary to operate.
“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” it said.
“This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment.” REUTERS

Iran's IRGC strikes tanker and threatens to target vessels beyond Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:04:30 UTC
00:04:30 KST

Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that vessels “violating” its designated routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region, as maritime agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed responsibility on Friday for setting an oil tanker ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz and threatened to pursue vessels it deems in violation beyond the strait and across the wider region, as maritime security agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.
The IRGC Navy said it targeted the engine room and propulsion system of the MV Sun Shine, a tanker belonging to the company Natwit, after the vessel attempted to use what it described as an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section. The attack caused a fire on board.
In a statement, the IRGC warned that action against "violating" vessels would no longer be confined to the Strait of Hormuz and that any ship using what it deems unauthorised routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region.
Companies it accuses of co-operating with the US would be sanctioned and all their vessels targeted, it added.
The IRGC laid blame for the incidents in the strait on the US military, accusing Washington of interfering in the decisions of shipping and insurance companies and paying "large bribes" to induce compliance.
"Direct responsibility for these incidents and the escalation of tensions in maritime transport in the region lies with the aggressive US army," the statement said.
Tehran's Friday prayer leader separately told his weekly sermon that the strait would remain closed until Iran's conditions were fully met.
Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Javad Ali-Akbari said Iran had set out "seven conditions" and would decide its next steps once they were met, adding that military readiness had improved, weak points had been addressed, and Iran's strategy had shifted from defence to offence.
Iran has said it controls the Strait of Hormuz and will not permit military forces from hostile countries in the area, vowing to respond "decisively" to any attempt to disrupt its management of the strait.
Lanes clear, CENTCOM says
US Central Command said on Friday it had cleared the strait's main shipping lanes, removed naval mines from principal transit routes, and declared them open to all vessels not in violation of US maritime sanctions against Iran.
Thousands of commercial ships had passed through safely as a result, CENTCOM said.
The competing claims came as the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported that an LPG carrier was struck by unknown projectiles on Friday morning, 13 nautical miles west of Al-Jazira in the United Arab Emirates, causing a major fire that was later brought under control.
UKMTO had reported the previous day that an oil tanker north of Qatari waters was struck by several projectiles resulting in casualties, in the first such attack in six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, the maritime intelligence company Vanguard reported that a tanker had caught fire roughly 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, identifying the vessel as probably the Dalkut, sailing under the Marshall Islands flag.
At least 12 attacks, attempted attacks or harassment incidents targeting oil tankers and gas carriers were recorded in the strait between 28 September and 5 October, the highest weekly figure since the war began on 28 February, according to media reports.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments normally pass, has been effectively closed since the outbreak of the war, following Iranian missile and drone strikes on commercial vessels and a US Navy blockade of Iranian ports.
The latest data indicate that oil exports from other countries in the region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels in recent days.

Yemen humanitarian crisis 'sharply worsens' as fighting displaces over 200,000: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:04:15 UTC
00:04:15 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Yemen's humanitarian crisis has "sharply worsened" amid renewed fighting that has displaced more than 200,000 people since early August, a senior UN humanitarian official warned Friday.
Mohamed Yahya, assistant secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and deputy emergency relief coordinator, delivered the warning during a UN Security Council briefing on behalf of UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher.
"Today, I must warn the Council that Yemen's humanitarian crisis has sharply worsened. Further inaction will cost lives," Yahya said.
He said escalating fighting over the past two months had forced families already exhausted by more than a decade of conflict to flee their homes.
Many displaced families had depleted their savings, lost livelihoods and had few options for safety, he added.
According to Yahya, more than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since early August, the highest level of new displacement since the 2022 truce.
Nearly 4,000 others have crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia, he said.
Yahya warned that women and children were "paying the highest price" as the conflict intensified.
He cited figures from the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights showing that at least 46 civilians had been killed and more than 130 injured since early August.
Yemen's health system was being pushed "closer to collapse" as conflict-related casualties placed additional pressure on overstretched facilities, he said.
Yahya warned that inadequate resources would deepen the crisis, make recovery more difficult and costly, and leave vulnerable families less able to withstand future shocks. 
Children at 'disproportionate risk'
Yahya stressed that a political solution was essential to preventing further suffering.
"Further fighting will have severe humanitarian consequences. It will displace more people and further restrict humanitarian access," he said.
"The people of Yemen need more than our concern and our outrage. They need our collective action, our concrete support, and our unwavering commitment to deliver."
Inger Ashing, chief executive officer of Save the Children International, also addressed the Security Council, warning that the escalation threatened children's safety, education and well-being.
For too many children in Yemen, conflict had turned education from a pathway to opportunity into a refuge from danger, she said.
"Yemen is a country of tremendous vibrance and hope. This latest escalation risks reversing its fragile recovery," Ashing said.
She warned that the country faced a "deadly convergence" of conflict, displacement, economic decline and a surge in infectious and waterborne diseases.
Ashing said children were at "disproportionate risk" from explosive weapons.
"Without urgent action, more children will be pushed deeper into hardship, with lasting consequences for their survival, learning, and protection," she said.

Trump’s planned DC arch faces new lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:04:01 UTC
00:04:01 KST

Trump’s planned DC arch faces new lawsuit
A Virginia county governing board filed the suit, claiming the planning for the monument near DC was rushed.
Local authorities in Arlington, Virginia, have sued the United States Department of the Interior and the National Park Service, seeking to block President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch.
The 250-foot (76-metre) arch project could win approval as early as next month. It is modelled on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and is planned to be built near Arlington National Cemetery, just across the Potomac River from Washington.
The Arlington County governing board said in its lawsuit on Thursday that the project within a busy traffic corridor will cause “significant harm” to its residents and likely require changes to nearby flight paths. It is the first governmental body to take legal action against Trump’s planned monument.
Lawyers argue that the National Park Service failed to conduct a thorough review and that the arch will harm public safety by clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services.
“The National Park Service, the agency responsible for projects on national park land such as Memorial Circle, is proceeding full speed towards ground-disturbing construction,” the lawsuit said. “Although the agency has claimed that a final decision to construct the Arch has not yet been made and purports to be engaged in a routine decisional process, that rushed process appears to be a pretext designed to shore up justifications for building the Arch in accordance with the President’s repeated marching orders.”
The lawsuit asks that “the agency’s feverish pace towards construction of the arch” be halted to ensure that the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act be followed and proper analysis and testing be done.
“The Arlington County Board has filed this lawsuit because our community has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project,” Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a statement. He added that the county has acted in good faith in the review process, pointing out the “severe, unique and wide-ranging negative impacts” the project will have on the county and its residents, only to see them ignored.
The Interior Department emailed a short statement: “The Department continues to follow all laws and regulations.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.
The proposed arch would be within the airport’s main approach and departure corridors. The Federal Aviation Administration’s safety determination requires the arch to be marked with a flame atop the structure and floodlight projectors to make it noticeable for pilots. Some aviation experts have raised safety concerns given its proximity to the airport’s main approach and departure corridor.
The FAA dropped an earlier requirement for red obstruction lights, which it generally mandates on buildings more than 200 feet (61 metres) tall near airports, such as the nearby 169-metre (554-foot) Washington Monument.
The arch is part of Trump’s broader push to remake Washington, including renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, redeveloping a golf course in East Potomac Park and adding his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Preservationists say the projects would alter some of the capital’s most prominent historic landmarks.
Though the arch has received early approval from the US Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued in federal court in Washington, DC, saying the project needs approval by Congress. The judge in that lawsuit said the administration must give the court 48 hours before undertaking any activities related to, or in preparation for, construction of the arch.
Last month, Trump said he would convert the arch into a military complex capable of deploying drones and positioning snipers.

It has been dubbed "the PISA shock". Countries that had been used to their school pupils performing well in test scores are seeing a plunge in standards. The PISA test is an international assessment led by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which measures how well 15‑year‑olds in over 80 countries apply reading, mathematics and science skills to real‑world problems. In the latest rankings, France's results were the worst it has ever had, and Germany's school pupils got their worst PISA report card too.
When it comes to EU member states in the global PISA rankings, the top five performers are Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Austria and Poland. France hovers in 27th place, while the bottom five performers are Malta, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Cyprus.

ICC condemns sweeping US sanctions as assault on international law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday condemned sweeping U.S. sanctions targeting the tribunal, calling them an attack on the foundations of international law and warning that history would judge efforts to undermine its independence.
The measures represent "an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," the court said in a statement, stressing that no individual should be above the law.
The Trump administration announced sanctions against the ICC on Friday, hours after a former judge at the tribunal was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, setting the stage for renewed diplomatic tensions between Washington and its European allies.
Unlike previous restrictions targeting individual judges and prosecutors, the latest measures could penalize companies and financial institutions providing services to the court, potentially disrupting its operations.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement first reported by Reuters.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he added.
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan denounced the decision, saying the restrictions were designed to weaken international justice but would not prevent the tribunal from carrying out its mandate.
"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan told Reuters.
"Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions," she added.
Washington has repeatedly criticized the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli officials over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Israel's genocidal military offensive in Gaza.
Established in 2002 to prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, the Hague-based tribunal has 125 member states, including all European Union countries and every NATO member except the United States and Türkiye.
The court has historically received strong support from European governments, many of which are close U.S. allies.
Nobel recognition highlights pressure on international justice
The sanctions announcement came shortly after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who served on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
The Nobel committee said the decision was intended to draw attention to growing political pressure on international judicial institutions.
In its citation, the committee said the award sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when judges and international legal bodies were facing political attacks.
"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the committee said.
The timing of the award and Washington's announcement underscored tensions over the authority and independence of international courts.
US grants limited exemptions as ICC prepares for disruption
Despite the broad restrictions, the U.S. Treasury Department issued four general licenses shortly after the announcement, allowing certain transactions involving telecommunications, software, pension payments and ICC detainees to continue.
U.S. sanctions generally prohibit American companies from conducting business with designated organizations, potentially forcing banks to close accounts, insurers to withdraw coverage and technology providers to suspend services.
The Trump administration previously sanctioned individual ICC officials during the president's first term. Those restrictions were lifted under former President Joe Biden.
Washington imposed additional sanctions shortly after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
Anticipating broader measures, ICC officials have spent months preparing contingency arrangements, including replacing Microsoft software with open-source alternatives and securing new banking and health insurance services.
Earlier this week, ICC Registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler urged the European Union to consider activating its blocking mechanism, a legal instrument intended to protect European entities from the extraterritorial effects of foreign sanctions.
Rubio said Washington had postponed the latest measures to allow ICC member states to address U.S. objections, but those efforts had failed to produce an acceptable outcome.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said, urging U.S. allies that belong to the tribunal to intervene.
He added that Washington expected countries relying on American military support to help restrain the court's activities.
The secretary of state said the sanctions were structured to leave room for negotiations with countries party to the Rome Statute, the treaty establishing the ICC.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said.
The court, however, maintained that its investigations and prosecutions would continue despite the restrictions, reaffirming its commitment to pursuing accountability for serious international crimes.

No correlation between SIR deletions &amp; poll results in Bengal: chief electoral officer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:02:31 UTC
00:02:31 KST

Refuting the claims made in the YouTube video -- which relied on electoral data from 25 seats with highest and lowest SIR deletions, and pointed to -10.5% and -5.3% swing respectively, for the TMC --, West Bengal's top electoral officer said that 'the electoral data....does not support the political narrative'
NEW DELHI: The chief electoral officer (CEO) of West Bengal on Friday dismissed as "misleading and speculative" claims made in an "analysis" posted on YouTube that deletions made during special intensive revision (SIR) in West Bengal had a direct bearing on the outcome of the recent assembly elections in the state.In a post on X, the CEO quoted the analysis by DeKoder and countered it with the electoral data from five West Bengal seats that saw the highest SIR deletions; four of them were won by the Trinamool Congress, and the only one went to the BJP. As for the five constituencies with the least SIR deletions, the BJP ended up winning in all.Refuting the claims made in the YouTube video -- which relied on electoral data from 25 seats with highest and lowest SIR deletions, and pointed to -10.5% and -5.3% swing respectively, for the TMC --, West Bengal's top electoral officer said that "the electoral data....does not support the political narrative".The CEO also dismissed the claim that women accounted for 62% of the electors deleted through SIR in West Bengal. "The claim...is unverified. As per the total data on deletion of invalid entries (excluding adjudication), around 50% or half of the deletions related to women," he posted on X.
As regards the DeKoder claim that deletions of Muslim electors in West Bengal were 52% more than those of non-Muslim electors, the CEO pointed out that there is no data based on the religious identity of the electors at the end of ECI.
"Hence the analysis claimed is based on mere unverified assumptions," he posted."...The facts do not support the allegations," the CEO stated and asserted that no voter can be deleted without due process. "Issuance of notice, an opportunity for hearing and a speaking order by the ERO (electoral registration officer) are part of the safeguards. Appeals are available at two levels," he added.The CEO underlined that SIR was not about deleting genuine electors but about protecting the integrity of the electoral roll and was being conducted as per Article 324 of the Constitution and Section 21 of the RP Act 1950, with due process and safeguards."SIR is a lawful, transparent and ongoing exercise to ensure that every eligible elector is on the roll and that ineligible entries are removed. Electoral rolls must be based on facts -- not speculation," he noted.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

PARIS, October 9. /TASS/. The unrest linked to high school student protests in France has caused "at least €30 million" in damage, AFP reported, citing the French Education Ministry.
A source confirmed the estimated damage to the news agency, based on reports from regional authorities. Officials have registered "a clear decline in the intensity" of demonstrations for several days now. The protests have become more localized of late, "either because of local politicization or amid actual problems in the areas concerned."
Of the 141 education establishments closed this Friday, most are in the capital region of Ile-de-France, as well as in northern and western France and the outskirts of Lyon.
High school student protests broke out in the capital region of Ile-de-France in late September and have since spread across the country. Demonstrators are protesting against overloaded schedules, teacher shortages and other problems facing the education system. In some areas, protests escalated into unrest and clashes with police. Law enforcement officers have so far detained almost 6,900 people, 86% of them minors.

How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:00:39 UTC
00:00:39 KST

How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice
On September 20, 2026, Ukraine launched another large-scale drone attack on the Moscow region. One drone hit a high-rise apartment building in Kotelniki, southeast of Moscow. Another had struck the same building in June. Neither strike killed anyone, but the attacks badly frightened many people in the neighborhood. Reporters from Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, visited the Novye Kotelniki residential complex to see how repairs were progressing after the two attacks and how residents had responded. Meduza is translating their report in full.
‘People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up’
Drivers struggle to find parking in this densely populated neighborhood in Kotelniki, outside Moscow. Shoppers wait in short lines at grocery store checkouts. It’s a warm, sunny weekend day, yet the courtyard of the Novye Kotelniki residential complex is unusually empty.
On September 20, a Ukrainian drone struck one of the complex’s high-rise buildings for the second time. The first strike came on June 18, 2026. The drone crashed into almost the same spot on the courtyard side, in the upper third of the building, and exploded.
A black scorch mark stands out against the beige-and-brown exterior, with a hole at its center. All that remains of the balconies on floors 19–22 is twisted metal and rebar. Some of the facade tiles have broken off.
The few residents walking in the courtyard occasionally look up at the building and whisper to one another. Many decline to tell Bereg how the constant drone alerts have changed their lives. “What is there to say?” says a woman of about 40 in a black hijab, waving off the question, though she had just been discussing that very subject with a friend.
Olga, a blonde woman in a trench coat, comes out of a neighboring building with her two-year-old daughter. She says this is their first walk in the courtyard since the recent attack.
This time, she says, the property management company quickly cleared the broken glass and other debris from the courtyard. But she’s still scared: “You never know, she could pick up a piece of glass or something. You’re more scared for her than for yourself.”
On the day of the attack, Olga woke to explosions at four in the morning. She woke her husband. At first, he thought she was imagining things, but then he heard the explosions, too. Deciding it wasn’t safe to stay in their apartment, they carried their sleeping daughter downstairs to the ground floor, where neighbors had already gathered.
Olga stayed in the lobby until eight in the morning. Throughout that time, she could hear explosions outside. “It was a nightmare: People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up, and we were all looking for medicine for them,” she tells Bereg. “You feel like you’re in a war zone, and you can’t believe this is happening to you.”
Olga missed the summer attack — her family was away. Perhaps that’s why, unlike many of her neighbors, she hadn’t put a “go bag” with documents, medicine, and other essentials in her entryway. Before the September attacks, she had felt less anxious than others. Afterward, she no longer felt safe.
Still, her family’s daily routine hasn’t changed. She and her husband decided against moving their bed farther from the windows, figuring it wouldn’t save them. “Look at the size of that hole,” she says, gesturing toward the damaged high-rise.
“You keep thinking: God, what if it happens again tomorrow?” Olga says. “I was on sedatives for two days. I definitely don’t feel safe here. I’m stressed every day.”
Her family is considering moving, but unless the attacks become more frequent — “not once or twice, but practically every day” — she and her husband are unlikely to “seriously start looking into it.” Olga hopes things will “get back to normal” because “they [the Ukrainians] have already hit what they wanted to hit, and now they’ll calm down.” She means the Moscow oil refinery, the Ukrainian military’s target. But the high-rise stood in the path of the drones flying toward it.
A few things help Olga manage her anxiety: She’s become even more absorbed in caring for her child and stopped reading the news, although she used to scroll through neighborhood chats even at night. “There’s so much noise now, so many planted stories, so much fake news,” she says. “Even the [real] news — there’s so much of it. You watch all this, and the whole situation keeps playing over in your head. What for?”
Ruslan, who lives in the same complex as Olga, takes the opposite approach: He tries to read all the news. He says the drone attacks don’t make him anxious.
“I knew there’d be an attack — the elections and all that,” Ruslan says. He says the neighborhood has only been quiet for the last few days. Before that, neighbors often heard air defenses in action at night and early in the morning.
On September 20, Ruslan and his family counted “at least 40 explosions.” “We could see flashes in the sky from our window — almost like the ones over Israel!” he says excitedly. “There were about 10 a minute at one point.” He saw the drone crash into the neighboring building. He and his family were about to head out into the stairwell when they heard a loud noise outside the window and red light flooded the apartment.
Like Olga, Ruslan doesn’t have a “go bag,” and he says he won’t be getting one. He sees no need, because “our air defenses have gotten better at their job.” “Yeah, there are screwups. Unfortunately, they can’t intercept everything. But overall, our guys are doing their job, and they’re doing it well,” Ruslan says. “Every day on my way home from work, I see the air defense systems changing locations.”
He tells Bereg he believes there won’t be any more strikes on the neighborhood because they’re no longer worth it for Ukraine: “They launched so many, and the results were really poor. They understand it’s a waste of money.”
With a smirk, Ruslan recalls wondering during the first attack whether the target might have been the apartment building rather than the refinery — “maybe some general lives here.” But he quickly dismissed the idea: First, it was a large-scale attack, and second, “what general would live here?”
Ruslan believes Moscow and its immediate surroundings are now “very well protected” and that the authorities should focus on deploying air defense systems in other regions. That’s his only complaint about the security measures. “I think our government will take care of us, and everything will be fine. Our army will handle it,” he says. “Maybe I’m not that well informed, or maybe I’m too optimistic. But I think everything really is fine.”
The toll of Ukraine’s October attacks on the Moscow region
The next large-scale attack on the Moscow region came overnight on October 6. It struck communities northwest of Moscow, damaging private homes and nonresidential buildings in settlements in the Solnechnogorsk, Volokolamsk, Istra, and Domodedovo districts. Ukrainian Telegram channels that monitor attacks and the Russian outlet Astra also reported a fire at the Volodarskaya oil depot, southeast of Moscow. The Ukrainian strikes and Russian air defense operations killed two people and injured nine.
Ruslan’s school-age daughter looks at him admiringly. They chuckle together as they recall a neighbor who panicked during the latest attack. “Run, run, we’re under attack!” Ruslan says, imitating her, though he quickly adds that “everybody’s different.”
His daughter says that after the summer attack, one of her classmates transferred to another school — her family had decided to move. “They were renting [their apartment]. Maybe if we rented here instead of owning, we’d feel better about moving, too,” Ruslan says. “Plus, we’ve got a mortgage here — where are we gonna go?”
‘I’ll be working to pay the rent. I’m just scared to live here.’
A man in a black jacket, probably an employee of the property management company, walks through the courtyard with a ring of keys. He unlocks a door marked “Shelter” leading to the basement, looks inside, locks it again, and moves on to the next building. Each of the complex’s more than 20 high-rises has a shelter.
Residents of Novye Kotelniki say the management company told them the basements are kept locked because they contain “technical equipment that the engineers are responsible for.” In the event of a real threat, residents are to call the dispatch office. A staff member will then come during the attack and unlock the basement door. The company promises this will happen quickly.
But on September 20, residents of some buildings complained in the neighborhood Telegram chat that they hadn’t been able to get into the basements until after seven in the morning, although the large-scale attack began at four.
Signs reading “Shelter” have been hung at the basement entrances, but the management company has done little to equip the rooms, residents say. Some have benches; others don’t even have those, leaving people to sit on the concrete or stand.
Aleksandra, a resident in her mid-40s, is smoking near the entrance to one shelter. Asked how she feels about the increasingly frequent attacks, she says emphatically: “It’s really bad, really bad!”
Aleksandra lives in the building that drones have struck twice. Or rather, she used to — after the recent strike, she realized she was afraid to stay in her apartment. “As they say, what happens once might never happen again, but what happens a second time…” she says.
Aleksandra was home during both attacks. On June 18, she and her husband woke to repeated explosions and began getting ready to go to the shelter. As she was tying her sneakers, a drone crashed into the building. “I hear this huge bang — and plaster starts falling down in our apartment!” she tells Bereg. “I opened the door, and there was already smoke in the stairwell. We didn’t know if we’d be able to get downstairs.”
No one opened the shelter, and neighbors crowded onto the ground floor. “It all ended around eight, and that’s when they opened the basement,” Aleksandra says indignantly. “Well, what’s the point of going down there once it’s all over?”
On the day of the second drone strike, Aleksandra again heard “a lot of activity” as explosions kept going off. First, she went out onto the communal balcony to take a look. From there, she could see several fires near the Moscow oil refinery, the Mega shopping mall, and the Sadovod market. She was horrified. “I wake my husband up: ‘Get up, there’s a real war out there — everything’s burning, everything’s in flames!’” she says.
To reach the stairs, Aleksandra and her husband had to pass through the communal balcony. As soon as they opened its door, there was a loud explosion, and a wave of heat hit them. “I knew it had hit the building,” she says. “Something went bang, and things started falling.”
As we talk in the courtyard, there’s a crash in the distance, quiet but distinct. Aleksandra flinches and abruptly turns toward the sound.
“I think something fell at the construction site.”
“I react like that all the time now [to sudden noises],” Aleksandra says. “My nerves are completely shot. I went a week without proper sleep, even with Novo-Passit, glycine, and things to calm me down. I’d sleep for two hours, then be awake again.”
On September 20, Aleksandra and her husband waited for the explosions to stop, went back up to their apartment, packed everything they needed, and left for their dacha. They’re staying there temporarily but return to their apartment in Novye Kotelniki every few days.
“We’re living out of bags: one in the car, one at the dacha, and one here. We come back, wash up, do the laundry, hang it up, and head back out,” Aleksandra says. “We try to get everything done as fast as we can. They’ve just posted [on Telegram channels] again that apparently another large-scale attack is expected. Who knows?”
But they can’t stay at the dacha for long: It has almost no amenities, and the trip to work takes three hours. Driving every day proved too expensive, so they switched to public transportation.
Aleksandra took out a mortgage to buy her apartment. She has no other home and no relatives who can take her in. Now she’ll have to pay both her mortgage and the rent on a new place in a safer neighborhood. “I’ll be working to pay the rent. What else can I do?” she says with a sigh. “I don’t know what I’ll eat, but I’m just scared to live here.”
“Looking at the windows, I could tell that lots of people had left — almost no one was still here,” she says. “Today we packed up a bunch of bags and took a heater. And everyone coming toward us had bags, too. People are leaving, and no one wants to come back.”
‘I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here.’
Far fewer people go into the high-rise hit by the two drone attacks than into the other buildings. Many residents emerge carrying large bags — clearly, they’re leaving for a long time.
The lobby has two entrances: one from the courtyard, the other from the road. The courtyard entrance is now cordoned off with barriers wrapped in red and white tape. The concierge warns that residents can’t leave through that door, either. A chair braces it shut from inside, and a sign on it reads: “No entry! Risk of death!” It doesn’t explain the danger.
Another notice asks residents not to use the elevators between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. so they can be available to “construction workers repairing the building.” Residents ignore the request, and there are no workers in sight.
Residents say that for the first few days after the attack, the elevators ran only in the evenings. Those with apartments on the upper floors of the 25-story building had to take the stairs or enter through the neighboring stairwell, use the elevator there, and cross the roof to reach their own building. The management company temporarily opened access to the roof for that purpose. The elevators are now running, and access to the roof has been closed off again.
On many floors, boxes and bags of belongings are scattered about, along with plastic-wrapped crates of toys, black bags of construction debris, window frames, packages of building materials, and parts from household appliances.
The smell of smoke still lingers on the fifth and sixth floors. On September 20, burning debris landed on a windowsill and started a fire. On the upper floors, it smells of burned plastic.
The 21st floor suffered the worst damage. Workers had to remove the front panels from one elevator and the structure surrounding the shaft opening. A padlocked grille has replaced the door separating the elevator lobby from the apartments. The apartment the drone struck is on this floor.
Georgy, whose name has been changed, was home in a neighboring apartment at the time. He and his wife, Yelena, whose name has also been changed, were about to head downstairs when he heard an unusual humming sound from the direction of the balcony. “I go over to the balcony and realize it [the drone] is getting closer, but I can’t see it. I can’t figure out where it’s coming from,” he tells Bereg. “I look down — and there it is, coming from the direction of the quarry, heading straight at me.”
Georgy managed to shout to Yelena to run. He didn’t have time to get out of the way himself. The drone hit the neighboring apartment and exploded. The blast wave and a hail of fragments hit him.
His arms and legs were badly cut. Bleeding heavily, he got dressed and pulled on his sneakers. His wife retrieved their cat, which had hidden under the bathtub. They grabbed a bag of documents and jewelry they had prepared in advance and ran downstairs.
“If it had flown just a little higher, that would’ve been it — we wouldn’t be talking now,” Georgy says, visibly shaken as he looks at his bandaged wrists. “The explosion was unreal. I’d never experienced anything like it in my life. I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.”
The couple went to the home of friends who lived nearby. From their friends’ window, Georgy saw an ambulance arrive at the complex. He went over to the medics himself for first aid and to have them “record [him] as one of the injured.” A few hours later, the couple returned to their apartment for belongings, then went back to their friends’ home. After that, they went to Yelena’s relatives’ home, where they’re now staying.
Georgy shows photos of the wrecked apartment on his phone. The stretch ceilings have melted. The windows and balcony are gone, and everything is covered in soot. Furniture and appliances have toppled over, and fragments and pieces of the walls are scattered everywhere. After what he’s been through, Georgy tries to avoid going to Novye Kotelniki unless he absolutely has to. He arranged to meet Bereg’s reporter at a shopping mall in Moscow.
“I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here,” Georgy says. It wasn’t until several days later, he says, that he fully realized “what could have happened.” It’s been hard to cope with. The other day, he went to get a haircut, and the buzzing of the clippers made him uneasy.
“I barely slept for three nights. I asked my doctor to prescribe something to calm me down, but it’s still pretty tough,” Georgy says. “It’s okay, we’re strong, we’ll get through it. I think time heals.”
Moscow regional authorities are working out how to repair the apartment and pay compensation, but Georgy is avoiding those subjects for now. Over the past week, he’s had to return to the apartment several times to let in specialists who are to assess the damage from the attack, as well as local administration representatives and officers from the Investigative Committee, Russia’s criminal investigation agency. Those visits convinced him that he could no longer live in the complex, even if the building were fully repaired.
“When you go back there, you start shaking — the atmosphere’s different, the aura’s different,” he says. “I’ve developed a phobia of the place, so I want to get everything sorted out as soon as possible and put this nightmare behind me.”
Georgy’s neighbors are collecting signatures for a petition to the management company and the authorities. They’re demanding additional protection for the building that drones have now hit twice.
“It feels unfair that they can’t keep our homes or our lives safe. You don’t feel very safe in your own capital,” Georgy says.
He believes the air defenses can’t handle the number of drones flying toward Moscow. He sees only one way to guarantee an end to the attacks:
It wouldn’t hurt to end this military operation. One decision — and it would all be over.

How the Grand Canyon could have lost 1 billion years of geologic history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In the Grand Canyon, rock layers preserve a relatively continuous record of Earth’s geologic history going back about 2 billion years. But between 520 million and 1.8 billion years, the record is noticeably empty. It’s as if someone broke into a museum and made off with almost an entire wing’s worth of rocks, and sorting out “whodunnit” is one of the coldest cases in all geology.
Now, scientists studying the Grand Canyon’s rocks say that a gigantic Earth-spanning cliff —with a global glaciation as its accomplice — could be to blame for the heist.
The giant cliff started forming about 800 million years ago as an ancient supercontinent called Rodinia split apart, Thomas Gernon, an earth scientist at the University of Southampton in England, and colleagues report August 17 in Geology. Forces like rain and ice weathered and eroded the rock and, like waves at the beach steadily erasing one layer of sand after another, deleted a billion years of Earth’s history.
The group used computer models to simulate how ancient Earth evolved over hundreds of millions of years. They watched as the cliff — known as an escarpment — formed around the time in Earth’s history when rocks in the region vanished.
The escarpment most likely extended across much of a continent called Laurentia, the ancient precursor to North America. It stretched from what was to become Alaska all the way to Arizona and would have been about one to two kilometers high.
Spanning a continent
Some 65 million years ago, the Great Escarpment of Laurentia would have stretched across much of North America, including the spot that would one day become the Grand Canyon and the site of an enduring geologic mystery. The escarpment itself is thought to have formed around 800 million years ago.
“No study has previously suggested the existence of a continental-scale escarpment in the Grand Canyon region. Our study shows it’s a plausible, straightforward explanation for the immense erosion that took place in the Grand Canyon,” Gernon says. Such an immense cliff created steep slopes that were ideal places for the elements to loosen and make off with exposed rock.
And the escarpment had a lot of help when it came to its disappearing act: ice, lots and lots of ice. The theft of the rocks coincided with an extreme period of glaciation called Snowball Earth. Massive ice sheets formed and may have extended all the way from the poles to equatorial latitudes. As the ice expanded, it would have eroded great quantities of rock, helping create the gap in the record.
And the escarpment, due to its high elevation, would have created ideal conditions for Snowball Earth glaciers and ice sheets to form. In a separate study published in Science, Gernon and a team explained how an escarpment created by tectonic activity was responsible for the formation of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet starting some 34 million years ago. “The exposed rocky peaks of the escarpment would have acted as glacier factories,” Gernon says.
It remains unclear, however, whether the erosion that erased the rocks occurred before, during or after the Snowball Earth glaciations. “That’s the real hole that needs filling: pinning down the erosion history in space and time, continent by continent, precisely enough,” Gernon says.
Linking the disappearance of the rocks to verified events in Earth’s history such as the breakup of Rodinia bolsters the case, says Alan Collins, a geologist at Adelaide University in Australia who was not involved in the new study. Not only that, but Gernon’s team points to modern-day examples where similar erosive processes are at work, including a similar escarpment in Antarctica as well as one in South Africa.
Maybe not quite case closed yet, but “I find this very convincing,” Collins says.

I’m Still Convinced the iPod Was the Perfect Gadget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”
He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.
The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)
All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.
Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.
But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.
Adding to the excitement was Steve Jobs’ willingness to redesign the iPod every year. Apple could have maintained its original iPod for a long spell, but almost immediately the company began a series of significant reinventions. Every cycle yielded an iPod with a different size and shape. With each iteration, the iPod seemed to grow smaller and cooler. First came the mini, then came multiple variations of nanos and shuffles in crazy colors and configurations. iPhone updates have kept people buying, but without the fun of a total reshaping of the product.
Is there an alternate universe where Apple continued making the iPod as a dedicated digital music player? I called Tony Fadell to discuss. Fadell is often referred to as the father of the iPod; he headed its hardware team and delivered the product in an amazing sprint of less than a year. He later was deeply involved in developing the iPhone, and his post-Apple career includes cofounding Nest, becoming a successful tech investor, and writing a well-received book.
Fadell resigned from Apple in 2008 and consulted for two years after that, when Apple was still supporting the iPod. But he recalls Jobs and other execs agreeing that the device was on a course to oblivion, despite being a great product with an enthusiastic user base. With the iPhone proving to be a monster success that also helped boost the Macintosh, and Apple pursuing potentially mass-market innovations like the iPad, iPod sales were becoming less relevant to the company’s bottom line. Jobs was a relentless prioritizer, and his successor Tim Cook felt the same way.
Fadell says that there was very little hand-wringing about the iPod’s fate. “The discussion was about Apple [not] doing lower-value things,” he says. Yet he agrees with me that the iPod’s disappearance created a hole that hasn’t been filled.
In retrospect, he says, what made the iPod invaluable is what it didn’t do—connect with the internet. “Because the iPod wasn't connected, you didn’t have all these other things going on to distract you. Today, you get all the annoyance of being connected without being able to get the same listening experience. You can always be distracted and go somewhere else.”
“This thing should still exist,” he says.
A lot of people seem to agree. There are multiple active communities on Facebook and Reddit of refuseniks who go to great lengths to mod old iPods—putting in large flash drives, installing Bluetooth. There’s even an app that makes your iPhone look and play like an iPod Classic. It works great, but you’re still one swipe away from your feeds, your mail, and everything else in your life that isn’t as fun as music.
I ask Fadell how he regards the iPod’s legacy. Tellingly, his answer speaks to Apple’s history more than exhilaration for the product itself. “The iPhone never would have existed without it,” he says. “That means that the Apple we know of would never have existed without the iPod.” It helped turn a computer company with a limited user base into a consumer electronics giant.
“And the crazy thing is that it was exactly 25 years ago—which is half the years that Apple has existed. There was the Apple II, and then the Mac, and then, boom,” he adds.
I prefer to remember the iPod for what it was, not what it led to. Not long ago, I exhumed my iPod Classic. I have an old boombox with a cradle designed for the iPod, with the old 30-pin connector. I put it in shuffle mode and blissed out.
I suspect a lot of others might like to return to iPod Nation. New CEO John Ternus has no incentive to revive the product, of course. I do find it sad, however, that a generation exists that doesn’t know what it’s like to have a dedicated music device that will never interrupt a tune with calls, texts, and notifications. They don’t know what they’re missing.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
