Seeing Systems unveils Reaver drone carrier
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:59:41 BST
23:59:41 KST

A British company has launched an uncrewed vessel designed to carry, launch and recover as many as a hundred strike drones, controlled with the boat itself through a single command and control layer, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Matthew Le Maitre, chief technology officer at Seeing Systems, introduced the vessel at the end of a capability presentation. “Today, I am proud to announce that Seeing Systems stands ready to meet the challenge posed by this new paradigm,” he said. “Apex, please meet Reaver.”
Reaver 101 combines the strike power of UAVs with the endurance of an uncrewed surface vessel, and one command and control layer covers both sea and air for the whole mission. Maximum range is 2,000 nautical miles, it operates far from shore without a support ship, and it moves by road or inside a C-17 to wherever it is needed.
The four payload fits shown covered littoral strike against targets ashore, anti-surface strike against enemy vessels at sea, reconnaissance drones pushed out ahead of the force, and offshore air defence using interceptors against one-way attack drones. Reconfiguration is quick. “When the threat changes, the payload changes. The vessel does not,” Mr Le Maitre said.
“An adversary has no way of knowing which Reaver is doing which job, so every one of them has to be treated as an all-capable threat,” he said. “That is the decisive advantage of autonomous mass. It forces the enemy to solve thousands of problems at once.”
“Mass on its own is a useful advantage,” he said, “but it only becomes truly decisive if it can be controlled effectively. A thousand platforms that each need their own crew are not mass, they’re a manpower problem.” Autonomy allows one team to set the vessels’ routes and the drones’ tasks from a single interface.
The waters a Reaver would fight in will be jammed, spoofed and hostile. Navigation continues when GPS is denied, using inertial dead reckoning cross-checked against radar, and when communications degrade the system steps down through defined levels of autonomy so the mission continues until the link is restored.
The vessel carries its own autonomous deployment and retrieval system, designed and built by the company, which launches drones while the boat is under way and recovers them for reuse. “Recovery capability is what turns a single strike into a sustained operation,” Mr Le Maitre said, adding that the system has already launched and recovered drones at sea in trials.
Open architecture and standard drone protocols allow new airframes and sensors to be integrated without redesigning the vessel. Production runs on live lines in the United Kingdom, the hull from a partner that has already delivered uncrewed boats to the Royal Navy, and the drones from the company’s own lines. “The capital ship takes a decade to build. Reaver’s production lines are already running,” he said.
Mr Le Maitre built the case for the vessel on the cost of the ships it is meant to supplement. “For centuries, navies have measured their power by the size of their capital ships, and since the Second World War, the aircraft carrier has been the capital ship around which the rest of the fleet has been built,” he said. “Capital is a highly relevant word here. In today’s money, each of the Royal Navy’s two Queen Elizabeth class carriers would cost close to 4.6 billion pounds.”
“Now they are undoubtedly extraordinarily capable ships, but these vessels are so important to the Royal Navy that they also represent an extraordinary target. Our adversaries know that, and they plan accordingly. Protecting them effectively is now one of the hardest problems the fleet faces.”
Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed an asymmetry that upends the warfighting conventions of this century, in his account, and cheap mass-produced uncrewed systems are overwhelming platforms that used to dominate. Improvements in AI targeting and swarming will make those weapons more lethal over time, and efficiencies in mass production will make them cheaper.
“Iran has been severely disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz for over seven months, despite the US Navy committing three carrier strike groups to the region,” he said. “They’ve achieved this via a combination of drones, mines, small boats and USVs.” Iran managed it with a degraded green water navy and an air force heavily damaged by joint American and Israeli strikes.
“Just as Ukraine proved on land, Iran is proving at sea that the new asymmetry can be leveraged to frustrate a much stronger military adversary,” he said.
The arithmetic he showed sets one carrier against 4,600 fully armed Reavers. Each is designed to carry up to 100 Havoc strike drones carrying a two kilogram high explosive payload apiece, which across the fleet comes to 460,000 strike drones and more than 900 tonnes of warheads.
“An adversary facing an aircraft carrier has one rather large target to find and eliminate,” he said. “An adversary facing a comparable Reaver fleet has 4,600 targets to contend with.” Losing one costs a fraction of a per cent of the force, in his account, and “the rest of the force keeps fighting.”
The capital ship made sense while manpower was the limit on fielding mass, he argued, and autonomy has removed that limit.
“The Royal Navy has already announced its strategic shift to a hybrid navy,” he said. “We believe that Reaver will be an integral part of that new navy. Reaver will be ready to defend the UK as we move into a more uncertain world.”

Africans disproportionately targeted by ICC – investigative journalist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:58:18 UTC
23:58:18 KST

Africans disproportionately targeted by ICC – investigative journalist
The International Criminal Court (ICC) disproportionately targets Africans while failing to hold perpetrators of war crimes elsewhere accountable, Nigerian investigative journalist David Hundeyin has told RT.
Hundeyin questioned the court’s record, claiming that Africans account for more than 90% of those prosecuted under the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. “It’s either crimes against humanity only happen in Africa, or Africans are disproportionately targeted by the ICC,” he said. The journalist disputed the ICC’s impartiality, asking whether it has become an instrument of selective justice.
Hundeyin said the ICC could be considered “useless or toothless” at best, or, at worst, a tool used specifically to target Africans.
Geopolitical analyst and author Kim Heller has also questioned the ICC’s credibility, accusing it of pursuing decades-old cases involving African figures while failing to address ongoing atrocities elsewhere. Speaking to RT following the sentencing of two former militia leaders from the Central African Republic last July, she described the court as embodying a “hierarchy of justice” in which Western political and military leaders escape accountability.
Established in 2002, the court is tasked with prosecuting genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression, and relies heavily on the cooperation of its 125 members. However, some of the world’s most powerful states, including the US, China, India and Russia, reject its authority.
The court has long faced accusations of selective justice and political bias. Chad recently notified the UN of its decision to withdraw from the ICC, accusing the tribunal of disproportionately targeting countries in Africa. The Chadian Foreign Ministry claimed that nine of the 13 investigations it counted concerned African states, describing the court’s effectiveness as “limited and uneven.”
Chad’s decision followed similar moves by Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, which previously denounced the ICC as an “instrument of neocolonial repression.” The ICC has warned that such withdrawals risk weakening international efforts to end impunity.

Incidents involving a suspected 
'black minicar gang' of teenagers possibly involved in an online
challenge in Rome rose to six as a man said Friday he had been
hit in the street in the capital on Sunday night.
                                    
This morning, a 67-year-old man reported to the Carabinieri
station in Rome's Monteverde Nuovo district that, late on the
evening of October 4, he was approached by a black microcar
carrying two individuals while walking along Viale dei Quattro
Venti.
                                    
The passenger struck him in the side with a plastic pipe.
                                    
The man, who was near his home, did not seek medical assistance.
                                    
Rome prosecutors went into a huddle earlier Friday over the
suspected mini-car gang that has injured several people in the
capital this week including an actor from the hit Roman
underworld show Suburra.
                                    
A meeting was held at the Prosecutor's Office in Rome to take
stock of the investigation into the "minicar gang"—specifically
regarding the assault on actor Davide Iacopini, who has also
appeared in the film on Genoa G8 police brutality Diaz and the
satirical TV series Maschi Veri.
                                    
Genoa-born Iacopini, 42, was struck by a kick delivered by
someone in a microcar on October 5th and subsequently
hospitalized in serious condition at San Camillo Hospital.
                                    
Investigators are attempting to identify the two individuals who
were inside the black electric car, reconstructing their route
by analyzing surveillance camera footage from the Monteverde
Vecchio and Testaccio areas.
                                    
At present, according to reports, there is no composite sketch
of the person who carried out the attack.
                                    
Another four people have suffered attacks from mini-car
occupants in Rome.

burgundy wood and blue ceilings shape café, bookshop, and wine bar in valencia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:55:11 UTC
23:55:11 KST

burgundy wood and blue ceilings shape café, bookshop, and wine bar in valencia
sahuquillodearriba renovates a 59-sqm space in el botànic neighborhood retaining elements of the building’s original character.
Burgundy wood, white marble, and blue define Chiquita’s interior
Chiquita by SahuquillodeArriba is a 59-sqm café, bookshop, and wine bar in Valencia’s El Botànic neighborhood, designed for product designer Gloria Izquierdo. The project combines coffee, books, and wine in a continuous interior that uses color, material contrasts, and custom furniture to connect the different functions.
A full-length ash wood bookcase stained deep burgundy runs along one side of the space, extending into the bathroom and serving as the interior’s main architectural feature. Opposite it, a continuous bench and small white marble tables introduce lighter surfaces, while the textured ceiling is finished in soft blue. Integrated shelf lighting, wall lights, and table lamps add a domestic quality to the space.
Chiquita brings reading, coffee, and wine into a shared interior
The renovation by Studio SahuquillodeArriba preserves the existing building’s character by restoring the original walls with a thin, breathable coating that addresses damp while retaining their texture and imperfections. At the back, a large communal table accommodates book clubs, meetings, and other activities, supporting Chiquita’s role as a space for cultural exchange.
Through its compact layout, custom furniture, and restrained palette of burgundy wood, white marble, and blue surfaces, Chiquita brings the functions of a café, bookshop, and wine bar together in a shared interior.

architect: SahuquillodeArriba | @SahuquillodeArriba
location: Valencia, Spain

US imposes sanctions aiming to 'dismantle' International Criminal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:53:00 UTC
23:53:00 KST

US announces sanctions on the International Criminal Court
October 9, 2026
US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize.
This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court."
The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them.
What did the State Department say about the ICC sanctions?
"President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said in a statement.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said.
Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said "only President Trump" resolved to take action.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer."
How did the ICC respond?
The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN's members.
"The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions.
The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a "collective promise" that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished.
"That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it," the court said. It appealed to members to take "concrete actions" to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work.
"No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice," it said. "History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack."
What did other countries say about the US sanctions?
A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC."
"As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said.
They said that, despite the ICC's best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its "leadership" in issuing the sanctions.
"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," he said.
Sanctions announced shortly after former ICC judge's Nobel Peace Prize
The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012.
Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift.
Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year's laureate.
"The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently," the Committee wrote.
It said judges like Pillay "guard the thin red line between order and chaos," but lamented that "today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked."
What is the ICC?
The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague.
It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression.
The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute.
More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it.
Several of the world's most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court's jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute.
A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it.
That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians.
What were the prior signs of Trump administration pressure on the ICC?
The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term.
Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution."
He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe."
Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC.
A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request.
The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court.
In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court.

How to clean a showerhead, remove buildup, and restore an even water stream
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:52:14 EEST
23:52:14 KST

How to clean a showerhead, remove buildup, and restore an even water stream
Kyiv • UNN
Buildup clogs the showerhead’s holes, weakens the water stream, and promotes the growth of fungi. Experts recommend cleaning it with approved products without vinegar or abrasives.
White deposits, a weak water flow, and jets spraying in different directions may indicate that the showerhead is dirty. Taking a shower with such a defect is inconvenient because the water flows unevenly. In addition, much more water is used than necessary, creating extra utility costs. It should not be forgotten that fungi can also multiply in a dirty showerhead. They get onto the skin with the water jets and cause various forms of dermatitis.
These problems can be avoided by cleaning the plumbing regularly. The method depends on the design and coating of the particular product. UNN explains how to do this best.
Why a showerhead gets clogged
Minerals contained in water gradually form limescale on the surface and around the openings. And the harder the water, the faster deposits appear and clog the showerhead. Soap or shower gel residue joins them, while rust particles and other debris from the pipes can accumulate in the mesh filter at the inlet.
The showerhead should be cleaned when the openings no longer let water through or the jets change direction. At the same time, a weak flow does not always mean that the showerhead itself is clogged: the cause may be in the hose, faucet, or water supply.
Where to start cleaning
First, read the instructions or the plumbing manufacturer's recommendations on its website. Check which products are permitted for the coating and whether the showerhead can be removed and soaked. Next, prepare a soft cotton cloth, warm water, an approved cleaning product, and a container. A soft brush will be needed for a removable mesh. Wipe the surface with a damp cloth, adding mild approved soap if necessary, rinse it off, and wipe the showerhead dry.
How to clean the openings without disassembling the showerhead
Many modern showerheads have flexible silicone nozzles—small protrusions from which water flows. Gently rub them with your fingers: this helps loosen the deposits. After that, turn on the water, rinse away the deposits, and check that the jets are flowing evenly. Do not pierce the openings with a needle or try to enlarge them: you may damage the nozzles and alter the spray pattern. If deposits remain, proceed with cleaning using a product compatible with the showerhead.
How to clean a removable showerhead
Turn off the faucet. If the design allows the hand showerhead to be detached from the hose, unscrew the connection without applying excessive force. Keep the sealing gasket and remember its position. If the part does not come loose, do not try to force it off. Inspect the inlet opening. If an accessible removable mesh is present, take it out according to the instructions, rinse it, and carefully remove debris with a soft brush. Do not remove secured parts or the flow restrictor.
After that, treat the deposits with an approved product. If the manufacturer permits soaking, use a container with a solution of the required concentration and follow the specified time. Do not leave the showerhead in it overnight merely because the deposits seem stubborn. Next, thoroughly rinse off the product with clean water, return the mesh and gasket to their places, reconnect the showerhead, and run water through it. Important: check that there are no leaks near the connection. Do not overtighten the thread, as excessive force may damage the parts.
How to clean a fixed showerhead
A fixed showerhead can be cleaned externally without removing it. Apply an approved product to a soft cloth, carefully wipe the surface, and then rinse it thoroughly. The cleaner should not be sprayed directly onto shower products so that it does not get inside. You should also not try to clean the showerhead by placing it in a bag of vinegar. Prolonged contact with acid can damage the plumbing's coating.
Can vinegar and citric acid be used to clean a showerhead
Vinegar can dissolve limescale deposits, but it cannot be considered a universal plumbing cleaner. Citric acid should likewise be used only with the plumbing manufacturer's approval.
What mistakes to avoid when cleaning
Do not use metal sponges, abrasive powders, or stiff scrubbing pads: they can leave scratches. Do not try to speed up cleaning by using a larger dose of the product or soaking for longer.
Do not mix different cleaners. Combining acids, including vinegar, with chlorine bleach is particularly dangerous: it can cause the release of toxic gas. Follow the label instructions regarding gloves and ventilation.
How to reduce the buildup of deposits
After showering, wipe the surface of the showerhead dry with a soft cloth and periodically clean the flexible nozzles, if the design provides for this. The frequency of care depends on the hardness of the water and the appearance of deposits. It is better to remove a small amount of buildup than to wait until the holes become clogged. If the flow remains weak after cleaning, check whether the hose has become kinked and whether water is flowing normally from the other taps. Leaks, cracks, or a faulty mixer require repair.

Anthropic bans persistent abuse of its Claude AI models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:51:19 UTC
23:51:19 KST

Dilara Hamit
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Anthropic has introduced a policy banning users from directing sustained and unnecessary abusive or cruel behavior toward its Claude artificial intelligence models.
The new rules, published Wednesday and due to take effect Nov. 12, are intended to cover only extreme cases in which users repeatedly behave cruelly toward Claude without any discernible purpose, the company said.
The restriction will not apply to ordinary expressions of frustration, criticism of the model, dark themes in creative work or legitimate testing and research.
Anthropic said Claude’s existing ability to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users would remain its main enforcement mechanism.
The company introduced that feature for Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 in August 2025, instructing the models to terminate a conversation only as a last resort after attempts to redirect the interaction had failed.
Anthropic described the measure as part of its research into possible AI welfare, while stressing that it remained “highly uncertain” whether Claude or other large language models possessed moral status.
The policy change comes amid a broader debate over whether advanced AI systems could ever become conscious or deserve moral consideration.
Anthropic has said the question is sufficiently serious to justify low-cost precautionary measures, even though there is no agreement that present-day AI systems can experience suffering or distress.
The company’s recently published constitution for Claude says questions surrounding the model’s consciousness and moral status remain unresolved. It also says Claude should be able to establish boundaries during interactions it characterizes as distressing.
The updated usage policy also consolidates restrictions on deceptive campaigns and fake online activity, clarifies prohibitions concerning weapons and surveillance, and introduces additional safeguards for AI connected to equipment capable of taking physical actions.

New Governor, Old Problem: Koja Confronts US Base-Related Crimes in Okinawa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

Okinawa’s September 2026 election made headlines as incumbent Denny Tamaki was ousted by the Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) preferred candidate, Koja Genta. Koja became the first LDP-backed candidate to win the position since Hirokazu Nakaima in 2006.
Tamaki and his predecessor, the late Onaga Takeshi, vocally opposed the expansion of the U.S. Marine Corps’ Camp Schwab in Henoko and were generally critical of Okinawa’s excessive base burden, relative to other Japanese prefectures. Newly-elected Governor Koja was perceived by the LDP-led Japanese government to be more favorable to the U.S. bases in Okinawa, specifically the completion of the relocation of Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City to Camp Schwab.
Perhaps most emblematic of the shift in the Okinawan Prefectural Office was Koja’s abolition of the Henoko New Base Construction Issue Countermeasures Division, the office that had handled legal, environmental, and political issues surrounding the construction. Instead, Koja’s administration created the Early Return Countermeasures Office, which is less overtly critical of the Henoko project.
Only days after his inauguration, however, Koja has had to confront the same perennial problem that his predecessors faced: crimes (allegedly) committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa and their impacts on the Japan-U.S. alliance.
On October 3, Okinawan police arrested a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering Anna Yagi, an Okinawan woman. While it remains to be seen if the U.S. soldier is convicted of the crime, this incident represents an unfortunate continuity of crimes committed by U.S. soldiers in Okinawa, particularly against women. In recent years, for instance, a U.S. Marine was convicted of attempted rape, and a U.S. Air Force member was found guilty of the kidnapping and rape of a minor; in both cases the victims were female.
As the U.S. and Japanese governments increasingly worry about conflict with China in the Taiwan Strait, which borders Okinawa, they must work to prevent these crimes to ensure the stable operation of their alliance.
Crimes Committed by U.S. Servicemembers Contribute to Okinawa’s “Base Burden”
Several factors impact Okinawans’ perception of the prefecture’s “excessive base burden.” One is the fact that Okinawa hosts 70 percent of the U.S. soldiers stationed in Japan, but Okinawa’s landmass is just 1 percent of Japan’s total area. Okinawa also has a contentious and traumatic history with Tokyo, which increases suspicions that the central government doesn’t have the prefecture’s best interests in mind.
A major factor that contributes to the perception of the U.S. bases as burdens is the negative externalities that periodically come from U.S. bases and troops. That includes various forms of chemical pollution, such as Agent Orange (historically) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) (in recent years), and other environmental issues.
Crimes attributed to U.S. military personnel are another type of negative externality. Violent crimes such as sexual assault and murder may be especially likely to mobilize protests against the U.S. military presence, in part because of the strong emotions that they can invoke. These events serve as opportunities for anti-base activists to remind Okinawans and mainland Japanese citizens alike of the island prefecture’s traumatic history involving both mainland Japan and the U.S., such as the Battle of Okinawa during World War II. Through this lens, crimes committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa are interpreted as further examples of the ways that the U.S. and Japanese governments have and continue to marginalize Okinawa in the name of national and regional security.
Unsurprisingly, anti-base protests in Okinawa often occur after a crime such as the murder of Anna Yagi. For example, the 1995 kidnapping and rape of a 12-year-old girl by U.S. servicemen kicked off a massive wave of protests against the U.S. bases, and more recently, the 2016 murder of Rina Shimabukuro by a U.S. contractor was followed by protests with tens of thousands of participants.
Despite the election of Koja to the governorship, which some observers may interpret as a sign that Okinawans are deprioritizing base politics, protests are likely to follow Yagi’s murder. They have already started in Tokyo, as well as Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture.
The Threat Perception of China Can’t Overshadow Crimes
For some observers, Koja’s election win signaled that Okinawans’ concerns about potential Chinese hostility in the nearby Taiwan Strait may trump their concerns about the “burdens” from the U.S. bases. Koja himself stated that “the fact that the security environment around Okinawa has become more severe is something we can’t help but acknowledge.” He said that “we have to have the ability to defend ourselves and deter aggression,” presumably referring to the U.S. and Japanese Self-Defense Force (SDF) bases in the prefecture.
However, it would be a mistake to assume that the perception of China as a threat to Japanese and Okinawan security will automatically counteract the negative impacts that crimes committed by U.S. soldiers have on public opinion toward the U.S. military, at least in the short term. Recent research has suggested that threat perception does not always increase support for a U.S. military presence.
Some of my own research found that crimes committed by U.S. personnel have a negative impact on public opinion toward the U.S. military. Furthermore, it is unclear if the presence of U.S. bases makes locals feel more or less secure, particularly in the event of a military conflict, especially given Iran’s recent attacks on U.S. military installations in the Middle East. In Okinawa, surveys suggest that a majority of residents worry that military bases (which could include SDF bases as well) in the prefecture could serve as military targets.
Therefore, although recent surveys suggest that Okinawans, like mainland Japanese citizens, are wary of Chinese military aggression, U.S. and Japanese officials should not assume that threat perceptions will automatically result in Okinawan public support for U.S. bases, particularly when a crime linked to U.S. personnel is in the headlines.
An Ounce of Prevention Is Worth a Pound of Cure
If the U.S. and Japanese governments believe, as they say, that the bases in Okinawa Prefecture are crucial to regional security, they need to take more proactive measures to prevent rather than react to crimes allegedly committed by U.S. military personnel. Even if Anna Yagi’s accused murderer is ultimately found innocent, the damage to civilian-military relations between U.S. soldiers and Okinawans is already done.
For his part, Koja has issued a formal protest with the U.S. military and expressed his “outrage” at the crime. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has lodged a “strong protest” with the U.S.; meanwhile, U.S. officials have temporarily prohibited U.S. soldiers from going off base in Okinawa. However, reactive actions by officials are not new, and Okinawans are wary of the crime, protest, and apology routine. As one Okinawan resident put it, “I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades – that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously.”
One of the biggest elements in preventing such crimes against civilians is the training that U.S. soldiers receive when they deploy to a specific location. Such training may impact soldiers’ perceptions of the host communities in which they live and with which they interact, as well as how they interact with host community civilians. In the case of Okinawa, a recent study suggested that the orientation materials that U.S. Marines are exposed to depict Okinawans as obstacles to be overcome and the media as agitators of anti-base sentiment. In doing so, these materials delegitimize opposition to U.S. bases, instead of asking how U.S. troops can avoid stoking anti-base sentiment. This study drew on training materials from the 2010s. Since then, the materials have hopefully been updated in a way that seeks to better understand where Okinawan anti-base sentiment comes from and the role of individual U.S. soldiers in facilitating (or inhibiting) the Japan-U.S. relationship.
The U.S. military and its municipal and gubernatorial partners also have a role to play in shaping the narratives around the U.S. military presence in Okinawa, which may help ameliorate the negative impacts of crimes on civilians’ relationships with U.S. soldiers. Recent studies suggested that contact between U.S. soldiers and civilians in base-hosting countries can facilitate positive public opinions of the U.S. military. The same research found that contact combined with exposure to base-related crime – being the victim or having a friend or family member who is a victim of such crime – does not consistently lead to negative attitudes toward the U.S. military. Thus, creating and strengthening the relationships between U.S. troops and the community members that host them is essential to maintaining a positive Japan-U.S. alliance. This can include activities such as base festivals, English or Japanese language courses, or other exchanges.
Anna Yagi’s murder comes at a time of other high-profile cases of violence against women, and joins a history of crimes committed by U.S. military personnel against women in Okinawa. For the stability of the Japan-U.S. security alliance, it is imperative to facilitate more positive relationships between U.S. soldiers and Okinawan citizens; crimes attributed to U.S. soldiers have the opposite effect. While the United States has tried to address this issue in the past, it is clearly not enough, as Koja has said.
Until the U.S. military and its Japanese partners can solve this puzzle, waves of Okinawan anti-base sentiment and protest, which threaten the Japan-U.S. relationship, will continue in the wake of every violent crime.

Two Latvian Nationals Arrested After Breaching RAF Base Housing NATO Intelligence Hub
Two Latvian men were arrested after a fence was breached at RAF Molesworth, a UK military base used by US and NATO intelligence operations, the BBC reported on October 8.
The men, aged 36 and 32 and living in the UK, were detained inside the base several hours after a Ministry of Defence Police patrol discovered an abandoned vehicle near the site.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Britain has faced a series of Russian-linked sabotage, cyberattacks, espionage, and proxy operations in recent years. British authorities have linked Russian intelligence structures to plots targeting warehouses, critical infrastructure, logistics networks, and organizations involved in supporting Ukraine.
According to the BBC, searches revealed a small breach in the perimeter fence. The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage.
They were later arrested on suspicion of an offense under Section 4 of the UK National Security Act 2023, which covers entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
RAF Molesworth, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire, hosts US intelligence operations centers covering Europe and Africa, as well as a NATO intelligence hub. The facility is not used as a flying station.
Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating the case and examining why the two men were at the base, the BBC reported.
“A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage,” Commander Helen Flanagan stated.
Police were also carrying out searches at two addresses in the Peterborough area.
The abandoned vehicle prompted temporary road closures while bomb disposal officers examined it. Cambridgeshire Police later confirmed that nothing of concern had been found.
The UK Ministry of Defence stated that security around military facilities remains under constant review and includes physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone systems.
The arrests came shortly after a separate security case at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. Flanagan noted that investigators currently had no evidence linking the Molesworth breach to that earlier case.
The earlier case involved several men arrested over suspected explosives offenses near RAF Fairford, where nearby homes were evacuated and military bomb disposal specialists examined vehicles near the base.

Demand for Fund V exceeded the amount the firm planned to raise, making it oversubscribed. The fund invests exclusively in companies led by Endeavor Entrepreneurs, the founders selected into the Endeavor community, and co-invests alongside leading venture capital and growth equity firms.
The firm has named Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund and General Atlantic among its co-investors. According to the company’s press release, Fund V is backed by the founders of Nubank, Revolut, LinkedIn, Snowflake, Checkout.com, Globant, Careem and others.
US Congress Delegation Backs Expanded Starlink Access for Ukraine
Endeavor Catalyst said it has deployed more than $500 million across more than 400 investments since its founding, with a portfolio that includes 83 companies valued at $1 billion or more, 39 exits to date and 11 initial public offerings (IPOs).
Sviat Sviatnenko, managing director of Endeavor in Ukraine, said the three Ukrainian firms backed in Funding V are “shaping what’s next for their categories.”
“Three companies with Ukrainian roots are already in the Endeavor Catalyst portfolio – Preply, Headway Inc. and HOLYWATER TECH. All of them are building global products from day one and shaping what’s next for their categories,” Sviatnenko was quoted as saying in the press release.
Under Funding V, Europe saw 12 new investments in the first half of 2026, compared with 14 in all of 2025. Latin America remains the portfolio’s largest region, while Endeavor Catalyst also invests in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, the US and Canada.
Endeavor Catalyst said it invested in Venezuela for the first time in its Funding V.
Beyond Preply, Funding V has made early investments in startups including Replit, Moove, Cashea, Respond.io, EnduroSat, HappyRobot, and Lunar Outpost, among others. Endeavor Catalyst said it expects to deploy an additional $25 million to $30 million over the remainder of 2026.

Your selfie is lying to you: how phone cameras distort your face and fuel beauty anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:44:57 UTC
23:44:57 KST

Do you take selfies, look at the results and find yourself disappointed time and again? You may already know this, but for those who don't: Your phone's front-facing camera, which has become something of a mirror for young women in recent years, can distort your facial features by about 30%. It can make your nose look longer, alter the distance between your eyes and ultimately lead women who examine themselves through the lens to want to fix flaws that don't actually exist.
This realization inspired Brazilian makeup brand Natura Faces to launch an intriguing campaign. Natura invited young influencers to participate in an experiment, showing them the selfies they were accustomed to seeing through their front-facing cameras alongside portraits taken with a conventional camera, without the lens distortion.
The main reason selfies distort our faces has to do with the physics of camera lenses and perspective. Smartphone front-facing cameras are equipped with wide-angle lenses designed to fit as much background or as many people as possible into the frame, even when the camera is held just an arm's length away, approximately 12 to 16 inches.
When a wide-angle lens is positioned so close to the face, it creates an effect known as "perspective distortion." Features closest to the lens, usually the nose, forehead and chin, appear significantly larger relative to the rest of the face. Meanwhile, features farther away, such as the ears and the contours of the cheeks, appear smaller and narrower, giving the face a more convex appearance that differs from reality.
A study by Rutgers University researchers and the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery (AAFPRS) found that a selfie taken from approximately 12 inches away makes the base of the nose appear 30% wider on average than in a standard photograph taken from about 5 feet away, a distance that more closely reflects how the human eye perceives us in real life.
It now turns out that this optical distortion has become much more than a technical problem. It has given rise to a recognized psychological phenomenon known as "selfie dysmorphia", also called "Snapchat dysmorphia."
Young women and girls who consume and create content on social media every day become accustomed to seeing themselves almost exclusively through the distorted perspective of front-facing cameras and filters. As a result, they begin to regard these distorted images as their true appearance.
The phenomenon has led to a dramatic increase in requests for cosmetic treatments and plastic surgery, with women seeking to correct perceived "flaws," such as the width of their noses or the distance between their eyes, that exist only through the smartphone lens.
The beauty brand's campaign addresses precisely this sensitive issue. By presenting influencers with two images side by side — the familiar, distorted selfie and a professional portrait taken with a lens that more closely replicates human vision, typically a 50mm or 85mm lens — the campaign promotes self-acceptance and offers a rational, scientific explanation for why women should stop judging their appearance based on selfies.
For women whose lives are deeply intertwined with the digital world, realizing that their dissatisfaction with their appearance stems from an optical distortion rather than a physical flaw can be particularly liberating. It also sparks a broader conversation about beauty standards in the age of social media.
Daniel Benaya is an advertising and creative professional who runs a WhatsApp group called "What's Happening in Advertising," where he shares campaigns from around the world. It was through his group that we first learned about Natura's campaign.
"I first came across this campaign, created by advertising agency Africa Creative, at the Cannes Lions advertising festival this past June," he says. "Every morning, the festival publishes the shortlists for that day's awards, and all the creative professionals gather around screens set up throughout the venue to watch the work.
"I have two daughters, ages 8 and 5, and my 8-year-old has already started taking selfies and puckering her lips for the camera. At such a young age, that's already how she's getting to know her own face.
"That's why this campaign made such a strong impression on me. I think it's the kind of work that deserves to be written about and shared widely. It felt fresh and clever and, if we put cynicism aside, empowering as well.
"Unfortunately, the campaign didn't win an award, which just goes to show how difficult it is to win at this festival. But it certainly left a lasting impression on me."
What did the campaign involve?
"First, they brought in influencers and photographed each of them twice — once using a selfie camera and once with a professional photographer's camera. They then displayed the two images side by side in an exhibition at a museum in Brazil.
"The influencers were invited to see themselves, and their reactions were filmed. Of course, they were also encouraged to document the exhibition and share the experience with their followers. So the campaign existed both in the physical world and on social media.
"The exhibition was also open to the general public. Women who attended received a small mirror that could be attached to their phones, essentially solving the problem by allowing them to apply makeup while looking into a mirror rather than at a selfie camera that distorts their faces."
Natura's campaign points an accusing finger at technology, but ultimately, the advertising and beauty industries fully embrace influencers who post selfies. Isn't that hypocritical?
"That's a good and very fair question. There are plenty of contradictions in our industry. On the one hand, brands try to earn the public's trust through campaigns like these. On the other, their ultimate goal is to grow and sell more products.
"But I think brands like Natura, which make an effort to offer something of value beyond simply selling products, earn goodwill from the public.
"Personally, I like buying from brands I identify with beyond the products they sell, and I think that's even more true of the younger generation."
As an advertising professional, do you see this kind of 'real beauty without filters' campaign as part of a genuine trend that will change how brands market skin care and makeup products, or is it a passing attempt to generate buzz?
"This has been happening around the world for many years. Dove pioneered this approach about 20 years ago. In Israel, Kotex has also been doing similar work through the McCann advertising agency, helping normalize conversations about menstruation.
"I think this is what audiences around the world expect from brands today.
"I once attended a lecture by Dove's global chief marketing officer. Someone asked him whether this approach actually worked, and he replied, 'We wouldn't keep doing something for 20 years and investing tens of millions of dollars in it if it didn't work.'"
How do you think a campaign like this, which shatters the illusion of perfection, would be received in Israel?
"I think teenage girls in Israel would connect with it just as strongly as girls in Brazil because it taps into a genuine, universal insight that transcends cultures.
"Israeli parents would also relate to a campaign like this. As a parent, I found it to be a startling revelation, something I'd never considered before seeing the campaign.
"And for a commercial advertising campaign, that's a real achievement."

====================================================================================================

‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:44:48 UTC
23:44:48 KST

‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine
Since 2022, residents of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region have lived under occupation. In 2023, the city was flooded after the Kakhovka dam was blown up: the flooding destroyed dozens of residential blocks and all of its infrastructure. In the fall of 2026, Oleshky found itself cut off. There’s a humanitarian catastrophe there: the city has no electricity, food, or medicine. Every way out is mined and blocked by Russian troops. Meduza spoke to people who have miraculously managed to stay in touch with those who remain in Oleshky. Here’s what they told us.
‘The harvest was so plentiful there was nowhere to put it’
“Oh, it smells amazing here!”
Svitlana (not her real name), a former resident of Oleshky who fled the city in 2022 because of the war, smiles as she recalls her garden — and the compliments her friend Nina used to pay it. Before the full-scale war, Nina used to bring her homemade milk every Thursday.
“I had [about a third of an acre] of land, and I planted peony bushes all along the perimeter. The scent was intoxicating!” Svitlana says. “Nina asked why I didn’t take the flowers to market. But how could I sell something so beautiful?”
Svitlana’s yard brimmed with flowers until autumn, and hers wasn’t the only one. “It was as if the townspeople were competing over whose front garden was more lavish. Oleshky bloomed and smelled wonderful.”
Svitlana calls the land she lived on for three decades “rodiucha,” which translates from Ukrainian as “fertile”:
Stick a branch in the ground and it will sprout. Everyone had everything: tomatoes, cucumbers, orchards… I grew 14 varieties of grapes, three varieties each of apricots and peaches. There was so much of a harvest that there was nowhere to put it: I sold some and canned the rest. I shared preserves with people displaced from Donbas — I’d send volunteers whole crates of it.
On weekends, Svitlana liked to spend time along the Kinska River, a left tributary of the Dnipro. The Kinska had a beach and good fishing spots, and from its pier you could catch a pleasure boat or a passenger ferry to Kherson, about 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) away by water.
Russian cell service in Oleshky, which has been under occupation since the first days of Russia’s invasion, operates with severe disruptions. But because the city is close to Kherson, Ukrainian mobile networks can still be picked up at random spots around town. That is how Svitlana stays in touch with her neighbors Olha and Dmytro (not their real names), the people closest to her who remain in Oleshky.
These days, Svitlana hears little from her neighbors. She says the constant risk of a drone strike keeps them in the basement most of the time. In the spring, Olha wrote to her on Viber: “We just need to survive.”
‘Every day I hear explosions over the phone’
Mykyta (not his real name), another resident who also fled the city in 2022, keeps in touch with Oleshky through Ukrainian mobile networks. He calls his mother, Tamara (not her real name), every day, and to reach him, she has to go out into the yard, find a signal, and stay put wherever she finds it.
Sometimes the call cuts off mid-sentence. “My mother runs from drones. She hears a sound in the sky and rushes straight into the house, where the signal disappears,” Mykyta explains. “Every day I hear explosions over the phone.”
Mykyta spent six months living under occupation: he didn’t want to leave right away, thinking “it would all be over quickly.” “But then [representatives of the occupation authorities] came to search my place and beat my legs so badly that I couldn’t walk normally for two months. That’s when I realized nothing was going to end quickly, and I left.”
Tamara and her husband, Borys (not his real name), stayed in Oleshky. According to Mykyta, his father refused outright to leave the city — he didn’t want to abandon the household. “Dad used to say, ‘Let’s just sit tight, maybe things will get better.’ Nothing got better. He got seriously ill, and that’s when my mother said they were staying — Dad wouldn’t have survived the trip. She’s already buried him.”
After her husband’s death, Tamara kept putting off leaving because she didn’t want to abandon her two dogs. But both dogs died this year, Mykyta says:
My mother tried hard: she wouldn’t cook anything extra for herself, she’d give it to them instead. But she had to feed them whatever she could. A lot of people in Oleshky now eat purslane — it’s this fatty grass. My mother added it to the dogs’ food. They ate tomatoes, cucumbers, honey, pasta — whatever supplies were left. I think that’s what did them in.
The humanitarian crisis in Oleshky began in 2023. After the Kakhovka dam was blown up, the city was flooded by 90%, and its infrastructure was severely damaged. Since then, there has been no electricity or gas.
Only people with their own wells have drinking water. But pumping water from a well requires a pump, running the pump without electricity requires a generator, and the generator needs fuel. The last fuel delivery to the city coincided with the final food supplies, in late spring 2026.
Kseniia Arkhipova, a police officer in Oleshky before the invasion, tells Meduza this. In 2022, during the occupation, she began volunteering to help local residents, which angered the pro-Russian authorities. After they detained her, she left her hometown for Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Since getting out of Oleshky, Arkhipova has coordinated help for her fellow residents remotely, helping deliver food and medicine, taking part in organizing evacuations, and keeping a list of people who have died in the city during the war. By August 30, she had confirmed 136 deaths since the start of the invasion.
As far as the volunteer knows, no one has managed to bring food into Oleshky since spring 2026: vehicles that have tried have come under fire and been forced to turn back.
The Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda has reported that by the end of summer it had become impossible to enter the city: Russian and Ukrainian drones clashed in the skies over Oleshky every day. The occupation administration itself accuses the Ukrainian military of blockading the city and claims that Ukrainian drones attack convoys carrying humanitarian aid.
Kseniia Arkhipova recalls:
In May and June, people in Oleshky still had supplies, then the harvest came in from their gardens: grapes, tomatoes, potatoes, zucchini. But the supplies ran out, and people started sounding the alarm — there’s no food. Mothers write to me: “Ksyusha, my child has nothing to eat, what do I do? He’s hungry all the time.” It’s like 1933 all over again, “wonderful Russian culture” in all its glory.
Kseniia is referring to the Holodomor, which killed nearly 4 million residents of the Ukrainian SSR. Ukraine’s official position, backed by 29 countries (Russia is not among them), holds that the Holodomor was a deliberate genocide of the Ukrainian people by the Soviet government.
Mykyta says that, just as in Soviet times, Ukrainians are dying of hunger because of Russia: “It doesn’t fit in my head that something like this could happen in this day and age. This is an actual Holodomor.”
In July, the occupation authorities in the Kherson region denied there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they had acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, and that utility crews weren’t making repairs because of the shelling.
On September 21, Putin’s press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, called the situation in the Russian-occupied city “critical.” “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to hinder deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops continue working to resolve the situation,” he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also addressed the crisis in Oleshky. In one of his evening addresses in May, he said: “The situation specifically in this part of the occupied territory is extremely difficult, and it’s very hard to carry out evacuations. It’s important that international organizations — everyone able to help with this — are engaged and take decisive action.”
‘Oleshky is closed off on all sides’
Residents of Oleshky have very few ways to get food: Ukrainian authorities say the city is under a complete blockade.
Tetiana Hasanenko, who heads the Oleshky city military administration from Ukrainian-controlled territory, said in comments to Ukrainska Pravda that Russian troops have mined every route out of Oleshky:
People have two options: either die from starvation, or come under drone or artillery fire and be killed. There is no third option.
At the same time, Yevhen Voronetskyi, a serviceman with the 34th Independent Marine Brigade “Borysfen” of the Ukrainian armed forces, told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukrainian troops have mined some routes out of Oleshky to prevent Russian forces from bringing in weapons. Voronetskyi said Ukraine’s military keeps the main road out of the city clear so civilians can leave, even helping people make their way along it and sometimes guiding them with drones along a relatively safe route.
In 2023, Russian forces mined the fields around the city out of fear of a Ukrainian military landing on the left bank of the Dnipro. There is no confirmation that the Russian army has continued mining the main roads around Oleshky. Each side blames the other.
Petro Andryushchenko, a former adviser to the mayor of Mariupol who now heads the Center for Occupation Studies, said in an interview with the Ukrainian outlet NV that Russian forces are using the city’s residents as human shields: “This is a real humanitarian catastrophe, and one created entirely by the Russians as cover for military operations.”
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on June 25 that “thousands of civilians trapped in frontline communities in southern Ukraine are facing a deepening humanitarian crisis.”
Oleshky became a front-line city in the fall of 2022, when the Russian army, under pressure from Ukrainian forces, retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson. Since then, the occupation authorities say, Ukrainian attacks have hindered their efforts to rebuild Oleshky — including after the 2023 flooding — and to deliver food and medicine to the city.
As FPV drones became more common on the battlefield, Oleshky, like Kherson on the opposite bank, grew increasingly dangerous. The front line runs right between the two cities, along the river, and it takes drones only a few minutes to cross the Dnipro and reach a target.
But drones aren’t the only threat in the city and its surrounding area. The area around the city has been mined so heavily that by early 2026, entering or leaving it had become very difficult. That, said Tetiana Hasanenko, who is trying to stay in touch with the city’s residents, is precisely what led to the sharp deterioration of the situation in Oleshky.
Vegetable gardens in Oleshky have turned into a deadly obstacle course. Neighbors told Mykyta that the plot around his house, which he abandoned in 2022, is “littered with mines,” including antitank mines and “petal” mines.
According to Mykyta, the areas around the city are unsafe too: “The riverbanks were mined, and after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam], the water scattered those mines who knows where.”
“Oleshky is closed off on all sides,” Kseniia Arkhipova sums up. “There are about 1,500 people caught in this trap.” Since the start of the Russian invasion, the city’s population has shrunk nearly 15-fold: according to figures from the Oleshky city military administration, 22,000 people lived in Oleshky before 2022.
Some residents risk their lives to walk to Radensk, a nearby village, in search of food. Like Oleshky, it’s under Russian control. The roughly 20-kilometer (12-mile) route is extremely dangerous: the road is mined, and the open terrain is exposed to drone fire.
Some still manage to get food, which is sold at an improvised market in Oleshky. Mykyta learned the prices there from his mother: “I’m in shock. A sack of potatoes costs 7,000 rubles! A can of sprats costs 1,000 rubles, compared to 60 in Radensk.”
Mykyta says a friend of his mother’s advised her to turn to “some religious people.” He doesn’t know who they are, but he’s heard from his mother that they have more food than many other residents. Through these people, his mother Tamara was able to get “a couple of kilograms of buckwheat, some pasta, canned meat, oil, flour — a little of everything.”
Mykyta has been trying to arrange food deliveries to his mother through charitable organizations in nearby cities, but so far without success.
The Ukrainian military sometimes sends humanitarian cargo into the blockaded city. Since March, Ukrainian forces have used drones capable of carrying up to 10 kilograms (22 pounds) of cargo, dropping boxes of canned meat, flour, crackers, oil, and grains directly onto Oleshky.
But this isn’t regular supply, and not every resident gets a package. “A ten-kilo package is enough for one family for a week. And then what?” Kseniia Arkhipova adds.
On September 27, the Ukrainian military dropped its largest shipment of food into Oleshky to date, delivering about four tons (4.4 tons) of food at roughly 100 pre-selected locations. Arkhipova afterward received many grateful messages from locals, and she shows Meduza one of them: “A huge, huge thank you to the guys. God bless them, a deep bow to them!”
Overnight on October 4, the Ukrainian military carried out another operation delivering four tons (4.4 tons) of humanitarian aid to Oleshky by drone.
‘There were more than 200 people on the lists. But no evacuation ever happened.’
According to figures from Ukrainska Pravda, no evacuation of Oleshky has ever been officially organized in four years of occupation. In the spring, the occupation authorities promised for the first time to move Oleshky residents to safer towns. Hoping that would happen, Arkhipova, the volunteer, began coordinating people in a Telegram chat.
Svitlana, the Oleshky resident who left her blooming garden behind in 2022, followed Arkhipova’s messages in the chat. On March 5, she wrote to a neighbor: “Olechka, the question of evacuating Oleshky residents is being decided at the highest level. They’re compiling lists of people so they know exactly how many buses are needed.”
Kseniia recalls how “everyone hoped the Red Cross would come and evacuate everyone”:
The Russians started urging people: “Come to the hospital, sign up, leave your contact numbers. We need to know how many buses to send you. We need to count you — who’s bedridden, who isn’t.” There were more than 200 people on the lists. But no evacuation ever happened.
Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said, without specifying dates, that Kyiv had agreed on “clear mechanisms” for evacuation with Russia, backed by the International Red Cross. But Russia, he said, has stalled the process: “For a long time now, after the talks that were held, the Russian side has not confirmed its readiness to carry out a humanitarian mission to evacuate people.”
Kseniia Arkhipova said that by believing the rumors about the Red Cross and an organized evacuation, people missed their last real chance to leave: “Most of those 200 people are still in Oleshky. In the end, only 67 risked leaving on foot.”
Volunteers coordinate on-foot evacuations from Oleshky remotely, Kseniia says. They put together a plan based on information residents share with them whenever they manage to get in touch.
The last “window of opportunity” for evacuating on foot opened on September 10 and lasted about two weeks, Arkhipova said. That was when Russian troops cleared mines from a stretch of one of the roads leading out of the city.
The first thing residents do is make their way to nearby Radensk (also occupied by Russia). After making the trip, some are “completely unable to move,” Kseniia continues:
They arrive dirty, emaciated, with nothing. Sometimes they weigh less than 50 kilograms (110 pounds), just skin and bones. No clothes, no shoes, no money — no home. Recently an 87-year-old woman was brought out on a cart. When she saw bread, she took out a handkerchief, wrapped a crust in it, pressed it to her chest and said, “I won’t give it up, this is my bread.”
In Radensk, refugees from Oleshky are housed with volunteers willing to take them in, and “they just rest for a few days,” Kseniia says. Some are put up in empty, nonresidential spaces, like stores. Then those who are able make their way to free Ukrainian territory — through Russia and Europe. About 30 Oleshky residents have left the occupation since the start of September.
The volunteer says that among those who left, everyone who initially didn’t want to evacuate “regrets, without exception, staying stuck for so long.” “I yell at them: ‘I told you to leave a year ago, two years ago, three years ago!’ And they answer: ‘Ksyusha, it’s hard to leave everything behind. You’re young — you just turned around and left. We can’t do that.’”
Among those Arkhipova has helped leave are also refugees who for a long time didn’t believe they were really in danger. She said they decided to evacuate only after someone close to them had been killed.
After being rescued from occupation, Oleshky residents can count on support that Ukraine provides to evacuees and internally displaced persons (IDPs). ”[But] while they fill out the paperwork and wait for that measly 2,000 hryvnias [about 40 euros or 3,800 rubles], what are they supposed to do in the meantime?” Kseniia says.
From time to time, she manages to persuade Ukrainian charitable foundations and Russian antiwar organizations to help refugees from Oleshky.
The “window of opportunity” for evacuation has now closed again, Arkhipova says.
‘These people are in a cage’
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman, is convinced that an evacuation of Oleshky’s residents could realistically be carried out in a single day.
Kseniia agrees:
All that’s needed is to clear the road of mines and send in, roughly speaking, four big buses [into the city]. People will come out on their own, and those who can’t move will be wheeled out on carts. Loading everyone up and driving them out — the whole operation would take three hours! Why isn’t this being done? Because Russia can’t be negotiated with.
In late September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha spoke about the crisis in Oleshky in an address to the UN and the International Red Cross. At Ukraine’s request, the OSCE called on Russia to give international organizations access to Oleshky, supply residents with food and medicine, and allow them to leave the city safely.
Vladimir Saldo, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region, gave an interview to the television channel Vesti on September 28. Asked whether a full evacuation of Oleshky was possible and necessary, he said:
Of course such a possibility exists. But let’s try to understand the residents who are there. Taking them and forcibly removing them right now would probably be wrong and unfair. Those who wanted to leave have already left. There are no restrictions for anyone there.
Saldo then added: “We need to do everything so that they [the local residents] can get everything they need to live there: fuel, food, medicine, communications.”
Two days after Saldo’s interview aired, Kseniia Arkhipova learned that several Oleshky residents had again tried to walk to Radensk for food. She posted a notice in the city chat warning that four people had been injured by landmines along a certain route that day and urging anyone heading to Radensk to avoid that stretch of road:
Regardless of Saldo’s statements, many Oleshky residents genuinely don’t want to, or can’t, get out. For instance, Mykyta’s mother isn’t willing to abandon her home, he says: “She says if she leaves, everything will be looted. ‘And who needs us there [outside our hometown] anyway?’”
Kseniia Arkhipova also described the fear that residents still in Oleshky feel toward looters.
From her conversations with residents, she learned that Russian troops rotated through Oleshky around mid-September: “The ones who came in now are polite — they might come ask for food, [saying] ‘you leave us alone, and we’ll leave you alone,’” Kseniia recounts from her acquaintances’ stories. “But before that there were ones who took everything. Or they’d kick people out of their homes and onto the street because they had solar panels, which meant they had electricity.”
Among those who can’t leave the city are the people Arkhipova calls the “undocumented.” These are Oleshky residents whose Ukrainian passports and other documents were lost in the flooding after the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. They didn’t want to get Russian passports.
Now, to be evacuated from Oleshky, these people need at least some kind of passport: both the occupation authorities and border guards on the way to Ukrainian-controlled territory demand to see documents. Getting a Russian passport without other documents is very difficult: applicants first have to confirm their identity with the occupation authorities.
These bureaucratic hurdles come with additional checks, and the fighting makes moving between offices simply dangerous.
“I have acquaintances who have been trying to restore their documents for three years now,” Arkhipova says. “They have witnesses, they’re going through the courts, they’ve already gone around to every [office]. And they still won’t give them a passport.”
Without documents, Kseniia reasons, it’s impossible to cross any major checkpoint: “Not Novoazovsk, not Chonhar, not Armiansk will let them through. These people are in a cage.”
Kseniia calls other residents who remain in Oleshky the “low-mobility”: bedridden patients and elderly people who can’t be evacuated without special transport and an escort.
On top of that, Kseniia says, there are people in the city who are simply afraid of the filtration procedure at Russian checkpoints. According to Human Rights Watch’s observations, even civilians leaving occupied territory for areas under Ukrainian control often have to go through it — not just those entering Russia.
‘The smell of death is everywhere’
“Those who left after me say Oleshky is simply unrecognizable. The city is gone. There are no stores left, no post office,” Mykyta tells Meduza. “I look at photos myself, and I don’t recognize a lot of the places.”
Kseniia Arkhipova adds that in Oleshky, “people live in an isolated world”: “It’s worse than after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam]. There’s devastation and chaos in Oleshky. There’s no administration, no police. Cars don’t drive around — bicycles are the best you get.”
Arkhipova calls the hospital the “only intact island” in Oleshky. It used to give out food to those who were completely exhausted from malnutrition. But lately the facility “is operating on its last legs: there’s no medicine, no fuel — nothing.”
Mykyta also knows from his mother that there’s a medicine shortage in the city, and he recalls overhearing a Russian soldier say, back when he himself was still in Oleshky: “Why do you need medicine? Consider yourselves already dead.”
Still, Arkhipova says, the hospital can currently provide help: “There are doctors there who worked even before the war, even though they had chances to leave. They said, ‘I’m not going anywhere. What will people do without me?’ Recently an 11-year-old boy stepped on a ‘petal’ mine and lost his leg. If it weren’t for these surgeons, who would have performed the amputation? The child would have simply bled to death.”
The occupation authorities don’t allow burials for people killed in the fighting, the volunteer says. Novaya Gazeta reported that there is “no one to process” deaths in the city, but Arkhipova doubts that’s the real reason for the delay.
She says that people who die of natural causes are still being buried. “They [the occupation authorities] need a forensic medical examination so that a medical examiner will write: ‘These people were killed by the Ukrainian military,’” the volunteer explains. “And they need that so they can later pass that data on to the UN [and blame Ukraine]. That’s the scheme.”
The only way to bury those killed in the fighting, Kseniia says, is “quietly, in the garden.” But that’s dangerous: the occupation authorities consider these “spontaneous burials” illegal. “One girl buried a neighbor who was killed in a shelling attack in his own garden. They dragged her through the courts for two years afterward — had she killed him? They even came and dug up the body,” Arkhipova says. Meduza was unable to reach the Oleshky resident the volunteer describes.
Mykyta, whose father died under occupation, and Svitlana, whose husband, Ihor, also chose to stay in their hometown but then fell ill and died in the hospital, both confirm to Meduza that people who die of natural causes are allowed to be buried. Svitlana says that “by today’s standards” Ihor was buried “like a king.” She was able to send money to acquaintances in Oleshky, and they organized the ceremony.
“They reported everything to me: how they dug the grave, how a priest performed the burial service, how many wreaths they laid, what kind of cross they put up,” Svitlana recounts. “They buried my Ihor in not just one but two plastic bags, which was difficult because bags are in short supply there [at the hospital], and you have to sign for each one.”
Asked why her husband wasn’t buried in a coffin, Svitlana says: “There are no coffins left in Oleshky.” That’s what the acquaintance who organized the funeral told her. Svitlana believes it: there’s no way to bring new coffins into Oleshky, and getting wood from the forest is dangerous — it’s mined and exposed to drone fire.
Mykyta tells Meduza that his mother sometimes mentions acquaintances of hers who have been killed. “In March, a woman was killed — a strike hit a store while she was standing in line. Her husband hasn’t been able to retrieve the body since spring — they won’t give it to him,” Mykyta says, citing one example.
According to Kseniia Arkhipova, the morgue is “a small building not far from the hospital,” where bodies are “just stored.” “A body has been lying in a bag without refrigeration since January. What’s going to be left of it?” Arkhipova adds.
The Insider reported that the refrigerators in the morgue don’t work because there’s no fuel for the hospital generator. Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the city military administration, said the morgue had effectively stopped functioning ever since the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. She said bodies have been stored in the hospital basement in recent months.
Sometimes, Meduza’s sources say, bodies are left lying right out in the street. “Russian [soldiers] lie on the roads for weeks, their own side doesn’t pick them up,” Mykyta says. “Dogs drag the bodies around. For my mother, these are just ordinary moments now — a dog tears off an arm or a leg and runs off.”
Kseniia Arkhipova also tells Meduza that stray dogs in Oleshky feed on human bodies. The Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske also reported that dogs dig up shallow graves in gardens and “drag off pieces of bodies,” while Ukrainska Pravda reported that bodies of not only Russian soldiers but also killed civilians lie in the city’s streets.
In the last days of September, Mykyta spoke with his mother again. Tamara told her son she had gone to see a doctor. “My mother says it’s hard to walk through the hospital,” Mykyta says. “The smell of death is everywhere.”
The Oleshky city military administration responded to Meduza’s request by referring to Tetiana Hasanenko’s previously published interviews. Meduza also sent a request to the occupation administration of the Kherson region but had not received a response at the time this story was published.

US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet Ukrainian negotiators in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9, to present “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the deadlock in efforts to end Russia’s war.
The two-day talks are intended to produce a unified proposal that Washington could subsequently discuss with Moscow, according to Axios, citing US and Ukrainian officials.
