Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One proposal under consideration is a limited ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure and grain shipments. Ukraine has expressed readiness to discuss such an arrangement, while Russia has shown little willingness to accept temporary measures.
“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” a US source told Axios, adding that Washington was attempting to mediate between the sides and develop a common proposal.
Who will attend the Miami talks?
Ukraine will be represented by Kyrylo Budanov, Rustem Umerov, Davyd Arakhamia, and Serhiy Kyslytsya, according to Axios.
Representatives of the White House National Security Council and US Treasury Department are also expected to participate. Washington invited national security advisers from the UK, France, and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the EU.
The meeting’s agenda is expected to include possible security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic recovery plan, and other elements of a potential settlement, Reuters reported.
14-Year-Old Girl Accused of Poisoning, Strangling Ukrainian Soldier on Russian Handler’s Video Call
Earlier on Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met with US President Donald Trump to present the latest American proposals and receive his feedback before the talks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Deputy National Security Adviser Mike Needham reportedly attended that meeting as well.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Kyiv was discussing a possible ceasefire covering energy facilities and grain shipments but avoided predicting whether an agreement could be reached.
“As for what might be realistic or more realistic, I am not ready to say yet,” Zelensky said. “I do not want to say something and then have Russia, as always, do the opposite out of spite. So let’s wait and see.”
Another Moscow trip may follow
Witkoff and Kushner could travel to Moscow later in October for further negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to a source cited by Axios. No date has been confirmed.
The two envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September and have since worked with Russian and Ukrainian representatives on an updated peace initiative.
The Trump administration is seeking to revive trilateral negotiations between the US, Ukraine, and Russia, but no new three-way meeting has been announced.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow agreed with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s assessment that the diplomatic process had reached a stalemate. However, Peskov rejected the idea of temporary or limited ceasefires and said Russia wanted a “comprehensive” settlement.
He also said there was currently no immediate prospect of a summit involving Trump, Zelensky, and Putin.
The Miami meeting will therefore test whether Washington’s new proposals can bridge fundamental differences between Kyiv and Moscow before Witkoff and Kushner potentially return to Russia.

Israeli settlers have planted dozens of Israeli flags at the entrance of a streetside Palestinian cafe in the West Bank, obscuring it from one side in what its owner described as a blatant act of intimidation.

Asia-Pacific Community: More Australians head to China for holidays, business
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:41:59 CST
23:41:59 KST

by Xinhua writer Xiong Wenyuan
MELBOURNE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Michael Bocse was heading to China to serve as best man at a friend's wedding, with plans to hike in the mountains, sample Chinese food and ride high-speed trains.
He and his friends Charlotte and Harriet Fairbairn planned to attend the wedding of an Australian groom and a Chinese bride in Changzhou, in east China's Jiangsu Province, and go hiking in southwest China's Yunnan Province. All three were visiting China for the first time.
Speaking to Xinhua recently at Melbourne Airport, they said visa-free entry had made the arrangements easier, although they would have made the trip anyway.
Their plans reflect growing Australian interest in visiting China. Australian residents made about 744,000 short-term trips to the Chinese mainland in the 2025-26 financial year, up nearly 14 percent from a year earlier, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
The increase outpaced the 3.7-percent rise in short-term overseas travel overall. The Chinese mainland moved from fifth to fourth among Australian residents' overseas destinations.
A representative of Air China's Melbourne office said the airline had expanded capacity on its Melbourne-Beijing route compared with a year earlier and was carrying more passengers, noting that local demand for business, study and leisure travel to China was also rising.
Holders of ordinary Australian passports can visit China visa-free for up to 30 days for tourism, business and other eligible purposes.
Another first-time visitor, Aleksey Trivailo, was heading to Beijing to join family members already traveling in China. An aerospace student at Melbourne's RMIT University, he was looking forward to "getting a feel for the culture" and enjoying Peking duck.
He was also interested in China's aerospace development and the opportunities it might offer in his field.
A spokesperson for the government of Australia's Victoria state said China was one of its most significant international tourism markets, highlighting the cultural connections created by two-way travel.
"Travel helps foster mutual understanding and cultural exchange, while supporting the links that connect Victoria and China," the spokesperson told Xinhua in a written response.
For Australian businessman Sharon Benjamin, China was already a familiar destination.
"Every time I come, I see a big change," he said.
His business develops environmentally friendly household products in Australia and works with Chinese manufacturers on tooling and production. Its products include plates and cups made from recycled or compostable materials.
This time, he hoped to buy machinery in China and import it into Australia. He described China as a "champion in manufacturing" and said visa-free access made it easier to arrange short business trips.
Rhys Roberts, national president of the Australia China Business Council, told Xinhua in a written interview that the council was hearing from more members traveling to China, including some for the first time.
"Visa-free entry has made a real difference, especially for smaller businesses, because it takes cost and lead time out of the trip and makes a short exploratory visit an easy decision," he said.
Roberts said the scale and pace of China's market, and the expectations of its consumers, were hard to appreciate from a distance. He identified premium food and beverages, health and wellness, education and tourism as areas of opportunity for Australian businesses.
"Relationships in China are built in person, and there is no substitute for being in the room," he said. ■

Thai police raid Chabad, Jewish institutions in Bangkok amid ongoing foreign business investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:41:58 UTC
23:41:58 KST

Thai authorities raided three Jewish institutions in Bangkok on Thursday, including the Chabad Bangkok Foundation, a Chabad kindergarten, and the Jewish Association of Thailand, as part of a broader investigation into what officials described as a "network of businesses and assets linked to Israeli nationals" in a country that restricts foreign ownership of businesses.
Thailand's Special Investigation Department (DSI), which operates under the country's Justice Ministry, said the investigation centers on suspicions that Thai nationals were used as nominees "for the purpose of conducting business activities and holding assets in violation of the law."
Rabbi Nechemya Wilhelm, the Chabad emissary in Bangkok, told Walla on Friday that authorities had informed him of plans to inspect foreign institutions operating in Thailand. He said Chabad staff had fully cooperated with investigators.
"We have nothing to hide," Wilhelm emphasized. "We operate strictly in accordance with Thai law, for the benefit of travelers and Jews, and engage in charity and acts of kindness for everyone. Our doors are always open."
"We welcomed them warmly and gave them every document they wanted," he added. "They said they were checking everything, not because they knew something was wrong, but because they had come to inspect."
Wilhelm stressed that the investigation had not disrupted Chabad's activities.
"We are continuing our activities as usual," he noted. "About 500 people are expected to come here this Shabbat, and there is nothing preventing that."
More than 10 investigative and law enforcement agencies participated in the raids, including the police, Revenue Department, Immigration Bureau, Anti-Money Laundering Office, and Lands Department.
Investigators are examining the identities of individuals who control the businesses and their ultimate beneficiaries, as well as funding sources, real estate transactions, company operations, and the Thai citizenship granted to some involved.
Thai Authorities investigate Chabad institutions in Bangkok
The latest operation focused primarily on Chabad-connected institutions. Among approximately 40 foreign workers, authorities identified three Myanmar nationals suspected of working without valid permits and remaining in Thailand illegally. All three are expected to be deported.
At the Chabad kindergarten offices in Bangkok's Bang Rak district, investigators seized documents relating to the registration of nonprofit organizations and companies, donations, membership records, land purchases, construction projects, tax payments, restaurants, hotels, and Chabad house operations.
The DSI said more than 61 companies were registered at the same address, with some listing the same individuals as directors or shareholders.
Wilhelm denied that Chabad had any connection to those companies, explaining that the documents were found at an accountant's office whose owner provides services to numerous businesses.
"It is natural for an accountant to work with other companies," he said. "That does not mean they are our companies or companies connected to us."
During a third raid, at the Jewish Association of Thailand in Bangkok's Khlong Toei district, authorities found two Laotian nationals suspected of working without permits. Legal proceedings were also initiated against their employer.
The Jewish Association of Thailand is a longstanding organization established before Chabad began operating in the country.
Authorities also raided the construction site of Beth Elisheva, Bangkok's oldest synagogue and a center of religious and social life for the city's longstanding Jewish community.
The Jewish Association of Thailand manages the site in the Sukhumvit area, while Chabad oversees religious activities there. A new synagogue is being built to replace the original building, which could no longer accommodate the community's needs and was demolished to make way for a modern structure.
The authorities' statement did not accuse the religious institutions themselves of committing offenses related to financing, property ownership, or business activities. No arrests of Israeli nationals were reported during the operation.
Raids follow investigation into alleged foreign ownership violations
The raids follow an earlier investigation in Thailand's Chonburi province involving a company called Cozy Beach View.
A day before the raids, the DSI announced that the company, an Israeli national serving as one of its directors, and a Thai shareholder had been summoned or charged in a separate case involving alleged violations of Thailand's Foreign Business Act.
Investigators suspect the Thai national helped a foreigner maintain ownership of a business without obtaining the required permits.
Thai authorities emphasized that the country remains open to foreign nationals seeking to invest and conduct business legally. However, they warned that local companies and Thai nominees could not be used to circumvent restrictions on foreign ownership of businesses and property.
Wilhelm reiterated that Chabad welcomed the investigation and remained confident that its activities complied with Thai law.
"They have every right to inspect, and we will be happy for them to check whatever needs to be checked," said Wilhelm.
"We obey the law, we cooperate, and we welcome any inspection, and we are confident they will see that everything is in order," he continued. "We are here for the many Israeli travelers and Jews who find themselves in the city or live here, and our doors are always open, and we are busy with charity and acts of kindness from morning until evening for anyone who needs it."

A casualty of war: Israel's breathtaking historical site remains out of reach after October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:41:54 UTC
23:41:54 KST

It’s one of the most stunning views in the Judean Desert, and maybe in all of the Middle East.
Over the Green Line from Jerusalem, on Road 1 heading toward the Dead Sea, a brown official Tourism Ministry sign beckons with “Wadi Kelt/St. George’s Monastery,” just before the left turn to enter the settlement of Mitzpe Jericho, about six km. east of Ma’aleh Adumim.
Instead of making a right past the checkpoint to enter the settlement, another Tourism Ministry sign directs drivers to the left in the direction of Wadi Kelt, past a number of community structures, including a farm and a brand new country club and outdoor pool, all in Area C of the West Bank (fully under Israeli military and civil control).
The road winds around from west to east for three kilometers until you arrive at a parking area across from an imposing stone archway topped by a cross.
A combination of a hustler’s shuk, a livestock display and a solemn religious trek – done up Middle Eastern style – the parking area outside St. George’s Monastery felt like a Tower of Babel collision of worlds.
Amid buses and minivans filled with tourists and pilgrims parked willy-nilly, Bedouin vendors like Ibrahim, a father of seven, aggressively hawked everything from beaded trinkets to freshly squeezed pomegranate juice (and probably some other things you might have to ask for in hushed tones).
Desert cowboys offer to lead visitors for about NIS 100 (haggling encouraged) down the steep 500 m. decline to the monastery grounds via well-worn donkeys, who were clearly less inclined and motivated than their handlers to make the draining journey.
For those who prefer not to descend to the monastery, there was another much more maneuverable horizontal path winding around the rocky enclave toward a panoramic expanse of the Judean desert overlooking Wadi Kelt.
Across the gorge is the stunning view – a fortress-like series of structures built into the severe rock formations of the Judean Desert, St. George’s Monastery – 4 km. from Jericho along Wadi Kelt – a world-class wonder that has attracted untold visitors, both Jewish and gentile, since Israel took control of the area after the 1967 Six Day War.
It’s the highlight of many tourists’ visit to Israel, according to Jerusalem-based tour guide Hannah Rosenberg. “It’s a magical place. Whenever I would bring a group of tourists to the Dead Sea or Masada, on the way back to Jerusalem, we’d take an unannounced detour and turn off to the lookout,” she said.
“They’d say ‘where are we going? I thought we were going back to Jerusalem.’ And I told them, ‘I have a little surprise.’
“I’d tell them, just walk for one minute and you’ll see what the big deal is. They were always stunned and fascinated. It was the ‘wow’ factor that they would always remember.”
Rosenberg was talking in the past tense because, for the last three years, ever since Oct. 7, the road leading to St. George’s Monastery has been blocked by a Gaza-worthy labyrinth of electronic-arm barriers, codes, and blockages – some erected by Mitzpe Jericho, some by the army.
Whether due to bona fide security concerns about visiting the site, which is also in Area C, or because the residents of Mitzpe Jericho no longer will tolerate an influx of tour buses and unsupervised (Palestinian) motorists driving past their settlement expansion to the west, the upshot is that one of the truly wondrous and breathtaking tourism sites in all of Israel has become inaccessible.
And nobody – from the Mitzpe Jericho residents, to the IDF, to the Tourism Ministry, to the ailing tour guide professionals – seems to be bothered by it.
ST. GEORGE’S Monastery was established in the 5th century by the Egyptian monk John of Thebes (St. John of Choziba), together with five Syrian hermits who were living in caves overlooking Wadi Kelt. The monastery is named after its most famous monk, St. George of Choziba, who lived in the 6th century.
At the time, it was common for monks to abandon worldly distractions and travel into the Judean Desert, where they would live in isolation in the caves of Wadi Kelt. In fact, the word “monastery” comes from the Greek, meaning “dwell alone.”
According to the site Historical Sites in Israel, in 1878, more than a thousand years after the destruction of the monastery by the Persians in 614 CE, a Greek monk devoted himself to restoring the monastery, which was completed in 1901. Later, in the 1950s, a bell tower was added.
The monastery’s location in Wadi Kelt makes it an attractive destination not only for hikers and tourists but also for its religious significance. It is thought to be the Biblical Valley of the Shadow, and it lies parallel to the old Roman road to Jericho, where the parable of the Good Samaritan was set.
The monastery complex was built on a long, narrow rock ledge on the northern bank of the wadi. Today, the monastery is divided into three main levels: the upper level, where an ancient cave is located. The middle level, where most of the residential buildings, churches, and the bell tower are located. The lower level, built of arches and containing the monastery’s storerooms and monks’ graves. There are also hermitages in the cliffs where the monks are secluded.
The churches are rich with religious paintings, icons, and mosaics. There are also reputed to be the bones of the monks massacred by the Persians in 614 CE. The crypt also holds the remains of the original five Syrian hermits who established the monastery with John of Thebes.
Estimates are that today there are between five and 10 monks living at the monastery. In 2001, during the Second Intifada, Father Georgios Tsibouktzakis (also known as Father Germanos), a Greek Orthodox monk and abbot at St. George’s, was shot and killed by a Palestinian terrorist in a drive-by shooting on the Jerusalem-Ma’aleh Adumim road. He was the only terror fatality on that road during the entire uprising.
Walking around the grounds is enchanting and other-worldly, like one was transported to the 14th-century set of The Name of the Rose. There’s barely an indication of any nods to modernity.
During an open house visit to the monastery six years ago, a monk explained to this reporter over a cup of tea that most of his brethren were Greek and Romanian. They lived under a rotation method that swapped them out of the isolated Spartan lifestyle every six months.
When asked where they procured supplies for the rugged location, he put down his teacup and matter-of-factly said, “Rami Levy.”
He said that the monks enjoyed the visits from the public, but also cherished their silence and isolation at the cliffside monastery. However, in recent years, those visits have shriveled to zero, and the isolation has increased.
The monastery is open to the public daily, except Sundays
TODAY, THE monastery is generally open to the public daily, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., except on Sundays. Entrance is free, and modest clothing is mandatory – no shorts for men, and women must cover their legs and shoulders.
However, attempts to get to the monastery and lookout are an exercise in futility and one – literally and figuratively – filled with potholes.
One roadblock directs you to a phone number that then directs you to a rocky dirt road some 5 km. away. There, you can drive the treacherous route for 20 minutes to circumvent the roadblock, only to be met with another electronic arm and a sign saying “This road is dangerous. It leads to Area A. No entrance without coordination of the IDF.”
In an attempt to learn who is responsible for the electronic roadblocks and the less-than-user-friendly alternate route that leads to a dead end, The Jerusalem Post reached out to Mitzpe Jericho, the IDF, the Tourism Ministry, and local residents.
In response to an email query from the Post about the electronic arms inside the settlement, Mitzpe Jericho’s local council head Aliza Pilichowski wrote: ”I don’t feel comfortable in my role as mayor talking to the press. I also have not set up anyone else to talk to the press.” Talk about a dead end.
A Mitzpe Jericho security official told the Post that the electronic arm was a necessity to prevent possible terror attacks on the road, which has been built up by the settlement in recent years. Open access by Palestinians driving past settlement businesses, farms, and the country club increases the likelihood of attack, he said.
Tour guide and Mitzpe Jericho resident Mordechai Weiss said that immediately after the Hamas-led massacres in Israel on Oct. 7, and in the subsequent month, there was a permanent IDF position where the electronic arm is now.
“It’s the way things have evolved leading to today’s barriers. It’s part of a whole new mindset,” said Weiss, who made aliyah from the US in 2003.
He explained that the monastery road had been the original road for travelers driving between Jerusalem and Jericho before Road 1 was built – for Palestinians and Israelis alike.
“At certain times before Oct. 7, there were mounds of dirt at the end of the monastery parking area preventing drivers from continuing into Jericho [and Area A, under the Palestinian Authority’s control], but other times there weren’t. It always depended on the security situation,” he said.
Ironically, with the road being closed to vehicles to get to the monastery, there’s no prohibition or barriers preventing hikers from trekking the 3 km. to the site via Wadi Kelt, provided they can reach the entrance either by walking from Mitzpe Jericho or taking the arduous Good Samaritan bypass road.
Wadi Kelt, which connects west to Ein Maboa below Alon and Ein Prat near Anatot, has long been a prime hiking destination, with lush growth and plenty of water holes.
However, its appeal was permanently marred in 1993, shortly after the onset of the Oslo Accords, when Palestinian terrorists shot and stabbed to death two Israeli hikers, Dror Forer and Aran Bachar. The echoes of the brutal murders have continued to resonate in the canyon and beyond ever since.
“Security has always been an issue in the area. When I moved to Mitzpe Jericho in 2003, there were still horror stories about the terror attack that happened 10 years before,” said Weiss. “But that never prevented people from hiking or going to St. George’s. That all changed since Oct. 7.”
A military representative familiar with the area dismissed the difficulties in reaching the area.
“Of course there’s free access to everyone; it’s a tourist site, and the army won’t prevent people from going to a tourist site,” he said. “There is the issue of the gates along the way, but those can always be opened with the proper coordination.”
According to tour guide Rosenberg, who is often in touch with the army when entering sensitive areas around the country, it’s not that easy post-Oct. 7.
“I’ve tried gaining access to the site following all the protocols, yet have never been able to reach the right number to coordinate a trip,” she said.
Even a reporter from The Jerusalem Post, with the paper’s military correspondent assisting with contacts deep inside the IDF, had to make numerous queries via various military bodies to reach a number to coordinate a visit.
When asked why the electronic arm had been erected along with the red warning sign at the entrance to the monastery road, the IDF Spokesman’s Office erroneously said that the monastery was in Area A, and then clarified that even if a location is in Area C but leads to Area A, visits must be coordinated with the IDF – an idiosyncratic change in policy since Oct. 7.
A spokesperson for the Tourism Ministry said the ministry doesn’t get involved with locations deemed as security risks by the military.
When asked why the prominent signage was still on the road directing drivers to the inaccessible area three years after it was closed, the spokesman said that plans were underway to cover them up.
Weiss downplayed the lack of access to St. George’s, saying that because of the drastic drop in tourism since Oct. 7, it hasn’t really been an issue.
“If there were a return to somewhat good old days and the demand returned, I assume there would be efforts to reopen it or for tour guides to find a way to get clearance. But I understand and appreciate the security risks,” said Weiss.
“The reality is that today, local tourists who come to the area now go to Café Al HaKatze on the edge of the desert in Mitzpe Jericho. You can’t see the monastery from there, but it’s an amazing view.”
IDF opens up travel with advance coordination
DURING HOL HAMOED Sukkot last month, the IDF, with a huge presence every couple hundred meters, opened up the roads and arms to organized groups – allowing groups who coordinated in advance to travel on the road to St. Georges and, then continuing to the outskirts of Jericho – still considered Area C and home to an impressive archaeological site, the Hasmonean Palaces, and the final palace built by King Herod.
Stopping at the monastery lookout, the vendors and the donkeys are gone, but the site remains pristine. And the view is as breathtaking as ever.
It seems that nobody is invested in changing the post-Oct. 7 status quo of keeping the road closed and denying everyone access to the exquisite location.
Are the security risks still there? Does it not suit Mitzpe Jericho’s interests to be a conduit to the site? Will the Tourism Ministry ever cover up or remove the misleading signage?
If there were a desire or a demand to reopen the road to the monastery, it seems like it could be done. Keeping it inaccessible doesn’t make any sense, according to Yisca Harani, a scholar of Christianity, tour guide, and lecturer, who has brought countless pilgrims to the site in the past.
“It is totally unacceptable,” she said, adding that the site is one of the most breathtaking and significant in all of Israel.
Keeping it behind gates exposes a certain inconsistency in the policy. Even as the road heading toward the lookout and the monastery is barricaded, the hiking path down below in Wadi Kelt is open.
If, as the red sign at the gate to the road entrance claims, the road is a security risk because it leads to Area A and Jericho, then erect an official barrier at the far end of the monastery parking area that prevents that passage. It would ostensibly take away the risk and block the contiguity between the monastery and Jericho.
But in the delicate disputed areas of the West Bank, and the power struggle chess match continually taking place between settlements, the IDF, the PA, and the Bedouin, change is painstaking.
St. George’s Monastery is a microcosm of that overlapping alphabet soup reality where security, tourism, settlements, and land intersect.
It’s a complex and historic area where the army is confused between Areas A and C; where a world-class tourism site is hidden behind barriers that serve the interests of real or perceived security needs and the natural growth of settlement communities; and where those tasked with the challenge of rebranding Israel as a tourist destination in some far-off, hoped-for era of stability don’t realize that there’s a treasure right in front of them that has become impossible to visit.■

Italy and Switzerland still contest Crans-Montana fire victim bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:41:33 UTC
23:41:33 KST

Italy and Switzerland still contest Crans-Montana fire victim bill
More than nine months after the Crans Montana fire tragedy, the Swiss government still doesn't know how to settle the bill for the medical care provided to the Italian victims – which amounts to CHF1.5 million, Swiss public broadcaster RTS has learned.
Italy continues to refuse to pay this sum, contrary to international agreements on the matter.
On January 1, Umberto Marcucci’s son, Manfredi – severely burned on his back, hands, and arms – was initially admitted to the intensive care unit at the hospital in Sion. He remained there for 15 hours before being airlifted to Milan.
More
Crans-Montana blaze exposes cracks in Switzerland’s image
In April, the Italian national received a copy of the bill sent by Switzerland to the Italian social security system of CHF66,800 francs. The sum that shocked Marcucci. “If I break my leg on a ski slope, it’s only fair that the Italian system reimburses me, but if I hurt myself in a bar due to someone’s negligence, and probably someone from the municipality or canton, then the very least Switzerland could do is suspend its reimbursement request until responsibility is established,” he told RTS.
Solution promised
In total, 12 Italian victims were treated in Swiss hospitals after the fire, for varying lengths of time. According to RTS, the total cost of their care is around CHF1.5 million.
This bill has sparked controversy. The Italian government stated as early as April that it would not cover these costs. However, an agreement between European countries stipulates that when someone receives treatment abroad, the costs are borne by the patient’s country of residence.
In early May, Swiss president Guy Parmelin promised a solution after a meeting with Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni. However, nine months after the tragedy, the Federal Council still doesn’t seem to have found a way.
The issue is sensitive. Switzerland has already released CHF35 million for the victims of the fire that claimed 41 lives and injured 115 people. The canton of Valais has released more than CHF2.3 million. The Beloved Foundation, funded in part by Valais, already has a budget of CHF24 million.
Opinion divided
Swiss Green Liberal parliamentarian Céline Weber is calling on the Federal Council to stand firm. “These agreements don’t just apply in good times, but also when, unfortunately, there are problems. And I expect Italy to respect the agreements that have been signed with Switzerland,” she said.
But Social Democrat Laurence Fehlmann Rielle is encouraging the government to forgive and forget. “Switzerland should make a gesture and take responsibility for the victims, given that the situation was particularly serious,” she said. The Federal Council is expected to decide soon.
Manfredi will be celebrating his 17th birthday in a few days. He will soon undergo another hand operation to try and regain more flexibility. But it is already known that the young man will no longer be able to play the guitar, one of his hobbies before the accident.

BRATISLAVA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia's trade balance swung to a deficit of 125 million euros (139.9 million U.S. dollars) in August, ending six consecutive months of trade surpluses, according to preliminary data released by the Slovak Statistics Office on Friday.
Slovakia's exports rose 5.4 percent year-on-year to 8.3 billion euros (9.29 billion dollars) in August, while imports increased 7 percent to 8.4 billion euros (9.40 billion dollars), the data showed. The country recorded a trade surplus of 2.3 million euros (2.6 million dollars) in August 2025.
Machinery and transport equipment remained the country's largest traded commodity category, accounting for nearly 57 percent of total exports and 47 percent of total imports.
Other European Union (EU) member states accounted for nearly 81 percent of Slovakia's exports in August, while imports from these countries made up about 64 percent of the total.
Exports to other EU member states increased by more than 8 percent year-on-year, while imports from the bloc rose over 11 percent. In contrast, exports to non-EU countries fell 6 percent, while imports from those countries edged up 0.1 percent.
The country posted a trade surplus of 1.5 billion euros (1.68 billion dollars) in the first eight months of 2026, unchanged from the same period a year earlier, according to the Statistics Office. ■

Verstappen takes F1 Singapore Sprint pole as Mercedes upgrade doubts persist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:41:18 CST
23:41:18 KST

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SINGAPORE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Max Verstappen claimed pole position for Saturday's Sprint race at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix, edging George Russell and Charles Leclerc in a closely contested qualifying session on Friday.
Fresh from his first victory of the season at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Verstappen continued his resurgence with a fastest lap of 1 minute, 31.156 seconds, beating Russell by 0.120 seconds, with Leclerc a further 0.123 seconds adrift.
However, the Red Bull driver faces an investigation for overtaking Lewis Hamilton under yellow flags during the opening qualifying session, potentially putting his pole position at risk.
"It's always close here in Singapore," Verstappen said. "You're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places."
"Once we bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more, but I did not expect this. Of course, I'm very happy to be first."
Verstappen acknowledged that Singapore's tight, twisting Marina Bay circuit continued to expose weaknesses in his Red Bull despite the team's improved form.
"I think the last few races we have been a lot stronger, but this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car, but we manage to drive with them as well as possible," he said.
Russell's second place offered encouragement for Mercedes, which has struggled to extract the expected performance from an aerodynamic upgrade introduced in Malaysia.
The Briton reverted to an older specification of the car for Singapore, while teammate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli continued with the newer package, allowing Mercedes to compare their performance directly.
Russell qualified five places ahead of Antonelli, who was seventh, raising further questions about the effectiveness of the upgrade, though the difference in specification alone does not establish whether the new parts are responsible.
Russell will start Sunday's main Grand Prix from the back of the grid after exceeding his permitted allocation of power unit components following an engine failure while running third in Malaysia.
Behind the leading trio, Oscar Piastri qualified fourth for McLaren, ahead of teammate Lando Norris, with Hamilton sixth for Ferrari. Liam Lawson, Isack Hadjar and Pierre Gasly completed the top 10.
Hadjar had a faster lap deleted for exceeding track limits, leaving him ninth.
The session was disrupted twice, first when Sergio Perez struck the barriers in the opening segment and damaged his front wing. Although the Mexican managed to continue, debris from his car subsequently prompted a red flag with just over six minutes remaining.
Perez was among six drivers eliminated in SQ1, along with Arvid Lindblad, Lance Stroll, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Carlos Sainz.
The second segment was delayed by approximately 10 minutes because of a timing system malfunction that initially prevented some lap times, including Gabriel Bortoleto's, from being registered.
"The start of SQ2 will be delayed due to an issue with timing systems, some lap times had not been registered," the FIA said in a statement, before confirming that the results had been corrected and the session could resume.
The disruption followed a separate software problem at last weekend's race in Malaysia, where a glitch in F1's wet-weather power unit software caused several cars to lose power during the formation laps, forcing the race start to be aborted while the FIA issued a software fix.
Leclerc topped SQ2 with a time of 1:32.246, ahead of Hamilton, while Russell survived a heavy lockup to progress to the final segment.
Franco Colapinto, Nico Hulkenberg, Oliver Bearman, Bortoleto, Fernando Alonso and Esteban Ocon were eliminated.
Singapore is hosting a Sprint weekend for the first time, with the shorter race offering a maximum of eight championship points before qualifying for Sunday's Grand Prix later on Saturday.
Overtaking opportunities are expected to be limited on the narrow street circuit, placing particular importance on grid position. With no mandatory pit stops in the Sprint, drivers will have fewer strategic opportunities to gain places.
For Antonelli, who leads the championship, the reduced points available and the proximity of Grand Prix qualifying may encourage a conservative approach rather than risking an incident in pursuit of minor gains.
Singapore has also historically proved an unpredictable venue for Formula 1's dominant teams. In 2023, it was the only race Red Bull failed to win, while Mercedes struggled at Marina Bay in 2015 despite dominating much of that season.
Friday's result suggests the circuit could once again upset the established competitive order, with Verstappen's recent resurgence and Mercedes' contrasting car specifications adding intrigue ahead of Saturday's Sprint. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of military aggression against its territory, calling for urgent United Nations (UN) intervention amid escalating diplomatic tensions.
Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos made the remarks while briefing visiting UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed on Eritrea's "continued aggression" against Ethiopia and its implications for regional peace and security, the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement issued late Thursday.
Emphasizing the urgent need for a clear and principled UN response to the situation, Timothewos also demanded "the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean forces from Ethiopian territory."
The Ethiopian foreign minister further highlighted the East African country's "right to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity" in accordance with international law.
In a separate statement, Ethiopia's State Minister of Foreign Affairs Berhanu Tsegaye also highlighted the deteriorating situation along the shared frontier, specifically pointing to Eritrea's "continued aggression and direct military involvement across different fronts along the border."
He emphasized that addressing this "unprovoked aggression is critical to preserving regional stability, safeguarding ongoing peace efforts, and ensuring accountability across the Horn of Africa."
Ethiopia's accusations follow a rapid breakdown in diplomatic relations between the two Horn of Africa countries, amid growing allegations by Ethiopian officials that Asmara is supporting Ethiopian armed rebel groups.
Earlier this month, Ethiopia announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara, the Eritrean capital, "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."
Ethiopia also expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats for "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security in breach of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations," prompting Eritrea to announce a complete severance of bilateral ties.
Rejecting the allegations, Eritrea accused Ethiopia of "pursuing an agenda of incessant hostility" and claimed Ethiopia provides weapons and support "to an assortment of Eritrean armed opposition groups" to stoke internal conflict aimed at achieving regime change.
Experts and political analysts attribute the political friction to the continued intense clashes in Ethiopia's Tigray region, pitting the Ethiopian National Defense Force and its allied forces against troops loyal to the Tigray People's Liberation Front and its allied armed groups.
This military escalation unfolds against the backdrop of the devastating two-year war from November 2020 to November 2022, which caused a massive humanitarian crisis before being formally halted by the Pretoria peace accord in South Africa.
As Ethiopian federal forces expand control in Tigray, after capturing the regional capital Mekelle, analysts are raising alarms about a dangerous spillover across the region. ■

Kenya, China hold photo exhibition to promote wildlife conservation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:41:12 CST
23:41:12 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- An international photography exhibition and charity event was held on Thursday in Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, to promote the conservation of iconic wildlife species in their natural habitats.
The event was jointly organized by the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS), the Kenya Chinese Youth Association, and a Chinese delegation of wildlife photographers specializing in ecological photography.
Erustus Kanga, director general of the KWS, said Kenya and China have a long-standing relationship and are committed to protecting wildlife heritage and ecological health for the benefit of local communities.
Kanga praised Chinese wildlife photographers for using images to tell stories about Kenya's natural heritage and inspire people worldwide to conserve threatened species.
"Wildlife photography is a powerful language. A simple image can cross borders, cultures and generations, inspiring people who may never have visited a national park to understand wildlife and why it should be protected," Kanga said in a speech read on his behalf by Gladys Kosgei, the KWS director in charge of planning, partnerships and enterprise.
Kanga said Kenya has strengthened cooperation with China in protecting wildlife across diverse landscapes, including savannah grasslands, forests, mountains, wetlands and marine ecosystems.
"As you return to China, I urge you to become ambassadors for Kenya's conservation story. Share what you have seen, what you have learned and what you have experienced. Encourage others to visit Kenya and support conservation," Kanga told the Chinese wildlife photographers.
Justina Yang, president of the Kenya Chinese Youth Association, said wildlife conservation had become an integral part of the China-Kenya friendship, which has flourished based on mutual trust.
Yang said Chinese nationals living in Kenya had supported local wildlife conservation activities, with renowned Chinese wildlife photographers regularly visiting national parks to capture images of iconic species in their natural habitats.
Xiao Ge, a Chinese wildlife photographer, said he was excited to visit Kenya and use his camera to capture and document the country's iconic landscapes, wildlife and people.
Over the years, Xiao noted, Chinese photographers and nature enthusiasts have traveled to Africa, using images to highlight the continent's natural beauty and inspire people on both sides to protect wildlife as a shared heritage. ■

NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Friday invoked the iconic “Jo darr gaya” (one who gets scared) dialogue from the 1975 blockbuster "Sholay" to target the government, as opposition parties continued their protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Kharge was referring to the sweeping restrictions imposed by the Delhi Police ahead of Saturday’s planned protest by youth pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other student organisations, which are demanding the removal or resignation of Kumar.Speaking to reporters in the Parliament House complex ahead of the opposition’s march to Rashtrapati Bhavan to meet President Droupadi Murmu over the issue, Kharge remarked, “They (the government) are scared. ‘Aur jo aadmi darta hai vo aaj nahi toh kal marta hai’ (a person who is scared will die, if not today then tomorrow).”His remark was an apparent reference to the iconic dialogue delivered by dacoit Gabbar Singh, the main antagonist played by Amjad Khan in the film.
Kharge also claimed that the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had openly stated that CEC Kumar had made a “mistake”.“Both commissioners themselves said that we raised objections several times and explained to Gyanesh Kumar, but he did not agree.
Despite the objections of the two election commissioners, the Modi government is not ready to remove Gyanesh Kumar from his post,” he added, referring to a media report that triggered the ongoing controversy.Describing Kumar as a “small fish”, Kharge alleged that he had the backing of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah.“Gyanesh Kumar is a small fish, but behind him are (Narendra) Modi-(Amit) Shah and their government. The Modi government wants all rights to be stripped away and dictatorship to be imposed. If dictatorship comes, democracy will end, which will also wipe out the Constitution and all rights. We are fighting for the sake of democracy, the constitution, and the people's interests,” Kharge stated.(With PTI inputs)
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Shi takes early lead at Women's China Open
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
22:41:06 CST
23:41:06 KST

SHANGHAI, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- A birdie on her final hole proved the difference for Shi Yuli on Friday, as the Beijing veteran carded a four-under 68 to take a one-stroke lead during first-round play of the 17th edition of the Women's China Open.
Playing on the links-style Yangtze Dunes layout at PGA Anying Golf Club on Shanghai's Chongming Island, veterans Cai Danlin and Sui Xiang were one shot back at the RMB1 million CLPG Tour event as each carded rounds of three-under 69 in the sunny and warm conditions.
Ren Yijia, the CLPG Tour points ranking leader, was two shots off the pace after a 70, tied for equal fourth with Chen Yulin and Thailand's Ornnicha Konsunthea. China's top amateur Liu Yuji, the World No. 16, was a shot further back in a group of eight players on one-under 71.
Shi, who captured her maiden win last year at the season-ending CLPG Tour Championship, got off to a strong start when she made birdie at her first hole, the 423-yard 10th hole, after beginning her round on the Yangtze Dunes' back nine. She would be in and around the lead throughout her afternoon round, carding five more birdies and two bogeys.
"I felt pretty good today. My driver was very consistent, and my approach shots were generally quite close to the pin, which gave me plenty of birdie opportunities. Two of my birdies came from putts of about a yard and a half," said Shi, the inaugural winner of last year's CLPG Tour points ranking.
"The course is playing at 6,704 yards this year, so the extra distance could make things a little more challenging for me. I'll probably need to use my long irons more often. I played pretty well here the last two times, so I'm looking forward to the week. The China Women's Open is a national-level championship, so winning a tournament of this stature would mean a lot to me." ■

In Russia, Missile Systems Research Institute and Center for Elimination of Ballistic Missiles Have Been Struck — General Staff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:41:06 UTC
23:41:06 KST

The Ukrainian Armed Forces struck the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region.
This was reported on October 9 by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on its Facebook page.
The facility near the village of Dalne Konstantinovo-5 belongs to the V. P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes—a subsidiary of JSC Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Operation Center Facilities (TsENKI).
The company is engaged in the development and production of launch and technical complexes, refueling equipment, as well as ground-, air-, and sea-based missile and space complexes. This is stated on their official website.
Another facility reported as having been destroyed by the General Staff was the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center near the village of Surovatikha in the same region.
The center is involved in the disposal of missile weapons, as well as the production, preparation, storage, and transportation of rocket fuel. In addition, the facility maintains and repairs missile delivery systems.
The General Staff noted that the strike on this facility was aimed at weakening the Russian military-industrial complex’s capabilities to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
Gleb Nikitin, governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, confirmed the nighttime drone attack on the region. According to him, infrastructure facilities were damaged by falling debris, but he described the damage as minor.
The Russian official also reported the death of a serviceman from the Bars-NN unit, who had participated in repelling the attack alongside forces from the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation and the National Guard of Russia.
According to reports from the Russian monitoring resource UAV Russia, drones were detected in several districts of the Nizhny Novgorod region on the night of October 9, specifically in the Sosnovsky and Kulebatsky districts. The threat was declared neutralized at 06:39.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on October 9, Ukrainian drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant in Russia’s Tver region, which manufactures rocket fuel components.
The TsENKI is a Russian organization responsible for operating the ground-based infrastructure of the rocket and space industry. Its structure includes enterprises that develop launch complexes, work with rocket fuel components, and maintain the relevant equipment.
The Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes was established in 2010 through the merger of two design bureaus. Its predecessors participated in the creation of launch infrastructure for the Soviet R-7 intercontinental ballistic missile and rocket and space complexes.
The Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center in the village of Surovatikha was established in 1993 on the basis of a missile neutralization and dismantlement station. Initially, its activities were related to the implementation of agreements on the reduction of strategic offensive weapons between Russia and the United States.
In 2009, the center became part of the JSC Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Operation Center Facilities (TsENKI). The organization’s 2018 report noted that, during the facility’s operation, 448 intercontinental ballistic missiles had been dismantled, and its activities also included work to extend the service life of missile systems.

China’s multilateral development funding rises tenfold since 2010: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:40:37 UTC
23:40:37 KST

Faisal Mahmud
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
China’s funding for multilateral development institutions has increased more than tenfold since 2010, though Beijing remains far behind European donors in financing international development, a study showed Thursday.
China’s contributions exceeded $3 billion in 2024, reflecting its expanding role in global financial institutions, according to the Washington-based Center for Global Development.
The European Union and its member states, however, remain the world’s largest collective providers of official development assistance, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
European Union institutions alone provided $6.4 billion to multilateral organizations in 2024, although that figure covers a broader category of development financing.
The study found that China has increasingly directed its contributions toward development banks rather than UN agencies and specialized funds.
Chinese financial platform Sina Finance also reported the findings, highlighting Beijing’s growing commitments despite its limited influence within multilateral institutions.
China pledged $1.5 billion to the World Bank’s International Development Association, becoming its fifth-largest donor, while its multilateral climate financing reached about $5.3 billion in 2025.
Despite those contributions, China holds about 6% of voting shares at the World Bank, less than half the proportion suggested by its share of the global economy.
Western countries have resisted changes to voting structures that would give Beijing greater influence.
The findings come as traditional Western donors face growing pressure to maintain development assistance amid tightening budgets and rising international financing needs.

Italian opposition hail Nobel Peace Prize for Pillay
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:40:22 CEST
23:40:22 KST

Italy's centre-left opposition on
Friday hailed the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to South African
human rights activist and jurist Navi Pillay and urged Premier
Giorgia Meloni to further condemn Israel's actions in Gaza,
which Pillay branded "genocide" last year.
                                    
The 5-Star Movement (M5S) said "we're sorry for Giorgia Meloni
who wanted to give the peace prize to Trump and for (Foreign
Minister Antonio) Tajani for whom international law only applies
'up to a certain point' (referring to the way Israel stopped the
Global Sumud Flotilla for Gaza, ed.), but this award presented
to jurist Navi Pillay is a vitally important recognition of the
role played by the United Nations and international justice
institutions—such as the ICC, against which Tajani has even
called for an investigation—in fearlessly exposing and
prosecuting criminals, no matter how powerful they may be; this
is precisely what Pillay did by acknowledging the 'genocide' in
Gaza and gathering thousands of pieces of evidence against
Netanyahu and Israel's military leadership."
Green-Left Alliance (AVS) co-leader Angelo Bonelli said "the
Nobel Prize awarded to Pillay honors a life dedicated to
international law, precisely at a time when international
justice is under attack.
                                    
"Criticizing a government is not antisemitism—which must always
be fought firmly.
                                    
"Invoking Nazism against those demanding justice for Gaza helps
neither Israel nor this cause.
                                    
"We call on the Meloni government and Minister Tajani to
distance themselves from (Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon)
Sa'ar's remarks. Yet we already know they will not do so: the
Meloni government will remain silent, just as it has throughout
these years, complicit in the face of the Netanyahu government's
crimes."
The Israeli foreign ministry said earlier that Nazi propaganda
chief Joseph Goebbels would be "applauding from Hell" the award
to Pillay, former head of the Rwanda genocide panel and chair of
last year's UN-commissioned commission of inquiry into Tel
Aviv's actions in the occupied Palestinian territories.
                                    
"Awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Pillay is not an act of
justice, but the grotesque exploitation of an honor to
legitimize hatred and prejudice against Israel," said the
ministry.
                                    
"Now that the Nobel committee has rewarded the greatest lie of
the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is surely applauding from
hell," the ministry stated.
                                    
"If there were a prize for lies, hatred, and defamatory
accusations, Pillay would be the clear favorite. Her role in the
relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and in
promoting allegations of genocide speaks for itself."
Meloni this week renewed her government's commitment to fighting
antisemitism in a message marking the third anniversary of the
"barbaric and horrific" October 7 attacks by Hamas on Israel.
                                    
She added:
"Precisely in the name of protecting the whole civilian
population involved, we cannot remain indifferent to the
dramatic, unacceptable suffering of the people of Gaza or the
escalating violence to which Palestinian civilians in the West
Bank are subjected.
                                    
"This spiral of violence must be broken."

Explainer: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:39:33 UTC
23:39:33 KST

Explainer: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
Oct 9 - The U.S. military plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting.
If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution.
Executions are generally conducted behind prison walls, and internet platforms and governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage.
HAS A LAWFUL EXECUTION EVER BEEN LIVESTREAMED OR BROADCAST TO THE PUBLIC BEFORE?
Death penalty experts consulted by Reuters said they were unaware of any previous lawful execution that had been livestreamed or broadcast to a public audience.
Execution footage has occasionally emerged after the event. The hanging of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein in 2006, for example, was seen around the world after official and unofficial recordings circulated online and through broadcasters, though it was not shown live.
Broadcasts and livestreams today are common for court proceedings, parliamentary debates and other state functions, but not for judicial executions.
HOW UNUSUAL IS THIS COMPARED WITH MODERN EXECUTION PRACTICES AROUND THE WORLD?
Public executions have become rare worldwide, with most countries that retain the death penalty carrying out executions away from public view.
According to Amnesty International, public executions recorded in recent years have largely been concentrated in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan.
The execution would also be notable in the United States. Public executions largely disappeared during the 20th century, and death penalty experts cited by Reuters said the last legally sanctioned public execution took place in 1936.
Hasan's execution would be the first carried out by firing squad by the U.S. military since the 1945 execution of Eddie Slovik, who was convicted of desertion during World War Two.
HOW HAS THE INTERNET CHANGED THE CIRCULATION OF EXECUTION FOOTAGE?
The internet has transformed execution imagery from a local event into content capable of reaching global audiences within minutes.
Militant groups such as Islamic State became notorious for producing professionally edited execution videos that were distributed online as propaganda and recruitment tools.
Criminal organisations, including Mexican drug cartels, have also circulated violent footage to intimidate rivals and project power.
The ability of users to rapidly copy, repost and redistribute content has made it more difficult for governments and technology companies to control the spread of such material.
WHAT HAS BEEN THE REACTION FROM GOVERNMENTS AND TECH COMPANIES?
Governments and technology companies have generally moved in the opposite direction, attempting to reduce rather than expand access to graphic execution footage.
Major social media platforms have spent years removing execution videos linked to extremist organisations and other violent groups.
One of the first public governmental reactions came from New Zealand, whose chief censor said authorities would have little practical ability to prevent residents from accessing a livestream while it was taking place.
Livestreams pose particular challenges for platforms because footage can be viewed, copied and redistributed before moderation systems can intervene.
Even countries that still conduct public executions have often restricted filming and broadcast rights. Saudi Arabia historically carried out public executions before spectators, but recording them was prohibited and such public executions had largely ceased by 2019. REUTERS

Ukraine has simplified the mechanism for leasing state-owned premises for providers and data centers — what changes to expect
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:38:50 EEST
23:38:50 KST

Ukraine has simplified the mechanism for leasing state-owned premises for providers and data centers — what changes to expect
Kyiv • UNN
Telecom businesses and data centers will be able to lease premises from state-owned companies without auctions. The simplified rules will apply during martial law and for six months after it.
Ukraine has simplified the leasing of premises belonging to state-owned companies for telecommunications businesses and data centers to enable rapid recovery after attacks. The Ministry of Digital Transformation reports this, citing a government decision, UNN reports.
The enemy is intensifying attacks on data centers and telecommunications infrastructure in an effort to leave Ukrainians without basic necessities. If servers or communications equipment are under threat from Russian strikes, companies have no time for lengthy waits to lease new premises. Telecommunications businesses and data centers can now lease space from state-owned companies through a simplified procedure, the statement says.
What is changing:
1️⃣ Auctions have been canceled. Providers and data center owners can lease state-owned companies’ property without electronic bidding.
2️⃣ Relocation has been accelerated. Equipment can be moved out of harm’s way and deployed at a new location within just a few days.
3️⃣ The rules have been established. The simplified procedure applies for the duration of martial law and for another six months thereafter.
The Ministry of Digital Transformation added that this decision is our investment in the resilience of Ukraine’s digital infrastructure.

More than 40% of Ukrainians may relocate due to worsening winter conditions - survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:38:48 EEST
23:38:48 KST

More than 40% of Ukrainians may relocate due to worsening winter conditions - survey
Kyiv • UNN
According to Gradus, 42% of Ukrainians do not have autonomous heating, backup electricity, or water supplies. Safety is the main reason for a possible relocation.
Over 40% of Ukrainians are considering moving due to deteriorating living conditions during the winter. This is stated in the results of a survey by Gradus, reports UNN.
Details
35% do not plan to change their place of residence even under difficult circumstances. Most respondents still depend on centralized electricity, water, and heating supplies.
42% live in homes without equipment for autonomous heating, electricity supply, or water reserves.
The main factor that could prompt people to move is safety. Those surveyed also cited limited access to medical care, worsening weather conditions, and problems with public transportation and education as factors that could potentially lead to relocation.
In the event of relocation, almost half of those surveyed would consider temporary displacement within Ukraine. This could involve a neighboring settlement or another region. At the same time, one in five allows for the possibility of leaving the country.
Reminder
The Russian Foreign Ministry recommended that foreign citizens and diplomats staying in Kyiv leave the Ukrainian capital and not come to Ukraine at all.

Bab al Mandab cleared of Houthi militia as fighting continues: Saudi envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:38:18 UTC
23:38:18 KST

Saudi Arabia’s ambassador to Yemen has said that the Bab al Mandab Strait had been cleared of Houthi militia, and Yemeni government troops reported continuing fierce clashes around the strategic waterway.
“Blessed Friday, and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia,” Mohammed Al Jaber wrote on X on Friday, without providing further details.
A Yemeni military source told Anadolu, speaking on condition of anonymity, that government forces launched an operation Friday morning to establish full control over the strait and Mayun Island, which overlooks the key maritime passage.
The operation involves the Southern Giants Brigades and Nation’s Shield Forces, with support from the Saudi-led coalition, the source said.
Government forces pursue remaining Houthi militias
Yemeni government forces said heavy fighting was continuing around the waterway.
The Nation’s Shield Forces said their units, alongside the Southern Giants Brigades, were pursuing remaining Houthi militia in the area.
Strategic waterway at centre of renewed fighting
Yemen has been embroiled in conflict since the Houthi militia seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in 2014.
A Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The latest escalation, which began in July, has marked the most extensive fighting since a UN-brokered truce brought relative calm in 2022.
As clashes intensified in September, the Houthi militias seized key areas in Hudaydah and Taiz provinces and advanced as far as Mayun Island in the Bab al Mandab Strait.
Government forces launched Operation Dawn of Yemen this week to retake Houthi-held territory and restore control over the strategically important area.
The Bab al Mandab connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a vital route for international shipping between Europe and Asia.

No drone debris that could help identify the source of an attack on two merchant ships in the Black Sea has been found, Bulgarian Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said at a briefing at the Chaika Naval Base in Varna, BNR correspondent Daniela Stoynova reported.
Stoyanov cautioned against speculation about who was behind the attack without evidence, noting that both Russia and Ukraine had denied involvement. He said the vessel Able had been badly damaged by fire and its engine room was flooded, but it remained afloat.
The minister also denied having met Kyrylo Budanov, chief of staff to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. “As far as I know, only the Prime Minister has had such a meeting,” he said.
Two merchant ships were struck by drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on 6 October. One of them, ALFA WATAN, sank, leaving its 12 crew members missing. An inspection confirmed that the vessel was carrying wheat.

Spying, involvement in criminal organisation and harming Austria: UP journalist Tkach reveals allegations against him in Vienna
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:38:00 EEST
23:38:00 KST

Spying, involvement in criminal organisation and harming Austria: UP journalist Tkach reveals allegations against him in Vienna
Mykhailo Tkach, head of investigative journalism at Ukrainska Pravda, has said that he and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko were accused of three offences after being detained in Vienna: espionage on behalf of Ukrainian military intelligence, involvement in a criminal organisation, and causing harm to Austria.
Source: Tkach in a video for UP
Quote: "At the start of the interrogation, I was given a document to sign. As far as I understand, it was the equivalent of a formal notice of suspicion. It listed three allegations against us. One was spying for Ukrainian military intelligence. Another was that involvement in these activities is classified as involvement in a criminal organisation. The third allegation, as far as I remember, concerned causing harm to Austria."
Details: Tkach said the law enforcement officers did not explain the grounds for the accusations during questioning. As the interview progressed, he concluded that there was no evidence against him or his colleague.
Quote: "We've worked in Vienna many times, always in public places, covering public figures and people about whom information was in the public interest. So hearing these allegations came as a shock to me."
Details: Tkach described what had happened as an "extraordinary misunderstanding". He also suggested that the detention might have resulted from information provided to Austrian law enforcement officers, possibly through manipulation.
He said the first round of questioning lasted around two hours. The Ukrainian consul arrived afterwards, which gave the journalist an opportunity to tell him about his detention. The questioning then resumed.
Tkach thanked the Ukrainian diplomats for their assistance, noting that he believes their intervention helped significantly.
Background:
- On 8 October, it was reported that Tkach had been detained in Vienna while carrying out an assignment from the editorial team involving tracking down the fugitive former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko.
- Tkach was in Austria with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko.
- The Ukrainian Embassy in Austria said it had asked the Austrian authorities to explain the circumstances surrounding Tkach's detention in Vienna.
- It later emerged that the Ukrainian consul had been granted access to Tkach and had spoken with him.
- In the morning, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry reported that Tkach had been released.

US to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution: Is that legal?​
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:37:08 UTC
23:37:08 KST

US to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution: Is that legal?
Rights groups and legal experts say the move could endanger minors, who are usually barred from witnessing executions in the US.
The Pentagon has said it will livestream the upcoming execution of convicted mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad – a first for the United States.
A Pentagon spokesperson made the announcement on Thursday, drawing uproar from legal quarters as experts and rights groups raised concerns that it could violate US and international laws and, in particular, put minors at risk.
The US military rarely invokes capital punishment, last executing an officer by hanging in 1961. Firing squads are even rarer, and were last used in the military in 1945.
Here’s what we know:
What was Hasan convicted of?
Nidal Malik Hasan, a then-Army major, opened fire at an Army processing centre in Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others.
An Army psychiatrist found he was acting in an effort to stop military deployments to Afghanistan and to halt the killing of fellow Muslims. Hasan was himself scheduled to be deployed later that month.
Following a lengthy military trial in which Hasan made little effort to defend himself, a jury convicted him in July 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of murder, and imposed the death penalty.
Although he said he acted on religious grounds and was found to have corresponded with al-Qaeda-linked elements, Hasan was not convicted of “terrorism” as the US military justice code does not have a stand-alone charge for it.
This week, the Pentagon said US President Donald Trump had given the go-ahead for Hasan to face a firing squad. The military requires presidential approval for executions, and only the president can stipulate a particular method.
When and where will Hasan be executed?
On Thursday, a Pentagon official said Hasan was to be executed at the same Fort Hood military base where he killed 13 people in 2009.
The official said the execution would be livestreamed.
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle set the execution date for December 3 at 1pm local time (18:00 GMT).
What has Hegseth said?
Speaking in a podcast interview this week, Hegseth said the livestream would act as a deterrent.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said during the interview with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec.
He added that the timing of the execution was symbolic. “We’re going to do it at one o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad.”
Who normally attends executions?
The rules vary in the 27 US states where death penalties are still in place.
Texas law allows up to five close relatives of the victim, a spiritual guide, justice officials, state-ordained chaplains, a judge, the sheriff, and the media to attend an execution.
All persons, however, must be adults older than 18.
When was the last public execution in the US?
It was on August 14, 1936. Rainey Bethea was publicly hanged in Owensboro, Kentucky, after confessing to the rape and killing of 70-year-old Lishia Edwards.
What does international law say about public executions?
The US is a signatory to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which bans torture, cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment.
While the convention does not completely ban the death penalty, it does strictly restrict its use to the “most serious crimes” and encourages its abolition.
Washington ratified it in 1992, but it issued reservations and stated that the US would retain the right to impose capital punishment as it sees fit.
Legal experts say the public execution of Hasan could violate the clause against degrading punishment under the convention. A livestream would likely also be recorded and shared widely.
What does US law say about who can witness executions?
British-American human rights lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented clients on death row in the US and founded the Louisiana Capital Assistance Center in New Orleans in 1993 to represent low-income individuals facing the death penalty, called the move “barbaric”.
He said a public execution broadcast in this manner would violate several laws in the US that prohibit the transmission of obscene, indecent, or graphic material, especially to minors.
There’s no single federal law stipulating who may witness executions, but death penalty states typically prohibit minors.
Likewise, the Army’s justice code (PDF) prohibits minors from witnessing an execution.
“I’ve watched six executions, and I suffer from PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder] to this day,” Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “It’s a nightmare, and you’ll have people who will have traumatic responses to it.”
Smith said several legal challenges are likely, and the Army will likely have to consider several factors if it does go ahead with broadcasting the execution.
Challengers are likely to question how the US military will prevent children from viewing the livestream, and how they will make Hasan’s shooting less ghastly based on the body parts targeted, he said.
Regarding using the public execution as a deterrent, Stafford Smith added the opposite could actually be more likely. He said it could end up “provoking more cases” and that Hasan could be seen as a “martyr” by some.
He added: “This is likely going to Congress. The Democrats will want to stop this. So that will be an interesting battle.”
How have politicians and rights groups responded?
Democrat Senator Chris Murphy called the move “disgusting” and compared it to executions carried out by the Islamic State (ISIL). “I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions [are] medieval,” he said in an interview with CNN.
Amnesty International Australia said Hegseth’s statements showed an “appalling disregard for human dignity”, and called on Melbourne to intervene.
Meanwhile, New Zealand’s national censor told rights groups urging it to protest that it has no authority to block internet users from viewing the livestream – a sign that governments attempting to restrict access might be hampered.
