On the Ground at the Power to the People Festival, a Day of Protest Music and Solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:35:51 UTC
23:35:51 KST

Tom Morello has been staging benefit shows since before Rage Against the Machine made him an icon: $10 at the door, proceeds to a homeless shelter, guitars loud enough to wage a sonic revolt against the establishment. Last year, while serving as musical director of Back to the Beginning, the Birmingham farewell concert for Ozzy Osbourne and Black Sabbath, he began imagining something bigger: a multigenerational, multigenre festival built on his foundational proposition that music can be an act of resistance—aimed squarely at Donald Trump and the forces he has unleashed.
"It's no accident that the concert was about three weeks out from the midterms," Morello told me after the Oct. 3 Power to the People show at Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Md., less than 30 minutes from the capital whose balance of power those elections will decide. "In a time where hatred and division are rife, this is a festival of love and solidarity. In a time where injustice is rampant, this is a festival celebrating those who are standing up against injustice. And in a time where artists are either being canceled or censoring themselves, it was a guarantee the artists were going to be able to play what they wanted to play and say what they wanted to say."
To that end, Morello assembled a sprawling roster of rebels and rock-n-roll royalty: Joan Baez and Public Enemy; Jack Black and the Dropkick Murphys; Cypress Hill and Nathaniel Rateliff; Killer Mike and Serj Tankian; Stephen Stills and Dave Matthews and the Foo Fighters. Headlining the event was Bruce Springsteen, fresh off a 20-show tour that had become a nightly rebuke of Trump, MAGA, and the authoritarian currents he saw threatening the American experiment.
Power to the People suggested a rebellious energy stirring at a moment when many artists had grown wary of speaking out, fearful of backlash, of alienating part of their audience, of the wrath of an administration that has repeatedly targeted prominent critics. "I feel as though we're trying to turn the tide and we're facing a tsunami," said Baez, who sang alongside Bob Dylan and Pete Seeger during the protest movements of the 1960s and '70s. Then she turned to the crowd. "You are the antidote in a world of cruelty and bullying." With Rateliff beside her, she launched into a haunting rendition of Woody Guthrie's "Deportee."
Inevitably, the place felt like a progressive family reunion: aging boomers who carry the counterculture as a kind of secular inheritance; younger activists animated by rage against corporate power, democratic erosion, and the war in Gaza; keffiyehs, protest shirts, and homemade placards scattered across the grounds. One read, Keep the Immigrants. Deport the Racists. MS NOW livestreamed the proceedings. It would be easy to dismiss the show as an exercise in preaching to the converted.
But movements have to begin somewhere, and politics is downstream of culture. If the message travels beyond the lawn, Power to the People may come to represent one of the seminal cultural events of the era: a gathering of artists, at a liminal moment in American life, turning their influence into a political insurgency to preserve the nation's democratic future.
Morello had been planning the festival for more than a year, but he says the "turning point" came after the Operation Metro Surge, when Trump administration deployed roughly 3,000 federal officers to Minneapolis this winter for the largest immigration-enforcement operation in the country, which culminated in the killings of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
"When you're putting on a show like this, managers and agents are not always eager to get involved," Morello told me. But after Minneapolis, something changed. "Artists started calling me up and raising their hand, saying, 'I understand you're putting on a festival. Can I be involved?'"
One was Ken Casey, frontman of the Dropkick Murphys, who tore through a 12-song set that ended with the band's signature anthem, "I'm Shipping Up to Boston," built around lyrics by Guthrie. "Days like today let us know that there's a community out there that wants to see a peaceful America, an empathetic America, a unified America, that wants to see control of our government given back to the people," Casey told me.
The concert began at one in the afternoon and ran for 10 hours, the history of American protest music compressed into a single day. During Morello's early-evening set, Tankian from System of a Down joined him for Audioslave's "Like a Stone," a tribute to Morello's late bandmate Chris Cornell. Macklemore, recently dropped as an opener on Ed Sheeran's tour because of pressure from New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft over the artist’s pro-Palestinian advocacy, had been invited but was unavailable. So he sent a video message that played on the giant screens. The controversy itself reinforced the festival's defiant argument—rebelling against a world where speaking out still carries a price.
The lineage grew explicit as the night wore on. Baez, Rateliff, and Matthews joined for "Deportee," then moved into the civil-rights standard "Ain't Gonna Let Nobody Turn Me Around." As they left the stage, Stephen Stills appeared and reached back to another era of upheaval with Buffalo Springfield's "For What It's Worth." Cypress Hill followed, then Public Enemy with their landmark "Fight the Power," then Dave Matthews. The Foo Fighters opened their set with "Times Like These," a song born of uncertainty and near-fracture for the band that transformed into an anthem of renewal. They closed with "Everlong." a track about the desire to make a perfect moment last forever, despite knowing that it can’t.
But the concert’s climax was Springsteen's set. At 76, he summoned the power and energy that have defined him over a half century, as he occupies yet another role now, too: the elder statesman among a generation of musicians deciding how much to risk by taking a stand. "When you have a guy that's at that stage of his life, he's done all the stuff, he's comfortable, he didn't have to go on the road and do that and put the crosshairs on himself, but he did it anyway," Casey said. "If artists can't take a lead from that, then my God, nobody's paying attention."
Springsteen opened with "Streets of Minneapolis," his protest song against Operation Metro Surge, written days after ICE flooded Minnesota's streets and murdered two protestors. He then brought Baez onstage for a searing acoustic rendition of Dylan’s "Chimes of Freedom.” From there the set erupted into anthemic rock fueled by righteous anger. He ripped through the Clash's "Clampdown" with Morello, then "The Ghost of Tom Joad," rekindling the version the two had performed on his recent Land of Hope and Dreams tour.
Grohl and Matthews returned to the stage, and Springsteen's set became an ensemble of generations of American rock musicians gathered around the protest-song tradition. Together they tore into two classics of the canon, Creedence Clearwater Revival's "Fortunate Son" and Neil Young's "Rockin' in the Free World."
When the last chords faded, they stayed onstage for a final coda as the rest of the day’s performers joined them onstage.
The festival was a reincarnation of the spirit of Guthrie, Seeger, and the musicians who advocated for working-class dignity and civil rights in the mid-twentieth century. Morello stepped forward to explain what they were about to sing—and why: Guthrie’s "This Land Is Your Land," but with the verses often omitted from popular renditions, in which the narrator encounters a "Private Property" sign and Americans standing hungry outside a relief office. The lines restored the song's original edge—an unofficial patriotic anthem that also challenges the country to make good on its promise that America belongs to everyone.
It was the version Springsteen sang with Seeger at Barack Obama's inaugural concert in January 2009, and one he resurrected last spring at Music America: The Songs That Shape Us, his concert at Monmouth University celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary, where he recruited the kind of star-level talent the President had been unable to marshal to Washington for the occasion.
For Morello, the song also evoked his mother, Mary Morello, who recently died at 102. A child of the Great Depression, she possessed an activist spirit, he said, feeding the homeless, helping recovering addicts earn their GEDs, and supporting her son's early punk bands. "Her fingerprints were all over this," Morello told me. "Her DNA was in every bit of this. I don't think it was any accident that this concert happened in a place called Mary Land."
It was also there, of course, because of its proximity to the White House, and so they closed with John Lennon's "Power to the People." Morello, Springsteen, and company wanted Trump to hear them, at a precarious moment for the President and the MAGA movement, with the midterms weeks away and his poll numbers at their lowest point of his second term. But the festival's message was ultimately a call to agency, a reminder that in a democracy it is the voters who get to determine their destiny.
"History is not something that happens," Morello told the crowd. "History is something we make."

CAFE III kicks in from 2027: Will your next car be cheaper to run?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:33:37 UTC
23:33:37 KST

What if your next car saves you more at the fuel station but costs more in the showroom?That is the next big question as Indian consumers are asking themselves while the government prepares to roll out its new Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE III) norms from April 1, 2027.Over the next five years, carmakers will have to make their passenger vehicle fleets progressively more fuel-efficient, potentially bringing more efficient petrol cars, hybrids, electric vehicles (EVs) and alternative-fuel models to the market.Notified by the ministry of power, the new rules will remain in force until March 31, 2032. They tighten fuel-consumption targets while offering incentives for cleaner technologies and ethanol-blended fuels. The fleet-average benchmark will fall from 3.996 litres per 100 km in 2027-28 to 3.3273 litres per 100 km in 2031-32, an improvement of around 16.7%.But what does that mean for your wallet? Will your next car go further on every litre, or will the technology needed to improve efficiency add to its price?The answer will depend on how automakers respond, and which car you choose.
Will your next car be cheaper to run?
Under the new norms, automakers will have to meet fuel-efficiency targets based on the average performance of their entire passenger vehicle fleet, rather than each model individually.
This will require carmakers to factor in the efficiency of their overall line-up when deciding which vehicles to develop, manufacture and sell.Jyoti Prakash Gadia, managing director of Resurgent India Limited, said the framework tightens efficiency requirements. It also adds new fleet-weighting rules and incentives for clean technology.“The primary modification made by CAFE III is to bring about increasingly stringent fuel economy pathway in conjunction with new fleet weighting and clean technology incentive provisions,” Gadia told TOI.He added that the framework strengthens the earlier fleet-averaging system. This, he said, was in response to rising car ownership and changes in automotive technology.Pankaj Sharma, founder and managing director of K2 Infragen Limited, said the stricter standards were necessary as the growing number of vehicles increased energy consumption. Improving transport efficiency would also help India reduce pollution and dependence on oil.For buyers, this could mean more fuel-efficient models on offer as carmakers work to meet their targets. Better engines, hybrid systems and electrification can cut energy use. Actual savings, though, will depend on the vehicle, driving conditions, fuel or electricity prices and how far you drive each year.The norms do not guarantee lower running costs for every owner. They set requirements for manufacturers’ fleets. They do not fix a fuel-efficiency figure or a saving for any single model.
Will car prices rise under CAFE III?
The cost of complying will depend on how each carmaker chooses to improve its fleet. More efficient engines, electrification and engineering changes could raise the price of some models. Competition and higher volumes may limit that rise over time.Gadia said the impact will differ from one manufacturer to another. He expects buyers to have a range of choices, including efficient petrol cars, hybrids, EVs and alternative-fuel vehicles.“Efficient Engines, Comprehensive Electrification, and Engineering might raise the cost of certain models but this would be limited due to competitive pressure and expected economies of scale from increasing volumes,” he said.Sharma also said the impact on prices would vary between brands and technologies. While more efficient engines and other innovations could increase costs, competition and economies of scale could help contain the rise.The rules could also push carmakers to review their line-ups, especially models that drag down their fleet average. Still, CAFE III does not force them to give up petrol engines or follow one technology path.For buyers, the difference between the purchase price and the total cost of owning a car will matter more. A costlier car can work out cheaper over several years if savings on fuel or electricity cover the extra price. The result will depend on the price gap, yearly usage, maintenance and energy costs.Gadia said buyers should remember that the purchase price is only one part of the calculation. The cost of running the car over its lifetime counts too.
Salient features of the CAFE III norms
EVs, hybrids and flex-fuel cars get a boost
CAFE III does not push carmakers towards a single route. Instead, it gives them incentives and room to choose different technologies.Battery electric vehicles (BEVs), range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), strong hybrids (SHEVs) and flex-fuel ethanol vehicles get volume derogation factors, commonly called super credits.These factors give such vehicles extra weight when a company’s fleet average is calculated, giving carmakers a reason to sell more of them.Under the notified framework:
BEVs and REEVs get a factor of 3.0.
PHEVs get 2.5, as do strong hybrids that run on flex-fuel ethanol.
Strong hybrids get 1.6.
Flex-fuel ethanol vehicles get 1.1
These incentives could eventually shape manufacturers’ future investment and product plans. But how many new models actually arrive will also depend on consumer demand, vehicle costs, charging infrastructure and fuel availability.“Absolutely, the regulations make EVs, hybrids and alternative fuel vehicles more attractive as these cars are seen as helping overall fleet efficiency in the interest of sustainability,” Gadia said.He cautioned that not every carmaker will take the same path. “But it doesn’t imply that all car manufacturers will use only one trajectory and phase out regular engines,” he added.Sharma said the incentives would encourage manufacturers to produce more electric, hybrid and alternative-fuel vehicles, but affordability, demand and manufacturing capacity would continue to influence their decisions.He also highlighted the importance of infrastructure in determining which vehicles consumers can conveniently use.“The role of infrastructure will be important for choosing convenient vehicles. It is hardly possible to call a good car convenient if there are no places where one could recharge or refuel it,” Sharma told TOI.For infrastructure providers, the shift towards cleaner vehicles also underlines the importance of dependable electricity supplies and transport connections. The availability of vehicles and the infrastructure required to operate them will need to develop together.Carmakers will therefore keep weighing market demand, financial viability, manufacturing capacity and infrastructure before choosing their technologies.
Ethanol and alternative fuels enter the compliance equation
CAFE III introduces a Carbon Neutrality Factor (CNF). It gives credit to certain renewable and low-carbon fuels when a fleet’s compliance is calculated.CNF treatment applies, under set conditions, to petrol vehicles running on ethanol blends, flex-fuel ethanol vehicles and compressed natural gas (CNG) vehicles. The rules set the following factors on tailpipe carbon dioxide emissions:
Ethanol-blended petrol vehicles: 8%
Flex-fuel ethanol vehicles: 22.3%
CNG vehicles: 5% or the notified compressed biogas blending percentage, whichever is higher
Diesel vehicles: depends on the applicable biofuel blending percentage
This gives carmakers one more way to meet their fleet targets, alongside better efficiency and electrification.Dr CK Jain, president of the General Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA), said recognising ethanol was significant because India's clean-mobility transition need not rely on electrification alone.“Ethanol offers a domestically produced, renewable fuel pathway that can complement vehicle electrification, reduce dependence on imported crude oil and create sustained demand for agricultural feedstocks,” Jain said.GEMA said the recognition of ethanol could encourage investments in flex-fuel and electrified flex-fuel technologies. Greater adoption could also strengthen the domestic ethanol value chain, supporting farmers and rural industries through sustained demand for agricultural feedstocks.The association said the need for cleaner transport went beyond reducing emissions. India also needs to strengthen energy security and create sustainable demand for domestically produced fuels.A framework that supports multiple decarbonisation pathways could allow automakers to innovate while helping India build on its existing ethanol ecosystem. However, the policy incentives will need to translate into greater availability of compatible vehicles, wider adoption of flex-fuel technology and higher ethanol consumption.For buyers, the real impact will depend on whether carmakers launch more compatible vehicles. It will also depend on whether suitable fuel and servicing are easy to find.
Aim behind CAFE III norms
Twelve fuel-saving technologies eligible for incentives
The list of recognised fuel-saving technologies grows from four to 12. This lets carmakers improve efficiency without changing the powertrain alone.The 12 technologies are:
Start-stop systems
Tyre-pressure monitoring
Regenerative braking
Six-speed or higher transmissions
Efficient alternators
Motor-generators
Exterior LED lighting
Advanced glass and glazing
Electric water pumps
High-efficiency air-conditioning
Solar-reflective paint
Pulse-width-modulated radiator fans
For each eligible technology in a vehicle, a manufacturer can claim a cut of 1g of CO₂ per km, up to a cap of 9g CO₂ per km. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways will develop the certification methods.Verification rules differ across the compliance period. In the first block, carmakers can claim savings through self-declaration. In the second block, claims must be backed by validated test results.This lets carmakers combine several small improvements across their models. Some of these cut energy use without asking buyers to switch fully to EVs.
New weight-based targets and compliance flexibility
CAFE III also changes how a vehicle’s weight affects its fuel-consumption target. The reference weight rises from 1,082 kg to 1,229 kg, an increase of about 13.6%.The revised target line is meant to be more weight-sensitive. Lighter vehicles get relatively softer targets, while heavier ones must meet tougher efficiency requirements.The applicable standard is worked out with a formula based on the average unladen mass of vehicles made or imported for sale in India. The constants in the formula change over the five years as the benchmarks tighten.Carmakers also get some flexibility in how they comply:
Those that beat their target can earn credits and carry them forward within the compliance block.
Those that fall short can use eligible credits, swap credits with other manufacturers, or buy credits through the Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s buyout mechanism.
The buyout price will rise from Rs 2,500 per g CO₂/km in 2027-28 to Rs 4,500 in 2031-32.
Credit trading will happen in a set annual window, and compliance will be checked at the end of each block.
Manufacturers selling fewer than 1,000 eligible vehicles in a reporting period are exempt from the fleet-average obligations.
Things car buyers should keep in mind
What should buyers consider from April 2027?
The standards will apply to new passenger vehicles made or imported for sale in India from April 1, 2027. That does not mean every car bought after that date will be cheaper to run.Gadia advised buyers to look at their travel needs and yearly mileage first. Only then can they judge whether the likely energy savings justify a higher upfront price.“From April 2027, people must look into the total cost of owning the car in terms of financing, energy used, maintenance, insurance, and even reselling,” he said.Sharma similarly advised consumers to consider their travel requirements, budgets and available infrastructure before making a purchase. For EV buyers, this includes assessing the possibility of charging at home, the reliability of public charging facilities, battery guarantees and after-sales service.Those considering hybrids or alternative-fuel vehicles should check fuel availability and the reach of maintenance networks. Sharma also stressed that safety remains important because fleet-level efficiency standards do not mean all individual models perform equally.Gadia also advised EV buyers to check access to reliable charging and the battery warranty. Across all categories, safety, reliability, insurance, maintenance and resale value will still matter.The economics will differ from buyer to buyer. Someone who drives long distances every year has more room to recover a higher purchase price through lower energy bills. Someone who drives little may not. So buyers should compare their expected savings with the upfront premium, rather than assume a more efficient car is always cheaper overall.
CAFE III aims to push the passenger vehicle industry towards steadily better fleet efficiency while letting carmakers choose from several technologies. Its effect on buyers will depend on how carmakers respond, how fast cleaner technologies arrive and how much of the efficiency gain shows up as lower real-world energy use.The takeaway for car buyers is to look beyond the showroom price. The new rules may bring more efficient cars to the market, but whether your next car is cheaper to run will depend on the model, the technology, the cost of energy and how you use the vehicle.

The Estonian Health Insurance Fund encourages people to complete an organ donor declaration  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:32:30 UTC
23:32:30 KST

TALLINN - Ahead of European Organ Donation Day on Saturday, the Estonian Health Insurance Fund and the Tartu University Hospital are encouraging people to take the important step of completing an organ donor declaration; more than 62,000 Estonians have already done so.
Unfortunately, as in the rest of Europe, the number of patients in Estonia needing a new organ is growing year by year. Currently, 72 people are awaiting a lifesaving transplant at the Tartu University Hospital. One organ donor can give a new life to up to eight people after their death.
According to Virge Pall, director of the Tartu University Hospital's Transplantation Centre, the need for an organ transplant can arise at any age and for a wide variety of reasons.
"In children, the most common reason for needing a transplant is congenital defects. In adults, it can be caused by chronic diseases, as well as acute illnesses and poisonings."
In Estonia, transplants of kidneys, livers, lungs, and pancreases are performed, as well as tissues such as corneas, blood vessels, bone tissue, and skin. For heart transplants, the Tartu University Hospital cooperates with Finland.
Over the last five years, a total of 283 organ transplants have been performed on Estonian patients. According to Pall, there are always fewer donor organs than people who need them.
"One reason for this is the public's lack of awareness and the resulting misconceptions. Therefore, it is very important that reliable information about donation and its medical, ethical, and legal aspects reaches everyone."
It is equally important to discuss the decision with loved ones and to formally complete the declaration of intent.
Completing the electronic declaration of intent is simple - all adults can do so on the health portal at www.terviseportaal.ee. From the menu, you need to select 'declarations of intent,' mark your decision, and confirm it with a digital signature. A signed declaration can be changed at any time on the portal.
Donating organs is an invaluable act that gives hope and a future to people whose lives are at risk of being cut short by an unexpected illness or accident. More information about organ donation can be found on the website https://www.elundidoonorlus.ee/.

Most outages were reported in the Kaunas region, but as the wind strengthened, more reports were coming from the coast, where ESO and contractor crews were already heading to repair faults, the company said in a statement.
According to the company, power supply to customers is being restored in an average of less than two hours.
Jolita Orentaite, head of the communications division at the Fire and Rescue Department, said winds were toppling trees along the coast, with one tree falling on three cars in Klaipeda.
"Most of the reports were received from Neringa and the city of Klaipeda," Orentaite added.
Orentaite said the first report of wind-related damage was received at around 8 a.m. on Friday, and by 10 a.m. about a dozen reports had been received, all from the coast. The strongest winds were expected around noon, she said.
According to ESO, the strongest wind gusts were forecast between noon and 2 p.m., particularly along the coast, where they could reach storm force in some areas. Reinforced crews across Lithuania were ready to respond to further reports, with about 200 ESO and contractor teams mobilised, compared with 60 on a normal day.
Additional crews were also being assembled for the weekend, and staffing at dispatch centres had been increased.

Trump sanctions entire ICC over Netanyahu warrant hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:30:59 UTC
23:30:59 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was named the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. 
The move, driven in part by Washington's opposition to arrest warrants issued for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, marks a major escalation in the administration's campaign against the court and threatens to put the United States on a diplomatic collision course with its European allies. The ICC denounced the sanctions as an assault on international law, while the European Union pledged to help keep the court operating.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement. "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate."
Unlike previous U.S. sanctions targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, Friday's measures target the institution itself, potentially penalizing companies that provide it with financial, technological and other essential services. The Trump administration has long opposed the court, particularly over its arrest warrants for Netanyahu and other Israeli officials, as well as a previous investigation into the conduct of U.S. troops in Afghanistan, which the court has since closed.
In a strongly worded statement Friday, the ICC rejected the sanctions and called on its 125 member states to ensure it could continue functioning. "It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," the court said.
The tribunal vowed to "fully discharge its mandate" to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression when member states are unwilling or unable to do so. However, it warned that it could not withstand the pressure without international support. "The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it," the statement said.
"This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment," the court added.
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan condemned the sanctions, telling Reuters they "must be condemned." She said the measures were designed to undermine international law but insisted the court would continue operating. "The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan said. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."
Nobel Peace Prize announcement highlights international divide
The sanctions came hours after the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay for her contributions to international criminal justice. Pillay served on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008 and has spent decades working to strengthen international legal institutions.
In its announcement, the Nobel Committee said it sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack." It added: "An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world." 
The timing underscored the sharp divide between Washington and supporters of the court. Established in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, the ICC has 125 member states, including every European Union country and all NATO members except the United States and Turkey. The court is based in the Netherlands, itself a member of both organizations, and has received strong public backing from several major U.S. allies.
Rubio warns allies: ‘either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC’
Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing sanctions against the court itself in the hope that the institution and countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address American concerns. He said those efforts had failed and called on U.S. allies to intervene.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said.
The European Commission responded by calling Washington's decision "deeply regrettable" and reaffirmed its support for the court's independence. In a statement Friday, it said the European Union would work closely with the ICC to ensure it could continue operating effectively.
The commission emphasized that the sanctions would not become applicable for six months, leaving time for negotiations. "As there is a six-month delay before the measures are applicable, there is room for dialogue," it said. The EU also declared itself ready to take "any necessary measures" to enable the court to carry out its work and pledged to cooperate with countries party to the Rome Statute to preserve its independence.
U.S. sanctions typically prohibit American companies from doing business with designated organizations, potentially forcing banks to close accounts, insurers to withdraw coverage and software providers to terminate services. A senior State Department official said the Treasury Department would issue licenses "to protect American interests," apparently allowing temporary exemptions from certain restrictions.
ICC officials have been preparing for months for the possibility of sanctions against the entire institution, including replacing Microsoft software with open-source alternatives and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance. Earlier this week, ICC Registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler urged the European Union to prepare a so-called blocking mechanism that could shield European businesses from the extraterritorial effects of American sanctions.
The latest measures go substantially further than the targeted sanctions Trump imposed on ICC officials during his first term, which were later lifted by former President Joe Biden. Washington resumed sanctioning court officials shortly after Trump returned to office in January 2025, but Friday's action represents a broader effort to restrict the court's ability to function.
Despite the escalating confrontation, Rubio said Washington was leaving open the possibility of negotiations with the ICC's member states. "We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," he said.

New bill sets conditions for fund investor payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:28:17 UTC
23:28:17 KST

The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) submitted a nine-article bill to parliament on Oct. 9 setting rules for fund liquidations and allowing advances of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to eligible investors.
AKP parliamentary group leader Abdullah Güler said repayments would be financed through the funds’ assets and money recovered from those responsible for losses, without Treasury contributions or other public funding.
The proposal covers funds ordered into liquidation by the Capital Markets Board (SPK) on Sept. 17 whose liquidation remains incomplete when the legislation takes effect.
Advances would be calculated from investors’ actual cash contributions and withdrawals, without an inflation adjustment.
Payments would depend on available cash, with the SPK authorized to determine how to distribute insufficient funds.
“This is not a sum to be paid unconditionally or upfront to everyone, nor a promise of final compensation,” Güler said.
Under the proposal, records held by the Central Securities Depository (MKK), Takasbank and custody and distribution institutions would be reconciled to establish investors’ entitlements.
Asset sales would remain under SPK supervision, with provisions intended to preserve their value during liquidation.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) would pursue amounts the SPK determines are owed by those responsible for fund losses.
Recovered money would be held in separate accounts for each fund and used for liquidation and investor repayments.
The bill would also allow the voluntary return of gains exceeding market benchmarks from transactions involving artificially priced fund units or shares.
People and institutions identified by the SPK as having participated in market manipulation, insider dealing or related abuses would be excluded from payments.
Güler said the Plan and Budget Commission was expected to consider the proposal next week, with a debate in the General Assembly to follow.
Meanwhile, the Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, reviewed preparations for the proposed advances at its fourth meeting, the Communications Directorate said on Oct. 9.
Officials also discussed ongoing liquidations and coordination between institutions handling the return of excessive gains.
Separately, Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş said she had filed criminal complaints against lawmakers Ümit Özlale, Cemal Enginyurt and Ali Mahir Başarır over allegations linking her family to the funds.
Özlale had questioned whether her father had traded in two of the funds.
Göktaş denied any family involvement, saying the records concerned another person with the same name.

One in 21 women and girls in Gaza killed or severely wounded amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:27:45 UTC
23:27:45 KST

Nearly 50,000 women and girls have been killed or severely wounded by Israel in Gaza since October 2023, equivalent to one in every 21 women and girls in the enclave, UN Women has said.
"More than 38,000 killed and 11,700 left with injuries so severe that they now live with lifelong disabilities," Sofia Calltorp, UN Women's chief of humanitarian action, told reporters in Geneva on Friday.
She said most casualties occurred during the first two years of the genocide, but violence has continued despite the ceasefire agreement entering into effect a year ago, with 277 women and girls killed since October 2025.
Nearly one million women and girls have been forced from their homes, while almost all remain displaced, many living in tents or among the ruins of their homes, she said.
Calltorp also warned that the number of female-headed households has doubled, with women now heading one in four households in Gaza.
Meanwhile, funding cuts have severely weakened women's organisations, with 13 of 14 surveyed reporting they can no longer meet growing needs.
All surveyed organisations reported increases in gender-based violence, poverty and mental health distress since 2025, while 13 reported rising child marriage.
UN Women called for full implementation of the ceasefire, respect for international law and accountability for violations.
"What we have found is a horrific amount of collective suffering, an immense amount of pain, and a level of resilience and strength that no woman should have to bear," Calltorp said.

According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, the head of state presented 20 apartment certificates to Heroes of Ukraine and the relatives of fallen defenders. The recipients included service members from the Ground Forces, Territorial Defense Forces, Navy, Air Force, Air Assault Forces, Support Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and National Guard of Ukraine.
They included pilots and service members who distinguished themselves in battles for the Kyiv region, Kyiv, and Mariupol in 2022; carried out missions in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Sumy regions; and took part in the Kursk operation.

China, EU reach understanding on hybrid vehicle trade amid efforts to ease tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:26:23 UTC
23:26:23 KST

Faisal Mahmud
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
China and the EU reached an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade following intensive negotiations, Beijing's Commerce Ministry announced Friday, signaling progress in efforts to ease bilateral trade tensions.
The understanding emerged from the second regular meeting of the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism in Beijing, attended by Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.
According to a joint statement released by the ministry, both sides reached an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade consistent with World Trade Organization rules.
They also agreed to explore reducing tariffs on certain products and continue procedures concerning price undertakings and reviews related to the EU's anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese electric vehicles.
China pledged to facilitate export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for Europe through a "green channel" mechanism.
The EU, meanwhile, agreed to help resolve priority licensing cases involving dual-use exports to China.
Both sides also agreed to improve transparency in export controls, address intellectual property concerns and strengthen cooperation on reforming the World Trade Organization.
The talks came amid longstanding trade disputes over Chinese electric vehicles, European market access and export restrictions on critical minerals.
Trade between China and the EU remains heavily weighted in Beijing's favor.
According to European Commission data, the bloc imported approximately $650 billion worth of goods from China in 2025, compared with exports of $232 billion, leaving a merchandise trade deficit of around $418 billion.
Machinery and vehicles accounted for more than half of manufactured imports from China, according to the data.
The imbalance has become a central concern in Brussels, which has urged Beijing to open its market further to European companies and address what it describes as unfair competition and industrial overcapacity.
The two sides agreed to hold their next ministerial-level meeting in March 2027, preceded by a video conference in January.

Presidential adviser: Russia begins using new satellite navigation antennas in Shahed UAVs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:26:07 EEST
23:26:07 KST

Russian Shahed-type drones used to attack Kyiv are being equipped with new, shielded satellite navigation antennas with 32 elements instead of the previous 16, Adviser to the President of Ukraine Serhiy (Flash) Beskrestnov said.
According to him, these CRPA antennas are designed to counter electronic warfare (EW) systems that create interference on satellite navigation frequencies, particularly GPS. The number of antenna elements affects its ability to suppress interference from EW systems.
Beskrestnov said the Shahed UAVs can locate a target either through radio control by an operator via a MESH modem or using satellite navigation signals. To counter the second guidance method, Ukrainian electronic warfare systems generate jamming, while the Russian side installs antennas on the drones capable of neutralizing such signals.
"Previously, we essentially needed to ensure that there were always 16 electronic warfare sources around the 'Shahed,' but now we essentially need twice as many," the presidential adviser said in a post shared on Facebook.
He said this technological race creates additional difficulties for Ukraine, since it is easier for the enemy to increase the number of antenna elements than it is for the Ukrainian side to increase the number of electronic warfare deployment points. "This race is difficult for us because it is easier for the enemy to increase the number of elements on an antenna than it is for us to add electronic warfare sites."

Central Asia’s Leaders Gather in Turkmenistan for 8th Consultative Meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

On October 8, Turkmenistan hosted a flurry of region meetings in Avaza, including the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Council of Heads of State, as well as related foreign minister-level meetings.
According to Turkmen state media, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov laid out “five key objectives,” which included “building the potential of the six-party format,” ensuring lasting peace and stability in the region, joint efforts “to transform Central Asia and Azerbaijan into key transport, logistics, energy, and industrial hubs on the continent in the East-West and North-South directions,” creating the conditions for “accelerated technological growth and the active implementation of artificial intelligence,” and finally, expanding “cultural, humanitarian, educational, and civilizational ties.”
These were all vaguely, and inoffensively, stated, as per Turkmen diplomatic style.
Remarks from Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev were more ambitious and concrete – or at least more readily accessible. Mirziyoyev remarked on the atmospheric change in Central Asian regional diplomacy. He pointed to the completion of the Treaty on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century. The treaty was signed during the fourth Consultative Meeting of Central Asian Leaders in 2022 by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. It took until 2025 for Tajikistan to sign on, and Turkmenistan only did so earlier this year, in July during a visit by Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev to Ashgabat.
Mirziyoyev did not remark on the gap between 2022 and 2026 for all five countries to sign onto the treaty; he also didn’t address the fact that while Azerbaijan has joined the grouping – and is taking over as chair – it isn’t a party to the treaty.
This is, perhaps, by design. Mirziyoyev did remark that “we do not seek to create cumbersome structures.”
The friendship treaty codifies this position, baking in possibilities while committing to little beyond words and consultation. The treaty lays out commitments to cooperate across a wide range of areas and build relations “on the basis of mutual respect, equality, understanding and comprehensive consideration of each other’s interests.”
But it contains hints of possible future pathways. For example, its Article 5 states that the parties “shall provide each other with comprehensive support and mutual assistance in matters of preventing threats to their independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.” It goes on to stipulate that should a situation arise that “poses a threat to the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity” of one of the parties, “appropriate consultations” may be held bilaterally or within the consultative format “in order to determine measures that will contribute to the effective prevention of the threat that has arisen.” That’s a long-winded diplomatic way of saying that should a crisis develop, the Central Asian states may act together to confront it.
Of course, history – and the track records of other regional groupings such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) or the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) – suggest that defaulting to inaction is the most likely outcome, even amid a crisis.
It’s hard to divorce the friendship treaty, which was signed by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan in July 2022, from the Russian invasion of Ukraine earlier that year. Similarly, Tajikistan only joined after its long-standing border disputes with Kyrgyzstan were settled. Turkmenistan, which maintains a foreign policy of “positive neutrality,” is the most surprising signatory by far – but that it did sign on may reflect less a change of heart in Ashgabat than the low commitments demanded by the treaty.
Grand outcomes aren’t necessary at every meeting to prove the value of a format. But at a certain point, the lowest hanging fruit – the ability to sit around a table together and discuss priorities amicably – has been picked. Mirziyoyev – and Kazakh president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev – have made clear that they have grander ambitions for what Central Asia can accomplish collectively. The economic sphere – particularly trade, transit, and investment – got special attention from both presidents and represents the next lowest hanging fruit. Who can argue with expanding trade?
In his remarks, Tokayev noted that intraregional trade amounted to approximately $13 billion, representing 8 percent of total trade turnover between the countries. He set the aim of reaching $20 billion. Tokayev suggested deepening regional trade cooperation, linking across borders the logistics centers most of the countries in the region are building. “In the near future,” he said, “we can link them together to build regional value chains. We have all the conditions for expanding cooperation in investment, energy, industry, and other strategic areas.” Tokayev referenced the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, while also noting that “North-South route, in cooperation with Russia, remains particularly important for Kazakhstan.”
Mirziyoyev argued that “economic cooperation must be elevated to a new level.” He noted the importance of continuing to address trade barriers, but looked to the future: “We have already reached a point where standard mutual trade is no longer sufficient; we need to create finished products together.”
Mirziyoyev closed with a focus on the youth and cooperation, saying that “it is important that students, young professionals, scientists, researchers and representatives of creative professions have more opportunities to communicate, learn from one another and work together.”
That’s a great sentiment, but delivered in light of virtual silence on the matter of Dr. Ikboljon Qoraboyev it rings hollow. Qoraboyev was a well-known Uzbek international relations professor at a top Kazakh university. He was was detained this summer in Kazakhstan, apparently on espionage charges, and there has been very little said officially about the case – either by Astana or Tashkent – since. It serves to highlight the distance between remarks delivered at a round table and the reality of what it takes to inspire and support cooperation and collaboration.
There is much hard work ahead for Central Asia.

2028 US presidential hopefuls making moves in November midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:22:41 UTC
23:22:41 KST

As most of the political world focuses on next month's midterm elections, the shadow primary for the 2028 presidential contest is quietly playing out in public view.
Democratic and Republican presidential prospects have been crisscrossing the country, raising money and tapping their political connections to help boost their parties' candidates — and their own White House ambitions.
Here's a closer look at some leading prospects and how what happens Nov. 3 may shape their political futures.
Vance steps up midterm campaign efforts
The 42-year-old has embarked on an extensive midterm campaign schedule from the Midwest to the South and Alaska, focused on the administration’s anti-fraud efforts.
A key state will be Ohio, which Vance briefly represented in the Senate.
Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance’s seat in 2025, is facing a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Democrat Amy Acton is in a close contest with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for governor.
The effectiveness of the conservative group Turning Point Action will also be closely watched. Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point co-founder Charlie Kirk and the organisation’s new leader, has already endorsed Vance’s potential presidential bid, and leaders have said they intend to use the group to support his campaign.
Vance has said he is not focused on running for president, but “trying to help elect Republicans.”
Newsom has a Southern strategy
Gavin Newsom leaves the California governor's office at the end of the year, and he's been among the most active Democrats throughout the midterms.
He's paid particular attention to the South, where he's campaigned with candidates up and down the ballot in states like Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina, and, not surprisingly, South Carolina, which will host the party's first presidential primary contest in 2028.
The Southern focus aligns with the mission of Newsom's political action committee, established in 2023 to help his party compete in red states. But it could also help endear him to Black voters, a key constituency within the Democratic base
Newsom's national profile and extensive email list have helped him develop relationships with Democratic officials in states like Nevada and New Hampshire, where his fundraising emails have generated a surge of donations.
Perhaps Newsom's biggest midterm contribution was backing Proposition 50, California's response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander.
California voters approved the proposition last year, creating a new congressional map that may let Democrats pick up as many as five additional US House seats in California this fall.
Shapiro is all about Pennsylvania
Among the Democrats considered potential 2028 presidential contenders, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro has largely concentrated his midterm political activities within his home state.
He hasn't visited any early primary states or campaigned with any midterm candidates beyond his state.
The approach reflects Shapiro's focus on consolidating his political position in Pennsylvania, a key presidential swing state.
Shapiro is considered the favourite to win reelection against his Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, and has directed political resources towards other races.
Beshear faces risk and reward
As chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear has expanded his national political activities during the midterms.
He’ll headline a get-out-the-vote tour through key states, beginning with Nevada on Oct. 22.
He's also been on a national book tour, letting him cosy up to influential Democrats in early states.
Still, Beshear’s spending decisions as chief of the governors association in 2026 may present the highest risk and reward for him heading into 2028.
He’s been active in supporting Democratic candidates in traditional swing states like Wisconsin, Michigan and Arizona while pushing into Republican-leaning states like Ohio and Iowa, places he argues could be critical in the next White House campaign.
But Democrats in other states are clamouring for more resources and warning Beshear of blowback if he doesn't deliver.
Under pressure, the governors association sent $1 million this week to help Gina Hinojosa, the candidate for Texas governor.
Cruz hits the road in Texas
Sen. Ted Cruz has long been one of his party's most active campaigners and fundraisers, and that's not changed as he openly weighs another presidential bid.
His PAC has spent more than $2.4 million this year on ads supporting midterm candidates, according to AdImpact, mostly to help Senate candidate Ken Paxton in his home state.
Cruz has travelled to Iowa three times, the first state on Republicans' nominating calendar and where he won the caucuses during the 2016 primary.
He’ll be in Alaska next week, and is also planning trips to South Carolina, North Carolina and most likely Michigan.
Pritzker's money plays Illinois
Gov. JB Pritzker is seeking his third term in November, but the Democrat has focused more on helping midterm candidates in other states. Pritzker's team says the billionaire Democrat has already donated $38 million to the party's midterm efforts.
More than other 2028 prospects, Pritzker has focused on the Texas governor's race, where he donated $1 million this week, plus $200,000 earlier.
He's also been active on the speaker circuit, having participated in more than 75 events across the country. He's expected to visit South Carolina before Election Day.
AOC's progressive politics face a test
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York has been increasingly open about a potential presidential run, which could position her among the Democratic Party's progressive contenders.
But first, she's trying to prove that brand of politics can succeed in a presidential swing state like Michigan, where she has thrown her weight behind Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. They appeared together this week at a New York City fundraiser, and she cast his campaign as a broader test for the progressive movement.
“If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” Ocasio-Cortez told the audience.
Ocasio-Cortez and other Democrats have acknowledged that she'll face questions about whether she can appeal to voters across the country.
Ocasio-Cortez argues an El-Sayed victory could challenge some of those assumptions.
Buttigieg is busy, too
Since leaving his job as transportation secretary under President Joe Biden, Pete Buttigieg has used his time to travel across the country, raising money and campaigning for Democrats on the ballot this year.
Buttigieg has endorsed nearly 100 candidates, from state legislative contests to Senate races, and has appeared on the campaign trail with roughly half of them, according to his team. He has visited 37 states since leaving office.
The range of those appearances also reflects his efforts to build connections across different parts of the Democratic Party.
Buttigieg has also campaigned for Democratic candidates in traditionally Republican areas, including Nancy Lacore, a US House candidate in South Carolina who campaigned with Buttigieg in August.
Ossoff’s Georgia audition
The Georgia senator is the only Democrat seeking re-election in a state Donald Trump carried in 2024, and the midterms are his whole ballgame.
He has spent the fall in a rolling argument with Trump-backed challenger Mike Collins, framing the administration’s conflicts of interest as a cost-of-living, AI, and war problem.
Polls put him up by roughly 7 to 10 points; Cook rates the race Lean Democratic, and he has already raised nearly $100 million. Early voting starts next week.
He insists the presidential chatter is fantasy. “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028,” he told local television last month, and he has repeated the line on national air. 
He has hosted fundraisers for the Georgia Democratic Party and its coordinated campaign, appeared with gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, and picked up an Obama ad this week. 
A senior Georgia Democrat told the Financial Times his aim is not merely to win, but to win by enough that “he could change his mind in 2028 or after.” On prediction markets, he is already the favourite for the Democratic nomination.
The risk is the same one that made him look vulnerable a year ago. Georgia still requires 50 percent to avoid a December runoff, Collins is hitting him as a coastal trust-fund radical, and a narrow win would leave the 2028 talk looking like hype.

Tunisian court dismisses case to dissolve publisher of ICIJ partner Inkyfada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:21:29 UTC
23:21:29 KST

PRESS FREEDOM
Tunisian court dismisses case to dissolve publisher of ICIJ partner Inkyfada
Despite the court victory, Inkyfada and its parent company Al Khatt still struggle to recover funds frozen by authorities.
The Tunis Court of First Instance ruled this week to dismiss a case that would have shuttered media publisher Al Khatt, and with it, ICIJ partner Inkyfada. The ruling, praised by press freedom advocates, comes amid a severe crackdown on Tunisian media.
Tunisian authorities filed the dissolution request against Al Khatt, a nongovernmental organization that promotes independent journalism and media literacy, in May. The dissolution request was not based on a single claim, and it fit a larger pattern of censorship, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) told ICIJ at the time. The court finally ruled on Monday in Al Khatt’s favor.
“This decision is an encouraging signal, but it cannot mask the persistence of major concerns regarding the environment in which independent media operate,” Oussama Bouagila, director of RSF’s North Africa office, wrote to ICIJ. He condemned in particular authorities’ targeting of the independent news site Nawaat and needless detentions of multiple Tunisian journalists.
“The right of the Tunisian people to information is being undermined,” Bouagila said. “RSF calls on the Tunisian authorities to continue down the path to reform, to ensure the release of the detained journalists, and to establish the conditions for free and safe journalism.”
Al Khatt publishes and partly funds Inkyfada, a longtime ICIJ partner that has contributed to several cross-border investigations, including the Panama Papers, the Pandora Papers and the Implant Files.
Malek Khadhraoui, executive director of Al Khatt and publication director of Inkyfada, said that the organization’s victory in court “does not end our difficulties.”
Since 2023, Tunisian authorities have targeted Al Khatt’s finances under the guise of regulatory action, including blocking the organization’s bank transfers, sometimes for months at a time.
“We have still received no explanation,” Khadhraoui wrote to ICIJ. “We will pursue every legal avenue to recover these funds, and we will keep publishing.”
In a press release, Al Khatt stated that it stood by organizations and journalists facing similar attacks in Tunisia.
Since 2022, Tunisian authorities have weaponized a law criminalizing “rumours and fake news” to pursue politically motivated censorship. Six of the 14 journalists prosecuted in Tunisia between April 2025 and April 2026 were prosecuted under this law, according to the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists’ annual report. Last week, the government amended the law to replace prison sentences with fines, but press freedom advocates warn the government can still use it to attack critics of the country’s leadership.
“[Al Khatt] hopes that civil society will be protected and supported as an indispensable partner in public life, and that everyone who practises journalism will be guaranteed the right to work freely and without fear of prosecution,” the statement reads.

Europe’s changing face: How migration is reshaping the continent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:20:35 UTC
23:20:35 KST

Europe’s changing face: How migration is reshaping the continent
The native population in several European countries could become a minority within the next two decades if current demographic trends continue, according to a new model projecting the long-term effects of migration and declining birth rates.
Meanwhile, European governments continue to portray migration as an investment in the future, even as local communities grapple with high housing costs, overstretched public services, and persistent failures in border enforcement.
Who is doing the counting?
The Demography Dashboard was published earlier this week by the Institute for Remigration (IFR), run by Austrian activist and author Martin Sellner. He campaigns for sharply reducing immigration and encouraging or enforcing migrant departures, with the aim of preserving native majorities.
The model uses official national population statistics to project how migration, births, and deaths could change Europe’s population. It generally carries forward migration levels averaged over 2015-2024 and holds birth and death rates constant.
When will Europeans become a minority in their own country? The IFR Demography Dashboard answers that question - and shows how remigration could change the course. https://t.co/alL0saMOhb
— Institute for Remigration (@remigrationinst) October 5, 2026
Its “migrant” category includes arrivals from Africa, the Middle East, and elsewhere, as well as other European countries, both inside and outside the EU. Depending on the country, it also includes locally born descendants and people who have acquired a national passport. Citizenship alone does not remove someone from the category: Germany, for example, counts people who were born without German citizenship or have at least one parent who was.
“Native” generally means people without that migration background, but the definitions vary. Britain’s calculation uses ethnicity instead – White British and White Irish people count as native, while all other ethnic groups fall into the model’s migrant category, regardless of birthplace or passport.
The IFR’s projected dates show what could happen if its assumptions about migration, fertility, and mortality hold. According to Eurostat data, the EU’s fertility rate has dropped from 1.54 children per woman in 2014 to 1.34 in 2024, below the 2.1 replacement level. Deaths have outnumbered births since 2012, with 10.7 deaths against 7.9 births per 1,000 residents in 2024.
A generation of change
Switzerland is projected to cross the dashboard’s 50% threshold first, in 2038, from a modeled migrant-background share of 41.2% in 2026. Belgians will become a minority in their own country in 2044, Germany will cross the threshold a year later, and Sweden a year after that (2046). Their modeled immigrant starting shares were respectively 36.6%, 32%, and 36.8%.
The UK is also expected to reach that threshold in 2053, starting at 27.2%, while Spain follows in 2057, from a 25.4% base. For France, the dashboard cites a separate study projecting a similar shift around 2050 under its high-migration scenario.
Sustained immigration, alongside aging populations and low birth rates, are the primary drivers of the demographic shifts, according to dashboard data. Arrivals also include workers, students, family members, and asylum seekers from Africa, the Middle East, and elsewhere. Ukrainians have added another large European component, with some 4.43 million holding temporary protection in the EU at the end of July.
More arrivals, fewer affordable homes
Across Europe, immigration has added demand for housing and public services that were already struggling to cope. Spain and Ireland are stark examples of governments admitting newcomers without ensuring there are enough homes and infrastructure.
In Spain, immigration-driven population growth has outpaced housing construction, while soaring rents have pushed residents into the streets. The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home of 70 years last month has become a rallying point for sprawling protests across the country. The woman died on October 7.
Immigration is the main driver of housing demand in both Ireland and Spain. It is long past time government slowed the pace of worker and student visa issuance to ease housing demand growth. It should not be controversial to say demand needs to managed, and it is certainly not anti-immigration never mind anti-immigrant.
— Dan O'Brien (@danobrien20) October 6, 2026
In Ireland and Britain, taxpayer-funded accommodation for asylum seekers has fueled resentment among residents struggling to rent or buy. Ireland’s purchase of Dublin’s Citywest Hotel for asylum accommodation prompted protests over the loss of a local amenity in an area already short of facilities.
Britain’s asylum accommodation contracts, meanwhile, are projected to cost £15.3 billion ($21.2 billion) over a decade, more than triple the original estimate. Private providers have amassed substantial profits while communities face added pressure on housing and services.
Security failures
The influx of migrants to Europe over the past decade has also contributed to a major security debate, sharpened by attacks involving people who should already have been removed, or whose dangerous behavior was known to the authorities.
Deadly suspected terrorist attacks have taken place in France, Germany, and Britain involving migrants, exposing failures in screening, monitoring, and deportation enforcement.
Foreign nationals accounted for 42.9% of identified violent-crime suspects in Germany in 2025, disproportionately represented even as recorded violent crime declined, according to police figures.
New video released of the illegals t3rrorizing Paris. (Legal) French citizens / passengers of the subway were trapped as they’re attacked by the fighting age men whom President Macron & his husband imported. Is this what the EU leaders wanted for the first world? https://t.co/O9vYsyJW8l
— The Beringer Project (@BradBeringer) October 2, 2026
Crackdown on dissent
Drawing attention to the issue, however, has been effectively banned in some European countries. In Britain, the overzealous crackdown on “anti-migrant sentiment” has extended to criminally prosecuting locals for social media posts opposing uncontrolled migration, or even something as mundane as waving the British flag in public.
In Spain, a group citing police inaction over crime and irregular migration has taken matters into its own hands, launching street patrols and handing suspected thieves to police. Its activities, however, are now the subject of a “hate crimes” investigation.
Former French presidential candidate Eric Zemmour has also faced prosecution over his immigration rhetoric. In September 2025, France’s highest court upheld a €15,000 fine for racial insults and inciting hatred over a speech in which he described immigrants as “colonizers” and Muslim clothing as the “uniforms of an occupation army.”
Growing backlash
Hundreds of thousands of people across Europe voiced their opposition to migration policies during the summer. Large marches were held in London, Madrid, and Dublin that saw protesters demanding stronger border controls and an end to governments leaving local communities to absorb the consequences.
The authorities, however, have frequently responded by condemning the protests rather than addressing their complaints. Ahead of May’s London march, the British prime minister accused its organizers of “peddling hate and division.”
Meanwhile, parties promising tighter controls have continued to gain public support. In Germany, an October 3 poll put the right-wing AfD at 30%, well ahead of the governing CDU/CSU’s 18%.
Washington’s warning
Europe’s immigration policies have also drawn criticism from abroad. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked the approach, accusing European leaders of “destroying your heritage” through migration policies adopted in the name of being politically correct. His administration has put border restrictions and deportations at the center of its own approach.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a similar warning at February’s Munich Security Conference, saying mass migration threatened “the cohesion of our societies, the continuity of our culture, and the future of our people.”
Speaking in Athens on Wednesday, he accused Western governments of opening borders while surrendering sovereignty to global bureaucracies. He criticized the fashion of prioritizing the “global community over one’s own people” and called for cooperation to secure Europe’s borders against mass migration.
Orders to leave, little effect
European governments have increasingly promised tougher migration controls, but enforcement continues to lag. In the second quarter of 2026, EU countries issued around 110,000 orders to leave, while fewer than 37,000 people were actually returned outside the bloc.
July’s Ceuta invasion, which saw some 72,000 people cross from Morocco into the Spanish North African exclave in a single day, further exposed the cracks in what Brussels claims is a comprehensive migration policy.
Appeals, missing documents, and countries refusing to take people back have repeatedly delayed removals, while European governments’ own asylum laws have created further bureaucratic barriers to deportations.
Moving detention abroad has offered no simple solution either. Britain abandoned its Rwanda scheme in 2024 after spending nearly a billion dollars only to ultimately relocate four volunteers. Italy’s attempts to offshore asylum processing to Albania were also blocked by the courts, which allowed Rome to use just one of the centers to hold migrants awaiting deportation.
The pressure has also exposed divisions within Europe’s supposedly border-free Schengen area. Germany, France, Austria, and several other members have reinstated checks on travelers arriving from neighboring countries, citing migration and security concerns. Following the Ceuta crisis, Italy also reinstated border checks on all air and sea routes from Spain, with Madrid responding in kind.
The EU’s Migration and Asylum Pact, applied since June, has promised faster screening, asylum decisions, and returns. However, it has so far been unable to clear backlogs, carry out removals at the necessary pace, or give communities relief, instead adding yet another layer of procedures.

Planning to return to Ukraine now or in the future? The “Dodomu” platform can help you prepare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

Over the years of full-scale war, millions of Ukrainians have started building lives in other countries. Data from the Centre for Economic Strategy shows that 43% of Ukrainians abroad plan or are rather inclined to plan to return to Ukraine. Some are considering this possibility for the future, while others do not yet know where they will be living in a year or two. The decision to return is rarely simple: it involves safety, employment, housing, children’s education, loved ones, and many other circumstances.
Today, in EU countries alone, 4.43 million people who left Ukraine remain under temporary protection. The largest number is in Germany: approximately 1.29 million, or nearly a third of the total in the EU. At the same time, for most people this is not a decision for the near term: around 80% of those considering returning link it to the end of the war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But even if relocating is not on the table right now, practical questions could already have arisen. Where are you going to live after returning? How do you find housing if you are not going back to your hometown? What social and medical services will be available, and where should you turn if you need help?
Answers to these questions are often scattered across the websites of various government agencies, communities, and organisations. Gathering the information required on your own could mean scrolling through dozens of pages. The “Dodomu” platform, dodomu.unity.gov.ua, brings useful resources together in one place and helps you understand the next steps if you are considering returning to Ukraine.
Dodomu was developed within the YOUA “Shaping New Paths, Building Ukraine’s Future”, implemented on behalf of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH in cooperation with the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine. According to the project, no Ukrainian state budget funds were used to develop or operate the platform.
What You Need to Know If You Are Considering Returning
Where should you start, and what should you take into account in your specific situation? On the “Dodomu” platform, you can create a personalised return plan. You answer a few questions and receive steps and recommendations tailored specifically to you.
This plan will help you figure out which documents you need to arrange; how to organise the transport of personal belongings, a car, or pets; where to look for housing and employment; how to enrol a child in school or nursery; and what support you can count on. It also includes opportunities for education, retraining, or starting your own business.
                                                                                                                                                                         Note: The screenshot shows an English translation of the Dodomu website (dodomu.unity.gov.ua). The original website is in Ukrainian.                             
What if you are not returning to the place you left?
Over the years of war, the very meaning of “returning” has changed for many people. A hometown may now be in temporarily occupied territory or may have suffered heavily from the war. Jobs, schools, and familiar surroundings may have changed too. That is why returning to Ukraine does not always mean going back to the same flat, city, or community.
In this situation, it is important to understand, even before moving, what life might look like in a different place.
The “Dodomu” website already features 149 communities, and the number is gradually growing. Each one has its own “profile” with information on services and infrastructure, employment and education conditions, transport connections, leisure options, and contact information for administrative service centres (TsNAPs), social protection departments, and community representatives.
                                                                                                                                                                         Note: The screenshot shows an English translation of the Dodomu website (dodomu.unity.gov.ua). The original website is in Ukrainian.                             
While still abroad, you can learn more about a given community: what job and education opportunities exist there, what infrastructure is available, and where to turn after arriving. This makes it possible to compare different options and get a clearer picture of what life might look like after returning.
Support Is Also Available Abroad
The platform also features an interactive map of Unity Hubs for Ukrainians and partner organisations in various countries. It includes contact details and information about services which are available — consultations on staying in host countries as well as on opportunities in Ukraine.
In Germany, which currently hosts the largest number of Ukrainians under temporary protection in the EU, Unity Hub Berlin has been operating since April 2026 as the first Unity Hub for Ukrainians in Europe. Here, people can get information on the conditions for staying in Germany, consultations on social and pension matters in Ukraine, as well as advice on a possible return and how to prepare for it.
“Dodomu” Is Still Evolving, and Users Can Help Shape It
“Dodomu” is currently being piloted. Since its launch in June 2026, the platform has recorded over 50,000 visits from various countries around the world.
The pilot allows the service to be improved based on feedback from the people it was created for. All users can leave feedback or a suggestion — sharing what information is missing, what was hard to find, what does not work smoothly, or what should be added.
This feedback helps the team better understand the real needs of Ukrainians abroad and gradually make the platform more convenient and useful.
                                                                                                                                                                         Note: The screenshot shows an English translation of the Dodomu website (dodomu.unity.gov.ua). The original website is in Ukrainian.                             
The decision to return remains an open question for many Ukrainians abroad. But it is possible to prepare for it now, so that when the time comes to decide, there will be far less uncertainty. That is exactly what the “Dodomu” platform is designed for: helping people find the information they need and put together a personal plan for returning to Ukraine.
The project provides technical assistance only and does not influence individual decisions about returning to Ukraine. Participation in its activities and use of its services are entirely voluntary for people considering return, those who have already decided to return, and those currently reintegrating after returning to Ukraine.
