Estonia plans up to €5 million payments to municipalities that allow wind farms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Estonia plans up to €5 million payments to municipalities that allow wind farms
Minister of Energy Erkki Keldo has sent for approval a draft regulation that would create the possibility to pay local governments up to €5 million in support to encourage the construction of wind farms on their territory.
The purpose of the measure, called Tuulehoo preemia (Wind Speed Bonus), is to increase the readiness of local governments to carry out wind‑energy developments, especially in the most time‑consuming stages of planning and permit procedures, the Ministry of Climate said.
The maximum amount of support is up to five million euros per municipality, divided into two parts: the first part can be applied for after the planning has been established, and the second part once construction permits for the turbines have been issued. The right to apply for support arises when the established plans foresee at least five wind turbines.
According to the ministry's press release, the support can be used to improve local life — for example, renovating schools and other public buildings, building pedestrian and cycling paths, creating local energy and storage solutions, and improving crisis preparedness.
The total volume of the bonus support is at least 12 million euros, planned for 2027 and 2028. The measure will be financed from the sale of emission allowances (CO₂ quotas) up to 12 million euros and from the state budget.
The bonus does not mean that a municipality must establish a wind‑farm plan or issue a construction permit. All existing requirements remain in force: necessary studies and environmental impact assessments must be carried out, and local residents must be involved, the ministry explained.
At the same time, it was added that the bonus payment does not replace the wind‑turbine fee. While the turbine fee provides local governments and residents with long‑term annual income throughout the wind farm's operating life, Tuulehoo preemia enables local benefits to arise earlier — at the planning and construction‑permit stage.
The Ministry of Climate expressed hope that the planned bonus will also contribute to the state's long‑term goal of increasing energy security and the share of clean energy, and ensuring affordable electricity prices.
"Onshore wind will be one of the most cost‑effective ways to produce electricity in the coming years, and it increases access to low electricity prices. To reduce dependence on fossil‑fuel imports, we need affordable, renewable, domestic production. Therefore, developing wind farms is of strategic importance, and we cannot allow the construction of new parks across Estonia to stall. This is why we are creating the bonus. The local community must feel that changes in their living environment bring them practical benefits. Developing wind farms should be cooperation that benefits everyone," Keldo said in the press release.

Your Favorite Song Might Make Pain Hurt Less
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:13:38 UTC
23:13:38 KST

No one much likes the pain of a needle stick at a doctor’s office or hospital. But according to a new study in Frontiers in Pain Research, there’s one thing that can ease the sting: music. Listening to just the right soundtrack may be its own kind of anesthetic—one that could be useful for needle insertions and other painful medical procedures.
“Although a needle puncture is a minor procedure, the level of pain can vary significantly from person to person,” said radiologist and lead author Dr. Andrei-Cristinel Dragnea of University Hospital Zürich, in a statement that accompanied the release of the study. “In modern medicine, the goal of treating physicians is not only to provide a successful diagnosis and therapy, but also to ensure that the procedure causes as little discomfort as possible.”
To conduct their research, Dragnea and his colleagues studied 204 people who were undergoing an MRI of the brain, spine, head, or neck, and divided them into four groups. One group listened to soft relaxation music similar to what’s played during a massage; one listened to a Mozart composition; one listened to their personal favorite songs; and the fourth, a control group, did not listen to music. For the first three groups, the music was played before, during, and after the insertion of a cannula, which is a port-like tube slid into a vein for the purpose of administering medication, general anesthetic, or contrast dye before an MRI.
The Mozart music was not just any selection, but Sonata K488, written for two pianos, in D major. This song made headlines in 1993 when a study published in the journal Nature found that listening to classical music—and that composition in particular—was linked to improved memory, problem-solving, and spatial-temporal reasoning. Though the mechanism involved wasn’t firmly established, the finding gave rise to what became known in science as the "Mozart effect.” The songs chosen by the group that listened to their favorite tunes included, among others, AC/DC’s Safe in New York City, Lionel Richie’s Hello, and the Crash Test Dummies’ Mmm Mmm Mmm Mmm.
People were asked to rate their pain before and after the cannula insertion. Those who listened to the soft relaxation music or no music had no significant pain reduction before, during, or after the procedure. There are possible reasons the lilting, generic music was ineffective. “Relaxation music is usually characterized by a slow speed and low volume, and does not show noticeable dynamics,” said Dr. Meritxell Garcia Alzamora, a neuroradiologist at the University Hospital Zürich and senior author of the study, in a statement. “These characteristics may have contributed to the patients disregarding relaxation music, which would explain the lack of pain relief.”
The other two groups did show some pain relief after listening to music. Those who heard the Mozart composition and those who listened to their favorite songs experienced significant pain reduction two minutes after the procedure. The “favorite music” group even had a bonus pain-relief perk that no other group experienced: just 30 seconds after the procedure, they rated their pain lower than the other groups, compared to their baseline.
Why does some music appear to have an analgesic effect? The researchers did not try to answer the question definitively, but their findings did raise some possibilities. Listening to music, they write in the study, may trigger the release of endorphins, chemical messengers that bind to opioid receptors to reduce or eliminate pain. Music may also calm the body down, with a resulting reduction of blood pressure, heart rate, anxiety, and stress—all of which may reduce pain. Being distracted by music may also engage the brain’s limbic system and prefrontal networks, activating pain mediation networks. Those neural regions are known to have a somewhat delayed effect, which could explain why people experienced relief two minutes after the needle. It’s possible, too, the researchers concede, that the music wasn’t what was responsible for reduced pain, but rather the presence of a friendly, distracting experimenter in the room.
Going forward, the investigators plan to explore other types of classical music beyond Mozart that may have similar—or even superior—pain-relieving benefits. They also hope to determine if music can serve as an analgesic for more severe pain than needle sticks.
There are a lot of pharmacological approaches in an anesthesiologist’s toolkit. Music—no-cost, easy, and absent risk—could be a valuable drug-free addition.

Ethiopia and Eritrea accuse one another of launching war
Eritrea denies backing TPLF as Ethiopia alleges collusion, further straining their already volatile relationship.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an “all-out invasion” in a message to the United Nations Security Council, while Eritrea says it is facing a “war of aggression” from its neighbour.
“The all-out invasion of parts of northern Ethiopia by Eritrea is a matter of public record,” said a letter by Ethiopia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Gedion Timothewos, which was shared with news agencies on Friday.
“It is a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence,” added the letter dated Thursday and addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.
Gedion said that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and demanded their withdrawal, just days after the two nations cut diplomatic ties.
Eritrea’s Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel rejected Ethiopia’s claims.
“The Ethiopian regime has been pursuing, in effect, an unprovoked war of aggression against Eritrea for more than three years now,” he said on X.
Yemane said Asmara had shown restraint since landlocked Ethiopia had essentially declared a war against Eritrea when it stated in 2023 that it would gain access to the sea.
Citing statements made by Ethiopian officials, Yemane accused Addis Ababa of using the current conflict to take Assab, an Eritrean port, in order to restore access to the Red Sea.
Eritrea also denied Ethiopia’s claim that it is backing the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which is part of an alliance of seven armed groups that has been attempting to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government since September.
Over the past week, Ethiopia’s army has pushed back the TPLF and seized the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle.
Witnesses also told the AFP news agency that rebels had lost the Tigrayan cities of Shire and Adigrat. Eritrean troops were reportedly seen in Adigrat before Ethiopian drone strikes hit them, according to several witnesses.
Tumultuous history
Ethiopia and Eritrea have traded accusations since the reported incursions by Eritrean troops this week raised fears of outright war in the region, where the two nations have fought previous conflicts.
The stakes have been raised this time around by conflicts in the Horn of Africa region and tensions across the Red Sea.
Diplomatic ties between the two have collapsed amid the escalation: Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country last week. In response, Eritrea announced it was severing ties.
The neighbours have a tumultuous history, as Eritrea won independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and they fought a border war for two years in 1998.
Relations improved slightly in 2018 when Abiy took power in Addis Ababa, and Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.
Eritrea, however, was not part of the peace deal that ended the war, which soured ties soon afterwards.
Tensions are also fuelled by Abiy’s repeated claim that landlocked Ethiopia – which lost its access to the coast when Eritrea secured independence – has a right to sea access, which Eritrea sees as a threat to seize its Red Sea port of Assab.

"No warning shots were known to have been fired," Mantoo said.
The office stressed that all detentions must comply with international law and that detainees' fundamental rights must be respected.
"No person may be detained absent proper basis in international law, and the important procedural guarantees under applicable international human rights and humanitarian law that protect any individual taken into custody must be fully respected," Mantoo said.

Sources told the agency on October 8 that the meeting would take place on Friday and would include preparations for trilateral Ukraine-USA-Russia talks. The information was confirmed by sources in the negotiating group and the Office of the President of Ukraine.
The delegation includes National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov, first deputy head of the Presidential Office Serhiy Kyslytsia, and Servant of the People parliamentary faction leader David Arakhamia.
Axios previously reported, citing American and Ukrainian officials, that U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would meet the Ukrainian negotiating team and European officials in Miami on Friday to present new proposals aimed at breaking the deadlock in Russia's war against Ukraine.
Axios journalist Barak Ravid, citing an unnamed official, reported that Witkoff and Kushner had received briefings from Trump earlier this week ahead of the meeting with the Ukrainian delegation.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in Pryluky that the Ukrainian negotiating team was in Europe and was due to travel to the United States on Friday and Saturday.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed Ukraine's readiness to participate in trilateral peace talks in October and to consider different ceasefire arrangements, including an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact.
On October 1, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha told journalists that four proposals for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire with Russia had been put forward by the United States, India, Turkey and Egypt. Ukraine was ready for both an energy ceasefire and a Black Sea ceasefire, but only as a combined arrangement, he said.
“We are ready for different ceasefire formats, including an unconditional ceasefire along the current line of contact. We have conveyed all of this, and the Americans have accepted it and are also working on this track,” Sybiha said.
On September 12, Budanov told Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Yalta European Strategy meeting in Kyiv, organized by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation, that another round of trilateral peace talks could take place in October.
“We are preparing. For October,” Budanov said when asked whether preparations were under way for the next round of talks.

"We were detained like terrorists": UP journalist Mykhailo Tkach describes his detention in Vienna
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:11:00 EEST
23:11:00 KST

"We were detained like terrorists": UP journalist Mykhailo Tkach describes his detention in Vienna
Mykhailo Tkach, head of investigative journalism at Ukrainska Pravda, has described how armed masked men smashed the windows of his car and dragged him and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko out onto the road as they were arrested in Vienna. One of the men then knelt on Tkach's neck as he repeatedly insisted he was a journalist.
Source: Tkach in a video for UP
Quote: "It felt as if we were being treated like terrorists. They didn't speak to us at all. There was just a shocking amount of shouting – they were all yelling and pointing their weapons at us, and there was virtually no communication."
Details: Tkach said he and Bondarenko were driving between filming locations when their car stopped at a traffic light about 3-5 km from central Vienna. At that moment, seven armed masked men ran up to the car, smashed the windows and pointed their weapons at the journalists.
Tkach said he immediately raised his hand and told the men in English that he was a journalist. The men pulled Tkach and Bondarenko out of the car, forced them face down onto the road, searched them, and taped their hands behind their backs.
Quote: "I kept repeating that I was a journalist, but one of the men knelt on my neck and shouted at me to shut up.
Then they dragged me away – there was an archway nearby, so they dragged me through this archway, shoved my face against the wall and told me to keep quiet."
Details: According to Tkach, the masked men who detained him did not identify themselves or explain what they were doing. He saw no badges and did not immediately notice any police markings, so for the first 30-40 minutes he believed he and Bondarenko were being abducted.
He said he only realised the men were police officers when they led him out of the archway and he saw police cars. The journalist was then placed in a separate compartment in a minivan, which drove off with its sirens on for about 20 minutes.
Tkach said he has not seen Bondarenko since their detention. He recalled seeing shards of glass from the smashed car window fly into the cameraman's face.
At the police station, all of Tkach's belongings were confiscated and he was ordered to take off his shoes and placed in a solitary cell. He said he waited there for about two hours without any explanation, despite repeatedly asking officers why he had been detained. A doctor also visited him during that time to ask how he was feeling.
Eventually Tkach was taken to another room and told to strip naked. His clothes were confiscated, but his belongings were later returned. He was weighed and measured.
He was then asked to sign a document in German. When he refused on the grounds that he did not understand what it said, the police officer became angry and started shouting, he said.
Tkach was then taken to two people he believed were investigators. It was only then that a meaningful conversation began, he said.
Background:
- On 8 October, it was reported that Tkach had been detained in Vienna while carrying out an assignment from the editorial team involving tracking down the fugitive former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko.
- Tkach was in Austria with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko.
- The Ukrainian Embassy in Austria said it had asked the Austrian authorities to explain the circumstances surrounding Tkach's detention in Vienna.
- It later emerged that the Ukrainian consul had been granted access to Tkach and had spoken with him.
- In the morning, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry reported that Tkach had been released.
- Ukrainska Pravda editor-in-chief Sevğil Musaieva reported that Tkach had been released after being detained in Vienna, but the editorial team was unable to contact him, and that cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko had been injured during the detention.
- Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner stated that Tkach had been released following his detention in Vienna, but cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko remains in custody. The minister said the Ukrainians were detained on suspicion of espionage.

EU Urges Bulgaria to Help Identify Those Behind Black Sea Drone Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:11:00 UTC
23:11:00 KST

Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova
				
				
			  
			
            Bulgaria needs to take a more active role in identifying those responsible for drone attacks near Byala if it wants the European Union to impose sanctions on the perpetrators, EU officials in Brussels told Bulgarian media Club Z.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) presented ambassadors from EU member states with a new package of 12 proposed sanctions against Russia on the previous day, in response to recent hybrid attacks, including a drone incident in Leipzig in early August. This prompted questions about whether similar measures were being considered over the Black Sea incidents on October 6.
“For sanctions in the Council of the EU, Member States expect to be more active in trying to identify the perpetrators of the hybrid attacks and then propose legal entities and names to make progress,” the Brussels representatives told Club Z.
The EEAS proposal is expected to be discussed at the Foreign Affairs Council in Luxembourg on October 12, but Brussels stressed that this does not mean sanctions related to the activity will be adopted at that meeting.
The EU Council could also approve 1,569 proposed listings submitted last month. These include 743 individuals and 826 organizations, along with 77 additional entries connected to Russia’s parliamentary elections in September. The latter group includes candidates who took part in voting in Ukrainian territories illegally occupied by Russia, as well as several elected officials.
EU member states are also discussing ways to reduce the number of Russian diplomats in the bloc, according to the sources. The aim is to sharply restrict or even stop Russian hybrid attacks across the EU. Tightening existing visa restrictions for Russian citizens is under consideration for the same purpose of limiting subversive activity.
“We see how Russians are involved in hybrid attacks. We need to carefully examine how much they can travel around Europe. Some may be in good faith, but we need to examine them more seriously. The perpetrators of hybrid activity are mostly people around international organizations based in European capitals, accredited Russian diplomats. We also have a problem with ex-combatants from the war with Ukraine and we need to study the military files of visa applicants. Especially for fighters, we expect an agreement soon,” the Brussels representatives said.
They emphasized that substantial work remained, adding that the measures were not intended to punish the Russian population as a whole, but to strengthen the EU’s protection through visa controls.

US immigration chiefs defend shooting of New York man, attack 'sanctuary' policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:09:42 UTC
23:09:42 KST

US immigration chiefs defend shooting of New York man, attack 'sanctuary' policies
NEW YORK, Oct 9 - US immigration officials defended federal agents on Friday who shot and wounded a New York City man in his car with a young child believed to be his son in the back seat and rebuked Mayor Zohran Mamdani for his condemnation of immigration agents.
US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference that officers did not know the child was in the car at the time they opened fire and accused the man, a Dominican who was the target of the operation, of endangering both officers and the child.
The man, identified by officials as Oscar Belgal, refused to exit his car when approached by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on Thursday afternoon in Marble Hill, Manhattan's northernmost neighborhood.
Before Belgal, federal immigration officers had shot at least 21 people, killing 7 of them, across the US since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 promising record-breaking deportations, an unusually high number for civil law enforcement operations.
Marcos Charles, a senior ICE official, said at the press conference that Belgal accelerated his car and struck two ICE vehicles and appeared to be "going towards officers" when they began shooting.
In other violent incidents, initial accounts from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security have repeatedly been contradicted by video and other evidence, sometimes in court, and Reuters was unable to verify Charles' account.
Belgal suffered a superficial wound to his neck, Charles said. He is being held in a detention facility outside New York state. Belgal's 5-year-old son was in the back seat at the time, according to police.
Belgal can be seen sitting by a car with his hands cuffed behind him and patches of what appear to be fresh blood on the tarmac in a three-minute body-worn camera video released by the New York Police Department on Friday, with several agents dressed in plain clothes standing around him. One is holding a rifle and wearing a fluorescent reflective vest.
A crowd of angry onlookers gathered outside a corner store shouts at the agents from the sidewalk. Several city police officers pick up Belgal by his arms and legs, put him in their car and take him to a hospital.
"Yo, put pressure, put pressure!" one of the police officers instructs his colleagues with Belgal in the back of the police car.
Mullin said body-worn camera video from ICE agents would also be released.
Belgal is a Dominican who is in the country illegally and had previously evaded an effort by ICE agents to apprehend him in September, according to US officials. He pleaded guilty last year to fourth-degree grand larceny for stealing something from another person, leading to a sentence of five years on probation, and is due in court in December on charges of criminal sale of a controlled substance, to which he pleaded not guilty, according to New York court records.
Speaking to reporters late on Thursday at the scene of the shooting, Mamdani, noting he himself was an immigrant, condemned ICE as "rotten to the core" and said he had tried unsuccessfully to secure Belgal's release in phone calls with Trump and Mullin.
Mamdani said the shooting is "further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbors than they could ever have claimed to save."
In response on Friday, Mullin attacked Mamdani and criticized New York's "sanctuary" policies, which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authorities unless a person has been convicted of violent or otherwise serious felonies.
Trump says aggressive efforts to deport immigrants are necessary to protect the safety of native-born Americans.
Public defenders at agencies that have represented Belgal in court also condemned the shooting.
Legal Aid said in a statement the shooting amounted to "an urgent call to rein in ICE's use of force and hold federal immigration agents accountable," calling on city prosecutors to investigate the agents involved. REUTERS

Bangladesh’s mango diplomacy with India has reached its limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:09:16 UTC
23:09:16 KST

Bangladesh’s mango diplomacy with India has reached its limits
Cultural gestures have kept relations from collapsing, but repairing ties with New Delhi will require difficult political negotiations.
For two years, Dhaka has deployed a soft diplomatic arsenal of prized Haribhanga mangoes, hilsa fish, jamdani fabrics, and Tangail sarees to keep its relationship with New Delhi from freezing into permanent estrangement. These gestures kept doors open, preserved public channels, and prevented temporary friction from decaying into absolute hostility.
Yet, as the dust settles, a cold geopolitical reality remains visible. Soft power can create an opening, but it cannot settle the hard politics waiting behind it. There comes an inevitable point in every strained diplomatic relationship when the mangoes have simply done all they can.
Since the mass uprising that began in Bangladesh in July 2024 and toppled Sheikh Hasina’s increasingly authoritarian rule of 15 years, Bangladesh has sought to avoid sharp confrontation with India. The instruments chosen by Dhaka were conspicuously soft.
Cultural programmes, textile exhibitions, hilsa festivals and trade gestures were paired with a determined effort by the Bangladeshi High Commission in New Delhi to keep talking to Indian counterparts, even when the respective governments had little pleasant to say to each other. This campaign was not entirely pointless. It was merely incapable of bearing the political weight eventually demanded of it.
A basket of mangoes can generate a momentary thaw. A saree exhibition can fill a grand room with appreciative visitors. A shipment of the coveted silvery delicacy of hilsa can evoke profound nostalgic warmth in Kolkata. None of these things, however, can determine the fate of Hasina, settle disputes over shared river waters, rebuild shattered political trust, or address the core security anxieties of two tightly interconnected neighbouring states.
That fundamental distinction – between keeping a diplomatic relationship alive and actually repairing its broken core – now defines the delicate balance between Bangladesh and India.
The limits of this approach were demonstrated clearly in 2025. In July, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus’s erstwhile interim administration dispatched 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) of high-grade Haribhanga mangoes to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, alongside additional consignments for senior officials and political leaders across New Delhi.
The gesture was interpreted as a deliberate signal that Dhaka sought normal, functional ties despite the intense bitterness that followed Hasina’s overthrow and her subsequent flight to Indian soil. The mangoes arrived swiftly on schedule. The heavy political problems remained exactly where they were.
Hasina remained in India while authorities in Dhaka pursued her formal extradition. The two capitals argued persistently over border management, transit rights, and the treatment of Bangladeshi citizens. Visa services, long a bellwether of bilateral warmth, were suspended and later resumed after Tarique Rahman’s BNP came to power in February this year. But the number of visas issued has still not returned to pre-2024 levels.
Unresolved questions concerning shared water resources, bilateral trade imbalances, and regional security continued to linger without resolution. Soft diplomacy was, at best, a pleasing sweetener rather than the main course.
Few pursued this softer strategy more visibly than Bangladesh’s outgoing envoy in New Delhi, M Riaz Hamidullah. Under his leadership, the High Commission experimented energetically with cultural outreach. The first jamdani exposition in Delhi, held in September 2025, brought traditional Bangladeshi weaving into an Indian artistic space where shared history was obvious.
In April 2026, the mission mounted another exhibition displaying 300 handloom sarees sourced directly from master weavers in Tangail and Pabna. The response from the Indian capital was positive.
As for cultural diplomacy, the initiative was a success. Indian connoisseurs arrived in droves, designers exchanged ideas, and sarees sold out within 24 hours. The shared Bengali cultural inheritance proved far easier to discuss than shared rivers. There was sound logic behind this tactic: building constituencies within Indian society who did not view Bangladesh strictly through the lens of immediate political quarrels provided a crucial buffer.
The diplomatic mistake lies in confusing access with real influence. A sold-out textile exhibition proves Indian admiration for Bangladeshi craftsmanship; it does not indicate agreement with Dhaka’s strategic posture. Cultural familiarity has never guaranteed political convergence in South Asia.
If it did, Dhaka and Kolkata would have settled every bilateral disagreement over hilsa-laden lunch decades ago. Indeed, even the fabric eventually ran into politics when the Tangail exhibition became entangled in contentious debates over heritage claims and geographical indication status.
Atmospherics inevitably run out of room. Sooner or later, formal political engagement must take over. Nothing illustrates this shift better than the continuing efforts to arrange a visit by Tarique Rahman to New Delhi. India extended invitations for both a direct bilateral visit and attendance at the BRICS summit in his capacity as chair of BIMSTEC.
Rahman did not make the journey. Dhaka noted that a high-level summit required an appropriate environment and mutual respect, while Indian officials publicly underscored that invitations had been extended without producing a visit.
This polite impasse revealed the true state of affairs. A prime ministerial visit requires a substantive agenda, careful political preparation, and deliverable outcomes that both leaders can sell to domestic audiences. India’s high commissioner in Dhaka, Dinesh Trivedi, has repeatedly urged direct top-level dialogue, emphasising that direct contact between leaders is necessary to resolve outstanding issues.
Soft diplomacy operates best when the underlying strategic foundation is already functional. When two governments agree on the fundamentals, cultural affinity adds warmth and colour. When they clash over fundamental interests, soft power can prevent complete rupture, but it cannot negotiate the terms of reconciliation.
India’s previous relationship with Dhaka rested on deep security cooperation, energy links, and established political arrangements. Hasina’s removal dismantled that comfortable architecture.
The leadership in Dhaka now demands a new equilibrium based strictly on sovereignty, reciprocity, and strategic flexibility. New Delhi maintains its own sharp concerns regarding regional security and Dhaka’s shifting external alignments.
These are complex matters involving trade treaties, water allocation, border enforcement, and intelligence cooperation. They cannot be managed by cultural envoys or resolved over dinner menus.
The gestures of the past two years were not failures; they preserved vital space during a turbulent political transition. But symbolism is now yielding diminishing returns. Both capitals understand that the next phase of South Asian geopolitics cannot be stitched together with fabric or negotiated over fruit. The mangoes succeeded in keeping the diplomatic door open. Real political bargaining must now walk through it.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

AfD and Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance in Saxony-Anhalt call for a halt to aid for Ukraine and an end to Russia sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:06:27 UTC
23:06:27 KST

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) have introduced a resolution in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament calling for an end to aid for Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia. Regional AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the state’s premier, posted a video on social media outlining the proposal. Political scientists interviewed by The Insider said the resolution has no legal force because Germany’s federal states do not have authority over foreign policy.
AfD and BSW lawmakers submitted the resolution to the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag (state parliament), calling for an end to military deliveries to Ukraine and the lifting of sanctions on Russia. The document states:
“The policy of sanctions against Russia, economic embargoes, and arms deliveries and financial aid to Ukraine has failed. The West’s one-sided partisanship in the war in Ukraine has not helped to end the war; rather, it prolongs the suffering of the population and increases the risk of the war spreading to other countries. The energy and economic war directed against Russia is causing massive damage to industry, commerce, and trade in Germany, as well as to our citizens.”
In the resolution, AfD and BSW call for diplomacy to become the main focus, for sanctions against Russia to be lifted immediately, and for financial and military support for Ukraine to end at once. The authors also call for Ukraine to retain neutral-state status while urging the Saxony-Anhalt government to “use all means at its disposal…to launch a corresponding initiative in the Bundesrat,” the German federal government’s upper legislative chamber.
Local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund wrote on X:
“Not even 24 hours have passed since the constituting session [the first meeting of the newly elected parliament], and we are already getting to work. We are applying for a peace initiative and a special session of the state parliament. End the war, end the payments to Ukraine!”
German political scientist Alex Yusupov, head of the Russia Program at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES), told The Insider that, from a legal standpoint, the resolution introduced by the far right and populist left has no force. He said the fact that AfD and BSW made foreign policy, rather than regional problems, the first initiative of the new state parliament shows that both parties “continue to pursue a public relations strategy rather than practical policymaking.”
“It is simply a resolution, meaning a public statement of the Landtag’s position, nothing more and nothing less. It is a call to action and an appeal,” Yusupov added.
Dimitri Stratievski, director of the Eastern Europe Centre Berlin (Osteuropa-Zentrum Berlin), told The Insider that all the issues raised in the resolution fall exclusively under the authority of Germany’s federal government, meaning AfD and BSW have no ability to carry out what they are demanding. He said:
“This is a populist move. But it is notable that, for their first test initiative, they chose an issue that has nothing to do with state-level politics. I think that was deliberate, because no concrete decisions are expected here and there is no political responsibility attached. Voters cannot hold these two parties accountable for promises they fail to keep. At the same time, AfD and BSW need to send signals to their voters.
As a rule, voters for right-wing and left-wing populists are not especially familiar with how powers are divided among different levels of government. And even if some are, it is not particularly important to them. They want the sense that their representatives in government are dealing with major issues. Ending weapons deliveries to Ukraine is also important to them because they believe it would save federal budget money at a difficult time.
In addition, to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, AfD would have to enter a coalition with the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance. And they very much do not want to do that. The far right is not enthusiastic about the prospect of partnering with people who spent a long time in the left-wing party and are supposed to be strong opponents of the right. BSW does not look like a reliable coalition partner for AfD. But a joint statement like this on Ukraine — which cannot have concrete political consequences — is a trial balloon and an attempt to demonstrate some common ground and pull the two parties closer together.”
Stratievski noted that Ulrich Siegmund is already presenting himself as the leader of Saxony-Anhalt, framing his statements as though they were being made on behalf of the state even though he has not yet become its premier:
“Siegmund is behaving like a state official without having any authority to do so, but he has repeatedly said that he will become the state premier in December. He is doing this deliberately. On the one hand, he is mobilizing supporters. On the other, he is trying to impose on his political opponents a sense that it is inevitable that he, Ulrich Siegmund, will become the next premier of Saxony-Anhalt. It is a psychological and political tactic designed to convey the idea that ’the matter is settled, and I am already behaving like the acting head of the state.’”
In early September, AfD finished first in Saxony-Anhalt’s state election with nearly 44% of the vote. The far-right party won 39 of the Landtag’s 83 seats. The left-populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance won five seats and said it was prepared to cooperate with AfD.
On Oct. 6, AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch, 35, became the first far-right politician in postwar German history to be elected speaker of a state parliament, taking the top post in the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag by a vote of 48-34. AfD and BSW together controlled 44 votes, meaning Rausch received support from at least four lawmakers outside either party. Because the ballot was secret, it is unclear who backed him, though speculation in Germany has focused on members of the CDU, the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The other parties in the Landtag had said they would not support Rausch.

Another Sudanese rebel commander defects to army – media
Unknown

Another Sudanese rebel commander defects to army – media
Another senior commander of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has defected to the Sudanese army, bringing around 300 fighters and 30 military vehicles with him, The Sudan Times reported on Thursday.
Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari, who identified himself as commander of the RSF’s Special Tasks Group, announced his departure in a video circulated on Thursday. He described the conflict as a “futile war.”
“I, Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari ... announce my resignation and withdrawal from all military duties and responsibilities within the ranks of the Rapid Support Forces,” he said. Fanjari apologized to Sudanese families who had lost relatives, been displaced or suffered during the fighting.
The local news agency said the number of personnel accompanying Fanjari could not be independently verified, while the RSF has not publicly confirmed the scale of the reported defection.
The move comes as Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has ruled out negotiations with the RSF, pledging to continue military operations until the paramilitary group is defeated. “We say it again: We have no negotiations with anyone, we are not speaking with anyone, and we have nothing to do with anyone,” Burhan said on Tuesday during a visit to Northern State.
Sudan’s conflict erupted in April 2023 following months of tensions between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
Several senior RSF commanders have switched sides since 2024. Abuagla Keikal, commander of the Sudan Shield Forces, defected in October that year, followed by Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as Al-Nour al-Qubba, in April 2026 and Ali Rizqallah, also known as Al-Savana, in May 2026.
More recently, around 200 RSF fighters led by Abubakr Hamouda Dahloub, identified as the group’s intelligence chief in North Kordofan, joined the army in late August, Sudan’s state news agency SUNA reported. Another 50 fighters reportedly defected in Omdurman in September, according to the Sudan Tribune. On Saturday, an additional 106 fighters, including 18 officers, from the paramilitary group reportedly switched sides in North Darfur.

Estonia pushes firm to drop Russian supplier after EU strategic project nod

Estonia pushes firm to drop Russian supplier after EU strategic project nod
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) expects NPM Silmet to set a deadline for ending the use of Russian raw materials as it receives EU backing for a major expansion.
The European Commission on Friday selected Silmet 2.0 as one of 46 new strategic projects for bolstering the EU's supply of critical raw materials. Tsahkna said the project must come with a firm deadline for ending the company's reliance on Russian raw materials.
"We will work with the European Commission to set a clear deadline for NPM Silmet to stop using Russian raw materials," he said, emphasizing that the company must move quickly to alternative suppliers as with strategic status comes responsibility.
"We cannot allow an industry critical to Europe's security to remain dependent on supplies from an aggressor state," the minister added.
Silmet 2.0 is an investment and development plan to adapt the Sillamäe-based plant's infrastructure and production processes to new raw material sources, allowing its strategically important output for Europe to continue.
Alongside ramping up pressure on Russia via sanctions, Europe also has to strengthen its own production capacity and find new sources of supply, Tsahkna said, adding that the Silmet project would help bolster the EU's economic security.
"Estonia continues to support strong sanctions against Russia," he stressed.
Russian supplier dropped from sanctions package
Earlier this week, Estonia successfully pushed to exclude a Russian company that supplies rare earth metals to NPM Silmet from the EU's proposed 22nd sanctions package against Russia, which is awaiting formal approval.
The Foreign Ministry says NPM Silmet plays a crucial role in Europe's critical raw materials supply chain, with its products used in the electronics, medicine, automotive, aviation and defense industries.
EU strategic projects aim to secure supplies of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on third countries.

Israel opens first-ever booth at Morocco defence show with firms behind Gaza drones, bombs
Israel’s Ministry of Defence announced on Thursday that it had participated for the first time in a defence exhibition in Morocco, with experts telling The New Arab that this marks a more "public" relationship between the two countries.
In a statement, the ministry said it opened a pavilion at the Marrakesh Airshow 2026 for the first time, and that it also marked the first time it had participated in such an event in the kingdom since the signing of the controversial Abraham Accords of 2020.
“Eight Israeli defense companies exhibited advanced, combat-proven technologies at the show, including loitering munitions, AI-powered robotic systems, autonomous navigation capabilities for UAVs, laser guidance for FPV drones, satellite communications, and more,” the statement read.
“Alongside the IMOD pavilion, Israel's three major defense industries, Elbit Systems, IAI - Israel Aerospace Industries, and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, also exhibited, presenting solutions across the air, land, sea, space, intelligence, cyber, and digital domains,” it continued.
The Israeli ministry further said its attendance at the exhibition formed part of a strategy to increase defence exports and cooperation with countries around the world.
Their participation at the expo comes at the same time Gaza marked three years since the start of the genocide, where Israeli forces have killed over 74,000 people since October 2023.
Israeli arms firms frequently market weapons tested in the occupied Palestinian territories as "battle tested".
The expo, which started on 7 October, takes place every two years and sees firms from the space and military industries showcase their latest offerings.
Many activists and campaigners have lambasted Israel’s attendance at the event, calling it a sign of warming relations between the two.
Yassin Akouh, an independent journalist specialising in Morocco and author of Colonial Curse (Koloniale Vloek), a book on the colonial legacy in Morocco, told The New Arab that the relationship between Rabat and Tel Aviv is not new.
"This relationship is not new. Under Hassan II, Morocco and Israel cooperated for decades, mostly behind closed doors...what has changed since 2020 is not the relationship itself. What has changed is that it now happens in the open, and increasingly in the military and security sphere. The role of the the pro-Israel lobby in shaping American policy in the region, is well documented and should not be underestimated," he said.
He also noted his surprise at seeing some support for normalisation in Morocco.
"What shocks me is how shameless it has all become," he said, but noted that much of the population still stands in solidarity with the Palestinians.
"Moroccan society remains deeply attached to the Palestinian cause. Since October 2023, tens of thousands have repeatedly taken to the streets, and ending normalisation has become a constant demand. In general, the state tolerates the marches but has prosecuted activists who went further online," he said.
"What comes next? Ambassadors, investment and tax agreements, more direct flights, high-level visits and, above all, deeper defence cooperation. I don't expect mass unrest over this alone. The anger is real, but the monarchy is a red line, and the king's foreign policy is not open to public debate. Still, the gap between the palace and the street is growing, and every new step widens it," he continued.
Last month, nationwide protests in Morocco demanded an end to normalisation with Israel, as well as stronger solidarity with Palestinians.
The demonstrations followed a 16 September announcement in New York by Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz that Morocco and Israel would upgrade their liaison offices to embassies and appoint ambassadors.
Morocco and Israel recently agreed to expand in the air travel sector, with direct flights operated by carriers from both nations resuming and plans for high-level visits drawn up and set to take place in the coming months.

US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, hours after former judge wins Nobel
- The Trump administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, hours after former judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, deepening tensions with European allies.
- Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with the “rogue court” and cut off resources, over ICC cases involving Israeli officials and past scrutiny of US troops in Afghanistan.
- The ICC and EU allies face pressure to respond, as the court prepares for wider sanctions that could hit banking, software and services, while Washington demands the court “rein in” its actions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Oct 9, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.
The Oct 9 move would go much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
Washington has long been angry over ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the US and Turkey.
It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries, including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Oct 9 for her work in international criminal justice, served as a judge on the ICC’s Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008. In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack”.
“An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world,” the committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
He did not provide further details, but a senior State Department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licences “to protect American interests”, an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions.
US expects allies to ‘rein in the court’
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during Trump’s first term, which were rescinded under then president Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court’s registrar, Osvaldo Zavala Giler, called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called “blocking mechanism” that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the US had delayed its sanctions, hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.
“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defence, to rein in the court,” Rubio said.
“We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly,” Rubio said. REUTERS

OPSGROUP, a membership-based organisation with almost 10,000 aviation professionals that shares flight risk information, sent a "do not fly" warning for Saudi Arabia to its members on Friday, citing risks of sustained missile attacks and "misjudgment" in defensive responses.
"We now recommend avoiding operations in Saudi Arabia entirely, including the use of Saudi airports as en route alternates," it said in the memo shared with Reuters.
AIRLINES SUSPEND FLIGHTS

Canadians ‘worried’ about US travel as Trump’s policies make travelers feel unwelcome: Former premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:03:15 UTC
23:03:15 KST

Fahri Aksüt
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
US President Donald Trump’s immigration and border policies make Canadians uneasy about traveling to the US for the first time, a concern reflected in tourism figures, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said.
Trudeau, speaking at the opening session on Friday of the World Travel & Tourism Council’s (WTTC) 26th Global Summit held in the Maltese capital of Valletta, stated that for the first time, many Canadians are “worried” about crossing the border.
“In the past number of years, the US hasn’t been very good at making travelers feel welcome, whether it’s the thickening of the borders, the worries about what can happen if you get arrested at the border,” he said. “Because, for decades, generations, Canadians and Americans criss-crossing our shared border, the longest unmilitarized border in the world, has been something we almost took for granted, and the family, personal, and business connections have been huge and strong.”
Trudeau stated that the real issue is Washington’s attitude towards Canada, particularly “this disrespect that the president has shown, in terms of saying it’s not a real country.”
“I think, first of all, (it’s important to) understand that some governments get along, some governments don't get along, and that's the reality,” he said. “Looking at what, how people are feeling — like, even when we were facing difficulties with the United States, we didn't impose penalties or raise prices or make it more difficult for people to travel to the United States, for example.”
The former prime minister noted that the number of Canadians traveling to the US declined by more than 20% and that, to compensate, American tour operators, airlines, and hotels lowered their prices, but to no avail in changing Canadians' travel preferences.
“At places like Florida, Arizona, even nearby places like Maine or elsewhere, (they’re) coming to tell Canadians, ‘it’s okay, we still like you, Please come back’ — we know Canadians still like Americans, Americans still like Canadians, but conflict between governments and disrespect from the US government has caused Canadians to say, ‘Okay, let's look at other places to go,’ and that has been a really important shift, but also a telling one, that how the mood of a country, how people are made to feel welcome, is an extremely important part of tourism,” he said.
He recalled that early bookings for the North American World Cup were affected because travelers felt hesitant about entering the US.
“Now, the US actually was very successful in welcoming lots of people from around the world who had a wonderful experience discovering North America, discovering how wonderful and nice Americans are. But at the same time, in the run-up to the World Cup, we saw that bookings were down, we saw people worried about going to the United States, not sure if they wanted to go to the United States, and there was a point at which people were worrying that it might not be a huge success. It ended up being a success, but countries need to be a little more consistent. If they want tourism dollars, they have to show themselves as being open to the world, which is something that Canada always did well,” he added.

Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
The 85-year-old South African judge has spent decades fighting apartheid and genocide.
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the fifth South African to win it.
Making the announcement on Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee praised Pillay for her decades-long efforts to prosecute genocide and war crimes, which have been marked by “judicial rigour, personal integrity and considerable courage”.
From defending activists in apartheid-era South Africa, to more recently overseeing a United Nations inquiry which declared Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, the 85-year-old, who is also a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has specialised in international law for decades.
Here’s what we know about her life and why she has been awarded the world’s top peace prize:
Who is Pillay?
Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi Pillay, was born in the racially segregated city of Durban in South Africa’s Natal province in 1940 to parents of Tamil descent.
After earning a law degree from the University of Natal, she became the first woman in Natal province to start her own law firm. Early in her career, she helped defend numerous anti-apartheid activists in the country.
She later became the first woman of colour to sit on the High Court of South Africa. She went on to preside over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), which prosecuted those charged with humanitarian crimes during the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Pillay was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) from 2008 to 2014. More recently she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory which determined last year that Israel is responsible for carrying out genocide in Gaza.
Currently, Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice, acting in a case in which Myanmar is accused of genocide against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.
What work is she best known for?
Pillay has spent much of her life advocating for human rights in her home South Africa and abroad. While studying, she took part in boycotts and marches against apartheid. She later joined the legal defence of some of the country’s most prominent anti-apartheid figures, such as Phyllis Naidoo and Strini Moodley.
In 1973, Pillay took on a case that helped secure basic rights, including legal access, for political prisoners on Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was jailed.
In a 2016 interview with the Diplomatic Courier, Pillay said her early human rights work was “shaped by what (she) had experienced under apartheid”.
“I used many of the challenges to my advantage, I had to learn international humanitarian law so as to defend cases of racial discrimination,” she said.
Pillay oversaw a UN commission of inquiry which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
In a statement on the report, Pillay urged UN member states to do everything they can to establish a ceasefire in Gaza and to “ensure justice and accountability for all victims”.
What has she been awarded the Nobel Prize for?
The Nobel committee said Pillay was being honoured for her “efforts to promote peace and international law”.
It called her one of “the great defenders of international legal principles in our time”, having helped hold states and national leaders to account and bring “hope to victims of violence and conflict”.
The committee stressed the role Pillay played in the Rwandan genocide tribunal, saying her influence helped establish “that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide”.
“In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” said the committee.
Why is her win so significant?
The committee said honouring Pillay is especially important at a time when international law “is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack”.
That message was echoed by rights advocates and international officials.
The UN’s rights chief, Volker Turk, said her award was “a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security and prosperity”.
International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane said the award carried special significance “at a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law”.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa praised the award as a tribute to Pillay’s “courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.
Haakon Gjerlow, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said it “sends a clear message that peace depends not only on political leadership, but on strong, credible international institutions and the courageous people who dedicate their lives to defending them .”
Ashok Swain, a professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, told Al Jazeera that the selection of Pillay was a “pleasant surprise” and the “best possible choice”.
He said the Nobel committee likely took into consideration Pillay’s lifelong record fighting genocide and apartheid. He added that the award to the South African jurist could also be read as a message to United States President Donald Trump, who has long argued that he is deserving of the peace prize and whose administration has clashed with South Africa over debunked claims that white Afrikaners are facing “genocide”.
Furthermore, last year, the Trump administration issued sanctions against members of the ICC in what many critics saw as an attack on the system of international law.
The ICC had previously issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The ICC responded by describing the US sanctions as a “flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution” and the victims of war crimes around the world. It said it would continue its work “without regard to any restriction, pressure or threat”.
How has Pillay responded?
Pillay appeared to learn of the award as media reports circulated, telling a group of supporters applauding her: “I don’t know about this. So my question is: Is it true?”
She also jokingly referenced Trump, saying, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
Once the news was confirmed, Pillay said she would dedicate the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes”.
“This award strengthens my conviction that we must stand together in defence of the rule of law, in defence of independent courts and an international legal order based on principle.”
Earlier, the Nobel committee said it had struggled to get in touch with Pillay to notify her. “If you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up,” said committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Launch Institute and Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Disposal Facility
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian missile-related facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region overnight on October 9, targeting infrastructure involved in missile launch systems and the disposal of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the strikes, identifying the targets as a branch of the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and a facility responsible for dismantling intercontinental ballistic missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces hit a facility belonging to the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes, a branch of the Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure, near the settlement of Dalneye Konstantinovo-5.
The institute specializes in the development, maintenance, and operation of missile launch positions, fueling equipment, and missile control systems, making it part of Russia's missile infrastructure.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian forces targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near the settlement of Surovatikha, also in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
The General Staff said the strike was intended to weaken Russia's military-industrial capacity to produce explosives and components used in rocket propellants.
In addition to the two facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Russia's Tver region.
The Redkino Experimental Plant is a major chemical production facility in Russia’s Tver region, specializing in small-batch manufacturing of specialty chemicals. The enterprise produces more than 40 types of chemical products supplied to Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Its product range includes ferrocene-based compounds used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, alongside specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These substances serve both civilian industrial purposes and military production needs.
Ukrainian forces also targeted the Lukoil-Ukhtaneftepererabotka oil refinery in Ukhta, Russia's Komi Republic, approximately 1,700 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, as Kyiv continues strikes against Russian energy facilities in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian territory.

Fjord Details a Family’s Sudden Nightmare in Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:02:05 UTC
23:02:05 KST

Romanian filmmaker Cristian Mungiu makes thoughtful movies about social issues that cross international borders: In 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days, a young Romanian woman risks her life for an illegal abortion. R.M.N. explores xeno-phobia in a small Transylvanian village, dissecting the complexity of spontaneous human impulses in the process. Mungiu’s films can spur us to think anew about issues we’d rather keep in the background, and they can at times be deeply moving. They can also feel dreary and instructive, in an eat-your-vegetables way.
Mungiu’s Fjord, which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes earlier in the year, offers a healthy dose of very nutritious vegetables, and in places the story almost—almost—stretches the bounds of believability. But its actors, including Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, as well as two young newcomers, make you believe in one family’s sudden nightmare. Do the authorities entrusted to protect our children always know what’s best for them? Fjord suggests, provocatively, that the answer may not always be yes.
Mihai Gheorghiu (Stan), who is Romanian, and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Reinsve) have just relocated with their five children from Romania to Norway, to be closer to Lisbet’s parents. Mihai and Lisbet are also deeply religious, and appear to be raising their children in a sometimes strict but undeniably loving home. One day, at the children’s new school, an instructor charged with protecting the students’ welfare notices a bruise on the shoulder of the eldest Gheorghiu daughter, Elia (Vanessa Ceban). The administrator takes swift action, and before Mihai and Lisbet can fully grasp what’s happening, their children—including their infant, who’s still breastfeeding—are whisked into foster homes. Their struggle to reunite their family involves risky twists and a great deal of frustrating bureaucracy.
Unless you know Norway’s judicial system, you might be tempted to wonder: Could one family really be broken up that fast, with so little evidence? Mungiu’s premise seems somewhat far-fetched, intensified for dramatic reasons, though it’s worth noting that his script is based on a real-life case in Norway. And recently, in the U.S., Child Protective Services interviewed the children of former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, separating the children from their fathers for 24 hours, after receiving a tip alleging that they were at risk. The report was proved false, but the incident shows how easily a system designed to protect kids might be manipulated.
Regardless, the plausibility of Fjord’s premise is academic in the context of the performances given by Stan and Reinsve. Reinsve (so terrific in 2025’s Sentimental Value) is resolutely unglamorous here, a dutiful wife and mother decked out in dowdy clothes. But her distress over the loss of her children crosses the planes of her face like a muted shadow; you sense some anger beneath that meek veneer. And Stan, who is Romanian American, gives layers of complexity to Mihai as a father figure. He clearly loves his kids, but he also has a temper. Stan doesn’t make Mihai easy to read, just as the movie around him doesn’t offer any easy conclusions.
Yet amid all the child-custody drama Fjord lays before us, a subplot involving the deepening friendship between Elia and a neighbor couple’s daughter, Noora (Henrikke Lund-Olsen), ends up being the film’s most powerful and moving element. These two young teenagers aren’t just navigating a new friendship; they’re exploring feelings that may or may not be the roots of romantic love. Sometimes kids tell us what we need to know about life, even if it’s not always the lesson we expect or want. And sometimes they steal a movie away from the grownups. Fjord, perhaps unbeknownst even to the man who made it, really belongs to them.

The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said.
Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005.

Kyiv has 700 generators, but they cannot power city's main facilities
Around 700 generators are currently installed at Kyiv's heating and water supply facilities. However, the city's largest and most critical facilities require separate power plants to ensure a reliable backup power supply.
Source: Petro Panteleiev, acting First Deputy Head of Kyiv City State Administration, at a press briefing on 9 October
Details: The generators are used at boiler houses, heating substations, local pumping stations and other facilities. For example, 155 public drinking water pump rooms, which provide an additional source of drinking water in the event of temporary disruptions to the centralised system, are equipped with them.
"However, backup power for the main heating and water supply facilities can only be provided by building new diesel power plants or cogeneration units," Panteleiev said.
He noted that some backup power projects under Kyiv's Resilience Plan are already up and running, while the rest are scheduled to be completed by the end of the year, in line with the original plan.
Panteleiev added that utility workers are gradually stabilising the water supply in the city's Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts, where reduced pressure has been recorded.

- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously said that Kyiv's city authorities have almost completely failed to implement the necessary measures to protect energy infrastructure.
- The government has unblocked payments for some projects under Kyiv's Resilience Plan, specifically backup heating supplies, the construction of cogeneration plants and measures to ensure an uninterrupted power supply to water infrastructure.

South African human rights lawyer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting international justice and accountability for serious crimes.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the award Friday in Oslo, recognizing Pillay’s contributions to prosecuting war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
The committee praised her courage and integrity in advancing international law and defending human rights.
“Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict,” the committee said.
Pillay, 85, began her legal career in South Africa during apartheid, challenging racial discrimination and defending people who opposed the system.

She also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, overseeing international efforts to protect fundamental rights.
According to the committee, Pillay has consistently emphasized that individuals and governments must respect the rule of law.
The committee said the award was intended to highlight the importance of legal institutions in maintaining peace and resolving conflicts without violence.
The Nobel Peace Prize includes 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately 8 million DKK.
The prize was established under the will of Swedish inventor and chemist Alfred Nobel.
It recognizes individuals or organizations whose work has made significant contributions to peace, in accordance with the principles outlined in his will.
