In parched Hungary, volunteers build their own dams to hold onto vanishing water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:09:32 UTC
22:09:32 KST

In parched Hungary, volunteers build their own dams to hold onto vanishing water
LADANY-VOLGY, Hungary, Oct 9 - In a bone-dry valley in Hungary, forest workers and volunteers piled up terraces of logs and deadwood, hoping to catch any trickles of water that make it down the hillside when the rains finally come.
In other areas, other groups fanned out, building barriers across streams and small creeks — their own man-made "beaver dams" designed to pool water and prepare the landscape for an even hotter, drier future.
As of this week, they were still waiting for that rain after a drought-hit summer that brought river levels to record lows, disrupting everything from cargo barges to the country's Paks nuclear plant, which relies on flows of cooling water from the Danube.
But the teams working under the banner of the grassroots, volunteer "Water Guardians Movement" kept on building, getting ready.
'WE CAN IMPROVE THE SITUATION'
"The wells (on my farm) have practically run dry," said Bence Bardos, a forest engineer leading the team building terraces in the Ladany valley in eastern Hungary near the border with Slovakia.
"This is the impact from climate change and our special geography in the Carpathian basin."
There was little locals could do about that, he said. "But we can improve the situation by small steps, by reversing the water runoff and drainage," the 36-year-old added.
The volunteers are turning out in their hundreds to help the country build structures to retain rainwater and restore wetlands — techniques that mark a sharp turnaround from the past, when programmes focused on managing floods, not droughts.
Nearly a quarter of the country lies on floodplains, and experts spent decades draining wetlands and building canals to channel water away from the fields and open up more land for agriculture.
"We have regulated our rivers, cutting their bends, which means the rivers flow faster, which drains ground water nearby," Diana Ürge-Vorsatz, a professor at the Central European University in Vienna, said.
Much of that now needed to go into reverse. The important thing now was to "restore the original natural conditions as much as possible, to allow rivers to flow on longer routes and thus slower, and retain ground water in the winter-spring," Ürge-Vorsatz added.
The government announced a new strategy in August which prioritised "natural water retention methods" and, far from draining fields, said some farmland should be deliberately flooded.
RESEARCHERS 'CAN'T PERFORM A RAIN DANCE'
Agriculture, one of the planks of Hungary's economy, has borne the brunt of the drier conditions.
Many farmers have given up on maize and shifted to alternatives, as researchers work on drought-resistant varieties.
This was the first year when the harvested area of maize in Hungary fell below the area planted with sunflowers, said Zoltan Kende, associate professor at the Institute of Agronomy at the MATE University.
But even sunflowers have suffered from the drought.
"We have shown that dry weather alters the fatty acid composition of sunflowers, resulting in a change in oil quality," Kende added.
Researchers could not "perform a rain dance" but there were recommendations they could make on cultivation and other methods to help adaptation, he said.
"For each cultivated plant species, we investigate the optimal factors as for temperature, moisture ... that result in the fastest germination. This approach helps enhance resilience against drought damage."
Hungary's central bank has said the drought damage to agriculture would cut economic growth by 0.4 percentage points in 2026.
The challenges were already there to see as the volunteers worked on the slopes of Ladany valley.
Borbala Kanizsay, who was there with her husband, said the creek that ran past their nearby house ran dry in May for the first time she could remember. Most of her parched trees shed their leaves in July.
A "terrible sight," the 41-year-old added. "We must adapt to this situation that our climate has changed, and we must strive to keep Hungary a liveable place." REUTERS

The Treasury said Shelton will advise Bessent on currency policy, "with a particular focus on evaluating financial conditions in China."
Shelton is not known as a China expert. She authored "The Coming Soviet Crash" in 1989, followed by "Money Meltdown," about the need for a unified international monetary regime, in 1994. Before joining Treasury, Shelton was a senior fellow at the Independent Institute, a free market think tank, and, before that, at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University. She holds a Ph.D. in business administration from the University of Utah.
"Throughout her career, she has specialized in analyzing the internal monetary and financial conditions of nations and their impact on exchange rates," The Treasury said in its announcement, which will be released later Friday.
A bipartisan group of senators, including all Democrats and a handful of Republicans, rejected President Donald Trump's 2019 nomination of Shelton as a Fed governor over her views on Fed independence, her support for the gold standard and her questioning whether the U.S. needed a central bank.
Her appointment comes at what looks to be a time of turmoil at the Treasury regarding high-level personnel. A recent Wall Street Journal story cataloged seven Senate-confirmed officials who have left the department through the end of August. Only one position has been filled.
Bessent recently named David Zervos, former chief market strategist at Jefferies, as a counselor — the same job title as Shelton. Neither Shelton nor Zervos require Senate approval.
Correction: Shelton authored "Money Meltdown" in 1994. An earlier version misstated the year. David Zervos is former chief market strategist at Jefferies. An earlier version misspelled the firm's name.

Ukraine pushes Russia back in Donetsk as military, civilian casualties soar
Russia is fighting for settlements it once firmly held in Donetsk, and has retreated from many others, as Operation Vivaldi unfolds.
Russian forces continue to retreat in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
The Kremlin-aligned channel Rybar, on Telegram, said on October 7 that Moscow’s forces were losing villages south of Lyman, a town they have tried to capture as a springboard to mount a full-scale offensive on the “fortress belt” cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
A Ukrainian counteroffensive named “Operation Vivaldi” this year has reclaimed 175 square kilometres (67 square miles) of previously occupied land around Lyman.
“The enemy is using successes in the Lyman direction to develop attacks [east of Sloviansk], where Russian troops are forced to defend previously occupied positions and expend resources on restoring control, instead of launching their own offensive,” wrote Rybar.
“It is becoming increasingly clear that the possibility of storming the urban area [of Sloviansk] is receding into the more distant future.”
A key battle seems to be building for the village of Kryva Luka east of Sloviansk, which sits on high ground on the Russian-held right bank of the Siversky-Donets River, and which could serve as a base to launch counterattacks further east.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Reuters news agency that Operation Vivaldi was successful but incomplete.
To get as far as Kryva Luka, Russian sources acknowledged that Ukraine has recaptured settlements west of it. They blamed the Russian communications strategy of claiming settlements that have not been captured, giving away the plan of attack.
“Premature statements” aided Ukraine, said Rybar. “Some villages were declared liberated even before Russian units arrived, which allowed the enemy to accumulate forces there and launch counterattacks.”
Ukraine built up reserves in the Lyman area before unfolding its counteroffensive. That preparation seems to be yielding results.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said its campaign to disrupt the flow of Russian ammunition and fuel to the front struck a record number of air defence assets and targets more than 50km (30 miles) away in September.
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed Russia had captured 1,300sq km (500sq miles) of Ukraine in September, echoing claims by his generals.
The Institute for the Study of War, which monitors territorial advances using geolocated, open-source data, said Russia actually lost 80sq km (30sq miles) during that month.
The Russian casualty rate rose to a record for 2026 of 46,230 in September, according to Ukraine’s military.
Of these, 33,087 – more than 70 percent – were confirmed kills, said Ukraine.
The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said enemy casualties were up by 40 percent in the first five days of October, compared with the same period in September.
The Ukrainian military on October 7 counted 1,545,950 Russian dead and wounded for the entire full-scale invasion since 2022.
Putin’s response
Putin’s response has been to intensify bombing, causing civilian suffering.
Twenty-two people, five of them children, were killed in the city of Pryluky, in the northern Chernihiv region, when a Russian cruise missile demolished a five-storey apartment building on October 7, Putin’s birthday.
“Today, for Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘gifted’ the destruction of a residential building in Pryluky,” said Zelenskyy.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia unleashed 130 drones and 48 cruise missiles across 12 regions that day, as well as ballistics. At least two more people died in Kyiv and two in Oleksandria.
At least 30 people died in Kramatorsk on October 8, when a Russian bomb struck two city buses. Video of the emergency response showed bodies strewn across an avenue and in a park.
Recent analysis of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones Russia increasingly uses for many of its attacks makes it unlikely that these attacks on nonmilitary targets are accidental.
Ukraine’s military intelligence said the attacks use satellite and sophisticated inertial navigation systems, as well as a camera that reads landmark features and checks them against an on-board database – all three systems working in concert to ensure accurate navigation.
Ukraine has responded to the jet-powered drones by speeding up delivery of F-16 fighters from its allies, which are proving an effective first line of defence.
“Currently, F-16s are destroying between 50 percent and 60 percent of the drone attacks,” said Zelenskyy.
Ukraine is also testing five new types of interceptor drones, the most successful of which is 30 percent effective, and experimenting with small-scale missiles, Zelenskyy said.
A dozen AI-driven heavy machine-gun turrets have been placed around Kyiv as a last line of defence, with dozens more planned around the country.
These are a “facility-level” defence, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, a senior Defence Ministry adviser. “It can protect a warehouse, factory, bridge, or power substation.”
Russia has begun hitting bridges across the Dnipro River, striking Kyiv’s southern and northern bridges seven times in the first four days of October. It has previously struck the building where Ukraine’s cabinet met, as well as energy facilities feeding the city, in an effort to cause a blackout.
Russia’s jet-powered drones travel at more than 500km (310 miles) per hour and are more difficult to intercept than its propeller-driven Shahed drones.
Despite this, during the October 7 strike, Ukraine’s Air Force said it intercepted 80 percent of the jet-powered drones, 95 percent of the propeller-driven drones and 80 percent of cruise missiles.
On October 7, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv to announce a 1.3-billion-euro ($1.46bn) military aid package, and to sign agreements worth 8.5 billion euros ($9.5bn) to jointly develop drone defences and other weapons with Ukraine.
Merz’s visit was an important political gesture following recent elections in two German states where the pro-Russian AfD trounced his governing CDU party.
Ukraine continued long-range strikes inside Russia.
These struck refineries in Volgograd on October 2 and Bashkortostan on October 8, as part of a strategy to starve the Russian economy and military of fuel.
“Over 51 percent of the enemy’s oil refining capacity has been disabled,” said Ukraine’s military.
Ukraine also hit the Samara linear production and dispatch station, which its General Staff described as “a major hub for receiving, storing, and blending oil”.
The staff said eleven 20,000-tonne storage tanks and three 50,000-tonne storage tanks had been destroyed.
“The facility blends high- and low-sulfur oil from various fields to produce the export grade of oil known as Urals, which accounts for up to 50 percent of the total volume of Russian oil exports,” the military said.
Ukraine also struck military targets. On October 7, it struck the Astrakhan Gas Processing Plant, which extracts gaseous sulphur for use in explosives.
On October 4, it destroyed a Sukhoi Su-35 multi-role fighter and a Sukhoi Su-34 fighter-bomber on the Adygea airfield, and also hit the Seshcha airfield in Bryansk.
Its campaign of mid-range strikes to destroy Russian power supply in occupied areas had reached 456 between July 6 and October 3.

China Studies Ukraine as a Live War Lab—and Turns Battlefield Lessons Into PLA Training
China is conducting a large-scale, systematic study of Russia’s war against Ukraine, treating the battlefield as a “live textbook,” according to a new study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) published on October 7.
CSIS analysts reviewed more than 90 verified Chinese sources published between July 2022 and August 2026 and found that Chinese military thinkers are closely tracking how warfare is evolving in Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Some Chinese analysts have described 2024 as “the first year of the global drone war,” reflecting the degree to which unmanned systems have reshaped operations on land, at sea, and in the air.
Since that time, they are feeding lessons from drones, electronic warfare, naval attacks, and deep strikes into the modernization of the People’s Liberation Army,
According to the study, Chinese specialists can identify and document new battlefield tactics within roughly four months of their appearance, although integrating those lessons into doctrine, training, or procurement generally takes at least a year.
The PLA is studying the war largely from the perspective of a force that could itself become the target of similar tactics, placing particular emphasis on defensive measures. Ukrainian operations involving naval drones and strikes against Russian air bases have attracted especially close attention.
One of the clearest examples came after Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb in June 2025, when Ukrainian forces struck Russian strategic bombers at airfields deep inside Russia. Just 4.5 months later, according to CSIS, Chinese troops were already practicing defenses against comparable infiltration tactics.
China is also closely examining Ukraine’s use of fiber-optic FPV drones, which resist conventional radio-frequency jamming, as well as the evolving contest between unmanned systems and electronic warfare. Elements of those lessons are already appearing in Chinese military exercises.
To accelerate that process, the PLA has expanded reforms to its military education system and established new specialized universities intended to prepare personnel for emerging forms of warfare.
China’s defense industry is moving in parallel. CSIS found that Chinese companies are already displaying weapons influenced by lessons from Ukraine, including laser and microwave systems designed to defeat large numbers of drones.
The research suggests Beijing is not simply observing which weapons perform well, but studying how entire battlefield systems interact—from reconnaissance and electronic warfare to logistics, command structures, and layered drone defenses.
Previously, reports emerged that China was accelerating its naval modernization by constructing what appears to be the world’s first mothership designed to deploy full-sized uncrewed submarines.

Warnings before mobile traffic cameras reduced fines by 90 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

Warnings before mobile traffic cameras reduced fines by 90 percent
Speeding fines have dropped nearly 90% since July's higher intervention threshold and the August rollout of warning signs before mobile speed cameras. But the police says safer road design, not enforcement, is the real key to improving traffic safety.
The higher intervention threshold for speeding, which took effect in July, brought a drop of more than half in speeding violations. The impact of the warning signs introduced in August in front of mobile speed cameras has been even more noticeable — according to data from the first full month of use, the detection of violations has decreased by approximately 90 percent.
If in September of last year mobile speed cameras issued 26,228 fines, then in September of this year mobile cameras across Estonia issued a total of 2,939 fines, according to police statistics.
"This September there were two fewer cameras operating compared to last year, and part of the working time was spent installing warning signs, but this does not change the overall picture — the number of fines today is very small," said the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) spokesperson Uku Tampere.
Most drivers comply with speed limits
PPA traffic‑supervision chief Taavi Kirss explained that placing warning signs before mobile cameras has made their effect similar to stationary speed cameras.
"At the specific location where there is a speed camera with a warning sign, speeds are correctly reduced, and it is safer there, and violations generally do not occur," Kirss said. At the same time, he noted that once drivers leave the camera's area of influence, they often accelerate back to their usual speed. "If traffic supervision is not visible, there is no risk of being caught," he said.
According to the Transport Administration's latest survey, 77 percent of drivers comply with the speed limit, but for the rest, speeding remains a problem, Kirss noted.
According to Kirss, installing warning signs has not been without practical issues. Problems have been identified with placing signs in the landscape, and there have been situations where large trucks passing by have knocked the signs over.
The reduction in fines — and thus fine revenue — does not concern the police. "We have not looked at it, and fine revenue is not important from the police perspective. Our goal is directed at safety and reducing traffic accidents," Kirss emphasized.
Asked whether the police, having lost one effective method of catching speeders, plan to bring more patrols onto the roads or use alternative measures, Kirss answered no.
"The number of patrols will not increase; it remains the same as it has always been," he confirmed. Traffic will continue to be calmed with existing tools: mobile and stationary speed cameras and daily police patrols.
Safe infrastructure replaces supervision
The police's main expectation for lawmakers is to make the traffic environment and infrastructure safer. According to Kirss, logical and safe infrastructure reduces the direct need for police supervision, because movement in such an environment is inherently safer and more understandable for drivers.
As a successful example, he pointed to Tallinn, where speed limits in the city center were lowered in 2024.
"Initially, this reduced pedestrian‑related traffic accidents by about 50 percent. Today it has remained around 30 percent, and I think that is a very good number," Kirss said.
On highways, the police consider most important the construction of roads where lanes are separated and the risk of head‑on collisions is minimized.
"Places where different road users can move in their own lanes are significantly safer than those where speeds differ and the risk of collision is high," he added.
Since 1 July, the PPA raised the intervention threshold for mobile speed cameras. Mobile cameras now issue fines only starting from 6 km/h over the limit (previously 3 km/h), to avoid penalizing momentary carelessness. The change applies only to PPA‑operated mobile speed cameras, of which there are eight across Estonia. Stationary cameras still intervene starting at 3 km/h over the limit.
In May, three MPs — Valdo Randpere, Madis Timpson, and Marek Reinaas — initiated a law amendment requiring the police to use a warning sign before a mobile speed camera. The amendment was adopted despite police objections and entered into force on 1 August.

Is China seeking to restrict Taiwan's cultural presence?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:04:00 UTC
22:04:00 KST

Is China seeking to restrict Taiwan's cultural presence?
October 9, 2026
When Taiwaneseauthor Yang Shuang-zi's "Taiwan Travelogue" won the 2026 International Booker Prize, it marked a historic breakthrough on the global stage. But behind the triumph lay a sharp geopolitical reality.
On stage, Lin King, who translated the book into English, gave voice to the anxiety looming over Taiwan, where she spent a large part of her childhood.
"In 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, I made the explicit decision that rather than translating Sinophone works indiscriminately, I would only translate writing from Taiwan for the foreseeable future. I will continue to do so until the day comes that my homeland's sovereignty is no longer a provocation or a punchline — until no English speaker feels comfortable saying to me, 'I really should come visit you in Taiwan while it still exists.'" she said in her acceptance speech.
Literature and politics
"Taiwan Travelogue" follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tour. As she and her Taiwanese interpreter explore local street food together, a subtle intimacy unfolds between them. The narrative centers Taiwan's history rather than Beijing's preferred "Greater China" framework.
"Literature and politics are directly connected," Yang told DW. "Politics determines the allocation of resources, and the allocation of resources determines which works get pulled out, held up high and defined as 'good literature.' The idea that politics can just be kept out of it doesn't exist."
A few days after the 2026 International Booker Prize was announced, China's Taiwan Affairs Office reacted by saying the following: "Writers from both sides of the Taiwan Strait should firmly uphold a national standpoint, respect historical facts, and squarely face the immense suffering inflicted upon the Chinese people ... by Japan's war of aggression and fascism."
"From China's perspective, they do not want to see Taiwan's voice gain prominence." Yang said.
Her book demonstrates that Taiwanese culture is shaped by multiple historical strands — including Indigenous, Japanese colonial and local Han influences, rather than being merely a "branch of Chinese culture."
During Yang's German book tour this October, an event at the Literaturhaus in the southern German city of Munich sparked controversy when the writer's interpreter significantly shortened certain statements concerning Taiwan, China, history and politics. The interpreter later admitted that there had been oversights and shortcomings in the translation but denied deliberately deleting content due to their political stance or the situation in Taiwan.
Taiwan and China
Beijing claims Taiwan as a Chinese province and has long threatened to use force to bring the island under its control. Taiwan's democratically elected president has rejected Beijing's assertion that its laws apply to Taiwan.
Since 1949, Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence, maintaining its own government, military, and legal systems while facing ongoing military pressure from Beijing.
China's international overreach?
China's monitoring of Taiwanese international engagement reaches far further than words over a literature prize.
"The target of suppression and harassment primarily include outspoken individuals, exiled activists, diaspora community organizers, alongside their family members and close affiliates back home, " said said Dr. Yan-ho Lai, a senior fellow of Georgetown Center for Asian Law. "From the PRC's (People's Republic of China) eyes, these groups are a threat to regime security, as they are able to amplify the dissenting voices and alternative stories of China to the West."
In April this year, Taiwanese barista Lin Shao-hsing, also known as Bala, won the 2026 World Latte Art Championship in the United States. Soon after, all mention of Taiwan as it related to Bala's win was removed from the official World Coffee Championships website.
It now says that Bala was representing "the competition body of Chinese Taipei," a term often used in international contests, such as the Olympics, to refer to Taiwan, but almost never used in Taiwan itself.
According to a 2026 poll by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center, the vast majority of people in Taiwan identify as "Taiwanese," while only 2.5% identify as Chinese.
In 2024, China allegedly planned to stage a "car collision" during Taiwanese Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim's visit to the Czech capiutal Prague. Czech intelligence officials told local media that the incident had been part of a much larger and escalatory plan by Chinese diplomats and intelligence officers working out of the Chinese embassy in Prague.
In early October this year, the FBI said authorities arrested a woman in California for allegedly spying on the son of Taiwan's president. According to the US Department of Justice, the woman had traveled to Seattle in 2025 under instructions from Beijing to monitor the Taiwanese president's son and his family, capturing photos, video footage, and license plate information.
During a press conference on October 6, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it "consistently opposes the hype surrounding so-called 'Chinese spies' and the smearing and vilification of China."
"It reflects the ambiguity and limitation of international law, that the PRC using soft power to restrict the visibility of Taiwan may not directly fall into international law arena, as Taiwan is not recognized by international bodies as a sovereign state party." said Dr. Lai.

US military prepares options for three-day strike campaign against Iran
The US military is preparing options for a three-day campaign of intense strikes on Iran, The New York Times reported on Thursday, citing US officials.
At President Donald Trump’s direction, the Pentagon has drawn up plans to target Iran’s arsenal of drones and missiles, energy facilities and other military sites, the newspaper reported. The preparations come as three US aircraft carriers are expected to be in the Middle East soon in a major show of force.
The timing of any potential attacks remains unclear. Trump has said there have been "productive discussions" with Iran and claimed there would be no attack before the 3 November midterm elections.
But tensions between Washington and Tehran remain high.
Although the US has not struck targets in Iran for weeks, low-level hostilities continue in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains largely blockaded by Iranian forces. The US military has also imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports, rattling global energy markets.
Iran has threatened to retaliate with full force if the US and Israel resume their war, which began on 28 February and quickly drew much of the region into a wider conflict.
US officials told the NYT that Trump’s national security team and the Pentagon had presented him with five proposals in recent months for major military operations targeting Iran or Yemen’s Houthi movement, which is engaged in a conflict with Saudi Arabia and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. Trump rejected each proposal but has now again ordered officials to prepare options for possible strikes.
The plans centre on a short, intense campaign lasting about three days, the newspaper reported. Potential targets include Iran’s missile and drone stockpiles, which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has reportedly replenished since the early stages of the war, as well as energy facilities, command centres and the IRGC’s main headquarters.
Senior national security officials discussed the plans at a meeting led by Vice President JD Vance at Camp David last Friday, according to people familiar with the discussions.
The preparations coincide with a significant US naval deployment. The USS Theodore Roosevelt left San Diego last week and is expected to join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington in the Middle East, potentially by the end of October.
The deployment would mark the first time since 2003 that three US aircraft carriers have been in the Middle East simultaneously. Each carrier strike group includes other warships, while the wider deployment is expected to put more than 20,000 sailors and Marines at sea alongside hundreds of aircraft by the end of October, according to the report.
The build-up is expected to be temporary. The USS George Washington is due to return to its home base in Japan shortly after the Theodore Roosevelt arrives next month to replace it.
Citing unnamed security sources, Israeli news site Walla recently reported that around 3,000 US troops are deployed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defence systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations, according to the report.
Despite the military build-up, there is no certainty that Trump will authorise further attacks, even after the midterm elections, the NYT reported.
Senior US officials are concerned that an expanded campaign could further deplete global stocks of defensive weapons needed to protect American bases in the Middle East. They are also worried about the US military’s ability to intercept Iranian attacks.

Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s AI data infrastructure

Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development efforts, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down a major data hub in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company’s AI models are housed.
Yandex, which operates under close government observation, said the attacks had struck at the core of its operations and that it was trying to maintain its services.
“Our teams are working day and night to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one,” it said in a statement.
The company operates numerous apps that many Russians consider essential, as well as social media networks.
Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
Damage from the attacks has forced some services to suspend operations. Roughly 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after an attack.
“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Ryazan strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”

A drone attack sparked a fire at a plant in Redkino in the Tver region, but it was quickly extinguished, the local governor said.
The Ukhta oil refinery belonging to the state giant Lukoil, 1,900km (1,180 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was also struck, according to Zelenskyy.
Meanwhile, Russia’s air campaign has continued to hit civilians, despite the Kremlin’s insistence that it only attacks military targets.
Overnight strikes killed one and injured seven in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional defence official Ivan Fedorov said on the Telegram messaging app.
Russia also struck a cargo vessel in Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Mykolaiv, the Ministry of Defence in Moscow said, according to state news agency RIA Novosti. The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian military.

France’s seafood problem starts elsewhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:01:11 UTC
22:01:11 KST

France’s seafood problem starts elsewhere
Much of the fishmeal and fish oil that support seafood consumed in France come from global supply chains linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food insecurity in poorer countries.
On March 6, 2024, Pascal Goumain, the president of Saumon de France, was presenting his company’s salmon pens in Cherbourg as part of France’s food future. In an interview, Goumain described plans to adapt the farm to climate change and pointed to official backing for expansion. “The French Ministry of Agriculture set an objective to farm 20,000 tonnes of salmon in France by 2030,” Goumain said. The promise of fish farming, he argued, is that it is both sustainable and important for food sovereignty. “We should be a leading aquaculture country,” he said, “but we’re falling behind.”
The industry and government pitch of aquaculture in France has been straightforward: People want more seafood, the limit of what can be viably pulled from the wild is quickly being reached, and fish farming is the way to meet the growing demand while slowing the collapse of the oceans. “The quantities caught are not sufficient to feed consumers,” former minister of the sea Annick Girardin said in 2021. The Haut-Commissariat au Plan on fish farming echoed the point in 2023, asserting that in a context of climate change and overfishing, the “responsible development” of aquaculture could expand supply without undermining the fishing sector.
Globally, the ocean-sustainability argument for fish farming – “grow more, so we can catch less” – is one of the reasons that the $313-billion aquaculture industry is currently the fastest-growing food sector, and why half of the seafood eaten around the world is now farm-raised rather than caught at sea.
There is a problem, though. “The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in France – salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream – are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained. Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil, ingredients made by cooking and pulverising wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, DC. These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, violent protests typically spurred by the horrid stench from fishmeal factories, and escalating geopolitical tensions as countries compete for scarce sources of protein. What economists often call “externalities", these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.
In Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export. In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, on farms, and in factories. In other countries, like India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labour strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish.
The four-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fishmeal ships at sea. The goal was to chronicle what economists call this industry’s “externalities” – the hidden and displaced social costs of producing this feed that rarely appear on the balance sheets of the seafood companies that depend on it.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The investigation revealed that the fishmeal industry also contributes to geopolitical tensions.
For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity. In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal, after a fisher was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fishmeal boat. Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara, a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various UN resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illegal catch into fishmeal in Western Saharan plants, then exporting it to farms globally labeled as Moroccan. A violent clash over trucks, many of them carrying this fish and fishmeal out of Western Sahara, led to the collapse of a 29-year ceasefire between the countries in 2020. As recently as 2024, a Western Saharan fishmeal plant supplied fish oil to a French importer named S.A.S. Ch. Daudruy Van Cauwenberghe & Fils, which advertises supplements for animal feed on its website, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that maps seafood supply chains. S.A.S. Ch. Daudruy Van Cauwenberghe & Fils did not respond to a request for comment.
Read moreThe Saya de Malha Bank, a 'forgotten ecosystem' in need of protection
France’s greatest exposure to these problems comes less from home-grown salmon than from the more than €6 billion worth of seafood the country imports annually, including shrimp, trout, tilapia, and other forms of fish that rely heavily on fishmeal and fish oil. For example, shrimp raised on farms in Ecuador and sold at major grocers in France such as E.LeClerc, Cora, and Carrefour is fed fishmeal from plants throughout Latin America that have been tied to at least five worker deaths, 20 cases of illegal fishing, and over a half dozen instances of civil unrest from neighbours protesting the stench from fishmeal factories, the investigation found. Carrefour Group, which also owns Cora, said it was immediately launching an investigation into the issues concerning its supply chain and “will take all necessary measures in the event of confirmed non-compliance", which could include the exclusion of sources of supply “that do not meet our ethical and environmental standards". E.Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment.
More than sixty percent of the salmon eaten in France comes from farms in Norway, which rely heavily on imported fish feed made from wild-caught fish. The feed raising this salmon is linked to a range of documented impacts, including food insecurity in Western Africa, pollution from waste and chemicals, and the spread of parasites and disease to wild fish populations. A 2024 Science Advances review found that about 87 percent of global fishmeal goes to aquaculture, compared with roughly seven percent to pigs and about five percent to poultry.
The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden from the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, in particular as feed for fish, chickens, and pigs. The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets. For example, less than 30 percent of the fleet had publicly available location information, and less than 25 percent had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.
Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the vessels in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species. At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths. The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.
“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Pauly. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
Natural food web 'now shaped by industrial design'
For most of human history, we ate what ecosystems produced on their own: wild fish, grazing animals, and crops grown for people. Livestock survived largely on grass and agricultural leftovers that humans didn’t eat. Today, we do something different: We grow or catch food that people could eat and feed it to animals instead, especially in industrial livestock and fish farming. These calories are converted before they’re consumed.
Read morePosidonia meadows: Lungs of the seas at risk
This global transformation has rewired the trophic chain, turning farms and oceans into engineered calorie-processing systems. The natural food web, consisting of who eats what and how energy moves from plants to animals to humans, is no longer mainly determined by ecosystems. It’s now shaped by industrial design. Animals have become less like savings accounts that turn waste into food, and more like biological factories steered by globally traded feed commodities such as soy and fishmeal. Roughly 90 percent of the catch used to produce fishmeal globally is edible for humans, according to a 2017 study published in the Fish and Fisheries journal. Most fishmeal plants around the world rely on whole fish rather than processing waste or inedible byproducts, further intensifying local protein scarcity.
The science of animal feed – combining corn, soy, grains, and ingredients like fishmeal to raise livestock faster, more efficiently, and at a larger scale – has been central to the rise of modern civilisation. Techniques of animal husbandry emerged roughly 12,000 years ago in the so-called Fertile Crescent, a region stretching from Mesopotamia to Egypt. Alongside innovations such as irrigation and the plough, the domestication of livestock enabled humans to build stable food systems, settle permanently, and eventually develop cities. As farming shifted from grazing animals on open land to penning them, humans assumed responsibility for providing balanced diets, an early precursor to today’s industrial feed systems.
In her 2021 book The Fishmeal Revolution, Kristin A. Wintersteen traces how the Humboldt Current – a cold, nutrient-rich upwelling system along the Pacific coast of South America – was reimagined as a protein mine. That shift, she argues, turned Peru into a global fishmeal superpower, responsible for roughly a quarter of worldwide production. Fishmeal became a critical input fueling the post-World War II expansion of industrial chicken and hog farming, and later aquaculture, particularly in northern Europe and the United States. Since then, this model spread far beyond Peru, including to West Africa and Southeast Asia.
Modern aquaculture does have benefits. Fish farming provides millions of people with year-round access to affordable protein. In India, for example, aquaculture is a crucial source of jobs, especially for women. In Bangladesh, fish farming has driven an overall decline in the price of fish, making it more accessible for lower-income households. Even accounting for feed ingredients like soy and fishmeal, and transportation to the US, certain farmed fish, including tilapia and Atlantic salmon, emit less greenhouse gas per pound than beef or pork.
Read moreForced labour, disease and conflict: The hidden side of industrial fishing in Saya de Malha
Harvesting bivalves, like clams, oysters, scallops, and mussels, is an especially sustainable type of aquaculture, since these species do not require feed. This kind of farming also has a very low carbon footprint and produces shells that can function as a form of carbon capture, according to a 2020 paper by Nature Food. As of 2022, roughly a third of global aquaculture did not require external feed inputs. France is the European Union’s second-largest producer of farmed seafood by volume, behind Spain, with bivalves accounting for nearly 80 percent of what the country grows.
The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fishmeal and fish oil, and especially on the use of whole fish or fish that people can eat. However, as aquaculture overall grows, so too does demand for fishmeal. The total amount of global fishmeal production is predicted to rise by nearly 10 percent, mostly from trimmings, between 2022 and 2032, according to the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization. Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from IFFO, the international fishmeal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system". She added that her organisation’s “role is not to advise which markets should use fishmeal and fish oil". “Sustainability frameworks won’t work if they ignore real-world economics,” she said, and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat".
France has not only been a consumer of farmed seafood. It has also tried to help find alternatives to fishmeal. In northern France, inside a vast warehouse, millions of mealworm larvae wriggled in stacked trays at Ynsect, a company that promised to mass-produce insect protein as a replacement for fishmeal in livestock and aquaculture feed. When the firm broke ground in 2021 on what was billed as the world’s largest insect farm, France’s agriculture minister hailed it as a symbol of the country’s “reconquest of protein sovereignty". Investors poured more than half a billion dollars into the company.
Read moreIn the Saya de Malha Bank, sharks are being hunted to extinction for their fins
But the fix proved harder than the pitch. By 2022, Ynsect had suffered more than $105 million in losses, largely because demand from feed buyers remained weak. In 2023, the company said it would shift away from the lower-margin business of feed for fish and farm animals, focusing instead on higher-end pet food markets. Its retreat illustrated a broader problem with alternatives to fishmeal: Even when a substitute looks promising in theory, it frequently struggles with cost, nutrition, and scale. Alternatives often lack the full range of nutrients that support the growth of farmed fish, especially omega-3. Certain “green” options, like insect meal, are expensive, and there has been limited interest among feed companies to pay a premium for them as a result.
Insects, moreover, turned out not to be as circular a solution as advertised. One of the industry’s main selling points was that larvae could be raised on waste. But in the European Union, disease-prevention rules largely bar insect producers from feeding them household food waste, manure, or catering scraps. Instead, most producers must rely on feed-grade crops. As a result, a sector promoted as a way to ease pressure on oceans has, in many cases, ended up competing with people and livestock for the same agricultural resources. The lesson from Ynsect was not that replacing fishmeal is impossible. It was that there is no easy substitute waiting in the wings.
Forced labour and land appropriation
For now, the pattern persists: Wild fish are caught and rendered into feed, while the costs of this production are left elsewhere. And reporting across several continents and oceans showed just how varied those costs can be. In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks while demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal. In Russia, fish processing workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore. “People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.
The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labour and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. In 2025, France imported more than $124 million worth of seafood from China, which is rapidly expanding its aquaculture industry. China now raises more than four times the amount of fish it catches. One of the fastest-growing regions in this boom is China’s mountainous and desert inland west, particularly Tibet and Xinjiang, two regions known for intense political repression.
In Tibet, the Chinese government has relocated roughly half a million Tibetans, leveling villages and monasteries for development projects such as hydroelectric dams and fish farms. This effort often uses coercive tactics, including repeated home visits, threats of criminal prosecution, and warnings that utilities could be cut off for those who refused to move, according to a 2024 Human Rights Watch report. In response to these sorts of policies, at least 169 Tibetans have set themselves on fire, typically on camera, outside police stations, monasteries, or public squares. In Xinjiang, more than a million people have been held in detention camps, and the government has engaged in large-scale land seizures, forced sterilizations, and criminal penalties for speaking native languages or practicing religious and cultural traditions.
The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, much of which is exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States. China’s effort to promote fish farming in Tibet and Xinjiang is partly facilitated by severe state repression, including the widespread appropriation of land, intense police surveillance, and the incarceration of tens of thousands of local residents. The United States bans all goods produced “wholly or in part” by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region on the presumption that they were made with state-sponsored forced labor. No such law exists for Tibet. EU law, which applies in France, does not single out China but prohibits products made with forced labor from being placed or made available on the EU market, including imports.
Sustainability smokescreens
As the production of seafood has become more globalised, its supply chains have stretched longer, and it has become tougher for consumers to know whether it was harvested sustainably or legally. Most grocers who sell seafood are in the dark as well because tracking is difficult and costly. Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said this is partly because grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. The other reason may be plausible deniability, he added. “Companies can escape blame or the need to fix problems if they’re unaware of them.”
Where government regulators have proven lacking in ensuring that supply chains are free from unsustainable, illegal, or unethical practices, industry-led certification programs have sought to fill the gap. Critics say these programmes serve more as a sustainability smokescreen, giving downstream customers a way to avoid looking deeper into their supply chains. The programmes generally focus on environmental crimes, while mostly overlooking labour abuses on ships. Their biggest weakness, according to researchers, is that they do not actually track seafood fully, which results in false reassurances for consumers.
Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at the strategic litigation non-profit group Corporate Accountability Lab, said that on land – at processing plants or on farms – certification programmes rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the guarantees given by managers at the factories. Instead, the programmes frequently alert companies before inspectors show up, which gives them a chance to clean up the scene so there are no violations. At sea, these programmes also often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors directly visit and check conditions offshore on vessels, where crimes are most common. Certification programmes are rife with conflicts of interest, since they are typically funded by the companies that they are supposed to police, Brudney added.
The various organisations that make up the certification industry emphasize that each plays its own role and cannot be held accountable for others’ responsibilities. For example, Devan Meserve, a spokesperson for The Global Seafood Alliance, which runs a programme called Best Aquaculture Practices, said that her organisation represents the “most comprehensive programme for farmed seafood", partially because it covers the “entire aquaculture production chain". Protecting workers on the fishing vessels that supply feed mills is, however, an “immense challenge", she noted, because audits occur strictly at port and do not witness harvest conditions. Meserve added that her organisation helps the industry counter illegal and overfishing by requiring feed mills to source most of the fish they use in fishmeal or fish oil from fisheries accredited by certification programmes like MarinTrust and Marine Stewardship Council.
Partly bolstered by these certification programmes, seafood companies routinely make marketing claims about the ethics and sustainability of their seafood. Often, these claims fail to reckon with crimes or social concerns further up their supply chains, including on the ships or plants that produce the feed for the fish farms. This disconnect is creating growing legal risk for seafood companies and grocers. Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies across six US jurisdictions. The legal complaints focused on a common pattern: marketing claims that portrayed products as sustainable or ethically sourced, paired with supply chain evidence that suggested otherwise. Plaintiffs challenged language such as “sustainable", “eco-friendly", “all-natural", “wild-caught,” and “from the coast of Maine", as well as claims of superior worker-safety standards.
In at least four cases, the use of fishmeal or fish oil and their link to industrial fishing and ecosystem depletion were central to arguments that the products were not environmentally sustainable. Additional allegations included forced labour on fishing vessels and reliance on harmful pesticides and antibiotics. During this same period, seafood companies have paid more than $2 million in settlement fees to resolve false-advertising cases. The Outlaw Ocean investigation assessed more than 800 seafood companies that made marketing claims comparable to – or stronger than – those cited in the lawsuits and found that over half of the companies had documented crimes or concerns within their supply chains.
Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with the Canadian sustainable seafood group SeaChoice, said many industries have already had to begin reckoning with the human rights and environmental abuses buried in their supply chains. She cited sweatshop garments, blood diamonds, and fair-trade coffee as examples. Seafood, she said, has been slower to face that kind of scrutiny. But as the world searches for more protein and leans further into aquaculture, that may change, particularly if more governments begin restricting imports tied to illegality or unsustainable practices. “That’s when investors will begin to see material, not just reputational, risk,” she said, “and companies will have to adjust".
The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.
The Outlaw Ocean Project is a non-profit journalism organisation based in Washington DC that produces investigative stories about human rights, labour and environmental concerns on the two thirds of the planet covered by water. The organisation is run by Ian Urbina, an award-winning journalist who used to work for The New York Times.
Most of the stories are reported at least partially at sea. In the United States, the group publishes its stories in various news outlets, including the New Yorker, NBC News, The Atlantic and The Washington Post. The reporting is also regularly translated into other languages, particularly French and Spanish, and broadcast in partnership with dozens of foreign newspapers, magazines, radio and television outlets.

Latvia must have one of most efficient judicial systems in Europe - Kulbergs  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:54 UTC
22:00:54 KST

RIGA - Latvia must have one of the five most efficient judicial systems in Europe, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) said Friday at the conference "The Court Beyond the Codes: The Role of the Supreme Court in the Development of the State and Society".
He pointed out that it is not the government’s role to tell the courts how to rule, but rather to ensure that the courts have the necessary resources and personnel.
At the same time, the prime minister said that he sees every day how court rulings are changing the country. Meanwhile, in the recent Saeima elections, the people have spoken in favor of change. Kulbergs pointed out that if there is a desire for change, it must also take place in the economy, and the economy must be the top priority for the next 4-8 years.
"For this to happen, investment is needed. For there to be investment, the key is a solid foundation - a fair and swift trial. I emphasize: a swift trial!" said the prime minister.
The politician cited the latest data on the trials of corruption cases as an example, noting that, on average, such cases take three years to be heard in the first instance.
Likewise, he said, for companies, the specific outcome of a court decision may not be decisive, but the speed at which the decision is reached is crucial, because during the proceedings a company may go bankrupt and disappear, and then, in the end, the whole process would be pointless.
"An effective court system is the foundation of the economy. If we have a swift and fair court system, with an emphasis on speed, then that is the key foundation for promoting competitiveness and entrepreneurship," Kulbergs emphasized.
Speaking about security, the prime minister noted that we are living in a time of hybrid operations targeting Latvia, sanctions evasion, and information operations. The rule of law serves as a line of defense in these circumstances. A country where the courts work quickly and fairly is less vulnerable, he noted.
The prime minister also emphasized that court decisions must be understandable and well-explained.
"If we want real change in the country - the change voters have voted for - then that change must also take place in the courts. And Latvia must be among the five most effective judicial systems in Europe. That must be our goal. Just as I have said about public administration," Kulbergs noted, adding that technology and artificial intelligence can certainly help achieve this speed.
Following Kulbergs’ speech, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court asked to meet with him, to which the prime minister replied with a laugh, "Only if we are going to talk about speed".
As previously reported, the conference is attended by judges - senators, presidents of regional courts and district (city) courts, judges from the Constitutional Court and the General Court of the European Union, as well as chief justices and judges from 14 European countries.
Also participating in the conference are faculty members from the University of Latvia, Faculty of Law and other faculties, officials from the judicial system, representatives from several ministries, as well as representatives from the Foreign Investors’ Council in Latvia.

Number of passengers served at Riga Airport remains flat in January-September  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

RIGA - Riga Airport served 5.32 million passengers in the first nine months of this year, which is the same as during the respective period last year, the airport informed LETA.
In the first nine months of this year, the airport handled 48,800 flights, which is 2 percent more than during the same period a year ago, while the volume of air cargo handled increased by 46 percent to 20,700 tons.
The airport notes that the proportion of transit and transfer passengers in the first nine months of this year has increased from 20 percent to 22 percent compared to the same period last year.
In September 2026, Riga Airport served 623,400 passengers, which is two percent more than in July 2025. This past July, 25 percent of passengers used Riga as a connecting airport.
In September of this year, Riga Airport handled 623,400 passengers and 5,693 flights, which is on par with last year’s levels. Meanwhile, cargo traffic continued to grow in September, reaching 1,997 tons, a 19 percent increase compared to September of last year. The average load factor in September remained stable at 78 percent.
The airport added that Latvia’s national airline airBaltic, carried 4 percent more passengers in the first three quarters of this year than in the same period last year, Polish airline LOT, by increasing flight frequency on the Warsaw-Riga route, has increased its passenger numbers by 21 percent since the beginning of the year, while the number of passengers served by Turkish Airlines in Riga has increased by 10 percent, and Finnair served 9 percent more. Meanwhile, Irish low-cost airline Ryanair served 17 percent fewer passengers in the first nine months of this year than in the same period last year.
As reported, Riga Airport handled 7.111 million passengers last year, which is at the same level as in 2024. but nine percent less than in 2019, or before the Covid-19 pandemic.
The airport handled 63,155 flights last year, which is about as many as in 2024, while handling of air cargo increased by seven percent year-on-year to 20,147 tons.
Riga Airport is the largest air traffic hub in the Baltic countries.

Klaipėda Port showcases the future of smart operations with a private 5G network trial and design  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

Trials of a private 5G network at Klaipėda Port in Lithuania have successfully concluded, marking a key milestone in defining the port’s digital future. Santa Monica Networks and Latvian telecommunications provider LMT (LMT Group) have completed the comprehensive design phase for a potential port-wide private network and demonstrated concrete, practical applications directly to port company executives, illustrating how 5G technology can optimize daily workflows.
According to Mindaugas Žiūkas, Director of Santa Monica Networks, as the port increasingly digitizes its operations, reliable connectivity is becoming crucial as the foundation for a growing number of machines, devices, and daily processes, not just for human communication. "Numerous processes take place simultaneously at the Port of Klaipėda, making it clearly evident where technology can deliver practical benefits, such as boosting operational efficiency, automating more processes, and reliably managing machinery and data. For us, as a strategic IT partner, this is one of the most significant projects of recent years and an opportunity to leverage our expertise to help modernize the port that connects Lithuania to the world," said M. Žiūkas during the event.
Autonomous systems demonstrate private 5G applications
Executives and IT specialists from companies operating at the Port of Klaipėda attended the demonstration. Santa Monica Networks, LMT, and their technology partners showcased specific private 5G use cases in a real-world port environment and discussed with port representatives how these solutions could further modernize the port.
Atlas demonstrated its autonomous drone-in-a-box solution, combining AtlasNEST with the AtlasPRO unmanned aerial system to enable persistent remote monitoring and autonomous operations. The integrated system enables remote deployment, operation, recovery, and recharging of the drone, supporting inspection, situational awareness, and monitoring missions in complex and hard-to-reach port environments.
LVR Flote, a provider of port technical services in Latvian ports, demonstrated its uncrewed surface vessel, the Otter USV, which is used for hydrographic surveys of the harbor bed. LVR Flote also presented a tool to improve the transfer and processing of large survey datasets and a data pre-processing tool that applies initial filtering before detailed quality control by hydrographers. Combined with 5G connectivity, these solutions are intended to reduce manual work, shorten the time between data collection and analysis, and support faster operational decision-making in ports.
“At LVR Flote, we see strong potential in using digitalization and data more effectively to support better, data-based decisions – whether in fleet management, hydrographic surveys or other operational areas. For any digital solution to work in practice, safe, reliable and secure connectivity is essential, especially in critical infrastructure such as ports,” said Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote.
According to Algis Latakas, Director General of the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority, technological development is crucial for the port not only in terms of modernization but also regarding competitiveness.
“Today’s market rewards those who are fast, reliable, flexible, and resilient. A private 5G network could unlock even more opportunities for the Port of Klaipėda by enabling the implementation of advanced solutions, process automation, and increased operational capacity, while ensuring uninterrupted connectivity and secure data transmission, even in extraordinary situations. Resilient, modern, and flexible – that is how we envision the future of the Port of Klaipėda, and that is the port we are building every day,” says Algis Latakas, Director General of the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority.
Increasing use of digital solutions in port operations
A private 5G network would give the port greater control over connectivity management. The port could independently decide which processes are prioritized, which devices can connect to the network, and keep certain sensitive operational data within its own infrastructure. This contributes to an increase in security, and would help ensure controlled communication and coordinated action during incidents.
According to Aigars Runcis, Director of the Ventures Department at LMT, the solutions demonstrated in Klaipėda represent only a fraction of the potential applications for private 5G technology in a port environment. "Private 5G is not connectivity for its own sake – it is the foundation for smarter, safer, and more efficient port operations. Demonstrations in Klaipėda show how unmanned systems and mission-critical communications can already deliver practical benefits, while the same connectivity platform can support a wide range of other solutions as the port ecosystem evolves. Our goal is to help ports build infrastructure that enables continued digitalization and automation, while boosting operational efficiency and resilience," said A. Runčis.
LMT brings practical experience in deploying private 5G networks in ports to the Klaipėda project. The LMT Group installed the first private 5G network in the Baltic states at the Baltic Container Terminal (BCT) in the Port of Riga. Covering an area of over 50 hectares, the network is already used in daily operations, ensuring connectivity for mobile machinery and facilitating mission-critical communications. The team is also applying this experience to develop solutions for other ports.

Largest short film industry in the Baltics recognises outstanding projects from Baltic countries and Italy
Welcoming filmmaking talents from the countries of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania - alongside guest country Italy - the 14th edition of the Baltic Pitching Forum (BPF) saw filmmakers come to Lithuania’s capital of Vilnius to pitch 12 projects to key industry figures, alongside participating in a series of seminars, talks, lectures, and training sessions.
The pitches culminated in the BPF Awards held in the opulent surroundings of the Italian Embassy in Vilnius on Thursday evening
Lithuanian animation Meat Jelly (dir. Emilė Maigytė, prod. Marija Lenkutytė-Bartoševič, Agnė Adomėnė) was awarded a place at the European Short Film Co-production Forum “Euro Connection” 2027, which is part of the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival in France. The film is an ode to self-acceptance and love of which the BPF Panel said:
“With sharp visual inspiration and liberating humour, this animation project takes us on a self-reflective journey of emancipation from the norm.”
For the first time not one, but two projects received an invitation to the ShorTO Film Market 2027 and its sessions – Lithuanian mixed-media animation Walks. I Love, Therefore I Am (dir. Gintarė Valevičiūtė-Brazauskienė, prod. Justė Beniušytė and Estonian hand-painted animation Blue Tower (dir. Mari Koff, prod. Sergo Kibus, Kadriann Kibus). The BPF Panel said of the films:
“The “You Only Pitch Twice” award goes to Walks. I Love, Therefore I Am for its layered story based on an extensive archival research which reminds us about the importance of singular acts of Resistance in the wider Story and of building a meaningful relationship with the past and the memories. Exceptionally another project – Blue Tower – is receiving an award for ShorTO, going to the Think Outside the Keyframe session. A compelling animation project with a long journey in front of it for which we want to be among the first who believed in it, providing the floor for the first steps of your path.”
Walks. I Love, Therefore I Am also won the Producers’ Jury MEDIA Award, initiated by the Creative Europe MEDIA Desks in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Italy, and accompanied by a €1000 cash prize. The Producers’ Jury said:
“This prize recognises the well-thought-out hybrid form that naturally emerges from the real story and the extensive research that mirrors its multi-layered complexity. We want to encourage the creative vision and the team behind it to continue the mission of the character whose story they are telling, and to inspire action through love.”
The Jury also gave a special mention to the Italian short film project Creature! (dir. Irene Dionisio, prods. Emanuele Segre, Alessandro Bernard, Valentina Velardi). According to the jury, this mention was for:
“It’s strong artistic approach and visual quality, which reflect the director's visionary talent. Through a subtle dramatic approach, the important topics of empathy and openness towards difference unfold through the eyes of a child discovering both death and the miracle of life.”
Introduced last year, the Riga IFF Award grants one project the invitation to the SHORT RIGA Test Screenings event in 2027 or 2028, depending on the project’s timeline. The award was given to Latvian fiction short film project Seeing John Malkovich (dir. Ildze Felsberga, prod. Zane Gulbe), a surrealistic comedy that looks at what happens to a small East European capital when a major Hollywood star comes to town. As Lauma Kaudzīte, manager of SHORT RIGA, said: “We are pleased to present the award to a promising project by a talented emerging director with a distinctive artistic voice and an original vision. Its playful and self-reflexive approach, exploring the blurred boundaries between reality, fiction and cinematic perception, promises a compelling meta-cinematic experience. The project is further strengthened by the support of an experienced and established production company, providing a solid foundation for the director’s vision to be brought to the screen.”
For the third year in a row, one project received the Up Records Sound Post-Production Award – established by the Vilnius-based Up Records studio. This prize offers the winners post-production services worth €2000. The award went to Walks. I Love, Therefore I Am. Saulius Urbanavičius, the sound post-production supervisor at Up Records, said:
“The film’s exploration of memory, hope and fragile line between remembering and forgetting feels especially relevant today, offering a wonderful opportunity for sound to become an essential part of the story.”
This year, the Baltic Pitching Forum introduced a new prize – the Baltic Talent Digital Strategy award, initiated by Baltic Talents Agency. The winner receives a consultancy session with Baltic Talents Agency to sharpen its digital presence ahead of its festival launch, covering EPK development, social media strategy, and positioning materials for the market and press. The inaugural winner of the award is Seeing John Malkovich (dir. Ildze Felsberga, prod. Zane Gulbe). According to Simona Inta and Viktorija Cook, founders of the Baltic Talent Agency:
“We chose to give our award to the project that felt closest to what we often talk about between ourselves, and that partly inspired us to create our agency. Here in the Baltics, we still carry a bit of a stigma that someone famous is better than us, that they are from another world. We crave to see and touch the legend. But we forget that we are becoming the legends ourselves.”
The Baltic Film Student Choice Award, initiated by students from the National Film School KIMO (Lithuania), Latvian Academy of Culture and the Baltic Film and Media School (Estonia) who attended the BPF, also saw Seeing John Malkovich triumphant. The students said of their decision:
“The genre of the chosen project is a breath of fresh air. Us students saw the honest passion of the creators that was radiating throughout the room. The project reflects on the feeling of what it's like being from a small country and it really makes you want to seek John Malkovich yourself.”

This year’s Producers Jury consisted of Dagnė Vildžiūnaitė (Just a Moment, Lithuania), Maie Rosmann (Estonia), Antra Cilinska (Juris Podnieks Studio) and Enrica Capra (Graffiti, Italy).

About 900 working-age people in Latvia die due to external causes each year  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:37 UTC
22:00:37 KST

RIGA - External causes of death in Latvia claim an average 1,400 lives each year, including approximately 900 people of working age, according to data from the State Chancellery and the Welfare Ministry, which were presented today at a meeting of the Council on Demographic Affairs.
As the Welfare Ministry's spokesman Egils Zarins informed LETA, at the meeting, which was chaired today by Krists Avots, Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, representatives from the State Chancellery and the Health Ministry presented data on external causes of death, their impact on society as a whole, the country’s demographic trends, and the national economy.
External causes of death account for 24 percent of all potential years of life lost up to the age of 64. The most common causes of death in this category are traffic accidents, falls, drowning, poisoning, violence, exposure to cold, fires, and suicides.
Last year, Latvia recorded 240 suicides and 234 fatal falls. There were also 171 cases of alcohol and drug poisoning, while 121 people lost their lives in traffic accidents. Also in 2025, 92 people drowned, 72 froze to death, and 34 were murdered. Of all these cases, 629 involved alcohol consumption, while psychoactive substances were involved in 102 cases.
To reduce and prevent such deadly accidents and incidents, close cooperation is needed among the health, education, traffic safety, law enforcement, and social sectors. Experts also pointed to the need for a long-term approach that combines prevention, public awareness, and cross-sectoral cooperation.
The Welfare Ministry notes that educational issues were also discussed at the meeting. The Education and Science Ministry gave a presentation on the current situation regarding the implementation of the Program at School education funding model.
At the same time, the council discussed options for providing free meals in schools through the 9th grade.
The Council on Demographic Affairs is an advisory and coordinating state institution established to promote a unified national demographic policy and its implementation at all levels of government. The council evaluates and coordinates the implementation of the national demographic policy and informs the media about demographic policy matters.

He stated that airBaltic has made additional adjustments to the upcoming winter schedule. In line with seasonal demand, flights from Riga to Bucharest, Romania; Sofia, Bulgaria; Budapest, Hungary; and Oulu, Finland, will not operate during the winter season, but are scheduled to resume during the summer season. Flights from Riga to Innsbruck, Austria, will also be suspended.
