Cocktail of the week: All Roads’ daiquiri – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:28 UTC
21:00:28 KST

Our daiquiri sums up what All Roads is all about: familiar flavours with a little twist. Pineapple, rum and lime are a classic combination, and the addition of scotch bonnet jam brings a subtle warmth that makes this just as good for those first crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day.
All Roads daiquiri
Serves 1
For the pineapple and scotch bonnet jam
75g fresh pineapple, roughly chopped
30g caster sugar
1 small slice scotch bonnet chilli, or more to taste, or 1 pinch chilli flakes
For the drink
10ml overproof white rum – we use Wray & Nephew
45ml white rum – we use Havana Club 3-Year-Old
25ml fresh lime juice
30g pineapple and scotch bonnet jam (see above and method)
First make the jam. Put the pineapple and caster sugar in a saucepan and cook over a low heat until the fruit begins to soften. Blend smooth – we use a stick blender – then add the scotch bonnet to taste and keep cooking gently for 20-25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the jam thickens and turns lightly golden. Take off the heat, leave to cool completely, then lift out and discard the chilli (if using chilli flakes, leave them in). Decant into a small jar or container and keep in the fridge until needed.
To build the drink, put everything in a cocktail shaker filled with ice, shake hard until well chilled, then double strain into a chilled coupe.
- Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, All Roads, London SW9

====================================================================================================

Which cities dominated 2020 voter fraud talk? A city’s Black population was the best predictor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

White Americans who hold racially resentful attitudes are particularly prone to believing claims of election fraud, especially when those allegations target predominantly Black communities. The authors argue that such claims give people who feel threatened by Black political power a way to reject election results they dislike while still professing support for democracy. The findings were published in Political Behavior.
To understand this reaction, social scientists often examine racial resentment. In political research, this concept does not simply refer to overt hatred; instead, it describes a subtle belief system that downplays systemic barriers faced by Black Americans and views minority political or economic gains as unearned. According to the social theories the authors draw on, when members of an advantaged group feel their social standing is slipping, they often look for ways to protect their position.
Following landmark political shifts, scholars began documenting how these racial attitudes influence trust in the voting process. For instance, a 2016 study showed that racial resentment was linked to suspicions of widespread election misconduct following the historic election of Barack Obama. Later work deepened this connection: a 2021 study found that racially resentful White Americans tend to become less satisfied with democracy when their preferred candidate loses an election.
Fraud allegations may also serve a particular purpose for dissatisfied voters. In a 2021 survey experiment, researchers found that exposure to unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud lowered people’s confidence in the integrity of elections without reducing their support for democracy itself. These findings raised a question the new study set out to answer: whether fraud accusations carry a racial charge that makes them especially persuasive to resentful White voters.
To test this dynamic, a research team led by Kevin T. Morris of the Brennan Center for Justice and Ian Shapiro of Tennessee State University conducted three distinct investigations. The authors sought to understand how racial attitudes interact with claims of election malfeasance.
“The motivation for this study was an urge to understand whether and how racial considerations shaped people’s trust in the 2020 general election,” Shapiro told PsyPost. “I suspected that fraud narratives, with their focus on crime, provided a vehicle for some White Americans to perceive specific elections as corrupt while maintaining trust in a system that had traditionally benefited them.”
The authors first examined whether real-world public discussions of election fraud actually focused on Black communities. They analyzed approximately 2.7 million public posts published on Twitter in 2020 containing the phrase “voter fraud.” From that collection, the researchers isolated about 95,000 posts that mentioned American cities with at least 100,000 residents, comparing those mentions against local demographic data and election tallies.
The social media data showed that cities with larger Black populations appeared far more often in voter fraud conversations, a pattern driven by the period after the election; before Election Day, none of the city characteristics the researchers examined predicted how often a city was mentioned.
The 10 cities mentioned most often relative to their size, a list that included Detroit, Philadelphia, and Atlanta, had an average Black population share of about 36 percent, compared with about 16 percent for the large cities in the analysis and under 7 percent for U.S. municipalities overall. In statistical models, a city’s Black population share was the only reliable predictor of these mentions; how strongly a city voted for Joe Biden was not related to how often it came up.
“I think what surprised me most was how clearly racial composition mattered in predicting which places became targets of social media fraud narratives,” Shapiro said. “Partisanship and racial politics are closely linked, but the only predictor of how frequently a city was mentioned on social media was the Black share of the population. Not even Biden’s vote share was associated with fraud narratives, other things equal.”
“Prior to election night, narratives about fraud were all over the place. They were prevalent but lacked shape,” Shapiro explained. “On election night in 2020 and in the weeks after, attention narrowed to specific places that became focal points for fraud accusations. Those places were not random.”
Next, the researchers evaluated how these public narratives corresponded to shifts in individual attitudes over time. They examined data from roughly 4,300 White participants in the 2020 Cooperative Election Study who answered questions about election confidence both before and after Election Day. The authors tracked changes in confidence while controlling for conservative ideology, support for Donald Trump, age, gender, education, income, and Fox News viewership.
Confidence in the election dropped sharply among White Trump supporters after Election Day, as is typical for voters whose candidate loses. But even after accounting for this pattern, along with ideology and the other factors, higher racial resentment was associated with an additional decline in confidence. This link held among Trump supporters, whereas resentment was not related to changes in election confidence among White supporters of Biden.
“Trump voters generally trusted the election less after it looked like he had lost. That’s normal,” Shapiro observed. “But confidence fell off a cliff among Trump supporters who scored higher in racial resentment, following the election and the accompanying focus on Black cities.”
To test whether racial cues directly cause people to believe fraud claims, the researchers conducted an online survey experiment in July 2024 with 1,500 White American adults. Participants read a mock news report describing either an apolitical story about a local restaurant, allegations of voter fraud in a fictional suburban city portrayed as largely White, or identical allegations in an “inner-city” described as predominantly Black. The stories included matching photographs of either White or Black election workers, voters, and local election administrators. After completing the questions, participants were debriefed and informed that the city was fictional and that election fraud is rare.
Across the entire sample, reading about fraud increased suspicion compared to reading about the restaurant, but participants overall did not view the Black city as more fraudulent than the White city. Important differences emerged, however, when examining specific subgroups. White Republicans who read about the predominantly Black city scored an average of 0.65 on a scale measuring belief in fraud, compared with 0.58 for Republicans who read about the White city, a gap of 0.07 points, or about 12 percent. This partisan comparison was not part of the authors’ preregistered analysis plan.
Personal levels of racial resentment also shaped how participants responded. Participants with higher resentment showed elevated suspicion of fraud even when assigned to read about the restaurant, and the fraud stories moved their beliefs considerably more than those of less resentful participants. Resentful participants also tended to find accusations more believable when they targeted the Black city, though this pattern was statistically reliable for only one of the resentment measures, and the authors describe the evidence as somewhat mixed. Fraud beliefs lined up more closely with resentment toward Black Americans than with White consciousness, a measure of attachment to one’s own racial group.
“The survey experiment confirms prior findings that just talking about fraud can substantially affect how much of it people think is happening,” Shapiro noted. “Despite fraud being so rare, words have power. And when those words are tied to tangible places for a political purpose, the effects can be substantial.”
These findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that White Americans who felt their racial group faced widespread mistreatment were consistently more skeptical of election fairness from 2012 to 2020. That earlier research measured perceived discrimination against White Americans rather than resentment toward Black Americans. It also found that strong White identity without a sense of grievance went along with greater faith in elections, which is broadly consistent with the new study’s finding that White consciousness tracked fraud beliefs less closely than resentment.
The results also support research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which indicated that higher levels of racial resentment are tied to broader anti-democratic views among White Americans. Morris and Shapiro argue that skepticism about ballot integrity often intersects with underlying anxieties regarding multiracial governance.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The social media analysis relied on public posts from Twitter, which may not capture the complete range of political discussion experienced by ordinary citizens offline. In addition, the researchers could not distinguish between posts promoting fraud claims and those seeking to debunk them, and some messages could have been amplified by automated accounts or foreign entities rather than regular voters.
Shapiro also emphasized that the investigation centered on how narratives are received rather than how political leaders strategize behind closed doors. “The data we use can’t really tell us about the motivations behind elite-driven narratives,” he told PsyPost. “The paper didn’t directly show people Trump’s social media posts or anything like that.”
“However, it’s not a stretch to suspect that the narratives we see spreading on social media took some structure and encouragement from elites,” Shapiro added. “A lot of agenda setting and attitude formation happens from the top down. This study is more about where and among whom these racial narratives find, excuse me for this, fertile ground.”
Shapiro is now examining how these rhetoric-driven policies affect the electorate. “I’m looking into how restrictive laws passed in response to these narratives turn people off from voting,” he explained. “I’m interested in what psychological mechanisms drive that process for different people.”
Reflecting on the democratic stakes, Shapiro stressed the broader danger these narratives pose to public trust. “This study is important because we’re in an era when people are cynical about all sorts of institutions, including elections,” he remarked. “But things like losers’ consent—accepting election results even when your side loses—and the belief that elections are a viable way to hold leaders accountable are at the heart of democratic functioning. Politically convenient narratives about crime and race threaten these pillars of democratic life.”
The study, “On Fertile Ground: How Racial Resentment Primes White Americans To Believe Fraud Accusations,” was authored by Kevin T. Morris and Ian Shapiro.

Rosalind Eleazar Gives One of the Year's Best Performances in the Acerbic and Tender Misty Green
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

It was probably around 100 years ago that stalwart Hollywood star Marie Dressler said, “You’re only as good as your last picture.” Today, that hard-nosed observation not only holds; in a culture measured out in here-today-gone-tomorrow limited series and independent films that fail to find their audience, it’s more apt, and more potentially heartbreaking, than ever.
Misty Green, the title character and the heartbeat of Chris Rock’s fourth feature film as a director, is living out Dressler’s maxim. Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar, is a gifted singer and actor who desperately needs a break. But there are good reasons she’s not going to get it. Even though she has an Emmy from her role in a hit series, she’s on her way to being forgotten. She has no patience for Hollywood BS and refuses to play the usual games. But she’s also prickly and unpleasant—she has alienated most of the people who might be able to help her—and a self-destructive streak hinders her further: She’d rather go out for a night of clubbing and coke than stay in and learn her lines for the next day’s important audition.
So now she’s in desperate straits. Essentially homeless, she’s been camping out in the apartment of a rich—and dead—ex-lover, but the guy’s angry widow has just given her seven days to pack up and vacate. During all this, her fragile brother, Jay (Daniel Kaluuya), who has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and whom she loves deeply, shows up at the flat that’s not even her own, needing more from her than she can provide.
We’ve seen the story of the wannabe comeback kid before. And Misty Green isn’t always a thoroughly graceful film. One of the weaker links may be the character played by Rock himself, Jordan, a director who wants to help Misty but harbors amorous feelings that don’t feel wholly believable; Misty could use some help, but she may not need that kind of savior. But overall, Rock’s writing is sharp and perceptive, and he’s attuned not just to the horrors of trying to make it in Hollywood, but also to Misty’s specific plight—and to the reality that she’s at times almost repugnantly dislikable.
Eleazar, best known for her role in Slow Horses, knows just how to shape this character without ever softening her. Misty is gifted, arrogant, impossible; at times, you begin to wonder if she even deserves a break. But Eleazar, giving one of the best performances of the year, tears our expectations to shreds: Who are we to decide what she deserves? At one point, during an audition, one of the men in charge of potentially hiring her blurts out, “Are you mixed?” and her eyes, moments ago dancing with fire, become glacier cold.
Misty has made her way along a path paved with irrelevant, if not outright racist and sexist, questions and assumptions—it’s little wonder she can barely take any more. But even stronger than her resentment is her belief that she still has something to give. It may be a stereotype to characterize actors as needy people, but Eleazar captures an almost existential longing that goes beyond garden-variety neediness. And at her lowest moment, Misty’s desperation becomes nearly unbearable to watch. Eleazar brings us right to the knifepoint of her degradation, and it pierces us too.
But Rock wouldn’t leave Misty in despair; he gives her the empathetic yet unsentimental ending she deserves. It’s almost impossible to like Misty, and yet, in a film that’s both acerbic and tender, Eleazar makes us love her, almost against our will. Hollywood, a place of dreams, can be inhumane to those who dream the biggest. Misty Green opens a safe space for them—without the false promise of a happy ending.

Why South Korea and Ukraine Are Fighting Over Two Prisoners of War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

On Sept. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine spoke at the UN General Assembly about the military support Russia was getting from North Korea and the deaths of North Korean soldiers on the Ukrainian front. “Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” he revealed. He seemed to be trying to highlight the global reach of Russia’s war and also hoping that the revelation would increase popular and political support in Seoul for providing weapons and aid to Ukraine.
Zelensky ended up igniting a diplomatic dispute between Ukraine and South Korea. Seoul claimed that Ukraine had agreed to keep the transfer confidential; Kyiv denied that such an agreement existed and downplayed the episode as a misunderstanding. Now South Korea is recalling its ambassador to Ukraine.
The quarrel over diplomatic protocol highlights the human cost paid by two soldiers caught in a geopolitical conflict linking European and Northeast Asian security. Their story captures the complicated geopolitics of the two Koreas now playing out on a European battlefield. It also underscores South Korea’s push for inter-Korean peace, even as North Korea tests Seoul’s patience by launching hypersonic missiles and planting landmines.
The men from North Korea
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured while fighting in the Kursk region of Russia in January 2025. They were part of a 10,000-strong North Korean contingent reinforcing Russian troops on the front line. Shortly after their capture, Ukraine’s military released video footage of the two soldiers. The images helped confirm North Korea’s direct involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war. Human Rights Watch raised concerns about Ukraine’s decision to release the video and expose the soldiers, given the potential repercussions for their families in North Korea, including torture, forced labor, imprisonment, or execution.
North Korean soldiers are instructed to take their own lives rather than risk capture. One of the captured soldiers reportedly attempted suicide before a Ukrainian medic stopped him. In North Korea’s eyes, a soldier who survives by surrendering, or worse by defecting to the South, is a traitor. Under the regime’s well-documented system of collective punishment, three generations of a defector’s family can face retribution through guilt by association.
By revealing the prisoner of war transfer to South Korea in New York, Zelensky offered Pyongyang an incentive to make an example of these soldiers’ families to demonstrate the consequences of defection. This stands in stark contrast to the regime’s response to the deaths of North Korean soldiers in Russia. Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, promised their surviving families a “beautiful life” and granted them new luxury apartments.
The North Korean regime may have already tracked down the families of the prisoners of war after Ukraine confirmed their capture in January 2025. But Zelensky’s disclosure at the United Nations renewed the danger facing the two soldiers now resettled in South Korea, a point Seoul highlighted in its protest to Kyiv. A life in South Korea offers these soldiers personal safety, but one could imagine it might come at a crushing cost: abandoning their homes and living with the guilt that their families may suffer in their place.
Mending the rupture between Seoul and Kyiv
If this episode were only about the two North Korean soldiers, their resettlement might have passed unnoticed. The diplomatic kerfuffle between Kyiv and Seoul is rooted in the different geopolitical narratives that each nation seeks to project, or in Seoul’s case, downplay.
For Ukraine, publicizing the presence and resettlement of North Korean prisoners of war provides a valuable opportunity to solicit support from South Korea, a major arms exporter and a vital partner to NATO. Since 2022, Kyiv has been urging Seoul to supply it with lethal weapons, including Patriot interceptors and 155mm artillery shells. In light of Pyongyang’s direct military support for Moscow, Ukraine has intensified pressure on South Korea to move beyond non-lethal military, humanitarian, and economic assistance.
For South Korea, Ukraine’s public disclosure of the resettlement of these soldiers undermines its diplomatic outreach to North Korea. In his address to the UN General Assembly, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea reiterated his vision of inclusive, peaceful coexistence built on “respect for each other’s systems” and the restoration of cross-border trust with North Korea. Accepting North Korean soldiers while publicly promoting dialogue weakens Lee’s reassurances to Pyongyang that Seoul desires “stable, peaceful coexistence.”
Pyongyang has maintained silence regarding these two soldiers. But North Korea considers South Korea’s reception of defectors as part of an effort to undermine its regime and eventually bring about unification on Seoul’s terms. While North Korea now defines the Koreas as two separate states, article four of South Korea’s constitution commits the nation to “peaceful unification based on the basic free and democratic order.”
As two nations dedicated to promoting freedom and democratic principles, South Korea and Ukraine must look beyond this diplomatic disagreement to protect their partnership. Seoul provided $400 million in aid to Ukraine in 2024 and announced $2.3 billion in long-term reconstruction aid through 2027. In return, Ukraine offers critical, real-world intelligence on North Korean military tactics and the weapons technology Pyongyang receives from Russia.
Given the complex legal situation of North Korean combatants captured by Ukrainian forces, Kyiv and Seoul must establish a protocol for handling North Korean prisoners of war and non-combatant defectors who seek asylum in South Korea. The need for such a policy will only grow. Similar episodes may unfold as the presence of North Korean troops and laborers in Russia grows, increasing the potential for future defections. Zelensky recently warned that another 10,000 troops from North Korea could soon be deployed in Russia.
With Kyiv’s cooperation, Seoul should affirm its commitment to accept future North Korean prisoners who voluntarily request resettlement, subject to standard security screening. That policy must fully comply with South Korean law and uphold international humanitarian principles and the values of a democratic society. To safeguard these individuals, both governments should protect prisoners’ identities, grant confidential access to impartial humanitarian representatives, and ensure that decisions are not made under coercion. Prisoners of war should not be forcibly repatriated, and public announcements of their transfer must be avoided without their explicit consent.
Crucially, not every captured North Korean soldier will want to go to South Korea. Their wishes must be determined through private, independent interviews conducted without pressure from governments, intelligence agencies, advocacy groups, or the media. Both governments may have followed such protocols. It remains unclear whether Ukraine eventually deviated from the agreed approach script or whether there was simply miscommunication.
Yet for the two soldiers already resettled, no policy can erase the personal toll. They must now rebuild their lives in a country they were raised to view as the enemy while carrying the lingering anguish about the fate of the families they left behind.

Developers crowd into Lüganuse as municipality navigates project surge

Developers crowd into Lüganuse as municipality navigates project surge
Lüganuse municipality in Ida‑Viru County has become a favorite location for various developers, which has forced the municipality to hire additional staff to process planning applications.
In Lüganuse, VKG and Kiviõli Keemiatööstus are expanding their oil‑shale mines; the state wants to establish two defense‑industry parks in the municipality; both a nuclear power plant and a VKG limestone‑product factory are being planned for the area.
A large part of the new Haljala–Kukruse section of the Tallinn–Narva highway, which will be publicly presented on Monday, also falls within Lüganuse's borders. In addition, various wind‑farm developers are showing active interest in the municipality, said Lüganuse Municipal Council Chairman Mart Kivistik.
"At the moment we have five detailed plans, four special plans, and one has been established — Evecon Energia's. In reality, this is an enormous burden for our small municipality. Initially more than 160 positions were launched. I think the real number will remain around one hundred, because so many locations will fall away," Kivistik said.
According to Gregor Raudvere, board member of Varja Windfarm, which wants to build wind farms in Lüganuse, the municipality's advantage is its favorable location and the low level of local opposition.
"In Lüganuse, I would say the attitude of residents is certainly one factor that speaks in its favor — this has been mentioned a lot elsewhere too. But Lüganuse also has very good wind conditions, Lüganuse has the Püssi substation, which is one of the largest node substations in Estonia, and there is a lot of free land and people who are willing to allow turbines to be erected on their land," Raudvere said.
For the municipality, the interest of various industries means that additional workforce is needed to make the proceedings run more smoothly, Kivistik noted.
"It is quite a large resource cost to answer all kinds of inquiries and matters that come with all of this. In that sense, we have created additional positions," Kivistik said.
In various proceedings, the municipal council chairman has been bothered by the fact that the experts assessing impacts tend to view the processes more from the developer's perspective than from that of the local resident.
"I would say from my own experience, since I have attended many of these meetings, that experts should explain more substantively and the presentations should be better, more prepared and impartial," Kivistik said.
Lüganuse municipality was formed by the merger of the former Lüganuse, Sonda and Maidla municipalities and the towns of Püssi and Kiviõli. The municipality has almost 8,000 residents, most of whom live in the town of Kiviõli.

Amid heartache of Nepal flooding disaster, fear remains

Amid heartache of Nepal flooding disaster, fear remains
Six weeks after Nepal’s deadly flooding disaster, communities are still struggling to rebuild their lives, but they will need sustained help as global warming increases the risk of another Himalayan catastrophe, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Friday.
At least 1,400 people were killed, including 84 children, and nearly 5,300 people are still missing, after a mountain of glacial ice and rock collapsed into the Bhotekoshi, Upper Trishuli and Narayani-Gandak rivers in late August, unleashing a massive torrent that washed away bridges and homes.
Lasting trauma
In an update from Kathmandu, UNICEF spokesperson James Elder highlighted the traumatic experience of 16-year-old Sahara, who he met this week at a technical training supported by the agency. “Her mum was swept away by the floods and killed. Through tears, Sahara told me, ‘It's not nice to live without a mum.’”
Today, areas of impacted towns and villages “look like war zones”, Mr. Elder stressed, while access to some communities in Rasuwa remains difficult.
“They continue to receive airlifted relief supplies in the most isolated areas,” said Caroline Holt, Director for Disasters, Climate and Crises at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC). “In the hardest-hit locations, families face disrupted markets, higher transport costs and shortages of essential goods as roads and communications are gradually restored.”
"Unless the world acts to reduce climate risks, we will keep returning to the same valleys after the next flood and after the next landslide, and yet again find children paying the highest price. This is true in Nepal, across Asia, across the Pacific and around the world," James Elder - UNICEF
Security call
The IFRC official stressed the urgent need to support those impacted by the disaster.
“People need more than assistance to survive, they need confidence in their future, they need to know where they live, how they will earn an income and when their children can return to school,” she said.
Among those requiring urgent assistance are Shushila and her husband, Jivan, after floodwater more than two metres high surged through their home, destroying their tailor’s shop and tea store.
“They escaped with the clothes they were wearing, and nothing else," Mr. Elder said. "Shushila told me, ‘Maybe it would have been better if we weren't able to escape.’ That is the stress and trauma brought on by inaction elsewhere in the world,” Mr. Elder noted, adding that UNICEF has supported Shushila and Jivan’s family with cash assistance. “With so many needs, how did they prioritize their spending? On their children; books, stationery and clothes."
COP31 call
International support for vulnerable countries, including Nepal, that are on the front line of climate change is critical, as the Himalayas warm “about twice as fast as the global average”, Mr. Elder said.
Noting that Nepal produces only 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse emissions, the UNICEF spokesperson welcomed declarations of support from States parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) “to avert, minimize and address loss and damage. But for countries like Nepal, those commitments have to quickly translate into support that reaches affected families on the ground,” he said, ahead of this year’s UNFCCC summit (COP31) in Antalya, Turkïye, from 9-20 November.
"Unless the world acts to reduce climate risks, we will keep returning to the same valleys after the next flood and after the next landslide, and yet again find children paying the highest price. This is true in Nepal, across Asia, across the Pacific and around the world," said Mr. Elder.

‘Serious blow’: Guterres condemns new US sanctions on International Criminal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Serious blow’: Guterres condemns new US sanctions on International Criminal Court
The United States has imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing on Friday to “dismantle the ICC, brick by brick” unless it ends what Washington regards as a “threat” to its citizens.
The court hit back forcefully, calling the step unprecedented, following sanction measures by the US already in place against 13 judges and prosecutors.
Attack on ‘international legal order’
The ICC described the measure as “an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order”.
The designation, the court said, is aimed at disrupting its operations and “intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the court”. But, it will not be deterred.
“The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” said ICC President Tomoko Akane.
Read our explainer on the ICC here
Stand up and be counted
Yet, the court acknowledged that it cannot stand alone.
“Its fate now rests also in the hands of the States that created it,” the statement said, adding that the Rome Statute’s promise “is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it”.
“No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice. History will judge this moment,” it concluded.
Rubio: ‘We will end the ICC’
Announcing the sanctions, Mr. Rubio said the US would “ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate”.
“America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it,” he added.
Mr. Rubio said the door to diplomacy remained open, but he issued a stark warning. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” he said, adding that Washington expected allies to “rein in the court”.
Guterres condemns move
UN Secretary-General António Guterres strongly criticised the US decision, according to his spokesperson, Stéphane Dujarric.
The UN chief condemned the new sanctions against the court “as an institution”.
Mr. Guterres was “deeply alarmed” by the expected impact on the court’s “continued ability to perform its important mandates” and called the sanctions “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar”.
He reiterated his “unwavering support for the independence of the court and its officials” and called on all States to uphold their commitments under international law.
The UN remains committed to cooperating with the ICC under the relationship agreement approved by the General Assembly on 13 September 2004, the statement added.
Sanctions ‘directly injures’ victims
Independent UN human rights experts warned separately that the US sanctions were a “brash attempt” to dismantle a collective international legal system to hold perpetrators of the gravest crimes to account.
They called on States committed to the rule of law to stand together in defence of the court and its independence.
“Sanctioning the institution entrusted with delivering justice for the gravest international crimes is an assault on the foundations of international accountability and rule of law,” the experts said.
“No State should place itself beyond the reach of the law by intimidating the court established to enforce it and attempting to dismantle it.”
The UN Human Rights Council-appointed experts – who are not employed by the UN and receive no salary for their work – added that the attack “directly injures the victims of atrocities and their advocates, who rely on the ICC for justice, accountability and reparation”.

Livestreaming US execution would breach prohibition of torture, UN rights office warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

Livestreaming US execution would breach prohibition of torture, UN rights office warns
The UN human rights office (OHCHR) on Friday warned that livestreaming a planned execution by firing squad in the United States would amount to a public execution and breach the absolute prohibition on torture.
The statement came after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed to publicly execute Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death by a military jury after being convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
OHCHR’s Shabia Mantoo was responding to a question from journalists at a press briefing in Geneva.
She noted that the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, in response to public executions in Afghanistan and Iran had previously stressed that such executions “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.
“Failure to respect this prohibition would inevitably render the execution arbitrary in nature, and result in a violation of the right to life and the absolute prohibition of torture,” the spokesperson added.
UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said during Friday’s press briefing in New York that the “possibility of…a government executing someone in public or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent”.
Call to halt Tennessee execution
Earlier this month, OHCHR also called on the authorities in the US state of Tennessee not to pursue any further attempts to execute Christa Pike, saying her case highlights why the death penalty should be abolished.
“The death penalty has no place in any society, and Christa Pike’s case lays bare the multiple reasons why capital punishment should be abolished,” said UN Human Rights Office spokesperson Ravina Shamdasani.
“Her prolonged suffering is abhorrent, and cruel. Key fair trial concerns remain unresolved,” she said.
Ms. Pike survived a botched execution attempt and regained consciousness on 6 October.
Responding to the botched execution, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada has said he will be stepping down at the end of this month.
Executions on the rise
In a report to the Human Rights Council on the question of the death penalty, published in August 2025, UN Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed steady progress towards abolition worldwide, but expressed concern that a diminishing number of countries were substantially increasing the number of executions.
The report, which cites figures from Amnesty International, noted that 1,518 executions were recorded in 15 countries in 2024, a 32 per cent increase from 2023.
In the United States, the report noted that the President signed an executive order on 20 January 2025 lifting the federal moratorium on the death penalty, and that South Carolina had carried out an execution by firing squad in March that year – the first in the US in 15 years.
“Pending abolition, States must not violate article 7 of the Covenant by carrying out executions that are cruel, unnecessarily painful or humiliating,” the report states, referring to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political scientist’s view: “Where will we make the cuts?” – Rajevskis warns of the cost of banning grain transit

20:59:43 KST

Latvia is planning to ban the transit of grain from Russia and Belarus, but it remains unclear how thoroughly the consequences of such a decision have been assessed. While the move might provide political satisfaction, what impact would it have on Latvia’s economy? Filips Rajevskis, political scientist and co-founder of Mediju tilts, stresses that the “grain issue” needs to be considered from a broader perspective.
The political scientist points out that grain transported through Latvia in transit is mainly traded by American commodity traders. “Of course, there may always be moral objections, but we must take into account that the grain no longer belongs to Russians and that this is not a Russian business. It is the business of our strategic partners – major American commodity traders who handle these transactions. This means their country’s interests are also involved,” Rajevskis says.
He also stresses the importance of examining how Latvia’s neighbours are acting. “Estonia was very quick to announce that it would not transport any grain. That is logical because Estonia has never been a grain transit country. Therefore, its loud announcements do not really mean much. At the same time, we can see that Estonia quietly secures an exemption from sanctions for a Russian magnesium plant to protect its own economic interests. It is not loud statements but quiet actions that reveal countries’ real economic interests. Latvia must finally understand, both in its foreign policy and its external economic policy, that we have national interests of our own. We should not harm our partners who guarantee our security either.”
When BNN noted that Lithuania had announced plans to propose a complete halt to grain transit at both Baltic and European Union level, Rajevskis responded that attention should be paid not to what Lithuanian officials say, but to what is happening at the Klaipėda terminal, where potash is handled. “That will be potash purchased by American traders, and they will continue handling it without any concerns. Latvia is also a transit country for potash. So we need to approach this issue sensibly and realistically.

Russian scientists make calculations to improve Arctic energy resource extraction safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:59:35 UTC
20:59:35 KST

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. Russian mathematicians and geologists conducted a series of experiments and calculations, where they for the first time studied how unilateral warming of frozen rocks in the Arctic increases the risk of gas emissions that threaten infrastructures and personnel. Results of these experiments and calculations will help make resource extraction safer, press service of Skoltech (part of the VEB.RF group) said.
"We have shown how metastable methane hydrates behave in frozen rocks when heated," the press service quoted Skoltech's leading researcher Evgeny Chuvilin as saying. "Previously, many models considered only a decrease in pressure as the cause of hydrate decomposition. But in the Arctic, a well is heating the frozen rock, and the process develops somewhat differently. We can see that the pore hydrate begins to decompose at temperatures below zero, well before the frozen rock begins thawing."
Huge reserves of so-called methane hydrates or clathrates lay inside the marine and onshore permafrost deposits in the Russian and foreign Arctic, the scientist and his colleagues said. This is what scientists call water and methane compounds that remain stable at low temperatures, high pressures, or at a combination of both. Human activity and global warming are destabilizing them, leading to a sharp release of gas and to formation of giant funnels, domes and other peculiar structures.
The proximity of such deposits to oil and gas wells may destabilize methane hydrates, since these structures can heat the upper layer of frozen rocks during the natural resources' extraction. With this in mind, Russian scientists conducted a series of experiments with analogues of Arctic permafrost deposits containing methane hydrates, and used them to create a computer model of these deposits.
The conducted experiments and calculations have shown that with unilateral heating, the hydrates decomposition begins at minus 1.1 degrees Celsius, while the ice began to melt only at minus 0.01 degrees Celsius. In other words, with prolonged thermal exposure, hydrate decomposition outstrips ice melting, which must be taken into account when extracting natural resources in the Arctic.
"We can see that the pore hydrate begins to decompose at temperatures below zero, even before the frozen rock begins to melt," the scientist said in conclusion. "This changes the estimate of how quickly a gas release zone may form around the well. This means that the intra-permafrost hydrate decomposition zone is formed earlier than we have thought, and this must be taken into account when designing production wells so that not to receive an unexpected influx of annular gas or a soil subsidence area around the well."

Swiss gene therapy for blindness makes further encouraging progress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:59:28 UTC
20:59:28 KST

Swiss gene therapy for blindness makes further encouraging progress
Eye researchers at the Swiss city of Basel are hopeful of a breakthrough in the treatment for blind people after initial positive indications that a new form of therapy works.
Blind people learning to see. What sounds like a fairy tale is becoming reality – at least in a certain sense. A new therapy for the retinal disease retinitis pigmentosa, which has so far only been tested on a small number of people, is showing astonishing results.
With its help, blind people were able to recognize at least the outlines of certain objects. This is reported in the renowned scientific journal New England Journal of Medicine.
Stefan Futterknecht from the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel (IOB) is a co-author of this recently published study. He is convinced that these findings will be very beneficial.
More
Blind patient gets “bionic eye” implant
“This has laid the foundation for the development of more precise and effective therapies in the future, said Futterknecht, who described the study as a “milestone for restoring vision.”
Outlines of objects are seen
Five years ago, the first study of this gene therapy was conducted, at that time in Paris and with a single person. That man gained his first visual impressions through the therapy.
After initial treatments proved effective on the anonymous test subject, the IOB have moved to the next stage.
Of the ten participants in the expanded, new study, most experienced an improvement, said Futterknecht. “Seven out of ten people had an increase in light sensitivity.” Furthermore, four out of eight people were able to see the outlines of even small objects, such as a matchbox.
Being able to recognize a door could greatly simplify everyday life, according to the study. Furthermore, those who practiced more with the glasses saw better.
However, this milestone is far from being the end of the road. “We are still a long way from patients being able to read or having the kind of vision we are used to,” said Futterknecht. Now, work is underway to improve various elements of the therapy, including the proteins that make cells light-sensitive.
Potential benefits
Ideally, patients treated should be able to see again without glasses. The long-term hope is “to restore vision as much as possible,” says Futterknecht.
Specifically, all participants in the study suffer from retinitis pigmentosa, but its origins differ. Futterknecht says this shows that the new gene therapy has the potential to benefit many blind people, not just a specific, small group.
Optogenetic therapy does not address every single cause of the various forms of this disease, in which, in advanced stages, the light-sensitive retinal cells barely function. Instead, it enables other cells in the retina to respond to light.

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim unveiled the national budget for 2027 on Friday with a focus on easing the cost of living through tax breaks, a higher minimum wage and other measures while also seeking to develop the country's burgeoning technology sector.
Malaysia's Budget 2027, totaling 459.8 billion ringgit (112.5 billion U.S. dollars), aims to turn resilient economic growth into real gains for the people with better wages, smarter targeted support, stronger fiscal discipline and a bold push towards higher-value industries, Anwar, who is also finance minister, told parliament in his budget speech.
Among measures aimed at easing the cost of living is raising the minimum wage to 2,000 ringgit from the current 1,700 ringgit starting in June 2027, with the exception of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises with annual sales below 50 million ringgit.
The government will also introduce a minimum monthly salary of 2,500 ringgit for semi-skilled workers and graduates as the initial step in reforming the wage framework. Middle-class citizens will benefit through increased individual income tax relief and reduced tax rates for selected income brackets.
Meanwhile, the government will extend green tax incentives to Dec. 31, 2030. Companies investing in green technology projects, electric vehicle charging stations or green assets for their own use will be eligible for up to 100 percent investment tax allowances.
A 100 million ringgit fund will support early-stage semiconductor and advanced manufacturing companies in Penang state as part of efforts to strengthen regional industrial development and attract investment beyond established economic centers. Other technology hubs in other states will also be supported to attract global semiconductor investments, create skilled jobs and expand business opportunities for local companies.
It will also implement a preferential five percent tax rate on income generated from global services hub activities for new companies, starting on Jan. 1, 2027, to facilitate business operations and make it easier for global companies to operate in Malaysia. ■

Interview: AI ethics should reflect common values of humanity, says UK AI expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:58:05 CST
20:58:05 KST

by Shao Haijun
ZAANDAM, THE NETHERLANDS, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly capable, humanity needs to consider not only what AI can do, but also what values should guide its development and use, according to Nigel Shadbolt, a member of the UK Government's Council for Science and Technology.
"As our AI systems become more capable, we would like them to embody the best of us," Shadbolt, also a Distinguished Senior Scientist at the Institute of Ethics in AI and Professor of Computer Science at the University of Oxford, told Xinhua in an exclusive interview on Wednesday on the sidelines of the World Summit AI, held on Oct. 7-8 in Zaandam, the Netherlands.
The rapid development of AI has brought major opportunities, but also created new forms of risk, raising fundamental questions about how increasingly capable systems should be designed and governed.
Shadbolt identified three broad areas of concern.
"The first is the misuse of AI by humans," he explained. "AI can accelerate drug discovery and scientific research, but the same capabilities could also be exploited by malicious actors to launch cyber-attacks, commit fraud, develop biological weapons or other harmful purposes."
"The second is the possibility that AI systems may pursue their assigned goals in unexpected ways," he said. Recent incidents involving advanced AI agents have highlighted this concern. For example, an AI agent developed by OpenAI reportedly breached a data portal linked to Australia's universal healthcare system in June.
"Highly capable systems could, for example, cheat, hack into systems or obtain credentials in ways their developers had not anticipated," he said.
A third concern is whether increasingly advanced AI could eventually become difficult for humans to control. While Shadbolt said he was not primarily focused on existential risks from hypothetical super intelligence, he argued that researchers should continue to examine the challenges presented by recursive self-improvement, AI systems developing evermore capable versions of themselves.
Technical safeguards and regulation are therefore necessary, but they may not be sufficient on their own. Shadbolt argued that sets of values should also be encoded into AI systems to help guide their behavior.
"What values do we put into the system? And how can we be confident that the model can't be persuaded to act in a way that suddenly has it cheating, lying or pretending to be less capable than it is?" he said.
He emphasized the goal should not be to impose one particular ethical tradition in the world. Instead, there may be room to identify values that can be shared across different societies and systems of governance.
"We do share a common set of values about what we think is desirable," he said.
Different societies have different philosophical and cultural traditions, ranging from utilitarianism and social contract theory to rule-based ethics and traditions emphasizing respect and social obligations. Some of these principles, he noted, have parallels with values found in Confucian thought.
"I'd like to believe that there is scope for agreement on some of those ideas -- what would common, shared ethical values look like," he said.
Shadbolt also called for more inclusive AI governance and greater international cooperation to ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain aligned with human interests. A more inclusive approach should address not only AI safety, but also data, intellectual property, consent and the distribution of economic benefits.
Ultimately, Shadbolt argued, AI governance needs to combine technological innovation with shared human values, ensuring that increasingly powerful AI systems serve not only national or commercial interests, but also the broader interests of humanity. ■

EU seeks to ban Russian diplomats from travelling outside host countries
On 12 October, the EU Foreign Affairs Council will discuss the possibility of introducing further restrictions on the movement of Russian diplomats between EU member states, potentially including a complete ban on travel outside the country to which they are accredited.
Source: European Pravda, citing several European diplomats and a senior EU official familiar with the preparations for the discussion
Details: European Pravda's sources indicate that the EU wants either to ban Russian diplomats from travelling outside their host country altogether or require them to obtain prior permission from any EU member state they intend to travel through.
The diplomats noted that several EU countries support significantly tightening restrictions on Russian diplomats' freedom of movement within the Schengen area.
Quote from one diplomat: "Until now, Russian diplomats have been able to notify their host country and travel wherever they want. Now we want to impose a blanket restriction."
Details: Another European Pravda source stressed that a significant proportion of Russian diplomats in the EU are intelligence officers, which is one of the main reasons the EU wants to restrict their freedom of movement.
Quote from another diplomat: "The logical next step would be to allow Russian diplomats to travel only within the country to which they are accredited. For example, a Russian diplomat accredited in France would not be allowed to travel to Germany or Belgium."
Details: Meanwhile, the EU is also considering a less restrictive option: requiring Russian diplomats to obtain permission from both their host country and the countries they intend to visit, rather than simply notifying them of travel within the Schengen area.
European Pravda's sources also highlighted the large number of Russian diplomats accredited to international organisations based in European capitals. They said the EU is interested in reducing their numbers and tightening oversight.
European Pravda notes that the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting on 12 October will be for discussion only, with no decision on new restrictions on Russian diplomats expected.
EU diplomats first want to gauge the level of political support for further measures restricting Russian diplomats' travel.
Furthermore, on 14 October, the EU Council's visa working group is due to discuss a German initiative on a common restrictive approach to issuing visas to Russian citizens, the use of visas with limited territorial validity and visa-related provisions in the EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia.
Background:
- In October 2025, as part of the 19th package of sanctions against Russia, the EU introduced a requirement for Russian diplomats to notify EU member states in advance of any travel outside the country to which they are accredited. The rules came into force on 25 January 2026.
- Since the summer, the EU has also been discussing restricting visa issuance to those who have fought in Ukraine for Russia. The EU included a mechanism to ban visas for Russian military personnel in its 21st sanctions package, but the ban itself has not yet come into force.
- In September, Hungary announced its decision to expel 10 staff members of the Russian embassy for activities deemed "unacceptable for diplomats" under the Vienna Convention.
- In early September, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski called for Russian diplomats to be allowed to travel only within the countries to which they are accredited, and for limits to be imposed on the number of accreditations they can hold.

Thieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian winery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:57:49 UTC
20:57:49 KST

Thousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind in Italy.
A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off.
Among the bottles targeted were those most prized by wine collectors and consumers, including Solaia, Guado al Tasso and Tignanello, notable as one of the first red wines in the Tuscany region to be produced without white grapes. All the stolen bottles, ranging in price between €120 and €400 a bottle, are from the firm’s 2023 vintage.
The theft occurred on Saturday as the company, based in the hilltop town of Cortona, prepared for a major shipment to buyers abroad. The robbery was discovered only when staff arrived for work on Monday morning.
“The gang was very prepared,” Renzo Cotarella, chief executive of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere della Sera. “A theft of this scale and value has never happened before in Italy.”
He said he had “great confidence” that investigators would trace the stolen wine, which included 3,000 bottles, some of them magnum-sized, of Barolo Ginestra.
“Two trucks full of merchandise can’t just disappear into thin air,” he added. “The Tuscan roads are full of cameras. Perhaps with a bit of luck we’ll be able to recover at least some of the bottles.”
There have been several thefts at wineries in Italy in recent months, including one in Alba in the northern Piedmont region in mid-September.
But Cotarella, who suspects the same gang could have been involved, never imagined a theft of such scale would happen to his company. Unfortunately, its insurance policy does not cover the robbery of wine at such huge value.
“We had always considered the possibility of having a few cases of wine being stolen during their transportation, but certainly not that two trucks manage to enter the cellar and make off with such a huge haul,” he told Corriere.
Such large wine robberies were usually meticulously prepared and would probably be carried out by those with an intimate knowledge of wine themselves, Corriere suggested, with the target destination possibly collectors, bars or restaurants. However, a sudden increase in the supply of such wines could raise suspicion.
As the investigators continue their search, Cotarella said the company, which was established in 1385, has warned customers to be wary of any offers of its wine outside official channels.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said his carrier is weighing whether to go ahead with debuting a flight between Atlanta and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after attacks claimed by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have escalated there.
The flights between Riyadh and Delta's biggest hub are scheduled to begin on Oct. 23.
Three people were killed in attacks at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as the Houthis stepped up strikes in the country, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said.
"Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," Bastian told CNBC in an interview. "Safety is is going to make the call."
He said that the airline will let customers know of its decision soon. German airline Lufthansa said it was pausing flights into Saudi Arabia through at least Oct. 16, a spokesman told CNBC.
Delta is planning to operate the Atlanta-Riyadh flight daily from Oct. 23 to Oct. 30 before moving to three-times-a-week service. When it announced the route earlier this year, Delta said it would be the first nonstop service between the U.S. and Riyadh operated by a U.S. airline.

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. The level of trust among Russians in President Vladimir Putin stands at 72.5%, according to a survey conducted by the All-Russian Center for Public Opinion Research (VTsIOM) from September 28 to October 4 among 1,600 adult Russians.
"When asked about trust in Putin, 72.5% of survey participants answered positively, while the level of approval for the president’s activities stands at 68.6%," the pollster noted in its materials.
The Russian government’s performance is approved by 44.6% of respondents, while 44.1% approve of the work of Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin. Trust in Mishustin stands at 54.1%.
Respondents also expressed their attitudes toward the leaders of parliamentary parties. Trust in Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov stands at 36.7%, A Just Russia leader Sergey Mironov at 26.7%, Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR) leader Leonid Slutsky at 22.7%, and New People party chairman Alexey Nechayev at 13.7%.
Support for United Russia stands at 31.9%, the Communist Party at 18.8%, the LDPR at 9.3%, A Just Russia at 4.6%, and New People at 11.6%.

Details
The former prince left Royal Lodge at the beginning of this year and currently resides on the Sandringham estate. Andrew fully vacated the property and paid £1.8 million for repairs and restoration work.
It is noted that Andrew was entitled to compensation because, under the terms of the lease, he surrendered it early, within the first 25 years.
Andrew lived in the 30-room mansion on the Windsor Estate grounds for more than 20 years.
The lease on Royal Lodge has been terminated, and our focus is now on the future use of the property and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the country through its early return

2026/27 PGPL: Tractor remain top
TEHRAN - The first day of Matchweek 8 in the 2026/27 Persian Gulf Pro League (PGPL) concluded with six matches, as Tractor maintained their position at the top of the table following a 1–1 draw against Esteghlal.
Sepahan, Gol Gohar and Aluminum also strengthened their positions with results that brought them to 13 points.
In the most anticipated fixture, Tractor drew 1–1 with Esteghlal at Yadegar-e Imam Stadium in Tabriz. The result left Tractor top with 17 points, while Esteghlal remained second with 16.
Sepahan recorded one of the biggest victories of the round, thrashing Fajr Sepasi 6–1. The win took Moharram Navidkia’s side to 13 points and lifted them to fourth place. Fajr Sepasi remained 13th with seven points.

Elsewhere, Aluminum drew 1–1 with Malavan, while Nassaji shared the same scoreline with Zob Ahan. Aluminum moved to 13 points, while Nassaji and Malavan reached nine and eight points respectively.
In the final match of the day, Foolad Khuzestan beat Mes Shahr-e Babak 2–1 to climb to seventh with 12 points. Mes remained 17th with five points.
At the end of the day, Tractor lead with 17 points, followed by Esteghlal on 16. Persepolis sit third with 13 points and a game in hand, while Aluminium, Sepahan and Gol Gohar remain close behind.

Russia plans to allocate over $141.51 mln for Arctic, Antarctic research through 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:56:18 UTC
20:56:18 KST

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. Russia’s draft federal budget for 2027-2029 allocates more than 12 bln rubles ($141.51 mln) for polar expeditions in the Arctic and Antarctica, Russian Deputy Natural Resources and Environment Minister Konstantin Tsyganov said at a meeting of the State Duma Committee on Ecology, Natural Resources, and Environmental Protection.
"In September 2024, polar expeditions began aboard the new ice-resistant North Pole platform, and in December of the same year, the new Vostok wintering complex was commissioned in Antarctica. To support their operations, as well as those of four other year-round and five seasonal stations in Antarctica and the expedition to the Spitsbergen archipelago, the draft budget allocates more than 12 bln rubles," Tsyganov said.
In addition, 2.3 bln rubles ($27.12 mln) will be allocated to developing the state environmental monitoring system in the Arctic.

‘I want to thank President Putin’, Trump says after agreeing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel – US politics live
Prominent Republicans joined Democrats to condemn president for lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and administration’s plan to livestream execution of Fort Hood attacker
Republicans join Democrats to condemn Trump's oil deal with Putin and plan to livestream execution of Fort Hood gunman
A number of prominent Republicans joined Democrats on Friday to condemn Donald Trump for lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and the plan to livestream the execution of the former army major who carried out the Fort Hood attack in 2009.
“Trump started a stupid & illegal war in Iran that has driven up diesel prices. Now he wants to bankroll Putin’s illegal war against Ukraine by buying diesel from him,” senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, wrote in response to the news of Trump’s deal with Putin to lift sanctions and import Russian diesel. “One strategic disaster after the next.”
“70% of Americans support Ukraine,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, chimed in. “Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities. The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”
“This announcement is a disgrace,” senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, wrote. “You know how Trump could bring down gas and diesel prices? By ending his illegal war with Iran. Instead, he’s going to help fund Putin’s war machine.”
Warren also joined her Democratic colleagues, Jeanne Shaheen, of New Hampshire, anf Chuck Schumer, of New York, in a statement denouncing Trump’s deal with Putin.
“President Trump’s announcement that the United States will allow global purchases of Russian diesel for six months, is a total betrayal of Ukraine, our European allies and American national security,” the Democratic senators wrote. “After launching a war with Iran that has spiked gas and diesel prices for every American, the President is resorting to desperate ‘deals’ with a murderous dictator to attempt to clean up his own mess.
“Through the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, we gave the president significant authorities and leverage against China and Russia to bring Putin’s war to an end with a negotiated settlement,” congressman Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican posted on social media. “Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin’s war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days.”
“Putin throws lifeline to try to save Trump in the midterms,” senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat, wrote. “In return, American dollars go to Russia and get put toward killing innocent Ukrainians. Trump/Russia right out in the open.”
Congressman Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, agreed, writing: “Infuriating—but this is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia. Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he’s *lifting* sanctions on Russian fossil fuels.”
“The Fort Hood shooting was a horrific act of violence that took 13 innocent lives and devastated military families,” senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat, wrote. But there is a fundamental difference between carrying out a lawful sentence and turning an execution into a public spectacle.”
“Public executions are the hallmark of authoritarian regimes like Iran and North Korea, not the United States of America,” he added. “There is a reason that almost no countries in the world engage in this barbaric practice. Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory, fuel radicalization, and put American service members, diplomats, and citizens overseas at greater risk.”
“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” congressman Tom Barrett, a Michigan Republican fighting to hold his seat in a tight race with progressive Democrat Will Lawrence, posted. “Nidal Hasan is an evil person ... That does not change the fact that our American values should strive to elevate human dignity. Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.”
“There is no need to livestream any execution, including this one,” senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican posted. “I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America. It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks. How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision.
“I support bringing this terrorist to justice,” congressman Michael Baumgartner, a Washington Republican, wrote of the execution of the Fort Hood attacker. “I do not support the public livestream of the execution. This should be reconsidered.”
“Who still carries out public executions: The Iranian regime The North Korean regime The Taliban in Afghanistan Al-Shabaab in Somalia,” Nikki Haley, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the 2024 Republican nomination before supporting him, posted on social media. “That is not the company we want to keep or the country we want to be.”
A crowd of Trump supporters waiting for the president to appear at a rally in Syracuse, New York was just treated to the song, Rich Men North of Richmond, blasting oujt over arena loudspeakers.
The song, by Oliver Anthony, includes a pointed reference to the sway of Jeffrey Epstein, the late convicted sex offender Donald Trump socialized with for nearly two decades.
“I wish politicians would look out for miners/ And not just minors on an island somewhere,” Anthony’s voice sang, to no discernible reaction from the president’s fans.

Trump suggests final decision has not been made on whether execution of Fort Hood gunman will be streamed live
On his way to a rally for Republicans in upstate New York on Friday, Donald Trump was asked about the controversy over his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, saying that the execution of the gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009 would be livestreamed.
Hours after his vice-president, JD Vance, said that he did not know if the killing of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist, would be streamed live, Trump was asked by a reporter: “Do you want the execution of the Fort Hood shooter to be livestreamed? And are you worried that the video would be used as propaganda?”
“Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump said. “But he will be, uh, killed. He will be, through firing squad. He killed 13, 14 people,” the president said.
“He’s totally nuts, so I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes,” Trump continued. “And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
The president then ignored a follow-up question about whether he would watch the execution.
Several Republican lawmakers joined Democrats and human rights advocates in condemning Hegseth’s idea that the execution should be streamed live.
Minutes later, Trump leaned in to listen to a follow-up question from a Brazilian correspondent, Raquel Krähenbühl, who asked, in slightly imperfect English: “Did you personally authorize or approve the execution, the livestream execution of the Fort Hood-”
“Did I approve?” Trump cut in to ask.
“Did you approve?” the reporter repeated.
“Absolutely,” Trump said, although it was not entirely clear if he either heard or was responding to the part of the question about the execution being streamed live.
As Trump walked away, Krähenbühl sought to clarify, shouting “the live-streaming?” but the president did not reply audibly.
The correspondent for Brazil’s TV Globo later shared video of her exchange with Trump on social media, in which he did appear to nod in response to her follow-up question about the live stream.
'I want to thank President Putin', Trump says, after agreeing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel ahead of midterms
As he left the White House on Friday for a rally in New York state, flanked by the former boxer Mike Tyson, Donald Trump extended his thanks to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, for agreeing to sell diesel fuel to the US in return for the lifting of US sanctions on fuel exports from Russia, even as Russia’s deadly war on Ukraine continues.
When a reporter asked Trump to comment on the response from Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said “that you are weak”, Trump ignored the question and turned to the rest op the press corps to boast about the deal.
“I think you heard about the oil deal with Russia. That is a big deal,” Trump said.
“That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country. And I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you. We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel which is what we want, so: thank you,” the president said.
“Zelenskyy said you are weak because of it,” the reporter told Trump. “He just criticized you.”
“Who said that?” Trump leaned in and asked.
“Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, just said you are weak because of the deal you made with Putin,” the journalist replied.
Trump then stepped away and called on another journalist instead of responding.
Minutes later, another reporter returned to the subject, telling Trump: “President Zelenskyy said the diesel deal is a weak move by a strong partner that will only prolong the war.”
When that reporter asked, “Is this emboldening-” Trump cut in to ask: “By a strong what?”
“By a strong partner that will only prolong the war,” the reporter said.
“Well, we are a strong partner,” Trump said.
“Will this embolden Putin?” the reporter asked.
“Well, no; we need oil for the world and this is diesel which is what we need. So, we’re very happy to get it,” Trump said. “We’re very happy to get it. Look, we need it. Oil prices are already dropping like a rock. So, we’re very happy to get it.”
Zelenskyy denounces Trump's decision to lift diesel sanctions on Russia as 'weak'
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced Donald Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions on Russia, to let the US buy diesel fuel from the nation that kills Ukrainian civilians daily, in an interview with Axios on Friday.
Zelenskyy, who had traveled to Washington to plead with US lawmakers to pass tougher sanctions on Russia last month, reportedly told Axios on Friday that Trump’s decision, was “not fair and not honest” and “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin”.
“It looks absolutely terrible,” he added.
Ukraine’s president also criticized Trump’s decision in a statement on social media, in which he wrote:
Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill, there must be support for Ukraine in protecting lives, and there must be pressure on Russia for its war. And today, there was a conversation between the leaders of America and Russia. A conversation that leads to something different. …
Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness. It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world. …
Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will “repay” the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis. We count on America’s fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one.
As Republican senators met Zelenskyy to discuss tougher sanctions on Russia, Trump struck deal with Putin to buy diesel
Donald Trump’s surprise announcement on Friday, that the US will buy diesel from Russia, and is lifting sanctions for six months to enable Russia to export diesel freely, came as two Republican senators, Kevin Cramer of North Dakota and Roger Wicker of Mississippi, were in Kyiv meeting with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to discuss implementing the tough new Russia sanctions law signed by Trump just three weeks ago.

Trump says he struck a deal with Putin for Russia to sell diesel to US, weeks after signing Russia sanctions law
Just weeks after signing a new law that gave him the authority to impose tariffs on countries that buy fuel from Russia despite US sanctions, Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US will now be buying fuel from Russia.
Writing on social media, Trump said that he stuck a deal with Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, “wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace,” to be followed by another 4.5m tons of diesel fuel exports.
A short time later, the US treasury’s office of foreign assets control announced that, at Trump’s direction, it had lifted sanctions on the sale of Russian diesel to the global market, “including importation into the United States for six months.
Trump claimed that the deal, which suspends an effort to punish Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, would soon drive down the cost of fuel in the US, which has been a concern to voters casting ballots in the midterm elections.
The Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, signed into law on 18 September, authorized the president to impose tariffs on countries “facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion”, but also gave him broad authority to waive any sanctions or tariffs. Those provisions had led some Democrats to oppose the legislation, arguing that it delegated too much authority to Trump.

Writing on social media, Donald Trump confirmed on Friday that he has appointed a rightwing commentator, Katie Zacharia, as the new White House press secretary.

“She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!”

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance was asked about how he squares his Christian faith with the Pentagon’s decision to broadcast the execution – for the first time in US history. He went on to say that if the decision is made to livestream he was “not going to be watching it”.

Senator John Curtis, a Republican from Utah, said “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment”. Meanwhile, Rob Bresnahan – a GOP congressman who is facing a competitive re-election battle for his central Pennsylvania district – said the victims and their families’ pain “deserves respect, not a public show”.
