Trump envoy kept financial ties to firm behind $15 billion Hormuz-bypass oil pipeline plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:41:58 UTC
20:41:58 KST

Thomas Barrack, a top US diplomat in the Middle East, advocated for a firm run by his business partner to take part in the development of an oil pipeline from Iraq to Syria, three people said, activities which appear to violate federal ethics rules.
In July, Iraq and Syria signed memorandums of understanding with a consortium made up of the company, Californian investment group TI Capital, along with Chevron and Qatar’s UCC Holding, to carry out technical and financial studies in preparation for rehabilitating the pipeline, which would skirt the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.
Barrack, US presidential special envoy to both Iraq and Syria as well as Ambassador to Turkey, has a longstanding business relationship with TI Capital and its founder Ziad Ghandour. At the time of his confirmation hearings in 2025 he had a financial interest entitling him to as much as a fifth of the profits from a real-estate venture near San Francisco, California and managed by TI Capital - with Ghandour as chief executive - that he said he intended to retain, public records show.
During engagements with Syrian and Iraqi officials after the start of the war in Iran, Barrack pressed for Ghandour's firm to be included in the project, according to two of the people, who have direct knowledge of the discussions.
On June 16, a month before the consortium agreement was signed, Barrack and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi issued a joint statement that commended Iraq's decision "to advance a memorandum of understanding with TI Capital to rehabilitate the Kirkuk-Baniyas Pipeline." The statement made no mention of Chevron or UCC in connection with the pipeline.
Reuters found no evidence that Barrack stands to profit from the pipeline or other projects. His ties to Ghandour would not constitute a criminal conflict of interest unless he stood to directly profit from the pipeline itself, two ethics lawyers told Reuters.
However, Barrack's relationship with Ghandour makes such advocacy "a serious problem" under the regulation that prohibits officials from participating in matters that call into question their impartiality because of a personal or business relationship, said Richard Painter, a former chief White House ethics lawyer and a professor at the University of Minnesota Law School.
The impartiality rule, which is not a criminal statute, can be triggered by the involvement of a business associate in a project, regardless of whether the official has a financial interest of his own.
“The ethical concern is the appearance of a conflict of interest," said Ann Skeet, interim executive director at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics in Santa Clara University.
Asked what Barrack would have needed to do to comply, Painter said: "Have nothing to do with this pipeline. Completely recuse. Say this is not a matter I participate in."
Don Fox, a former general counsel and acting director of the US Office of Government Ethics, said that promotion of TI Capital by Barrack would additionally violate a regulation prohibiting officials from using their office to endorse any enterprise or for the private gain of people they are affiliated with.
Barrack has not filed a conflict-of-interest waiver with the US Office of Government Ethics regarding his ties to the company as it participates in the project, according to a Reuters records request. Waivers allow officials with potential conflicts of interest to participate in matters that would otherwise require the employee be recused.
In a signed ethics agreement before his confirmation hearings last year, he committed to recusing himself from matters directly affecting the financial interests of the real-estate venture unless he first obtained such a waiver.
Barrack’s office and Chevron declined to comment. TI Capital, Ghandour and UCC did not respond to requests for comment.
In a July 17 post on X, Barrack said the involvement of US companies in Iraq and Syria was “a new paradigm” aimed at bringing clarity and opportunity to the region.
A fourth ethics lawyer said it was up to the State Department to decide whether its employee's financial holdings create a potential conflict of interest.
"Ambassador Barrack has no affiliation with, role in, or financial interest in the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline project," a State Department spokesperson told Reuters, while acknowledging Barrack’s relationship with the TI Capital real-estate venture.
His public comments on the pipeline reflect "long-standing, publicly stated US policy interest in regional energy integration," the spokesperson said, adding that Barrack was certified to be in compliance with ethics rules.
The disclosed interest: Barrack declared an equity stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment
In a financial disclosure filed with the US Office of Government Ethics in March 2025, before assuming his diplomatic roles, Barrack declared an equity stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment LLC, a venture building a large housing project near San Francisco. The filing did not disclose the size of the stake, but said he was entitled to 20% of the company’s profits when the earnings reach an established minimum.
ACD-TI is managed by TI Capital and headed by Ghandour, California state corporate records show. Reuters was unable to find contact details for a company representative and did not get a response to questions sent to its postal correspondence address.
The filing said the profit-sharing arrangement was in return for services he provided to the company. Barrack also disclosed to the OGE a paid consulting role with the venture in 2024. The filing does not say whether or how much he was paid.
In a separate signed ethics agreement dated March 7, 2025, three weeks before his Senate confirmation hearing, Barrack listed ACD-TI Oakley among assets he would retain rather than sell.
Bypassing Hormuz via the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline
The historic Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline, which for decades moved Iraqi crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast, faced sporadic shutdowns from the early 1980s and has been out of action since the US invasion of Iraq in 2003. Mothballed plans to revive it received new impetus this year when, under US attack, Iran restricted traffic through Hormuz, pushing oil prices higher.
Several people told Reuters in August the pipeline would take at least four years and cost $15 billion to build.
The idea of bringing TI Capital into the regional project was raised by Barrack in May at the Milken Institute Global Conference in Los Angeles, a third person with direct knowledge of the conversation told Reuters. The discussion, they added, took place on the sidelines of the event.
With the US war on Iran raging, Barrack and Ghandour also participated in an invite-only panel at the conference, where they discussed in more general terms the need for new energy supply lines in the Middle East, the person said.
A Milken Institute spokesperson declined to provide details of the panel discussion, saying it was closed to the media.
Barrack has engaged in business with Ghandour since at least 2020, when the two men created a $250 million blank-check SPAC that was dissolved after Barrack was arrested in 2021 on charges of acting as an unregistered agent of the United Arab Emirates. He was acquitted in 2022.
The Iraqi cabinet named TI Capital later in July as part of another consortium with UCC Holding and ConocoPhillips to assess the Akkas gas field, one of Iraq's largest undeveloped reserves. On its website, the firm claims involvement in projects at Syria's Tartous port, without providing details. Syria’s port authority did not reply to questions about TI Capital, and Reuters could not verify its role in Tartous. ConocoPhillips did not reply to a request for comment.
A person close to Barrack said the ambassador trusted Ghandour to help implement US President Donald Trump’s regional strategy of bringing Iraq and Syria closer to the US. “Ziad is the chosen man. Hand-picked by Barrack,” the person said.
The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department.

Just how sunlike is the sun?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:41:08 UTC
20:41:08 KST

Is the sun a sunlike star?
If you’re not an astronomer, the obvious answer is yes. That’s tautological! Sunlike stars are stars like the sun. The sun is the sun, so it’s the most sunlike of them all!
Astronomers, though, can be persnickety. When asked that question, they immediately shoot another right back: What do you mean by “sunlike”?
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
That’s a fair response. If the definition is too broad, the sun starts to look a little funny, appearing quite unlike other stars. For a much tighter definition—well, it’s still a little off but not nearly as much.
So why ask this question in the first place?
Astronomers like to look at large populations of objects because bigger sample sizes should better reveal trends in their properties. This can lead to greater insights on their structure, their characteristics and the physics that underlie it all.
We already know a lot about the sun, given that it’s the nearest star in the universe to us. If we then compare it with other, similar stars, we can extrapolate the properties we know to those we may not, thus learning more about them, too.
For example, when compared with stars of similar mass, the sun sits right at the average in terms of its temperature and the amount of energy that it emits. In those cases, it’s quite normal.
But stars have other properties! An important one for a star is its amount of magnetic activity, which depends on the strength and variability of its magnetic field and the effect that field has on the star and its immediate surroundings. Research published in the journal Science in 2020 suggested that the sun was not normal when compared with the magnetic activity of other, similar stars. Our very own star was instead something of an underachiever.
Magnetic fields are extremely complex phenomena. They can, however, be explored in stars using a surprisingly simple method: looking at star spots—sunspots on other stars.
At the risk of oversimplifying, magnetism is created when charged particles (such as electrons, protons or ionized atoms) move around. In general, the more coherently these particles move as a group, the stronger the magnetic field is. All of them ping-ponging around higgledy-piggledy won’t generate a magnetic field, but a cloud of them moving along together will.
The sun and stars like it aren’t just miasmas of incandescent plasma. They have internal layers, such as each’s core, where energy is generated by thermonuclear fusion power. At some distance above that, material heated by the core rises up, just like warm air rises in Earth’s atmosphere, flowing upward until it reaches the star’s surface. It then radiates its heat into space, cools and sinks back down in a process called convection. It’s like a conveyor belt of heat, and there are many thousands of such towers of upward-and-downward-flowing cells in the sun.
But that gas is hot enough to have electrons stripped from its atoms, making it ionized. Each vast tower of flowing material therefore creates its own magnetic field, which it drags along as it flows vertically. Sometimes, the magnetic fields from neighboring convection cells get tangled together, and when these tangles reach the surface, they prevent material from easily flowing back down. So that stuff spends more time at the surface, where it cools a bit more than usual. Cooler gas doesn’t glow as brightly, so these patches are a little bit darker than the surrounding material. These are the aforementioned star spots. And besides looking menacingly dark, they are sites of enhanced magnetic activity.
It’s easy to see them on the sun, but detecting them on distant stars is much harder. It is possible, however, because stars rotate. As one does, star spots spinning into view can slightly dim the star, as seen from afar, with bigger spots or groups of spots causing greater dimming. The star brightens again when the spots rotate back out of view. By carefully measuring the star’s fluctuating brightness, we can get a measure of its star spot activity and use that as a proxy for its magnetic field.
This is more important than you might think because a star’s magnetic field isn’t constant. The sun, for example, has a roughly 11-year cycle in which the magnetic field waxes and wanes in strength. When it’s strong, the number of sunspots increases. At the peak of the cycle, the sun blasts out more solar flares, as well as coronal mass ejections, immense explosions of material that scream outward into the solar system. These can profoundly affect our orbiting satellites and power grid, so understanding the sun’s magnetic activity actually very much impacts us here on Earth.
And this is where the sun appeared anomalous in the 2020 research: it didn’t show as much magnetic activity as similar stars. So maybe the sun is a magnetic weakling.
A team of astronomers wanted to take a closer look at this. The scientists used data from NASA’s exoplanet-hunting satellite Kepler, which searched for exoplanets via very precise, high-cadence brightness measurements of hundreds of thousands of stars. Those measurements, it turns out, can be used to look for star spots as well.
Their results, published in 2023 in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics, is that the sun is indeed less active compared with other stars in a broad range of characteristics such as temperature and mass. But by narrowing the range of these parameters—for instance, by only looking at stars whose temperature was within 100 degrees Celsius of that of the sun—they found our home star is only a tad bit less active, well within the range of normal.
So the sun is a sunlike star.
Still, why are the other stars stronger at all? If they have the same properties as the sun, what makes them more magnetically excited?
The answer, the team found, is that the stars observed by Kepler are composed of somewhat higher levels of heavy elements. Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, with much smaller amounts of elements like iron, carbon, and so on. But these trace elements can have an outsize effect on overall stellar characteristics.
For example, heavy elements are better at absorbing heat from the core, which affects the size of a star’s convective layer. More heavy elements make the convective layer deeper, allowing it to generate a more powerful magnetic field.
Surprisingly, this also affects a star’s rotation. Stars like the sun blow a wind of subatomic particles; in the case of the sun, we call it the solar wind. As the star spins, the magnetic field coming out of the surface catches that wind and sweeps it up. This imparts a drag on the star—imagine spinning around on your heels while holding an open trash bag; the bag will act like a parachute, slowing you. Over millions and billions of years, the drag from a star’s magnetic field slows its rotation, and in fact, the astronomers found that stars with stronger magnetism tended to rotate more slowly.
So that dash of heavier elements in other stars has wide-ranging effects and shows that, in the end, it’s not so much that the sun isn’t sunlike but rather that astronomers need to do a little extra bookkeeping when they compare it with other stars.
It’s reassuring to know the sun is sunlike after all. And while that might seem like a silly question, it actually reveals a lot of fascinating science behind stars and their behavior. It also forces us to question our assumptions, something every scientist (and everybody) should do.

In Pictures: Weirdest and most thought-provoking statues of Donald Trump over the years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:40:41 UTC
20:40:41 KST

Following the headline-grabbing statue "The Orange Plague" by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, which was displayed this week at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, we take a look back at some of the ways artists have depicted Trump in satirical, humorous and thought-provoking ways.
Donald Trump has been immortalised by artists on countless occasions, with creatives using their talents to poke fun, criticise, educate, and even warn.
From signs and murals to carnival floats, the divisive POTUS has inspired many to remind the public that the arts are a vital way to comment, inform and inspire.
One artform which has been an effective favourite for many wishing to represent Trump is the sculpted figure. It makes sense since Trump has shown a clear preference for classical and gilded aesthetics; statues play on the man’s perception of monumentalism as being a reflection of power. Artists therefore use oversized or flashy statues to better reflect and lampoon Trump’s ego, as well as comment on the pitfalls of gaudish effigies which so often betray a sense of narcissism.
In effect, the momuments strike at the heart of Trump's sensibilities and symbolically cast him as the eagle in Aesop’s fable – a figure undone by a self-infliction. In this case, a marked proclivity for oversized effigies.
The latest example has been "The Orange Plague", the 2.6-meter statue by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt.
Coated with 23-karat gold, the artwork also known as “The King of Injustice” shows a nude Trump holding a comically sized golf club in one hand, a set of scales in the other, all while sitting on the back of a smaller, frailer man.
Beneath the statue is a plaque which reads: "I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back. - The King of Injustice."
According to Galschiøt, the work is a “satirical outcry” against Trump’s volatile climate and foreign policies.
The statue was previously displayed at the “hands off Greenland” demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier this year and the COP30 UN Climate Summit in Belém, Brazil last year. It has just finished its short stint at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg and is heading to the COP31 UN Climate Conference next month in Antalya, Türkiye.
Before we see “The Orange Plague” once more, here are other notable statues of Trump which have amused spectators and sought to reflect what certain people think of the current leader of the free world.
"The Emperor Has No Balls"
Artist: Indecline
Year: 2016
Original location: Cleveland, Los Angeles, New York City, San Francisco, Seattle
Description: Not one, but five 1.95m-tall statues were installed in five major cities in the US. Made of clay and silicone, the statues show a naked Trump with bits missing. The title will clue you which. The monuments were all promptly taken down, with the greatest official statement being from the New York City Parks Department, whose phrasing was perfection. They said that it “stands firmly against any unpermitted erection in city parks, no matter how small”.
"Dump Trump"
Artist: Don Lessem
Year: 2019
Original location: Trafalgar Square, London
Description: The 4.9m-tall statue depicts Donald Trump sitting on a golden toilet and on his phone, wearing a MAGA hat with the words “Impeach Me!” on the headwear. The statue was spotted during Trump’s visit to the United Kingdom. It was also seen during the Trump-organised Salute To America in Washington D.C. on 4 July 2019. Also worth noting is that the effigy emitted noises of flatulence and featured audio of Trump catchphrases like “I’m a very stable genius” and “fake news”.
"Statue of Illiberty"
Artist: Tomaž Schlegl
Year: 2019
Original location: Near Kamnik, Slovenia
Description: The wooden statue was erected only weeks after architect / artist Tomaž Schlegl’s Melenia Trump statue, which was placed in her home town of Sevnica. That one was destroyed by fire. “Statue of Illiberty” showed Trump with his arm raised in the style of the Statue of Liberty, but featured two sides. One side was Trump’s face (with luscious red lips); the other face was an image of a “vampire”, a monstruous image which served as something of a warning. And wouldn’t you know it, this statue was also burned down a year later.
"In Honor of a Lifetime of Sexual Assault"
Artist: Anonymous
Year: 2024
Original location: Portland and Philadelphia
Description: Two satirical statues, approximately 2.4m tall, which were spray painted gold, showing Trump grinning and making a grabbing gesture with his right hand. The plaque accompanying the statues was a direct quote from Trump from the infamous Access Hollywood tape: “I just start kissing them. It's like a magnet. Just kiss. I don't even wait. And when you're a star they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab them by the pussy. You can do anything.”
"Best Friends Forever"
Artist: The Secret Handshake
Year: 2025
Original location: National Mall, Washington D.C.
Description: Otherwise known as “Why Can’t We Be Friends?”, this 3.7 meter-tall statue depicts Donald Trump and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein merrily holding hands and frolicking. It was created in protest of the relationship between Trump and Epstein and as a way to call out the sexual misconduct allegations against Trump and the redaction of the Epstein Files. The statue was constructed from foam, resin, wood and coloured to appear bronze. The center plaque read: "In Honor of Friendship Month – We celebrate the long-lasting bond between President Donald J. Trump and his “closest friend” Jeffrey Epstein.” It was dismantled by the US Park Police within 24 hours of installation but "Best Friends Forever" was temporarily reinstalled at various other locations in Washington D.C.
"King of the World"
Artist: The Secret Handshake
Year: 2026
Original location: National Mall, Washington D.C.
Description: The 3.6m statue was seen this year as a companion piece to "Best Friends Forever", as it also depicts Trump and Epstein. This time, the anonymous artists belonging to The Secret Handshake mimicked the Jack and Rose pose from Titanic. The plaque accompanying it read: "The tragic love story between Jack and Rose was built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches. This monument honors the bond between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein, a friendship seemingly built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches."

A theft worth €5 million has occurred
at the Marchesi Antinori facility in Cortona (Arezzo), as
thieves made off with 30,000 bottles produced by the Florentine
winery—all from the 2023 vintage—including 10,000 bottles of
their most prestigious product Solaia, Corriere della Sera and
the Financial Times reported Friday.
                                    
According to the Italian newspaper, this is the largest wine
heist by value ever to take place in Italy.
                                    
A group of at least seven people carried out the operation last
Sunday night, managing to haul away a shipment of Solaia,
Tignanello, and Guado al Tasso—wines ranging in price from €120
to €300 per bottle.
                                    
After disabling the alarm system and putting the cellar's
security cameras out of commission, the thieves reportedly
entered with two trucks and loaded the bottles using the
company's own forklifts.
                                    
The theft was only discovered on Monday morning when employees
arrived and found the wine missing.
                                    
"It is certainly a highly organized gang," Renzo Cotarella, CEO
of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere.
                                    
"Perhaps the same one that has targeted other wineries in Italy
in recent months. A theft of this magnitude and value has
certainly never happened in Italy before."
The stolen stock could be destined for collectors or venue
owners, though it is likely to raise suspicions—particularly
regarding the Solaia, of which only about 60,000 to 70,000
bottles are produced annually.
                                    
"We are informing our customers around the world," the company
explained—as reported by the Italian newspaper—"we want to warn
them to be wary of offers made outside official channels."
"We still hope to recover the wine; two trucks cannot simply
vanish," Cotarella told the FT.
                                    
"These wines are highly valuable, and I don't understand how
they could be sold worldwide without being detected," he added,
noting that Antinori also aims to "protect the market" by
warning potential buyers that bottles offered by unusual sources
at attractive prices could be stolen goods.

'Grand odysseys': Why historic travel and legendary journeys are trending for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:40:21 UTC
20:40:21 KST

Skyscanner’s 2027 travel trends report points to growing demand for historic trails, ancient ruins and iconic destinations brought to life on screen, as travellers look to the past for a sense of connection in a fast-paced world.
It’s the season when travel companies start to reveal their predictions for the following year, and now Skyscanner has launched its 2027 Travel Trends report.
Pairing global search insights and research from more than 28,000 travellers, the report uses data from the likes of TikTok, ClassPass, Wise, Universal Music Group for Brands, and AllTrails.
Among the new trends for 2027 is history-focussed travel, which follows on from a trend which has already seen significant traction this year thanks, in no small part, to The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of Homer's epic poem.
Skyscanner has called this particular trend “Grand Odysseys”, and suggests that its popularity is down to travellers trying to escape a fast-paced world. They’re seeking out history which offers context and grounds them in timeless human stories.
Next year will see tourists following sacred walking trails, exploring legendary ruins and turning to the past to enrich their often overwhelming present.
Skyscanner’s research found that cinematic releases have been driving real-world bookings, with films and TV shows including The Odyssey and Gladiator proving particularly inspiring.
Data from TikTok backs this up, too, showing that video views for cinematic travel content are up +346% year on year, while posts featuring #HeroJourney are up some +452%.
The Odyssey reportedly prompted a third of people to plan a trip inspired by the epic, and the data shows that almost half – 43% – of Millennials have been inspired by films and TV set in antiquity, from Troy to the tales of Ancient Greece.
And 24% of them have taken it further and travelled in the footsteps of ancient stories, a figure which rises to 30% among Gen Z.
The top historic hikes for 2027
Among Skyscanner’s partners for the report was the app AllTrails, which revealed its top five walking trails to experience historical travel on foot in 2027.
In first place is Corfu’s Cape Drastis Loop. The popular route on the Greek island is said to be ancient author Homer’s mythical land of Phaeacia, where a shipwrecked Odysseus shared the story of his epic 10-year journey home.
Next up was the route between Horcones Viewpoint, Horcones Lagoon and Espejo Lagoon in Argentina. Walkers can experience shimmering glacial lakes as they walk in the shadow of Mount Aconcagua, South America’s highest peak.
In third place was China’s Xi’an City Wall. Here, visitors can stroll along impressive Ming Dynasty walls where ancient gateways, sweeping views and centuries of history unfold below.
In fourth is Monte Santa Caterina in Favignana, Italy. Adventurous travellers can climb to Favignana’s highest point, which is home to a historic castle with a rich history linked to the island, long associated with Odysseus’ legendary voyage.
Finally, Rizes Cave, or the Cave of Eumaeus, in Ithaca, Greece continues The Odyssey theme. Here, walkers will pass through olive groves above the Ionian before arriving at a cave where Odysseus sought refuge after returning home in the epic tale.
“It’s grounding to visit a trail and realise you’re seeing the same rugged peaks, ancient forests, and horizons that travellers did thousands of years ago,” said Shelby Eagleburger, head of data integrity at AllTrails.
“Historic routes remind us that exploring the outdoors is a universal human experience, and it connects us across generations. How we travel evolves, but the pull of natural landscapes stays the same.”
Skyscanner’s top trends for 2027
Grand Odysseys is one of seven trends featured in the Skyscanner report, all of which show a shift in traveller behaviour.
The prediction trends also include “Signal Severance”, which is linked to the fact that one in four Gen Z travellers plan to disconnect in 2027.
Many of us are craving a less connected world and are seeking out remote travel spots, or places where it’s possible to switch off entirely.
Skyscanner found that digital detox spots in Finland, including Kittilä and Rovaniemi, are seeing rising demand.
Most of us like to bring back a keepsake from a trip – whose fridge isn’t covered in magnets? But for 2027, Skyscanner believes that the best souvenirs are the ones you have to travel for, with travellers increasingly building itineraries around unique regional apparel, artisanal crafts and location-exclusive items.
One in four travellers have taken a trip specifically for items they couldn't buy online, including the vastly popular Trader Joe's tote from the United States and merchandise from the Ritz Paris.
Weddings and travel often go hand-in-hand and, increasingly, couples are choosing to move away from gendered celebrations and are embracing the “sten do”, a combination of stag and hen parties. The report shows that 25% of travellers are opting for these combined celebrations abroad as they’re more fun, less expensive and easier to organise.
If you’re into fitness and wellbeing, you may already be an aficionado of the gym-cation, but it’s set to be a huge trend in 2027.
The report found that 67% of millennials are more likely to book a hotel which serves a nutritious breakfast, and 40% of Gen Z travellers said they prioritise hotels with gyms. TikTok data also showed a +659% year-on-year increase in video views for "Gym Hotel" content.
Increasingly, many travellers are opting to base a trip around seeing live music and experiencing unusual events.
Cultural immersion is a priority as traditional carnivals rank highly for both Gen Z (33%) and Millennials (30%), while 25% of those surveyed said the setting of a concert is almost as important as the set list, with fans hoping for gigs held in the likes of ancient caves or pyramids.
Finally, the “currency chasers” trend is set to be huge in 2027. Those keen to save cash are plumping for destinations where they can take advantage of positive foreign exchange rates.
According to the data, 45% of Gen Z and 40% of Millennial travellers have switched destinations to get more bang for their buck. Vietnam is a particularly popular choice for this trend, as the currency means tourists can spend relatively little while making the most of the beautiful Asian nation.

Russia gains ground as France retreats: why Africa is shifting and Ukraine is under fire
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:40:00 EEST
20:40:00 KST

Russia gains ground as France retreats: why Africa is shifting and Ukraine is under fire
In May 2026, Emmanuel Macron chose Nairobi for one of the last major African gatherings of his presidency. Kenya is English-speaking, was never a French colony and sits far from the West African countries where France's position has deteriorated most sharply.
The Africa Forward summit was presented by Paris as evidence of a renewed relationship based on investment, innovation and joint decision-making rather than the old French pré carré, or privileged sphere of influence.
Between 2022 and 2025, French forces withdrew from Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger and handed back permanent bases in Chad, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire and Gabon. Djibouti is now the main exception .
It is easy to read that sequence as a simple exchange of powers: France leaves, Russia moves in. In the central Sahel, the Russian advance is real.
But France has not disappeared from Africa, and Russia has not replaced it as a complete economic or diplomatic partner. Paris is already rebuilding military cooperation in a different form, including discreet deployments in Benin, renewed discussions with Chad and a new defence relationship with Kenya.
The objective is no longer a chain of large permanent bases, but smaller arrangements built around requests from individual governments.
How France began to lose Africa
When France launched Operation Serval in Mali in 2013, its immediate military objective was clear: stop jihadist forces advancing towards the south of the country.
Serval was followed by Barkhane, a much larger regional counterterrorism operation that kept thousands of French troops across the Sahel for years.
France became not merely one foreign partner among others but the most visible external actor responsible for security.
That visibility eventually became a liability.
Jihadist violence continued to spread through Mali and into Burkina Faso and Niger. French forces could kill commanders and disrupt armed groups, but they could not repair weak institutions, local conflicts, corruption or the lack of state authority across enormous territories.
The military relationship also sat on top of older grievances. French interventions after independence, support for authoritarian governments, the CFA franc, restrictive visa policies and the dense political networks associated with Françafrique had already made the relationship unusually sensitive.
France had allowed its African policy to be excessively militarised, while its attempts to redefine the relationship came too late to prevent the security crisis from dominating it.
The coups in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger gave this frustration a political vehicle. Their new military leaders made sovereignty central to their legitimacy and presented the removal of French troops as evidence that the old hierarchy was ending. Turning away from Paris was therefore useful domestically as well as diplomatically.
Russian information campaigns amplified anti-French narratives, sometimes aggressively.
But Moscow did not invent the grievances on which they relied.
France's own Senate acknowledged in 2025 that the deterioration of its image reflected a genuine loss of influence and a challenge to its status as a privileged interlocutor, even if some anti-French narratives were manipulated from outside.
What Russia is betting on
France's economic position has weakened over time, particularly as China, Türkiye, Gulf states and others have expanded. But it remains substantial.
A 2025 French Senate report found France was still one of sub-Saharan Africa's main suppliers and its second-largest foreign investor by accumulated direct investment. Thousands of French companies remain active across the continent.
In several Sahel states, Moscow has concentrated its offer around the institutions closest to political power: armed forces, military training, intelligence, weapons and regime security.
Russian instructors arrived in Niger after the military authorities broke with Western security partners.
In Mali, Wagner fighters operated alongside the army before being replaced by Africa Corps, now much more directly connected to Russia's Defence Ministry.
Burkina Faso has also developed Russian military and security cooperation.
For military governments, this is a different kind of partnership from the European model.
Russia's relationships in the region have generally been transactional, centred on security assistance and political survival, while making fewer public demands over democratic transition or governance.
That does not mean African leaders have simply exchanged dependence on France for obedience to Moscow. They have made choices they consider useful, often while simultaneously cultivating Türkiye, China, Gulf countries, the United States or European states.
A company investing in telecommunications or infrastructure may matter enormously to an economy.
A foreign actor training presidential guards, supplying weapons or working alongside the national intelligence service can matter more immediately to the survival of a government.
The transformation from Wagner to Africa Corps has made the relationship even more explicit. Wagner gave Moscow some plausible distance from operations committed by a nominally private organisation.
Africa Corps is is tied much more directly to the Russian state. That gives the Kremlin greater control, but it also makes it harder to separate Moscow from what happens on the ground.
Russian strategy in Africa
Mali was supposed to demonstrate the superiority of the new security partnership.
The junta expelled its old Western partners, brought in Russian forces and promised a more sovereign approach to defeating jihadist and separatist groups. Russian-backed forces did help Bamako retake Kidal in 2023, an important symbolic victory.
In April 2026, jihadist and Tuareg forces launched coordinated attacks across the country, including against Bamako and strategic sites in the north and centre.
Further attacks followed during the summer. In September, sources cited by Reuters said more than 100 Malian soldiers had been killed in a single assault in Dioura, while another attack targeted the airport at Sévaré, where Russian personnel were also present.
Africa Corps has not solved the problem that eventually consumed France's presence in Mali: military operations can weaken armed groups without creating a functioning political and security order.
The circumstances are different. France operated as part of a much larger international architecture involving European forces, the United Nations and regional partners.
The Malian junta deliberately dismantled much of that framework and replaced it with a far narrower Russian partnership. Before the coup, roughly 20,000 international and regional personnel were deployed in Mali; the current Russian contingent is estimated at between 1,000 and 2,500.
There are also serious allegations of abuses by both Malian forces and their Russian partners. Human Rights Watch accused Africa Corps of carrying out an indiscriminate airstrike that killed civilians in June, while other monitoring organisations have linked violence against civilians to the worsening insurgency.
For Moscow, this creates a problem France knows well.
The more a foreign power presents itself as the partner capable of delivering security, the harder it becomes to treat continuing insecurity as somebody else's failure. Russia's advantage in the Sahel is therefore real but not irreversible.
It is also highly uneven across Africa.
Russia's African strategy since 2022 has been shaped increasingly by the consequences of its war against Ukraine.
Russia has sought more diplomatic partners, economic relationships and security footholds while trying to reduce the effect of Western isolation.
Russia presents itself as an opponent of Western domination and frequently draws on the Soviet Union's support for anti-colonial movements. Its invasion and occupation of Ukrainian territory sit awkwardly with that image.
But pointing out the contradiction does not automatically neutralise it. Where European governments are remembered through colonial rule, military interventions or unequal political relationships, arguments about Western double standards can still resonate.
The connection with the war is no longer only diplomatic. Ukraine said in February that more than 1,700 citizens of African countries were serving in Russia's armed forces, many recruited through deceptive schemes.
New opportunities for Ukraine in Africa
Ukraine's diplomatic presence on the continent was thin when the full-scale invasion began. That has changed quickly.
Eight new Ukrainian embassies have opened in Africa in recent years, bringing the total number of diplomatic missions to 18, with further expansion planned.
Kyiv has also begun defining its African policy around trade, agriculture, technology, education, defence cooperation and food security rather than treating relations primarily as a search for votes at the United Nations.
That change reflects the same reality France has been forced to confront: African governments don’t not want to be treated primarily through somebody else's geopolitical priorities.
France has finally begun adapting to that environment as well. The Nairobi summit in May was deliberately built around economic investment, private capital, technology and a partnership co-hosted by an African government rather than another France-led summit in Paris. The fact that Macron chose Kenya also reflected a broader attempt to build relationships beyond France's former colonial sphere.
That shift is relevant to Ukraine because French and Ukrainian interests overlap without being identical. Both countries have reasons to limit Russia's ability to turn military partnerships into wider diplomatic influence. But Ukraine does not carry France's colonial history, and France cannot erase it simply by changing the language of its partnerships.
The collapse of the old French model therefore did more than create an opening for Russia. It demonstrated the limits of a relationship in which an outside power becomes too closely associated with the security and political choices of another state.
Mali suggests it may now be learning the other half of it. As Russia becomes more closely tied to governments and security forces, continued instability is becoming harder to separate from the Russian presence itself.
Charlotte Guillou-Clerc,
Journalist (France)

But the former prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for giving up the lease early on the 98-acre property, meaning his total costs came to £1.5m.
Recouping costs for dilapidations is a standard process when exiting a lease, and the Guardian understands the repairs covered the entire estate, which includes several properties, gardens and large outbuildings.
Andrew was entitled to compensation because, as per the terms of his lease, he surrendered it within the first 25 years.
The Times reported that King Charles had contributed to the repair costs.

He was forced to move into Marsh Farm on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk amid public outcry about the rent he paid on the Royal Lodge.
In June, a National Audit Office investigation revealed that the late queen’s second son received an unknown amount of private income from subletting three cottages on the Royal Lodge estate while paying a peppercorn rent – a small, symbolic payment – for more than two decades.
The crown estate spokesperson said the property would now be marketed by two nationally recognised agents for its proposed future use.
On Thursday, Mountbatten-Windsor won a legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home. The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.
Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.
The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.
The arrest followed information that emerged from the Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein. Police began searching the former duke’s residence on the Sandringham estate and the Royal Lodge on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.
Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

Almost all Gaza residents need shelter as El Niño threatens flooding, UN agency says
GENEVA, Oct 9 - Almost all of Gaza's population need tents or help with shelter ahead of winter, with the El Niño weather phenomenon expected to bring heavier rainfall, while supplies remain scarce due to Israeli restrictions, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
The El Niño — which could be the strongest ever, according to the UN weather agency — could further weaken unsafe buildings, and cause flooding amid the enclave’s heavily damaged drainage systems, the IOM said.
Almost 2 million people inside the enclave, largely devastated by the war launched by Israel in response to Hamas' assault in October 2023, require assistance, but only about 17% of the needs for winter shelter supplies have been met by humanitarian actors, IOM Director General Amy Pope said.
"Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," Pope said, adding that constraints by Israeli authorities are making it hard for agencies to scale up their responses.
Some 8,600 emergency shelter kits, comprising wood, a tarpaulin and some basic materials, have not been allowed by Israeli authorities to enter Gaza, as they have been determined as dual use, the IOM said.
COGAT, the Israeli military arm that oversees aid flows into Gaza, did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment. Israel cites security concerns for its curbs on Gaza.
IOM said they had been able to bring in some tarpaulin and tents, but that it was not enough at the current scale needed in Gaza.
More than half of all tents and makeshift shelters in the enclave need replacing as they are in poor condition, the IOM said, warning that there are few alternatives with war-damaged buildings posing safety risks.
More than 3,600 structures were identified in August as dangerous and at risk of collapse, while around 1.8 million people are living in displacement sites - most in flood-risk areas, the IOM said. REUTERS

Latvian army takes delivery of first Hunter fighting vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:39:18 UTC
20:39:18 KST

- Latvia’s armed forces received their first ASCOD-based Hunter infantry fighting vehicle on Oct. 7, about 20 months after signing the first contract.
- Latvia has ordered 84 Hunters worth almost €800 million, with final assembly in Valmiera and all deliveries planned by 2029.
Latvia’s armed forces have taken delivery of their first Hunter infantry fighting vehicle, a tracked armored vehicle based on General Dynamics European Land Systems’ ASCOD design, about 20 months after the country signed its first contract.
The vehicle was handed over on Oct. 7 in the presence of Defense Minister Raivis Melnis, and GDELS said this week that it was ready for delivery a year and a half after the program began. Latvia has ordered 84 Hunters in two batches of 42, signed in January and June 2025, in a program worth almost €800 million (about $929 million). The Latvian Ministry of Defense plans to receive all 84 by 2029. Neither the ministry nor the company has said how many vehicles will be delivered by the end of this year.
The Hunter, called Mednieks in Latvian, is a version of the ASCOD platform built by GDELS-Santa Bárbara Sistemas in Spain and adapted for Latvia. It carries a crew of three and up to six fully equipped soldiers, has armor rated to NATO Level 4, and is armed with an automatic cannon, anti-tank missiles and a machine gun mounted in Elbit Systems’ unmanned UT30 Mk2 turret. Its 1,100-horsepower engine gives it a top speed of about 70 km/h (43 mph) and a range of about 500 km (311 miles). Soldiers of the Latvian Land Forces Mechanized Infantry Brigade, which will operate the vehicle, chose the name.
The Hunters will gradually replace the British-built CVR(T) tracked vehicles Latvia bought secondhand over the past decade.
Final assembly takes place in Latvia. GDELS supplies the vehicle hulls and major components, and Defence Partnership Latvia, a joint venture of Patria Latvia and local firm Unitruck, assembles them at its plant in Valmiera, which also builds Patria 6×6 armored personnel carriers. In June, the first Hunter hull arrived in Latvia to begin local assembly. Latvia signed a separate maintenance subcontract in September 2025 that runs through 2037, and the program requires at least 30% Latvian industrial participation.
GDELS said the program is also moving into counter-drone work. In August, Latvia’s defense ministry tested GDELS counter-drone systems mounted on the Hunter at the Ādaži military base, though no decision on fitting them to the fleet has been announced.
Latvia also joined the international ASCOD user group last year, signing a letter of intent with Spain and Austria, which already operate the vehicle, to cooperate on training, support and upgrades.
The ministry has said the rest of the 84 vehicles will arrive in batches through 2029.

Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of provoking war as Tigray rebels retreat

Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of provoking war as Tigray rebels retreat
Ethiopia and Eritrea on Friday accused each other of starting a "war of agresson" days after the two countries severed diplomatic ties. Ethiopian officals estimate that up to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers are present in Tigray supporting rebels who last month launched attacks against federal forces.
Ethiopia and Eritrea each accused the other of starting a war of aggression on Friday as an internal Ethiopian conflict threatened to escalate into a regional war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing rebels in its northern Tigray state, who launched attacks against federal forces last month.
The two countries severed diplomatic relations, and over the past week, Eritrean troops have been seen in northern Tigray with Ethiopia launching drone strikes against their forces.
A foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP they estimated 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in Tigray.
Eritrea's conduct is "a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos wrote in a letter to diplomats.
Eritrea's information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, responded on X that it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from Ethiopia.
Watch moreEthiopia and Eritrea break diplomatic ties over conflict
Over the past week, the Ethiopian army has pushed back the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and seized their capital city, Mekelle, with Ethiopian Airlines saying flights to the city would resume from October 11.
There are also signs that federal forces have pushed back the Eritrean troops with heavy drone strikes.
Rebels lose cities
Witnesses told AFP on Friday that the rebels had lost two other cities in Tigray: Shire and Adigrat.
An aid worker in Shire said TPLF fighters and the local administration left on Wednesday.
"Looters are operating in the city, and four people were killed and 11 injured in an exchange of gunfire related to the looting," he said, adding that pro-government forces were yet to enter the city.
Eritrean forces were seen in Adigrat in recent days before being targeted by Ethiopian drone strikes, according to a conflict monitor and witnesses.
The rebels were retreating to Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, according to a Tigrayan official from a TPLF dissident faction.
Kjetil Tronvoll, regional specialist at Oslo New University College, told AFP that the TPLF was "withering", with low morale and frustration with their leaders.
"Many are defecting and going back to their villages," he said.
"I do not believe (Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed) will stop at the border," Tronvoll said.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab.
"The hysterical infatuation with the Red Sea must also be seen with previous intentions to wage a war of invasion against Eritrea," the Eritrean information minister said.
Authorities in both countries have not responded to AFP requests for comment.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and fought a brutal border war from 1998 to 2000.
Relations improved with the rise to power of Abiy in 2018 and Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia during the latter's 2020-2022 civil war against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
But relations deteriorated after the war, with Eritrea angry over the way it was concluded and fearing an Ethiopian invasion.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Lebanon's new media law targets ownership, funding transparency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:36:48 UTC
20:36:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon's new media law targets transparency over funding and ownership
Lebanon's media law passed, on 12 August, after more than 16 years of parliamentary deliberation, replaced the 1962 Publications Law, which predated the rise of the internet, social media, and other digital technologies.
The new law, introduced after years of calls to update outdated legislation, incorporates several reforms long sought by journalists and civil society organisations; most significantly, the introduction of rules governing media ownership and requiring transparency for media outlets' funding sources.
The law places transparency in media ownership and funding among the key requirements for regulating the sector. Articles 15, 16 and 17 provide for the establishment of a dedicated register at the National Media Authority containing details of owners and directors, as well as the names of shareholders who hold more than 5% of shares or stakes, their ownership percentages and the holders of economic rights.
The law requires the authority to publish this information and make it available to the public, allowing people to trace who owns media outlets and identify the interests associated with them.
Transparency does not stop at ownership. Article 18 requires media outlets to disclose their financial information and various sources of income, including advertising, subscriptions, sales, loans, and cash and in-kind grants, while specifying the sources of loans and grants.
Article 19 also gives the National Media Authority the power to verify the accuracy of this information, including by appointing auditors. This means the law moves media ownership and funding from the realm of information unavailable to the public into a legal framework that requires disclosure and accountability.
Layal Behnam, programme director at the Maharat Foundation, which participated in drafting the law through parliamentary committees, explained the importance of this reform in comments to The New Arab.
"Media outlets are not ordinary commercial institutions. They help shape public opinion, and citizens therefore have the right to know the identity of the owner of the media outlet through which they obtain news and information. They also have the right to know who has the power to influence its editorial line," she said.
"This knowledge is particularly important in the Lebanese context, where media ownership intersects with political and economic interests," she added.
"Most media outlets are directly or indirectly linked to political figures or forces. The transparency stipulated by the law therefore allows citizens to read the news not only through its content but also by understanding the context and potential interests behind it," she further noted.
She explained that "pluralism is not simply about having a large number of media outlets but about ensuring genuine diversity in interests, ownership and voices".
Similarly, MP Halima Kaakour told The New Arab that "this provision lies at the heart of the principles of transparency, democracy and good governance in the media sector".
"There is no doubt that many media outlets have not welcomed it because it forces them to disclose their funding sources and, consequently, reveals their agendas in every television programme or political position. In other words, it shows why they attack one political side or another," she said.
However, media outlets did not publicly express their opposition to the provision, because, as Kaakour argued, "it is difficult for them to publicly reject transparency in ownership and funding sources".
"But they exploited our opposition to Articles 104 and 105, which criminalise the deliberate fabrication of misleading information and false news in vague terms, to raise their voices against those provisions. They did not do so to preserve the gains introduced by the law, as we did, but rather to prevent its passage and send it back for further study," she added.
This partly echoes Behnam's comments.
Kaakour further noted that "some media institutions managed to influence certain formulations during earlier stages of the law's review by parliamentary committees".
“This was evident in the provisions setting ownership limits. Some earlier drafts stipulated that a single person should not own more than 10% of a television or radio station. This became a clear subject of debate and objection until the provision was removed from the final version”, she said.
Ayman Mhanna, executive director of the Samir Kassir Foundation, distinguished transparency in media ownership and transparency in funding sources in comments to The New Arab.
Regarding ownership, he said, "Anyone can obtain a document from the commercial register showing the shareholders in media outlets under the Right to Information Law".
"The problem arises when investigating actual ownership. Examining the names of shareholders in media outlets shows that some work as employees in other companies owned by businessmen. This raises questions about whether they are merely nominal owners acting on behalf of actual owners who prefer not to disclose their identities," he pointed out.
On sources of funding, Mhanna said that "many media outlets say their funding comes from advertising, which is normal. But when the funding behind that advertising is linked to political and economic interests, we are looking at a different picture".
"For example, the Association of Banks in Lebanon announced that it had allocated a large sum to support Lebanese media in the coming period," he explained. "In theory, this is justifiable, since anyone with an interest seeks ways to make their voice heard through the media. But the question is whether advertising funding will affect the editorial line or be limited to placing advertisements for food, furniture, cars and other products."
"Will this funding, for example, be used to support particular candidates who align with the interests of the Association of Banks in the next elections?" he rhetorically asked, and then said, "the answers to these questions are not addressed in the new law. Instead, they require investigative journalism to highlight the extent to which advertising funding influences editorial lines".
In the same vein, Behnam believes that "knowing the identities of media owners is not enough; funders must also be disclosed. We believe that, in some cases, identifying the funder is more important than identifying the owner".
"Media institutions have substantial financial costs. If they do not have sufficient revenue, they will depend on loans, grants or ongoing funding from a political or economic entity," she explained.
"It is precisely at this point that a relationship of influence can emerge, even if the political or economic entity does not own shares in the media outlet," she added.
The reform introduced by Lebanon's new media law is a positive development, but in Lebanon, the real test always lies in implementation.
On this, MP Kaakour explained "the law provides mechanisms and means to compel media institutions to be transparent about their ownership and funding sources."
"Article 19 gives the National Media Authority the power to audit the information submitted by institutions and their owners, using all available means of verification, including appointing auditors to ensure the accuracy of their declarations," she added.
The matter does not end there. According to Kaakour, "Article 20 sets out penalties for violating transparency and disclosure obligations. It imposes a fine on the media institution or its owners for failing to meet disclosure requirements, in addition to requiring them to rectify the violation. In the event of repeated violations or delays in compliance, the fine is doubled".
"What we need is a genuine willingness on the part of the executive authorities to implement Lebanon's media law, as well as a genuine willingness on the part of media outlets to comply with its provisions rather than evade or circumvent them," she explained.
The New Arab is publishing this article as part of a joint fellowship programme between the Lebanese Journalists Syndicate and the Qraib programme, in support of and raising awareness about media law reforms.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

Former US ambassador to Israel Jack Lew has said he struggled to persuade Israeli officials to prioritise the safety of Israeli-American hostages following Hamas’ October 2023 blitz.
“There was no obligation that was greater for an American diplomat than worrying about Americans,” Lew said at a Columbia University event on Wednesday, according to Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
“While the issue of the hostages was right at the top of my concerns, it was nowhere near the top of the concerns of the interlocutors I had in the government,” he added.
Lew said the Israeli government took advantage of then-US President Joe Biden’s support during the ensuing war, arguing that Washington had limited ability to influence Israel’s conduct because Israeli officials knew Biden was reluctant to significantly reduce US assistance.
“Unless you’re willing to say, ‘Do it our way or we’re going to be leaving you on your own,’ you didn’t have the leverage to make the kind of difference that you would have liked,” Lew said.
Biden “wasn’t going to abandon Israel — there was no credible scenario in which he was going to abandon Israel — and I think that was taken advantage of,” he added.
Israel’s war on Gaza has included excessive air and ground attacks, a siege and a ground offensive since October 2023.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since then, according to Gaza’s health authorities.
The Israeli army has continued its attacks despite a ceasefire deal that took effect on October 10 2025, with more than 1,460 Palestinians killed and over 5,160 wounded in Israeli violations of the truce, according to the figures provided.

France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:35:00 BST
20:35:00 KST

France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests
- Published
The French government has made its first sign of giving ground to teenage protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday evening, at the end of another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.
The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18, since protests began centred around demands for more resources in secondary education.
In what unions have billed as Act Four of the three-week movement, some 71,000 people staged protests across the country on Thursday, with 24,000 gathering at the Bastille in Paris.
Police once again intervened with tear-gas to disperse groups who attacked them with paving stones and homemade fireworks.
In Bordeaux, a lycée, or high school, was ransacked by protesters, and in Marseille a deputy-head was beaten up.
On Friday, some 140 lycées - out of 3,500 - were totally or partially closed, a big drop on previous days. But another day of action has been called for next Tuesday.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published1 day ago
Geffray's announcement was the first material concession to the protesters' complaints.
It has long been recognised by all concerned in French education that too many school hours are being lost because of absent teachers and their non-replacement by available supply staff.
The minister said that thanks to new software coming online at the ministry, it would be possible to direct 3,000 supply teachers to the 500 or so lycées identified as being in the greatest need.
Many of these schools are likely to be in high-immigration city suburbs, where the lack of teachers is most acute.
Geffray also said that more money would be made available under an already existing scheme for those teachers who want to work overtime hours in order to plug gaps.
And he promised that students' grievances would be taken into account in forthcoming discussions on the education section of the 2027 state budget.
But the offer contained no major promise of new investment on a scale likely to appease protesters.
The government is wary of appearing to buy social peace because it knows France's precarious debt situation is being followed closely by international money markets.
Reaction from student leaders has been guarded to say the least.
Nathanaël Combary, who represents the most moderate of the three main lycée unions Renouveau Lycéen (Lycée Renewal), said students were waiting to see how the promise was carried out in practice: "We've had some announcements which correspond to part of our demands. But obviously people want to see the money and more concrete results."
"As long as we do not have €10bn on the table, we will continue our action," said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Etudiante (Student Union), which is close to the radical-left France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Mélenchon praised Thursday's demonstrations, saying on X that the students had "retaken the Bastille".
But at the other end of the political spectrum, a spokesman for the hard-right National Rally (RN) condemned the government's concessions.
"The message is: if you break things, you get given stuff," said Laurent Jacobelli. "When you burn cars, attack police, you gain something in return. It's the legitimisation of violence."
The movement is the most serious student unrest in France in many years, and comes against a backdrop of rising tension in the country - with anger over rising fuel prices and distress in the farming sector also liable to trigger protests.
Next Saturday, 17 October, has been earmarked as a day of demonstrations by a revived "yellow vest" movement, which forced the government to halt a rise in fuel taxes after protests and riots in 2018.
In addition, the approach of presidential elections in April and May - in which both hard right and hard left are expected to perform strongly - is exacerbating the mood of confrontation.
The government is hoping that the approach of half-term holidays at the end of next week - as well as the arrival of colder and wetter weather - will take some of the sting out of the protests.

Putin says Russia-CIS trade exceeded $110B in 2025, rose 12% in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:34:06 UTC
20:34:06 KST

Kanyshai Butun
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Trade between Russia and members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) exceeded $110 billion in 2025 and rose a further 12% in the first half of 2026, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday.
Speaking at a meeting of CIS leaders in Turkmenistan, Putin called for removing trade “barriers” to improve cooperation among CIS members.
“Is it possible to move even faster? It probably is. What needs to be done for that? Barriers need to be removed,” he said.
Putin said cooperation spans science, education, culture, tourism, health care, environmental protection, sports and youth policy.
He stressed the importance of protecting shared history and preventing its falsification, saying young people should know about the achievements of Soviet-era peoples and their ancestors’ contributions during World War II.
Putin said CIS leaders would adopt a separate statement on preserving historical memory. He welcomed proposals to designate 2028 as the Year of Social Development and 2029 as the Year of Transport within the bloc, saying joint initiatives could demonstrate the benefits of cooperation.
Putin thanked Turkmenistan for its leadership of the CIS this year, and said Uzbekistan would assume the bloc’s rotating chairmanship on Jan. 1. He pledged Russia’s support to Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in the role.
Putin also invited CIS leaders to an informal gathering in St. Petersburg on Dec. 21 to discuss current and future issues.
The CIS leaders' summit opened with a restricted-format meeting attended by the presidents of Russia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and CIS Secretary General Sergey Lebedev. Talks continued in an expanded format with the participation of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
A number of agreement were signed after the meeting, the Kremlin said.

Voting to begin in local elections in the Czech Republic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:34:00 UTC
20:34:00 KST

Czechs vote in local elections, a test for PM Andrej Babis
October 9, 2026
Voters in the Czech Republic begin casting ballots in local polls on Friday to elect local representatives as well as one-third of the Senate's members.
The elections are being seen as a test of popularity for the populist billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
Babis took power last December after forming a coalition with two small political groups. His party, the ANO, or YES, won big in parliamentary elections last year after he was able to tap into people's economic frustration, playing into a sentiment that the center-right government at that time was spending too much on Ukraine.
But Babis ran into challenges as well after having formed a government, with the opposition challenging his widening budget deficit — which is when the government spends more than it earns. But he survived a no-confidence vote in parliament earlier this month.
Babis, 72, founded the Patriots for Europe in the European Parliament with former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and other far-right parties.
Housing shortage is big issue in Czech cities
More than 8 million eligible voters are set to elect municipal and town councils in more than 6,200 districts nationwide.
Housing shortages, a big theme in major European cities including Berlin and Madrid, is a top concern for voters in the Czech Republic's major cities too.
As for the Senate, a third of the seats are up for grabs, as they are every two years.
The vote will determine whether the liberal and conservative opposition can retain their majority in the chamber or whether the governing parties and their allies make gains.
President Petr Pavel drew attention ahead of the vote because he said he was not going to be able to cast his ballot since he was on a private holiday outside Europe.
"The president regrets the planning error," his spokesman said.

The remote employment termination service has become available in Diia for people in the temporarily occupied territories

The remote employment termination service has become available in Diia for people in the temporarily occupied territories
Kyiv • UNN
Employees in the temporarily occupied territories and areas of hostilities can resign through Diia. The application is signed online, and the termination takes effect the following day.
Ukrainians who are officially employed in temporarily occupied territories or areas of active hostilities can now terminate their employment relationship with their employer via the "Diia" app. This was reported by the Ministry of Economy and Environment, UNN writes.
Details
The first online service under the new digital labor market ecosystem, "Obrii," has been launched in the "Obrii.Robota" section of the "Diia" app. Previously, terminating such contracts required contacting the employment service or the employer directly and waiting for paper documents to be processed.
According to the State Employment Service, since the beginning of the full-scale war, 11,714 citizens have applied with such requests, while 65,000 legal entities were registered in the TOT in 2022.
How to use it
To complete the dismissal process, you need to update the "Diia" app to the latest version. The procedure is fully automated:
-  The user submits an application through the app and signs it using "Diia.Signature." 
-  The system automatically checks whether the employer is included in the list of TOTs or areas of active hostilities. 
-  After successful processing, the system records the dismissal date, notifies the employer, and updates the data in state registers. 
-  The dismissal takes effect automatically on the day after the application is registered, without any additional confirmations. 
As noted by Oleksandr Tsybort, Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment of Ukraine for Digital Development, Digital Transformations, and Digitalization, formal employment in occupied territories had previously been a barrier to finding new official employment, obtaining unemployed status, or pursuing professional development. The new service is intended to remove this obstacle.
The ministry also adds that grants for professional development will soon appear in "Obrii"—financial assistance for education and retraining.
