PROFILE – Navi Pillay: Nobel laureate who led UN inquiry that found genocide in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:29:57 UTC
20:29:57 KST

- Pillay led UN inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza
- ‘When clear signs, evidence of genocide emerge, the absence of action to stop it amounts to complicity,’ she says
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, the South African jurist who led a UN inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee honored the 85-year-old “for her efforts to promote peace and international law,” placing particular emphasis on her career holding states and political leaders accountable.
Pillay’s work on Gaza became one of the most consequential and controversial chapters of that career.
From 2021 until November 2025, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel. Established by the UN Human Rights Council, the commission investigated violations committed by all sides and collected evidence that could be used in future legal proceedings.
Its first major report following Oct. 7, 2023, found in June 2024 that Israeli authorities were responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity during military operations in Gaza. It also concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes during their attacks in Israel, including deliberately killing civilians and taking hostages.
“It is imperative that all those who have committed crimes be held accountable,” Pillay said at the time, arguing that adherence to international law was the only way to end recurring cycles of violence and retaliation.
The commission’s investigation later focused on Israel’s attacks on hospitals and the broader destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system. In October 2024, it accused Israeli forces of deliberately attacking medical facilities and personnel, as well as mistreating Palestinian detainees.
“By targeting healthcare facilities, Israel is targeting the right to health itself,” Pillay said, warning that the destruction would have lasting consequences for Gaza’s civilian population.
“Children in particular have borne the brunt of these attacks, suffering both directly and indirectly from the collapse of the health system,” she added.
 
‘Absence of action amounts to complicity’
In September 2025, the commission issued its most far-reaching conclusion: that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed four of the five acts defined as genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
These included killing members of a protected group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately imposing conditions calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction and taking measures intended to prevent births.
The commission also concluded that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Isaac Herzog and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant had incited genocide and that Israeli authorities had failed to punish them for it.
Pillay said the evidence showed “an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza” and placed responsibility with Israeli authorities at the highest levels.
She also directed criticism at governments continuing to arm or politically support Israel.
“When clear signs and evidence of genocide emerge, the absence of action to stop it amounts to complicity,” she said.
The commission called on states to halt transfers of weapons and equipment that could be used to commit genocidal acts, prevent companies and individuals under their jurisdiction from contributing to them and support accountability proceedings.
Israel rejected the findings, accused the commission of bias and maintained that its military campaign targeted Hamas rather than the Palestinian population.
The commission’s determination was not a binding judicial ruling and it did not speak for the UN as a whole. The International Court of Justice is separately considering South Africa’s genocide case against Israel.
Pillay stepped down from the commission in November 2025, citing her age, medical issues and other commitments.
 
From apartheid to international justice
Born in Durban in 1941 into a South African family of Indian origin, Pillay began her legal career under apartheid, when racial and gender discrimination restricted both her professional opportunities and the rights of her clients.
In 1967, she became the first woman to establish a law practice in the province of Natal. She represented anti-apartheid activists and trade unionists, exposed allegations of torture and helped secure rights for political prisoners held on Robben Island.
Her work attracted the attention of apartheid-era security authorities, and she was denied a passport for years.
After apartheid ended, President Nelson Mandela appointed Pillay as an acting judge on the South African High Court in 1995, making her its first non-white woman judge.
That same year, she joined the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, later serving as its president. Pillay sat on the panel that decided the landmark case against Jean-Paul Akayesu, the first conviction for genocide by an international tribunal.
The judgment also established that rape and sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the intention of destroying a protected group, an enduring contribution to international criminal law.
Pillay subsequently served as a judge at the International Criminal Court from 2003 to 2008 and as UN high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014. She currently serves as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar.
Announcing the award, the Nobel Committee said Pillay’s career demonstrated how international law could provide accountability for victims and offer an alternative to violence at a time when courts and legal institutions were facing growing political attacks.
The Nobel Peace Prize, carrying an award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million), will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10.

US wants to livestream a firing squad execution. People are calling it 'beyond disgusting'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:29:50 UTC
20:29:50 KST

The US government is preparing to livestream a man’s execution by firing squad — the first in decades — turning a military killing into something the public can watch unfold on screen.
The Pentagon says the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, is planned for December 3. But the decision to broadcast it has triggered a question that goes far beyond the death penalty: why does the government want an audience for an execution?
Even some supporters of capital punishment are recoiling at the prospect. Critics say the livestream risks turning the deliberate taking of a human life into a public spectacle, raising uncomfortable questions about what the state wants viewers to see and what watching such an event is supposed to achieve.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended the decision as a way to demonstrate the serious consequences of such crimes.
One of the most striking reactions came from Alyssa Farah Griffin, a television host and former official of US President Donald Trump’s administration who has said she supports capital punishment.
Livestreaming an execution, she argued, however, was “toxic for society” and “bad for the human soul” of those watching.
This execution plan would represent a significant departure from modern US practice, in which executions have generally been conducted privately. The United States has not held a public execution since 1936.
The planned firing squad would be the first US military firing-squad execution since 1945.
Actor Henry Winkler also expressed disbelief at the announcement, writing on X: “Live execution?? Is this where we are now?”
Novelist Joyce Carol Oates raised questions about the consequences for viewers, particularly children, and the lasting effect of witnessing a person being killed by the state.
Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the decision.
Representative Betty McCollum argued that Hasan should be held accountable for his crimes but that turning the execution into a media spectacle was inappropriate for the US military. Senator Patty Murray similarly distinguished between accountability and broadcasting a person's death for public consumption.
Much of the criticism focuses on why the government would want an audience for an execution in the first place.
Senator Thom Tillis called public executions “beyond disgusting” and likened them to practices in dictatorships, Senator Chris Murphy said it was “disgusting” and asked if America was “mimicking ISIS (Daesh).”
Legal questions remain
The proposal has also drawn scrutiny from legal experts, who distinguish between the military's authority to carry out an execution and its authority to broadcast one.
Other experts have pointed to the possibility of further legal challenges. Eugene Fidell, a Yale Law School lecturer specialising in military law, has said Hasan could pursue federal habeas corpus proceedings challenging the legality of his detention or execution.
Attorney John Galligan, long involved with Hasan, called the Fort Hood location and public angle “political theater” not great for confidence in the justice system. He also raised concerns about notification and access to legal counsel in connection with the presidential approval of the execution.
When many states have had setbacks carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
The risks of lethal injection were underscored by the case of Christa Pike, a Tennessee death-row inmate who survived two doses of the execution drug pentobarbital during a botched execution attempt just last week, suffering serious injuries.
“Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner,” he said. “I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasise — the ‘lethality culture.’”
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said the announcement raises many legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution, and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
New Zealand’s concern
New Zealand's national censor, meanwhile, said on Friday it would not have the authority to block internet users in the country from accessing the livestream of the execution, as rights groups pressed governments to protest.
"The Classification Office cannot classify a livestream event as it is taking place, and we, nor any other body, has the authority to block access to a livestream event," a spokesperson for New Zealand's Classification Office said in a statement.
New Zealand Chief Censor Caroline Flora said the threshold for banning content under New Zealand law was high and required balancing freedom of expression with the likelihood of harm.
"Distressing as content may be, it is not always unlawful," she said, adding that she could not speculate on the likely classification of something before it exists.
Double standards
Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on February 28.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on January 14. “It’s stopping, and there’s no plan for executions.”
In his State of the Union address just days before launching the Iran war, Trump reiterated, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked on Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

====================================================================================================

IKEA Stopped Selling in Russia. But its Former Belarusian Supplier Filled the Gap — With Strikingly Similar Furniture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

When the Swedish furniture giant IKEA exited Russia and Belarus in 2022 in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it instructed its suppliers to do the same. A Lithuanian supplier complied, and stopped sourcing IKEA products from its Belarusian factory.
But the Belarusian factory didn’t stop exporting furniture after losing the rights to IKEA designs. Instead, it appears to have filled an IKEA-shaped void in the Russian market, exporting pieces that are strikingly similar to the Swedish designs.
The website of one Russian retailer even told customers that “IKEA's departure doesn't mean you have to give up your familiar interior design style,” adding that they “now have the opportunity to buy those same beloved products.”
“Yes, their appearance and names have changed slightly,” the blurb on the website said. “But the design, quality, ease of purchase, and ease of assembly remain unchanged.”
IKEA said it could not comment on individual cases, but noted that it “continuously monitors potential infringements” on its intellectual property rights.
“How we approach individual matters depends on a range of legal and practical considerations that may differ from market to market,” IKEA added in an emailed response to questions from OCCRP’s media partners, Belarusian Investigative Center and 15mins.
In response to questions about the similarities between the IKEA products and the furniture produced in Belarus, Novus Industry, the company that owns the factory, said it “manufactures products based on designs and blueprints provided by its customers.”
Until last month, Novus Industry was owned by Lithuanian businessman Sigitas Paulauskas. He also owns the Lithuanian furniture and timber conglomerate VMG Group, which has continued to supply IKEA with items that are not manufactured in Belarus.
IKEA said it had found no sign that Belarusian products had entered its supply chain, which would be a potential breach of European Union sanctions.
“Based on the information available to us at this stage, including sanctions screening and publicly available information, we have found no evidence that our supplier has acted in breach of applicable sanctions,” IKEA said.
Paulauskas said his “exit from the business in Belarus began immediately after Russia's open aggression in Ukraine” in 2022. He said he had not participated since 2017 in the operational governance of Novus Industry, and that the formal transfer of management to local executives began in 2023.
Novus Industry confirmed Paulauskas’ comments in its response to questions from reporters.
The sale of Novus Industry was not finalized until last month, Paulauskas said. The process took a long time due to “finding an investor, their due diligence process, Belarusian laws regulating share transfers to foreign entities, active sanctions regimes, and the necessity of obtaining creditor consents.”
Paulauskas added that Novus Industry “has no right to manufacture products based on IKEA designs.”
Cecilia Wahlberg, a senior lecturer in industrial design at Sweden’s Konstfack University, examined images of products exported to Russia from the Belarusian factory. She said some pieces differed enough that they would not likely be considered an infringement on IKEA products, but others showed “apparent similarities in the design and measurements.”
“I would think that the factories that are producing the ‘new’ non-IKEA furniture are using the same production drawings and machinery that were used for producing the IKEA furniture,” she said.
"Defending design rights internationally is unfortunately both hard and expensive, which is why a lot of independent designers find themselves copied at a larger scale and are more or less unable to do anything about it,” Wahlberg added.
Russia has become Novus Industry’s key market. Around 70 percent of its production was being sent there in 2024, the company’s director told local media that year. Belarusian customs data obtained by BIC shows the factory directly exported more than $30 million worth of goods to Russia between March 2023 and May 2025.

This handout photograph taken and released by the Donetsk Region Prosecutor's Office on October 8, 2026 shows one of the two passenger buses struck by projectiles in Kramatorsk, near the frontline in eastern Ukraine (AFP Photo)
Urgent repairs are being carried out in Ukraine after Russian strikes on the country's electricity network, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 9.
Russia has admitted targeting the grid in a repeat of its deliberate tactic in the nearly five-year war of hitting power and heating before winter.
Several regions have been hit by power cuts already, while rolling blackouts have been introduced to ease pressure on the system, including in the capital, Kiev.
Zelensky said in a post on X that the Russian strikes had caused "extensive damage to power grids and electricity transmission facilities."
"Restoration work is underway around the clock."
On Oct. 8 night, all three lines of the Kiev metro were temporarily suspended due to power disruptions, cutting services, as well as lights and escalators.
Large parts of the city's historic center also went dark, with shops and restaurants keeping the lights on using generators.
The strikes, using powerful ballistic and cruise missiles as well as attack drones, have forced operators to introduce rolling outages while parts of the city were also without water for several hours earlier this week.
City mayor Vitali Klitschko told AFP in an interview on Oct. 8 that Kiev, which has seen bridges and other key infrastructure attacked, was now in "survival" mode as winter approaches.
Residents in the city have been making plans in case the energy system is knocked out again during the months of sub-zero temperatures.
Last year, Kiev was plunged into darkness and bitter cold for weeks when Russia hit power and heating infrastructure, as temperatures dropped as low as -20 degrees Celsius.
Zelensky in his post said he had told military and government officials that "slow-walking" winter resilience plans was "completely unacceptable", after concerns about contingencies.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone strike damaged a data center belonging to Russian technology giant Yandex. The company said on Oct. 9 that several modules at the center in Russia’s Kaluga region had been “completely disabled.”
Russian attacks have killed dozens of civilians across Ukraine over the past days using a mix of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. On Oct. 8, a Russian guided bomb exploded next to public buses filled with passengers in eastern Ukraine, killing 30 people.
A day earlier, a Russian missile strike killed 22 people, including five children, in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky.
Meanwhile President Donald Trump’s envoys were to meet Ukrainian and European officials in Miami on Oct. 8 to discuss “new ideas” and seek a unified proposal to end the war with Russia, two U.S. sources told AFP.
“The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the U.S. tomorrow,” Zelensky said on Oct. 8. “The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group.”
“The American negotiators also invited national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union”, one of the U.S. sources familiar with the talks told AFP.

People seeking safety in Greece are trapped in uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:27:40 UTC
20:27:40 KST

“I have been running away all my life,” says Samuel*, from Eritrea. “I have already experienced so much trauma, and I don’t know if I can handle or face another struggle. I’m sick of this life.”
For a person seeking safety, these words capture the weight of an uncertain and re-traumatising reality, as well as an unimaginable future. Unfortunately, Samuel’s is not an isolated experience. For over 10 years, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) psychologists in Greece have been supporting numerous people experiencing profound feelings of helplessness, hopelessness, fear, and despair.
Many of our patients have faced traumatic events – including torture, imprisonment, and the loss of loved ones – and undergone a dangerous journey to escape war, conflict, and persecution. When they arrive in Greece, their physical and psychological health further deteriorate because of restrictive European Union (EU) migration policies of deterrence and containment. 
“Many people arrive in Greece already emotionally and physically exhausted from the exposure to unsafe conditions they faced in their country of origin and during the journey,” says Anzhelika Iastremska, MSF psychologist on Lesbos. “For many, arrival is associated with the expectation of finally reaching safety and stability. However, barriers in accessing healthcare, opaque asylum procedures, and poor living conditions may contribute to ongoing psychological distress and feelings of hopelessness.”
When the system deepens trauma
Restrictive policies, deterrence measures, barriers to accessing healthcare, precarious living conditions, and complex asylum procedures can contribute to a cycle of trauma, creating an environment of perpetual uncertainty that severely degrades people’s mental health and leaves them in deep psychological distress.
For many of our patients, living isolated in remote prison-like reception facilities, with high barbed wire fences, contributes to their trauma.
“The environment of the reception facility often functions as a constant traumatic reminder for survivors of detention, violence, or persecution,” says Georgia Kotitsa, MSF psychologist on Lesbos. “Many patients describe feeling trapped, unsafe, and deprived of autonomy. For some individuals, for example those who have survived imprisonment or torture, the restrictive conditions, constant surveillance, and lack of privacy within the reception facilities trigger intense re-traumatisation.”
Moreover, complex and fast-track asylum procedures offer limited time to secure individualised counselling and legal assistance, and patients report difficulties in understanding and navigating the process. This severely worsens their mental health, preventing them from finding any sense of stability.
People live in a state of limbo, overstressed, being transferred from one facility or one city to another, through opaque asylum processes, with little information about what will happen next. Many live with the fear of rejection and deportation while they struggle to access healthcare, understand their rights and what the future holds, in an increasingly restrictive environment.
The environment of the reception facility often functions as a constant traumatic reminder for survivors of detention, violence, or persecution.
Georgia Kotitsa, MSF psychologist on Lesbos
“Reaching Athens is not the end of their journey for many patients but the beginning of a different struggle,” says Katerina Kavakou, MSF psychologist in Athens. “They need to navigate unfamiliar systems in a huge city, language barriers, precarious employment, insecure housing, and the uncertainty of what comes next.”
Barriers to accessing healthcare
Since January 2026, MSF psychologists have conducted over 900 mental health consultations on the islands of Lesbos and Samos. Some of the main gaps they see in their daily work concern accessibility and continuity of mental health care. Their observations and patient reports suggest that the current healthcare system fails to provide sustained psychological and psychiatric support that people seeking safety in Greece urgently need, leaving them stuck in cycles of uncertainty and distress.
Services and interpretation are often limited, especially when it comes to trauma-informed care and support, which takes each person’s individual needs and experiences into consideration. At the same time, follow-up consultations are often inconsistent, which can result in missed appointments and interruptions in treatment.
MSF teams have documented a wide range of consequences over the years. Many of our patients describe signs of depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic stress, sleep disorders, excessive worrying, and suicidal thoughts.
Dreams out of reach
“I meet people who want to work, go to university, and continue their dreams,” says Nikolina Kazaki, MSF psychologist in Samos. “But the lack of support deprives them of the ability to build a new life and creates a devastating sense of despair and hopelessness.”
I meet people who want to work, go to university, and continue their dreams. But the lack of support deprives them of the ability to build a new life and creates a devastating sense of despair and hopelessness.
Nikolina Kazaki, MSF psychologist in Samos
For over 10 years, MSF has provided psychological support to refugees, asylum seekers, and people in vulnerable situations in Greece, with a focus on victims and survivors of violence. Our teams offer a safe and inclusive space, where people can be heard and supported through a multidisciplinary and holistic approach that goes beyond medical and psychological care. Social workers also contribute to this care by helping people with broader social and practical challenges.
However, these efforts seem like a drop in the ocean when compared with the complexity of people’s needs and the significant gap between the level of support currently available and the realities faced by many refugees and asylum seekers.
“People need more comprehensive support systems, with better integration programmes and uninterrupted access to healthcare,” says Kazaki. “When you’re struggling to find a safe place to live, access healthcare, earn a living, or simply feel secure, the constant pressure can become unbearable, leaving you feeling trapped, exhausted, and hopeless.”
Moving forward against the odds
Despite the perilous journey, the uncertainty, and the numerous barriers, refugees and asylum seekers continue to move forward, adapt to new realities, care for their families, and look for ways to rebuild their lives.
“We meet people that are parents, students, friends, community members, workers, with dreams and hopes,” says Kavakou.
MSF sees that people need improved access to physical and mental health and social services, alongside better living conditions and dignified reception. At the same time, clearer, more informed procedures are necessary to reduce uncertainty, facilitate integration, and support people in this demanding journey to rebuild a sense of safety and stability.
* Name changed to protect identity.

Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:27:35 UTC
20:27:35 KST

Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
Most recently, the 85-year-old chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide.
Announcing the prize in Oslo, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said it was going to someone who “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict”.
Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay said “if you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
The award comes as the system of international justice is under attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to dismantle the International Criminal Court “brick by brick, if necessary”, and the US has sanctioned several of its staff.
Pillay played a significant role in the anti-apartheid movement in her homeland as a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela and other activists. She went on to serve as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, spending the last four of her eight years there as its president.
She was one of the ICC’s first judges, sitting in the appeals chamber from 2003 until 2008, when she stepped down to become UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
In 2019, she was appointed as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice by the Gambia, which had filed genocide proceedings against Myanmar over its treatment of the Rohingya minority.
Last year, as chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, she said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
In a post on social media, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” she said.
The prize is administered by the Nobel Foundation and comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (around €1.07 million).

Finance ministers strike market supercop deal despite Brussels’ objections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:27:33 UTC
20:27:33 KST

European Commissioner for Financial Services and the Savings and Investments Union Maria Luis Albuquerque during the meeting of the College of the European Commissioners in Brussels, Belgium on May 21, 2025.
LUXEMBOURG — EU finance ministers struck a compromise to beef up the bloc’s markets watchdog Friday, but the deal exposed divisions over national control and exemptions that critics say favor the biggest member countries.
Most finance ministers backed the Council’s position on MISP, a package of bills to integrate and police financial markets. At its heart is a plan to give the EU’s securities regulator powers to oversee major financial players — a flagship bid to make Europe a stronger investment hub, where European companies can seek investors without traveling to Wall Street.
But capitals stopped short of handing the future watchdog too much autonomy, triggering a hard rebuke from the European Commission.
Advertisement
“We deeply regret that the compromise now on the table falls significantly short of the level of ambition needed,” Finance Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque told ministers during Friday’s public Ecofin debate in Luxembourg. “We need [the European Securities and Markets Authority] to become an effective supervisor. The current compromise text would not allow for that.”
France spearheaded a last-minute push over dinner Thursday to strengthen the watchdog’s executive powers. Paris took issue with a rule that would allow nine national supervisors to force the watchdog’s executive board to submit draft decisions for further scrutiny before they’re adopted. The Irish EU presidency tweaked the rule overnight to limit national supervisors’ ability to delay decisions and preserve the watchdog’s power to act in emergencies, according to a compromise document obtained by POLITICO.
That was enough for France and most other countries. But not for the Commission, nor European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who was equally critical of the Council compromise. Beyond the governance concerns, Albuquerque took aim at supervisory carve-outs that the Irish introduced to accommodate Germany’s push to exclude its stock exchange, Deutsche Börse, from EU oversight.
The carve-out club
The carve-out shields stock exchanges from direct EU supervision unless they meet certain thresholds for trading activity and cross-border reach. Spain’s stock exchange, Bolsas y Mercados Españoles, would also benefit from the carve-outs, triggering criticism from smaller EU countries that accused the waiver of granting the bloc’s largest nations preferential treatment.
Belgium was particularly critical because its Brussels-based securities depository Euroclear is expected to come under direct EU oversight and face supervisory fees, while some major stock exchanges could remain under national oversight. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever will take the issue to EU leaders at the end of next week.
“We cannot support the carve-outs. The package includes as many ins as there are outs,” Belgian Finance Minister Jan Jambon said during Friday’s public debate. “I think Germany has won in certain cases.”
Advertisement
As a peace offering, Berlin backed a review clause that would allow the Commission to revisit the carve-outs two years after the supervisory rules start applying. Any changes would require new legislation, however.
“The carve-out is temporary,” Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, who backed the deal, told journalists Thursday. “If that exchange were to grow, it would also fall under [EU supervision]. This is also intended to ensure that Dutch companies or pan-European companies such as Euronext are not put at a disadvantage.”
Friday’s deal puts pressure on MEPs to agree Parliament’s position so negotiations on a final text can begin. The Commission hopes future legislative negotiations will provide a second chance to improve the text, which also threatens to increase pressure on the EU budget.
Under the compromise, the EU budget would shoulder 60% of the cost of ESMA’s activities not covered by industry fees, with national supervisors paying the remaining 40%.
“The Commission cannot accept a significant increase in the EU budget contribution in light of the difficult discussion at [the Multiannual Financial Framework],” Albuquerque said amid a bitter budget battle that threatens to shave hundreds of billions of euros off the proposed €2 trillion cash pot. “I sincerely hope that the European Parliament will be more ambitious.”

Four Dead After Two Cars Collide Near Pleven
Four young people were killed and another person was seriously injured in a head-on collision between two cars on the road linking Pleven and the village of Yasen
Pleven declared a day of mourning on October 9 for the four young people killed in a crash on the road between the city and the village of Yasen, with Mayor Valentin Hristov announcing the decision.
The victims were between 18 and 21 years old. Three were from Pleven, while the young woman who died was from Blagoevgrad. The two victims traveling in the Opel were students at the Medical University in Pleven.
According to the District Prosecutor’s Office, shortly before 11 p.m., a 20-year-old Opel driver entered the oncoming lane and collided with a BMW. The crash killed the BMW’s 18-year-old driver and his 21-year-old front-seat passenger. The other two fatalities were the Opel’s 20-year-old female front passenger and a 20-year-old man sitting in the back.
The Opel driver was the only survivor. He was taken to a hospital in Pleven and admitted to its Neurosurgery Clinic in stable condition.
Inspections at the crash site continued in the morning, while the road had remained closed for 12 hours. Driving at an inappropriate speed was considered the most likely cause of the collision.
The force of the impact scattered evidence of the crash across a stretch of about 200 meters, bTV reported. Investigators found medical and Bible textbooks, along with books on motor transport, among the wreckage.
The road is in poor condition and had been scheduled for renovation, but the funding was redirected last year to address Pleven’s water crisis.
The high school declared three days of mourning for the young people who died, calling the incident a major loss for the academic and student community and the entire city. The flag outside Pleven Municipality was also lowered to half-mast as a gesture of sympathy for the bereaved families.
“There are no words that can comfort loved ones in such a loss. It is especially difficult when young people leave this world!” Pleven Municipality said in a social media post.
The local administration extended its condolences to the families and relatives of the four victims.
“This loss is a huge tragedy for Pleven. Today Pleven mourns! Tribute to their memory!” the municipal statement added.

Conversations with the Sea: A love letter to Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:26:20 UTC
20:26:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Conversations with the Sea: Palestinian film director Muayad Alayan's love letter to a Jerusalem under occupation
Muayad Alayan’s fourth feature, Conversations with the Sea, is currently touring the global A-category film festivals.
After premiering almost simultaneously at the Venice and Toronto International Film Festivals, it is soon heading to the Warsaw Film Festival.
In the UK, it will screen at the Leeds Film Festival, as well as the Bristol and London Palestine Film Festivals, while preparing for its local theatrical release.
The film follows Kamal, a 60-year-old Palestinian man from Jerusalem, who is ordered by an Israeli authority to repay a substantial social security debt supposedly owed by his son, Wael. The problem is that Wael drowned in the Red Sea decades ago, yet his death was never officially recorded.
Kamal is therefore forced to prove that his son is dead, while the absence of official confirmation leaves open the possibility that Wael may still be alive.
His search takes him through hospitals, memories, family histories and the fragmented geography of Jerusalem.
What begins as a bureaucratic obligation gradually becomes a search for a missing son, and an exploration of guilt, family, displacement and the intergenerational trauma left by decades of conflict.
Based in Jerusalem and co-founder of the Bethlehem-based Palcine Productions, Muayad Alayan studied film in San Francisco and made his feature-length debut with Love Theft and Other Entanglements (2015), a dark romantic comedy that premiered in the 65th Berlinale Panorama section.
His sophomore political drama about forbidden love, The Reports on Sarah and Saleem (2018), won the Special Jury Prize in the Hivos Tiger Competition and the Hubert Bals Fund Audience Award at the Rotterdam International Film Festival, where he also presented his next work, A House in Jerusalem (2023), a film about ghosts and the supernatural dimensions of displacement.
Conversations with the Sea is perhaps his boldest political film, though it does not overshadow its poetic texture.
Although it is a fiction film, the plot’s point of departure comes from real life, raising questions that reach beyond the story and into the realities that shaped it.
The New Arab: The starting point of Conversations with the Sea is absurdist — a father being asked to repay a debt allegedly owed by his dead son. Where did that story come from?
Muayad Alayan: It happened to my wife's family. Her brother had died more than 20 years ago, and then the family received a demand from an Israeli security agency asking them to pay a large amount of money connected to him.
They had to go and find hospital records and prove that he was dead. It was very painful and insulting, because you are basically being asked to argue whether your son or your brother is actually dead or alive.
I witnessed what happened, but because it was very sensitive, I didn't immediately think, "I'm going to make a film about this." Then, about a year later, I got permission from the family to fictionalise it. So I ended up dramatising it, but in some way, it is inspired by the lives of Palestinians in Jerusalem.
How much of the film grew out of things you had witnessed yourself in Jerusalem?
I've been making documentaries and working as a cinematographer in East Jerusalem for a long time. I met many families and heard many stories.
You see people dealing with debt, imprisonment, losing their homes and properties, and being displaced. Sometimes these things happen through very complicated bureaucratic mechanisms; other times, through direct pressure.
What interested me was how all of this enters people's everyday lives. You don't necessarily wake up every morning thinking about politics. You have to go to work, raise your children and pay your bills. But politics is constantly entering your life.
I didn't want to make a film about a heroic character who is fighting some enormous battle. I am more interested in an ordinary person simply trying to live.
Conversations with the Sea features different generations of Palestinians in Jerusalem. As hinted at in the film, the older ones did not want to pay taxes to the Israeli state because they were sure the situation was temporary. How is this variety of views reflected in the city?
Every generation carries something different. My uncle's generation, for example, was very influenced by communism and genuinely believed that the [Israeli] occupation would end. His generation had a certain confidence that history was moving in a particular direction.
Then you have the generation of the 1980s, and the First Intifada, followed by the 1990s, when the peace process gave people hope again that maybe something was going to change.
The next generations inherited all of that history, but also the disappointment. There isn't necessarily acceptance, but rather a lot of depression and a feeling that the future has already been decided for you. The film is trying to capture that.
There is a Palestinian artist, Sliman Mansour, whose paintings I have always found very interesting. If you look at his work across the decades, you can almost see how his imagination of Palestine changes. The same thing happens with people. The city changes alongside people and political reality.
The question of home is central to Kamal's story, making property and displacement key themes as well.
I've worked on documentaries following Palestinian families in Jerusalem, and I remember one project involving around 12 families.
All of them were being pushed out in one way or another. None of them had simply decided, "We don't want this house anymore, let's sell it." That wasn't the story.
People left because they worried about their children, faced enormous pressure, or dealt with legal or financial mechanisms that made staying increasingly difficult.
Displacement doesn't always look like someone coming and physically removing you from your home. It can take many forms, and that's what I wanted to show.
Some people's lives were made so difficult that eventually they had to leave. The future of a neighbourhood can be made to look like something designed to keep its inhabitants out.
The film also includes several different Israeli characters and perspectives, with the boldest example being Kamal at the Israeli dinner, listening to their talk about the education of Palestinian children. What did you want to achieve by having that range?
I didn't want to create a film where every Israeli character is exactly the same. There are settlers, people from the political right, liberals, intellectuals, people who come from abroad. A wide variety, indeed.
But I wanted to pay attention to the fact that the Palestinian population itself is often missing from conversations about what Jerusalem should look like in the future.
Israelis talk about solutions, plans and how the city should be organised, but nobody asked the people who have been living there for hundreds and hundreds of years what they want. That question was important to me.
In your Director’s Statement, you describe Conversations with the Sea as a love-and-hate letter to Jerusalem. What has changed most dramatically in the city since you were growing up there?
The visual memory of Jerusalem is changing. Some people have lived in Jerusalem all their lives but can no longer access parts of the city.
You have the separation barrier and Palestinian homes that have been occupied by Israelis. An old urban landscape that is being transformed.
And then there are the villages around Jerusalem. You can go to some of these places and see Israeli artists living in Palestinian villages and new communities developing around them.
But the film isn't simply saying, "Look at what is happening politically." It's also about memory.
When you are older, you remember what a street looked like 30 or 40 years ago. You remember who lived there or a shop that doesn't exist anymore.
A city can live, but it can also disappear gradually through the eyes of the people who remember it. That's why I see the film as a love letter to my only home and my only city.
There is nostalgia for what it used to be, and grief over what it's being forced to become.
You shot in Jerusalem during a difficult period. What was it like to actually make a feature film there?
It was very difficult. For the last three years, production in Jerusalem has become incredibly complicated.
We couldn't have large crews outside, block streets or announce that we were filming. So we developed what I call a "shoot and run" style.
We had very small exterior crews, sometimes no more than eight people, and different bases in different places. We used small cars and trolleys to move equipment and work very quickly.
Behind that apparently chaotic way of working, however, there was always a very precise plan.
We kept backup memory cards hidden in different places, a second camera body ready to be brought in, and different crew members prepared to move ahead and shoot in another location if we were stopped.
So, while I'm happy that the film looks smooth, there was a whole matrix of planning behind it.
This makes me think of Iranian cinema and how it deals with restrictions on filming in public. Iranian filmmakers often have to work inside, in cars or in other confined spaces. Your film, by contrast, seems to have had more freedom in its exteriors, although I imagine you still had to find ways around the restrictions.
It's funny you mention Iranian cinema, because I watch a lot of Iranian films. In fact, it also influenced our choice of equipment.
We shot with a Red Komodo, which Jafar Panahi used for his last feature. We chose it because it was compact, could be operated seamlessly and wouldn't attract too much attention.
My Italian director of photography wanted to use a much bigger camera, but I told him, "We're the locals. Trust us." If you want to shoot in these places without getting into trouble, you either have to look like amateurs with a small camera or like a news crew.
There is always something worth filming in Jerusalem, so if you fit into one of those categories, you can get away with a lot more. If you try to make the production look complicated, you will get into trouble.
Did the restrictions change the way the film looks?
Definitely. Sometimes limitations force you to make decisions that you might not otherwise make. You become very conscious of the geography, thinking about where you can park, where the crew can stand, how quickly you can move, what happens if somebody stops you.
For interiors, it was easier. But once you go outside, everything becomes more complicated.
We also had to use Bethlehem and Ramallah for certain things when we couldn't shoot in Jerusalem. So the production itself became part of the experience of making a film about Jerusalem.
Kamel El-Basha plays Kamal. What did he bring to the character personally?
I've known Kamel for more than 20 years. He was in my first short film, Lesh Sabreen?, and in my first two features as well. He is from Jerusalem and grew up in and around the Old City.
At a young age, he was also a political prisoner. He grew up around a bakery belonging to his uncle, like the one in the film, and he remembers the city in a very physical way, knowing the gestures, the streets and the way people speak to each other.
During the film's preparation, Kamel gave me many small details. Sometimes it was the way he wore his hat, a simple gesture, a street name, or something from his own family history.
These details are difficult to invent if you haven't lived there.
Did his own experience affect the way he understood Kamal?
Very much. At the Q&A in Venice, Kamel said that Kamal was like him, but also like his father and his grandfather. He said he hoped his grandson would not have to live the same reality.
I think Kamel really understands this kind of feeling, what it means to live in a pressure cooker. Something that Palestine puts us in.
For me, the relationship between Kamal and his family was also very important. It's not only about the political pressure outside the house, but also inside the family. How do you deal with guilt and grief? How do you reconcile with people you have hurt?
Those are human questions, but they become much more intense when you are living under constant pressure.
The film begins with a bureaucratic problem but becomes increasingly emotional. What did you want audiences to take from that?
I wanted people to see the human being before the political metaphor. There is a tendency to look at Palestinian characters and immediately ask what they represent politically.
But Kamal isn't a symbol. He is a man who has made mistakes and regrets. He loves his family, though he has a complicated relationship with his children.
He's not a hero, and that's important to me because most people are not heroes. They are just trying to live their lives.
The title refers to the sea, which is connected to Wael's disappearance. But the film seems to be interested in many different forms of disappearance.
The sea takes Wael, but other kinds of disappearance happen around him.
People disappear from neighbourhoods, homes and memories disappear, streets change, families become separated. Sometimes a person is physically there, but the world around them has become unrecognisable. That is part of what I was trying to explore.
Jerusalem is haunted by fear. You have soldiers, armed settlers, demolitions, evacuations, arrests, injuries and deaths. Cycles of violence and fear all around.
But at the same time, people continue living.
They fall in love, have children, search for work, try to make money, argue with their families, but also look for moments of happiness.
That contradiction interests me.
Mariana Hristova is a freelance film critic, cultural journalist, and programmer. She contributes to national and international outlets and has curated programs for Filmoteca de Catalunya, Arxiu Xènctric, and goEast Wiesbaden, among others. Her professional interests include cinema from the European peripheries and archival and amateur films

Two men accused of being tasked by Iran to carry out hostile surveillance on the Israeli Embassy in London, Britain's oldest synagogue, and other Israeli or Jewish targets pleaded not guilty on Friday.
Nematollah Shahsavani, a 41-year-old dual Iranian-British national, and Alireza Farasati, a 22-year-old Iranian national, appeared at London's Old Bailey court and denied a single offense under the National Security Act.
The pair are among several individuals who have been charged in separate cases with acting on behalf of Iran in Britain.
Britain has recently accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the US-linked RAF Fairford military base, with seven men arrested and then released on bail.
Iran has denied any involvement in hostile activity in Britain, including the alleged RAF Fairford plot, after which the US removed its B-1 bombers from the base.
The pair are alleged to have gathered information and undertaken reconnaissance in July and August 2025, with a list of targets including the Israeli Embassy, the Israeli Consulate, and London's Bevis Marks Synagogue.
Unnamed individual of interest to Iran one alleged target of surveillance
Judge Bobbie Cheema-Grubb said one of the alleged targets also included an unnamed individual "of intelligence interest" to Iran.
After they were charged in March, Britain's Foreign Office said it had summoned Iran's ambassador to the UK.
Shahsavani and Farasati were remanded in custody ahead of their next court appearance in February, with their trial due to begin in April.
Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in hostile activity in Britain, which authorities say has markedly increased since the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023 that triggered the subsequent war in Gaza.

====================================================================================================

Israel cannot heal from October 7 without confronting its failures - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:25:20 UTC
20:25:20 KST

All you had to do on Wednesday was turn on the radio.
The songs playing were the same ones Israelis are used to hearing on Remembrance Day for the Fallen of Israel’s Wars and on Holocaust Remembrance Day. Songs of grief, sadness, and tragedy. Songs that capture the nation’s pain and the weight of its collective memory.
It was Israel’s way of marking October 7.
And what we learned on Wednesday is that a new day has been added to Israel’s calendar of remembrance. Not just another date to commemorate, but a day that represents a raw and open wound, one that continues to haunt us and will likely do so for generations.
What made this third anniversary significant was how different it was from the previous two. On the first anniversary in 2024, Israel was still in the midst of the war. The IDF was fighting in Gaza and Lebanon, negotiations over the hostages were dragging on, soldiers were being killed, and there was not yet an end in sight
The second anniversary, in 2025, came as Israel was approaching a breakthrough in the hostage negotiations. Just days later, the remaining living hostages returned home, accompanied by a celebratory visit by US President Donald Trump.
This year was different since it was the first time that people could look back. All of the hostages are home, and while the IDF remains in control of most of the Gaza Strip and occasional airstrikes continue, the high-intensity stage of the war is, for now, behind us.
Yes, Hamas has yet to disarm. It remains in control of roughly one-third of Gaza, where it has been replenishing its ranks and rearming itself. But a full-scale Israeli offensive does not currently appear to be in the cards. And with elections just weeks away, this created something Israel has not really had until now: an opportunity for a deeper and more genuine national reckoning.
The question, though, is what will we do with it.
When we think about October 7 and how it will be remembered, one of the most important questions is how we ensure that this moment in our history does not dissipate over time. How do we make sure it does not simply become another date on the calendar, gradually fading from our consciousness as the years pass?
The closest parallel in Israeli history is, of course, the Yom Kippur War of 1973, a war that shares many of the same characteristics as October 7: an extraordinary intelligence failure, a devastating operational failure, and a failure of political leadership.
I think that what made the Yom Kippur War such a seminal moment in Israeli history was not just the failure itself or the terrible price in lives that Israel paid. It was what happened afterward: Israel established a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures, and its findings led to resignations, the dismissal of senior military officers, and fundamental changes in Israel’s defense and intelligence establishments.
The commission was far from perfect, but its work forced the country to confront what had happened. Lessons were learned, books were written, and investigations were conducted. The country began the difficult process of not just understanding what went wrong but also reckoning with that knowledge.
We will never be able to put October 7 behind us, nor should we. The murder of 1,200 people, the kidnapping of 251 hostages, the destruction of entire communities, and the heroism and sacrifice of so many Israelis will forever be part of our national ethos.
But as long as there is no comprehensive investigation, Israel will struggle to close this chapter in a way that allows it to heal and, just as importantly, to learn.
This is why a state commission of inquiry into October 7 is existential for Israel. It is existential because we need to heal, and because we need to learn the lessons necessary to ensure the mistakes are never repeated.
Confronting the faliures of October 7
And here is the hard truth: three years after the massacre, Israel has already fallen into two new “conceptziyot” – dangerous paradigms of thinking that, if left unchallenged, could cause immense harm in the years ahead.
The first is the belief that we can somehow move forward without a full investigation. Three years have passed, and Israel has still not established a state commission of inquiry. Yes, the IDF has conducted internal investigations, but those have focused on tactical and operational failures and are far from being enough.
They do not provide the comprehensive examination needed of the government, the cabinet, the National Security Council, the intelligence agencies, and the political decisions that shaped Israel’s policies toward Hamas and Gaza in the years leading up to the attack.
The refusal to establish such a commission illustrates a dangerous belief among the politicians preventing it: that Israel does not really need this reckoning, that it can somehow continue without confronting the full extent of what went wrong. They are mistaken.
But there is a second “conceptziya,” one that is no less dangerous. It is the belief that every problem Israel faces is a nail and every solution is a hammer.
There is a problem in the West Bank? Send in the IDF. There is a problem in Gaza? Expand military control. Negotiations with Lebanon are stalling? Increase the IDF presence. There are security concerns in Syria? Continue holding territory.
Every challenge is increasingly met with the same response: more military force, more control, and more operations.
There is no question that Israel needs a strong military and that we need a doctrine of preemptive action. October 7 taught us the catastrophic consequences of containment and failing to maintain the readiness needed to defend our borders.
But as essential as it is, military power cannot alone solve the challenges Israel faces.
It was commendable that Avigdor Liberman, the head of Yisrael Beytenu, published a plan this week for dealing with the conflict with the Palestinians.
His proposal calls for dismantling the Palestinian Authority and transferring responsibility for the West Bank to Jordan through some form of security arrangement.
Is it realistic? I don’t think so. Jordan has no interest in assuming such responsibility, most Israelis are unlikely to support the idea, and the Americans as well as the Europeans are unlikely to endorse it.
But that is beside the point, since at least Liberman is talking about the issue. At least he is putting forward a plan, and at least he recognizes that the conflict requires more than deploying another infantry battalion.
That is more than can be said for his partners in the opposition. Does anyone know what Naftali Bennett’s plan is for the West Bank? What does Gadi Eisenkot believe should happen beyond saying a few weeks ago that a two-state solution is delusional? What is not delusional, Gadi? What is the alternative?
And then, of course, there is Benjamin Netanyahu, widely viewed as Israel’s most prominent opponent of a two-state solution. Yet when you look back at his political career, he has repeatedly taken steps that kept the possibility of such an outcome alive.
In the 1990s, he met repeatedly with Yasser Arafat, signed the Hebron Agreement, and continued implementing parts of the Oslo process initiated by Yitzhak Rabin.
In 2009, after returning as prime minister, he gave his famous Bar-Ilan speech, explicitly endorsed a demilitarized Palestinian state alongside Israel, and continued to support that possibility during his dealings with US president Barack Obama. Even during Trump’s first term, he endorsed the American peace plan, which envisioned a pathway to Palestinian statehood.
Even more recently, Netanyahu accepted Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan, whose final clauses explicitly recognize the possibility of a credible pathway toward Palestinian self-determination and eventual statehood.
This does not mean Netanyahu wants a Palestinian state today, and the steps he has taken in recent years in Judea and Samaria make that quite clear.
But it does demonstrate something important: even a leader so strongly identified with opposition to Palestinian statehood has for the last 20 years recognized the need to keep a political horizon on the table.
The problem today is that almost nobody in Israeli politics seems willing to have an honest conversation about what that horizon should look like.
Not Netanyahu. Not Bennett. Not Eisenkot. And, with the exception of Liberman’s proposal, hardly anyone else.
This is the second dangerous conception Israel must confront: the belief that we can continue indefinitely without a political strategy, that military superiority alone will resolve our challenges, and that the absence of an immediate solution justifies the absence of any plan.
Israel today is militarily stronger than it was on October 7, 2023. Hamas has been weakened, Hezbollah has been hit with devastating blows, and Iran’s nuclear program remains mostly under rubble. The regional balance of power has shifted dramatically in Israel’s favor.
These are extraordinary achievements. But military achievements are not an end in themselves. They are supposed to create the conditions for something else, and if we do not translate them into diplomatic and political opportunities, we risk finding ourselves back where we started.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

====================================================================================================

October 7 haunts Netanyahu's election campaign, but his bloc holds its ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:25:02 UTC
20:25:02 KST

A few months back, when talk of early elections was abundant, conventional wisdom held that they would take place sometime in September.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, this thinking went, would not want to go to the people in October, when ceremonies marking three years since October 7 would bring memories of that tragedy painfully back to the surface.
That assumption made sense. It also proved wrong.
Netanyahu did not call early elections that would have let him pick a more convenient date. Instead, he decided to see his term through to the very end – October 27.
Perhaps he calculated that by then, the emotional weight of this week’s commemorations would have eased, overtaken by other news and events.
Or perhaps he concluded that the date made little difference: whether the election was held on September 1 or October 27, October 7 would cast a long shadow over everything else.
If October 7 would be there regardless, he might as well finish his term – itself a remarkable political feat considering the magnitude of the disaster and the seething anger directed at him and his government in its immediate aftermath.
Still, this week offered a reminder of why an October election might have seemed an unappealing prospect.
October 7 commemorations bring national mourning into election campaign
The country essentially just went through four days of remembrance, beginning on Simchat Torah, the Hebrew date of the attack, continuing through the 24th of Tishrei, the official state memorial day, and extending through October 7 itself, when a massive citizen-organized ceremony was held at Ganei Yehoshua.
Television, radio, and the print media were filled with harrowing accounts – stories of horrific tragedy and remarkable heroism. The grief was palpable. So, too, were many unresolved questions, including what Netanyahu knew and when he knew it, and why he continues to refuse to establish a state commission of inquiry.
Was it politically wise, then, to hold an election just 20 days after the nation revisited its deepest wounds?
The polls suggest the answer is less obvious than expected.
From October 1 to October 7, nine major polls were taken for eight media organizations, with Channel 14 publishing two. Their simple average put the Netanyahu bloc – Likud, Shas, United Torah Judaism, Religious Zionist Party-Zehut, Otzma Yehudit, and Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party – ahead with 55.5 seats.
That compares with 50 for the opposition bloc of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu, and Yair Golan’s Democrats. The two Arab parties averaged 13 seats, with the remaining 1.5 going to parties that cross the electoral threshold in some polls.
There is a caveat. For months, the Channel 14 and i24 polls have been outliers, giving the Likud significantly more seats than the other surveys. Exclude them, and the two blocs are in a virtual dead heat: 52.17 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc and 51.83 for its opponents.
Both remain well below the 61 seats needed to form a government. But comparing those figures with nine polls in early May and nine others in late September puts them in perspective.
Opposition's lead over Netanyahu's bloc narrows
Excluding Channel 14 and i24, Netanyahu’s bloc averaged 51.5 seats in the May polls, compared with 57.83 for the opposition – an opposition advantage of more than six seats. By late September, that gap had narrowed to less than one seat: 51.75 for Netanyahu’s bloc and 52.63 for its opponents.
During the first week of October, Netanyahu’s bloc edged ahead. The striking point is that the gap has closed because the change bloc has lost ground, not because the Netanyahu bloc has significantly increased.
Netanyahu’s bloc has gained only about two-thirds of a seat since May. But the opposition has lost six. In some five months, therefore, a clear opposition advantage – at least in the polls – has become a virtual tie.
These averages cannot establish whether this week’s commemorations changed anyone’s vote. They do show that a week spent reopening the wounds of October 7 did not coincide with an erosion of support for Netanyahu’s bloc or an increase in support for the other side.
The wounds are still raw, but what that will translate into at the ballot box remains contested.
And while other issues – foremost the haredi conscription issue – are consequential in this campaign, questions about reported warnings from Egypt and the UAE before the Hamas attack, what Netanyahu knew, and whether he acted appropriately have brought the campaign back to October 7 and its origins.
October 7 shapes competing election narratives for Netanyahu and the opposition
For both sides, October 7 is central to this election. What divides them is what they want voters to see when they look back.
The opposition wants voters to focus on the colossal failures of that day, the failures that preceded it, and the refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry.
Its argument turns on this question: can a prime minister who has neither taken responsibility nor allowed a full, independent accounting be trusted to prevent the next disaster?
Netanyahu wants voters to focus on what came afterward: the blows delivered to Israel’s enemies and the changes in the region that he argues have made the country stronger and safer.
Last week’s flydubai incident gave both sides fresh ammunition for their arguments.
Bennett, Eisenkot use flydubai security failures to challenge Netanyahu's record
For Bennett and Eisenkot, the apparent security failures surrounding the flight provide a way to bring the argument about October 7 into the present. They can argue that this is not only about a catastrophe three years ago. Even after the military achievements since then, serious vulnerabilities remain.
The passengers’ resourcefulness and courage helped avert disaster. But citizens rescuing themselves is hardly a substitute for institutions doing their jobs.
That is the connection the opposition wants voters to make: extraordinary people stepping into a vacuum left by a system that should have protected them. The heroism deserves celebration. The vacuum demands investigation.
October 7 and the attempted hijacking differ enormously in scale and circumstances. But one relevant question is common to both: whether familiar habits – complacency, gaps in oversight, fragmented responsibility – are again visible, and whether those responsible will identify and correct them.
Politically, the flydubai saga gives Bennett and Eisenkot an opening to make their points. This incident challenges the proposition that the military achievements since October 7 mean the government’s machinery is now functioning as it should. Flydubai shows that this is not the case.
Both candidates can use the flight to illustrate a major theme of their campaign: competence. Who can identify gaps, assign responsibility, and follow through? Security depends on the daily business of governing, as well as on decisions made in the war cabinet. Somebody has to ensure procedures work and problems are addressed.
Netanyahu highlights diplomatic achievements in flydubai crisis
Netanyahu, meanwhile, has an answer.
He can point to the Saudi assistance and the Emirati role in bringing the passengers home as evidence that the regional relationships he helped build have real value. The cooperation shown during this crisis reflects the new Middle East that emerged through his actions since October 7.
That argument has substance. Israelis in distress received help in a region where, not so long ago, the prospect of such cooperation would have seemed impossible. Don’t forget, only a few years ago Israeli planes could not fly over Saudi Arabia, let alone land at a joint civilian-military airfield when in need.
The Abraham Accords did not remove hostility or erase the barriers to normalization with Saudi Arabia. They did, however, help create relationships that can deliver assistance when Israelis need it.
Here, too, the flydubai incident makes both sides’ campaign arguments tangible.
For the Eisenkot and Bennett campaigns, talk of government competence is often abstract. A plane plunging while passengers struggle to save it makes this idea concrete.
Likewise, “failure to take responsibility” is abstract, while hearing officials explain after the flydubai incident that the matter is not in their jurisdiction makes it concrete.
And for Netanyahu’s campaign, a “new Middle East” can sound like a slogan. But enlisting Saudi and Emirati assistance in bringing Israelis safely home gives it practical meaning.
The campaigns will draw different lessons from the same flight. Netanyahu will point to the regional cooperation that helped bring Israelis home. His opponents will point to the failures that put them in danger in the first place and the officials who have been passing around the responsibility ever since.
Both arguments go to the heart of this election: whom can Israelis trust to keep them safe?
This week’s polls suggest that the answer does not follow automatically from the pain of October 7. The wounds remain raw, but Netanyahu’s bloc has held its ground. His opponents still have to convince voters that the failures outweigh the achievements, and that they can provide better protection.
The campaigns will make sure that October 7 – and its long aftermath – and flydubai are on voters’ minds when they enter the polling booth.
The question is which will weigh more heavily: the failures Netanyahu’s opponents want them to remember, or the achievements he wants them to recognize.
For now, tellingly, neither side has established a clear advantage in the polls.

Tuscan winemaker Antinori sees red after $6 million theft

Tuscan winemaker Antinori sees red after $6 million theft
ROME, Oct 9 - Thieves stole around 30,000 bottles of premium wine worth about €5 million ($5.8 million) from a Marchesi Antinori warehouse in Tuscany, Italy's largest family-run winemaker said on Friday.
Antinori, which dates back to 1385 and now exports to 170 countries, has alerted customers worldwide to be wary of offers outside official sales channels following last weekend's heist and is still hopeful of recovering the stolen wine.
It said the thieves took 8,000 to 10,000 bottles of Solaia, one of Italy's most sought-after labels, as well as Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. The wines retail from €150, but some of the rarest vintages can fetch thousands of euros per bottle.
The theft is the latest in a series in Italy, following another in July at the renowned Banfi winery in Montalcino.
While such crimes have traditionally involved smaller quantities or a handful of high-value bottles, from restaurants, private cellars or during distribution, recent cases have involved larger stocks held at wineries.
Florence-based Antinori said surveillance camera footage showed seven masked men entering its storage facility in Cortona last weekend and disabling its alarm systems before loading thousands of cases of the Tuscan red wines onto two trucks.
Antinori said the timing and execution of the theft, which was discovered on Monday morning when staff arrived at the warehouse and is now being investigated by Italian police, suggested a highly organised group was involved.
The operation was facilitated by the fact that the wines had been prepared for a shipment to foreign distributors, allowing the thieves to remove a large quantity of high-value bottles quickly, a representative for Antinori told Reuters. REUTERS

France students plan more protests, UN 'concerned' over violence
Unknown

2026-10-09

20:23:35 KST

Breadcrumb
France's students plan more protests, UN 'concerned' over violence
Students in France were largely back in the classroom Friday following days of protests demanding better education, with the UN voicing "concern" over the sometimes violent clashes ignited by police action.
Tens of thousands have taken to the streets across France since students in late September began blocking entrances to high schools, which in turn saw squads of riot police deployed.
The students—most aged 15 to 18—have complained of absent teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
More than 6,800 people have been detained since the start of the demonstrations, of whom 86 percent are children, the justice ministry said Friday.
The United Nations said Friday it was watching the events "with concern" and urging people on all sides to remain peaceful.
"We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent," said Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights agency.
While the demonstrations have been largely peaceful, some protesters have started fires and vandalised bus shelters.
In response, police have used tear gas, batons and blast balls, leading to accusations from rights groups and the children of a disproportionate use of force.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
A 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, and the government has suspended the use of the weapon.
Substitute teachers
On Thursday evening in the capital Paris, police said they used tear gas in Bastille square to disperse some "high-risk profiles".
In a bid to placate the anger, Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has also promised a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October, while Economy Minister Roland Lescure said there was room to address demands for more school resources within the highly constrained 2027 budget.
In the current draft budget, education has the second largest increase in funding—after defence—with a boost of 1.4 percent to 90.9 billion euros.
Of the 3,700 high schools across France, called lycees, only 141 were closed on Friday, the education ministry reported.
Last Friday, some 800 schools had closed due to the protests.
But many students told AFP they were not relenting, with organisers calling for large-scale demonstrations next week.
"We're saving our energy for next week," said one 16-year-old student in Toulouse.
Alice, a high school student in Marseille, said the education minister's announcements "are a first step but they're not enough."

Ukrainian Freediver Nataliia Zharkova Dives 113 Meters to Win World Championship Gold
Ukrainian freediver Nataliia Zharkova has won a gold medal at the 2026 Freediving World Championships in Limassol, Cyprus, after completing a 113-meter dive in the Constant Weight (CWT) discipline, the deepest successful women's dive in the event.
According to Suspilne Sport, the championships were held from September 30 to October 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The women's CWT competition took place on the final day of women's events. In this discipline, athletes descend and ascend using a monofin or bifins while maintaining constant weight, without adding or removing ballast during the dive.
Hungarian freediver Zsófia Törőcsik initially declared a 115-meter attempt but turned early at a depth of 108 meters, resulting in penalty points that affected her final standing.
Zharkova subsequently attempted a 113-meter dive, successfully reaching the declared depth and completing her performance without penalties. Her result secured the gold medal and the best women's performance in the discipline at the championships.
France's Jade Agboton claimed silver with a 101-meter dive, while Törőcsik finished third despite reaching 108 meters because of the penalties incurred during her attempt.
According to Suspilne Sport, Zharkova's victory also contributed to her overall performance at the championships. The Ukrainian athlete finished sixth in the combined standings with 284 points.
Her achievement follows another milestone for Ukrainian freediving on the international stage. In November 2025, Ukrainian freediver Kateryna Sadurska set a new world record in the Constant Weight No Fins discipline, reaching a depth of 86 meters during the Blue Element competition in Dominica.
Sadurska completed the record-breaking dive in 3 minutes and 32 seconds, taking ten strokes during her descent before entering freefall and another 31 strokes to return to the surface.
