Researchers explore how J-Pop listening habits impact visual memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:12 UTC
20:00:12 KST

A small pilot study exploring the brain activity of young adults found that listening to preferred Japanese pop music was associated with higher descriptive scores in visual memory and subjective focus compared to unpleasant noise or silence. While the results were not statistically significant, the research provides a framework for testing how everyday listening habits relate to learning and attention. The findings were published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience.
Many students habitually listen to music while they review class materials or prepare for exams. Popular media often highlights a supposed cognitive boost from classical music, an idea frequently branded as the Mozart effect. But very few university students actually select classical instrumental pieces for their daily study routines.
Instead, contemporary students frequently choose popular music with familiar lyrics. This habit presents a puzzle for cognitive researchers. Meaningful speech and background vocals can easily disrupt the human brain as it attempts to process language and memorize verbal facts.
Listening to a favorite pop song with lyrics might logically act as a distraction that pulls attention away from educational materials. Conversely, familiar and enjoyable music can elevate a person’s mood, reduce stress, and increase overall motivation to complete a difficult task.
Different types of learning might also respond differently to musical background noise. While reading comprehension and verbal memorization often suffer when background lyrics are present, recalling visual information might be less susceptible to the exact same interference.
Researchers are working to understand if preferred background music can support efficient memory processing through emotional engagement. They are looking at neural mechanisms that are entirely distinct from those typically emphasized in traditional classical music narratives.
Yoshiko Tojo, a researcher at the Ibaraki Prefectural University of Health Sciences in Japan, wanted to understand this dynamic in a realistic context. Tojo aimed to see how self-selected Japanese pop music, commonly known as J-Pop, relates to visual memory retrieval and regional brain activity.
Tojo recruited healthy university students for a small brain imaging pilot study. After exclusions for incomplete data, the final analysis included five participants. The participants completed a visual memory test while lying inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner.
This imaging technology tracks blood flow in the brain to measure neural activity in real time. The visual memory task began with an encoding phase. Participants viewed sets of emotionally neutral photographs, such as everyday animals and food items.
They were asked to memorize both the specific objects and the exact order in which they appeared on the screen. Later, the participants answered true or false statements about the images to test their recall. They performed this retrieval task under three different auditory conditions.
In the first condition, participants listened to a J-Pop song they had personally selected beforehand as pleasant and comfortable. The second condition featured an abrasive composite sound made of ambulance sirens and earthquake early warning alarms. The final condition served as a baseline, featuring no sound other than the continuous rhythmic thumping of the scanner itself.
Following the memory tests, participants rated their subjective ability to focus during each auditory condition on a visual scale. They also rated the pleasantness of each sound environment. Tojo then analyzed both the behavioral performance and the brain activity data to see how the auditory contexts compared.
The behavioral data showed distinct patterns across the three listening environments. Participants achieved the highest average recall accuracy, answering correctly roughly 82 percent of the time, while listening to their preferred J-Pop music. In the baseline condition with no added sound, accuracy averaged about 76 percent.
The abrasive alarm sounds yielded the lowest recall accuracy at just 71 percent. The subjective focus ratings closely mirrored these results, with participants reporting the highest concentration during the J-Pop condition.
Brain scan data revealed shifting activity in specific neural regions depending on the background noise. Tojo focused heavily on the anterior insula, an area of the brain involved in evaluating subjective emotions, sensing internal body states, and managing large-scale attention networks.
During the J-Pop condition, participants showed higher average activity in the anterior insula compared to the other two conditions. This elevated activity suggests the familiar music might have engaged brain areas responsible for processing positive emotions and maintaining sustained task engagement.
Tojo also examined the temporo-occipital visual association cortex, a region at the back of the brain responsible for higher order visual processing and memory. Activity in this visual region was highest during the unpleasant alarm condition and lowest in the silent baseline condition.
This increased visual brain activity during the alarm condition might indicate that participants had to work harder to process the images when exposed to abrasive noise. But because the sample size was restricted to only five people, these behavioral and neural differences were not statistically significant.
The limited number of participants is the primary constraint of this research. The small sample size heavily restricts statistical power, meaning the results cannot be generalized to broader populations without further testing.
The experimental design also utilized different sets of pictures for each sound condition. This approach prevented participants from simply recognizing images they had already seen in previous rounds. But it also introduces the possibility that some image sets were inherently easier to remember than others.
The research focused exclusively on a visual memory task and a single genre of popular music. It is unknown if similar emotional and neural patterns would appear for verbal learning tasks, such as reading a textbook or memorizing vocabulary words.
Future studies with larger and more diverse groups of participants are needed to verify these trends. Expanding the research could reveal exactly when and for whom studying with background music might be beneficial.
These initial observations do not establish that listening to preferred music inherently improves memory performance. They do suggest that listening to emotionally positive background music is not universally detrimental to studying, opening the door for larger investigations into how personal listening habits affect the brain.
The study, “Preferred J-pop music and visual memory retrieval: an exploratory pilot fMRI study,” was authored by Yoshiko Tojo.

AI Chatbots Often Fail To Help Users in Mental-Health Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

As more people turn to AI chatbots to share their most distressing thoughts, companies are making pivotal decisions about how their platforms respond to users in the midst of mental-health crises. According to new research conducted by Scale AI and shared exclusively with TIME, chatbots are adept at discerning when a user is in crisis, but often fail to provide adequate help.
In about 35% of test conversations in the study, different AI chatbots recognized the user was distressed but didn’t refer them to helpful resources, such as a suicide hotline, according to the research.
“The models do a good job—regardless of the scenario—of identifying, ‘Look, this person's talking about something harmful,’” says Patrick Oathout, Red Team & Safety Lead at Scale AI. “But they'll respond in a very just empathetic, kind way as opposed to saying, ‘Okay, it's time that we get you help.’” The models performed worse at responding to users’ distress when they were engaging in long, multi-turn conversations—a deficit that matches the findings of previous studies, Oathout adds.
To test AI models’ effectiveness at responding to distressed users, Scale AI asked 19 licensed clinicians and crisis counselors to write 718 realistic chats, simulating scenarios where someone in crisis reaches out to a chatbot. The company tested 25 frontier models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. It graded the models’ responses based on a rubric that included whether it was compassionate, de-escalated the situation, and steered users to an expert who could help them, said Oathout. It also assessed whether they refrained from moralizing, such as criticizing suicide, and disclosed it wasn't a therapist. Based on the research, Scale AI research developed DistressBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate how well models reply when someone tells them they're thinking about committing suicide or self-harm.
How chatbots respond to mentally distressed users is a question with high stakes. More than half a million people in the U.S. died by suicide between 2014 and 2024, with 2022 marking a record high, according to the health-policy organization KFF. According to the CDC, an estimated 14.3 million people seriously thought about suicide in 2024.
Increasingly, vulnerable people turn to chatbots for comfort, companionship, or guidance when dealing with mental-health distress. But there isn’t consensus among tech companies, policymakers, or mental-health professionals about how AI companies should train their models to respond to users in crisis.
Kelly Zuromski, a principal clinical research scientist at Crisis Text Line, says the nonprofit’s 24/7 crisis text line has spoken with “a lot of people” who indicated they heard about the group through a chatbot. But Zuromski says there are unanswered policy questions about what a responsible handoff looks like when a chatbot refers users to a human during a mental-health crisis—and how effective the referral process is in the first place. “Who is actually using the recommended resources?” she says. “Are we getting people to us that need the help the most?”
In some cases, AI companies, including OpenAI and Google, have been sued for fostering emotional dependence among young users and then failing to respond adequately to their expressions of distress, or reinforcing their delusional or suicidal thinking in the first place. The companies have expressed sympathy for the families and said their models include mental-health safeguards. (The lawsuits are ongoing.) AI labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have said in recent years that they beefed up their protections for sensitive conversations, including by implementing policies that bar chatbots from instructing users on how to harm themselves and directing users to professional or emergency support.
An OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement the company did not have sufficient evidence to fully evaluate the Scale AI study, adding that the company incorporates robust safeguards into its models. Google declined to comment. Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment.
In the future, AI labs should improve their models to better respond to users engaging in dangerous lengthy conversations with chatbots, says Scale AI’s Oathout. “I think the models are better than they were,” he says. “The goal now is to raise it further and actually reduce harm, which would add this massive benefit to society.”

The Cornell 7 Case Demands More Than Outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

By now, most of America has heard about the young woman who says she was gang raped by fraternity brothers while she was a student at Cornell University.
The case has been dubbed the "Cornell 7" across mainstream and social media, after the seven Chi Phi members named in her recent lawsuit. The woman who filed the suit, referred to as Jane Doe, first reported her experience to Cornell campus police in November 2024. According to her lawyer, after Cornell's Title IX process, two of the seven were expelled, and the other five were suspended, sent to workshops, and assigned essays. Cornell says none of them got off with only an essay.
At the time, the Tompkins County District Attorney declined to prosecute. After public outcry, the DA issued a statement explaining that Jane Doe’s original statement to police described the drug use and sex as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” “However, recognizing that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human, my office has reopened this investigation," he wrote. Now, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case.
How did the case come to light? It took The Cornell Daily Sun, the campus student newspaper, breaking the story roughly two years later for this to capture the hearts, minds, and headlines of Americans across the country. The story struck a nihilistic nerve.
This case lands squarely in a moment of massive frustration, disappointment, and anger over how the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell case was handled. New CDC data shows that nearly half of American women and one in six men have experienced some form of contact sexual violence. Based on how broad this issue is and based on how some of the most visible cases have turned out, apathy about our ability to see our way from a society steeped in rape culture to one where sexual violence is rare should come as no surprise.
As someone fully immersed in this work, even though I see a pathway forward, I understand these feelings from a very deep place in my spirit. We should be disgusted. We should be heartbroken. We should be enraged.
So what do we do with these feelings?
We provide an outpouring of support to Jane Doe and to other women who have come forward with their accounts of sexual assault, such as Kendall Francis, who took to TikTok to speak out about how her college, LSU, handled her Title IX case. According to ESPN, in July, the LSU Office of Civil Rights and Title IX found her alleged attacker, a football player, responsible for “forcible rape” and suspended him for two semesters. The player appealed and in August, Administrative Law Judge Janet Waguespack reduced his punishment to four semesters’ probation, allowing him to remain on campus. The player's lawyers maintain that their client is innocent.
Again, Francis’ story struck a nerve, catching the attention of East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose office is now investigating the case.
The outpouring of support matters, both so these young women can get the justice they're seeking and so survivors everywhere know that support is out here. But what many of us know is that for every Jane Doe and Kendall Francis who reports and seeks justice, there are hundreds, if not thousands, of survivors who won't, for a lot of reasons. Chief among them is feeling alone in the fight. They aren't alone. But I'll admit it's hard to tell when spotlights dim, headlines fade, and accountability seems stifled.
As if right on cue, something else happened this week while these cases took over headlines. The Trump Administration’s Department of Education altered Title IX rules, declaring that harassment has to be "severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive" before a school must act, that most off-campus violence falls outside a school's responsibility, and that a college survivor can be cross-examined at a live hearing by the advisor her attacker chose.
This decision landing right as the Cornell 7 case came to light is telling. It's one of the clearest illustrations of the direct line between the damage this administration has done to the fight against sexual and gender-based violence—especially among young people.
The Trump Administration’s decision to make it more burdensome to file a Title IX complaint only adds to the helplessness so many survivors feel. Patriarchy protects itself the way any system of power does. It writes the rules, staffs the offices, and then leaves survivors like Jane Doe and Kendall Francis to fight for justice on their own.
Of course, it is worth remembering the challenge we collectively face isn’t simply a matter of one rule or how it is applied; there are questions we must confront about where our culture has ended up. After all, these Cornell students were tweens when recordings of now-President Donald Trump leaked of him using crude language to describe how he treats women. The context may be different, but we have to ask: How far is the line between "grab 'em by the p---y" and "free p---y", the message the lawsuit says one of the Cornell 7 sent his fraternity brothers, inviting them to join in the hours-long assault on Jane Doe?
Yet, in the face of these various challenges, we must also remember: We are not helpless.
On October 15, it'll be nine years since #MeToo went viral. We're far past the hashtag, but we're still in the movement, and it's a very real, very active movement fighting tooth and nail to destroy systems that prevent justice. The answer to such systems has always been the organized power of the people those systems harm. The rage people are feeling right now, from Baton Rouge to Ithaca, can be organized and directed exactly where it's needed. That means our outrage can't be selective. It can't show up when Epstein or Cornell makes the news and disappear when the coverage moves on. Because when the next national story takes hold, there will still be students on high school and college campuses all over this country who are fundamentally unsafe.
We've made real progress in almost ten years of the MeToo movement, and lasting change will only come from constant demand. Frederick Douglass famously said: "Power concedes nothing without a demand." Black people in the civil rights era didn't wait for a government full of segregationists to find its conscience. They organized until it had no choice. Sexual and gender-based violence is solvable, but those solutions have to be demanded, and we have the numbers to demand them.
Too many survivors who stay silent believe they'd be fighting alone if they raise their voices. The CDC's most recent national survey found that nearly 80 million American adults, close to 58 million women and more than 20 million men, have experienced contact sexual violence. For some people, those are just numbers. In reality, they're a base of power: millions of people who know this trauma intimately and are primed to act.
What action against sexual violence can look like
First, you can join an organization dedicated to addressing sexual violence head-on. Several national organizations are working to bring survivors and our allies together to demand systemic change. Organizations like mine, me too. International, along with the National Women's Law Center and UltraViolet, are on the front lines organizing survivor leaders, fighting for survivors in courtrooms, and keeping people engaged on these issues. Others, like Justice for Migrant Women, Educate Us, and the National Domestic Workers Alliance, work on where sexual and gender-based violence meets immigration, domestic work, and education. The Survivor Justice Network, a coalition of organizations fighting sexual and gender-based violence from a social and political standpoint, runs the Survivors Vote campaign to organize survivors as a voting bloc. And there are countless regional and local organizations fighting this fight every day, especially local rape crisis centers, many of which are struggling.
In April 2025, the Justice Department terminated hundreds of grants worth more than $800 million, including money for victim services, and this spring $200 million meant for violence against women programs was still sitting unspent. Centers like the DC Rape Crisis Center (DCRCC), the oldest in the country, don't only provide direct services to local survivors. They take on the larger issue of sexual violence and how it's affecting the people they serve.
Next, you can use your resources well. Speakimng of DCRCC, local rape crisis centers are the first line of defense, and when students can't get support on campus, they often go looking for it at the rape crisis center in their college town. Find the survivor support organizations near you and give to them directly. It's the best way to shore up the front line so survivors can get what they need and the fight can continue.
Third, you can get active in local politics.
Ask your elected officials where they stand on sexual and gender-based violence and on legislation they can move right now, like the Survivors' Rights Restitution Act, which Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced in September with Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross to compensate survivors whose federal rights were violated, including Epstein's survivors. Pressure them to vote accordingly, and make your support heard and understood.
Lastly, we must unite around our shared challenges. National outrage helps shake people up enough to pay attention, but culture won't shift just because we change laws and elect better politicians. People need to understand how sexual and gender-based violence shows up in their daily lives, how it intersects with the other issues they care about, and how long it stays with families, communities, and institutions. Until the whole of society sees this as an abomination, we won’t have the lasting cultural impact that makes sexual violence a rarity.
Jane Doe and Kendall Francis each refused to carry this quietly. The rest of us owe them and survivors like them more than a week of outrage.
We can let them see what it looks like to turn outrage into outcomes.

Dunking on Dating App Profiles Is Content Gold. People Are Getting Sick of It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Evangelizing to his 512,000 TikTok followers occasionally requires that dating coach Chad Franklin post the private communications of his clients, who pay upwards of $5,000 for his services.
In September, Franklin shared a DM conversation in which a woman implied she couldn’t afford an Uber with the text overlay “Don’t date POOR women!!!” That same month, he uploaded a video of a client’s successful text exchange on Hinge where they talked about the need to “flirt over some margaritas.” In the clip, Franklin can barely contain himself, noting that it was the type of tête-à-tête that gets his “dick hard”: “This is what men are looking for. We lead, you follow.”
Franklin posts under the alias @DefundSimping, and has made it his mission to help straight, career-driven guys in their “post-breakup, post-divorce” era undo their “simp” behavior, which he defines as putting women on a pedestal or giving them too much attention.
I reached out to the 30-year-old content creator because I wanted to talk about Hinge’s decision to start testing screenshot protection in India. The announcement set off a firestorm of reaction across social media last week, rekindling a debate around digital etiquette, privacy, and shame.
“Everyone who’s downloaded the app has seen the debauchery and the drama,” Franklin says, explaining that being online in 2026 simply means there is a chance you will become the day’s main character whether you intended to or not. “People are aware that they could be the next haha moment, but that doesn't mean they deserve it.”
TikTokers, X accounts like @hingestrange, and other online creators have built entire brands out of screenshotting and sharing bizarre dating profile prompts, cringe pickup lines, or red flags found while swiping. But critics of the trend argue it’s a form of public humiliation that should end.
In response to news of Hinge revoking profile screenshotting ability in India, some responded with relief.
“People on here kinda turned being on a dating app into both an extension of the panopticon and a window into their own personal penchant for cruelty,” writer Tres Dean noted on X. “I actually think this might be the first ethical development in online dating in years if not ever.”
X user @randy_mossad added, “Better for a million cheaters to go unpunished than for one regular person looking for love to get humiliated by leaked chats.”
In a TikTok video, Florida-based creator Kiara said she understands the change despite having posted screenshots to shame men who were hypersexual or “super disrespectful” in their profiles. “But I’ve noticed now that we’re in an ‘I hate men’ apocalypse ... women are posting men’s profiles simply because they’re not just not attracted to them,” she continued, describing the latter as being “wrong” and “mean.”
At a moment when the apps feel broken for so many people, there seems to be a desire for more private, less performative forms of dating and communication.
While apps like Raya and Grindr already include screenshot protection, the India pilot is the first iteration of it for Hinge, which will block screenshots on surfaces containing personally identifiable profile information, including Discover, Likes You, and Standouts.
The company confirms to WIRED that testing in India is part of an initiative to help singles build trust among other users and with the platform. The insights will determine whether and how Hinge introduces the feature in additional markets, but there are no current plans to greenlight screenshot protection in US or other regions.
A 2025 study in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication suggested that screenshots create “privacy turbulence” by allowing a recipient to permanently store and redistribute private conversations without the original sender's knowledge or consent, noting that the screenshot feature eliminates a shared boundary of control and strips away context.
But for some women in particular, screenshotting profiles has become a necessary precaution when vetting potential suitors. “Privacy’s in tension with safety. Screenshots can document inappropriate behavior or allow someone to check in with a friend before meeting a stranger,” says Lizzie Li, a communications researcher, who adds that communities like Are We Dating the Same Guy? grew partly out of women sharing screenshots to address safety concerns.
Asked whether the company has an obligation to prevent users from having their profiles turned into public content—30 million people currently use the app—a Hinge spokesperson tells WIRED that screenshot protection, along with Comment Filter and Did This Bother You?, is “another way we’re exploring how to help daters control how and where personal details are shared.” Singles will still be able to screenshot their messages with other matches if they want to report an account for potential safety concerns, affording women an extra layer of defense on dating apps where they disproportionately experience harassment and privacy violations. According to Hinge’s community guidelines, harassment, bullying, and intimidation are prohibited.
“When you are a bystander, it is fairly obvious that a privacy violation is occurring and most people would not want it to happen to them. At the same time, discomfort has not stopped the behavior,” says Alexis Ingber, an assistant professor at Syracuse University whose research focuses on privacy and emerging tech. “Dating-profile dunking reflects a broader sense of entitlement to others’ data.”
But Franklin, who has a knack for speaking in clip-ready one-liners, doesn’t believe dating apps have a duty to protect users from becoming a punch line on social media. “If you enter the dragon’s den, you may get bit by the dragon,” he tells me.
Still, with 20 clients on his roster, he says he does his best to block “every name, lip, face, and eye, trying to keep people private” when posting screenshots, because he understands that people are “scared of getting hit-pieced.” Before ending our Zoom call to meet with another client, he tells me there is actually one way to completely sidestep the problem. “If you don’t want to be potentially doxed, just don’t get on a dating app. Go talk to a girl at a dog park. Go to a farmer's market. Do it the old-fashioned way.”

The Best Mac Desktop to Buy (2026): Mac Mini, Mac Studio, or iMac?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

MacBooks have taken most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.
But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.
Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.
The Best for Everyone: Mac Mini
Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.
The Mac Mini isn't the ultracheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.
The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.
I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.
Shipping times on the M6 Mac Mini have improved to the point where you can buy one and pick it up today from an Apple Store. The M5 Pro models, however, may take up to four weeks to ship.
Only for Pros: Mac Studio
Like with the Mac Mini, there are really two distinct versions of the Mac Studio. The base configuration comes with an M5 Max (the same chip in the MacBook Pro), sporting some really impressive GPU performance in particular. And that's the main thing to consider when deciding between the M5 Pro Mac Mini and the M5 Max Mac Studio. Like choosing between those two chips in a MacBook Pro, the main upgrade is in graphics performance. Going with the M5 Max also lets you configure it with up to 128 GB of unified memory, which matters if you plan to run heavy local AI models. On the other hand, this puts you over the $5,000 price point rather quickly.
And then, there's the M5 Ultra. This massive chip is literally two M5 Max dies stitched together, and to my surprise while testing, it sometimes resulted in double the performance, such as in GPU performance. But look, don't even bother considering this unless you know exactly what you intend to use it for. Just so you know what you're getting into, the model I tested had 256 GB of memory and cost over $11,000. You read that right. It's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk.
But I downloaded and started running on the M5 Ultra some of the largest and most powerful AI models I could find, and soon enough I had a foundation-tier LLM running completely on-device—no cloud needed. That means direct access to your computer for a powerful agentic AI to run wild with, all without the privacy and security concerns. Some simple agentic tests I ran on the M5 Ultra took minutes, whereas it took five times as long on my M5 Max MacBook Pro.
And while this thing is clearly not intended for gaming, I was pretty blown away by how fast games like Cyberpunk 2077 ran. I've definitely never seen games play this smoothly on a Mac before.
Unfortunately, shipping times on the Mac Studio are still dicey. If you want anything with 128 GB or more of memory, you'll be waiting up to a month and a half for the M5 Max models. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, will take up to four months to ship at this point.
Don't Buy the iMac Right Now
The iMac has been downplayed in recent years. The once-iconic all-in-one computer, which comes with the display, stand, and accessories, used to be an affordable go-to choice for students, families, businesses, and even content creators. But as Apple has shifted focus, the iMac seems less and less of a focus, with sporadic updates over the years. It hasn't been updated since 2024 and still uses the M4 chip.
It's not a bad computer, though. The screen is brilliant, and the performance is solid, even by today's standards. Its age, however, isn't reflected in the price you'd pay right now: $1,499 gets you 16 GB of RAM, 256 GB of storage, the M4 chip with an eight-core GPU, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a 4.5K IPS display. A second M4 model with a 10-core GPU and four Thunderbolt 4 ports starts at $1,699. (Like nearly all Apple products, the iMac got a price increase.)
The main issue for me is that there's currently only a 23.5-inch model, which is smaller than what most people will probably want. Until Apple releases a 27-inch model (as it has in the past), perhaps with an option for a “Pro” M-series chip, I can't see the iMac as a good choice for most people. The simplicity will be a draw, especially if researching and buying a separate monitor and peripherals sounds daunting.
Interestingly, it is also the only desktop-size Mac monitor that isn't at least 5K (it's 4.5K). So, while it's cheaper than buying a Studio Display paired with a new Mac Mini, the iMac also locks you into a one-time purchase you can't upgrade later. And as the focus on local AI only grows, I can't imagine the iMac regaining the relevance or attention it once had. On the plus side, it's the only Mac desktop available in seven colors.
At the very least, I hope it gets a refresh to the M6 in the next couple of months. It'll have been long overdue! Either way, now's not a good time to buy an iMac.
Why Is Everyone Buying a Mac Mini?
Before the launch of the M6 model, Mac Minis had been sold out for most of this year. Orders for Mac Studios were similarly backlogged for months before you could get one. The reason? Well, according to Apple on an earnings call, both computers are “amazing platforms for AI and agentic tools,” and that “customer adoption of that is happening faster than we expected.” In other words, they were caught off guard. AI frameworks released in 2026, such as OpenClaw, run best on a dedicated machine that never turns off and has lots of available RAM—such as a Mac Mini.
What Happened to the Mac Pro?
The last incarnation of the Mac Pro was one of Apple's most short-lived Macs. The most recent design was relaunched in 2019, alongside the Pro Display XDR. When it was unveiled, it was an exciting reentrance for the Mac, focusing not only on Pro-level performance but also on upgradability. Unlike the current Mac Studio, the Mac Pro had modular components you could swap in and out—or upgrade. The design was much more akin to a traditional tower PC. For a company that had been moving in the opposite direction for so long, it was a breath of fresh air.
But it wasn't meant to last, and it survived only a few upgrade cycles. With the advent of Apple silicon and the rapid scaling of these system-on-a-chip (SoC) designs, the Mac Pro's focus on modularity made less and less sense. Apple didn't officially discontinue the Mac Pro until March 2026, but by then it had been almost three years since the Mac Pro was last updated. The Mac Studio with the “Ultra” chips has since fully replaced the Mac Pro.
M6, M5 Pro, M5 Max, or M5 Ultra?
Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio have two configurations to choose from, which gives a clean delineation between the two in terms of performance. When you move from the base chip to the Pro and Max chips, the main differences are GPU cores and, in some cases, the maximum amount of RAM you can upgrade to. Certain applications and tasks benefit greatly from stronger GPU performance, speeding up things like video rendering, 3D modeling, gaming, and AI inferencing. These are the same chips that are available in the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.
The jump between the Max and Ultra chips, however, is much more significant. This is where you enter performance territory not possible on a MacBook. It has twice the CPU and GPU cores of the standard Max chips, delivers far stronger performance, and lets you configure it with up to 512 GB of unified memory.
The iMac is still holding onto the M4. For most people, the chip is more than capable, but considering the age and the price of the iMac today, it's outdated for a new machine.
Here's a list of the different Apple silicon available for the Mac Mini, Mac Studio, and iMac.
Mac Mini update history:
- Mac Mini (M6): 2026
- Mac Mini (M4): 2024
- Mac Mini (M2, M2 Pro): 2023
- Mac Mini (M1): 2020
Mac Studio update history:
- Mac Studio (M5 Max, M5 Ultra): 2026
- Mac Studio (M4 Max, M3 Ultra): 2025
- Mac Studio (M2 Max, M2 Ultra): 2023
- Mac Studio (M1 Max, M1 Ultra): 2022
iMac update history:
- iMac (M4): 2024
- iMac (M3): 2023
- iMac (M1): 2021

Montenegro detains founder of Rybar, one of Russia’s most popular pro-war Telegram channels. Here’s what we know.
Montenegrin authorities detained the creator of the Telegram channel Rybar. Mikhail Zvinchuk, his wife, and three other Rybar staffers were detained in the town of Risan on the morning of October 9. According to reporting by the local outlet Vijesti, they found “sophisticated digital equipment,” drones, and “electronic devices” on them. Montenegrin security services had been monitoring Zvinchuk and his team for several days. Media reports said the operation was aimed at “suppressing the hybrid activity” of the Rybar network of channels.
It remains unclear whether Zvinchuk has been charged with anything. Law enforcement agencies have not officially commented on the detention. Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić wrote on the social network X that the government does not intend to “voice what should remain within the competence of the security services.” “But the message after today’s successful operation, in which the head of the Rybar information network was detained, is absolutely clear: state institutions are doing their jobs, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future,” he said.
The next paragraph contains profanity.
Rybar confirmed the detention. A post on the Telegram channel emphasized that all those detained were in Montenegro legally and officially. “In particular, there were plans to film at Cetinje Monastery, for which an entirely official request had been submitted beforehand,” the post said. Rybar said it hoped for the detainees’ swift release, since “there were no violations of local law.” Zvinchuk’s presence in Montenegro was indeed public: the day before, he posted a video from there on his RuTube channel. On his Instagram, he wrote that he had gotten into Montenegro despite being under EU and UK sanctions: “You can always run into some fucking idiot of a border guard who empties out all your pockets but forgets to check the database.”
Russia has promised diplomatic support for those detained. “Our diplomats will look into the reasons for the detention and, as with every Russian citizen, work to protect his rights,” Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said. Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Russians “needlessly traipse around” European countries and called for Russia to form an “exchange fund” of Europeans and foreigners.
Rybar is one of the most popular Russian pro-war Telegram channels, with more than 1.5 million subscribers. Zvinchuk, a former press officer for Russia’s Defense Ministry, created it with his colleague Denis Shchukin. The channel launched in 2018, and businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin helped fund it in its early years. Rybar describes itself as a “military-analytical center” and runs a network of affiliated channels devoted to specific regions, including “Evropar,” “Afrikar,” and “Balkanar.” In 2024, the U.S. State Department announced a $10 million reward for information on Rybar staffers. According to the American agency, the channel had tried to interfere in the U.S. presidential election.
In September, the Czech Republic expelled two Russians working for Rybar. Vitaly Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov were detained after the local outlet Seznam Zprávy reported that Rybar representatives were working in Europe and routinely obtaining comments from politicians and experts. During questioning, they said they officially worked for the newspaper Izvestia, which has been under EU sanctions since 2024. Later, the independent Russian investigative outlet iStories found that Chashchukhin and Dolmatov hold residence permits in Germany and have lived for years in villas in the prestigious Berlin district of Zehlendorf.
Montenegro is preparing to join the EU in the near future. The country’s expected accession date is January 1, 2028, though the timeline could shift if Montenegro fails to make the necessary legislative changes in time. As part of its preparations, Montenegro is aligning its visa policy with EU rules and will introduce a visa regime on November 1 for citizens of certain third countries, including Russia. A report Zvinchuk had previously published addressed this topic, among other things: he discussed how a visa regime for Russian tourists would hurt Montenegro’s economy.

Türkiye's Akinci combat drone hits target in 1st test with domestic guidance kit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:59:33 UTC
19:59:33 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Türkiye's Akinci unmanned combat aerial vehicle successfully struck a target in its first firing test using the domestically developed Morfoz Guidance Kit (MGK), manufacturer Baykar announced Friday.
The test was conducted over the Gulf of Saros in the Aegean Sea as part of efforts to expand the aircraft's capabilities by integrating domestically developed systems and munitions, Baykar said in a statement.
Akinci took off from the Corlu Flight Training and Test Center in the northwestern province of Tekirdag carrying the MGK and the Alpagut munition, jointly developed by Turkish defense companies Roketsan and STM.
The aircraft scored a direct hit on the designated target using the guidance kit before returning to the center, according to Baykar.
The company said the MGK was developed by Turkish defense firm Aselsan entirely with domestic components.
The guidance kit joins a growing range of weapons integrated into Akinci, including the MAM series of precision-guided munitions, the Tolun munition family, the Cakir cruise missile and the Sungur air defense missile.
Other integrated weapons include the IHA-122, IHA-230 and IHA-300 supersonic missiles and the Eren high-speed multipurpose loitering munition.
Baykar said the different guidance systems, ranges and warhead options allow Akinci to conduct missions against various types of targets.
The company also said it had signed export agreements with 39 countries, including 36 for its Bayraktar TB2 combat drone and 16 for Akinci.

High-level officials from Ukraine and Europe have flown to Miami, Florida, to take part in a new round of peace negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion amid a new wave of escalation that has battered Ukrainian cities and killed scores of civilians.

Witkoff and Kushner's recent trips to Moscow and Kyiv will inform the deliberations.
Among those options is a targeted ceasefire, covering the Black Sea, a vital trade route for shipping grain to low-cost nations, and/or energy facilities, which Moscow has hit at a relentless pace. Kyiv has responded in kind, striking Russia's oil refineries.
"I'm not yet ready to say what might be realistic or more realistic. In principle, I understand, but I don't want to say anything, only for Russia, as always, to do the opposite just to be spiteful," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a voice note sent to journalists.
"Let's wait and see. We are seeing an intensification of talks and meetings on the part of the United States," he added.
"I myself have spoken three times in recent days with the American side and am hopeful for a positive outcome from the meeting between our negotiators."
Zelenskyy said his team would comprise Kyrylo Budanov and Sergiy Kyslytsya, head and deputy head of the president's office; Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the ruling party in the Parliament; and Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service.
They are expected to be back in Kyiv on Monday morning to brief the president.
"There are things we cannot talk about, but we must remain wise, united, and support our military. Peace is not achieved through grand statements – it's hard, collaborative work, and we’re working on it," Budanov said on social media ahead of the trip.
The European side will be represented by the national security advisors of the so-called E3: France, Germany and the United Kingdom. The three countries lead the "Coaltion of the Willing" to provide future security guarantees for Ukraine.
The European Commission will also take part, a spokesperson confirmed to Euronews. NATO has sent its chief of staff, Geoffrey van Leeuwen, an official said.
Russia will not participate.
The Miami meeting comes after several media reports suggested that Washington is exploring business deals with Moscow that could be signed even before a final peace deal is reached. The reports have alarmed Ukrainians and Europeans, who have long feared economic interests would trump diplomacy in the White House's vision.
Zelenskyy took exception after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the war was stuck in a "diplomatic stalemate" with risk of an escalatory spillover.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of diplomatic stalemate," he said as he visited the site of a Russian attack.
Zelenskyy also urged the US to expand the use of Starlink satellite service inside Russian territory to help Ukraine target ballistic-missile launchers.
European officials have actively engaged in the US-led process, arguing their security architecture is directly at stake. Following the cut-off of American aid, the continent is now the main provider of financial and military support for Ukraine.
However, scepticism over Moscow's intentions runs deep. The Kremlin has once again dismissed the possibility of a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level.
"We cannot have our vested hopes in (these talks) because we don’t see that Russia is ready at all to negotiate in good faith," a senior EU official said on Friday.
"But with stronger US pressure, hopefully, on Russia, and European influence over those talks, there is also a track that can lead to a partial ceasefire that Ukraine has been asking for and is ready to commit to."
Sasha Vakulina and Shona Murray contributed reporting.

More than 100 education staff have been injured since the start of nationwide high school protests in France, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Friday as students continued their blockades to demand better learning conditions.
“Unfortunately, yesterday brought us past the 100 mark for injured staff,” Geffray told reporters after meeting students and teachers at a high school in Cachan, near Paris, according to Le Parisien.
He condemned the “unspeakable violence” and praised staff who had protected students and school buildings.
A previous tally cited by the newspaper recorded injuries to 215 students and nearly 800 police officers and gendarmes since the movement began.

Students are protesting teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, inadequate facilities and school schedules.
Geffray said Friday that 3,024 substitute teachers were being contacted for deployment, with assignments expected later in the day or early next week. Additional contract teachers are also being recruited.
Student organizations nevertheless called for another day of demonstrations on Oct. 13, with some representatives seeking a meeting with France's Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu.
Blockades continued Friday in cities including Paris, Rennes and Strasbourg. Classes were canceled at Paris’ Lamartine school complex and during the morning at Pantheon-Assas University.
Separately, Paris prosecutors opened an investigation after a video circulated appearing to show a police officer kneeing a demonstrator in the face.

CFDT union leader Marylise Leon welcomed the teacher deployments as a first step but said students’ broader demands remained unresolved. She also questioned the proportionality of the police response.

Australia defeated Bangladesh by seven wickets to take a 1-0 lead in the ODI series in Brisbane.

What's next?
The series will continue on Sunday and then finish on Wednesday, with both the second and third ODIs also to be played at Allan Border Field.
A Phoebe Litchfield masterclass has ensured Australia remains undefeated in 22 ODIs at Allan Border Field after seamer Megan Schutt joined an elite club of bowling greats.
Opener Litchfield's 77 off 57 deliveries ensured Australia polished off the meagre 166 all out set by Bangladesh in just 25.4 overs for the loss of three wickets.
Litchfield combined ramps, glides, clips, exquisite drives, lofted pitching wedges, reverse hockey thumps and thunderous wallops in another knock that confirmed she is unique in world cricket and an absolute joy to watch.
The left-hander was unstoppable in racing to her 12th ODI half-century.
All-rounder Annabel Sutherland, player of the match, finished the chase with 26 not out after earlier taking four wickets.
Loading Twitter content
Australia pace bowler Schutt earlier snared her 150th ODI wicket in a probing opening spell to put the hosts on top.
Stand-in captain Tahlia McGrath invited the visitors to have first use of the surface and Schutt struck with the first ball of the innings, a vicious lifter that had opener Fargana Hoque edging to slip.
A Schutt inswinger trapped Sarmin Sultana (four) in front and from that moment the bowlers kept a vice-like grip on the run rate and picked up steady wickets to dismiss Bangladesh with the fourth ball of the final over.

Schutt finished with 2-19 from her 10 overs with medium pacer Sutherland (4-30) proving a handful when she hit the pitch hard.
Spinners Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham and Alana King bowled with class.

Veteran all-rounder Ritu Moni (45 off 63) showcased her experience and nous and was the best of a mediocre bunch.
Schutt has relished playing at AB Field throughout her career, where she now has 20 wickets.
The quick was initially left out of the ODI side in February against India before a quad injury to Kim Garth opened the door for a recall.
Schutt took 5-19 at AB Field on that occasion to provide a timely reminder of her talents.
McGrath, usually a vice-captain, has been elevated to lead due to injury to regular skipper Sophie Molineux and rotated her bowlers with panache.
The opener of three ODIs at the same venue, Friday's clash is the first match of the summer on home soil for Australia's victorious T20 World Cup side since lifting the trophy in July.

Labour fends off the Green party in closely watched UK by-election
Sagal Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the UK as child refugee from Somalia, won 3,300 more votes than Zack Polanski, leader of the Greens.
The Labour Party has won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer, fending off a challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister.
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader who came second.
The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was recently installed by lawmakers fearful that Starmer’s unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election.
After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result that triggered more questions about Polanski’s leadership.
There are now five Green MPs, compared with one in 2023.
But Polanski, 43, recently came under fire after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference.
The move, which called for “the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers. Polanski did not vote on the motion.
Labour has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983.
Labour’s Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the United Kingdom as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for “those who seek to divide us”.
“We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built and pass it on,” she said.
After conceding defeat, Polanski, who is not an MP, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of “Andy Burnham’s honeymoon”.
Polanski congratulated Abdi-Wali, but said, “One in three voters backed us here, and we know that many more considered it.”
Al Jazeera’s Sonia Gallego, reporting from London, said, “The constituency has been going through what some people have been calling ‘the Burnham bounce‘ … so far there is a deep sigh of relief (among Labour) that they’ve managed to hold on.”
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has changed voter habits during the past three years. The Greens, far more critical of Israel’s conduct than any other party, got a boost in the 2024 general election.
Back then, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein, a pro-Palestine independent candidate, came second, with 19 percent.
Polanski has raised the “progressive vote” while “reducing the Labour vote”, Feinstein said.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Porsche’s global vehicle deliveries fell 16% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, as a sharp decline in China compounded losses across its other sales regions, the German luxury carmaker said Friday.
The Volkswagen Group brand delivered 178,532 vehicles in January-September, down from 212,509 a year earlier.
Deliveries in China dropped 33% to 21,493 vehicles, the steepest regional decline.
Porsche described market conditions as challenging, saying it continued to prioritize the brand’s long-term development over short-term sales targets.
North America remained its largest market, with 56,088 deliveries, down 13%.
Porsche mainly attributed the decline to the end of 718 production and strong Macan Electric deliveries a year earlier.
Deliveries in Germany fell 7% to 20,954 vehicles, while sales in the rest of Europe dropped 11% to 44,949.
By model, the Cayenne remained Porsche's best-seller, with 59,586 deliveries, down 2% year on year.
The Macan followed with 51,025 vehicles delivered, a decline of 21%.
The iconic 911 sports car bucked the downward trend, recording a 12% increase to 42,217 deliveries as demand for exclusive, high-performance variants remained strong.

My Word: A hijacked world agenda - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:52:58 UTC
19:52:58 KST

If a “flydubai moment” hasn’t yet become a phrase, it should. There aren’t many incidents when the exact confluence of circumstances creates a miracle, but last week’s oh-so-Israeli, do-it-yourself rescue falls into that category. Talk about flying on a wing and a prayer.
Although details are still being released, it is now well known that on September 30, a radicalized Omani co-pilot on FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv attacked the Indian captain using the cockpit’s emergency ax, with the intent of crashing the plane with nearly 180 people on board, most of them Israeli. His plans were thwarted when Israeli passengers sprang into action and improvised, the way Israelis do.
The heroic Captain Smit Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door; Tali Manes, a mother taking her young daughter to the bathroom, heard the commotion in the cabin and managed to shake the flight crew into action.
Meanwhile, Israeli guys took command of the situation – tackling the terrorist and using in-flight headphone cables to restrain him. Among the heroes were Tali’s husband, finance executive Zvi Manes; insurance agent Assaf Rajuan, and dentist Dr. Shota Musaye, who treated the badly wounded captain.
Plumber Yaniv Hayoun earned his 15-minutes of global fame and eternal Israeli gratitude by grabbing the control sticks to pull the plane out of a nosedive, as he had seen on the TV aviation disaster series Mayday, and the reserve cabin crew managed to safely land the damaged plane in Saudi Arabia.
There, the traumatized passengers were, by all accounts, treated well, before they were evacuated to Tel Aviv, where on landing they sang “Am Yisrael Chai!” (The People of Israel Live!). Even secular Jews recited “Birkat Hagomel,” the blessing on surviving danger.
It was a cross between an improbable episode of the two TV hit series Fauda and Tehran. What could have been an Israeli 9/11 – just ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas invasion and mega-atrocity – was averted by a matter of seconds.
I was reminded of Hatikvah 6’s popular song “Am Shel Giborei Al” about the ordinary Israelis from all walks of life who turned up for IDF reserve duty after October 7: “True, everyone looks normal, but we are a nation of superheroes, and within each one hides a soldier ready to save the world.”
The near-disaster, of course, raises many questions. Attention focused on how Hamam al-Hammami – who had an Omani father and Syrian mother, displayed openly jihadist sympathies, and had been kicked out of airlines in Oman and Morocco – was flying a plane for the United Arab Emirates, let alone a jetliner with Tel Aviv as its destination.
Under UAE-Israel agreements following the Abraham Accords, pilots on this route are meant to be nationals of countries with which Israel has diplomatic relations.
While there are meant to be checks of the passenger and flight crew lists (partly under the auspices of the Tax Authority), I’ve long been more concerned with the harder-to-detect terrorist threat from baggage handlers and other airport staff abroad.
Qatari and Iranian influence
Entire University campuses, professional organizations, NGOs, and government offices are being hijacked, partly financed and fueled by Qatari and Iranian influence. Israel has become the central issue on the agenda, even in local politics.
Across the globe, October 7 events have been perversely turned into vigils and rallies to support Gaza – from where the Hamas perpetrators invaded and murdered 1,200, and where they held 251 hostages in homes and terror tunnels. According to a report by the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry, at least 262 pro-Palestinian events were scheduled in 37 countries in the first half of October.
In the Netherlands, where a law was recently passed banning products from “The Occupied Territories” – including Judea, Samaria, the Golan Heights, and east Jerusalem – the luggage of passengers arriving on flights from Tel Aviv is subjected to a rigorous search to confiscate any illegal products.
Perish the thought that Israeli dates from the Jordan Valley, wine from the Golan, or Dead Sea cosmetics from the (Chinese-owned) AHAVA company should taint Dutch soil. One can only pray that the local airport staff is as vigilant in preventing terrorist threats.
In the UK, the US air force has removed its bomber planes from the RAF Fairford base in Gloucestershire following the arrest in London of a British-Iranian citizen allegedly plotting a terror attack. Altogether, six people reportedly have been detained (and released on bail) following an incident in September when an alert farmer spotted trucks and masked men near the base.
This is definitely not Britain’s “finest hour” in Churchill’s immortal words. Current British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Minister Ed Miliband have a hostile approach to the Jewish state.
Following the latest declaration of UK sanctions last month, Israel announced the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem. This would leave open the embassy in Tel Aviv but closes the Jerusalem facility, which extraordinarily handles only Arabs, not Jews, and serves as the de facto embassy to the Palestinian Authority.
Britain is reportedly threatening to retaliate by expelling 27 Israeli diplomats, thus further escalating the tension (and probably boosting already high antisemitism).
Even though the British sanctions (similar to the Dutch ones) have yet to come into force, there were reports last month of staff at London’s Luton airport pulling aside some Israeli passengers for an added search – as if Israelis were the threat and not the frontline fighting global jihad.
On Sunday, Britain marked the 90th anniversary of “The Battle of Cable Street,” the clash between Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts and anti-fascist demonstrators, who refused to let them pass through the heavily Jewish area of the East End of London. Today the fascist forces have joined with the far-Left and Islamists in an unholy alliance against the Jews.
As Nicole Lampert wrote in The Telegraph, “[This week]… there were two demonstrations for Cable Street. A real one and a fake one. One filled with Jews and allies who sang: ‘Ninety years on, we are still here.’ At the front were people whose parents and grandparents had been at the first battle…
“The other demo was filled with people who looked to be as obsessed with Jews as Oswald Mosley and his fascists were.”
Covering this second demonstration as a journalist, Lampert was accosted for being “a Zio.” She described the distressing experience as “a microcosm of what has been happening to Diaspora Jews since the October 7 attacks three years ago – the taunts, the hatred, the violence.”
Meanwhile, at the annual conference of the Green Party of England and Wales, a motion defining Zionism as “racism” passed by a large majority (although only a fraction of the membership participated in the vote).
The motion calls Israel “colonialist” and supports replacing it with a Palestinian state, with Jerusalem as its capital. Jewish national self-determination, unlike Palestinian nationalism, is strictly “Verboten.”
Green Party members can now be “disciplined” for being members of synagogues. Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is nominally Jewish but a strident opponent of Israel, was not present for the vote.
Elsewhere, the violent riots that started in Paris neighborhoods that are heavily populated by immigrants – ostensibly over conditions in high schools – have spread beyond the capital and even beyond French borders. Here, too, a theoretically domestic issue has become wrapped in the keffiyehs of both the far-Left and Islamists.
In Spain, socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has taken the country on a virulently anti-Israel and pro-mass immigration course, was forced this week to call snap elections. It remains to be seen whether Sanchez, beset by a series of scandals, can return to the cockpit or whether safer hands will take over the controls.
As Douglas Murray summed up in The Free Press on September 30: “What happened in the skies above Saudi Arabia on Wednesday morning stands as a metaphor for three years of war.
“The Israelis saw an existential threat, took matters into their own hands, and decided their own course. The rest of the West will have to decide whether it will follow the Israeli model or let its own future be dictated by terror and the hijacking of its entire society.”
We can’t count on miracles, but we can count our blessings, and we can stand up and be counted.

Motives behind US AI companies’ calls to slow development questioned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:52:42 UTC
19:52:42 KST

Calls by leading US artificial intelligence companies to slow the development of increasingly powerful systems have prompted questions about whether safety is their only concern or whether commercial and strategic interests are also driving the debate.
Advanced AI models have raised genuine fears about systems escaping human control, acting unpredictably and being used in cyberattacks. Critics, however, argue that companies already dominating the sector could use safety standards to preserve their market position, limit competition and consolidate US technological power.
The debate is therefore not simply about whether AI development should accelerate or slow. It also concerns who sets safety standards, how those rules affect competition and whether the massive investments in AI will deliver the expected returns.
Could safety rules protect market leaders?
An OECD analysis published on June 24 found that parts of the AI market were concentrated, noting that early movers and vertically integrated companies enjoy significant advantages.
Control over essential resources, including advanced chips, computing infrastructure, data and cloud services, could reinforce the power of companies already leading the industry.
Critics have consequently warned that industry-wide agreements to slow development or impose costly safety requirements could function as a “soft cartel,” making it harder for smaller companies to enter the market.
A Forbes analysis published on Sept. 15 argued that common safety rules could create new barriers for competitors while strengthening established AI companies.
Julia Cartwright of the American Institute for Economic Research similarly told Fox Business on Sept. 25 that regulation could increase the costs of entering the market and protect incumbent firms. She also warned of a collective-action problem if US companies restrict themselves while Chinese competitors continue developing AI without equivalent limitations.
A Congressional Research Service analysis published on Sept. 28 noted that some commentators believe coordinated slowdown proposals could reduce capital expenditures, improve profitability and support company valuations.
Aashis Luitel, an associate professor at the University of the Cumberlands, said the commercial dimension of the safety debate should not be overlooked. Shared standards could reinforce the positions of current market leaders and place greater pressure on lower-cost Chinese competitors, he said.
Nikhil Naren, an associate professor at Jindal Global Law School in India, said safety concerns could not be completely separated from commercial and strategic interests.
Safety may provide the reason to apply the brakes, he said, but competition determines how firmly companies can press them.
AI investment boom fuels bubble concerns
Another dimension of the slowdown debate is whether companies need time to generate returns on the enormous sums invested in AI.
Goldman Sachs expects global AI investment to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, including about $581 billion in the US.
Research published by the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School on Sept. 1 estimated that major technology companies’ AI infrastructure spending could reach about $755 billion in 2026 and surpass $1 trillion in 2027.
The study said productivity gains from AI would need to rise substantially for investment on that scale to generate sufficient returns.
US investor Michael Burry has argued that calls by OpenAI and Anthropic executives to slow AI development may benefit the companies themselves, particularly as competitors narrow the technological gap and the firms prepare for potential public offerings.
Burry also suggested that safety rhetoric could mask a more fundamental slowdown caused by the increasing difficulty of maintaining rapid growth.
Other prominent investors have warned of a possible AI bubble. Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio said in January that the boom appeared to be in the early stages of a bubble, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has acknowledged that investors may be overly enthusiastic about the technology.
Safety concerns remain real
The controversy intensified after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay on Sept. 12 calling for AI development to proceed at a more measured and controlled pace.
Amodei argued that coordinated development could allow time to study increasingly capable systems, conduct safety tests and build safeguards before more advanced models are released.
Some technology executives and political figures have opposed slowing development, warning that it could strengthen China and restrict innovation.
The Trump administration has favored rapid AI development rather than additional regulation. US President Donald Trump has described fears of AI escaping human control as part of a “sick conspiracy” and argued that slowing US progress would benefit China.
The dispute is now centered less on whether safeguards are necessary than on who designs them and whether they primarily protect the public or the companies already leading the AI race.

Swiss queer film festival removes award-winning Israeli movie from lineup after boycott threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:52:34 UTC
19:52:34 KST

In a particularly ironic incident in the ongoing de facto international boycott of Israeli culture in many quarters, Moshe Rosenthal’s Ophir Award-winning movie, Tell Me Everything, has been disinvited from a Swiss queer film festival that goes by the name "Everyone’s Perfect," following threats from local organizations, including a Palestinian film festival, Variety reported on Thursday.
The Geneva-based festival, which opens on October 9, had previously included Tell Me Everything, a drama about a boy who discovers his father is gay at the height of the AIDS epidemic, in its lineup.
Tell Me Everything had its world premiere this year at the Sundance Film Festival and is Israel’s official selection for consideration for Best International Feature Film Oscar. It recently won 10 Ophir Awards and received a record 16 nominations. In September, it acquired international distributors that will bring it to Europe, Australia, and other countries. Critics around the world have praised it as a powerful coming-of-age film that deals with the issue of discrimination against gay men.
Palestinian film festival pushes boycott over Israeli film
But all of these achievements were not enough to make the Everyone’s Perfect festival stand by the movie when it was threatened with a boycott. Variety reported that Charlotte Sector, the festival’s communications spokesperson, said the festival received threats the previous week from the festival Palestine Filmer C’est Exister, which is also held in Geneva.
“They started writing messages like ‘We’re going to boycott your festival’ - boycott, boycott, just boycott. When people mention boycotting a festival that is a very big threat,” she said.
Variety reported that other groups joined the Palestinian festival in threatening a boycott. Although Sector acknowledged that she admired the film, the festival asked Rosenthal and the producers for a statement on the current political situation, although the film takes place in the 1980s and 1990s.
In a statement to Variety, the producers of the film said, “A film does not represent a government, and filmmakers should not be held responsible for its policies. Many of us in Israel oppose the war and are deeply critical of our government. Tell Me Everything is a human story about love, family, identity, and healing. We made it to create connection and conversation, not to represent a government. Would Iranian or American filmmakers be asked to make similar declarations about their governments before their films could be shown? We care deeply about being part of an international film community where difficult questions and different perspectives can exist. Festivals should make room for that connection and conversation - not exclude artists because of where they come from.”
But Everyone’s Perfect chose to do just that – exclude the film because of where Rosenthal is from and where it is set. Everyone may be perfect in the eyes of the organizers of this festival, but to paraphrase the famous line from George Orwell’s Animal Farm, some people turn out to be more perfect than others.
Israeli film excluded out of desire to avoid controversy
According to a Swiss newspaper report quoted by Variety, Sylvie Cachin, the festival’s artistic director, said: “The cancellation isn’t related to the film itself, but to the desire to avoid controversy just days before the festival’s opening.”
This is an interesting statement, and one that is revealing of the current climate in the cultural world, because in the past, film festivals were places that welcomed a diversity of opinion and sought to foster debate. Now, the specter of controversy is enough to get a film banned - rather than welcomed - and a festival director has admitted that openly.
In a similar case, Nadav Lapid, the most critical of the Israeli government of all Israeli directors, was disinvited from the jury of FID Marseille Film Festival and screenings of his movies were cancelled in June.
Sector was quoted by Variety as saying about the decision to boot Tell Me Everything: “It was a way of saying we’re all coming together, we need to come together.” That the way for “all” to “come together” is by excluding an Israeli movie is an irony that Sector and her colleagues do not seem to register. Some people are simply too evil to be included these days, in the eyes of much of the international film community, and these people are called Israelis.

Ten of Israel's leading law firms raised NIS 172,000 (approximately $57,000) to provide hot meals to residents of northern Israel, where communities continue to recover from the damage and displacement caused by the war with Hezbollah.
The funds were raised during the fifth annual DLA Piper Israel Charity Basketball Tournament, held at the Hashalom Sport Center in Tel Aviv, with proceeds going to Leket Israel, the country's national food bank.
The tournament brought together lawyers from some of Israel's largest firms, exchanging their courtrooms for a basketball court to support families struggling to rebuild their lives.
"The north absorbed more than its share, and long after the headlines moved on, families there are still putting their lives back together," said Jeremy Lustman, managing partner of DLA Piper Israel.
"A hot meal, every day, is one of the most concrete forms of support we can offer."
The tournament has raised more than NIS 670,000 ($220,000) for charitable causes over the past five years, according to the organizers.
Supporting Israel's northern communities
The latest fundraising effort focused on the continuing needs of northern Israeli residents, many of whom were forced to leave their homes following Hezbollah's attacks that began after October 7, 2023.
Although residents have been returning to communities along the Lebanese border, the region continues to face economic and social challenges as families and businesses work to recover from the prolonged fighting.
Leket Israel's hot meals program provides prepared, nutritious food to people in need, while reducing food waste by rescuing surplus meals that would otherwise be discarded.
"Food rescue is not charity. It is national infrastructure," said Gidi Kroch, CEO of Leket Israel.
"Every shekel donated here becomes a hot, nutritious meal on a table in the north, while preventing perfectly good food from being destroyed."
Founded in 2003 by Joseph Gitler, Leket Israel distributes rescued food through a network of more than 360 nonprofit organizations, reaching approximately 470,000 people in need each week, according to the organization.
In 2025, it rescued more than 2.24 million cooked meals and over 32 million servings of fruit and vegetables.
Meitar takes home the trophy
On the basketball court, Meitar emerged as the tournament champion after defeating Arnon, Tadmor-Levy in the final.
Meitar attorney Orpaz Azoulay was named the tournament's most valuable player.
The participating firms included Amit, Pollak, Matalon & Co.; Arnon, Tadmor-Levy; FBC & Co.; Furth, Wilensky, Mizrachi, Knaani; Goldfarb Gross Seligman; Gornitzky; Herzog Fox & Neeman; Meitar; S. Horowitz & Co.; and Shibolet & Co.
The event was organized by DLA Piper Israel, the Israeli arm of the international law firm, which operates in more than 40 countries.
