Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:51:54 UTC
19:51:54 KST

Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
South African jurist and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay was on Friday announced as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
She was honoured “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement.
The committee said the award was going “to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order,” noting that she “has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.”
Fighting hate, defending civilians
Ms. Pillay served as the UN human rights chief from September 2008 through August 2014, but her career has spanned more than 50 years - from fighting apartheid in her homeland to defending civilians in conflict zones.
She is a former chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and was appointed a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, in addition to serving as an ad hoc judge with the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's highest court.
“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the Nobel Committee said.
An ‘independent voice of justice’: Guterres
In a statement congratulating the new Nobel laureate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Ms. Pillay has shown “that the force of law must prevail over the law of force and that defending human rights is the surest safeguard against injustice.”
He hailed her as “a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice”, adding that “in its citation, the Nobel Committee reminded the world that peace must be built on lasting principles, not the will of the powerful."
A lifelong champion of human rights
Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was born in South Africa in 1941 to a Tamil Indian family and was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country.
As a lawyer, she acted as a defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists, exposing torture, and helping to establish key rights for prisoners on notorious Robben Island.
In her role as chair of the Independent International Commission, which is appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, she oversaw its 2025 report that said Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip constituted genocide.
Listen back to our interview with Ms. Pillay on the commission's report:
Human rights reaffirmed: Türk
On receiving the news of Ms. Pillay's honour, the current UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warmly congratulated the woman he described as a big sister.
“To say it is well deserved is a total understatement, and especially at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power, this award is particularly poignant,” he said, speaking in Geneva.
“It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security.”
Moreover, it is “a recognition, a reaffirmation, that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything - to peace, to security and prosperity,” he added.
Belief in international solidarity
In an October 2025 interview with UN News in Geneva, Ms. Pillay reflected on her lifetime of fighting for human rights, justice and equality.
“I didn't think apartheid would end in my lifetime,” she recalled. “So, what happened? We had the collective support of people all over the world, even children. If we can achieve that, we can have a better human rights protection system.”
Her experience in the anti-apartheid struggle shaped her belief in international solidarity, which she carried into her role as a judge and president of the ITCR, which prosecuted persons responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
During her eight years there, she helped establish groundbreaking legal precedents in the fight against genocide and gender-based violence.
As UN human rights chief, Ms. Pillay continued to champion the participation of civil society and victims’ voices in shaping global human rights standards.
“When the UN started, it was just a club for the States,” she told UN News. “Everything we have today for human rights protection didn’t happen just because the States woke up one day. It comes from the pressure of civil society. That’s why I value these institutions.”

The Meaning of It All: Ultimate Meaning, Everyday Meaning, Cosmic Meaning, Death, and Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:50:00 UTC
19:50:00 KST

Isaiah Berlin explained his move from philosophy to the history of ideas through the desire to know more at the end of his career than at the beginning. He was mistaken: philosophy often makes demonstrable progress. Focusing on our context, this is also the Golden Age of analytic exploration of the issue of the meaning of, or in, life. Without depreciating the value of the insights of the ages on this topic from Ecclesiastes onward, a great deal of progress has been made on it in the last generation. Rivka Weinberg’s splendid new book, The Meaning of It All, takes this progress considerably further in a number of important ways. Anyone reading Weinberg’s book will know and understand more about the meaning of life at the end of this book than they did at the beginning. Moreover, readers are doubly fortunate, because she accomplishes this in a relatively short, fast-moving, well-written, irreverent, personal, and entertaining book.
The book has an introduction and five chapters. The introduction does its introductory work, but also presents a significant conceptual contribution, a typology of meaning-related concepts. The kinds of meaning Weinberg suggests are Ultimate Meaning (UM), Everyday Meaning (EM), and Cosmic Meaning (CM), and we shall get to know them below. The characteristics of meaning are value, significance, impact, explanation, purpose, and point (xii). These distinctions are genuine innovations which significantly advance the discussion. Even those who doubt her further suggestions on life and its meaning will need to speak from now on more or less in these terms, at least as to what she calls the characteristics of meaning. This should help to make the whole debate more accurate, subtle, and sophisticated.
Beyond this conceptual contribution the book includes two ambitious moves, the “narrowing of focus” on meaning, in Chapters 1-3, and the depreciation of death and emphasis on time instead, in Chapters 4-5. In the first, Weinberg decisively argues that there is no Ultimate Meaning. Further, Cosmic Meaning is rather dubious and questionable, probably not even worth fussing about, so that even if we can make sense of some views within it, CM will not add much life to the meaning of life. This then leaves us with Everyday Meaning, which becomes, she claims, the proper locus of our endeavor for meaning. Many interesting philosophical and practical questions remain to be debated even then, but Weinberg’s discussion takes the Meaning of It All away from the majestic aspirations of ultimacy, the grand scheme of things, the view from nowhere, God, or the cosmos, to the mundane issues of taking care of our children and deciding whether to take up painting.
Unlike the Everyday and Cosmic varieties, where conceptual awareness of the plurality of the potential characteristics, and clarity as to their contextual relevance and interconnections, are crucial, Ultimate Meaning raises, according to Weinberg, only one question: does living have a point? Within our lives, our endeavors can have a point, but what is the point of living itself? This she says, is “metaphysically impossible” (68). Here I was not convinced, and inclined to try and keep UM alive. One way would be to modify the UM question. But even sticking to Weinberg’s conceptual use of the term, it wasn’t clear to me why UM is impossible. Is it that one cannot have UM of one’s life because one necessarily lives within life, and there is no way of being as it were both in and out? I was reminded here of Zeno’s movement-denying Arrow, which cannot move because clearly it can move neither within the space it occupies (no room for movement!) nor out of it (it’s never there!). But this isn’t correct (I just went to the fridge to get a drink).
Meaning seems mostly to be about value. Why cannot the UM be to partake in value? Luckily, we can do so, and that’s the point. What’s the point of that point, i.e., of doing so? Well, it has value. It’s valuable. One engages with, experiences, is enhanced by, contributes to, reacts to, and gains value. That seems to me an excellent point to life. Berlin would often approvingly quote Herzen, who said that the purpose of life is to live it. The ultimate point of life is to live, because (in addition to other benefits) this allows one to engage with value, and this has value, and makes one’s life valuable. What more could one want? Indeed, if we could miraculously bring ourselves to be conceived, it would make sense to do this both because we would thereby live, hopefully enjoy life, and gain Everyday Meaning, and because being such a being would have a value-based point, we would also gain Ultimate Meaning. The ability to engage with value provides the point of what Weinberg calls the meta-project of leading or running a life.
For example, in Chapter 10 of my recent book Paradoxical Ethics, I explain why opting, in one’s job or position, for making irreplaceable contributions can add value and thereby meaning to and in one’s life. One does this either by making the sort of contribution that would otherwise not be made, or by making the given contribution better than one’s likely replacement would. Such a consideration would of course fall under Weinberg’s Everyday Meaning, but why does it not generate Ultimate Meaning as well? After all, in irreplaceable contributions, one’s role in the world includes a gap that would not be filled except for oneself. Value provides the point of living, and one’s contribution adds unique value to the world. Weinberg, for example, has gained Ultimate Value by adding to the world a valuable book that would otherwise not have existed.
On Cosmic Meaning, Weinberg’s discussion often reminded me of Hume’s writing, when, for example, he makes fun of religious claims about miracles, or of the pursuit of the “monkish virtues”. CM, she shows, is much overrated. We repeatedly see how her diverse distinctions (significance, impact, explanation, purpose, etc.) are helpful. She is particularly effective when employing them while exploring the suggested “happy endings” of life; for example, exploring the idea of partaking in divine bliss or in a life of contemplation, in terms of purpose and value.
Relating usually involves actions, sentiments, and attitudes. So if our cosmic purpose is communion [with God], what happens when we achieve it? Do we just bask in its glow, sizzle in its warmth? As with happiness, that emotional state of feeling closeness does not, by itself, seem very meaningful. (76)
As she shows, “It’s not easy to imagine an end that provides a significantly meaningful, positive, and sensible explanation of the universe, no matter how much magic sauce we allow into the mix” (104).
The action largely lies, then, according to Weinberg, in Everyday Meaning. There is a sharp discussion of the objective-subjective question concerning meaning in life, and Weinberg rejects both subjectivism and Susan Wolf’s hybridism. Weinberg plausibly argues that objective meaning suffices in order to have a meaningful life, since we can mistakenly underestimate the actual, objective meaning of our own lives, but it would still be there. I particularly liked the discussions about the potential for meaning (both of humans as such and that of individual persons), about the risks of missing it, and about the great inequality in the Everyday Meaning of people’s lives. Weinberg is always on the lookout for cant and is excellent in not allowing the typical (perhaps especially common in the US) attempts to put a redeeming, positive gloss on the bad aspects of life (e.g., failure; see 62).
A large and venerable list of people, including Heidegger, Nussbaum, Sartre, Scheffler, Tolstoy, and Williams have sung the praises of death as enabling us to have meaning in life. Weinberg goes over the diverse arguments and convincingly finds them lacking. Eternal life could be just fine. Life under these conditions could still involve great risks of suffering or loss, and allow for achievement and purpose, even if never ending. Boredom need not ensue. Death is unnecessary.
What mostly matters for Everyday Meaning is not death, but time. There is too much of interest here to discuss, but just by way of illustration, Weinberg brings out the weakness and dangers of the “focus on the present”, a favorite of much popular psychology, as well as of the Stoics, and of followers of the Buddha. As she writes, “If you are interested in meaning this is extremely terrible advice” (154). Rather, her advice is: “Fully appreciating the past, experiencing the present, and anticipating the future” (161). She shows how value requires taking time, for example with love (155). Once again, the wealth of salient concepts—such as impact, significance, purpose, coherence, explanation—helps the reader to see this. They all require that we go beyond the present. Yet, now looking in the negative direction, it is again time, and not so much death, that threatens meaning, by wearing away the things we worked to achieve, thereby diminishing their impact, significance, and value.
The Meaning of It All is a magnificent book and an important contribution to our understanding both of the meaning of life and of the possibilities for living meaningful lives. The book will provide the conceptual Gold Standard for the distinct questions which need to be asked concerning the kinds of meaning (Ultimate, Cosmic, and Everyday) and, in particular, what Weinberg calls the characteristics of meaning. The book challenges other philosophers to try to make sense of Ultimate Meaning—for, Weinberg argues, this is simply impossible. The book also redraws the terrain of the debate concerning Cosmic Meaning, taking up the various religious and cosmological offers for CM, and finding them vague and unappetizing, when not completely senseless. Weinberg has many fascinating and wise things to say about Everyday Meaning, both philosophically and pragmatically. Her discussion here connects to her strategic depreciation of death and her emphasis on the crucial importance of time in seeking meaning in our lives. Throughout, she strikes a good balance between the critical puncturing of claims in an area that seems to invite pretentious nonsense, and awareness of the importance and value of thinking constructively and thereby assisting people’s efforts to make something meaningful of their lives in a tragic world. Anyone who wishes to see what the best kind of subtle, sensible, and courageous philosophical work has to say about The Meaning of It All must read this outstanding book. But take care to do so while you still have plenty of time left.

For some, IUD placement is painful. Does it have to be?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:49:01 UTC
19:49:01 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Intrauterine devices, more commonly known as IUDs, are some of the most effective forms of birth control options available. These small, T-shaped devices are placed directly into the uterus by way of the cervix, where they’re more than 99 percent effective at preventing pregnancy for years at a time. And copper IUDs, which rely on copper ions instead of hormones to limit sperm movement and egg fertilization, are also more than 99 percent effective as emergency contraception if placed within five days of unprotected sex.
But while IUDs are a set-it-and-forget-it solution, they do require a visit to the doctor for placement and eventual removal—and that process can be uncomfortable or even quite painful. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention now recommends that doctors counsel patients on pain medication options before an IUD insertion, but there’s not a lot of data out there about effective treatments. Options offered can include local anesthetic creams or injections directly to the cervix, conscious sedation or even full anesthesia—but there’s no real consensus on which intervention to use or how helpful some of them might be.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Today’s guest is the author of a recent study on a new method for mitigating the potential pain of IUD insertion. Helena Kopp Kallner is a professor at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden and senior consultant in obstetrics and gynecology at the Danderyd Hospital.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Helena Kopp Kallner: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: So you recently published a study on IUD insertion, but before we get into the research itself, I would love to give our listeners a little bit of context about IUDs. So could you tell us a little bit about what makes them such a great birth control option, but also what, you know, the potential downsides are that might keep some patients from getting them?
Kopp Kallner: So the very big upside with intrauterine contraception or IUDs is that they are user independent. So that means that you don’t have to think about taking something daily, weekly, monthly, or every three months. So it’s a type of fit-and-forget contraception, as we call it. That means that you have it placed, and then you don’t have to think about it. And, for some IUDs now, you can actually use them for up to eight or 10 years.
They’re also very, very effective, so perfect for young and highly fertile women who don’t wanna become pregnant just now. And for the hormonal IUDs, there’s also an upside with, like, reduction in menstrual flow, so you don’t bleed so much, and also reduction in menstrual pain. So those are the major upsides. But then the downside is that they can be painful to have fitted.
Feltman: Hmm. So tell me about, uh, how your new study came about?
Kopp Kallner: Well, actually, this has been quite a long process, as it usually is with clinical trials. But this was actually an idea that I had myself as I was fitting a lot of IUDs for very young women because I see a lot of very young women in my clinic with a lot of menstrual pain, and they are autistic, and they have lots of different issues. And I was just thinking that I needed to find something simple, so just like, “Okay, why don’t I just, like, inject some, local anesthetic through this, like, very, very thin catheter?” And then I was like, “Okay, now I have to do a study,” because I, I felt it worked. But then we started using a lower concentration of the same substance that we have been using now, and we did the pilot trial with around 80 patients. And then we got, like, near significance, and it was so annoying. And then we planned a larger study, so that’s what we have done now, and then we used a higher concentration of the local anesthetic. And it turned out that it, it works.
Feltman: So, prior to you trying this method, what pain relief and mitigation options were available to people getting IUDs inserted?
Kopp Kallner: I think the most common method still worldwide is just the use of anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen and paracetamol that you take before the IUD insertion, although there are so many trials that have shown that this is not effective.
It works fine for pain after the placement or insertion, but not prophylactically. I think the second most common method is probably to use what we call a paracervical block. So that’s an injection with local anesthetic into the tissue with a needle, which is given on both sides of the cervix and then numbs the cervix and the uterus. But it has also been shown in studies that that method in itself is painful. So usually gynecologists and midwives are a bit reluctant to use that method because they feel that in a lot of patients you actually cause more pain with what’s supposed to cure the pain than what actually causes the pain. We only use it for those who really feel they need it or where we really feel like this is going to be painful.
Feltman: Right. Well, and, it’s occurring to me, I’m, unfortunately intimately familiar with why IUD insertion is painful. But, for people listening who have never had an IUD, could you walk us through what the process of insertion actually is, and, and why there is so much opportunity for discomfort and even pain?
Kopp Kallner: Well, I mean, the highest scientific standard of insertion of an IUD is to use, first of all, you use a speculum. That speculum, it visualizes the cervix because the IUD has to be inserted through the cervix into the uterus. So you visualize the cervix, and in some places you also clean the cervix. We don’t do that much in Europe, but in the U.S. it’s usually done, with an antiseptic. And then because the uterus is actually a curved organ, and you’re going to insert something straight into a curved organ, so you have to straighten it out. And, I think a lot of people have a lot of fear of the straightening process because usually that’s done with a so-called tenaculum. And the tenaculum is a very evil-looking kind of instrument with two claws that you, sort of, put onto the cervix. And for some women they don’t feel a thing. It’s not painful. And for others, this is very painful.
And then after that, usually, you use a so-called sound, which is also a, kind of, a straight instrument, and you use that to measure the length of the cervix and the uterus so that you are sure that you put the IUD up into, like, the bottom of the uterus. And that can also be painful. So you put the sound into the uterus, and then after that you do the IUD insertion.
And the IUD insertion has basically three painful parts of it. First of all is when you put the IUD insertion tube through what’s called the inner os. That’s the upper part of the cervix, and that is a very pain-sensitive part of the uterus.
And then, uh, you release the arms of the IUD. So that means that the arms, they’re folded in into the insertion tube, and then when you release the arms, that can also be painful because the IUD suddenly becomes bigger, so it sort of distends the uterine cavity a bit. And that can also be painful.
And then there is the final part of it, and that is when you actually push those arms that you’ve just distended, you push them up into the top of the uterus. Now, all of this, it sounds like it takes a lot of time because I’m, I’m speaking slow. But this is a really fast process. So all in all, from the very start to the very finish, if you have a good provider, this is going to take, like, less than a minute total. But it can be a very painful minute.
Feltman: Right. And it, it seems like for a procedure that’s so common and that potentially causes so much discomfort and frightens people, there aren’t many options, certainly not options that are easy and worthwhile for providers to implement to deal with that pain. Why do you think there’s that gap?
Kopp Kallner: So first of all, I think that the, the pain has largely been ignored because it’s a very short-lasting pain in most instances. And secondly, it’s only until the few last years that we have really been starting to insert a lot of IUDs in women who have not had children before.
And we know that women who have had children, especially who have given birth vaginally, that they have less pain than those who never have. And IUDs have traditionally been used for women who have completed their family. But now we inserted a lot of them in the very young for the obvious reasons that I stated in the beginning, that it’s a very effective method and long-lasting, so it’s very suitable for young women.
And that, of course, has also brought this pain issue more to the attention of providers and women. So I think that there has been a lack of research, and recently there have been a lot of trials investigating different methods for pain relief with IUD insertions, but they have either been found ineffective or painful in themselves.
And there are a lot of methods out there used, and people tell me, like, “No, but you should have been doing this, and you should have been doing that. And I do this, and that works fine for me.” And I’m like, “Yes, but have you done the actual study? How do you know that it actually works? Perhaps it’s just, like, placebo that you’re offering to patients.” And I think women deserve more. Women deserve a method that has actually been proven to be effective in a study so that they know that they’re just not being offered placebo. And if you think that your method is so great then do the study. Show the women that it is effective. That is what I have been doing, and I’m actually very proud of that.
Feltman: Just anecdotally, I feel like people who I know or, you know, who I, I talk to because of my line of work, I think there’s so much fear, there often is so much actual discomfort and pain. People are so used to it being brushed aside that to some extent I think a provider offering anything goes such a long way into making a patient at least feel calmer. But to your point, how much better to have something that’s been empirically proven to actually help you.
Kopp Kallner: Yes.
Feltman: So let’s talk a little bit about the method that you tested. You mentioned that it’s a very small catheter. So just so our listeners understand since that, that might not be a word that they hear a lot in their, their everyday lives. Uh, so there’s no injection that’s being used to apply a local anesthetic. Is that correct?
Kopp Kallner: That is definitely correct. So this is a very, very thin, plastic catheter. And of course, maybe I should have looked up what it is in inches, but it’s 1.3 millimeters wide. So, it’s a very tiny catheter.
Feltman: So small that translating it to be inches would be meaningless. At that small, I think, I think most people in the U.S. would agree millimeters is much more useful.
Kopp Kallner: Oh, great. It’s also, like, extremely soft, so you can completely bend it in either direction. What I usually do is I, I show the catheter to the women when it’s still in its little package. And I say, “See how thin it is,” and then I bend it so that they see that it’s not sharp or anything.
And this little catheter is then attached to a syringe with the 10 milliliters of the mepivacaine then, which is the local anesthetic that we use. And so it just like, it slips into the uterus very nicely actually.
And what happens then is that this fluid, it just, slowly runs out of the cervix, and it forms like a little puddle inside the vagina, and it sort of, like, drenches the cervix in this local anesthetic fluid. And then we apply the tenaculum to that part of the cervix that has been in the puddle, so to speak.
So perhaps it actually numbs the cervix as well. But that, we haven’t really studied so much. We got, in the pilot trial that I spoke about with the lower concentration of the mepivacaine, there we saw that the absolutely most painful part of the whole procedure was the actual placement of the IUD.
So then we actually took away the pain assessment for the tenaculum and the, uh, the sounding because the most painful part was the IUD insertion.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, and speaking of that pain assessment, could you tell us about the results? You know, what kind of improvements did you see? And also what kind of feedback did you get from patients about efficacy?
Kopp Kallner: Yeah, so we measured pain uh, two different ways. First was on what is called the visual analog scale. It’s a 10-centimeters long line. And then the women had the pain scoring sheet, the visual analog scale, this 10 centimeter line in front of them during the IUD insertion.
And then we told them, like, “Okay, now you need to score,” and they scored. And it was like, “Now you need to score,” and they scored. So it was, like, an immediate pain assessment. So it’s not like something, like, “Oh, 10 minutes after I thought like, you know, I experienced this kinda thing I remember.” So it’s a very exact kind of pain assessment. So it’s from the absolute worst pain imaginable—sort of like, what if somebody were to saw off your legs with a really rusty saw and you had no anesthesia—to, like, you wake up in the morning, you’re completely pain free, the sun is shining. You score in between those.
And then we also asked women if the pain was tolerable. What is then tolerable? Well, that is subjective to you. Some people might think, like, “Oh, you know, this sawing off of the leg, well, that might be tolerable.” Very few, of course, feel that. And I think that maybe it’s not like the visual analog pain scale really that matters to the patient. What matters to the patient is that you walk out of there and you thought like, “This was okay.” “This was tolerable.” And what we could see was that we lowered the pain score, uh, in the visual analog scale.
But we also raised the proportion of individuals who thought that the pain was tolerable to 98.3%, I think it was. So that means that the absolute vast majority went out of the room with an okay experience, and I think that is the most important thing. Because what, what I think that we see in social media is we, you know, we see, like, women screaming or posting “This was the absolute worst experience I’ve ever had in my life.” We need to lower the proportion of women who have that just absolutely excruciating, painful, intolerable experience.
Feltman: Well, and is this a method that other practitioners could implement right now? Is there anything stopping a clinician from reading your study and offering this to their patients?
Kopp Kallner: No, I think this is enough. I mean we have, uh, now performed basically three studies with around 600 randomized individuals with this method. I mean, this is the highest level of evidence. It’s been consistent, the findings throughout all these trials.
And there have been no complications. No increased risk of infection has been seen. So I think just go ahead and implement this. And, if we have patients listening to this, I sincerely ask you to ask for this method because I think that doctors are hard to convince to try something new.
But if patients start asking for it, like, “Oh, I want this evidence-based pain relief,” and the doctor goes like, “Oh, what is that?” And they’re like, “Oh, do I have to educate you?” So I think that when we educate women, when we educate our patients, that’s when change happens more rapidly.
Feltman: Yeah. Well, thank you so much, uh, for coming on to talk to us today. This has been really great.
Kopp Kallner: Oh, thank you for having me.
Feltman: That’s all for this week on Science Quickly. We’ll be back on Monday with our usual news roundup.

Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.

Chair of Jewish Greens calls for Zack Polanski to resign after byelection loss

The chair of the Jewish Greens has called for Zack Polanski to step down as pressure increases on the Green leader to acknowledge anger within the party over a new policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for the state of Israel to be abolished.
The comments by Vivien Lichtenstein come after Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, criticised Polanski for a lack of leadership in missing the debate and vote at the weekend that resulted in the policy being passed.
However, another member of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.
Lichtenstein had said she was considering quitting the Green party of England and Wales following the vote at the party conference to adopt the policy, which states that Zionism is racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.
Polanski was not at the conference on Sunday when the motion was debated; instead he was campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which he finished second to Labour.
In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski, who is Jewish, said he would have voted against the motion had he attended. Two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.
Lichtenstein, speaking to Times Radio, said that even though Polanski was campaigning, he should have spoken and voted for the amendments online, which was an option. “He should have done that. And I think that was a big mistake on his part.”
She said she was surprised to hear Polanski say he had been working with Jewish members of the party, adding: “I don’t know which Jewish members of the party he’s been working with. It certainly hasn’t been with the Jewish Greens committee.”
Asked if Polanski should continue in his role, she replied: “No, I think he should resign.”
However, Annie Gottfried Cohen, who is communications officer of the Jewish Greens, said she and some other officers in the group disputed Lichtenstein’s claim that Polanski had not worked with Jewish members, saying he “held a long meeting with the Jewish Greens committee on this motion back in August”.
She said: “Vivien’s views do not represent all or even the majority of Jewish Greens, many of whom have been campaigning for Zack all week, and some of whom, myself included, are furious that she has made this call in her capacity as chair of Jewish Greens. A motion of no confidence in the chair is being tabled as a result, asking her to step down.”
A number of group members supported the motion and others were critical of only some parts of it, she said.
But Lucas, who remains one of the Greens’ best-known and popular figures, said on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.
Speaking to Newsnight, before the byelection result, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”
Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.
“Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection. I want him to speak now about what’s happened. I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. I think the jury is out about whether or not he will do that, but I very much hope he will.”
Jonathan Bartley, who was formerly the Green co-leader with Lucas and is now a councillor in Lambeth, south London, called on Polanski to “put his hands up” and apologise. “I think [the policy vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now from the Green party,” he told the BBC.
There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.

UN voices concern over student protests, high school blockades in France

Unknown Publisher

Beyza Binnur Donmez
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The UN human rights office on Friday expressed concern over incidents surrounding student protests and high school blockades in France, urging restraint and respect for the right to peaceful assembly.
"We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent," spokesperson Shabia Mantoo told reporters in Geneva, responding to a question from Anadolu.
Mantoo called on all sides to ensure that demonstrations remain peaceful and urged law enforcement authorities to avoid the disproportionate use of force.
"We call on everyone to ensure that they remain peaceful and that there is no disproportionate use of force by law enforcement," she said.
"And the right to peaceful assembly must be upheld," the spokesperson added.
The protests began in mid-September in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where high school students mobilized in support of teachers protesting staff shortages, before spreading to schools across France.
Students have demanded increased education funding, more teachers and support staff, improvements to deteriorating school buildings, smaller class sizes and changes to the Parcoursup university admissions system.
The demonstrations have intensified amid reports of clashes between protesters and police, including the use of tear gas and other crowd-control weapons that have left several students seriously injured.
French authorities have faced growing criticism over the police response, while the government has pledged to address students' grievances.

Feverish after a vaccine? The reason could be your gut microbiome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:48:29 UTC
19:48:29 KST

Vaccines pack a punch: The shots save lives, but they can also often cause minor side effects such as muscle soreness, fatigue and fever. Researchers have long wondered why some people develop these reactions while others seem to skate by unaffected. The reason, it turns out, may have to do with the bacteria in our guts.
In a new study published in Science on Thursday, researchers collected stool samples from more than 170 people before and after a second or third dose of a COVID vaccine. They found that people who experienced fever after the shot tended to share similar microbiome traits.
Specifically, people with worse fever tended to have more of a protein called flagellin in their systems than those with little to no fever. Flagellin makes up the tail-like structures, or flagella, that bacteria use to move—suggesting that the fever-associated microbes had greater “motility,” or ability to move around, explains Ruth Ley, the study’s senior author and director of the department of microbiome science at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen in Germany. The participants with high-fever symptoms also tended to have greater gut inflammation than their peers.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To investigate why, exactly, flagellin might influence fever, the researchers conducted a follow-up experiment in genetically engineered mice. They found that animals exposed to the fever-associated human bacteria showed a response equivalent to a fever in humans. This was particularly the case in those that could sense flagellin. Mice without flagellin receptors were less affected—indicating a direct link between flagellin and an immune system response.
On top of that, the levels of humans’ fever correlated with those of the equivalent reaction in mice, Ley says. “The worse the fever in the people, the more the temperature dropped in the mice,” she says. (Mice typically experience hypothermia as part of their immune response, which serves a similar function as a fever in humans.)
It’s still unclear why some people could have higher levels of flagellin in their guts than others. It may have something to do with diet: self-reported vegetarians tended to have lower flagellin levels, according to the study. But more research is needed to tease that out.
“It would make sense that, if you could tamp down the motility of the bacteria, we would predict that you wouldn’t react as strongly in terms of the fever,” Ley says. “But that’s all very much future research.”
Eventually, Ley hopes, the results could help fight this side effect of vaccines and, by extension, encourage higher vaccination rates.

Montenegrin authorities decided to expel Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the pro-Kremlin war blog Rybar, and four other Russian citizens for national security reasons, the local newspaper Vijesti reported on Oct. 9.
The blogger, his wife Valeria Zvinchuk, and three other associates — reported to be Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko — were detained earlier on Oct. 9 by Montenegrin law enforcement and security authorities in the town of Risan.
Zvinchuk is the founder of Rybar, one of Russia's most popular pro-war blogs, with over 1.5 million followers on Telegram. It focuses on battlefield developments in Ukraine while promoting pro-Russian propaganda about the war.
The channel's staff has been subject to U.K. and EU sanctions, and the U.S. announced a $10 million reward in 2024 for information on Rybar's activities.
"Today, employees of the Police Department, together with the National Security Agency and with the support of international partners, conducted a targeted and coordinated operation aimed at preventing, detecting, and neutralizing illegal activities on the territory of Montenegro," the Balkan country's police said.
The swift response prevented "potentially harmful actions" by the group on Montenegrin territory, according to the law enforcement agency.
The group was said to have arrived in the country less than two days ago. During the investigation, the Montenegrin police seized sophisticated digital equipment, including a drone, cameras, and several phones.
"Following the results of the criminal, operational, and intelligence investigation, it was established that these individuals cannot continue to stay in Montenegro, and in accordance with the Law on Foreigners, a decision was made to expel them for reasons of national and internal security," the police said.
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic previously confirmed Zvinchuk's detention, without disclosing further details about the operation.
"Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future," Spajic said on X.
Montenegro, a small nation in the Western Balkans, joined NATO in 2017 and is currently leading talks to join the EU.
Russia's Embassy has requested that Montenegro's authorities clarify the reasons for the detention of Zvinchuk and other Russian citizens, Russian state news agency TASS reported earlier on Oct. 9.
Separately, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Russian diplomats will work to protect Zvinchuk's rights.
Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's security council and former president known for his inflammatory rhetoric, issued threats against the West over the propagandist's detention.
"Now we will quite likely have to replenish our exchange pool with European and American morons to get our own people out," Medvedev said on his Telegram channel.

Acciaierie d'Italia has announced a suspension of production in Taranto pending a ruling from Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation, with plants in Genoa and Novi Ligure also set to shut down temporarily by 15 November.
Workers at all former Ilva sites in Italy are set to go on strike on 12 October, unions have announced, following Thursday's meeting with the government at Palazza Chigo.
Meanwhile, production at the hot end of the Taranto steelworks was suspended on Friday. More than 2,000 workers in Italy remain at risk of losing their jobs.
Acciaierie d’Italia has announced plans to shut down operations at plants in Taranto, Genoa, and Novi Ligure.
The undersecretary to the prime minister's office, Alfredo Mantovano, stressed the need for an emergency decree that includes social protections for workers and provides for a wage-support scheme that would not be tied to the closure of operations but would instead help keep the business going.
The government is expected to submit it at the next council of ministers, scheduled for Tuesday.
Taranto
On Friday, all production at the hot end of the Taranto steelworks was suspended, in compliance with a ruling by the Milan Court of Appeal.
The facilities will remain on heated standby, operating at the minimum technical level required to keep them warm but without producing steel.
Acciaierie d’Italia confirmed the move in a note sent to the prefect, local authorities, and law enforcement.
The shutdown will remain in place until the Court of Cassation rules on the appeals lodged by Ilva and Acciaierie d’Italia on 20 October.
'Completely unacceptable'
The company has also announced that by "15 November" there will be a "temporary general shutdown" of the former Ilva plants in Genoa and Novi Ligure.
"The announcement of a lockout is completely unacceptable," said the mayors of Genoa and Novi Ligure, Silvia Salis and Rocchino Muliere.
"It is an untenable prospect for workers, for Genoa and Novi Ligure, and for our country’s entire steel industry," Salis warned.
For the President of the Liguria Region, Marco Bucci, and his Piedmont counterpart, Alberto Cirio, "the announced closure of the former Ilva plants in Cornigliano, Novi Ligure and Racconigi is extremely serious news, not only for Liguria and Piedmont, but for the entire Italian steel industry, which is strategic for the country’s industrial future."
The trade unions also describe the idea of closure as "unacceptable."
"The workers have shown a great sense of responsibility, and we must therefore ensure that the cost of decisions and mistakes – which are not the workers’ fault – is not passed on to all the workers at the former Ilva plants," said Michele de Palma, feneral secretary of Fiom-Cgil, who was present at the meeting at Palazzo Chigi.
According to the USB, a country’s industrial strategy "is not decided by the judiciary," with Sasha Colautti, a member of the national executive, insisting that the government’s powerlessness in the face of the courts must not become an excuse.
This situation could take a further turn for the worse if the blast furnaces at Taranto were also to be taken off heat before the Court of Cassation issues its ruling.
The permanent shutdown of the hot end would leave no possibility of a subsequent restart, marking the definitive end to production and rendering any decision by the Supreme Court null and void.
Undersecretary Mantovano has stated that the government is "assessing whether there is scope to avoid a complete shutdown so as not to cause irreparable damage to the plants," before focusing on green steel production using DRI plants (which do not use blast furnaces) and electric furnaces, provided this is part of a "credible industrial plan."

The Race Illusion: On the Reality of Racialization and the Myth of Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:47:00 UTC
19:47:00 KST

Is race real? Are there human races? In the contemporary debate about the metaphysics and ontology of race, the most common answer is yes. Most people are racial realists, but they disagree about whether race is defined biologically—by reference to ancestry, genetics, etc.—or socially—by reference to culture, politics, etc. Adam Hochman bucks the recent realist trend in the metaphysics of race. He argues that there are no human races. Instead, he defends a thoroughgoing, and formidable, anti-realist account of race that he calls reconstructionist anti-realism. In my view, Hochman has provided the most convincing case for racial anti-realism since the work of Kwame Anthony Appiah and Naomi Zack in the early 1990s. (This is no small accomplishment!) The book makes a case for racial anti-realism that should be taken seriously for years to come.
Hochman divides the book into two parts. In Part I, he argues against biological realism. In Part II, he argues against social realism and considers some consequences of his anti-realist account. I will summarize each part and offer a few critical observations.
In Part I of the book, Hochman defines, and argues against, increasingly sophisticated versions of the biological theory of race. In Chapter 1, he considers the traditional view that races are human populations, where a population is a group of individuals that occupy a certain area, have shared ancestry, and are likely to have shared descendants. Hochman notes several problems with this view, but I will focus on two. First, the populations view appears to change the subject; there are many human populations that we would not consider races. Second, the populations view makes races scientifically trivial; such a notion of race would not tell us anything interesting about human biological diversity. Overall, Hochman dispatches these traditional views before moving on to more serious competing philosophical views in Chapter 2.
There, he argues against the most robust contemporary biological theory of race—the genetic cluster theory of race as articulated by Quayshawn Spencer. Spencer argues that human races can have a scientifically legitimate biological basis if we think of them as genetic clusters. Specifically, we think of racial concepts as picking out genetic clusters. Against Spencer, Hochman argues that Spencer’s theory faces the same problems as traditional biological theories of race. For example, Hochman argues that Spencer’s theory changes the topic, as genetic clusters give rise to different races than the ones that ordinary people will recognize. Hochman also thinks the view trivializes the notion of race, given that there are many genetic clusters. In Chapter 3, Hochman discusses several more theories of race by major figures in this area—Joshua Glasgow, Michael Hardimon, and Philip Kitcher—and argues that these views fail for similar reasons.
Hochman’s discussion of biological theories of race is comprehensive, rigorous, and compelling. He truly attempts to confront every major view in the area, and he gives substantive, extensive arguments against each biological account. While anti-realists have argued against biological theorists in the past, this book tackles the biological theories that have been offered most recently. This matters because it is tempting to think that recent advances in biology count in favor of biological realism. Hochman’s point is that biological realism still fails as a metaphysical thesis, despite what advances in genetic sequencing and mapping there might be. One worry about Hochman’s arguments, however, is that they feel a bit too familiar. While Hochman does not simply repeat existing arguments, it is true that the kinds of arguments he deploys against the biological theorist are well known. This is not to say that his arguments are unimportant. It is only to say that his arguments may not persuade people who are broadly familiar with the existing literature.
In Part II of the book, Hochman argues against social realism about race. On this view, racial kinds are social kinds, united by a common culture, recognition, or social structure. In Chapter 4, Hochman’s main issue with social theories of race is that they have what he calls an inflation problem. If we define race by reference to the social world, then we may end up inflating the concept of race. The clearest example of this is the distinction between race and ethnicity. The idea of an ethnic group includes factors surrounding shared ancestry and appearance, on the one hand, and culture, on the other. If races are essentially social, however, ethnic groups will count as racial groups because they include elements of culture and social recognition. Hochman criticizes Ásta’s conferralist account of race for different reasons. Ásta argues that we confer racial properties onto individuals in contexts.[1] Hochman thinks this kind of view makes racial properties come too easily. To use his example: the fact that we perceive someone as a witch does not make them a witch. Similarly, thinking that races are real should not make it so. Hochman discusses other social realist accounts of race, including Chike Jeffers’s cultural account of race and phenomenological approaches to race.
Hochman’s case against social realism was less persuasive to me than his criticisms of biological realism. This is because his arguments seemed to be against social constructionism, in general, not specifically against social constructionism in the metaphysics of race. The clearest example of this is his criticism of Ásta’s conferralist theory. According to conferralism, we socially construct the world by socially conferring properties onto groups and individuals. Hochman criticizes conferralism because it seems to rule out the possibility of major error about the social world; surely the world does not have whatever properties we think it does. This is a fair critique, but (a) it is not unique to the metaphysics of race, and (b) there are more general theories of social construction—ones that appeal to essences, grounding, anchoring, truthmaking, and so on—that respond to it.[2]
There are other signs that Hochman has issues with social constructionism, more generally. He thinks that the notion of social construction is radically ambiguous, to the point of “meaningless” (95). This too is a fair criticism, but it also seems like a more general point. Or at least, I wanted to see more argument for these claims. His critique of biological realism is almost twice as long as the critique of social realism, but, as far as I can tell, social realism is the most dominant position within social ontology.
Chapters 1-4 offer arguments against biological and social realist theories of race. Hochman considers, and rejects, the possibility of a purely negative metaphysical project. He calls unreconstructed anti-realism the view that races do not exist, and we do not need an alternative to race concepts. This view seems straightforward for anti-realists; if there are no races, then there is nothing further we need to explain. Hochman rejects this view because he thinks it is both metaphysically incomplete and “dangerous” (137).
The view is incomplete because it overlooks a non-trivial fact about the metaphysics of race: namely, that racialized groups and racialization exist. The view is dangerous because it leaves us without the resources to identify racism and historical racial injustices. The unreconstructed anti-realist says there are no races. But if there are no races, how do we explain interpersonal and institutional racism? Hochman thinks anti-realism is more plausible if we have good answers to such questions.
To this end, he defends reconstructionist anti-realism, which says that we should reform our understanding of groups that are believed to constitute races. Specifically, instead of talking about races, we would be better off talking about racialized groups and racialization. Hochman defines racialization as the process by which a group comes to be understood as a biological race. Racialized groups are the products of racialization. Hochman then gives a brief account of the advantages of his reconstructionist picture. First, he notes that the concept of racialization, unlike the concept of race, is a process concept; we must think of racialization as something that is done to us by others, while race is typically understood as who we are, biologically or socially. Second, he argues that the appeal to racialization would also be more advantageous when thinking about biomedical contexts. Race realists tend to attribute certain differences in the health of populations to race. The problem is that this kind of attribution can be dangerous, as people tend to think of race as genetic. If we talk about disparate health impacts in terms of racialized groups and racialization, it is harder to make this kind of mistake.
I found the discussion of racialization and racialized groups informative and fruitful. The chapter was informative because it explains how the anti-realist seeks to fill the explanatory gap that they are usually accused of being unable to fill. (“If there are no races, how could there be racism?”) It is fruitful because it asks new, and probably more interesting, questions within the metaphysics of race. For example, Hochman thinks we need a concept of racialization, but we should not bother with a theory of racialization. Insofar as I understand the dialectic, I disagree. Metaphysicians need theories of racialization because racialization often seems more explanatory than race.[3] Independently of who is right about this matter, it seems to be a point of disagreement that pushes the metaphysics of race toward new topics. This is a good thing.
I was also particularly impressed with the way that Hochman integrated the metaphysics of race with normative concerns about racism and racial injustice. In (what I call) critical social ontology, one does metaphysics with an eye toward critiquing or addressing social injustice.[4] Of course, critical social ontology has a danger of being done poorly; either we confuse metaphysics and politics, or we do both badly. Hochman’s case for reconstructionist anti-realism is clear about the distinction between metaphysics and value theory; it is metaphysically rigorous, and the recommendations seem practically sensible. It is hard to balance normative matters and social metaphysics, but Hochman succeeds in this task.
Adam Hochman’s The Race Illusion does not settle the debate on racial realism. (In philosophy, debates are never settled!) However, it does constitute the definitive case for racial anti-realism. If you are serious about the metaphysics of race, you should read this book.

German residential construction prices rise 5.5%, fastest pace in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:46:01 UTC
19:46:01 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Residential construction prices in Germany rose 5.5% year on year in August, their fastest increase in three years, according to official figures released Friday.
The increase accelerated from 5% in May, while prices rose 1% over the three-month period, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said.
The figures cover construction work on conventionally built residential buildings and include value-added tax.
Prices for structural work increased 5.4% from a year earlier, led by roofing, which rose 7.6%, and carpentry and timber construction, up 7.2%.
Concrete and masonry work, which account for the largest shares of structural work and the overall residential construction price index, became 4.3% and 4.2% more expensive, respectively.
Earthworks prices increased 6.1%.
Interior finishing costs rose 5.7% year on year, with electrical, security and information technology systems recording a 7.2% increase.
Prices for external thermal insulation systems climbed 5.7%, while heating and central hot-water systems, including heat pumps, rose 5.2%. Metalwork prices increased 5%.
Price increases also extended to maintenance and nonresidential construction.
Maintenance work on residential buildings, excluding cosmetic repairs, cost 6% more than a year earlier.
Prices for new office buildings rose 5.7%, while commercial building construction costs increased 5.5%.
Road construction recorded a sharper annual increase of 6.9%.

Heathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:45:25 UTC
19:45:25 KST

Infrastructure sends politicians berserk. Propose more money for the health service or reopening youth clubs and frowns break out all round. Can we afford it? But shout infrastructure and cheers go up. The word suggests glamour, chest-beating and “growth”. Reason flies out of the window.
The saga of Heathrow’s third runway beggars belief. A foreign-owned private company wants to make more money out of its cramped west London investment. The airlines are sceptical and passengers will have to pay surcharges higher than any in Europe. Meanwhile fields lie empty round its rival, Gatwick, and capacity at London’s third airport, Stansted, is underused.
The third runway is a nightmare. The official price tag is now a staggering £49bn but the overall budget for Heathrow’s expansion and operating expenditure could soar beyond £100bn. An unknown proportion of this will fall on the taxpayer. The proposal has been debated for 20 years and the opening constantly postponed. A date of 2035 has now become 2039. I would not take bets on 2045.
Sixty years ago, the British government agreed it was totally inappropriate for crowded and polluted Heathrow to expand in densely populated west London. Nor could an expanded Gatwick meet demand. The debate was over where to locate a new third airport. Sites in the Thames estuary and at Cublington and Stansted were researched. Stansted won. It already had an RAF base and it would service the expected growth in demand from London’s growing eastern reaches. Stansted opened in 1991.
The Tories privatised London’s airports. This turned what should have been a planned expansion into a battleground of feuding rivals. Each airport became a matter not of orderly growth but of quick profits, self-serving airline slots and a shifting army of amateur officials. Commissions came and went, in the grip of overpaid lobbyists. A Heathrow runway proposed by businessman Surinder Arora within the existing airport curtilage was brushed aside as insufficiently bold. As for Stansted, it was taken over by Manchester airport and is now hardly mentioned as an alternative to a third runway.
Airport public relations endlessly suggests it is about “business” and therefore relevant to “growth”, as if it were part of Andy Burnham’s re-industrialisation of Britain. Heathrow claims its new runway will create 100,000 jobs. But fewer than 15% of air travellers claim to be “on business”, and whatever happened to video conferencing reducing the need for intensive business air travel? As for Heathrow’s claim to be Britain’s leading cargo airport – “a quarter of all UK trade by value” – that is based, ludicrously, on the value of the gold ingots that form roughly 60% of the goods it transports. What banks shifting bullion has to do with growth is unclear.
Heathrow now has eerie echoes of HS2. Even its upper cost limit of £100bn is much the same. Both are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation. A third similar project is Hinkley Point nuclear power station, its cost currently rising through £50bn. Both the railway and the power station have been savaged by the National Audit Office. These projects are widely considered political white elephants and years from completion. Few dare say so. Meanwhile we should note that a new general hospital costs £1bn, as would rebuilding 50 secondary schools.
Stupefying sums are here being channelled into London and the south of England. That they have been born of the age of Boris Johnson’s “levelling up” and Burnham’s tilt to the north is bizarre. This week, conference politicians have cited budgets with endless savings: half a million off student exchanges here, a billion off quangos there. Yet no one mentioned that every year for the next decade John Healey’s Treasury will blow about £7bn just to relieve overcrowding on trains from London to Birmingham. This is almost 70% of his total rail investment.
The fact is that big infrastructure is monumental and sexy. No one boasts about building a care home, rather a fancy train or a nuclear power plant. One of Parkinson’s laws states that, while tiny items of corporate spending are debated for hours, big ones go through on the nod. They are too big to check and easy to promote.
It is absurd for the government to spend the next two decades upheaving Heathrow and tearing apart the M4 corridor for the profit of a band of foreign investors, when a simple alternative lies in growing Gatwick and Stansted. This whole debate is about tourism, and tourists can surely suffer the mild inconvenience of using the other two venues, as was intended half a century ago.
The rest of us – politicians not least – should realise that this is serious money. There are serious uses to which it should be put.
- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Palestinians set to delay legislative elections due to worsening conditions, letter says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Palestinians set to delay legislative elections due to worsening conditions, letter says
PARIS, Oct 9 - Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al Sheikh has informed France that a Palestinian legislative election planned for November 28 will be postponed, possibly until September 2027, because of worsening conditions throughout the Palestinian territories, according to a letter seen by Reuters.
"The assessment concluded that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for 28 November 2026 was based, have not materialized," said the letter, which was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and dated October 8.
It added that "holding them under the current circumstances faces fundamental obstacles affecting their inclusiveness, freedom of participation and the integrity of the electoral process."
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
Some officials within Abbas' Fatah party have demanded dialogue with Hamas and other factions to agree on a common national vision before proceeding with a vote. Others have cited obstructions to ballot boxes, election papers and ink entering Gaza, which they say would make voting impossible.
PALESTINIAN OFFICIALS SAY THEY EXPECTED US ACTION
The letter said Palestinian officials had expected conditions to improve through the implementation of US President Donald Trump's peace initiative and a UN Security Council resolution, including the deployment of international forces and Palestinian police in Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli troops.
It said the Palestinians had also anticipated US efforts to prevent further annexation of Palestinian territory in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, curb settler violence and secure the release of nearly $7 billion in Palestinian funds withheld by Israel.
"However, these steps, understandings and promises have not materialized. Rather, conditions have worsened throughout the Palestinian territory," the letter said, outlining in detail security issues in Gaza and the West Bank.
Based on their assessment, Palestinian officials recommended to Abbas "that the date of the legislative elections be adjusted by several months, and that dialogue continue to prepare the internal conditions", the letter said.
It added that Abbas had been advised to issue a decree adjusting the date for holding elections to the first half of September 2027.
Abbas, elected president of the PA in 2005, had reaffirmed plans to hold the elections during a speech to the United Nations on September 24.
FRANCE SAID ELECTIONS WERE ESSENTIAL
The letter was addressed to France after it recognised a Palestinian state in September 2025. As part of that decision France had urged that the planned legislative and presidential elections proceed, a written commitment that Abbas had made to President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, France's foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said it was essential for the elections to take place and hailed the launch of an EU mission to observe the elections.
"These elections will enable the Palestinian leadership to champion its people's legitimate aspirations with renewed legitimacy, while preserving the two-state solution," he said.
In the more than two decades since Abbas was elected as the successor to Fatah founder Yasser Arafat, the PA's public standing has sunk among Palestinians, who have grown to view it as ineffective and corrupt.
In 2007, the PA was driven out of the Gaza Strip by Hamas militants, who had won an election there on an anti-corruption platform. Abbas has ruled by decree since his mandate expired in 2009.
A peace process meant to lead to the creation of a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem collapsed in 2014, and expanding Israeli settlements have since carved up areas once slated for eventual Palestinian control. REUTERS

EU faces potential gas shortage as winter approaches: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:43:16 UTC
19:43:16 KST

Melike Pala
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The European Union could face a natural gas shortfall of up to 14 billion cubic meters this winter, equivalent to around 7% of the bloc's demand, amid depleted storage levels and disruptions to global energy supplies, according to energy reports.
A report by the US-based Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), shared with Politico on Friday, warned that the EU's gas reserves have fallen to just above 70%, their lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011.
The potential deficit could affect energy supplies equivalent to the consumption of 10 million to 12 million European households, raising concerns over higher electricity bills and possible energy-saving measures.
High prices have encouraged traders to sell gas during the summer rather than replenish storage facilities ahead of winter, leaving the bloc with a reduced buffer against supply disruptions.
The findings are also reflected in the 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG).
The report warned that storage levels could fall to as low as 11% under a cold-winter scenario if liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports are limited or remain at optimal levels.
To restore reserves to 30% by the end of winter, the EU could face a situation in which gas consumption equivalent to 7% of demand would have to be curtailed or supplies withheld from consumers, according to ENTSOG.
The EU's planned ban on long-term contracts for Russian LNG, due to take effect in January, is expected to reduce gas imports by a further 7 billion cubic meters, according to the IEEFA report.
Meanwhile, winter gas demand has risen over the past two years, while imports have remained largely flat, increasing the bloc’s dependence on stored supplies.
The EU could turn to additional LNG imports, particularly from the US, to offset potential supply losses.
However, replacing the missing volumes at current prices would cost an additional €3 billion, representing a 12% increase compared with the cost of the same volumes last year, according to IEEFA.

Forgotten trail camera yields 9 months of wildlife images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

Forgotten trail camera yields 9 months of wildlife images
A farmer in South Estonia who forgot about a trail camera he had set up found a wealth of nature photo on it once he retrieved it.
Tarvo Siilaberg, a Põlva County farmer, left the trail cam in a forest earlier this year and it soon passed from his mind. But once he remembered and located it, he found the fully working camera had been "visited" by moose, deer, cranes and other wildlife — including a bear.
The camera's battery and systems were still running, and its memory had not filled up either.
"Part of it was simple absent-mindedness. We have quite a few camera traps for animals and one ended up in a spot I couldn't remember for a long time," said Siilaberg, owner of Raja Farm.
When he went looking for the camera in the forest, he found it hard to spot because of its nature as a trail cam — well camouflaged.
Some of the visitors captured on the footage were more surprising than others.
"We already knew that a moose trail passes through our land, which is why we put the camera at the edge of the bog forest," Siilaberg explained.
"The camera was up at the edge of the forest, where the ditch bank meets the meadow — we happened to place it right at an animal crossroads," he said. "Deer appear in front of the trail camera about as often as you'd see a pigeon in the city."
One of the last images the camera captured before it was retrieved was also one of the most impressive: a bear.
"That was also the first photo I saw when I took the camera down from the tree. Then I knew there was something very good here," said Siilaberg, whose farm is in Kanassaare village in Põlva municipality.
"The picture of the cranes is my favorite," he said. "I hope to forget my camera in the forest again soon — then good things will start happening, if a person keeps their hands away. The result is definitely worth it."
Of the animals he had hoped to see, Siilaberg said he had wanted footage of a lynx, but there wasn't any.

In September 2025, more than 30 Russian Gerberadrones violated Polish airspace. Wreckage from the drones was later found at 27 locations across the country.
The Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office reported the findings.
An official decision lists 24 localities, including Chojny, Krzywowierzba-Kolonia, Cześniki, and Wyhalew.
However, the names of three other locations where drone debris was found have not been disclosed because the information is classified.
Some of the drones were found several dozen kilometers from Warsaw.
The drones crashed because they ran completely out of fuel during their long flights.
As previously reported, the Polish prosecutor’s office closed its investigation into the mass violation of the country’s airspace by Russian drones because it was unable to identify the individuals directly responsible.
Most of the case files, including the reasoning behind the decision to close the investigation, are classified. As a result, the prosecutor’s office has not publicly disclosed details about the identified flight paths, the methods used to control individual drones, or which specific drones were shot down by Polish and allied forces.
However, closing the investigation because the individuals directly responsible could not be identified does not mean that Polish authorities are denying the Russian origin of the drones.
A separate part of the investigation examined the actions of Polish military personnel during the interception of the drones. The prosecutor’s office concluded that the military acted within their authority and had legal grounds to open fire to destroy the aerial targets.
SIM cards issued by Polish mobile operators were also found in some of the Russian Gerbera drones that violated Polish airspace.
However, the prosecutor’s office has not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.
