Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:25:22 EEST
19:25:22 KST

South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who spent decades pursuing accountability for war crimes and human rights violations, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her contribution to international law. The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the award in Oslo on Friday, recognising the 85-year-old former UN human rights chief.
The committee credited Pillay with helping establish legal principles used to prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. Her career spans South Africa’s apartheid era, the prosecution of those responsible for the Rwandan genocide and investigations into alleged violations of international law in Gaza.
Announcing the decision, committee chairman Jørgen Watne Frydnes said Pillay had played a central role in developing international justice at a time when governments were challenging the authority of international courts.
“The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack,” Frydnes said.
Born in Durban in 1941 to a family of Indian Tamil descent, Pillay grew up under apartheid. The daughter of a bus driver, she became the first woman to establish a law practice in South Africa’s Natal province in 1967. She represented opponents of apartheid, including Nelson Mandela, before becoming the first non-white woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court.
Her international judicial career included eight years at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she served four years as president. She helped develop legal precedents recognising rape and sexual violence as acts constituting genocide and crimes against humanity.
Pillay subsequently served as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She also chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
That commission concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel rejected the findings, describing the report as “scandalous”.
Pillay currently serves as a judge in proceedings brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over allegations of genocide against the Rohingya population.
The announcement initially caught Pillay by surprise.
In a video shared on social media by Amnesty International’s secretary general Agnès Callamard, Pillay appears visibly surprised. She questions whether the news is genuine as colleagues congratulate her.
In the video, she also joked about US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly expressed his desire to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she told colleagues.
Speaking about criticism of her work investigating Gaza, she said: “Why would you need courage to speak the truth?”
Trump's administration has imposed sanctions on International Criminal Court judges and prosecutors amid disputes over investigations involving Israeli officials. Reuters reported that Washington was considering further measures against the court.
Asked whether the award addressed governments challenging international judicial institutions, Frydnes said it sent a message to those undermining the international legal system.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay, praising her work defending people subjected to persecution and discrimination.
The UN human rights office also welcomed the decision. Its spokesperson, Shabia Mantoo, told reporters in Geneva that the award recognised dedication to protecting human rights.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee considered 287 nominations this year, comprising 208 individuals and 79 organisations.
Pillay succeeds Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who received the 2025 prize.
The award includes 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million, a gold medal and a diploma. Pillay is due to receive the prize in Oslo on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

Russian authorities have lifted quarantine measures in the Irkutsk region following the unexplained death of an employee of an anti-plague research institute, even as the World Health Organization (WHO) says it still lacks enough information to assess the potential public health risk.
Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev announced on Thursday, Oct. 8, that the restrictions had been removed after experts completed preventive measures connected to what authorities described as a fatal case of “community-acquired pneumonia.”

Nearly 5,000 tests find no dangerous pathogens
The deceased employee, identified by independent Russian media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia.
She died overnight on Oct. 1-2 after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia of undetermined origin. Unconfirmed reports suggested she may have contracted pneumonic plague through exposure at the laboratory.
Russian authorities deny that a plague infection has been established.
Kobzev said Shipilova had been vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she handled. An investigation found no accidents involving pathogenic microorganisms at the institute, he added.
The governor said all people who had come into contact with Shipilova had undergone medical observation. Nearly 5,000 laboratory tests reportedly found no dangerous pathogens or infection-related health problems.
Around 200 people were placed in isolation after Shipilova’s death. WHO says it still lacks the full picture
Kobzev claimed that the WHO had publicly confirmed there was no danger to the population. The organization’s own statement was more cautious.

Ukraine expands drone strikes on data centres owned by Russia's Yandex

Ukraine hits second major tech site, expanding range of targets inside Russia
LONDON, Oct 9 - Ukraine struck and partly disabled a major data centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex on Friday in the second such action in successive days, widening the scope of its attacks inside Russia after Moscow hit data hubs in Ukraine.
Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia's AI development and is sometimes called Russia's Google, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
Ukrainian arms maker Firepoint said Kyiv had used its FP-1 one-way attack drones to mount the strike against what it called Yandex's biggest data centre and said that several of its modules had been completely knocked out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down Yandex's data hub in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed.
Yandex said it was facing a difficult challenge to maintain its services, used by millions of Russians daily for navigation, music, movies, food orders and other tasks. It also provides cloud computing services on which many businesses depend.
YANDEX SHARES FALL ON RUSSIAN EXCHANGE
Alexander Savitsky, who runs a start-up dating app called Pulse with 8,000 users, told Reuters that none of them had been able to access it since Thursday.
He said the company was unable to reach its backup database in Yandex Cloud and was getting an "internal error" message when trying to restore it elsewhere.
"We have no confirmation of actual data loss, but the situation is serious: the project represents three years of work," Savitsky said.
"The main risk is losing users and their trust: people can't use the app, and there's no telling how many will return once service is restored."
Yandex said it had struck a deal with other cloud providers to enable clients to swiftly move their data and services. Its shares fell by more than 4% on the Moscow exchange.
"The risks involve not only the potential temporary unavailability of Yandex services and lost revenue in specific segments but also the company's extensive base of B2B clients," said Maryana Lazaricheva, head of equity research at T-Investments.
She said the company could redistribute some of the load to its other data centres. "However, if the chain of attacks continues, this possibility vanishes, which could lead to even more severe consequences."
BOTH SIDES EXPAND RANGE OF ECONOMIC TARGETS
Locked in a deadly war of attrition after more than four years of fighting, both Russia and Ukraine have expanded drone attacks this year on infrastructure targets, from energy facilities and refineries to ports and vessels carrying oil and grain, e-commerce warehouses and, most recently, data centres.
The full scale of the disruption caused by the attacks was not immediately clear, although messages appeared on at least one Yandex app warning of potential problems in its operation.
Yandex said it was working around the clock to try to restore services which had been disrupted.
"Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one," it said.
Russia has struck Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
"We always respond in mirror-like fashion," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Thursday. He confirmed on Friday that his drones had struck the Kaluga data centre in what he called "our tit-for-tat response".
The regional governor said nine people had been injured in Ukraine's attacks, five of whom were being treated in hospital.
SPARTAK MOSCOW AMONG WEBSITES CITING DIFFICULTIES
Ukraine has previously targeted the warehouses of specific companies it deems central to Russia's economy, including dozens of sites operated by e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon. Russia responded by striking their Ukrainian equivalents.
Yandex operates five data centres, two of which have already been hit. It said in 2021 that the Sasovo data hub, which was struck on Thursday, hosted two of its three supercomputers built around Nvidia A100 chips, which it uses to train its YandexGPT large AI model. Yandex has declined to say whether the supercomputers were affected by the attack.
Multiple online services in Russia reported technical issues on Thursday, including real estate aggregator Cian, a book portal called Litmarket, and the websites of Russian Railways and professional football club Spartak Moscow.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres have forced some of them to suspend operations, while 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after one attack. Ukraine's digital minister told Reuters last month that the country was responding by moving digital infrastructure underground. REUTERS

NATO to conduct nuclear deterrence exercise in Italy without live ammunition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:25:09 UTC
19:25:09 KST

BRUSSELS, October 9. /TASS/. Starting October 13, NATO will begin its annual nuclear deterrence exercise, Steadfast Noon, in Italy, which will not involve live ammunition, the alliance’s press service reported.
It said that 17 countries will participate in the exercise. "No live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country," the statement says.
Three NATO members - the United States, France and the United Kingdom - are nuclear weapons states. NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements ensure that the benefits, responsibilities and risks of nuclear deterrence are shared across the Alliance. So, warheads from the countries possessing nuclear weapons can be deployed on delivery systems belonging to non-nuclear weapon states to make them more difficult to detect. This explains the number of participants in the nuclear exercises.

Trump envoy kept financial ties to firm behind $15 billion Hormuz-bypass oil pipeline plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:24:59 UTC
19:24:59 KST

Trump envoy kept financial ties to firm behind $15 billion Hormuz-bypass oil pipeline plan
DUBAI, Oct 9 - Thomas Barrack, a top US diplomat in the Middle East, advocated for a firm run by his business partner to take part in the development of an oil pipeline from Iraq to Syria, three people said, activities which appear to violate federal ethics rules.
In July, Iraq and Syria signed memorandums of understanding with a consortium made up of the company, Californian investment group TI Capital, along with Chevron and Qatar’s UCC Holding, to carry out technical and financial studies in preparation for rehabilitating the pipeline, which would skirt the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.
Barrack, US presidential special envoy to both Iraq and Syria as well as Ambassador to Turkey, has a longstanding business relationship with TI Capital and its founder Ziad Ghandour. At the time of his confirmation hearings in 2025 he had a financial interest entitling him to as much as a fifth of the profits from a real-estate venture near San Francisco, California and managed by TI Capital - with Ghandour as chief executive - that he said he intended to retain, public records show.
During engagements with Syrian and Iraqi officials after the start of the war in Iran, Barrack pressed for Ghandour's firm to be included in the project, according to two of the people, who have direct knowledge of the discussions.
On June 16, a month before the consortium agreement was signed, Barrack and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi issued a joint statement that commended Iraq's decision "to advance a memorandum of understanding with TI Capital to rehabilitate the Kirkuk-Baniyas Pipeline." The statement made no mention of Chevron or UCC in connection with the pipeline.
Reuters found no evidence that Barrack stands to profit from the pipeline or other projects. His ties to Ghandour would not constitute a criminal conflict of interest unless he stood to directly profit from the pipeline itself, two ethics lawyers told Reuters.
However, Barrack's relationship with Ghandour makes such advocacy "a serious problem" under the regulation that prohibits officials from participating in matters that call into question their impartiality because of a personal or business relationship, said Richard Painter, a former chief White House ethics lawyer and a professor at the University of Minnesota Law School.
The impartiality rule, which is not a criminal statute, can be triggered by the involvement of a business associate in a project, regardless of whether the official has a financial interest of his own.
“The ethical concern is the appearance of a conflict of interest," said Ann Skeet, interim executive director at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics in Santa Clara University.
Asked what Barrack would have needed to do to comply, Painter said: "Have nothing to do with this pipeline. Completely recuse. Say this is not a matter I participate in."
Don Fox, a former general counsel and acting director of the US Office of Government Ethics, said that promotion of TI Capital by Barrack would additionally violate a regulation prohibiting officials from using their office to endorse any enterprise or for the private gain of people they are affiliated with.
Barrack has not filed a conflict-of-interest waiver with the US Office of Government Ethics regarding his ties to the company as it participates in the project, according to a Reuters records request. Waivers allow officials with potential conflicts of interest to participate in matters that would otherwise require the employee be recused.
In a signed ethics agreement before his confirmation hearings last year, he committed to recusing himself from matters directly affecting the financial interests of the real-estate venture unless he first obtained such a waiver.
Barrack’s office and Chevron declined to comment. TI Capital, Ghandour and UCC did not respond to requests for comment.
In a July 17 post on X, Barrack said the involvement of US companies in Iraq and Syria was “a new paradigm” aimed at bringing clarity and opportunity to the region.
A fourth ethics lawyer said it was up to the State Department to decide whether its employee's financial holdings create a potential conflict of interest.
"Ambassador Barrack has no affiliation with, role in, or financial interest in the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline project," a State Department spokesperson told Reuters, while acknowledging Barrack’s relationship with the TI Capital real-estate venture.
His public comments on the pipeline reflect "long-standing, publicly stated US policy interest in regional energy integration," the spokesperson said, adding that Barrack was certified to be in compliance with ethics rules.
THE DISCLOSED INTEREST
In a financial disclosure filed with the US Office of Government Ethics in March 2025, before assuming his diplomatic roles, Barrack declared an equity stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment LLC, a venture building a large housing project near San Francisco. The filing did not disclose the size of the stake, but said he was entitled to 20% of the company’s profits when the earnings reach an established minimum.
ACD-TI is managed by TI Capital and headed by Ghandour, California state corporate records show. Reuters was unable to find contact details for a company representative, and did not get a response to questions sent to its postal correspondence address.
The filing said the profit sharing arrangement was in return for services he provided to the company. Barrack also disclosed to the OGE a paid consulting role with the venture in 2024. The filing does not say whether or how much he was paid.
In a separate signed ethics agreement dated March 7, 2025, three weeks before his Senate confirmation hearing, Barrack listed ACD-TI Oakley among assets he would retain rather than sell.
BYPASSING HORMUZ
The historic Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline, which for decades moved Iraqi crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast, faced sporadic shutdowns from the early 1980s and has been out of action since the US invasion of Iraq in 2003. Mothballed plans to revive it received new impetus this year when, under US attack, Iran restricted traffic through Hormuz, pushing oil prices higher.
Several people told Reuters in August the pipeline would take at least four years and cost $15 billion to build.
The idea of bringing TI Capital into the regional project was raised by Barrack in May at the Milken Institute Global Conference in Los Angeles, a third person with direct knowledge of the conversation told Reuters. The discussion, they added, took place on the sidelines of the event.
With the US war on Iran raging, Barrack and Ghandour also participated in an invite-only panel at the conference, where they discussed in more general terms the need for new energy supply lines in the Middle East, the person said.
A Milken Institute spokesperson declined to provide details of the panel discussion, saying it was closed to the media.
Barrack has engaged in business with Ghandour since at least 2020, when the two men created a $250 million blank-check SPAC that was dissolved after Barrack was arrested in 2021 on charges of acting as an unregistered agent of the United Arab Emirates. He was acquitted in 2022.
The Iraqi cabinet named TI Capital later in July as part of another consortium with UCC Holding and ConocoPhillips to assess the Akkas gas field, one of Iraq's largest undeveloped reserves. On its website, the firm claims involvement in projects at Syria's Tartous port, without providing details. Syria’s port authority did not reply to questions about TI Capital, and Reuters could not verify its role in Tartous. ConocoPhillips did not reply to a request for comment.
A person close to Barrack said the ambassador trusted Ghandour to help implement US President Donald Trump’s regional strategy of bringing Iraq and Syria closer to the US. “Ziad is the chosen man. Hand-picked by Barrack,” the person said.
The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department. REUTERS

GENEVA, October 9. /TASS/. More than 8,700 Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since May, and more than 4,200 patients have died, the World Health Organization (WHO) said.
According to its situation report, "as of October 6, 2026, the country had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 confirmed deaths," putting the case fatality rate at around 48.2%. Since the previous edition of the WHO’s Ebola situation report was published on September 25, the DRC has registered 775 new confirmed cases, including 379 deaths.
Since September 25, the Ebola outbreak has spread to the Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu province, expanding the "geographical reach of the epidemic." It currently affects 64 health zones in seven provinces in the eastern part of the country. Ituri province has been particularly hard hit.
The WHO said that "transmission remains intense at the national level, although the burden is unevenly distributed." In some areas, "there are clear signs that the epidemic is slowing, while in others it continues to intensify." The persistently high case fatality rate, along with the large number of deaths occurring outside healthcare facilities, "continues to indicate delays in disease detection and access to appropriate medical care."
The current Ebola outbreak began on May 15 in the DRC and Uganda. Ugandan authorities announced on July 28 that the outbreak in the country had ended. The WHO confirmed this on August 25. On October 6, Kenyan authorities reported the country’s first Ebola case. The infected person, a Kenyan national who had visited the DRC, died in hospital.

Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work.
For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems.
Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems.
She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities.
Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom.
“I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.”
In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling.
They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame.
The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead.
Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began.
Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended.
Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard.
Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires.
On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled.
Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them.
It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace.
“I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.”
Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams.
Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years.
The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another.
When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up.
In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone.
The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared.
There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam.
"These are my girls," she says again.
Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk.
Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks.
The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become.
Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings. Their futures still seemed to turn on exams, marks, university places and what their families could afford.
Maha remembers Sara Rayan laughing, and Ghaida, she says, is in Egypt now, studying dentistry.
Then, she reaches Lina al-Hour.
Here, she pauses, enlarges Lina’s face on the screen and falls silent. Her smile has disappeared. When she speaks again, her voice is quieter and catches slightly.
“This is my well-mannered student, Lina,” she says softly. “She is a martyr.”
On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. She was 18.
For a moment, the girls wrap their arms even tighter around one another in silence.
The photograph stays open on her phone.
Standing in the same schoolyard three years later, they tell one another they wish they could return to those days.
But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion.
Aya takes out her phone and holds it at arm's length, trying to recreate the selfie Sara took three years earlier.
“Sara should have been here to take it,” she says.
But Sara cannot come. She now works for an NGO, using her wages to help pay her university fees and contribute to her family's income.
Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders.
Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon.
Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women.
Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours.
“It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.”
After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology.
When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent.
But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees.
Aya turned to her older brother Yasser.
Seventeen years her senior, Yasser was a lawyer with his own practice, a wife and three children: Adnan, nine, Ahmad, seven, and three-year-old Ilaf. He helped support their parents and hoped one day to teach law at university.
“I used to always tell him, ‘You're a second father to me,’ because he was so kind to me, just like my father,” Aya says.
Aya remembers a summer's day in August 2023. Yasser, still dressed in his smart work clothes, came to take her from Nuseirat to the Islamic University of Gaza.
"Together, we went from department to department, trying to find a course that was affordable and that I would enjoy," she says.
Professors suggested engineering. But when they came out, Aya told Yasser she couldn't imagine herself studying computers or becoming an engineer.
“I could picture myself wearing a white coat, that's all,” she told him.
They tried health sciences next.
“Maybe I could study something in the medical field,” Aya suggested. “I really liked medical laboratory sciences.”
Yasser knew that his sister was giving up the version of university she had imagined. But he refused to let her see the decision as the end of something.
"Perhaps it's for the best," he told her. "Maybe one day you'll become a doctor in the field you choose to specialise in. You don't have to be a medical doctor; you could become a university professor with a PhD."
Then, he offered her a thought that has stayed with her. "He told me, 'Sometimes what is withheld from us can be better for us than what is given to us,' and I believe him."
Afterwards, he took her to Al-Taboun restaurant for lunch, while they kept talking about university and the choices available.
Aya enrolled in medical laboratory sciences, and Yasser bought her books and supplies. University had barely completed its first week when the war began.
A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house.
The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted.
She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to.
Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there.
On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food.
On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32.
Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation.
When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one.
“I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says.
Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained.
After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things.
"My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me."
She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat.
Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader, known as “the tall one”, had also imagined becoming a surgeon.
At school, she had loved Turkish dramas and anime and had a habit of doodling on her desk, much to the annoyance of her biology teacher. Those interests have since fallen away.
She graduated with 98.3 percent and enrolled in medicine at the Islamic University of Gaza on September 10, 2023.
Less than a month later, the war brought her studies to a halt.
Her father, Yunis Abd al-Qader, works as a paramedic with the Palestinian Red Crescent. During the war, he worked 24-hour shifts and returned home only for brief rest.
Lina worried each time he left.
“I would wonder if he would come back the next day," she says. "I wished I could be there with him, to help him through the difficult things he was seeing.”
Usually quiet and reserved, her father tried to spare the family the details of what he encountered. But sometimes, he came home exhausted, and the strain showed.
One account he shared stayed with Lina. After an Israeli strike, he had been recovering human remains. Initially, he believed they belonged to seven people. As he continued working, he realised there was an eighth.
Having witnessed the scale of amputations, fractures and other injuries, she wants to specialise in orthopaedic surgery.
As she continued her medical studies, Lina became close to another student, Shams Majdi.
Their friendship was still new when Lina struggled with a physiology problem and messaged Shams on WhatsApp for help.
Shams lived in northern Gaza, where internet access was unreliable. With Israeli quadcopters overhead, she travelled several kilometres to find a connection so she could help solve the problem with Lina over the phone.
Lina remembers the trouble her new friend took to help her.
Later, the two sat the same exam remotely, from different parts of Gaza.
Shams had again travelled away from home to find an internet connection.
After finishing the exam, Lina opened WhatsApp.
“Shams, did you get home?”
There was no reply.
Lina says Shams was usually quick to respond, when she could. So she waited.
About 45 minutes later, a message appeared in their medical college group announcing that Shams Majdi had been killed.
Lina stared at the name.
For about 10 minutes, she says that she struggled to comprehend that it was the same Shams whose reply she had been waiting for.
She opened their conversation again.
“Shams, where are you?”
“Tell me this is a lie.”
“Shams, reply.”
She kept sending messages throughout the day. None was answered.
Shams had been killed in an Israeli strike on her home, alongside members of her family.
For the following week, Lina says, she cried whenever she opened her medical books.
--
There had been another Lina in Maha's classroom.
Lina al-Hour, the quieter girl who loved novels and wrote letters to her friends, had also enrolled in medicine. She had attended her first week of university before the war began.
On November 17, 2023, an Israeli air strike hit her family's home. Lina was killed alongside her parents, siblings and other relatives.
With no surviving parent or sibling for Al Jazeera to interview, her former classmates and teacher helped piece together memories of her life.
Maha remembers the way she listened in class. The girls remember how easily they could make her laugh.
Lina Abd al-Qader remembers the strangeness of sharing a name with a friend who is now gone.
“I and my friend who was killed had the same name,” she says. “But my friend was killed, and I still cannot get over it.”
Ghaida Zaqout is now in Egypt, more than 300km (186 miles) from the schoolyard where she once posed with her classmates. Speaking to Al Jazeera by phone, she recalls how she used to fill her schoolbooks with drawings of the wooden houses she admired in Japanese anime, and dreamed of becoming an architect.
On October 20, 2023, Ghaida turned 18.
By then, her sister Asmaa, her husband and their two children had moved in after losing their home in an Israeli air strike. Her maternal uncle's family was staying with them, too. About 15 people were living under one roof.
Ghaida decided to make herself a small birthday cake.
She found eggs, flour and baking powder and began arranging the ingredients in the kitchen, joking with her sister's children as she worked.
Then, her aunt called with news that her cousin Majdi, 33, had been killed.
He had always made Ghaida laugh. At family birthdays, he liked to scoop cream from the cake and smear it across her face. A natural storyteller, he could turn even the simplest anecdote into something funny.
They had last seen each other on October 5, when the family went to Roots Cafe on Gaza's seafront.
Ghaida left the ingredients on the kitchen counter and went to check on her mother. She doesn't remember who eventually cleared away the eggs and flour.
Her mother had previously undergone surgery for breast cancer and was receiving follow-up treatment at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, including medication and radiotherapy. As her mother's treatment became harder to continue inside Gaza, because of the genocide, the family decided Ghaida would accompany her out.
Leaving presented a problem she had never imagined having to solve. "I thought, how can I fit 17 years of my life into one bag?" she says.
Ghaida began with paper. She gathered every certificate she could find, going all the way back to kindergarten: school results, awards, certificates from courses she had taken. She packed photographs of friends and family and the little gifts her friends had given her, keeping the messages and notes that came with them.
There were practical things too, like her charger, Lyon potato chips and Al Awda’s crackers, and her pair of white wool pyjamas, speckled with red cherries, that she particularly loved.
Then, there was the family archive.
They had an old camera that had been used to document their lives since before Ghaida was born, along with CDs and a box of photographs accumulated over generations. There were pictures of her grandparents, her mother as a student, her parents before they married, their wedding and the announcement of their marriage.
Ghaida wanted to take the box, but there wasn’t enough room for it.
What she remembers most clearly about packing was deciding what she could bear to leave.
"I wished I could carry the whole house with me," she says, "not the material things, but the things that had meaning for us. You know what I mean? The things that touched our hearts."
The photographs were among the things that stayed behind. Later, certain they would not be able to return, the family asked a relative to go back to the house. There were too many photographs for him to carry away, and they did not want their family pictures falling into other hands.
They asked the relative to burn them.
She crossed through Rafah with her mother and 16-year-old brother Abdul Rahman and eventually settled in Madinaty, in the east of Cairo.
That first day, they ate fried chicken. For the first time in months, the things that had become difficult in Gaza were suddenly easy. Food was available. There was electricity. She could sleep without hearing shelling or drones overhead.
Her friends were still in Gaza. Ghaida would call and hear about the difficulty of finding food and water. Then, she would look at what was available around her in Egypt.
She lost her appetite and her weight plummeted by more than 10kg (22 pounds).
"My soul is in Gaza," she says.
It was not until September 2025 that Ghaida finally began university. She was 19, a month short of 20, sitting among students two years younger.
And she was no longer studying architecture. She chose dentistry to help people in Gaza when she returns.
"If the crossings open permanently," she says, "I will return immediately."
Yasmin Abu Zaid had grown up as "the pampered one", in the words of her older sisters, and something she admits to herself.
She is the youngest of three sisters and remained the family's youngest child for 10 years, until her brother was born. She had few household responsibilities. If she asked for something, her family usually found a way to get it for her.
Her grandfather was particularly indulgent. Whenever he went to the market, he would return with something for Yasmin, food, sweets, whatever had caught his eye and made him think of her.
Within days of the war beginning, Yasmin's life changed.
Her family lived on the third floor of the Ain Jalut towers in Nuseirat, in an apartment along Salah al-Din Street. When a nearby mosque was bombed that October, their home was badly damaged. The family temporarily moved into her grandmother's nearby flat. But by December, Yasmin was fleeing shelling again with her sisters and other relatives. Eventually, they drove south to Rafah, where they found temporary shelter.
Their old apartment was bombed again on January 4, 2024. On a different floor of the same building, her father's goldsmithing workshop, where he worked with gold brought into Gaza from the occupied West Bank, Egypt and Dubai, was destroyed. He has not worked as a goldsmith since.
Then, on June 8, 2024, the apartment they had been displaced to was hit by Israeli fire.
Yasmin was near a window with her sisters and other relatives when a shell struck.
She remembers the explosion, although it was not as loud as she would have expected. Then, the room filled with white dust.
Yasmin could move her arms. She knew she was bleeding, but could not tell where she had been injured. Shrapnel had entered her chest, and she struggled to breathe. Through it all, she could hear the screams for help from her sisters, until one of them passed out.
“I kept closing my eyes because I was so exhausted, and I couldn’t breathe properly,” Yasmin says. “Every time I closed my eyes, I remembered my life before the war. I felt like what was happening was just a nightmare that I wanted to wake up from.”
As her breathing became more difficult, she says, “I genuinely felt like I was going to die.”
Her father managed to find and rescue her and her sisters, but Yasmin says many weren't as lucky. "During the war, I lost about 30 members of my extended family, killed by Israeli forces."
Her education stopped for roughly a year and a half.
When she returned, she chose psychology, the subject that had interested her when she was still the pampered schoolgirl worrying about exams. But now she encountered the material differently.
As Yasmin learned about trauma and children's behaviour, she began recognising some of what she was studying at home.
Her sister would wake crying after hearing explosions. Her younger brother would wake frightened and run. Yasmin had her own response to bombardment.
"I used to look at the wall and feel that it was going to explode in my face," she says.
Her studies have changed the work she imagined doing, too. The girl who had once thought about helping children with disabilities is now particularly interested in children living with trauma.
The subject has also given her a way of thinking about what happened to her own family.
"It had a big impact on helping me accept the bombing of our home, my father's workshop, and everything we have lost," she says.
Back in her classroom, Maha continues teaching mathematics, just as she did before the war. But much has changed.
With classrooms damaged and teachers killed or displaced, the school is struggling to accommodate its pupils. Maha now teaches classes of up to 45 girls, far more than before the war.
Many of her students have been displaced, some repeatedly. Others have lost relatives and classmates. Maha herself is less strict now, she says. "Attendance and rules once mattered. If a student failed to turn up or didn't keep up with homework, I wanted to know why."
Now, she may already know. A girl might have been displaced. Her parents may be afraid to let her travel to school because of shelling. She may have had little to eat.
During periods of severe hunger, Maha watched students trying to follow lessons after barely eating the day before.
"I can see it on their faces," she says. "The girls aren't smiling. Their expressions have changed. They look sad and exhausted."
One of the strongest students in another class began sitting at the back. Maha noticed that 10 or 15 minutes before the end of lessons, the girl would fall asleep. She asked her what was happening.
Both of the girl's parents had been killed. She was caring for her younger sisters while trying to continue her own education.
Although the war had kept formal education largely suspended, some teachers, like Maha, were trying to keep pupils learning where they could, squeezing in classes and exams.
Maha remembers a particular student who would always get top marks. In February 2025, the girl came to her, disappointed with her score of 14 out of 20 on a mathematics exam.
"I told her not to worry. I'd overlook this result and that she should focus on the next exam, and I'm sure she will do better. I said I'd use that mark instead," says Maha. And the girl left happy.
A few hours later, the girl's home was bombed. She was killed. Maha would place two photographs of the girl in the classroom. One on the back wall. Another hung beside the blackboard: a selfie of her smiling, both hands raised in V signs.
"Every time I looked at the photograph, it shook me," Maha says. "I would always remember that moment before she was killed, when she was sitting there worried about her grade."
One thought kept returning. "Thank God, I didn't disappoint her. I kept my promise to her and let her leave that day happy."
Now, the students at their desks finish the problems Maha has set for them.
In the corner by the window, a girl looks up from her desk.
“Miss, I’ve finished. Can you come and check my answers?”
Maha looks once more at the photograph from June 2023, before putting her phone away.

Scientists find hidden materials that could improve batteries and solar fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:20:23 UTC
19:20:23 KST

Scientists find hidden materials that could improve batteries and solar fuels
- Date:
- October 9, 2026
- Source:
- University of Warwick
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden world of “in-between” materials that briefly form as chemical ingredients are heated, revealing structures that conventional methods can miss. Among the discoveries is a previously unknown form of bismuth vanadate, a material widely studied for using sunlight to help produce clean hydrogen. The new version has a different atomic structure and interacts with light in a strikingly different way, potentially opening new possibilities for solar fuels, catalysts, and electronics.
- Share:
Researchers have uncovered previously unknown materials by closely following what happens as molecular precursors break apart and transform during heating. Among the discoveries is a new form of a well-studied clean energy material.
The research, published in Nature Communications, focuses on intermediate phases that appear while molecules are being converted into solid materials. These temporary stages are often overlooked because scientists typically concentrate on the final product. By capturing and studying them, the researchers found a possible route to materials that are difficult or impossible to obtain through conventional synthesis.
Hidden Stages During Material Formation
Dr. Sebastian Pike, Department of Chemistry, University of Warwick, said: "When materials are made by heating, scientists usually focus on the final product, the 'B' that results from 'A.' But this study shows that there are many fascinating stages in between 'A' and 'B,' and these hidden steps, could be just as important.
"We didn't know exactly what we would find going in, but we were confident there would be something interesting and unknown in the intermediate phases. We were thrilled to discover that some of these could have practical uses, even from the very first experiments."
The researchers began with specially designed 'single-source precursors', molecules containing all the elements needed to create a material. They then monitored how those molecules changed as temperatures increased.
This approach exposed several previously unknown material phases. One was a new, kinetically stabilized form of bismuth vanadate (BiVO4), which the researchers named β-BiVO4.
A New Form of Bismuth Vanadate
BiVO4 has attracted attention in clean energy research because of its useful "band gap" (the energy it needs to absorb sunlight and drive chemical reactions). Its properties allow it to absorb sunlight effectively while still supplying enough energy to split water and generate clean hydrogen fuel.
The newly identified β-BiVO4 has an atomic arrangement that differs from known forms of the material. It also has a significantly larger band gap, which changes the way it interacts with light.
Those differences could give researchers new ways to adjust materials for use in solar fuel production, catalysis, and electronics.
Potential for Next Generation Batteries
The newly discovered intermediate phases may also have uses beyond solar energy. Another hidden material identified during the experiments was able to store large amounts of lithium, raising the possibility that it could contribute to next-generation battery technologies.
Dr. Dominik Kubicki, School of Chemistry, University of Birmingham, said: "What's exciting is that these 'in-between' materials aren't just stepping stones -- they can have useful properties in their own right. By understanding and controlling how they form, we can start to design better materials for batteries, catalysis, and solar energy."
To observe these normally hidden states, the researchers combined several state-of-the-art techniques, including solid-state NMR spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and pair distribution function analysis.
Their results also showed that the precursor selected at the beginning of the process, along with the way that precursor decomposes, can strongly influence which materials form. By controlling those factors, researchers may be able to produce structures that are difficult to obtain using standard heating methods.
A New Route to Undiscovered Materials
The findings suggest that temporary stages in material formation could represent a largely unexplored source of useful compounds. Instead of treating intermediate structures only as brief steps on the way to a final material, scientists may be able to deliberately create and stabilize them for practical applications.
Dr. Pike concluded: "We only studied a few precursors here, but this work points to a broader opportunity in materials science. By carefully controlling temperature, precursor chemistry, and reaction pathways, there may be many more "hidden" but extremely useful materials to be found."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Warwick. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alexandria E. Hands, Thomas J. Barnes, Andrea Scarperi, Benjamin M. Gallant, Emanuele Vismara, Julia Wiktor, Stephen E. Brown, David Walker, Ashok S. Menon, Javier Castells-Gil, Dominik J. Kubicki, Sebastian D. Pike. Amorphous intermediates and discovery of a kinetic polymorph of BiVO4 from heating V Bi Zn single-source precursors. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-71702-7

Houthi missile strikes kill three at Riyadh airport including airline captain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:19:37 UTC
19:19:37 KST

Two missile strikes on King Khalid International Airport forced diplomats to shelter in place and delayed dozens of flights, as Yemen’s government claimed progress in its Red Sea counter-offensive. Houthi forces said they were holding their ground.
Three people including an airline pilot were killed in attacks on Riyadh's international airport on Thursday, Saudi Arabia said, after Yemen's Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the facility.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said two missile attacks on Thursday on the Saudi capital's airport and a Saudia Airlines aircraft there "resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens".
The national flag carrier on Friday confirmed the death of the plane's captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami in an incident at King Khalid International Airport, expressing "profound sadness" and "heartfelt condolences," and stating it honoured "his memory with deep respect and appreciation."
The missile strikes on Thursday forced diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city.
Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, while the airport advised travellers of the "necessity" to contact airlines before their trips.
The kingdom's civil defence agency also said "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh. It did not say if there were casualties there or provide details of the damage.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
The Houthis have also warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
'Crisis in everything'
The Houthis, whose heartlands are in Yemen's northwest, had already controlled the capital Sana'a and most of the country's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014.
Riyadh's military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.
Yet Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it backs have struggled to contain the Houthis' latest offensive, despite a pushback aimed at recapturing Red Sea territory including the area around the Bab el-Mandeb strait that is crucial to global energy flows.
After declaring its counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the group formally known as Ansar Allah insists it is holding its territory, and military sources on both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
In Yemen's Taiz, the Houthis are laying siege to the government-controlled city in the country's west, depriving residents of their main supply route to the government's temporary capital in Aden.
"There is a crisis in everything: water, gas, vegetables, everything essential", said Taiz resident Um Rian.

The Foreign Economic Relations Board of Türkiye (DEİK) and the European Business Summit (EBS) will co-host the second EU-Türkiye Business Summit in Brussels on Oct. 13, DEİK has announced.
The summit, to be held at Egmont Palace under the theme “Unlocking the Potential of the EU-Türkiye Economic Partnership,” will bring together senior policymakers, business leaders and investors from Türkiye and Europe.
Expected participants include Turkish Trade Minister Ömer Bolat, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic, Deputy Trade Minister Mustafa Tuzcu, Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the European Union Ambassador Yaprak Balkan, Türkiye’s Ambassador to Brussels Barış Tantekin, DEİK President Nail Olpak, DEİK Türkiye-Europe Business Councils Coordinating Chairman Mehmet Ali Yalçındağ, EBS Chief Executive Officer Arnaud Thysen, ambassadors, senior government officials, lawmakers, think tank leaders, CEOs of global companies and more than 500 business representatives.
Olpak said Türkiye and the EU are two major economic partners with strong ties built over decades, highly integrated production and value chains, and mutual investments.
He said the Türkiye-EU economic relationship should now be assessed not only through trade volumes but also in terms of competitiveness, production capacity, investment, technology, energy and supply-chain resilience.
“We are living through a period in which trade, production and investment decisions are being reshaped globally, while competitiveness, economic security and supply chains are becoming increasingly important. We believe that in this new era, the Türkiye-EU economic partnership should be placed on a more ambitious, inclusive and future-oriented footing,” Olpak said.
Olpak described the modernization of the Customs Union as one of the most important items on the agenda, saying the nearly 30-year-old arrangement has been one of the key achievements of economic integration between Türkiye and the EU.
“We view the modernization of the Customs Union not only as a solution to existing problems but also as a strategic step that will enhance the global competitiveness of both Türkiye and Europe. As the business community, we believe it is important to move beyond dialogue and achieve tangible progress on this issue,” he said.
Olpak added that Türkieye could be a strong partner in Europe’s transformation process, citing the country’s industrial infrastructure, manufacturing capabilities, renewable energy potential, logistics links, entrepreneurial private sector and integration into European value chains.
Yalçındağ said economic ties between Türkiye and the EU rest on a strong foundation but that their full potential has yet to be realized.
“The key issue before us today is to transform this strong foundation into deeper integration. With a combined population of nearly 600 million and an economic size exceeding $20 trillion, Türkiye and the EU together could create a powerful center of attraction on a global scale,” Yalçındağ said.
He said summit participants would discuss issues that will directly shape the future of the Türkiye-EU economic partnership, adding that closer cooperation could strengthen Europe’s competitiveness, energy security, manufacturing capacity and strategic resilience while generating benefits for both sides.

South African Human Rights Lawyer Navi Pillay Wins Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:17:49 UTC
19:17:49 KST

South African lawyer and human rights advocate Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
Pillay previously served as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and held senior positions as a judge and leader in international judicial institutions.
Born in Durban, South Africa, in 1941, Pillay became the first woman to establish her own law practice in Natal province in 1967. During apartheid, she defended activists persecuted by the authorities because of their political activities. In 1995, she became the first Black woman appointed to the Supreme Court of South Africa.
That same year, Pillay was elected a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, serving as its president from 1999 to 2003. Her work at the tribunal helped advance international jurisprudence recognizing that rape and sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide. In 2003, she joined the International Criminal Court in The Hague as a judge.
Pillay served as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014, working to protect fundamental rights and promote accountability for violations of international law. She also heads the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Her longstanding work has focused on advancing international justice and defending human rights, including efforts to investigate and prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Last year, the Nobel Peace Prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado in recognition of her efforts to defend democratic rights and support a peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy in Venezuela.
The Nobel Peace Prize is presented annually by the Norwegian Nobel Committee. It is one of five awards established in the will of Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel in 1895. While the other Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm, the Peace Prize ceremony is held in Oslo.

A drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, disabling several modules at the facility and threatening further disruptions to the company's services.
Several modules of the data center were completely disabled, Yandex said in a statement carried by pro-government Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
"Some Yandex services may experience disruptions as a result," the company said, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Yandex reported no injuries at the facility.
The attack came as drones struck other parts of Kaluga Oblast overnight, injuring nine people, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He also reported damage to houses in two districts of the oblast. Russian authorities claimed to have shot down 26 drones over the region.
Ukraine has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the attack on the Kaluga data center.
The strike marks the second reported attack on a Yandex data center in Russia in two days.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing the facility to suspend operations and disrupting parts of Yandex's cloud infrastructure.
The Sasovo facility houses tens of thousands of servers and two of the company's three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence models. Yandex said it was still assessing whether damaged equipment could be restored.
The attack coincided with reports of widespread internet disruptions across Russia, affecting banking services, transport websites, and online platforms.
Responding to questions about the Sasovo strike on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would continue retaliating against Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
"We responded to them," he added. "I cannot share all the details."
Russian forces struck several Ukrainian internet providers and data centers in Kyiv in late September, disrupting internet access for approximately 100,000 households, according to Ukrainian officials.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tensions within the opposition KMT are growing ahead of the local elections, with divisions over party leadership and defense policy drawing attention from Washington and Beijing, Nikkei Asia reported Friday.
KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) has faced criticism from figures aligned with the party establishment, some of whom have taken a different stance on President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) defense spending plans. Analysts say the split reflects competing views on cross-strait relations and the party’s direction.
A Washington-based analyst sympathetic to the KMT described the party as having “two centers of gravity”: one around Cheng and another centered on Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), who is seen as a possible contender for the KMT’s presidential nomination. Lu’s camp also includes figures connected to the party’s legislative caucus.
National Cheng Kung University assistant professor Chung San-ho (鍾燊豪) said infighting was weakening the party’s campaign efforts. “The party has suffered from a lack of coherent central leadership that can efficiently coordinate their prominent heavyweights,” he said.
The divisions have drawn greater attention as the KMT-led legislative majority considers next year’s defense budget amid uncertainty over US support under President Donald Trump and growing Chinese military pressure, Nikkei Asia reported. The party has repeatedly sought to block or revise Lai’s defense spending plans, prompting criticism from Washington and other governments.
The KMT publicly says its actions are intended to ensure accountability rather than weaken security. Some party figures have privately sought to distance themselves from Cheng, whose high-profile meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in April and questions about Lai’s defense buildup have fueled concerns about her approach to Beijing.
One foreign government official said some KMT politicians were trying to assure Washington that Cheng did not represent the whole party, saying they were “pro-US and pro-defense,” per Nikkei Asia. The official said some US policymakers increasingly viewed other KMT figures as potential partners on defense and institutional reforms.
Lu is seen by some as an alternative to Cheng. She belongs to a relatively US-friendly faction that includes former KMT Chair Eric Chu (朱立倫), Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安). Lu and Chu have previously expressed openness to higher defense spending, although they broadly share Cheng’s views on cross-strait relations.
Recent visits to the US by Lu, Han, and Cheng have highlighted the party’s efforts to maintain ties in Washington. A KMT delegation led by Legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) also met US Representative John Moolenaar last month. Moolenaar said concerns remained over the politicization of Taiwan’s security but that he believed all major parties recognized the urgent need to strengthen defense.
Diplomatic sources said US officials appeared supportive of Lu, while analysts said Beijing remained invested in Cheng’s leadership and could seek to undermine her rivals, per Nikkei Asia. Cheng has rejected claims of deep internal divisions, but another Washington-based analyst said tensions between her and Lu’s camp were real.
The local elections remain a common goal for the party, but Chung warned that the lack of coordination from party headquarters could hurt its prospects as local leaders focus on defending their constituencies. One KMT insider summed up the uncertainty by saying, “No one knows what will happen after the local elections.”

19:15:18 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD) has projected that global economic growth will be 2.6 percent in 2026, down from 2.9 percent in 2025.
In its Trade and Development Report 2026 released on Friday, UNCTAD said developing economies are expected to grow by 4 percent this year, easing from 4.7 percent in 2025.
In 2026, rising energy prices are pushing up trade values, while trade in goods and services is projected to expand by about 4 percent at constant prices, the report said.
According to the report, Asia is set to account for 59 percent of global growth in 2026. East Asia sits at the heart of the rapid expansion in semiconductors and advanced computing manufacturing.
The report noted that artificial intelligence (AI) products have become the main driver of merchandise trade, yet growth in AI-related trade does not automatically translate into broad development gains.
The report warned that the energy shock and financial instability are putting the global economy to the test.
It argued that the energy shock underscores the need to diversify energy supply. Addressing energy and supply bottlenecks is more effective against supply-driven inflation than broad monetary and fiscal tightening, the report said. ■

Palestinian Authority deputy chairman pushes off legislative election by several months - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:15:15 UTC
19:15:15 KST

Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al Sheikh has informed France that a Palestinian legislative election planned for November 28 will be postponed, possibly until September 2027, because of worsening conditions throughout the Palestinian territories, according to a letter seen by Reuters.
"The assessment concluded that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for 28 November 2026 was based, have not materialized," said the letter, which was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and dated October 8.
It added that "holding them under the current circumstances faces fundamental obstacles affecting their inclusiveness, freedom of participation and the integrity of the electoral process."
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
Some officials within Abbas' Fatah party have demanded dialogue with Hamas and other factions to agree on a common national vision before proceeding with a vote. Others have cited obstructions to ballot boxes, election papers and ink entering Gaza, which they say would make voting impossible.
Palestinian officials say they expected US action
The letter said Palestinian officials had expected conditions to improve through the implementation of US President Donald Trump's peace initiative and a UN Security Council resolution, including the deployment of international forces and Palestinian police in Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli troops.
It said the Palestinians had also anticipated US efforts to prevent further annexation of Palestinian territory in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, curb settler violence and secure the release of nearly $7 billion in Palestinian funds withheld by Israel.
"However, these steps, understandings and promises have not materialized. Rather, conditions have worsened throughout the Palestinian territory," the letter said, outlining in detail security issues in Gaza and the West Bank.
Based on their assessment, Palestinian officials recommended to Abbas "that the date of the legislative elections be adjusted by several months, and that dialog continue to prepare the internal conditions," the letter said.
It added that Abbas had been advised to issue a decree adjusting the date for holding elections to the first half of September 2027.
Abbas, elected president of the PA in 2005, had reaffirmed plans to hold the elections during a speech to the United Nations on September 24.
France said elections were essential
The letter was addressed to France after it recognized a Palestinian state in September 2025. As part of that decision, France had urged that the planned legislative and presidential elections proceed, a written commitment that Abbas had made to President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, France's foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said it was essential for the elections to take place and hailed the launch of an EU mission to observe the elections.
"These elections will enable the Palestinian leadership to champion its people's legitimate aspirations with renewed legitimacy, while preserving the two-state solution," he said.
In the more than two decades since Abbas was elected as the successor to Fatah founder Yasser Arafat, the PA's public standing has sunk among Palestinians, who have grown to view it as ineffective and corrupt.
In 2007, the PA was driven out of the Gaza Strip by Hamas militants, who had won an election there on an anti-corruption platform. Abbas has ruled by decree since his mandate expired in 2009.
A peace process meant to lead to the creation of a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem collapsed in 2014, and expanding Israeli settlements have since carved up areas once slated for eventual Palestinian control.
Israel allegedly blocks PA elections commission from east Jerusalem, Gaza
On Wednesday, Israel allegedly blocked the Palestinian Central Elections Commission from entering east Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip to monitor the November 28 elections, a Palestinian Authority official told the PA’s official WAFA news agency, as European Commission Vice President and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas renewed Europe’s commitment to deploying an election observation mission.
Though the CEC has yet to issue an official statement on the alleged block, CEC spokesperson Farid Taamallah confirmed the report to Agence France-Presse and insisted that the elections could still go ahead.
Taamallah has not yet responded to The Jerusalem Post’s request.
Danielle Greyman-Kennard contributed to this report.

Founder of Russian war blog Rybar arrested in Montenegro

Russian war blogger expelled from Montenegro for 'security reasons'
BELGRADE, Oct 9 - The founder of the influential Russian war blog Rybar was arrested in Montenegro and then expelled with three other Russians on Friday for national security reasons, police and the state security agency said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, who is also a former Russian Defence Ministry official, was detained with others including his wife in the Adriatic resort of Risan on charges of spreading "Russian influence", Pobjeda newspaper reported, citing sources.
Rybar — one of the most popular blogs on Russia's war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers — posted a message saying Zvinchuk and the others had been in the country legally and were planning to film at a monastery there.
RYBAR FACED BRITISH SANCTIONS
"Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released," Rybar said.
The Russian embassy in Podgorica said it had demanded clarification on the reasons for the arrests.
The blog is part of a network of sites and media feeds covering a wide range of Russian activities.
Britain imposed sanctions on 10 individuals linked to Rybar in July, saying the media company was resourced by the Russian state and "responsible for spreading false narratives about Ukraine and interfering in European elections, including in Moldova and Armenia".
Moscow has regularly denied accusations of misinformation and sabotage campaigns, saying the West is spreading anti-Russian propaganda.
Montenegro has long had fraught relations with Moscow. In 2016, authorities there accused Russia of plotting with a group of Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, a charge the Kremlin denied.
Ties soured further when the small Adriatic republic joined NATO in 2017.
Montenegro, a candidate for membership in the European Union, enforced sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine in 2022, banned Russian state media and expelled Russian diplomats for spying. In a retaliatory move, Moscow declared it an enemy state.
Montenegro's Prime Minister, Milojko Spajic, earlier announced the arrests and said there had been warnings that the country would face attempts to destabilise it and hybrid warfare - acts that fall short of direct military conflict.
"The message after today's successful operation ... is clear," he said. "Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future," he added.
Montenegrin police and the ANB state security agency said four Russian nationals they identified only by initials "were uncovered and processed".
"It was determined that these persons cannot continue their stay in Montenegro ... (and) it was decided to expel them from Montenegro for reasons of national and internal security of the state," the statement read.
