US diesel prices remain high despite Trump's moves to boost supplies
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Oct 9 - US diesel prices remain at near-record highs, up 70% since the US-Israeli war on Iran began despite two recent moves by President Donald Trump to boost supplies: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing the average US diesel price to $6.28 a gallon on Friday, according to motorist group AAA.
“Aside from a recession that hammers consumption, the only thing that can prevent oil prices from rising further and put them on a sharp downward trajectory is a durable end to conflicts in the Arabian Gulf and between Russia and Ukraine,” said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group. “Otherwise, policy options range from marginal to counterproductive.”
High fuel prices have made it harder for Trump and his Republican Party to defend narrow congressional majorities in the November 3 midterm elections. The cost of living is the top item cited by voters in a Reuters/Ipsos poll, and high diesel prices put particular pressure on traditional Republican constituencies: farmers, truckers and rural voters.
Trump’s approval rating is at a career-low 32%, according to the poll.
The administration has touted a G7 agreement to release 100 million barrels of oil and petroleum products as a major step to help ease prices, but those barrels appear to largely cover what remains of a March emergency release by International Energy Agency members, rather than new supply.
A White House official disputed that characterization, saying the earlier commitments were not specifically for refined products. The administration negotiated for the previously committed barrels to be front-loaded with diesel and released on a tight timeline beginning immediately, the official said.
The White House said Trump was focused on easing temporary disruptions while pursuing longer-term energy policies.
RED-DYED DIESEL
The administration's other major initiative, an executive order allowing red-dyed diesel on public roads through year-end, has drawn limited industry uptake. The fuel is chemically identical to what trucks normally burn but is tinted to show it is exempt from the 24.4-cent-per-gallon federal highway tax.
The order defers the federal tax and waives penalties for burning off-road fuel on highways. But major retailers and marketers remain wary of selling it because of unclear tax liabilities, logistical hurdles and the risk of fines when trucks cross state lines.
The tax savings are relatively small with diesel prices above $6 a gallon.
David Fialkov, who lobbies on behalf of NATSO, a trade group for truck stops and travel centers, said the White House appeared to be encouraging the supply chain to sell dyed fuel through channels not traditionally used for highway diesel, but said that most reputable retailers and marketers were unlikely to do so.
John Tirado, president of New Jersey-based commercial fuel supplier Summa Energy, called the red-dyed diesel plan “a Band-Aid on a much bigger problem.”
The White House said more than 4,000 retailers distribute dyed diesel. It said Treasury Department guidance will clarify the rules, allowing drivers to use it without federal tax or penalty. It said the savings should outweigh any detour costs for truckers seeking the fuel.
“The fundamental problem facing the US is not taxation but an exceptionally tight global market for refined products,” said Caspian Conran, lead economist at Baringa, citing disruptions to energy flows from the Middle East and reduced refining output elsewhere.
He described the measures as short-term steps ahead of the election that could provide “probably a few weeks of relief,” rather than a durable solution. REUTERS

The findings were uncovered as part of the ministry's efforts to identify and track foreign activists planning to enter Israel and the West Bank as part of organized international campaigns.
According to information collected by the ministry's National Command Center, the organization is currently recruiting international activists for a program that includes a stay of at least two weeks, training in "direct action," political and media training, and a commitment to continued political activity in their home countries after returning.
As presented by the organization, the program aims to go beyond maintaining a temporary presence on the ground. It seeks to turn participants into "catalysts" for further political organizing and activism in their home countries, as part of what the organization itself describes as "the broader confrontation with Zionism as a political project."
According to assessments, the program could help develop a long-term international network of activists, although the organization does not explicitly state this as an objective.
The registration page describes the initiative as being led by Palestinian organizers. According to a post on the organization's X/Twitter account, the application deadline was October 7, 2026.
International activists recruited ahead of olive harvest
The program joins several other campaigns identified as recruiting international activists to the West Bank ahead of the 2026 olive harvest season, including Go Palestine, Protect the Harvest, Faz3a, and the International Solidarity Movement. These organizations also describe their activities as providing a "protective presence" alongside Palestinian communities.
The experiences, training, and connections developed on the ground are intended to support continued political organizing in participants' home countries and contribute, in the words of the registration page, to "the broader confrontation with Zionism as a political project."
According to the registration page, Palestinian organizers and communities determine where volunteers will be deployed, which activities will take place, and when they will be carried out. Participants are required to follow these instructions, even in cases where they would have chosen to act differently.
Before beginning their accompaniment activities, participants are expected to undergo "training in nonviolence and direct action." The organization seeks to extend the program's influence beyond the volunteers' activities in the West Bank.
Applicants who have difficulty financing their travel are encouraged to indicate this, and many participants raise donations to fund their stays.
The registration page also addresses the possibility of being denied entry to Israel. Using the organization's terminology, it states that entry is controlled by the "Israeli occupation authorities" and that an applicant's chances of being admitted may be affected by their passport, name, travel history, family background, and publicly expressed political activity.
Applicants who are unable to enter through Israel may be referred to other activities.
Diaspora Affairs Ministry warns foreign activists
Avi Cohen-Scali, director-general of the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry, said, "The State of Israel will not serve as a playground for foreign anarchists. Anyone seeking to come here as part of an organized network whose purpose is to create provocations, disrupt public order, and act against the State of Israel should know that Israel identifies them, locates them, and will take action against them using all the legal tools at its disposal."
"The activity does not begin at Israel's entry points, nor does it end there. The ministry is working to map the activists, organizations, and infrastructure involved in these campaigns, transfer the information to the relevant authorities, and advance appropriate measures both inside and outside Israel, in accordance with the law and in cooperation with the relevant bodies," he added.
"We will act against the activists and the infrastructure behind them, both in Israel and abroad. The message is clear and unequivocal: Anyone who acts in an organized manner to undermine public order and harm the State of Israel and its legitimacy will encounter a state that is prepared, determined, and active, both at home and abroad."

SAO PAULO/BRASILIA, Oct 9 - Two starkly different visions for US-Brazil relations hang in the balance in Brazil’s presidential runoff, but the strategies of both Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva come with their own risks, experts said.
Bolsonaro heads toward the October 25 runoff with momentum after he secured 47% of the first-round vote to Lula’s 45%, following a campaign where both candidates’ relationships with Washington drew scrutiny.
The stakes are high. Brazil’s next president will have to navigate tensions between its first- and second-largest trading partners — China and the US — while shaping strategies on mineral development, industrialization, and regional cooperation.
Brazil and the US established a working group last month to drive negotiations over tariffs and a broader bilateral trade framework, with US access to Brazil's critical minerals and rare earths emerging as a key point of contention as Washington looks to reduce its dependence on China for those minerals.
If the challenger wins, "the Americans may prove reluctant to yield anything to Lula, preferring to wait and negotiate with Bolsonaro," said Rubens Barbosa, a former Brazilian ambassador to the US.
Lula's strategy toward the US has focused on defending Brazil's sovereignty after US President Donald Trump heaped pressure on Brazil to drop charges against Bolsonaro's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is now serving a 27-year sentence for trying to plot a coup.
A nationalist tone has framed Lula's engagement with Washington, while he prioritizes multilateralism and closer ties with the Global South, including the BRICS bloc, which includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, among other countries.
Though the approach helped his popularity at home, the leftist has enjoyed checkered progress in negotiations with Washington, experts told Reuters.
If Lula manages to win reelection, an incoming Congress dominated by right-wing parties could push a "weaker Lula" to change tack, said Monica de Bolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics in Washington.
"I believe there would be a lot of pressure on Lula to give in to some US demands regarding natural resources, as well as other issues," said de Bolle.
BOLSONARO’S GAMBLES
While "Lula has a well-established foreign policy," said Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat who served in the US and Europe, Bolsonaro's is a "blank slate."
The senator has a friendly relationship with the Trump administration, aided by his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former Brazilian congressman who has resided in the US since early last year and was convicted by Brazil's Supreme Court for inviting US intervention in their father's legal proceedings in 2025.
While neither brother has confirmed the rumors, a person close to the campaign told Reuters that the two have been discussing potential international roles for the younger sibling if the senator becomes Brazil's next president.
If Bolsonaro is elected president "there would be a foreign policy much more aligned with the United States than Brazil traditionally has had,” said de Bolle.
The family's close ties to the Trump administration could secure a more favorable negotiating environment with Washington, though Bolsonaro risks making concessions on key issues like strategic minerals, experts said.
"The path seems clear for good agreements," but Bolsonaro would face questions from supporters about Brazil's autonomy from the US and "more pressure to maintain an independent narrative," said Jean Castro, president of the Brazilian Association of Institutional and Governmental Relations.
Since launching his campaign, Bolsonaro has courted Trump, as well as other right-wing allies abroad like Argentina’s Javier Milei and Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella.
Bolsonaro and Trump have already aligned on strategy for combating organized crime. Visiting Washington in May, he urged Trump to designate major Brazilian criminal factions as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, a proposal Washington accepted but which Lula flatly rejected as intervention. Lula instead advocated for a national approach to address security with international cooperation.
Public opinion polls have shown Lula’s popularity got a bump from his frequent disagreements with Trump on trade and security, while other surveys showed Brazilians held Bolsonaro more responsible for tariffs imposed by Trump in July.
"He cannot adopt a stance that could be mistaken for subservience," said Castro. REUTERS

Best Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers (2026): Tested for Power, Battery Life, and Noise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:10:00 UTC
19:10:00 KST

Leaves are a problem of addition by subtraction: Just a couple of mature trees can drop enough debris that you need to remove, and in the process, consume hours of your weekends. Mowing leaves into mulch is a compelling option, but you’ll still need to wrangle them off driveways, walkways, flower beds, and patios. Gas blowers have long been the standard, but rising noise bans, finicky engines that are hard to start, and battery advances are cutting into their appeal.
If you’re on the fence about a leaf blower, know that owning one of any kind will reduce the amount of raking you do, but rarely eliminate it. For small yards, or if you (or your neighbor) have just one medium-sized deciduous tree, a rake and a tarp may be all you need. On the other hand, if you live in an arboretum, the long run time of a gas backpack blower may be worth the maintenance headaches—unless you’re willing to invest heavily in multiple batteries.
I’ve tested the newest crop of battery-powered blowers on everything from heavy fabric leaves to gravel, mulch, and even knocking over a concrete paver. Today’s models deliver serious clearing power without the gas-can hassle, though run time is always the primary trade-off. Here’s everything you need to know about battery-powered blowers.
Featured
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Overall
When factoring in overall performance along with the quality and diversity of Ego’s outdoor tool ecosystem, this blower is the best option for most users. In testing, it delivered gaslike power, easily knocking over a 5-pound brick paver on high speed where lesser machines required turbo mode, and it cleared the test patch of leaves without issue, without relying on turbo. Even with all that power, it was the second-quietest machine on turbo, registering about 89.7 decibels at an arm’s-length distance of 30 inches—though Ego still suggests hearing protection.
A bright, 1.75-inch LCD serves as the tool’s dashboard and is easy to read even in direct sunlight, though some details, like confirmation that a battery is installed, add clutter without much information. The electronic cruise control is intuitive: squeeze the variable-speed trigger to your desired speed, press the speed lock button, then release the trigger. The blower maintains that pace until you press the speed lock button again.
Ergonomically, the blower’s relatively narrow frame keeps the tool comfortable and tight to your body during operation, and the unit naturally pitches the nozzle towards the floor. A plastic grid covering the air intake and battery location helps prevent stray leaves from clogging the vents. The included fan nozzle widens the airflow for clearing hardscapes, though on a lawn, it can scatter leaves rather than help corral them. The tool sits securely on a wide base so it doesn’t tip very easily and has a stubby, 4.5-inch-long nozzle beneath the blower tube that works for drying a car or a grill.
Ego's was nearly the most expensive blower we tested, and its 56-volt battery powers a capable range of outdoor power equipment, from lawn mowers to string trimmers and chainsaws, making it a good choice for outfitting your garage or shed. The manufacturer has also branched into lifestyle gear, including portable power stations that run on its tool batteries, fans, wet-dry vacuums, and even a fun-looking minibike. The downside of this leaf blower is run time, which Ego attempts to offset by packaging the kit with two 4 amp-hour batteries. It had the shortest run time of the tested models, a direct trade-off for its high performance. The thinking is that you can charge one battery while using the other, which may work for most users since few people blow continuously for 11 minutes.
Best Budget
The Skil checks two important boxes for a battery-powered leaf blower: It was the least expensive model we tested and tied for the longest run time, at just over 33 minutes on high. Skil, a sister company to Ego, couldn’t match our top pick’s power—it would only knock over the brick on turbo and took a bit longer to push a brick-topped tarp—but it’s capable for most common leaf-blowing jobs. It was also the quietest blower in our test, registering 78.6 decibels on high, though Skil still recommends hearing protection.
The trigger system is as simple as it gets: Pull the variable-speed trigger, or rotate the dial with your thumb to set cruise control for longer sessions. Like most blowers, a separate button engages boost mode. The air intake is covered on all four sides by a black plastic grid that didn’t clog with leaves during testing, though if one gets sucked in it should be easy to pull off. This compact blower measures just under 36 inches long and is one of the few models that can stand upright when the battery is attached, which could help with storage.
Like the Ego, it has a short tube built into the housing, which is handy when you need high-volume airflow in a tight space. The secondary handle, while not very useful for clearing the lawn, makes the tool easier to rotate, position, and hold at awkward angles for jobs like clearing gutters, directing airflow around a vehicle for pushing water or snow, or clearing a workbench.
The Skil’s impressive run time is partly due to the 6-amp-hour battery it comes with, though the blower is also available with a slightly less capable 4-amp-hour battery for about $20 less. That 40-volt battery can power a range of core lawn and garden tools, including mowers, trimmers, and chainsaws, and the system has earned a solid reputation for performance and run time. Skil doesn’t yet have much in the lifestyle department—it does have a handy inverter which helps get more use out of the battery between weekends, but doesn’t offer the range of battery amp-hours Ego does.
Best Mix of Power and Run time
At the intersection of power and endurance, the Husqvarna 350iB feels as capable as the Ego but offers roughly three times the run time. This well-designed, capable tool costs as much as our winner, but delivers somewhat less value: It comes with only one battery, powers a smaller lineup of tools, and carries a three-year warranty instead of Ego’s five. In testing, it cleared our test patch of leaves with ease and, in turbo mode, knocked over the paver. It’s also relatively quiet at both high and turbo speeds, and recharges quickly in just under an hour and a half.
The 350iB’s high power is plenty strong for all but the most stubborn jobs. The tool is well-balanced, keeping the tube pitched slightly downward when walking. Thoughtful design details include punchy springs that help eject the battery, rubbery feet to protect the surface you set it on, and a second nozzle with a stiff plastic scraper that helps dislodge wet, matted leaves from a patio. The controls rely on graphics rather than words, but the buttons are intuitive to decipher.
If you’re new to outdoor power equipment and expect to build a system out to cover the basics, Husqvarna is a good choice to handle core lawn and garden tasks like lawn mowing, string trimming, and cutting wood with a chainsaw. The system doesn’t offer the variety of lifestyle tools that Ego or Ryobi do, however, and Husqvarna’s tools tend to cost more than comparable models. But for homeowners who prioritize power and run time, the 350iB makes a strong case for the Husqvarna system. The higher price and shorter warranty are the main trade-offs.
Best System
The Ryobi has an excellent mix of power and balance, plus a rubbery nozzle tip that makes it easy to pry debris off the ground. But price wise, it sits between better-performing models and our favorite budget pick. The blower’s power and ease of use are hampered by a scant 12-minute run time, despite having the largest amp-hour battery in the test. That short run time, combined with the long recharge time, makes it less practical for larger cleanup jobs, unless you have a second battery.
The Ryobi measured under 85 decibels on high. The rear intake is lined with foam that helps tame the noise. There’s no boost or turbo button here, so you pick between two cruise control settings for max power or max run time, or squeeze the variable speed trigger. It’s a capable blower, but its biggest advantage is the 40-volt system behind it: Ryobi offers one of the widest ranges of tools that use the same battery, making the platform, rather than any single tool’s performance, its strongest selling point.
Like nearly every outdoor power equipment manufacturer, Ryobi uses the same battery across a range of push mowers, string trimmers, and chainsaws. But the company also offers useful niche tools, including a leaf vacuum mulcher, handheld power washer, and log splitter. The same battery can power heavier-duty equipment, too, including a two-stage snow blower, rear-tine tiller, and auger. For someone planning to build out a broad outdoor power equipment collection, that range is a significant advantage.
Others Tested
Greenworks 80V Electric Leaf Blower for $190: This was a powerful blower with about 15 minutes of run time on high, which was longer than our favorite model. It also stayed well below 90 decibels, even in turbo mode. The blower is very narrow and comfortable to hold, and has a 4-year warranty on the battery, which was the longest in our test. Sometimes the tool is on sale for less than $200 as a kit, which is a good value for the power, and a recharge time of about 40 minutes. On sale, it’s about the same as our budget pick, which felt as powerful and had a longer run time.
FAQs
What to Look for (and What to Skip) in a Leaf Blower
Here’s what I’d focus on when buying a blower for leaf cleanup:
Volts: In the cordless power-tool arms race, leaf blower batteries range from 18 to 80 volts. Some of that difference is marketing trickery: an advertised 20-volt max battery or tool delivers essentially the same power as an 18-volt model, and the same goes for 36- and 40-volt options. But, unless you’re a minimalist who wants one battery to power everything from a drill/driver to lawn and garden gear, you’ll probably be happier with a leaf blower that uses at least a 36-volt battery. A few capable 18-volt blowers use two batteries—either simultaneously to mimic the power of a 36-volt tool or in succession to increase the run time—but they tend to cost more and only make sense if you already own the batteries. For smaller jobs, though, a standard, single-battery 18- or 20-volt blower may be all you need to clear a patio, clean out the garage or shed, or dry a car.
Amps: Volts get most of the marketing attention on the box, but a battery’s amp-hour rating tells you more about how long a blower runs. Think of voltage as the car’s engine and amp-hours as the size of the gas tank—you want to know both. Batteries with higher amp-hour ratings cost more than otherwise-similar battery voltages, and they tend to be heavier. For leaf blowers, manufacturers typically pair kits with batteries rated from 4 to 8 amp-hours. You can buy higher-capacity batteries separately, and it pays to know the range of options a manufacturer has. A battery with a higher amp-hour typically takes longer to charge.
Systems: Underestimating the range of tools a battery can power in pursuit of “the best” is, in my opinion, a mistake. Often, the difference between two top-performing tools is negligible, and with cordless power tools, that difference often comes down to run time, which you can address with a higher-capacity battery. If your garage is already stocked with one brand’s outdoor power equipment (OPE), it makes sense to stay within that platform and buy the blower as a bare tool, leveraging the batteries you already have. Switching brands just to buy “the best” probably isn’t worth it to introduce a whole new battery and charger.
If you’re new to OPE—and a leaf blower is a common first purchase—the breadth of tools that share the battery matters. Some manufacturers stick to the lawn and garden basics, so one battery can power a blower, mower, string trimmer, and hedge trimmer, while others offer a much wider range of tools, from log splitters to snow blowers, and even some handy lifestyle products like portable power stations. Before buying, consider what else you can power with the battery that comes with your leaf blower because, chances are, lording over leaves won’t be your only lawn and garden chore.
Traditional 18-volt power tool manufacturers—the ones who make drill/drivers and circular saws—all offer leaf blowers and the simplicity of a one-battery platform, but they’re not powerful enough to replace a gas unit. Ryobi, for example, uses 18-volt batteries across its traditional power tools, and some outdoor equipment, but its most capable gas alternative options run on 40-volt batteries.
Detent clasp: Blowers have two or more connection points: where the tube meets the housing and where the nozzle attaches to the tube. Look for models with a detent at those junctions—a small, often brightly colored spring-loaded clip that snaps into place with a satisfying click when the parts connect. I find these connections hold more securely and last longer than simple friction-fit attachments.
Stubby nozzle: Recently, blowers aimed at car detailers, with short tubes and sometimes a pistol grip, have become popular. Manufacturers responded by adding a stubby, 3- to 6-inch tube that the main blower attachment slides over. When you remove the longer tube, this short one works to direct the volume of air with an overall shorter tool length that’s easier to use around cars or in tight spots (the blower’s nozzle doesn’t fit on this stubby tube, though, so you lose some velocity).
What I’d Worry Less About:
Weight: Across the board, regardless of voltage, a good battery-powered blower will weigh about 10.5 pounds with the battery attached. If you need a lighter option, look for an 18-volt powered blower. Some have better balance than others, meaning that when you hold them without squeezing the trigger, as you would while walking around, the tool stays mostly level or the nozzle end tips down a bit. These models will cause less fatigue than one that forces you to rotate the nozzle upward. With the former, you only need to make a slight horizontal twisting motion to spread the stream of air. Most modern leaf blowers also draw air in a straight line through the rear of the tool, unlike gas-powered models with intakes mounted to the left or right of the engine. Those offset intakes can create a twisting motion that increases hand fatigue and may even suck in your pant leg.
CFM, MPH, and Newton: This sounds counterintuitive, considering how much marketing goes into boasting about a leaf blower’s cubic feet per minute (CFM) and MPH, but these figures are a guide, not necessarily the only reason to buy a specific model. A blower needs both to be useful: CFM tells you how much air it moves, while MPH tells you how fast that air is moving. But there’s no universally adopted testing method for these specifications when it comes to battery-powered blowers (ANSI/OPEI B175.2, the standard test on the books, applies only to internal combustion engines). That means brands can test their units differently — for example, measuring MPH where the motor meets the tube rather than at the end of the blower tube, which gives you a better sense of the airspeed you’ll actually get in use. Some CFM numbers are also measured with the unit running in its max, boost, or turbo setting, rather than on high speed.
Newtons, a unit of force, is a rating that’s appearing more frequently on the spec sheets of higher-voltage, battery-powered leaf blowers and is the best apples-to-apples comparison of blowing power. However, because there’s no testing code for battery-powered leaf blowers, reporting newtons is optional and, like CFM and MPH, consumers have no way of knowing whether the test is standardized. Generally speaking, a good midrange blower will produce around 20 newtons, while models that produce more are typically higher-performing units. Treat newtons as a guide rather than a definitive specification while buying.
Wide nozzles: Some blowers come with a wide-tip nozzle, which can be useful for clearing paved surfaces like patios and driveways or blowing water off flat surfaces. But in practice, it’s not enough of a game changer to be a deciding factor. The narrower nozzle is typically what you’ll use, and you can twist your hand back and forth to create a wider pattern when needed.
How Noisy Are Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers?
When tested from 30 inches away to approximate the noise you’d hear at arm’s length, the blowers ranged from 78.6 decibels on high to 95.2 decibels on turbo. Most user manuals recommend wearing hearing protection when using these tools, particularly for extended periods. By comparison, a handheld gas blower might produce 100 to 110 decibels. That might not sound like a lot more noise, but generally, a 10-decibel increase is perceived by the ear as roughly twice as loud.
Much of the noise reduction comes from eliminating the idling gas engine. Your neighbors will thank you for going battery-powered, too: In open air, sound typically drops by about 6 decibels each time you double your distance from the source. That means your neighbor across the street might hear your battery-powered blower at roughly the same volume as standing next to a washing machine.
What Else Are Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers Good For?
Besides clearing leaves and grass clippings, these fume-free tools are handy for all sorts of jobs. Use one to dry wet surfaces after rain or washing, including your car, patio furniture, or deck. In winter, a blower can remove a light dusting of snow from your car, making it easier to clear areas like the roof. With a cautious trigger finger, you can also clear dry leaves from gutters—just avoid wet, matted debris, which will only turn into a mess below. When grilling or firing up a pizza oven or outdoor fire pit, a gentle stream of air from a safe distance can help get the flames going. Indoors, a blower can clear dust from baseboard heating assemblies or remove lint from your dryer vent.
How I Tested Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers
I put each blower through a series of tests to gauge power, run time, noise, and ease of use. I spread about 8,800 3x3-inch polyester crafting leaves—nearly 4 pounds’ worth—over a measured 6-by-6-foot area and used each blower to clear the section, noting which models could do the job on high and which required a boost or turbo mode. To test blowing power, I placed a 5-pound concrete paver a fixed distance from the nozzle and recorded which machines could knock it over on high and which needed turbo.
For run time, I fully charged each battery, ran the blower at its highest standard speed, excluding any turbo or max settings, and timed how long it lasted. I measured noise with a smartphone decibel-meter app held 30 inches from the air intake while each blower ran on high and at any available turbo or max setting. I also performed practical tests to see how well each model moved gravel and wood chips and cleared water from surfaces such as a grill and patio furniture.

Candidate for Latvia’s State Chancellery director has only sports-related experience in public institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:09:46 UTC
19:09:46 KST

Kaspars Gorkšs, who has been nominated for the position of Director of Latvia’s State Chancellery, has previously gained experience in state or municipal institutions only in the field of sports, according to information provided by the State Chancellery to LETA about his professional background.
A second competition for the position of State Chancellery Director was announced on the 7th of August this year. One of the requirements was that candidates have experience working in state and/or municipal institutions.
Gorkšs currently works at the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia (LDDK), where he has served as Director General since the 3rd of April, 2023. At the same time, he has also been Director of the Jūrmala Football School since the 9th of November, 2020.
Previously, from March 2021 to October 2023, he was a board member of the Latvian Sports Federations Council. For three years, from March 2020 to March 2023, he served as Executive Director of the Latvian Association of Team Sports.
From March 2018 to October 2019, Gorkšs was President of the Latvian Football Federation.
According to information provided by the State Chancellery, Gorkšs also has teaching experience, having delivered lectures in the University of Latvia’s Sports Law course from September 2023 to August 2024.
Gorkšs studied at the University of Latvia, where he obtained a bachelor’s degree in law and a master’s degree in political science.
As previously reported, following the final round of the selection process, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) will submit the candidacy of LDDK Director General Kaspars Gorkšs for government approval as Director of the State Chancellery.
The government is scheduled to consider his appointment at its meeting on the 13th of October.
Kulbergs explained that he expects the State Chancellery to become a strong, data-driven centre of government that helps decisions be made more quickly and accurately.
“I believe Gorkšs has the appropriate experience to implement the changes I have outlined for the State Chancellery. All three finalists are strong leaders with experience both within and outside public administration, and I thank each of them for participating in the competition,” Kulbergs said.
Of the nine candidates who reached the second round, the evaluation committee selected three for the final stage: former Director General of the State Revenue Service and current sectoral attaché at the Central Finance and Contracting Agency Ieva Jaunzeme, Director of the Latvian School of Public Administration Agita Kalviņa, and Gorkšs.
During the third round, candidates were assessed on their management competencies, including strategic vision, decision-making and willingness to take responsibility,
 results orientation, change management and team leadership.
The selection process for the State Chancellery Director took place in three stages.
After evaluating 18 applications, nine candidates advanced to the second round, while three reached the final stage.
In accordance with the competition procedure, the candidate evaluation committee made a decision on the results of the third round and informed the prime minister.
As previously reported, former State Chancellery Director Raivis Kronbergs was detained in May in the so-called timber industry case.
He was initially suspended from his position, but the parties later agreed that Kronbergs would leave the post.
The State Chancellery serves as the centre of Latvia’s government. Its task is to ensure the functioning of the government and provide the prime minister and Cabinet with information based on data and research.
This includes conducting data analysis, assessing different policy scenarios and involving experts from various fields to support more accurate, evidence-based decision-making.
The State Chancellery is headed by its director, who is the country’s highest-ranking civil servant.
Since September 2015, the State Chancellery has been responsible for the centralised selection of heads of state institutions within Latvia’s direct public administration.

Bipartisan majority of Americans blame Trump policies for rising costs, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:09:41 UTC
19:09:41 KST

Bipartisan majority of Americans blame Trump policies for rising costs, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 - Some 78% of Americans blame President Donald Trump's policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that found majorities of Republicans and Democrats citing the cost of living as their top concern ahead of next month's midterm elections.
Fifty-seven percent of Trump's Republicans said that costs have been growing faster than their paychecks, a stark example of how his pursuit of import tariffs, war with Iran and other policies have clashed with a central 2024 campaign promise to kill inflation and lower prices "on day one."
Inflation instead has increased, to the point where the US Federal Reserve has pivoted to rate hikes to quell price increases policymakers have attributed to a variety of factors, including rising global energy costs following the start of the Iran war, and the administration's imposition of aggressive import taxes.
Concerns about the economy and the war have driven Trump's public approval to record lows and have been weighing on support for his party ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
About one in four Republicans disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy, a view shared by 63% of independents and 92% of Democrats. Disapproval was even sharper when it came to inflation, with 68% of all respondents and 40% of Republicans dissatisfied.
Jeffrey Talley, 65, a retired bank examiner from Mission Hills, Kansas, is a registered Republican, who said he voted for Trump in 2016 but not in 2020 or 2024 and now plans to vote for Democrat Adam Hamilton in what has become an unexpectedly competitive Senate race in the state.
"I'm pretty much against all the nonsense that's going on in the Middle East with the Iran war, and pushing up the price of gasoline ... that's been very disheartening," said Talley. He views the election as a chance to elect "somebody to put a check and balance on the craziness that's going on in the White House."
The six-day Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted online and nationwide and completed on Monday, gathered responses from 4,506 US adults. It had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for Americans in general and 3 points for Republicans, Democrats and independents.
'EVERYTHING HAS GONE UP'
The national average price of a gallon of gasoline was $4.36 on Thursday compared with $3.11 a year ago, while diesel fuel prices stood at $6.28 after a record run-up perhaps felt deepest in farm states including Kansas.
Another Kansan, 41-year-old Athena Barrett of Kansas City, said Trump's performance had motivated her to register to vote because "I don't really like what the president is doing."
"Gas prices ... food prices, the cost of living -- everything has gone up; what's going on with Iran, and all the stuff with immigration," said Barrett, who is Hispanic.
Hispanic voters supported Trump in large numbers in 2024, but polls have shown support eroding.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Trump had ended the "inflation crisis" of his predecessor in office, Democrat Joe Biden, by boosting the economy with tax cuts and lowering the costs of prescription drugs. "The president has delivered tangible wins for American families," Rogers said by email.
Inflation spiked to a 40-year high during Biden's term and played an important role in Trump's 2024 election victory.
Its persistence, albeit off the highs of the COVID pandemic, has meant higher daily prices for things like gas, ground beef and airline tickets as well as higher interest rates. The 30-year home mortgage is now at 7.5%, double what homebuyers were used to just six years ago.
Poll respondents cited the cost of living as a top issue in their decisions on how to vote, with 54% of respondents, including 40% of Republicans, saying they felt it had increased a lot in the last year, compared with 30% who said it was up only a little and 10% who said it was unchanged.
Some 78% of the respondents - including 64% of Republicans and 76% of independents - said some blame lies with the White House, with most Americans viewing tariffs as an important cause of higher prices.
LITTLE HIT TO SPENDING
The poll provided only limited indications of people cutting back on spending. Some 63% of respondents said they were eating out at restaurants less often, and 56% said they were spending less on entertainment or streaming services.
Smaller shares said they were driving less or falling behind on bills.
Economic data does show Americans in general still making modest gains in their income, even after accounting for taxes and rising prices. Overall hourly wage gains are growing roughly in line with the consumer price index, meaning much of any growth in pay is eaten up in higher prices, the type of treading water that can sour attitudes about the state of the economy.
Surveys of consumer confidence by both the Conference Board and the New York Federal Reserve have reflected a dim outlook.
Some of Trump's policies still resonate: 45% of respondents said unauthorized immigration was a root cause of higher prices, echoing the argument made by the administration that people in the country illegally create extra demand for things like housing, pushing up costs.
Herman Sims, 67, of Dallas, has voted Republican since 2012, and plans to continue doing so in a close Senate race between Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico even though he works for a trucking company hit hard by high diesel prices.
While he said he disagreed with Trump's decision to go to war with Iran, he would not vote for a Democrat: "What I've seen with the Democratic Party is they care more about themselves and will tell you anything, but they're more about spending." REUTERS

Montenegro Detains Founder of Russian Pro-War Channel Rybar
Unknown

Montenegro expelled Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Russian pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, and three other Russian nationals on Friday after detaining them in an operation targeting suspected Russian influence activities, police and the country’s National Security Agency said.
The agencies said the four could no longer remain in Montenegro “for reasons of national and internal security of the state.” Their statement identified the Russians only by their initials, but a police source confirmed their identities to Reuters.
Zvinchuk, a former Russian Defense Ministry press officer, was detained in the Adriatic resort town of Risan along with others including his wife, Rybar creative director Valeria Zvinchuk, local media reported.
Security sources told Vijesti that police and the National Security Agency (ANB) carried out the operation to counter “hybrid activities” by Russian information networks.
Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed the arrests earlier Friday, saying Montenegro had faced warnings of attempts to destabilize the country as it pursues European Union membership.
“Montenegro is protecting its interests and no one will endanger our European future,” Spajić wrote on X.
Intelligence agencies had monitored the group for several days after its arrival in Montenegro to film material about the Balkan country’s alignment with EU visa policies, the Russian news outlet Readovka reported.
Authorities suspected the material was intended to undermine Montenegro’s tourism industry, economy and national interests, according to the report.
Rybar said before the expulsion announcement that its team had entered Montenegro legally and planned to film at a local monastery.
The Russian Embassy in Podgorica said it had demanded clarification on the reasons for the arrests.
Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, said that Russia may need to "top up" its prisoner exchange fund with European and U.S. citizens in order to free its own citizens being held in Europe following Zvinchuk’s detention.
"Now, it is quite likely that we will have to replenish the exchange fund with European and American idiots in order to get our own people out. There’s no other way: when in Rome, do as the Romans do…," said Medvedev.
Rybar has about 1.5 million Telegram subscribers and publishes daily military analysis of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Zvinchuk is subject to Western sanctions. It also operates a broader network of websites and social media channels.
In October 2024, the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification of 19 individuals involved in managing Rybar-led social media channels, saying they had promoted Russia's political interests in the U.S. ahead of the 2024 presidential elections.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Ukraine's Diia government services app has added an online service allowing people to terminate their employment in temporarily occupied territories, the Digital Transformation Ministry said.
To use the service, users should open the Services section in Diia, select Obrii.Work and then "Termination of employment in temporarily occupied territories." They must verify their employment details, complete and review an application, and sign it using Diia.Signature, the ministry said in a Telegram post.

In June, the two ministries opened registration for closed beta testing of the first tools in the Obrii ecosystem. Development and integration costs for the current and following years have been estimated at $5 million to $10 million.

‘I would choose it again’: A Turkish bookbinder’s 60-year journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:04:02 UTC
19:04:02 KST

For nearly 60 years, Mehmet Karsli has dedicated himself to the patient, intricate art hidden beneath a book's cover.
“We only see the cover of a book, but there are many processes underneath it,” says the master bookbinder, who has spent much of his life repairing and restoring books.
The process involves carefully taking a book apart, repairing damaged pages, stitching them back together, applying glue, trimming the edges, and finally crafting a new cover.
Each stage demands attention to detail, and even the smallest mistake can undo hours of painstaking work.
“If you make a mistake in even one letter when lettering the cover, you have to discard it and make a new cover,” he tells TRT World.
Yet despite the craft's demanding nature, Karsli’s passion never faded.
“I have been in this profession for about 60 years, and believe me, I have never been tired of working.”
From apprentice to master
Born in 1951 in Musalikalesi village in the Akdagmadeni district of Yozgat, Karsli moved to Ankara at age nine.
After completing primary school, he began an apprenticeship at a bookbinding workshop in Hacettepe, balancing his early training with his education.
He spent his days learning the craft and attended middle school in the evenings. After graduating, he enrolled in the printing department of an industrial vocational high school.
His interest in books and bookbinding, however, began with something much simpler: the quality of paper.
At the time, Karsli recalls, good-quality paper was difficult to find. Most notebooks were made from second- or third-grade paper, which deteriorated easily when people erased writing.
But one of his friends, whose father worked as a printer, had notebooks made from better-quality paper. Their appearance caught Karsli's attention.
“He would come with beautiful notebooks, and that is how I became interested in this craft,” he says.
That early fascination eventually led him to a bookbinding workshop, where he discovered that learning the profession required far more than an interest in books.
The training followed a gradual process. Apprentices first learned by watching experienced bookbinders before moving on to stitching, repairing, rounding the spine, and cutting the book.
Making covers came much later.
“After learning to round the spine, you would only move on to making the covers after another year to a year and a half,” he tells TRT World.
Karsli likens the craft to a city's infrastructure, where much of the essential work remains hidden beneath the surface.
In traditional bookbinding, pages are stitched together, headbands are woven at the top and bottom of the spine, and the edges are trimmed. A board is then prepared to form the cover's foundation, before leather is thinned, shaped, and applied.
What appears to be a single finished object is, in fact, the result of numerous carefully executed stages.
The work beneath the cover
For Karsli, bookbinding began with the practical need to protect and hold written pages together.
“Bookbinding has existed since the invention of paper,” he says.
As writing on individual sheets became more common, people needed covers to keep the pages together and protect them from damage.
The craft's terminology also reflects its traditional materials. The word cilt, derived from the Arabic word for “skin” or “leather”, came to describe a book's protective covering, reflecting the widespread use of leather in traditional bindings.
Karsli distinguishes between two approaches to the profession: modern bookbinding and the traditional methods associated with Ottoman craftsmanship.
The classical tradition he describes belongs to a broader heritage of book arts that developed over centuries.
Important bookbinding examples emerged in Anatolia during the Seljuk period, and the craft later developed distinctive characteristics under the Ottomans.
In the classical Ottoman period, bookbinding was practised in palace workshops alongside calligraphy, illumination and miniature painting.
Its defining features include the decorative shamsa (a star-shaped, circular, or oval rosette medallion) and the headband, both of which require specialised techniques.
The headband is woven at the top and bottom of the book's spine, while the shamsa is a prominent decorative motif on traditional covers, often featuring vegetal or geometric patterns.
Restoring an old manuscript requires the same meticulous approach: first assess its condition, then carefully remove accumulated dirt.
“When a manuscript comes in, the first thing you do is give it a dry cleaning. After the dry cleaning, if there are any torn areas, you restore them,” he explains.
Once you've repaired the damaged sections, you stitch the pages together and begin work on the cover.
“After stitching it, you make the cover. Then you stamp the shamsa onto the cover. After the shamsa, you decorate it with gold or in a simple style. You weave the headband,” he explains.
“Then you glue the covers together, and a finished work of art emerges.”
What is particularly striking in Karsli’s story is that after decades in the profession, he chose to become a student again.
In 2010, his works were displayed at a group exhibition in Istanbul. Master bookbinder Islam Secen saw Karsli’s pieces there and expressed an interest in meeting him.
“He said, ‘I want to meet this master’.”
When Karsli later visited Istanbul, he sought out Secen not just to meet him, but to ask to become his student.
“I said to him, ‘Master, I sometimes receive questions about classical bookbinding, but I do not know this art. Could you teach me?’”
For the next year and a half, Karsli travelled regularly from Ankara to Istanbul to study classical bookbinding under Secen.
By then, he already had his own workshop and a steady stream of customers. Nevertheless, he made time for the training, closing his workshop every Friday evening and taking an overnight train to Istanbul.
“I went to Istanbul for a year and a half.”
“On Friday evening, I would close the workshop, take the train at night, and arrive in Istanbul in the morning.”
“I would attend the course, return in the evening, and open my workshop on Monday.”
Do it with love
Alongside his training and development as a bookbinder, Karsli built a career working in public institutions.
He began working at Ankara University's Faculty of Agriculture at a young age and secured a permanent position there when he turned 18.
In January 1982, he moved to Parliament, where he continued working until his retirement in 1996.
Retirement, however, did not mean stepping away from the profession. Instead, it gave him the opportunity to devote himself to his own workshop and the craft he had loved since childhood.
His decades of dedication have also brought recognition.
In the 60th year of his career, Karsli received an award from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, an honour he describes as one of the most meaningful moments of his life.
For a man who has spent much of his life learning, practising and teaching a centuries-old craft, the lesson he hopes to pass on extends well beyond bookbinding.
“Whatever you do, do what you love,” he tells TRT World.
“If you love what you do, you will surely succeed.”

NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:03:36 UTC
19:03:36 KST

NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Patients who use medicinal cannabis face having to switch to imported products after the only licensed grower in the Netherlands was declared bankrupt on Thursday.
A court in Groningen declared Veendam-based Bedrocan bankrupt two weeks after the company had applied for protection from its creditors. The firm, whose main growing site is in Emmeloord, employs around 70 people.
Bedrocan ran into trouble after the health ministry ended its contract at the start of this year. All medicinal cannabis sold in Dutch pharmacies is bought and distributed by the state-run Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC).
The ministry ended the deal in anticipation of a change in the law that will let growers sell directly to pharmacies. But health minister Sophie Hermans (VVD) told MPs in July that the change is not expected to take effect until July 1, 2028.
That left Bedrocan unable to supply the BMC and not allowed to sell to pharmacies itself, the Volkskrant reported. The state was by far its largest customer.
Limited stockpile
The BMC built up a stockpile of Bedrocan cannabis before the contract ended, but the minister said it was limited and had a finite shelf life. The BMC will switch to imported cannabis during 2027, with products matching current THC and CBD levels as closely as possible.
Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed medicinal cannabis, according to the Volkskrant. They include people with multiple sclerosis (MS), severe pain, certain forms of epilepsy, and patients in palliative care.
Patients fear a different variety will not work as well for them. Cannabis contains many compounds that together determine its effect, and the mix depends on the plant and how it is grown.
The MS association has written to Hermans warning that some long-term patients depend on a specific variety.
Bedrocan also supplied patients in other European countries through the BMC. The BMC is due to stop exporting at the end of 2026. In September, Bedrocan told foreign pharmacies and wholesalers to order from it directly.

Hong Kong outlines new liquidity reforms as US market rally pulls funds away
City is pressing ahead with market reforms as a surging US stock market intensifies competition for capital
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Hong Kong’s securities watchdog is renewing its push to boost market liquidity, setting out further reforms as emerging markets grapple with capital outflow pressure amid a rally in US equities and a strengthening dollar.
Speaking at a conference organised by the Asian Securities & Financial Markets Association (Asifma) on Friday, Julia Leung, CEO of the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), outlined measures ranging from extended trading hours and shorter settlement cycles to cross-market margining and board lot reform aimed at improving market liquidity and efficiency.
“The SFC is working with the HKEX [Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing] to develop margin offsets across its clearing houses,” Leung said, adding that the move would free up capital for “more productive” uses.
Leung also said the HKEX’s clearing house, OTC Clear, would enable same-day settlement for bond deposits and withdrawals later this year, streamlining the process and making non-cash collateral “a more attractive funding pool”.

Foreign Companies Employ 18.7% of Bulgaria’s Business Workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

Foreign-controlled companies employed 18.7% of Bulgaria’s business-economy workforce in 2023, according to Eurostat data, giving international capital a significant role in the country’s employment structure.
Across the European Union, enterprises under foreign control represented just 1.1% of all businesses but accounted for 15.5% of employment and 24% of total value added. The relatively small share of foreign-owned companies therefore corresponds to a much larger economic presence, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe.
In Bulgaria, 411,020 people worked for enterprises controlled by foreign companies in 2023, with their 18.7% share of employment standing 3.2 percentage points above the EU average.
Romania recorded a substantially higher proportion, with foreign-controlled enterprises employing 26.9% of the country’s business-economy workforce, or 1,301,612 people. Slovakia and Czechia were also among the EU countries with the largest shares, at 28.0% and 27.5%, respectively.
The figures vary considerably across the EU. Foreign-controlled companies employed 44.5% of the workforce in Luxembourg and 27.6% in Ireland. Their shares were considerably lower in the bloc’s largest economies, reaching 12.1% in Germany, 11.9% in France and 9.9% in Italy. Spain recorded 15.5%, equal to the EU average.
Eurostat said foreign-controlled enterprises are generally much larger than companies under domestic control, which explains why their economic contribution is substantially greater than their numerical share. Although they represented only 1.1% of enterprises in the EU, they generated 28.6% of turnover and 24.0% of value added.
The figures place international capital among the important factors supporting employment and production in Bulgaria, while also showing that the country remains behind several of its Eastern European counterparts. Romania’s proportion of workers employed by foreign-controlled enterprises, for example, was more than eight percentage points higher.
The differences also reflect varying forms of economic integration. According to Eurostat, countries with a strong presence of foreign companies tend to have a significant concentration of employment in manufacturing, while relatively low labor costs and participation in cross-border production chains are among the factors that attract international capital.
The statistics also show that the limited number of foreign-controlled enterprises does not mean they have a limited economic impact. Because these companies tend to be larger and more productive, international ownership represents an important route connecting the European economy to global value chains.
Bulgaria is part of this process, with almost one-fifth of its business-economy workforce employed by foreign-controlled companies, while its share remains below those recorded in Romania and the region’s leading countries. The country’s position in the European economy is therefore linked not only to the amount of capital it attracts but also to its ability to generate greater value added, more complex production and sustainable employment.

South African human rights lawyer wins Nobel Peace Prize

South African human rights lawyer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced at a press conference in Oslo on Friday.
According to the committee, Pillay has played a crucial role in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.

The prize comes with an award of 12 million SEK, equivalent to approximately 8 million DKK.
The Nobel Peace Prize was established under the will of Swedish chemist and inventor Alfred Nobel. According to his will, the prize is to be awarded to “the person or organization that has conferred the greatest benefit to mankind within peace”.

The attacks come amid an escalation in Yemen’s ongoing civil war, in which Saudi Arabia supports the internationally recognised government against the Houthi movement.
The Houthis have justified their attacks on Saudi airports by pointing to Saudi Arabia’s support for government forces in Yemen, Reuters reported.
The civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa.

Fire near Aarup disrupts train services across Denmark throughout Friday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

A fire in a railway signaling cabin near Aarup on Funen is causing major train disruptions across Denmark on Friday, with repairs potentially taking several weeks.
Michael Dyrborg, an area manager at Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, told Ritzau that almost everything inside the cabin had burned.
“It is too early to talk about a timeframe. We are getting an overview of the extent of the damage, but virtually everything inside has burned away,” he said.
A relay cabin is a small technical building along the railway that houses electronics and equipment used by the signaling system.
The fire has caused signal faults on the railway line between Middelfart and Odense. Dyrborg expects train services on the affected routes to remain disrupted for the rest of Friday.
“We are looking into whether it is possible to create some technical solutions so we can increase the speed and make traffic flow more smoothly,” he said.
Banedanmark has not yet said when normal train services are expected to resume.
The disruption is affecting services across Funen and other parts of the country.
According to DSB, Denmark’s national passenger railway operator, all trains between Fredericia and Copenhagen are experiencing delays, while all regional trains between Odense and Fredericia have been canceled.
Intercity trains running between Copenhagen and Fredericia via Roskilde are only operating as far as Odense, DSB said on its website.
Rail replacement buses have been deployed to replace the canceled regional trains on Funen. According to P4 Trafik, six buses were operating between Fredericia and Odense.
Passengers traveling between Jutland, Funen and Zealand can continue their journeys using some of the other trains still running, DSB said.
DSB employees are available at Odense and Fredericia stations to assist and guide passengers.
Both Banedanmark and DSB are urging travelers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s national journey planner, for updates.
Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.
The access began September 10 and was stopped October 2, lasting 21 days and 17 hours.
However, preliminary investigations suggest the unauthorized activity ended September 20, approximately 10 days after it began, according to a report submitted by the CPR office to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced Monday that personal information belonging to approximately 8.8 million people had been exposed, including names, addresses and CPR identification numbers.
The breach occurred through a small Danish company with legitimate access to the register.
According to DR, the company is based on Funen and shares ownership and an address with a larger business. Its identity has not been publicly confirmed.
Authorities discovered the incident after receiving an unusually large invoice for searches conducted through the company’s account.
Approximately 14 million CPR searches had been made using its access credentials.
“The number far exceeds the company’s customer base, and the company has indicated that they did not perform the lookups themselves,” the CPR office stated in its report.
Private companies and organizations can pay to access certain CPR information.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates party acknowledged that security measures had been inadequate.
She has requested a security review of the register following the breach.
The company had not responded to DR’s requests for comment as of Friday morning.
Sardine sales surge in Copenhagen as social media skincare trend gains popularity
Canned sardines are selling rapidly across Denmark, particularly around Copenhagen, as supermarkets report rising demand and occasional shortages.
Four major grocery retailers, Coop, Salling Group, Nemlig.com and Dagrofa, confirmed significant sales increases to TV 2 Kosmopol.
Coop, which operates 365, SuperBrugsen, Brugsen and Kvickly, reported a 170 percent increase in sardine sales in Denmark’s Capital Region between June and September 2026 compared with the same period last year.
Nationwide, Coop’s sales rose 163.5 percent.
Jacob Herbst Lassen, Coop Denmark’s press manager, said the sudden popularity has left some shelves with fewer products while purchasing teams work to replenish supplies.
Salling Group also reported pressure on availability, although spokesperson Alma Lyhne Kristensen said the company remained adequately stocked overall.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com said Greater Copenhagen and North Zealand accounted for 75 percent of its sardine sales.
Dagrofa, which operates Meny and Spar stores, reported that sales in the capital area had more than doubled compared with last year.
The surge may be connected to the social media trend “eat your skincare,” which promotes foods believed to benefit skin health.
Sardines have attracted attention for their omega-3 fatty acids, collagen and protein.
However, dermatologist and researcher Cæcilie Johansen cautioned that evidence linking sardine consumption directly to healthier skin remains limited.
She said some studies suggest omega-3 fatty acids may help with eczema, but the research involved large quantities.
Johansen emphasized that avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol and using sunscreen are more important measures for protecting skin health.
Denmark resumes citizenship and immigration cases after criminal records error
Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration has resumed processing citizenship applications that were suspended because of errors in the country’s Central Criminal Register.
The ministry announced the decision in a press release after the National Police concluded that the errors had only a very limited impact on the register.
Immigration authorities have also been instructed to restart affected cases involving permanent residence permits and family reunification, according to an update from the Danish Immigration Service.
The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.
The errors became public in early September when National Police Commissioner Lasse Boje informed politicians at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, that some criminal records had been deleted incorrectly.
Authorities had discovered the problem in June.
The National Police said further investigations would determine whether the errors had affected decisions made by other public authorities.
If problems are identified, police will work with the relevant authorities to determine how those cases should be handled.
The errors also disrupted the issuance of child protection certificates, which are background checks used to identify certain criminal convictions relevant to working with children.
Applications for these certificates were temporarily suspended while police reviewed the affected records.
The National Police reopened applications September 18.
During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.
Danish court rejects detention request for two Kosovo prison officers accused of assault
Two prison officers from Kosovo accused of assaulting an inmate at Copenhagen’s Vestre Prison will remain free while police investigate the allegations.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court rejected prosecutors’ request to hold the two men in pretrial detention Friday afternoon.
The decision upheld a ruling by Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday, which found insufficient grounds to detain them.
Both courts concluded there was no significant reason to believe the men would flee Denmark before a possible criminal trial.
The officers, aged 29 and 24, are undergoing training in Denmark ahead of assignments at Gjilan prison in Kosovo, which Denmark is renting to house prisoners.
According to police allegations, the two officers assaulted an inmate inside a cell at Vestre Prison around 4 p.m. Monday.
The inmate was allegedly pushed onto a bed before being punched in the face and body.
Police arrested the officers Tuesday morning, and prosecutors requested their detention the following day.
Both men deny using violence against the inmate.
During Wednesday’s hearing, a Copenhagen City Court judge found reasonable grounds to suspect the officers had committed the alleged assault.
However, the judge ruled that detention was unnecessary because both men reside in Denmark and are employed by Danmarks Fængsler, the Danish Prison and Probation Service.
Prosecutors challenged that decision, but the Eastern High Court reached the same conclusion Friday.
The investigation remains ongoing, and no decision has been made on whether the officers will face trial.
Once police complete their investigation, prosecutors will determine whether there is sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges before a court.

Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.
Business groups warn 200 DKK cruise passenger tax could drive tourists away
Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.
Dansk Industri (DI), the Confederation of Danish Industry, and Dansk Erhverv, a business organization representing companies across several sectors, are responding to the government’s proposal to introduce the tax from 2028.
“A cruise tax at this level will hit both the major cities and rural districts,” said Lars Bertolt Winther, head of tourism, culture and experiences at DI, in a press release.
Jesper Kronborg, industry director for transport at Dansk Erhverv, also criticized the proposal.
“In Dansk Erhverv’s view, it is a bad proposal, or at least a proposal that requires a very thorough analysis,” he said in a press release.
The government expects the tax to generate an additional 300 million DKK in annual revenue from 2028.
The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.
Figures from Statistics Denmark show that 1.1 million cruise passengers visited Denmark in 2025. The number of cruise ships calling at Danish ports increased by 16% compared with the previous year.
Copenhagen, Aarhus, Skagen and Rønne on the island of Bornholm are the country’s main cruise destinations. Together, they account for more than 98% of cruise passengers.
DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.
“Following the introduction of a high passenger tax, bookings dropped significantly, especially to the smaller ports, and the tax was subsequently lowered to limit the damaging effects,” Winther said.
“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.
According to the industry organization Danske Havne, which represents Danish ports, Iceland now charges 85 DKK per cruise passenger, while Greenland charges 50 DKK.
Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.

Danish exports fell by 3.3 percent in August, driven in part by a decline in goods exports to the United States, according to Statistics Denmark.
Total exports of goods and services amounted to 194 billion DKK in August, down 3.3 percent from July. Goods exports fell by 6.2 percent, while services exports rose by 0.7 percent.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, described the overall decline as “worryingly large”.
“But it is part of the story that a large part of the decline is concentrated around the US, where we also see fluctuations from month to month,” he wrote in a comment.

The August decline followed an increase in exports in July. Overall, Danish exports of goods and services rose by nearly 19 billion DKK, or more than 10 percent, between August 2025 and August 2026.
According to Kristensen, Danish exports have so far held up despite geopolitical unrest, higher energy prices and rising interest rates.
Still, the August figures are bad news for the Danish economy when viewed in isolation.
