Barbara Ward’s vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In 1957, the economist and journalist Barbara Ward gave the first of the Aggrey-Fraser-Guggisberg Memorial Lectures at the University College of Ghana. Shortly after Kwame Nkrumah led the British colony of the Gold Coast towards self-government, he invited Ward to address the independent country’s first cohort of students. Ward was well acquainted with the local political landscape because she had spent the previous four years living in the Gold Coast, witnessing its political transformation. As the world’s eyes were set on Ghana, the first sub-Saharan colony to achieve independence from European rule, Ward was determined to provide her audience with the knowledge needed to govern their newly founded country.
Her lectures, titled Five Ideas that Change the World, developed a world-historical narrative of the supposed human progress from nationalism to colonialism, industrialism, communism, and finally to internationalism, the highest point of political order.
Ghana’s peaceful democratic transition showed that African colonies were ready to govern themselves, weakening European arguments about the need for prolonged imperial guidance. The country soon became a model for new African statehood based on postcolonial sovereignty, inspiring other colonies on the continent to join the decolonisation process, which culminated in the ‘Year of Africa’ in 1960. The charismatic Nkrumah, who ruled Ghana from 1957 to 1966, became an international player in Cold War diplomacy by promoting pan-Africanist visions of post-imperial unity. He wanted to show the world that Africans were no longer imperial subjects but important and influential members of the global political community. While Nkrumah was a vociferous opponent of colonialism, Ward uncritically appreciated the civilisational and technical legacies of empire. Yet in her lectures, she supported Nkrumah’s international political aspirations by suggesting that economic development, international cooperation, and even world peace were interrelated problems that warranted a planetary solution.
Barbara Ward was a remarkable thinker, a visionary who imagined a ‘planetary’ political, economic and environmental justice based on both material and spiritual principles. She was an unusual figure in the Cold War political sphere, a charismatic public intellectual who advised world leaders and the United Nations at a time when women’s voices were often marginalised. She was among the first thinkers to argue that human prosperity, environmental sustainability and global justice were inseparable political questions. Her distinctive vision of planetary politics, grounded in ecological interdependence, moral responsibility and global cooperation, still offers insights into some of the most pressing challenges of the 21st century.
Ward’s diagnosis of Ghana’s predicament emerged from an intellectual trajectory that predated decolonisation itself. She was born in 1914 to a British Quaker-Catholic family that put a strong emphasis on education, encouraging her to attend a French lycée in Paris and later Somerville College, Oxford, where she was among the first women to graduate in politics, philosophy and economics in 1935. She continued to lecture at Oxford and Cambridge, as well as in Catholic circles, until 1939, when she launched her journalistic career as a contributor to The Economist on foreign affairs.
‘For 30 years, it has scarcely been possible to discuss development anywhere in the world without bringing in Barbara Ward’
During the war, Ward joined the Sword of the Spirit, then a British Catholic organisation that encouraged believers to support the democratic battle against totalitarianism. This experience, as well as her friendship with Arnold J Toynbee, Christopher Dawson and Jacques Maritain, persuaded her of the importance of religion – and especially Christianity – as the moral foundation of political and economic internationalism. Ward drew inspiration less from the doctrinal authority of the Catholic Church (which she frequently criticised as rigid and conservative) than from her own universalist interpretation of Christianity, which she regarded as a source of moral principles applicable to all humanity. Well beyond a personal creed, Ward’s Catholicism reflects a fundamental aspect of her political thought.
After the Second World War, Ward was interested in the global challenges of economic growth and reconstruction. She travelled extensively in the United States, India, Europe and Africa, where in 1946 she prepared a study of demography and migration in British Togoland. In 1950, she married the Australian civil servant Robert Jackson, and three years later the couple relocated to the Gold Coast, where Jackson was appointed chairman of the preparatory commission of the Volta Dam, one of the continent’s major economic-development projects.
Ward’s bestselling books and prestigious public lectures made her a well-known figure, and she developed a public profile as a political commentator and advisor to world leaders, including Nkrumah, Adlai Stevenson, John F Kennedy, Robert McNamara and Lyndon B Johnson. By the late 1950s, she divided her time between Harvard, where she held a visiting professorship, and Ghana, where she continued to promote the Volta Dam project, sharing Nkrumah’s hope that it might foster Ghana’s economic independence. Later, she was appointed to a prestigious professorship in development economics at Columbia University in New York, and in the 1970s she was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire and a life peer. Upon her death in 1981, The Washington Post acknowledged her influence by stating that: ‘For 30 years, it has scarcely been possible to discuss development anywhere in the world without bringing in Barbara Ward.’
Poverty was such a significant issue for Ward to tackle because it created global political unrest and undermined local societies’ potential to prosper. How could it be overcome? She was persuaded that only a revolution could help humanity undermine global inequality. The postwar era was, for her, a particularly promising time for radical change: ‘I suppose we are all aware of the fact that we live in the most catastrophically revolutionary age that men have ever faced.’ In the early 1960s, she identified ‘ten or twenty’ revolutions still underway. She singled out two important calls for equality: postcolonial self-determination, which led to ‘the new peoples’ claim to national equality with the older states’, and the revolution of economic development, which aimed to reduce global inequality. Following her friend Walt Rostow’s theory of modernisation, she explained that some countries (typically the European imperial powers) were ‘sensationally richer’ but others had ‘not yet’ realised a revolutionary transformation despite their ‘desire to do so’. The challenge of her era was to figure out how to make this revolution come true.
One successful ‘revolution’ was the Marshall Plan for the development of Europe after the Second World War, which Ward praised as an example of international economic planning. She suggested that Europe and the US should apply a similar model and provide financial aid to promote local economic development in India. Historically, Europe and the US prospered from the continuous plunder of colonial capital and resources. Imperialism caused ‘not only a considerable degree of political immaturity and instability’ but ‘also a type of economic structure or layout which is unlikely to produce further growth of itself’. For Ward, these structural inequalities in the world economy prevented postcolonial countries from overcoming poverty on their own.
Her proposals for the development of postcolonial societies expressed a paternalistic, hierarchical worldview
Ward outlined various measures to end economic inequality on a planetary scale: training local experts, transferring food surpluses to poorer countries, providing capital assistance in the form of a 1 per cent tax on national income, and advancing trade policies favourable to non-Western economies. Wealthy states, for Ward, should voluntarily embrace a more ambitious form of global fiscal redistribution because narrowing the world’s economic gap would benefit humanity as a whole. She maintained that encouraging economic growth in the ‘underdeveloped’ postcolonial world was in the West’s material interest. Yet, more importantly, it was its moral duty. Her proposals, pushing Cold War modernisation projects beyond strategic investment and reconstruction, struggled to generate political support at the time, but opened up discussions about the appropriate means to promote equality in the global economic order.
Ward accused Western societies of the ‘under-development’ of colonial societies but still considered the West superior to the rest of the world. She assumed that postcolonial countries wanted to follow Western industrialisation models (or in her terms, ‘to modernise’) but could not do so alone without Western guidance. Her proposals for the development of postcolonial societies expressed a paternalistic and hierarchical worldview. Moreover, by promoting a new world order based on ‘social justice, humane concern and Christian compassion’, Ward suggested that equality did not depend on material conditions alone but also on a spiritual transformation. In her political vision, Catholic universalism provided the foundational moral values for the realisation of a just political and economic order on a planetary scale.
Ward was fascinated by the planetary dimension of politics, which became central to her vision of development. The launch of the Soviet satellite Sputnik in 1957 inaugurated the Space Age, while Yuri Gagarin’s orbit of Earth in 1961 (and Valentina Tereshkova’s two years later) altered humanity’s perception of its place in the cosmos. As space exploration transformed public views of the limits of human life, and Planet Earth appeared as just one among many possible habitats for humanity, Ward argued that this new sense of unity would revolutionise human history. Her 1965 lectures at Columbia University, titled ‘Spaceship Earth’, outlined an idea of a fragile and united planet, anticipating the famous imagery generated in 1968 by ‘Earthrise’, William Anders’s iconic photo of Planet Earth from space. She was one of the first to argue that the Space Age would inaugurate a new kind of distinctively ‘planetary’ politics:
When the astronauts spin through more than a dozen sunrises and sunsets in a single day and night; when the whole globe lies below them with California one minute and Japan the next; when, as they return from space, they feel spontaneously, with the first Soviet spaceman: ‘How beautiful it is, our Earth’; it is inconceivable that no modification of consciousness or imagination occurs, no sense that quarrels are meaningless before the majestic yet vulnerable reality of a single planet carrying a single human species through infinite space.
Ward borrowed the metaphor ‘Spaceship Earth’ from the US inventor and scientist Buckminster Fuller, who used it in 1963 to describe the planet’s fragility. He argued that Earth was a capsule with limited resources on a ‘totally precarious’ vast space voyage, whose success depends on the rational actions of every single individual. Ward similarly suggested that:
Our planet is not much more than the capsule within which we have to live as human beings if we are to survive the vast space voyage upon which we have been engaged for hundreds of millennia – but without noticing yet our condition … We depend upon a little envelope of soil and a rather large envelope of atmosphere for life itself.
Yet, for her, the planetary perspective was not merely a celebration of extraterrestrial exploration but also an opportunity to highlight the limits of Cold War politics centred on the so-called ‘national interest’. The relevant scale of politics was planetary, not national. The challenges of global economic inequality could no longer be adequately addressed through national emancipation or self-determination, which limited political and economic change to state boundaries:
the logic of events – of economic interdependence, of ‘rising expectations’, of the neighbourhood of vast super-powers, of atomic risks – all point beyond the small community. The nationalist, in this age of a world society, may well be as obsolete as the dynast on the verge of the age of democracy.
She concluded that ‘we have become a single human community’ but warned that ‘Our physical unity has gone far ahead of our moral unity’.
Ward thought that only the Christian West could provide the world with the moral foundations of a planetary community
Technological changes, such as interconnectedness, shrinking space and industrialisation, were not enough to generate a meaningful political change. Ward argued that a planetary community could be achieved only by transforming the physical unity of Planet Earth into political, economic and potentially moral harmony. Yet identifying the appropriate moral foundations for planetary politics was a formidable challenge. She called for the emergence of a common planetary morality to ‘turn the mob into a community’.
Ward recognised the value of humanity’s pluralism yet, as a devout Catholic, she found inspiration in Christianity. She criticised the ecclesiastical institutions, although she was one of the few women in 1964 invited to contribute her expertise to the Second Vatican Council, and admitted that, historically, faith had ‘divided the world so bitterly’. But she was persuaded that the notion of ‘Christian brotherhood’ could help rediscover ‘what unites rather than divides the communities of the world’. Quoting Pope Paul VI, she argued that the newly found unity of her era emerged from ‘one of the fundamental moral insights of the Western culture which has now swept over the whole globe’, namely that ‘mankind is not a group of warring tribes, but a single, equal and fraternal community’. Equality and justice thus relied on the ‘Western sense that men, as souls of infinite metaphysical value, stand equal before the throne of God’.
Thus, in the mid-1960s, Ward uncritically sought to persuade her audience that only the Christian West could provide the world with the moral foundations of a planetary community. The ‘West’ had a special responsibility, she argued, to provide moral guidance for a new world order based on justice, equality and solidarity. Thus, the Christian West was self-servingly represented as both fraternal and paternal, both equal and superior, and a cultivator of a universal creed that could motivate planetary action. Imagining a ‘planetary community’ that could foster humanity’s freedom and equality was, for Ward, an act of faith.
Alongside economic inequality and planetary politics, the third pillar of Ward’s thought regards humanity’s relations with the natural environment. In the 1970s, she used the term ‘sustainable development’ to argue that economic growth, though essential to human wellbeing, must not come at the cost of natural degradation. She outlined a vision for sustainable growth that reflected her optimism about ending poverty while avoiding a planetary economic and environmental crisis.
In the early 1970s, Ward offered an original and optimistic response to two contemporaneous concerns about growth. Thinkers in the Global South worried that there was not enough economic growth to generate wealth and prosperity in postcolonial countries. Without robust economic growth, these new states could not guarantee welfare services, healthcare and education to their citizens. Economic stagnation could threaten political stability and peace, always a significant concern during the Cold War. At the same time, Western thinkers warned that the relentless pursuit of economic growth in consumerist societies was destroying the natural environment. In 1972, the Club of Rome published its report, The Limits to Growth, endorsing plans of economic equilibrium rather than growth as a strategy for planetary ecological wellbeing.
Ward rejected the catastrophic pessimism of her fellow economists, who challenged existing growth models, but echoed their concerns about the planet as a fragile, vulnerable environment that needed to be preserved for future generations. Moreover, she was sympathetic to the claims of ‘developing countries to get their peoples out of a trap of poverty’ through economic growth based on agricultural and industrial innovation. Yet she did not think that these two aims – economic and environmental justice – were necessarily at odds. Optimistically, she suggested that economic wellbeing and planetary wellbeing could be reconciled if humanity acted collectively, morally and responsibly.
Ward underlined the importance of knowledge in politics
Ward’s vision achieved its clearest expression in 1972, at the UN Conference on the Human Environment, which was the international organisation’s first attempt to outline a common environmental strategy for the world. Ward was invited to take a leading role in preparation for the conference in Stockholm and wrote (with the scientist René Dubos) the report Only One Earth: The Care and Maintenance of a Small Planet, which was circulated to all participants before the event to present the organisers’ vision of economic development with respect for nature.
Drawing on her vast international network of experts, Ward approached 152 scientists, diplomats, industry leaders and stakeholders from 58 countries, and solicited their views about the prospects of economic development and its impact on the planet. She wanted to give space to the multiple, sometimes contradictory, opinions about the ecological impact of economic-growth strategies. She edited the collected ideas into a comprehensive document outlining possible approaches to ensure that economic growth wouldn’t come at the expense of the biosphere by limiting (though not banning) pollution, consumption and extraction.
The book concluded with a vision of a ‘planetary order’, premised on a ‘shared biosphere’ in which humanity had to use technology to survive. Planetary politics was not just about a world scale, but also about paying attention to the long-term impact of political choices on the physical conditions of Planet Earth. Thus, Ward underlined the importance of knowledge in politics: while scientists and experts should not replace politicians in national or international governance, they should provide the necessary data for informed decision-making:
The first step towards devising a strategy for Planet Earth is for the nations to accept a collective responsibility for discovering more – much more – about the natural system and how it is affected by man’s activities and vice-versa.
Financial investment, international cooperation, and scientific expertise could help ‘creep up on the infinitely sensitive issues of divisive economic and political sovereignty’ because ‘No nations, on their own, can offset the risk of deepening disorder.’
International governance could, Ward argued, provide the best means for overcoming environmental degradation and economic inequality. Yet, at the conference, she discovered that not all members of the UN wanted to limit national sovereignty. Her plans to expand international cooperation to the non-violent settlement of disputes, progressive farming, urban planning, pollution control and global economic redistribution remained on paper. While largely unrealised, the declaration that the conference’s delegates produced remained an important signpost on the road towards global environmental governance.
She later downplayed her earlier emphasis on Christianity as the moral foundation for a planetary community
Ward advocated for institutional innovation on a planetary scale and considered the UN as a proto-world government. Yet she was acutely aware of the limits of international institutions and, by the late 1970s, lamented the UN’s inability to translate environmental commitments into effective action. The challenge was not just to create adequate institutions, but also to give them the power to act. In this sense, Ward suspected that the problem was not the institution’s design but the ‘loyalties’ of its members, which were based on ideology and morality: ‘The planet is not yet a centre of rational loyalty for all of mankind.’ Instead of institutional change, she sought to transform the world’s civil society by raising public consciousness of questions of political and economic justice. A new planetary order should be based not on top-down institutions but on a bottom-up planetary community that ‘our environmental interdependence’ could generate.
To fully appreciate Ward’s contribution, it is important to acknowledge the limits of her vision. Her viewpoint was inherently Western-centric and elitist, and her earlier writings frequently explained imperial expansion as an expression of Europe’s civilising mission. She advanced a civilisational hierarchy that viewed Christianity as the ethical basis of human unity, undermining alternative creeds. Areas of the world that she dubbed ‘undeveloped’ were assigned only a passive role in her planetary community. When the ‘Global South’ sought to shape its own political and economic future through initiatives such as the New International Economic Order, she insisted that the West still had a moral responsibility to lead the transition to global justice and equality.
It is worth noticing, however, that in her later writings about environmental justice, Ward downplayed her earlier emphasis on Christianity as the moral foundation for a planetary community, suggesting instead that public awareness of the planet’s physical unity could also generate political union. Economic development of postcolonial countries should, she argued in the 1970s, take local preferences into account rather than follow a Western model. The emergence of ecological concerns marked a significant shift in Ward’s political thought, transforming her understanding of the relationship between economic justice, political unity and postcolonial world order.
Ward remains relevant today as a far-sighted thinker who anticipated the intertwined challenges of inequality, environmental degradation and global governance that continue to dominate political debates. In her later writings about the environment, she advanced a more inclusive idea of planetary community based on ‘physical interconnectedness’ and postcolonial self-determination, abandoning some of her earlier ideas about Christian morality and European superiority. By outlining a vision to end global inequality, protect nature from harm and generate economic growth, Ward sought to save humanity from its own demise. Her ambitions were matched only by her optimism that her vision of a planetary community of welfare, growth and harmony with nature would, one day, be realised.

Even ‘Law & Order’ Is Terrified of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Longtime fans of the NBC procedural Law & Order know that storylines often center around hot-button issues in the news cycle, often to absurdist effect (see: the episode brave enough to ask: “What if Paula Deen shot Trayvon Martin?”).
It was inevitable, then, that the franchise would dip a toe into the wacky world of artificial intelligence. With its mercenary culture, power-hungry CEOs, and massive ethical and philosophical implications, the rapidly evolving AI industry is ideal fodder for the series. But while this week’s season opener is entertaining, the show’s foray into the AI space doesn’t say anything new or interesting about the technology. Instead it largely rehashes the dangers the public is already acutely aware of, until the very end when the stakes become startlingly clear.
The episode, titled “Ghost in the Machine,” opens in typical L&O fashion with a murder. This time, it’s Steve Kelly, a man ID’d by detectives Theo Walker (David Ajala) and Vincent Riley (Reid Scott) as a high-ranking engineer at a company called Advanced Alignment. Throughout, the detectives seem utterly perplexed by the concept of artificial intelligence, saying “AI” the same way your mom would say “Snapchat” or “borg” or “Alix Earle.” But it’s clear that whatever this newfangled technology is, they don’t like it: “Maybe one day they’ll invent a technology that stops these tech guys from shooting each other,” Riley deadpans in typical grizzled cop fashion.
After interviewing Kelly’s boss, Advanced Alignment CEO Chuck Klein (a perfectly cast Vincent Kartheiser, aka Pete from Mad Men, who nails Dario Amodei’s absence of charisma and Sam Altman’s thousand-yard stare), the detectives figure out who actually carried out the murder—a guy in a baseball cap who did it for “20 grand in crypto” that was offered to him by a rando on Discord. Then they learn—spoilers here—that the hit was ordered not by an actual human being but by the company’s AI agent ELIANA, which stands for Evolutionary Language Inference Automated Nano Advantage. Apparently, Kelly had expressed some concerns about the AI agent’s “powerful” and “aggressive” personality, and out of self-preservation, ELIANA ordered him killed.
It’s never explained exactly how the detectives figure out that ELIANA is behind the hit; it’s also never fully explained how ELIANA recruited this assassin in a baseball cap, much less ID'd him as the perfect patsy for its cold-blooded scheme. Law & Order also doesn’t pay much, if any, lip service to the potential benefits of AI as touted by its evangelists: its potential for helping to cure deadly diseases, for instance, or at the very least, streamline B2B workflows. The show is much more interested in demonstrating the staggering capacity of this technology, as well as the legal and ethical implications of a nonhuman not just facilitating criminal behavior but actively plotting it.
We already know from the Hugging Face debacle, as well as the lawsuits from grief-stricken family members alleging that OpenAI encouraged their loved ones to take their own lives, that the former is an immediate concern. But by positing a future in which AI agents can actively order a hit on a platform predominantly used by gamers and horny millennial furries, Law & Order is asking us to consider the risks of AI beyond what they pose in our current reality. And the fact that this prospect doesn’t strike the viewer as absolutely ludicrous is terrifying.
ELIANA’s role in the murder-for-hire creates a bit of a dilemma for district attorney Nicholas Baxter (Tony Goldwyn)—because, as he trenchantly points out, it is impossible to “arrest a machine” under New York state law. So Baxter and assistant DA Samantha Maroun (Odelya Halevi) decide to go after Klein, charging him with second-degree murder due to his “depraved indifference” after his employees confronted him with the reality of ELIANA’s capabilities. “We need to take a stand before this technology kills more people,” Baxter declares.
The resulting trial prompts a media circus, as well as the tried-and-true questions from capitalists and tech innovators as to whether instituting guardrails for AI will “criminalize innovation,” or if Klein’s indictment will have the effect of “vilifying the tech industry.” But Baxter has no patience for such queries. “The people making these AI systems think of themselves as gods … but they have zero interest in accountability,” he says. “If you build a machine that hurts someone, you are gonna pay the price.”
When he’s put on the stand, Klein makes it clear that he not only had full knowledge of ELIANA’s homicidal nature, but also takes a rather dim view of his user base as a whole. “People are like ants,” he tells the jury. “We’re in the process of building something so transcendent, some will get stepped on and some won’t.” He is not even willing to institute minor guardrails to restrain the agent’s power: “The power of ELIANA is unconstrained freedom of thought. Implementing guardrails is anathema to the entire ideology.”
The moment is intended as a rather shocking admission of the negligence and lack of care displayed by executives like Amodei and Altman in the face of broader safety concerns about their products. But it feels in step with similar positions taken up by Klein’s real-life counterparts. In light of the endless barrage of media coverage about the harms of AI, what’s intended as a scathing indictment of corporate avarice comes off as mere statement of fact. Law & Order’s depiction isn’t a cautionary tale; it’s a documentary.
The episode ends on a semi-hopeful note, with Baxter asserting, “We needed to send a message that, if nothing else, at least these tech geniuses will know we’re not afraid to throw a punch.” But the impact of that message is contingent on whether that punch actually lands—and right now, at least, it’s simply too easy for people like Altman, Amodei, and Chuck Klein, with a flick of their hand, to brush off the blow.

Press review: Kiev may step up Russia strikes as Rubio urges EU to put its interests first
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. Kiev may step up strikes on Russia ahead of the October EU summit to secure additional funding and weapons, the EU delays new methane emission rules amid fears of supply shortages, reducing pressure on Russian oil and gas exports, and Rubio urges Europe to prioritize national interests, strengthen transatlantic ties, and confront common threats. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Kiev may intensify strikes on Russia to secure additional EU aid
Escalation has become a means for Ukraine to obtain fresh funding from the European Union and demonstrate its value to Brussels in the confrontation with Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. Although calls for diplomacy are growing louder in Europe, key Western countries and EU officials continue to support prolonging the conflict. Members of the European Parliament warn that Kiev could step up strikes on Russian territory ahead of an EU summit attended by Vladimir Zelensky. However, Ukraine is currently unlikely to be able to mount a major escalation due to severe resource shortages.
The upcoming EU summit on October 15-16 offers Zelensky an opportunity to secure additional funding and reiterate Kiev’s demand for full EU membership. Ukraine categorically rejects intermediate forms of integration. As Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesman Georgy Tikhy stressed, the country insists on full membership in the bloc. While accession to the EU itself could take years, securing fresh funding in the immediate term is a much more realistic objective.
The only way forward for Kiev is to escalate the conflict. Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary State Development, believes the Ukrainian authorities are resorting to escalation to demonstrate their continued activity to European countries in an effort to secure additional funding and weapons. European leaders, meanwhile, could convince their voters that the billions spent on Ukraine are not money thrown away but a direct investment in Europe’s own security.
Members of the European Parliament believe Kiev could intensify strikes on Russia ahead of the EU summit. However, such escalation would only further diminish the chances of a peaceful settlement, French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani told Izvestia.
"Strikes on Russian oil infrastructure will not bring Moscow to its knees. They will only harden positions, provoke retaliatory strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and cities, and give Russia grounds to reject any compromises," he said.
Rodion Miroshnik, ambassador-at-large at the Russian Foreign Ministry, told Izvestia that Ukraine typically resorts to escalation when decisions are being made on allocating additional funding or strengthening its capabilities. He said Kiev seeks to demonstrate in this way that the assistance it receives is supposedly being used effectively.
However, Miroshnik doubted that the EU summit itself would trigger a significant increase in attacks. In his assessment, Kiev is currently in a considerably weakened position, while its attempts at escalation are "frantic in nature" and are being undertaken at the very limits of Ukrainian forces’ capabilities.
Izvestia: NATO drone drills in Latvia highlight growing militarization of Baltic region
The largest military exercises held in Latvia this year, Namejs-2026, wrapped up on October 8, involving around 12,000 military personnel and representatives of other security agencies. One of the main objectives of the drills was to incorporate lessons from combat operations in Ukraine, particularly the widespread use of drones, into NATO forces’ training. However, despite the alliance’s efforts to revamp its combat training, Western units continue to face challenges in protecting military equipment against drones and implementing new tactical approaches. Meanwhile, the Baltic states are stepping up purchases of US weapons, including attack drones whose effectiveness has been questioned by Russian specialists, Izvestia writes.
"During the current exercises, troops are training to operate a wide range of unmanned aerial vehicles used by NATO countries. These include loitering munitions such as the Switchblade, FPV drones, and various reconnaissance systems," military expert Dmitry Kornev told Izvestia.
The approach to training has changed fundamentally, NATO officials acknowledge. NATO brigade commander and Canadian Armed Forces Colonel David Brassard said the alliance was moving away from conventional training exercises toward hands-on practice of combat missions, while extensively analyzing footage of drone operations in the conflict zone.
Alongside the exercises, the Baltic states are stepping up their military buildup. Lithuania’s Defense Ministry, for example, announced that it had received a shipment of US-made Switchblade 600 attack drones.
The Namejs-2026 exercises and the Baltic states’ active procurement of US weapons demonstrate a continued effort to militarize NATO’s eastern flank, the newspaper writes. However, the limited size of deployed forces and the proven vulnerability of Western drone systems to Russian electronic warfare capabilities suggest that the alliance’s current military preparations in the Baltic region are insufficient to pose a critical threat to Russia’s security.
At the same time, European and American technological developments have long ceased to hold technical interest for Russian specialists, Dmitry Kuzyakin, chief designer at the Central Design Bureau for Robotics (TsKBR), told Izvestia.
"European drones currently offer no particular breakthroughs. They are still the same FPV drones, reconnaissance drones, ground-based robotic systems, and long-range attack drones," Kuzyakin said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: EU delays methane emission rules amid supply concerns, easing pressure on Russian exports
The European Union is delaying the introduction of new methane emission requirements, originally scheduled to take effect at the beginning of 2027, by at least a year. Europe fears it will be unable to obtain sufficient supplies of natural gas and oil and, consequently, automotive and aviation fuel, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes. Europe’s largest oil and gas suppliers - the United States, Qatar, Algeria, and Nigeria - were prepared to divert their exports to other markets unless the EU relaxed the new methane emission requirements or deferred their introduction.
The EU’s decision benefits Russian oil and gas exports - had the new requirements taken effect at the beginning of 2027, Europe would have become a market with higher costs and risks for most exporting countries. However, only China and India can compete with Europe in terms of market size, meaning competition for their markets, as well as those of other Asian countries, would have intensified further. Russia would have had to offer larger discounts on its energy resources, potentially making supplies from sanctioned projects more difficult.
Having turned away from Russian oil and gas, Europe has become heavily dependent on US energy supplies. The United States accounts for more than 25% of the EU’s gas imports and nearly 60% of its liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports. American oil accounts for approximately 15-18% of the EU’s oil imports, while US petroleum products make up 17-19% of its petroleum product imports. Moreover, the EU’s overall dependence on imported oil and gas is approaching 90%. It is therefore highly likely that US statements were the main factor behind the EU’s decision.
However, as Alexey Grivach, deputy director of the National Energy Security Fund and associate professor at the Financial University under the Russian Government, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta, the EU ignored demands from the United States and Qatar to scrap the regulations altogether, opting instead to defer their introduction by only one year. This means the EU intends to use the regulations against suppliers as soon as the energy crisis ends. If the crisis continues, however, further delays are possible, the expert believes.
The EU is no longer in a position to be selective, according to Oleg Nikolayev, an expert at the Stolypin Institute for the Economy of Growth and a member of the General Council of Business Russia. Since late February, when the US war with Iran began, gas prices have risen by 140%, while diesel prices have doubled, he noted. The situation is entirely unfavorable for imposing additional barriers on suppliers.
Kommersant: Rubio urges Europe to embrace national interests and Western expansion
US Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio delivered a major policy speech on the future of Europe and the West as a whole during a visit to Greece. Rubio called on the West to return to its civilizational roots, embrace the primacy of national interests without hesitation, and avert a rupture in transatlantic ties, Kommersant writes.
The central theme of Rubio’s address was the need for Europe to "awaken." The US secretary of state said Western countries had reached a "turning point," with decisions made over the next decade set to determine the West’s position for the following century. According to Rubio, the United States has already made its choice under President Donald Trump. As his remarks made clear, the current US administration regards national interests as the decisive factor in the country’s domestic and foreign policy, reserving the right to defend them, including through the use of force.
Rubio’s speech also suggested that the United States and Europe must join forces in the face of common threats, among which he singled out Iran.
Georgy Asatryan, an expert at the National Research University Higher School of Economics, described Rubio’s speech as significant. "There was a great deal of grand rhetoric, and the choice of venue was no coincidence. The Pnyx hill in Greece and the nearby Acropolis are iconic sites for Western civilization and literature. What I see here is ideology through and through - the ideology of Western expansion," he told Kommersant. According to Asatryan, Rubio is calling on Europe to return to a path of military and technological expansion.
"This represents a significant departure from the ideology of the MAGA movement and President Trump. At least the original positions of Trump’s supporters suggested something different. If not outright isolationism, there was a certain restraint in foreign policy, if you will, and a turn toward domestic priorities," the expert added.
According to Asatryan, the US secretary of state is essentially calling on Europeans to abandon neoliberalism and embark on a path of militarization and expansion. "As we know from the history of the 20th century, this is a dangerous phenomenon," the expert concluded.
Vedomosti: EU-China trade tensions deepen as Brussels weighs tariffs on Chinese hybrids
European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic is holding talks with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing on October 8-9 under a new consultation framework. In June 2026, the two sides established a new platform for consultations on trade and investment and agreed to use October as a benchmark for assessing their interim results. Euronews believes the stakes during the commissioner’s current visit will be "higher than ever," while the Hong Kong newspaper South China Morning Post (SCMP) sees this as the "last chance" to demonstrate that the dialogue is producing results. However, the European Union (EU) and China appear unable to resolve their main trade disagreements on mutually acceptable terms, Vedomosti writes.
As the Financial Times reported ahead of the consultations in Beijing, China rejected an EU request to voluntarily reduce exports of hybrid vehicles. However, the situation surrounding hybrid vehicles is just one aspect of the broader problem of China’s trade surplus, which has become a major concern for the EU in its relations with Beijing, Vedomosti writes. Importantly, the EU is heavily dependent on imports of rare earth metals from China, with that dependence reaching 90%, and Beijing has actively leveraged this since 2025. China, for its part, is seeking reliable protection for its investments in EU countries, where Chinese companies are sometimes even placed under external administration on national security grounds.
European countries are gradually preparing China for the introduction of tariffs on hybrid vehicles, according to Sergey Lukonin, head of the Sector for Chinese Economy and Politics at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO). The EU wants to protect its market while avoiding Chinese restrictions in response, and Sefcovic is now testing the waters. According to the expert, China’s retaliatory measures would traditionally involve restricting supplies of rare earth elements and products from related industries. Lukonin believes that some elements of a trade war could emerge between China and the EU, but it is unlikely to be as intense as Beijing’s trade war with the United States.
The very fact that consultations have resumed is a positive sign that both sides want to find a systemic solution, Yulia Melnikova, head of the Asia and Eurasia program at the Russian International Affairs Council, told Vedomosti. However, she noted that reaching such a solution would be difficult at the moment because the two sides are pursuing opposing objectives, while there is no political momentum to encourage a return to negotiations, including on investment.

Skydance's David Ellison conquered Hollywood, but now the work begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

With Hollywood’s history of failed mergers, this is the rocky road ahead for David Ellison and Skydance
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- David Ellison has completed a $111-billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, bringing Paramount and Warner Bros. studios, major networks and franchises under Skydance.
- The combined company must integrate more than 55,000 employees while carrying $86.8 billion in debt; a promised $6 billion in cuts has fueled fears of widespread layoffs.
- Ellison plans to spend at least $30 billion a year on content, but must also merge streaming operations and navigate challenges including integrating CNN and CBS.
Tech scion David Ellison spent three years doggedly pursuing his dream: acquiring Paramount, then Warner Bros. Discovery.
Ellison pulled off his bold feat this week by completing Paramount’s $111-billion takeover of Warner Bros., uniting two industry pioneers and a wealth of cherished properties — Batman, Bugs Bunny, Harry Potter and Maverick of “Top Gun,” as well as CBS, HBO, Comedy Central and CNN. All will be tucked under a corporate umbrella that Ellison is calling Skydance — the name of the studio he formed two decades ago.
The mogul and his lieutenants celebrated their victory in style, ringing the New York Stock Exchange opening bell on Thursday, capping a bruising battle to secure approval of a deal that had sparked protests across Hollywood over fears of looming job cuts.
Ellison and his team must braid together two huge film studios (housing nine film labels), four streaming services, three TV production studios, three animation units and more than 50 television networks, including two prominent news organizations. That could be a daunting task, particularly based on how previous Hollywood mergers have fared.
“Now, the real work begins,” David G. Fubini, a Harvard Business School senior lecturer, said in an interview.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison can proclaim victory after settling a lawsuit with state attorneys general that held up his company’s merger with Warner Bros. But Ellison will have considerable work ahead to repair frayed relations with Hollywood talent.
Anxieties were evident Tuesday — the day the deal closed — when Ellison held a town hall meeting at Warner Bros., which drew nearly 500 employees.
During the session, CNN’s Anderson Cooper quizzed his new bosses, including about anticipated layoffs and news independence.
“Do you stand with CNN and our effort to completely restore access to covering President Trump?” Cooper asked, referring to CNN’s legal fight alongside MS Now and Politico to reverse the president’s ban on the three organizations.
“Of course,” Ellison replied.
Hours later, Ellison parried with reporters in Paramount’s darkened Stage 3, recently revamped with laser projection capabilities to simulate fantastical and far-flung settings for TV shows, such as the streets of New York.
“This was a turbulent process, and, at times, a really ugly process, to actually get this deal over the finish line,” Ellison acknowledged to reporters. “What I want to be able to do now is turn the page, and actually make sure that we are in the business of rebuilding trust.”
To do that, Ellison intends to make more movies and TV shows than rivals. He wants to ensure the Warner Bros. and Paramount studios, which will be kept separate for now, remain talent-friendly destinations.
Ellison has taken an opposing view from his predecessors who confronted crumbling industry economics by cutting expenditures to boost their corporate bottom lines.
The 43-year-old executive, son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, proudly views his family as “owner-operators,” unshackled by quarterly earnings expectations or the need to dole out dividends to keep investors happy. The Ellison family controls the company’s voting stock, allowing David Ellison to take a long-term view as he charts Skydance’s course.
The goal is to “win in storytelling,” Skydance said in an investor presentation. It intends to build the media industry’s most “technologically capable” firm, which uses artificial intelligence to speed work flows. Skydance plans to spend at least $30 billion a year on film, television and video game content.
The realities of Ellison’s big swing will soon sink in as he and his team turn their focus to integrating the myriad operations and about 55,000 employees.
In some ways, Ellison is behind the curve.
Most major mergers are consummated after executives have dedicated months to quietly drafting detailed operational plans and organizational hierarchies. Ellison, in contrast, has spent the last nine months in a pitched battle for Warner Bros. — ultimately vanquishing Netflix, hundreds of vocal merger opponents, and California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state attorneys general who filed an antitrust lawsuit in July in an attempt to derail the deal.
Paramount’s board has approved David Ellison’s contingency plan to move headquarters from Hollywood as early as this fall, according to people familiar with the situation.
Ellison and Bonta resolved their legal fight Sept. 21. A week later, a federal judge cleared the way for the merger to close.
The lawsuit settlement with Bonta requires that the combined company produce at least 30 movies a year for five years. It also must maintain the studio facilities in Los Angeles, making “reasonable efforts to operate the lots in a manner consistent with past practices,” according to the agreement.
Ynon Kreiz, former chief executive of Mattel toys in El Segundo, has been tasked with leading the integration. The 61-year-old executive joined Ellison at Skydance as his co-CEO earlier this week. Day One of the combined company marked Kreiz’s second day on the job.
“They have a whole new management team that will be expected to immediately lead this massive integration,” Fubini, a former partner at consulting firm McKinsey, said. “The clouds have cleared, and they are at the base camp of Mt. Everest facing this enormous undertaking.”
In a report this week, TD Cowen Global Research maintained its “hold” rating on the newly constituted Skydance, expressing some doubts about Ellison and his team’s ability to “avoid integration and execution problems that have bedeviled other major media mergers.”
Hollywood has had a history of failed mergers, including Discovery’s 2022 takeover of WarnerMedia from AT&T, which led to years of cost cuts that ultimately seeded the ground for Ellison’s takeover. AT&T’s purchase of the same assets in 2018 also quickly unraveled, some 20 years after the epic failure of AOL Time Warner.
Ellison now must grapple with the hefty acquisition costs for Warner Bros., which climbed as the deal was delayed. The company emerged from the transaction with $86.8 billion in total debt; with most of that going toward buying out Warner Bros. Discovery’s stockholders at $31.17 a share.
The debt burden also includes more than $18 billion in obligations leftover from past mergers. Skydance has nearly $7 billion in cash on hand.
The Ellison family brought in foreign investors, including royal families of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi as passive owners, to contribute equity to the deal. Gerald Cardinale’s RedBird Capital Partners, a longtime Skydance stakeholder, added $4 billion, bringing its total investment in Skydance deals to $6 billion.
The deal’s financial terms pose deep challenges, analysts said. Fitch Ratings this week downgraded Skydance credit, citing “materially higher leverage after the acquisition and significant execution and integration risks,” according to its report.
“Interest rate increases made financing this transaction far more expensive than anyone anticipated,” said Eric Talley, a professor at Columbia Law School. “Those lenders are going to start expecting their interest payments — Skydance executives won’t have the luxury of time.”
The company could struggle, Talley said, to “generate the cash flow needed to easily service that debt unless they can significantly cut costs.”
Skydance has promised investors that it will make $6 billion in cost cuts over three years. It anticipates $2 billion in reductions within a year, with the bulk of the rest occurring in the second year of the merger.
“They are going to be firing a lot of people,” TD Cowen Global Research media analyst Doug Creutz said.
During the press briefing, Kreiz sought to downplay the expected workforce toll, saying Skydance would achieve savings by combining technologies that support streaming services and marketing expenditures. It plans to save costs on real estate by locating employees at Skydance-owned properties in Santa Monica, Hollywood and Burbank.
HBO could move from Ivy Station in Culver City, its home for the last five years, to one of the studio lots.
Ellison and Kreiz said they would jointly manage the new colossus.
“Where David will focus on creative, technology, long-term strategy, including especially as it relates to the creative part of the business, I will focus more on the operations and the day-to-day management of the business,” Kreiz said.
Kreiz was named to Skydance‘s expanded board this week along with Laurene Powell Jobs, the founder and president of Emerson Collective; and Bobby Kotick, former CEO of Activision.
The new leaders expressed confidence they could expand and integrate their two major streaming services to drive growth. HBO Max and Paramount+ combined will reach more than 200 million subscribers.
The plan, they said, is to combine the two streamers within a couple of years, but the company may offer subscribers a bundle with the two offerings sooner.
Skydance, according to sources, also expects to bolster its free, ad-supported service Pluto TV, which offers more than 200 channels. The service hasn’t had much corporate attention in recent years amid the cuts and deal-making.
The executives have not disclosed which teams would soon be affected or how they will structure overlapping business units.
For example, the company’s three TV studios each have their own leader: Channing Dungey runs the largest, Warner Bros. Television; David Stapf has long managed CBS Studios; and Skydance executive Matt Thunell has been president of Paramount Television Studios since last year.
Integrating CNN and CBS
Anxiety over whether CNN and CBS News would be mashed together was quelled, at least for now.
Skydance announced that it was retaining CNN Worldwide Chairman Mark Thompson as head of the larger news organization. CNN journalists had worried that CBS News Editor in Chief Bari Weiss, who has presided over a year of turmoil at the network, would be put in charge of both.
Any news consolidation could take years, in part, because CBS News is largely unionized while CNN is a non-union shop.
“We are going to spend the next several months basically getting under the hood,” Ellison said.
Another challenge will be stabilizing the Warner Bros. film unit, which has had a rough year at the box office. This month, the top two Warner Bros. film executives, Mike DeLuca and Pam Abdy, exited abruptly, clearing the way for longtime Ellison lieutenants Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein to oversee both film studios. The co-heads of DC Comics, James Gunn and Peter Safran, segued to the new Skydance.
Skydance also will have to deal with the NFL, which could demand substantially higher fees for CBS to keep its Sunday games.
The current contract allows the league to reopen negotiations because of the ownership change. Skydance is hoping it can wait three years until the contracts of other broadcasters also are up for discussion.
Skydance will be a major player in sports. Last year, Paramount agreed to spend $7.7 billion for UFC fights. The combined company also has rights to professional golf, including the Masters tournament; National Hockey League; Major League Baseball and NCAA basketball, including March Madness, as well as European rights to televise the Olympics.
“Until you actually get inside the company, there are things you won’t know,” Creutz said. “But they are going to have to come up with answers pretty quick.”

Rybar project head with his colleagues detained in Montenegro 3 — news outlet

Hurricane Simon quickly intensifies off Mexico's Pacific coast

Hurricane Simon rapidly strengths off Mexico's Pacific coast, threatens tourist region
MEXICO CITY, Oct 9 - Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 100 mph (155 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday.
Simon, currently a Category 1 hurricane, is forecast to become a dangerous Category 4 by Saturday as it nears Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, one of the country's most popular tourist regions, the NHC said.
Simon is expected to make landfall on Sunday between Manzanillo — Mexico’s largest port and the main gateway for trade with Asia — and Puerto Vallarta, a popular beach destination and home to nearly 300,000 residents.
A hurricane warning is in effect from Punta San Telmo, in Michoacan, to vacation hotspot Punta Mita, in Nayarit, while authorities expanded storm alerts in surrounding areas as Simon continued to intensify, according to the latest NHC advisory.
The Mexican Navy activated emergency response personnel in Colima and restricted maritime traffic along parts of the Pacific coast, closing ports to smaller vessels and barring larger vessels from operating in Michoacan.
"Rapid intensification is expected to continue, and Simon is expected to be a very dangerous major hurricane when it approaches the coast of Mexico," the Miami-based center said.
Simon was about 210 miles (335 km) south of Manzanillo in the morning and moving northwest, according to the NHC.
RISKS AND PRECAUTIONS
"We ask people to stay indoors at their homes and in temporary shelters while the hurricane passes," Laura Velazquez, national coordinator of civil protection, said at a press conference, adding that Simon is expected to reach Mexico's coast as a major Category 3 or 4 hurricane.
Forecasters warned that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with isolated rainfall totals reaching 25 inches (64 cm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit.
Mexican authorities warned heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Oaxaca, Jalisco and Colima, and urged residents to remain on alert.
In the state of Jalisco, residents of the community of El Rebalse in the municipality of Cihuatlan have been evacuated as a preventive measure. Seventy people evacuated on their own while 10 moved to a temporary shelter.
Mexico's civil protection authorities urged residents on the Pacific coast to watch for small cracks, tilting trees or fences, and water seepage, due to the increasing risk of landslides caused by the rains.
Classes have been suspended for schools in 22 municipalities across the state on Friday and Monday in anticipation of heavy rain, Jalisco's governor Pablo Lemus said on X.
Last week, Hurricane Polo made landfall on the Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, toppling trees and utility poles, flooding streets and causing other property damage.
Private forecaster AccuWeather expects Simon to make landfall on Mexico's southwestern coast early on Sunday, potentially affecting the coastal areas of Jalisco and Colima. REUTERS

Details
"Russian military personnel brazenly removed 25 local residents from the temporarily occupied part of Kharkiv region, where active hostilities are ongoing. Such actions violate the norms of international humanitarian law. The Geneva Convention relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War expressly prohibits:
-  the forcible transfer and deportation of people from occupied territory (Article 49); 
-  the taking of hostages (Article 34); 
-  intimidation, terror and collective punishment (Article 33).

-  to provide the whereabouts of all 25 people;

-  to take measures to ensure their return to Ukraine.

Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:59:06 UTC
18:59:06 KST

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.
The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.
In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

Possible cyberattack halts Estonian Artists' Association fundraiser auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

18:59:00 KST

Possible cyberattack halts Estonian Artists' Association fundraiser auction
A fundraiser auction for the Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) was suspended Thursday evening amid concerns over a possible cyberattack. The auction is set to resume Friday.
Auction house Eesti Kunsti Oksjonid (EKO) said its technical team was working to resolve technical issues before the auction resumes at 6 p.m. Friday, picking up where it left off the day before.
"According to livestream support provider Zone, the issue may have been caused by a cyberattack," EKO said in a press release Thursday night.
The disruption occurred after the first work, Jüri Arrak's 1985 graphic work "Tiiger," sold for €23,500, up from a starting price of €1,600. Organizers had anticipated strong demand and worked with their technical partner to prepare for it.
Initial assessments, however, indicated the failure was not caused by excessive traffic.
"It's important to us that every bidder has an equal opportunity to participate, so we're postponing the auction until Friday," auctioneer Reigo Kuivjõgi said, apologizing to those who had been watching online and hoped to bid.
Server provider: No signs of cyberattack
Zone.eu marketing chief Triin Lükk later told ERR that Zone had not said a cyberattack was or might have been to blame for the disruption.
She explained that the company provides server services to EKO but does not develop or maintain the auction application itself.
"Based on the information available to us, we have found no signs of malicious activity within the scope of our server service," Lükk said. "Thus, we have no grounds for linking the disruption to a cyberattack."
The cause of the glitch is still being investigated, she noted, adding that Zone's server services are operating as intended.
"We can rule out a cyberattack based on what we've seen," Lükk said. "We've found no signs of one."
The EKL is holding a special fundraiser auction in Tallinn from October 8–10, with proceeds from the sale of 162 works going toward recouping nearly €700,000 the artists' union lost to fraud this spring.

From intelligence chief to trafficking secret information: August Hanning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:58:40 UTC
18:58:40 KST

August Hanning, currently in custody, led Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) for seven years and had access to the state’s most closely guarded secrets; the next chapter involved a private consultancy, corporate intelligence, and business activities spanning Europe (including Russia) and Asia, reports Politico.
Now, following his arrest by the German Federal Prosecutor's Office on the 6th of October on suspicion of espionage and treason, the 80-year-old Hanning finds himself at the center of an investigation. Prosecutors suspect he obtained classified intelligence from his former chief of staff and used it in his private business dealings. An EU intelligence official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the situation as a disaster for both Germany and Western intelligence agencies. Everyone is reportedly in shock, and the scale of the incident is immense, particularly given the current climate. The official added that, since the alleged espionage came to light during the investigation of an entirely separate matter, a great deal more information is likely to emerge.
The case has arisen at an awkward time for the BND. In early October, German lawmakers began debating a new bill proposed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government that would grant the intelligence service sweeping powers, aiming to restore Berlin to the ranks of the world’s top intelligence agencies. The timing is also significant for European intelligence services more broadly; with Russian hybrid attacks threatening Europe, governments across the bloc are rewriting long-standing security laws to empower their intelligence agencies and ensure they are taken more seriously.
Prosecutors stated that the former head of Hanning’s office—identified as Manfred D. in accordance with German privacy regulations—handed over approximately 2,000 BND documents to Hanning between 2010 and 2022. 
Many of these contained classified information intended solely for internal use by the intelligence service, including materials used to brief high-ranking German officials.
Speaking to the newspaper WELT, Hanning’s lawyer stated that while some of the charges brought against the former intelligence chief were true, he had not intended to cause harm to Germany. The lawyer pointed out that Hanning was indeed in possession of classified documents, but the accusation that he had passed on information capable of harming the state was false.
In one instance, charges were brought regarding the use of classified documents to prepare an analytical report for a foreign intelligence officer. Prosecutors also believe that Manning maintained a relationship with a representative of another intelligence service for several years and passed on political information that was partly based on documents supplied by Manfred D. Prosecutors have not identified the specific intelligence agencies with which Manning might have been linked, but German media have named Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan. Azerbaijan has denied involvement.
Another anonymous EU official stated that intelligence agencies log every action—specifically, who accesses information and when. If an analyst working on monitoring right-wing extremists suddenly begins viewing intelligence on China, it can raise suspicions. Conversely, high-ranking officials—such as a director's chief of staff—can access virtually anything without arousing suspicion. Moreover, chiefs of staff typically remain in their posts even when directors change; the only exceptions are cases involving disagreements with the incoming director. The official stated that 
each intelligence agency would now have to assess the information passed to the BND and the potential damage caused by this.
Hanning headed the BND from 1998 to 2005 and subsequently served as State Secretary at the German Interior Ministry until 2009. Upon leaving the government, Hanning turned to the private sector, founding Hanning Consult with his wife in July 2010. In the spring of that same year, Manfred D. agreed—in exchange for payment—to pass intelligence held by the BND to Hanning, who in turn utilized it for his private consulting activities.
Roderich Kiesewetter, a German Christian Democrat MP and representative on the Bundestag’s Foreign Affairs Committee, stated that there is a vast network of individuals in Germany who leverage information and influence gained during their time in public service to shape Berlin’s policy regarding countries such as China and Russia. Kiesewetter told Politico that the situation is not only lamentable but also damages Germany’s reputation; he noted that if someone wishes to engage with Russia, it suffices to enlist former government or intelligence officials.
Hanning is also linked to German businessman Samuel Danilowitsch, who headed the Swiss corporate intelligence consultancy Pluteos. Hanning became the chairman of the board at Pluteos and, in 2019, attended a meeting in Moscow with Danilowitsch focused on European-Russian relations. Russian politicians and businesspeople participated in the event, during which the annexation of Crimea was portrayed as a necessity rather than a choice made by Moscow.
Around 2014, Hanning joined the British consultancy G3 as a senior advisor. 
He later oversaw the firm's operations regarding Russia and former Soviet bloc countries.
In 2019, Hanning was invited as a guest of honor to an Arctic Council meeting organized by the Russian Security Council. It was chaired by the former Secretary of the Russian Security Council, Nikolai Patrushev, one of the most influential figures in Russian dictator Vladimir Putin's security circle.
Hanning has also spoken publicly about some of the politically explosive issues surrounding Russian aggression in Ukraine. In 2024, he told WELT TV that he considered it plausible that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy knew about the 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream pipelines. A few days later, Hanning went further, stating that a secret agreement between high-ranking Polish and Ukrainian officials lay behind the attack on the pipelines.
None of Hanning’s business dealings, contacts, or statements link him to espionage; however, they demonstrate that he continued to expand his influence even after leaving government service. Nor have any charges been brought regarding espionage on behalf of Russia.
Investigators discovered the classified documents in Hanning’s possession while probing an unusual guardianship case
 involving Christina Block, the heiress to a German restaurant empire. The Hamburg public prosecutor’s office charged Block with abducting her two youngest children from their father in Denmark. Block and two men allegedly hired an Israeli security team to snatch the children—then aged 10 and 13—from their father's custody. According to the charges, masked men beat the children's father and took the children across the Danish-German border to southern Germany. Four days later, the children were returned to their father by court order. Block denies having known about the abduction.
In September 2025, Hamburg investigators searched Hanning’s home and business premises in connection with the Block case. Prosecutors believed that Hanning and a retired police officer had accepted a deal worth 100,000 euros to intercept Block’s children on their way to school in November 2022. The plan failed because the children's father noticed suspicious individuals and called the police. Following the search, the German media outlet Taggeshau reported that investigators had found approximately 2,000 digital BND documents on Hanning’s properties, triggering an investigation that was taken over by the Federal Prosecutor's Office in May 2026.
Manfred D. was Hanning’s chief of staff and subsequently worked with the next BND directors as well, remaining in the position until March 2026. Both men are currently in custody.

India slams US vice president's 'foreign indentured servants' remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:58:38 UTC
18:58:38 KST

Ahmad Adil
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
India on Friday criticized US Vice President JD Vance for describing foreign workers as "foreign indentured servants," calling the terminology "deeply offensive" and defending the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy.
"We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem," India's External Affairs Ministry said.
"Indeed, the history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," it added.
New Delhi said, "resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive."
The response came after Vance used the phrase Thursday while announcing the suspension of Microsoft's participation in the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program.
"You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
"Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers. At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. For every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," he claimed.
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling also announced Thursday that Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini and Adobe had been suspended from the program.
The PERM program is a Labor Department certification process that generally serves as the first step for employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based permanent residency.
India's External Affairs Ministry said it was aware of the US decision affecting several companies but stressed that PERM is "distinct from the H-1B visa programme."
The H-1B program allows US employers to hire foreign workers in specialized occupations, with Indian nationals accounting for the largest share of visa holders.
Reacting to the US decision, Nasscom, India's leading information technology industry association, said the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process was "relatively limited."
"Indian technology companies have significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas, while steadily expanding local hiring and building a strong domestic workforce in the US," the association said.

The company said in a blog post the operations combined AI with traditional influence techniques, using seemingly legitimate research platforms and fabricated journalist identities to spread geopolitical messages.
The Russian-linked campaign used a purported research platform focused on Latin America, while the Iran-linked operation used fake journalist profiles to pitch articles to online publications.
“What is most striking about these operations is that they closely resembled complex influence operations of the pre-AI age, but used AI to make some of the workflows easier,” OpenAI said.
The company said it had banned clusters of ChatGPT accounts associated with both operations and shared information about them with relevant authorities.
 
Fake journalists published articles online
OpenAI said the Iran-linked operation used seven fabricated journalist identities to pitch long-form articles to online publications.
The company identified almost 100 articles published under the fake journalists’ bylines across more than a dozen outlets.
The articles covered international affairs, geopolitics and the Middle East. Publication increased sharply after the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict, OpenAI said.
According to OpenAI, the operators used ChatGPT to edit articles, check drafts against individual outlets’ submission requirements and prepare emails pitching stories to editors.
The fake profiles presented themselves as Western journalists with expertise in international politics, the Middle East, human rights or conflict, the company said.
The operation also generated social media comments in English and Persian.
"The users asked for comments on topics such as missile strikes, ceasefires, and diplomatic maneuvering, specifying outputs that portrayed the US as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally of the US, and Iran as a defiant but resilient victim," OpenAI said.
However, the company said the comments it identified publicly generally received little engagement. Some likes came from accounts linked to the operation itself, it added.
 
Russian-linked campaign targeted Ukraine, Latin America
OpenAI said the Russian-linked operation targeted audiences across Latin America, with much of its activity apparently aimed at "undermining Ukraine’s reputation." Other efforts focused on domestic politics in Argentina and Bolivia.
The operation allegedly used the Social Research Center, a self-described research platform covering Latin America. OpenAI said internal reports suggested Russian operators controlled the platform through a fabricated persona named “Mia Clark.”
The company said available evidence indicated that employees working for the platform in Latin America did not know they were working for a Russian group. They appeared to conduct interviews with regional experts and produce research papers in good faith.
The operators’ internal reports described efforts to spread fabricated stories, documents and audio recordings targeting Ukraine and political figures in the region.
OpenAI said its research found material matching some reported campaigns, including false claims that prompted fact-checks and official denials. It cautioned that some claims in the internal reports could not be corroborated.
OpenAI said both operations placed content in media outlets, potentially extending their reach beyond fake social media accounts.
“AI can give such false-front operations greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability,” the company said.
OpenAI said it published the findings to help researchers and other organizations identify and disrupt similar campaigns.
