Taiwan rejects Beijing’s ‘reunification’ myth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:24:37 UTC
17:24:37 KST

In the modern geopolitical theater of the Taiwan Strait, the vocabulary of “unification” is wielded not as a democratic negotiation, but as an authoritarian mandate.
China consistently frames its ambitions toward Taiwan through the lens of an inevitable “reunification,” or tongyi, presenting it as the compulsory correction of a historical anomaly left behind by the Chinese Civil War.
This rhetoric has sharpened dangerously. In his Sept. 30, 2026, National Day address, Chinese leader Xi Jinping escalated Beijing’s rhetoric, vowing to “resolutely combat separatist forces advocating Taiwan independence, and oppose interference by external forces … and advance the great cause of national reunification.”
However, Taiwan fundamentally rejects this terminology. From the perspective of Taipei and the vast majority of its citizens, Taiwan has never been part of the People’s Republic of China, which was established by the Chinese Communist Party in 1949, long after Taiwan’s separate historical and political trajectory began.
Consequently, Taiwanese society views Beijing’s rhetoric not as the peaceful bringing together of a divided people, but as a historical distortion and euphemism for military annexation by a totalitarian communist regime.
A collective shield
For Taiwan, navigating this existential threat requires looking toward a future rooted in robust defense and strategic solidarity.
To prevent an authoritarian imposition of “unification,” Taipei must continue working alongside its global partners to build credible deterrence against Chinese aggression.
Preserving stability across the Western Pacific requires a structural security matrix combining agile executive diplomacy, robust legislative anchors, and deep regional burden-sharing among the United States, partners along the First Island Chain — stretching from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines — and democratic countries worldwide.
The strength of these ties was on display on Oct. 5, when the German Institute Taipei hosted its official reception celebrating German Unity Day. High-ranking Taiwanese officials attended the gathering, which celebrated the values-based partnership between Taipei and Berlin.
A traditional Taiwanese proverb captures the essence of this regional reality: “When people are of one heart, their combined strength can break metal” (人心同，鐵石成).
While Taiwan continues to strengthen its domestic resilience and asymmetric military preparedness, its survival also depends on the interlocking strength of democratic partners. Just as fragmented elements become harder to break when aligned toward a single purpose, the shared commitment of free countries creates a structural barrier Beijing cannot easily overcome.
The geopolitical dictionary of 1990
Taiwan’s defensive struggle stands in profound contrast to how Europe resolved its own division decades ago.
Every year on Oct. 3, Germany observes Tag der Deutschen Einheit — German Unity Day. To the outside world, the holiday is frequently understood as commemorating German reunification.
Yet the distinction between these terms is not merely a quirk of translation. It represents a deeper debate over history, national identity, and the balance between remembering the past and building a democratic future.
To understand why the terminology mattered, one must look back to the frantic diplomacy of 1990. When the Berlin Wall fell on Nov. 9, 1989, language immediately became a geopolitical tool.
West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl carefully navigated the deep anxieties of global powers. The term “reunification,” or Wiedervereinigung, carried historical baggage that could evoke the restoration of a powerful unified German state in the center of Europe.
By officially framing the project as Einheit, or unity, in the domestic Unification Treaty — signed in East Berlin’s Kronprinzenpalais on Aug. 31, 1990, by negotiators Wolfgang Schauble and Gunther Krause — the state signaled a forward-looking democratic project.
This message was reinforced externally by West German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher and East Germany’s last democratically elected prime minister, Lothar de Maiziere.
Together with the four victorious Allied powers of World War II, the two German states negotiated the landmark Two Plus Four Treaty, officially the Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany.
Signed in Moscow on Sept. 12, 1990, the treaty granted Germany full external sovereignty and finalized its international borders, assuring the world that a united Germany sought peace rather than territorial restoration.
The price of accession
Even this democratic and consensual path did not erase internal friction. The legal mechanism used to unite the two German states remains central to debates about what followed.
Rather than invoking Article 146 of the West German Basic Law — which could have opened the way for a new constitution adopted by Germans in both East and West — Kohl’s government used Article 23.
Legally and strategically, this allowed the German Democratic Republic to dissolve its provinces and rapidly accede to West Germany’s constitutional framework while the geopolitical window for unity remained open.
Domestically, however, the rapid mechanism meant East Germany was effectively absorbed rather than merged. Consequently, a narrative emerged in the East of a Beitritt, or annexation, masquerading as partnership.
Decades later, Germany’s economic, political, and cultural institutions remain heavily shaped by Western structures.
This internal rift remains politically volatile. During his October 2026 Unity Day address in Bremen, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier acknowledged “bitter setbacks” and warned that political demagoguery and persistent divisions continue to threaten Germany’s internal cohesion.
This German linguistic and historical tightrope was further complicated by the moral responsibilities of the state, particularly concerning Germany’s Jewish community and Holocaust memory.
The choice of Oct. 3 as the national holiday was itself a deliberate pivot away from a date that would have carried far more spontaneous joy: Nov. 9, the day the Berlin Wall opened.
Nov. 9 was also the date of the 1938 November Pogroms, often known internationally as Kristallnacht, when the Nazi regime orchestrated a violent wave of anti-Jewish attacks across Germany.
To celebrate a triumphant national awakening on the anniversary of one of the darkest chapters in Jewish history was deemed unacceptable.
By choosing Oct. 3 — the date the Unification Treaty took legal effect — Germany codified an important principle: national celebration would not overwrite historical memory.
For the Jewish community, the preference for “unity” over “reunification” also offered a psychological safeguard. “Unity” implied a constitutional commitment to democratic values, human rights, and pluralism.
“Reunification,” by contrast, could hint at the restoration of a historical German state.
Conclusion
This divergence underscores the irreconcilability of the German and Chinese models.
If China were to impose annexation on Taiwan, it would not be an act equivalent to Germany’s democratic unification. Taiwan’s political system, public opinion, and right to self-determination would be overridden rather than incorporated through consent.
Words such as “unity,” “unification,” and “reunification” are never politically neutral.
In the German context, the language of unity exists within an ongoing effort to bridge cultural, economic, and political divides inside a democratic constitutional order. Beijing’s use of “reunification,” by contrast, asserts a predetermined political outcome for a society it does not govern.
Germany’s history demonstrates that bringing divided societies together requires legal legitimacy, democratic consent, and international agreement.
By rejecting Beijing’s imposed baseline of “reunification,” Taiwan insists on the essential principle underlying any legitimate political union: genuine unity cannot be created through coercion.

Why Asian parents are trapped in a private tuition arms race
From Singapore to South Korea, fear of falling behind fuels a costly cycle of extra lessons despite the toll it takes on children
Grace often hears other Singapore mothers debating how much private tuition their children need. Some rush to enrol their offspring in multiple classes before they turn five, while others try to resist the pressure to add lessons outside school.
She enrolled her two children, now aged four and seven, in Chinese tuition when they were three to give them greater exposure to their ancestral tongue.
“Neither of their parents speaks fluent Mandarin at home … I guess there is some degree of pressure involved too,” said Grace, 38, the founder of a creative agency.
Her dilemma reflects a wider tension across Asia, where parents continue to invest in private tuition to give their children an academic edge, despite growing concerns over the stress placed on young learners and the widening gap between families who can afford extra classes and those who cannot.

INTERVIEW – Space weapons a ‘concern,’ but capabilities not new: UN space chief on US disclosure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:23:16 UTC
17:23:16 KST

The US disclosure that it has deployed weapons in orbit does raise concerns over the safety and sustainability of an increasingly crowded space environment, even if the capabilities themselves are not new, according to the head of the UN’s space office.
Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA), said her Vienna-based office deals with the safety and sustainability of space activities. Security, she said, falls under the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs.
“So we are not concerned with security in principle. However, to the extent that these things can affect sustainability and safety, it is a concern,” she told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya.
“I don’t believe that the US has put capabilities out there which do not already exist. The difference is that they have announced it.”
On Sept. 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told a defense conference in Maryland that the US has “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” It was the first official acknowledgment that Washington has weapons in orbit.
Meink did not identify the systems.
In a statement to The War Zone, a US defense news website, a Space Force spokesperson said space control involves “kinetic and non-kinetic means” to affect adversary capabilities “through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary.”
China’s Foreign Ministry urged Washington “to stop expanding its military buildup in outer space.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow believes space should be free of weapons and called for its complete demilitarization.
Opening the congress in Antalya on Monday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan also warned against the militarization of space, saying that sending weapons there or turning it into an arena for an arms race would be “totally wrong.”
European Space Agency (ESA) Director General Josef Aschbacher, also speaking to Anadolu at the congress, said Europe does not deploy weapons in space but is watching developments “very carefully.”
At the center of the debate is the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the foundation of international space law and a treaty to which the US, Russia and China are parties.
The treaty declares space free for exploration and use by all states. Under its Article IV, parties may not place nuclear weapons or any other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or station them anywhere in space.
The treaty does not, however, prohibit conventional weapons in Earth orbit.
Michael Schmitt, an international law professor and retired US Air Force military lawyer, wrote in Just Security, a law and policy journal based at New York University, on Sept. 23 that placing conventional weapons in orbit does not in itself violate international law.
He noted, however, that their legality depends on how they are used and the circumstances of their deployment.
Russia and China have long pushed for a treaty banning all weapons in space, which the US rejects, and there is still no agreed definition of a “space weapon.”
A UN working group on preventing an arms race in outer space is scheduled to meet next in Geneva on Nov. 23-27.
The most visible weapons are anti-satellite (ASAT) systems, designed to disable or destroy satellites. Only four countries have destroyed satellites in orbit in tests: the US, Russia, China and India.
Holla-Maini said the most pressing issue in space governance today is the traffic coordination.
According to the European Space Agency’s latest space environment report, more than 300 launches placed over 4,000 new payloads into orbit in 2025 alone, driven largely by commercial satellite constellations.
Close calls between satellites are increasingly common, and operators do not always know whom to contact.
"We have more and more objects being launched into space ... and it is increasing collision risk because of increased congestion," she said.
The governance challenge is also extending to the Moon as governments and private companies prepare for more lunar missions and potential resource use.
More than 100 lunar missions are expected by 2030, many of them commercial. Holla-Maini rejected the idea that the UN is falling behind in setting rules for them. She pointed to three tracks under the 104-member UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS).
The first is the Action Team on Lunar Activities Consultation, set up in 2024 on Romania’s initiative. It is drafting recommendations through 2027 on how countries should consult each other on lunar missions.
The second is a working group on space resources, which released an initial draft set of principles in 2025. The rules would cover activities such as extracting water ice, helium-3 and lunar soil.
The third is the UN-backed International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems. Experts there are working on lunar navigation and a common lunar time standard, which Holla-Maini described as “effectively a time zone for the Moon.” Washington ordered NASA in 2024 to develop a Coordinated Lunar Time.
“All of these three mechanisms combined and their work is absolutely what we need now, today, to make sure that the moon remains a domain for peaceful space exploration and activity,” she said.
Last November, UNOOSA hosted a conference in Vienna on the commercial lunar landscape, where around 40 companies presented their plans to member states, according to Holla-Maini.
“You cannot take decisions on rules if you don’t know what is going to happen,” said Holla-Maini, who joined the UN in 2023 after nearly two decades leading the Global Satellite Operators Association. "I think it's our responsible duty to bring industry into the dialogue without giving them decision-making power. That is for the member states."
The congestion concern also extends to a newer idea, moving data centers into space. Driven by the soaring energy demands of AI, several companies are developing orbital computing platforms that would run on continuous solar power.
Holla-Maini said the idea is not new but has gained visibility. She described it as interesting because it could draw on solar energy and on the cold of space for cooling.
“The problem from the UN side, whether it’s data centers in space, whether it’s more satellites in space, is congestion,” she said.
“We worry about so many objects being launched into space and not enough coordination and communication between the different actors ... If we’re going to continue to put more objects into space, we also need to start looking at debris remediation, cleaning space.”
AI is already embedded in space operations, from analyzing satellite imagery to steering spacecraft. SpaceX has reported to US regulators that its Starlink satellites performed about 300,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers in 2025, using an onboard autonomous system that decides when to move.
In September 2025, UNOOSA published a policy brief on responsible AI in space and Earth observation. It sets out five objectives, including transparent AI for space operations and safeguards for data integrity.
Holla-Maini said those protections are particularly important for UNOOSA because the office supplies satellite imagery to developing countries during disasters.
“Because the imagery that we provide is literally used for life-saving activities, we cannot afford for it to be tampered with or manipulated using AI or other tools,” she said. She added that UNOOSA wants to work with companies on a digital fingerprint to authenticate such imagery.
She also cautioned against relying on AI for collision avoidance, since satellite locations and maneuver plans are not publicly available.
“AI cannot take a decision on something which is not public, and that is problematic. So we need to maintain human in the loop.”
The International Astronautical Congress, organized by the International Astronautical Federation and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency, with SAHA Istanbul as co-host, is being held in Türkiye for the first time from Oct. 5-9.
On Türkiye, Holla-Maini recalled the country’s response to the 2023 Türkiye-Syria earthquakes, when Turkish companies provided satellite imagery and communications support. She also pointed to satellite operator TURKSAT’s long track record in the region.
She highlighted Ankara’s plan to build a spaceport in Somalia as another example of its expanding international ambitions.
“This is sending strong signals about international collaboration and cooperation and how Türkiye sees itself as a major player on the global stage,” she said.

"Bloody Friday" - security at schools has been tightened in Poland due to reports of possible attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Threats of attacks on schools spread across Poland on October 9 following two attacks in the Masovian Voivodeship. Police detained two 17-year-old teenagers.
Poles are being warned on social media about allegedly planned attacks on schools on October 9, following an entire series of incidents in the east of the country. Police have increased security at educational institutions. In some cities, they have been closed altogether. Euronews reports, UNN writes.
Details
On Thursday, reports about allegedly planned attacks on Polish schools began spreading actively on social media. Students and their parents exchanged screenshots and videos warning about a so-called "Bloody Friday," allegedly planned for October 9.
The reports emerged amid a series of serious incidents in the Masovian Voivodeship. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old man attacked nine people with a knife at a school in Ostrołęka. The next day, in the settlement of Leszczydół-Nowiny, a 15-year-old former student attacked three people; a 37-year-old school employee died from her injuries.
Police to patrol near schools
Amid growing anxiety, police announced additional preventive measures. Chief Commander of Police Inspector General Marek Boroń said that law enforcement officers would patrol near educational institutions starting Friday morning.
"The police will do everything to ensure that schools are properly protected," Boroń said. He added that patrols had appeared near schools as early as Thursday and were maintaining contact with representatives of educational institutions. On Friday, police officers will cooperate with principals, teachers, and local authorities.
The Chief Commander of Police also urged students and parents to report any reasonable suspicions regarding preparations for violence to teachers or law enforcement officers. Law enforcement agencies will verify the information received.
Boroń also noted that the number of reports about potential threats had increased significantly after the attack in Ostrołęka. In addition, he urged people to treat information about allegedly planned attacks with caution.
17-year-old teenager detained
One of the reasons for the heightened anxiety was a video that spread online. According to the Interia portal, the video concerned allegedly planned attacks on schools as part of a "Bloody Friday." Local media reported that its author threatened to carry out a "massacre in Przasnysz."
Local police promptly took up the case. They detained a 17-year-old resident of Przasnysz County who is likely the author of the video.
Police detained a 17-year-old resident of Przasnysz County who is likely the author of the video circulating online. Procedural actions are being carried out with the teenager
Alarming reports also emerged in other localities. In Sierpc, police detained a 17-year-old teenager who, according to eyewitnesses, spoke of intending to harm someone at a school. Two knives were found on him. In this case, the students and teachers who notified police about his behavior played a key role.
Authorities in several localities in the Masovian Voivodeship ordered the partial or complete closure of schools on Friday.

court observed that it could not consider easing the restrictions unless the denial of permission was challenged."If there is no permission for protests, it will be an unlawful protest," Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed.Sibal, appearing for CPM MP M A Baby, argued that every citizen had the right to protest, even spontaneously.The Supreme Court said the right to peaceful protest at a designated place existed, but holding a demonstration without permission could expose protesters to prosecution.The bench also indicated that it could consider easing the restrictions if the organisers challenged the denial of permission and gave assurances about the gathering.The court said it could seek details about the number of people expected to attend, along with undertakings that protesters would remain peaceful and not carry weapons.Such assurances could allow the court to reconsider restrictions imposed over possible law and order concerns.Meanwhile, CJP founder Abhijeet there.Dipke also criticised the Centre over the cancellation of trains to Delhi ahead of Saturday's protest."Shut down entire country if you are scared of youth," he said, taking aim at the government over the restrictions.Delhi Police had earlier denied permission for the proposed protest, citing short notice, alleged violations during a previous demonstration and concerns over public safety, law and order and traffic management.Joint commissioner of police Nupur Prasad said the police had received an application from CJP co-convener Saurav Das seeking permission for a protest over the accountability of the Chief Election Commissioner."This intimation was considered, and it was found that the intimation was given in a very short span of time, whereas as per the prescribed guideline, the intimation has to be received 10 days prior to the protest that is planned," she said.Prasad also pointed to the party's conduct during an earlier protest at the same venue."Further, it is also important to mention that on an earlier occasion, when the Cockroach Janta Party was given permission to hold a protest there, they did not follow the lawful directions and did not follow their own undertakings given at that point in time," she said.
She added that Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which allows preventive restrictions to maintain public order, was in force in the New Delhi area.Police warned that anyone violating the restrictions could face legal action.The restrictions come ahead of Saturday's planned CJP protest, with several trains to New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin cancelled and restrictions proposed at Metro stations.

U.S. Marine Corps wants AI to spot aircraft failures early
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:21:22 UTC
17:21:22 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps selected SteerBridge Strategies to develop AI tools for aviation supply, predictive maintenance and planning after a 34-day selection process.
- The selection is not a contract award, and any agreement depends on finalizing a statement of work.
The U.S. Marine Corps has picked SteerBridge Strategies, a small veteran-owned company in Vienna, Virginia, to work on artificial intelligence tools meant to predict aircraft maintenance needs and manage aviation spare parts, after a selection process the service said took 34 days from approved requirement to vendor notification.
The Marine Corps’ aviation acquisition office at Patuxent River, Maryland, announced the selection on Oct. 8. It said the tools, which it calls predictive super intelligence and machine learning technologies, are intended to help forecast parts demand, anticipate maintenance and support planning decisions for Marine aviation units. The selection is not a contract award, and the office said any agreement still depends on negotiating and finalizing a statement of work and completing other acquisition steps. No value, timeline or list of aircraft types was disclosed.
The service ran the competition through an Other Transaction Authority process, a faster route the Pentagon uses for prototypes, with the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium handling the solicitation. Companies submitted white papers and videos for review. The Marine Corps said the effort carries out a directive from the secretary of war to speed up software acquisition.
“This agile approach demonstrates that we can shorten the timeline from identifying an operational need to delivering a capability to our Marines,” said Lt. Gen. William Swan, the deputy commandant for aviation. “Accelerating our acquisition speed is essential to maintaining our competitive edge and driving the modernization goals outlined in the Marine Corps Aviation Plan.”
The 2026 Marine Corps Aviation Plan, released in February, makes AI-enabled sustainment a central goal, built around three lines of effort: dynamic aviation supply, predictive maintenance and data-driven operational planning. The idea is to replace scheduled inspections and surprise breakdowns with maintenance timed to data that shows when a part is likely to fail, so parts and mechanics can be in place before an aircraft goes down.
The service has already begun testing the approach. In April, Marine Corps aviation officials said they were feeding KC-130J tanker data into an AI system and planned to give a maintenance assessment tool to a unit at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, Arizona. Swan said then that if the tools could forecast part failures with around 90 percent probability, that would be good enough.
“The effort aligns directly with DoW objectives to accelerate acquisition timelines, strengthen collaboration with industry, and modernize acquisition processes,” said Maj. Gen. David Walsh, deputy portfolio acquisition executive for Marine Corps aviation.
SteerBridge is a certified service-disabled veteran-owned small business. The company says its aviation division already supports Marine Corps F-35 sustainment and analytics work.
Under the planned prototype, the government and the company will test and refine the tools for Marine aviation maintenance, supply and planning.

Nobel Peace Prize bets for Russian dissident’s widow surge on Polymarket
STOCKHOLM – Bets for who will take home the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize surged overnight on Polymarket, echoing similar events a year ago when a website hacking likely leaked the winner’s name.
Yulia Navalnaya, widow of the late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny, has suddenly emerged as front runner in betting on the Polymarket platform before the announcement due later on Oct 9.
Her odds went as high as 65.5% at one point, now sitting at around 46% with more than US$1.7 million (S$2.2 million) in betting volume. The event overall has a volume of just over US$30 million.
In 2025, a leak of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado’s name triggered an unusual betting surge on the Polymarket platform hours before she was unveiled as the award recipient.
The Venezuelan opposition leader had not previously been considered a favourite for the 2025 prize.
An investigation by the Norwegian Nobel Institute assisted by security authorities later concluded that an individual or a state actor may have illegally gained access to its website in a cyber breach.
Navalnaya, from exile, has carried on her husband’s campaign after his February 2024 death in an Arctic prison that his supporters and Western governments blamed on the authoritarian regime of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Arguably the most prestigious prize in global diplomacy, the Nobel Peace Prize has stirred more controversy.
In 2025, US President Donald Trump, who has long coveted the award, aggressively campaigned to obtain the award, in vain. Earlier in 2026, Machado gifted her medal to Trump, stunning Norway.
The Nobel prizes are annual awards for achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, peace and literature. They were established in the will of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite who died in 1896.
All except the Peace Prize are awarded in Stockholm, and the awards in 2026 come with 12 million kronor (S$1.5 million) of money. BLOOMBERG

The warning comes amid renewed fighting in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces have been battling armed groups linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Reports from the region also indicate that Ethiopian military drones struck vehicles allegedly carrying Eritrean soldiers near Adigrat on Thursday. The reported attacks and claims of casualties have not been independently verified.
Ethiopia and Eritrea fought alongside each other during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, but relations have since deteriorated sharply, with both governments accusing the other of threatening regional stability.
Tensions have also intensified over Ethiopia's pursuit of access to the Red Sea, particularly the Eritrean port of Assab, which Asmara maintains is part of its sovereign territory.

Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon have a new Grand Mufti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:20:00 UTC
17:20:00 KST

Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon have a new Grand Mufti
October 9, 2026
The reis-ul-ulema or Grand Mufti of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the head of the country's Islamic community, represents the interests of Muslims before the state, expresses himself on political, moral and social issues and defends the independence of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina against attempts at foreign influence.
Having served two seven-year terms, the current Grand Mufti, Husein Kavazovic, is no longer permitted to run.
Three candidates are competing to become his successor: Salem Dedovic, the Mufti of Mostar, Nedzad Grabus, the Mufti of Sarajevo, and Mensur Malkic, the head of the Directorate for Religious Affairs of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Grand Mufti's envoy.
While Malkic's focus lies in strengthening the Islamic Community in religious and institutional terms, Dedovic has stated that he sees the office in a more political light and would like it to become more engaged in social debates. Grabus, who has the most international experience as the former Grand Mufti of Slovenia, says he would like to strengthen the community in times of globalization and secularization.
"No other Islamic personality in Europe holds a position like the Reis-ul-ulema in Sarajevo," said Imam Benjamin Idriz, the head of the Islamic Community in the Bavarian city of Penzberg and the chair of the Munich Forum for Islam. "That's why the importance of this election extends far beyond the country, to Muslims and non-Muslims alike, across Europe."
The President of the Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Germany (IGBD), Zenahir Mrakovic, said that the "election is important to us, because historically, theologically and institutionally, we share close ties with the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina."
"Bosniak" is the name Bosnian Muslims use for themselves. With around 100 communities across the country, the IGBD is one of Germany's smaller Muslim associations.
Muslims have lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina for centuries. Islam was introduced to the population when to Ottoman Empire spread through southeastern Europe. The organizational structure of the Islamic Communities was established after the Berlin Congress in 1878, which, among other things, placed Bosnia and Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian rule.
Following the example of Christian churches, the Austro-Hungarian rulers soon officially recognized Islam as a religious community and in 1882, they founded the Council of Ulema and appointed the first Reis-ul-ulema as president.
Unique self-organization of the Muslim faith
This kind of Islamic self-organization could become a model for Muslims across Europe. The Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina is independent from the state and is financed with donations, membership fees and zakat, a form of charity given by Muslims.
The Islamic Community has its own sort of parliament, the Sabor, and a Constitutional Court that ensures the community's actions are in line with the constitution of the country in which it operates. The Riyaset is the community's highest executive body, responsible for implementing decisions. Its headquarters are in Sarajevo.
In the 150 years since its founding, the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina has survived numerous political upheavals and repeatedly adapted to new circumstances. After the Ottoman Empire came the Habsburg monarchy and Austro-Hungarian rule, then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito. Following Tito's death, the Bosnian War for independence ended in 1995 with the Dayton Accords.
Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a secular state with a democratic constitutional order. Time and again, the Islamic Community has clearly distanced itself from radical tendencies. It has a history of cooperation and coexistence with Jewish and Christian communities.
This has also left an impression on the roughly 400,000 Bosnian Muslims living in Germany.
"In the process of institutionalizing Islam in Germany, the experience of the Bosniaks' Islamic Community should be taken more strongly into account," said Esnaf Begic, a former imam and a lecturer at the Institute for Islamic Theology at Osnabrück University. "We are autochthonous European Muslims and to a certain extent, we share more similarities with Germans than with Muslims from Afghanistan, Iran or Saudi Arabia."
Mrakovic, head of the IGBD, agrees that Bosnia's experience with organizing religious life in a democratic and pluralistic society could also be useful to other Muslim communities. "It's not about telling other people how to live their Islamic faith but about learning from our own experiences: how we preserve our religious identity while remaining a natural part of European, democratic society.
An office in challenging times
The new head of Bosnian Muslims will be assuming his role in challenging times. Statehood in Bosnia and Herzegovina remains fragile, and foreign actors are vying for more influence. "Attempts to exert more influence aren't only coming from Ankara or Riyah, but also from Washington, Berlin or Brussels. They, too are, trying to act upon the Reis-ul-ulema in their own interest," Begic said.
In Europe, anti-Muslim racism and Islamophobia have reached levels that are becoming increasingly frightening for Muslims. Right-wing populists are on the rise, and extremist parties are attracting more and more supporters bent on denying Muslims the right to participate in society.
Given the circumstances, the new Reis-ul-ulema will be expected to employ the full democratic and historical legitimacy of his office to actively engage in debates about Islam in Europe.
This is what Idriz, the imam from Penzberg, hopes for, too. He believes the new Reis-ul-ulema could inspire more confidence not only in Bosniaks, but in all European Muslims, while signaling to majority societies that Islam is a part of Europe, and that it affirms and embraces values such as the rule of law, gender equality and freedom of expression. "In the future, the Reis-ul-ulema should lay an even stronger emphasis on this," Idriz said.
This article was originally published in German.

Strong winds leave 2,500 electricity customers without power in Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:20:00 UTC
17:20:00 KST

Strong winds left about 2,500 electricity customers without power in Lithuania’s Klaipėda and Kaunas regions on Friday morning, as authorities warned that the strongest gusts were expected around midday.
The figure had risen from about 2,200 customers earlier in the morning, according to ESO, the country’s electricity distribution operator.
“We can see that the weather forecasts are changing. The wind is expected to be strongest between noon and 14:00, but it has already shown its strength this morning,” ESO spokeswoman Rasa Juodkienė told LRT RADO on Friday.
Most outages were reported in the Kaunas region, but reports from the coastal area were increasing as winds strengthened. ESO and contractor crews were being dispatched to repair the damage, the company said.
On average, electricity supplies are restored in less than two hours, according to ESO.
Fallen trees also caused problems along the coast. Jolita Orentaitė, head of the Fire and Rescue Department’s communications division, told BNS that a tree in Klaipėda fell onto three cars.
Most reports of wind-related damage came from the resort municipality of Neringa and the city of Klaipėda, she said.
The first report of wind damage was received at about 08:00. By 10:00, authorities had received about 10 reports, all from the coast. The strongest winds were expected around noon, Orentaitė said.
ESO forecast the most intense gusts between noon and 14:00, particularly along the coast, where they could reach severe-storm levels in some areas.
The company said it had mobilised about 200 crews of its own and contractors across Lithuania to respond to outages, compared with about 60 on a typical day. Additional crews were being organised for the weekend, and staffing at dispatch centres had also been increased.
ESO said it had informed municipalities in advance about the forecast storm and urged them to request generators if needed.

What Pakistan Will and Won’t Do in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:18:00 UTC
17:18:00 KST

On October 5, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan moved ahead to activate their defense commitments and provide military capabilities agreed under the Mecca Defense Alliance. The decision came after weeks of Houthi drone and missile strikes against Saudi Arabia, even as the Houthis were ramping up their ground operations along the Red Sea coast.
Regardless of how the crisis plays out, the Houthi conflict has turned out to be the first major test of the Mecca Pact. The alliance must strike a balance. It has to demonstrate that its commitments have real military value without crossing the line into becoming an interventionist force or getting bogged down in a prolonged war of attrition.
For Pakistan, the Houthi crisis is a particularly difficult strategic problem.
There is broad agreement within Pakistan’s strategic community that the Mecca Pact is defensive rather than offensive. However, Pakistan cannot simply sit on the sidelines as the regional security environment goes downhill and its own defensive commitments come under strain. If the alliance cannot show up when one of its members faces a serious security challenge, its deterrent value could quickly erode.
At the same time, Pakistan is alive to the costs of direct intervention. Deploying large numbers of troops into Yemen would pile on additional pressure on an already stretched military, which is grappling with counterterrorism challenges at home and the threat from India. It could also put a strain on its relations with Iran and, perhaps most importantly, lock Islamabad into a commitment from which it would find it difficult to pull out without paying a heavy strategic price.
Diplomatically, Islamabad is trying to persuade Iran into restraining the Houthis. Nonetheless, there are limits to what Tehran can or is willing to do. Iranian influence over Houthi decision-making is significant but is not unlimited. The Houthis have an axe to grind when it comes to Saudi Arabia. Moreover, Tehran has little obvious incentive to do away with a source of pressure on Saudi Arabia while it is itself preparing for another round with the United States. Therefore, diplomacy is unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.
Pakistan must demonstrate that the Mecca Pact has real teeth and practical military value. To understand what that support might look like, it is necessary to understand the alliance’s objectives and the means available to achieve them.
Pakistan understands that wiping out the Houthis altogether is neither realistic nor desirable. Even if such an objective were militarily achievable, the costs would be high. Sustained Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, combined with the consequences of further stoking Yemen’s civil war, could make the price of total military victory prohibitively high.
The more realistic objective, therefore, is to constrain the Houthis’ ability to dominate the Bab al-Mandeb and tip the military balance sufficiently to open up space for a political settlement.
Any military support that Pakistan or Türkiye provides to Saudi Arabia or Saudi-backed forces in Yemen should be understood in this light.
Operationally, it would make little sense for Pakistan to send in large conventional ground forces to Yemen simply to put the brakes on Houthi advances. The decisive fighting is taking place in southwestern Yemen, particularly around Taiz and Mocha. These areas are far from the Saudi border. Operating a large Pakistani expeditionary force there would be logistically difficult and risky.
What is needed instead is a capable and better-organized anti-Houthi force in southwestern Yemen. This is where Pakistan and Türkiye can add value. Both countries can supply weapons and other military assistance to Saudi-backed forces, beefing up their ability to conduct counteroffensives. They can also help with command-and-control structures, where weaknesses have contributed to the inability of anti-Houthi forces to push back against recent Houthi advances.
Pakistan also has extensive experience with special operations and counterterrorism, particularly from its campaigns in Afghanistan. Türkiye, meanwhile, has built up considerable experience operating specialized forces in Syria and Iraq. Therefore, both could provide specialized personnel and advisers potentially inside Yemen without committing to large conventional formations. In this sense, Pakistan and Türkiye could contribute through force augmentation rather than direct intervention.
Another potential priority would be breaking up Houthi command structures. The Houthis have become more organized and militarily sophisticated, but they still retain many characteristics of a networked armed movement. Weakening their command and communications could pay off more than attempting to wear down the organization through conventional territorial warfare alone. Pakistan and Türkiye’s intelligence-gathering experience could offer useful lessons for Saudi Arabia and its local partners in this regard.
The alliance must also brace for further attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. Saudi Arabia’s air-defense network could come under increasing pressure if Houthi missile and drone attacks intensify. Already, Saudi air-defense stockpiles are thinned due to Iranian attacks and continued Houthi onslaughts. Therefore, Pakistan and Türkiye would provide additional air-defense capabilities and personnel to shield critical infrastructure and strategic facilities.
Saudi Arabia already has a substantial air force and does not necessarily require Pakistani fighter aircraft or pilots. What it needs more urgently is support in battlefield operational planning, target identification and air-combat support functions. Such assistance could improve both the effectiveness and intensity of Saudi air operations.
This broader role explains why deployment of as many as 40,000 Pakistani troops should not be read as preparation for a conventional Pakistani ground war in Yemen.
Nonetheless, there are limits to what Pakistan can pull off. The operationalization of the Mecca Pact’s joint command remains in its infancy. Moreover, it is unclear how effectively Pakistan’s military capabilities can be integrated into a conflict with a very different geography and political environment. Pakistan also has considerably less experience in indirectly shaping a battlefield by strengthening another state’s forces.
There is another uncertainty. The strategic objectives of Pakistan and Saudi Arabia may not stay in lockstep as the conflict evolves. Riyadh may ultimately seek to tip the balance of power in Yemen decisively in its favor. Islamabad, by contrast, is likely to remain committed to its defense obligations while seeking to steer clear of a prolonged military commitment. The two countries’ objectives may overlap during the initial phase of the crisis, but they could diverge as the conflict drags on.
A far more serious crisis could flare up if Iran or its allies in Iraq move to support the Houthis. Iraqi militias have already attacked Saudi Arabia several times, including strikes on the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline. While Iran’s direct intervention remains off the table for the moment, the situation would change if the US resumes massive strikes on Iran, including on energy infrastructure. Iran will surely hit back at Gulf energy infrastructure, Saudi Arabia’s included. The conflict would then spill over beyond Yemen.
How the Mecca Defense Alliance manages the Houthi crisis will shape not only the integrity of the Mecca Pact but also its credibility as a foundation for the emerging regional security order.

Swiss Valcambi gold refiner plans Hong Kong expansion

Swiss Valcambi gold refiner plans Hong Kong expansion
Switzerland's Valcambi, one of the world’s largest gold refiners, plans to open a new plant in Hong Kong, bolstering the city’s push to become a global bullion hub.
The Swiss firm signed a letter of intent with Hong Kong’s sole steelmaker Shiu Wing Steel to establish a new precious metals refining company that will also provide vaulting services.
“Asia is a key market for the precious metals industry and will continue to play an increasingly important role in its future,” Simone Knobloch, chief executive officer of Valcambi, said in a press release on Thursday.
More
The dark secrets of Switzerland’s largest gold refinery
Valcambi’s move comes as Hong Kong vies with Singapore to develop Asia’s premier gold trading center. On Tuesday, Hong Kong’s secretary for financial services and the treasury bureau Christopher Hui used an annual industry gathering in Italy to pitch plans to expand the city’s gold sector.
“Our focus right now is really to get the infrastructure right, where we ensure that that our system is robust and, at the same time, credible in such a way that we continue to draw investors’ interest to participate,” Hui said in an interview on the sidelines of the London Bullion Market Association’s conference in Sorrento.
This week, Hui toured Valcambi’s Swiss facility, as well as those of other major refiners including MKS PAMP and Argor-Heraeus. The new refinery, Valcambi’s first outside Switzerland, will be located in Shiu Wing Steel’s plant in northwest Hong Kong.
More
Swiss gold imports come under scrutiny as G7 targets Russia
As part of Hong Kong’s initiative, it launched trial operations of a gold clearing system in July, along with a new price benchmark, and has secured the participation from the biggest Chinese banks and major international bullion banks like JPMorgan Chase and HSBC Holdings. It’s also planning to launch yuan-priced gold futures, while exploring more preferential policies for gold traders.
Hong Kong is taking a “whole-value-chain approach,” said Hui. “Like London, we have storage, we have OTC contract; like Switzerland, we want to have refineries; like the US, we want to have gold futures.”
Developing Hong Kong’s gold market is a top priority before his official term finishes at the end of June, Hui said. Last month, gold was highlighted in the city’s first ever five-year plan, with bullion seen as “an entry point” for expanding the Chinese yuan’s usage in global markets.

Kovalskyi undertook personnel reshuffles in the prosecutor&apos;s office: who lost their positions and which inspections are ongoing
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:14:59 EEST
17:14:59 KST

Kovalskyi undertook personnel reshuffles in the prosecutor's office: who lost their positions and which inspections are ongoing
Kyiv • UNN
The Prosecutor General's Office dismissed eight prosecutors and four officials over the “Carthage” case. A large-scale personnel audit has begun.
Eight prosecutors were dismissed from the Prosecutor General's Office as part of the "Carthage" case, and a large-scale personnel audit was launched. Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalskyi reported this on October 9 on social media, UNN reports.
Details
According to Kovalskyi, after being appointed to the position, he held working meetings with the heads of the PGO's departments and regional prosecutor's offices, analyzed their activities, and began reviewing personnel decisions.
"The prosecutor's office cannot demand accountability from others if it is not ready to demand it from itself. Wherever there are questions regarding integrity, the quality of management, or the accountability of heads, there must be appropriate decisions," Kovalskyi emphasized.
The acting Prosecutor General also reported that, in connection with the circumstances being investigated as part of Operation "Carthage," eight people were dismissed from the prosecutor's offices, seven of whom worked at the PGO. Another four people were dismissed from administrative positions, including the head of the Information Technology Department and the head of the division for combating criminal offenses in the field of cybersecurity. In addition, 24 prosecutors underwent polygraph examinations. The information obtained was handed over to the commission conducting the official investigation.
They also managed to complete the official investigation into Aidyn Khudiiev, the former deputy head of a PGO department. Its results will be submitted to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of Prosecutors (QDCP), and the position he held has already been abolished. In addition, an official investigation is ongoing into the former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko's departure abroad. The circumstances surrounding the organization of his business trip are currently being examined.
A separate official investigation is being conducted into Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the PGO's Department of International Cooperation, who was detained as part of the "Carthage" case. Investigators are examining the circumstances of his possible use of official powers for private interests and interference in the work of other prosecutors. A disciplinary complaint against him is under consideration by the QDCP. The position he held has also been abolished.
Another area of change was a personnel audit of appointments to administrative positions. Based on its initial results, the PGO dismissed the head of a department and the head of a division of one of the departments. In regional and district prosecutor's offices, 16 prosecutors were dismissed from administrative positions, including the heads of the Vyshhorod District Prosecutor's Office of Kyiv Region and the Vyzhnytsia District Prosecutor's Office of Chernivtsi Region. Orders have also already been issued to dismiss the deputy heads of the Khmelnytskyi and Volyn regional prosecutor's offices.
Kovalskyi separately reported the decision to dismiss the heads of the Kharkiv and Volyn regional prosecutor's offices from their administrative positions. According to him, this is only the first stage of reforming the prosecutor's office. Going forward, he plans to continue the personnel audit, evaluate the performance of heads, improve management processes, and strengthen internal security.

Australia asks U.S. for $300M Tomahawk planning system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:14:35 UTC
17:14:35 KST

- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $300 million sale of Tomahawk mission planning systems and support to Australia.
- Australia first fired a Tomahawk from HMAS Brisbane in December 2024 and plans to field the missile on destroyers, frigates and future submarines.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible $300 million sale to Australia of the systems and support it needs to plan Tomahawk cruise missile strikes, adding mission-planning capability to the long-range missiles the Royal Australian Navy began acquiring in 2023.
The package covers a Theater Mission Planning Center with its associated communications systems, the Tomahawk Mission Planning System, and program management, engineering, training and logistics support for developing and delivering the planning system, according to the Oct. 8 notification to Congress. The approval does not mean the sale is final; the quantities, contract terms and timeline will be set if Australia moves ahead.
A Tomahawk does not simply fly in a straight line to its target. Before launch, planners build a route for the missile, with waypoints over land and sea, terrain and navigation data, and the aim point it is meant to hit. The Theater Mission Planning Center is the system the United States uses to prepare and distribute that data to launching ships and submarines, and the State Department said the sale would strengthen Australia’s Tomahawk capability and deepen its interoperability with U.S. maritime forces.
The principal contractors would be BAE Systems in San Diego, California; Tapestry Solutions, a Boeing subsidiary in St. Louis, Missouri; Peraton in San Jose, California; and Leidos in Virginia Beach, Virginia. The State Department said the sale would not require sending additional U.S. government or contractor personnel to Australia and would not affect U.S. readiness.
Australia announced in 2023 that it would buy Tomahawks for its Hobart-class destroyers and later its Hunter-class frigates, with more than 200 missiles planned. The missiles are also intended for the Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarines Australia is set to receive under the AUKUS agreement in the early 2030s. Canberra says the Tomahawk has a range of up to 2,500 km (about 1,550 miles), making it the longest-reaching strike weapon in the Australian Defence Force.
In December 2024, the destroyer HMAS Brisbane fired a Tomahawk for the first time during a test off San Diego, making Australia the third country, after the United States and the United Kingdom, to acquire and fire the missile. That firing followed Australian Navy tests earlier that year of the Naval Strike Missile and Standard Missile-6 from another Hobart-class destroyer, HMAS Sydney.

Ukraine reruns its Vivaldi playbook outside Kramatorsk and pushes Russia back across the Siverskyi Donets, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:14:26 UTC
17:14:26 KST

Ukrainian forces are advancing east of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, and even Russian milbloggers now acknowledge it, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said on 8 October. The gains may follow months of groundwork like the one that preceded Operation Vivaldi near Lyman, which Ukraine says returned 176 km² to its control. Russian commentators are already doubting that Moscow can reach the two cities.
Russia's years-long push on the Fortress Belt, the chain of cities anchoring Ukraine's defense in Donetsk Oblast, has been stalling since Vivaldi began. Unable to take those cities, Russia keeps hitting them from the air. On 8 October, a Russian bomb killed 30 people on two buses in Kramatorsk.
Across the Siverskyi Donets
Russian milbloggers said Ukrainian forces liberated Ozerne and advanced east of Pyskunivka toward Kryva Luka, ISW reported. They also acknowledged that Ukrainian troops drove Russian forces out of Pyskunivka. Ukrainians are now counterattacking toward Kryva Luka from the west and northwest, from across the river.
Vivaldi counteroffensive advanced after Ukraine took Russia’s drones out of the fight, ISW assesses
ISW called the repeated Russian claims of a river crossing notable, because the Siverskyi Donets is a significant natural obstacle. Kryva Luka is a dominant height just south of the river. From there, Ukraine could launch further counterattacks. Ukrainian forces appear to have pushed Russian troops off both banks in this area, ISW assessed.
The heights Russia wanted
After Vivaldi cleared ground near Lyman in September, Russia shifted its push south toward Mykolaivka and Sloviansk. Russian forces likely see Mykolaivka, just east of Sloviansk, as a primary objective, ISW said. Its heights would favor an offensive on the city. Ukrainian pushes northeast and southeast of the town now deny Russia that terrain.
East of Kramatorsk, milbloggers claimed Ukrainians liberated Malynivka and advanced between Fedorivka Druha and Holubivka. They also reported gains into southern Minkivka and near Fedorivka. The lines remain tangled. Geolocated footage shows Ukrainian forces striking a Russian position in central Tykhonivka after what ISW assesses was a Russian infiltration.
ISW said the counterattacks may point to a broader Ukrainian goal: pushing Russian forces east, away from the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk area and toward the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas Canal.
The Vivaldi playbook
The counterattacks have run for weeks. On 29 September, Ukrainian military observer Kostiantyn Mashovets reported them in the same areas, saying Russia's 3rd Combined Arms Army had failed to make significant gains. ISW assesses that the attacks build on months of shaping meant to wear down Russia's offensive capacity.
Vivaldi’s secret weapon was the targeting, not the robots: Third Corps reconnaissance mapped Russian command nodes, then hit them to cause panic
Before Vivaldi, Ukrainian forces targeted Russian drone operators, gaining drone superiority before the counteroffensive. They used the same approach ahead of their Oleksandrivka counterattacks in early 2026.
Moscow appears to see the pattern. A Ukrainian military official said on 7 October that Russia is moving drone units and Spetsnaz from quieter sectors to the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk direction. Ukraine also reorganized its command in and around Donetsk Oblast in early September, which may be blunting Russian attacks from the east, ISW said.
"Distant" and "doomed"
One Russian milblogger called an advance toward the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk area a "distant" prospect, ISW reported. A Russian offensive from Siversk toward Sloviansk may be "doomed" to failure or heavy losses unless Russia retakes the forests south of Lyman, he said.
The counterattacks east of the two cities appear to support Vivaldi, ISW assessed. Together with Russia's defeat north of the river, they could disrupt Russia's offensive toward Sloviansk from the east entirely.
If Ukraine holds Kryva Luka and keeps Russia off the Mykolaivka heights, Moscow's pincer on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk loses the ground it was built on.

Siberian Plague Fears Persist Despite Russia’s Completed Health Checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:13:22 UTC
17:13:22 KST

Russia has completed health monitoring of everyone who had contact with a laboratory worker who died at a Siberian plague research institute, authorities said Thursday, reiterating that tests of nearly 5,000 samples had found no dangerous pathogens.
Statements from Russia’s health watchdog and the regional governor said the checks on contacts of Darya Shipilova, 28, had concluded. Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said the investigation had been conducted thoroughly despite intense media attention.
"Amidst intense media scrutiny, the specialists thoroughly investigated the situation. It was a test, but we passed it in worthy fashion," Kobzev said.
However, Russian authorities have not definitively established whether Shipilova’s death on October 2 was caused by plague, despite requests for further information from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United States.
Officials have said she died of pneumonia whose origin remains unknown. They have also stated that Shipilova was properly vaccinated and that no microorganisms associated with her work were found in her body.
WHO senior official Maria Van Kerkhove said Wednesday that the organization wanted details of the laboratory tests performed, including which pathogens had been examined. She questioned the lack of clarity over the cause of death, asking, "if this individual didn't die from plague, then how did she die?"
Russia maintains that it has supplied the WHO with complete information through established procedures.
Health authorities worldwide and international media have paid particular attention to pneumonia cases with unexplained causes since the COVID-19 pandemic began with a cluster of rapidly spreading, fatal respiratory illnesses in China. However, the cause of an individual case of pneumonia often cannot be identified.
Pneumonia can result from conditions other than plague, including other bacterial infections and viral respiratory diseases such as COVID-19 and influenza.
The case has also prompted broader concerns about transparency and biosecurity at Russia’s anti-plague research facilities. Reports have described widespread speculation after Shipilova’s death in the Siberian city of Shelekhov, about 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk, where she worked as a laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute.
Early accounts suggested she had become ill after breaking a test tube. An official in a neighboring region initially said she had died of plague before revising the statement to say it was a possibility. Russian authorities have denied that plague was the cause, describing her illness as pneumonia of unknown origin. An independent regional news outlet reported that nearly 200 people had been placed in quarantine.
Plague remains a real but relatively uncommon disease. It is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which infects fleas and the small mammals that host them. There are three types, depending on which part of the body is affected. Pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs, has been suspected in Shipilova’s case, although pneumonia can develop for many different reasons.
The disease can be fatal but is treatable, and global case numbers are far lower than in the past. There are approximately 1,000 to 2,000 cases worldwide annually, with only a few in the United States. Last year, a young man died of pneumonic plague in Arizona. By comparison, seasonal influenza kills thousands of people in the United States each year.
The word plague also carries a heavy historical association. The Black Death killed at least a third of Europe’s population, about 25 million people, in the 1300s. Bubonic plague affects the lymph nodes, while plague doctors’ beaked masks became an enduring image of the disease during the 1600s, when treatments were lacking.
The term has long been used more broadly to describe devastating events. The Bible recounts 10 plagues that preceded the Hebrews’ exodus, including water turning to blood, locusts, frogs, hail, boils, darkness and the death of firstborn children. During the Black Death, people had little understanding of bacteria and viruses, and the disease was often seen as a supernatural punishment. Over time, plague also became a general term for rapidly spreading infectious diseases with high mortality rates.
The COVID-19 pandemic revived those associations. Although COVID-19 was caused by a virus rather than the plague bacterium, it killed 7 million people worldwide and brought widespread mask-wearing, lockdowns and overwhelmed hospitals, while many families were unable to be with loved ones at the time of their deaths.
Epidemiologists have said the possibility of plague in Russia is less concerning than some alternatives, including a new virus capable of spreading through asymptomatic carriers. Plague can usually be treated effectively with antibiotics, which can also be used preventively for people exposed to an infected person.
The disease is not highly contagious. Even pneumonic plague, its most contagious form, generally requires close contact to spread, making transmission through simply sharing a room unlikely. Symptoms can emerge within a day, reducing the period during which an infected person might spread the disease unknowingly. Hantavirus, by contrast, can take as long as 42 days to produce symptoms, requiring extended quarantine for exposed people.
Nevertheless, the lack of transparency surrounding the Siberian case has raised concerns among biosecurity specialists. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has identified pneumonic plague as a disease with potential for use as a biological weapon, and Russia has a history of biological weapons research. The possibility that a pathogen could have been altered in a laboratory to resist antibiotics has also been raised, although this remains hypothetical and multiple antibiotic treatments are available.
The concerns of specialists do not mean that the general public faces an immediate threat. Epidemiologists writing in the newsletter Your Local Epidemiologist said their role was to assess potential risks, but that public concern was not warranted at present because individuals had nothing to do in response and the risk of plague reaching the United States was "essentially nil."
In Shelekhov, residents told CNN that they had received little reliable information about Shipilova’s death, despite the international attention and calls from the WHO and the United States for clarification. Six days after the news broke, there was still no official confirmation that plague had caused her death.
A 36-year-old resident who identified herself only as Evgeniya said daily life appeared unchanged. She said she was not panicking but had heard from a friend who worked as a pharmacist that people had begun buying antibiotics after rumors of plague spread.
Russia’s health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Shipilova had died of pneumonia of unknown origin. The agency played down the possibility that her illness was connected to her work while moving quickly to isolate her contacts.
Although the Kremlin repeatedly urged the public to rely on updates from the agency, Evgeniya said many people she knew did not trust official statements.
"There is no official information, and we don’t trust it anyway. There are a lot of rumors, but what is actually happening remains unclear," she said.
Other residents expressed confidence in the authorities’ account. Ekaterina, 26, told CNN that she saw no reason for concern because everyone who had been in contact with Shipilova had been isolated.
"People are not giving in to panic and are carrying on with their lives as usual," she said.
She also argued that medical treatment made the situation different from the coronavirus pandemic. "It’s the 21st century now, and there is treatment for plague. This is not like coronavirus, which was something unknown to people. The outlook is much better. So, to sum it all up: Everything is fine. We are following safety measures and not giving in to the madness," Ekaterina said.
A 27-year-old pharmacist in Irkutsk, also named Ekaterina, described a brief rush to buy protective supplies at her workplace on Saturday, including masks, antiseptics and tetracycline antibiotics.
"People were, of course, afraid of getting infected," she told CNN. She said the rush lasted only one day and that conditions had since returned to normal.
Another resident, 38-year-old Alina, described the situation as ordinary apart from increased social media coverage, which she dismissed as panic disconnected from reality.
An unnamed Russian clinician told independent outlet Lyudi Baikala, which has extensively covered the case, that he was unconvinced by the health watchdog’s assertion that Shipilova’s illness was unrelated to her professional activities. He said laboratory confirmation could take up to 10 days and that it was too early to identify the pathogen conclusively.
"it is impossible to definitively identify the pathogen just one day after the autopsy," the clinician said.
Residents quoted by Lyudi Baikala also described disinfection operations at an apartment building believed to have been Shipilova’s home in Irkutsk. They said three vehicles arrived on Friday night and personnel wearing gas masks and orange suits emerged carrying containers before disinfecting the entrances.
"The smell was unbearable and very acrid," a woman in her 40s who lived in the building told the outlet.
She said the workers told residents they had been sent by the health watchdog. According to her account, they said a young woman had died of a deadly virus but that they knew no further details. CNN said it could not independently verify the account of the disinfection.
Shipilova’s mother, Svetlana Shipilova, was also in quarantine at an Irkutsk hospital. Speaking to local outlet Glubina, she said her daughter had not yet been buried.
"After all, who would bury her when we’re sitting here in detention? She was such a hard worker. A pure, such a pure soul," she said.
Other residents described a sense of resignation toward official statements and restricted access to information. Yulia, 25, told CNN that people were accustomed to uncertainty.
"Information is always limited. I think it’s like that in every region," she said.
One Irkutsk resident used dark humor on Telegram to describe what he saw as the euphemistic language of Russian official communications.
"An explosion is a bang. A recession is negative growth. A crash is a hard landing. A fire is smoke. A retreat is a gesture of goodwill," he wrote.
He continued by comparing the authorities’ description of the case to their handling of other crises: "The plague is pneumonia of unknown origin… Anyone who catches this pneumonia of unknown origin should wrap themselves in a sheet and crawl to the cemetery. But do it slowly, because the main thing is not to create problems for the authorities."

====================================================================================================

Finland: The world's happiest country has a debt problem it can no longer ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:12:00 UTC
17:12:00 KST

Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter
October 9, 2026
There's an uneasy mood in Finland, the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years. A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.
With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.
Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.
Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic
Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.
Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.
The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.
EU scrutiny over growing deficit
Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.
"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.
Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.
National Coalition rules out tax hikes
To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.
While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.
Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."
While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.
With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.
"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.
Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.
Finland rearms after Russia's full-scale invasion
Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.
During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.
With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.
While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.
On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.
Markets give Helsinki time to reform
Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.
On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.
Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.
On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.
Markets give Helsinki time to reform
Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.
On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.
Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.
