Suppressing Palestinian resistance: US charity under fire for  AI monitoring of Gaza classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:56:29 UTC
16:56:29 KST

A US charity in Gaza plans to record classroom conversations and use artificial intelligence to flag speech deemed “hateful” or “inciting.”
The plans laid out by the founder of the Gaza Children Village in a webinar last month have elicited ethical, safety and privacy concerns from some Palestinian and advocacy groups and at least one of the charity's partners.
There is no indication the charity intends to share its classrooms’ recordings with anybody else, but concerns about the potential misuse of surveillance technology are heightened in Gaza after three years of Israel’s genocidal war. The Israeli military has used AI to sift through intercepted communications to, among other things, identify targets for strikes.
Palestinian rights groups have been critical of the charity's education agenda more broadly, saying it is unaccountable to local and UN agencies that have long managed Gaza’s schools. Who controls education in Gaza is one of many unresolved questions about its postwar governance.
It is unclear when the classroom monitoring is supposed to begin, what specific language will be flagged, and whether teachers, students and their families have been told about the plans.
The charity's founder and CEO is Dr David Hasan, a neurosurgeon born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents who now teaches at Duke University medical school in Durham, North Carolina.
The charity has raised money largely from individual donors, including American Jews, and says it's partnering with North American, Israeli and European aid organisations and hospitals.
The schools' lessons are mostly built around the Palestinian Authority curriculum, but language that he says “glorified violence“ was removed, Hasan has said.
Hasan declined to comment for or provide examples of curriculum changes.
On a webinar last month with humanitarian groups, Hasan said the reason to monitor classrooms is to help train teachers in how to uphold a curriculum that he had previously said was aimed at “de-radicalisation.”
“I know it’s controversial, but trust me, it’s the only way we feel for us to survive and deliver this curriculum,” Hasan said.
The rhetoric of ‘de-radicalisation’ is what Israel and its supporters have often used to undermine Palestinian resistance and rewrite history, which is replete with Zionist atrocities in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Israel has maintained a crippling land, air, and sea blockade on Gaza since 2007.
Since October 7 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 in its genocide in Gaza, while around 90 percent of the besieged enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian and UN figures.
Monitoring classrooms opens ‘Pandora’s box'
Two people affiliated with the charity expressed concerns when notified about the possibility of classroom monitoring.
“Cameras to monitor the performance of students and teachers is acceptable. But cameras to silence students and teachers from being able to have a free exchange in a classroom are not acceptable,” said Bishara Bahbah, a Palestinian American political activist on the charity's board. He said he wasn't aware of the monitoring plans and that they haven't been raised with the board.
Bahbah said that with so few functioning schools in Gaza, the charity's top priority is getting more kids in classrooms.
An official at an aid group that partners with the Gaza Children Village said the use of cameras could prompt it to reconsider working with them. Using AI to monitor people’s words opens a “Pandora’s box,” said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Six current and former teachers at Academies of Hope declined to comment.
The system will flag language deemed ‘hateful’
Under the plans outlined by Hasan in various communications, recordings of classroom conversations will be analysed by an AI-powered system to detect “anti-Semitic,” “inciting" or “hateful” language.
If such language is detected, a warning will be sent to Hasan, who can then contact the teacher to understand the context and provide feedback, Hasan said in the September webinar. He said recordings are stored for 72 hours.
Palestinians in Gaza are especially concerned about surveillance technology
Concerns regarding surveillance technology remain acute in Gaza amid Israel's genocidal war and extensive monitoring by Israeli forces.
"Israel has weaponised information to such a dystopian degree that many Palestinians feel they cannot utter a word, type a thought, or twitch an eye without fearing it could be seized upon,” said Amjad Iraqi, senior Israel and Palestinian Territories analyst for the International Crisis Group.
Groups opposed to the charity's curriculum say Palestinians are being stripped of their autonomy in deciding what to teach their children.
“It is very concerning, they’re trying to control the minds of new generations,” said Ines Abdel Razek, co-director of the Palestine Institute for Public Diplomacy, an advocacy group.
The Palestinian Authority, which has limited autonomy in parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank, and UNRWA should be supported in rebuilding schools in Gaza, she said.

'PERM distinct from H-1B visa': MEA on US move to suspend certain firms from green card programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:56:18 UTC
16:56:18 KST

File photo: MEA says US move against tech firms may affect green card process, not H-1B status
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Friday said the US government's decision to suspend several technology companies from the employment-based green card programme would not, by itself, affect existing H-1B visas or the status of visa holders and their dependents.The ministry said the suspension of applications under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme could, however, affect the permanent residency process for eligible employees of the companies concerned.“We are aware of the US Department of Labour’s decision concerning the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme for certain companies. It should be noted that PERM is distinct from the H-1B visa programme,” the MEA said in a statement.
“The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents, though there could be some impact on the permanent-residency/Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies,” it added.The ministry also emphasised the economic benefits of skilled talent moving between India and the US, saying the latest measures did not advance the shared ambitions of the two countries.
“It should also be clear that talent mobility adds value to both economies. While it creates opportunities for Indians, it equally helps US companies with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US,” the MEA said.“This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact. The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries,” it added.
Which companies have been suspended?
The US department of labour has suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini from the PERM programme. The department said it would not accept new applications from the affected companies or process their pending applications amid multiple active federal investigations.US labour secretary Keith Sonderling said the companies had collectively sought millions of foreign workers and received hundreds of thousands of approvals under employment-based immigration programmes.“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.The administration has alleged that companies misused employment-based immigration programmes to replace American workers with foreign employees. These are allegations made by US officials; the announcement cited ongoing investigations.
What is PERM, and how is it different from H-1B?
PERM is a labour-certification process that allows an eligible US employer to sponsor a foreign worker for employment-based permanent residency, commonly known as a green card. Before certifying an application, the US department of labour must establish that there are not enough qualified and available American workers for the job and that employing the foreign worker would not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.
The H-1B programme, by contrast, allows US employers to hire skilled foreign workers temporarily for specialised occupations. The PERM suspension does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas, but it could disrupt a route to permanent residency for employees whose employers are sponsoring them through the programme.The move comes amid a wider crackdown by the Trump administration on skilled foreign labour. A day before the announcement, the US department of homeland security proposed new fees for F-1 international students seeking to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT), describing the measure as an effort to protect American workers and strengthen the integrity of the immigration system.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:53:15 KST

Strike drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant in Russia’s Tver region overnight on October 9. The facility manufactures chemical products used by Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on this.
Footage published online shows strike drones flying overhead, followed by explosions and a fire near the plant. Local residents also reported Russian air defense activity in the area.
Tver region governor Vitaliy Korolyov confirmed that a fire broke out at the plant in the settlement of Redkino following a drone attack. According to him, the plant’s employees were evacuated to a shelter in time, and no one was injured. The fire has since been extinguished.
The facility is one of the major chemical industrial sites in the Tver region.
The plant produces specialty chemicals in small batches and manufactures more than 40 types of products for the aviation, aerospace, and other industries.
Its products include ferrocene derivatives, which are used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, as well as specialty materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives.
According to the Security Service of Ukraine, the plant manufactures components for the special fuel Decilin-M, used in Russia’s Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
In September 2025, the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on the facility. The British government cited its activities in Russia’s strategically important defense and chemical sectors as the basis for the restrictions.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant was targeted twice by strike drones in a single night on June 27, 2024.
At the time, Russian sources reported that plant personnel had been evacuated, while Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that four drones had been intercepted over the Tver region.
The plant was also targeted in September 2023 and, according to monitoring channels, in February 2026.

South Africa withdraws asylum directive after anti-migrant violence
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 9 - South Africa's Department of Home Affairs said on Friday it had withdrawn a directive allowing the intake of asylum applications, a day after anti-migrant protests turned violent in Johannesburg and Durban.
The directive had sought to implement a July 7 Constitutional Court ruling that said asylum seekers cannot be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.
Home Affairs said in a statement that the directive was issued as an operational measure, and the implementation had overwhelmed refugee reception offices within days, put officials at risk and led to threats to public safety and order.
The government has blamed disinformation over the court's ruling, adding that it did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants.
Africa's biggest economy grapples with a surge in anti-immigrant protests that have strained relations with other African countries and forced thousands of foreign nationals to leave.
Migrants are often blamed for unemployment, crime and pressure on public services, accusations that social scientists say are unsupported by evidence.
Rioters torched 14 vehicles in the coastal city of Durban and 10 in Johannesburg's Soweto township on Thursday. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.
A top police official, Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane, told a press briefing in Soweto on Friday, near the remains of torched vehicles, that calm had returned to the area.

Drone Strike on Yandex Data Center Triggers Widespread Internet Outages Across Russia
Russia’s internet segment suffered widespread outages on October 8, hours after a retaliatory Ukrainian drone strike hit a Yandex data center in the Ryazan region.
The Moscow Times reported that disruptions began around 4 p.m., citing Russian outage-monitoring services Sboy.rf and Downdetector. Problems affected banks, retailers, mobile operators, transportation services, streaming platforms, Google, YouTube, RuTube, and several major Russian websites.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Avito recorded the largest number of complaints, with more than 14,000 reports during the day. The most serious disruptions were reported in Moscow and St. Petersburg, where users also experienced problems with T-Bank, internet provider SkyNet, and the Mango Office cloud service.
The outages followed an overnight drone attack on a Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region. The Moscow Times reported that a fire broke out at the facility, while users experienced problems accessing Yandex Disk, Yandex Documents, and other company services.
The disruption also affected online bus-ticket sales in the Moscow region. MosTransAvto linked the problem to the suspension of a data center supporting its online ticketing system and estimated that restoration could take up to 24 hours.
Several major Russian media websites, including RBC, RIA Novosti, Kommersant, Vedomosti, Interfax, and Vesti, also experienced access problems. Some remained unavailable even through VPN connections.
Russian Railways acknowledged that "some users" could encounter difficulties accessing its website because of the operation of "external services," while its passenger application remained functional.
The incident followed reports that the Sasovo facility had suspended operations after the drone strike. Yandex could not immediately confirm whether the damaged data center could be fully restored. The site reportedly housed two of the company’s three supercomputers, making it an important part of Yandex’s computing infrastructure.
Earlier on October 8, it was reported that Yandex had blurred all four of its Cloud data centers on its mapping service, including the facility struck by drones in the Ryazan region.
The concealed sites are located in Mytishchi, Sasovo, Kaluga, and Vladimir. The Sasovo facility, with an electrical capacity of up to 12 megawatts, shares an industrial site with the Sasta machine-tool plant. The plant was also struck overnight and is reportedly linked to supply chains supporting Russia’s Iskander ballistic missile production.

Germany Extends Protection for Ukrainians to 2028, Tightens Rules for Military-Age Men
Germany has extended temporary protection status for Ukrainian refugees until March 4, 2028, while establishing special conditions for newly arrived men of military age.
The updated regulation, enacted by the Federal Ministry of the Interior and published in the country's official legal gazette, Bundesgesetzblatt, takes effect on October 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the amended transitional residence framework, men subject to military service must meet specific requirements to qualify for temporary protection.
They are required to show proof of completed military obligations, demonstrate that they crossed the Ukrainian border legally, or provide official documentation certifying exemption from mobilization.
The European Commission planned to update its temporary protection directive in July 2026, requiring newly arriving Ukrainians to present official documentation proving their exemption from military mobilization to obtain temporary protection status in the EU.
The measure was designed to target first-time applicants, both men and women, without affecting the roughly 4.3 million Ukrainians already residing in the bloc with protected status, including over 1.2 million in Germany and nearly 960,000 in Poland.
Scheduled to take effect in March 2027, the policy reflected a broader trend among member states, such as Denmark, which had introduced separate legislative measures to restrict refugee status for military-aged Ukrainian men.

Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:48:15 UTC
16:48:15 KST

Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
Communications minister points users to Google Maps and a locally developed app as alternatives to the Google-owned service.
Iraq is set to ban the popular navigation app Waze, which was founded in Israel.
Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad announced the move on Tuesday. It has prompted discussions in Iraq over whether the country can build its own alternative and whether banning one app protects users’ location data.
What has Iraq decided and why?
The Ministry of Communications plans to block the use of Waze by the end of December, according to the Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada.
Sanad told the broadcaster Rudaw that it would take effect some time at the start of 2027.
He made the announcement on the sidelines of the Hitex 2026 technology exhibition in Erbil, the capital of the semiautonomous Kurdish region in northern Iraq.
“Because it comes from the entity [Israel] and is Israeli-made, we will ban it at the beginning of 2027,” he said.
What is Waze?
Waze is a widely used navigation app. Hundreds of motorists, including taxi drivers, use it to get around. The service relies on users to report traffic jams, accidents and police checkpoints as they happen.
It was developed in Israel, and Google bought it in 2013 for nearly $1bn.
Waze’s privacy policy lets it collect users’ locations, routes, destinations, search histories and device details, depending on their settings.
Pooled across many users over time, such data have security value because they can reveal movement patterns, peak times and unusual changes.
Rudaw reported that the app has been the subject of security discussions in Iraq over its alerts being used to avoid checkpoints although Sanad did not link the ban to that issue.
Why does the Israeli connection matter in Iraq?
Iraq does not recognise Israel or have diplomatic relations with it and has formally been at war with it since 1948.
A 2022 law criminalises any diplomatic, political, military, economic or cultural ties with Israel. Its penalties include life imprisonment and the death penalty. It was passed by 275 votes in the 329-seat Council of Representatives.
The law applies to all Iraqi citizens, state institutions and media as well as private companies and foreign entities operating in the country, including the Kurdish region.
Sanad has not specifically said Waze must be blocked under the antinormalisation law.
Distrust of Israel has been bolstered by the US-Israel war on Iran. The United States and its allies have targeted Iraq’s Iran-aligned militias with air strikes and economic measures.
During the war, Iraq also faced a serious case of Israeli infiltration. In May, US media reported that Israel had built two secret military outposts deep inside Iraq’s desert to support its war on Iran.
One post was nearly exposed by a local shepherd who stumbled upon it and was killed.
What alternatives is the government offering?
Sanad said users could switch to Google Maps or Iraqi navigation apps.
Communications Ministry spokesman Omar al-Amiri said in remarks carried by Al-Mada that Waze would be replaced by a yet-to-be-named Iraqi app.
He said the app would run without technical problems.
Al-Mada also quoted Iraqi technology researcher Mustafa Kamel al-Sharif as saying a national alternative would take more than an app with an Iraqi map and logo.
It would need accurate geographic databases, a constantly updated road network, routing systems and live data on traffic, accidents and closures, he said.
He also told the newspaper that the crux of the issue lies in how Iraq regulates its citizens’ data and other services may also collect sensitive data similar to Waze.
What remains unclear?
The ministry has not said how the block will be enforced or whether it will cover the Kurdish region. It has also not set out the ban’s legal basis or said when the Iraqi app will launch.
Another unknown is why Google Maps, owned by the same parent company, Alphabet, would remain available or serve as an alternative.
The government has also not answered why Waze is being banned now when its Israeli roots have been long known.

More work visas, less temporary housing: Czechia changes rules for Ukrainians
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:45:06 EEST
16:45:06 KST

More work visas, less temporary housing: Czechia changes rules for Ukrainians
Kyiv • UNN
The Czech government plans to allow Ukrainians with temporary protection to apply for work visas and employee cards. The number of places in humanitarian housing will be reduced from 20,000 to 10,000.
In the Czech Republic, the government approved amendments to several government regulations concerning the possibilities for Ukrainian citizens to stay in the Czech Republic. Among other things, they expand the possibilities for obtaining work visas and residence permits. UNN reports this with reference to Radio Prague International.
Details
The changes, as stated in the accompanying documents, are aimed at facilitating the arrival of Ukrainian citizens in the Czech Republic and are being adopted following recent restrictions on granting temporary protection to people liable for military service. They also take into account the provision of opportunities for a gradual transition from the temporary protection regime to the regime of standard residence permits for certain groups of people who wish to work in the Czech Republic, including after the end of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Among such standard residence permits, the most common are precisely those that the current government proposal would make more broadly available to Ukrainians in the Czech Republic. These are, on the one hand, a short-term visa for employment purposes and, on the other, a long-term residence permit for employment purposes pursuant to §42g of the Foreign Nationals’ Residence Act, the so-called "employee card" (zaměstnanecká karta).
Restrictions to be lifted
Access to them is also to be opened to people with temporary protection in the Czech Republic — at present, they do not have it.
"The proposed change returns economically motivated migration to the standard framework appropriate to it, separates it from the humanitarian temporary protection regime, and represents a step toward the systematic and proper targeted use of individual residence permits," the authors of the proposal said.
Currently, long-term migration from Ukraine to the Czech Republic is possible, in particular, for the purpose of family reunification, full-time study at a university, or employment. Applications are accepted at Czech consular offices in Kyiv and Lviv.
Ukrainian citizens who are staying in Ukrainian territory (and are entitled to leave it), as well as those staying in other countries, including with temporary protection in other EU member states, may apply at these consular offices for an "employee card" (zaměstnanecká karta), a "blue card" (modrá karta — a long-term residence permit for employment in positions requiring a high level of qualification), and special work visas (mimořádné pracovní vízum) within government migration programs and the established annual quotas, which are fully sufficient.
However, the current rules do not allow Ukrainian citizens who have or previously had temporary protection in the Czech Republic to apply for an "employee card" at Czech consular offices in Ukraine. This restriction is now to be lifted.
"The unemployment rate in the Czech Republic and the shortage of workers in a number of sectors of the national economy are currently, despite the presence of approximately 150,000 people with temporary protection who are employed at this time, at the same level as before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In 2021, almost 27,700 "employee cards" were issued to Ukrainian citizens. In addition, Ukrainian citizens also actively used short-term work trips on the basis of short-term employment visas, of which more than 185,500 were issued in 2021," the document says.
Humanitarian housing to be halved
Another proposed change concerns halving the number of places allocated for the temporary humanitarian accommodation of newly arrived refugees. People who have nowhere to stay may receive such state-funded housing for up to 90 days after obtaining temporary protection.
There are currently 20,000 such places reserved; there will be 10,000. However, as noted in the cover letter, this will not worsen the actual situation of refugees.
As the authors of the proposal noted, in 2026 approximately 300 people are staying in such accommodation in the Czech Republic; on average, 17 people are placed there each week, representing 1.3% of all those who received temporary protection during the week. In 2024–2025, as of the end of those years, around 500 people were staying in humanitarian accommodation; such accommodation was provided to an average of 45 people per week, which accounted for about 3% of all newly arrived people with temporary protection.
Therefore, the document states, the number of 10,000 reserved places is also expected to be entirely sufficient in the event of an unexpected increase in the number of newly arrived applicants for temporary protection.

tim walker traces five decades of queer activism through portraiture in ‘fairyland’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:45:03 UTC
16:45:03 KST

tim walker traces five decades of queer activism through portraiture in ‘fairyland’
from pioneering activists and healthcare workers to drag performers and musicians, 250 portraits trace how queer communities have shaped british cultural life through resistance, solidarity, and self-expression.
tim walker explores queer history through 250 portraits
British photographer Tim Walker turns his fantastical visual language toward Queer history in Fairyland: Love and Legends, a major exhibition opening at the National Portrait Gallery in London today, October 9th, 2026. Curated by Susanna Brown and designed by Walker’s longtime collaborator Shona Heath, the exhibition brings together around 250 specially created portraits of activists, artists, performers, and cultural figures, including Isaac Julien, Ian McKellen, and Chappell Roan. The exhibition brings together five years of work with Queer people and their allies in Britain and beyond, reflecting a new direction in Tim Walker’s photography.
On view until February 7th, 2027, Fairyland brings together people whose lives and work have shaped many overlapping narratives of Queer history, moving between generations and connecting the activism of the 1970s and 80s with contemporary voices working across art, fashion, music, film, and politics. Its title reclaims the word ‘fairy,’ historically used as a homophobic slur, as an expression of identity and belonging. Walker approaches this reclamation through the wit, theatricality, and sensitivity that have long defined his photography.
‘Fairyland: Love and Legends’ as a record of queer history
The exhibition opens with portraits of activists who advocated for the right to love during the 1970s and 80s, including founding members of the Gay Liberation Front and Stonewall, among them Olivette Cole-Wilson, Andrew Lumsden, Lisa Power, and Tom Robinson. Walker draws on sixteenth-century Tudor portraiture by Hans Holbein the Younger and Nicholas Hilliard to present these figures as an imagined Queer aristocracy, a reference that places people who have often been marginalized within a tradition historically associated with power, status, and official remembrance.
Other portraits bring together campaigners, writers, and cultural figures whose work has helped make Queer lives visible. Ted Brown, Caroline Paige, Gilli Salvat, and Peter Tatchell appear alongside storytellers including filmmaker James Ivory and author Sarah Waters. The British photographer also asks sitters to bring objects with personal significance to their sessions, allowing individual histories to enter the frame. Author Jane Cholmeley presents the original shop sign from Silver Moon Women’s Bookshop, founded in 1984, while photographer Sunil Gupta holds his camera. Filmmaker Isaac Julien clasps a conch shell associated with his pioneering 1989 film Looking for Langston. These objects offer material connections to the places, practices, and cultural histories through which identities are formed and preserved. Walker photographs many of his subjects against simple white backgrounds, recalling the portraiture of Richard Avedon, whom he assisted in the 1990s, giving the sitters and their chosen objects room to carry the narrative.
remembering the hiv/aids crisis through solidarity
A section of the exhibition addresses the HIV/AIDS crisis of the 1980s through portraits of healthcare professionals, nurses, and musicians who contributed to the response of the period. Those who worked to develop effective treatments and improve care appear alongside artists whose music became part of the era’s cultural landscape, including Marc Almond, Holly Johnson, and Jimmy Somerville. ‘The brilliance of their music boomed despite the fear of mortality and discrimination. I wanted to bring that disco to the ward, to celebrate the tireless work to spread awareness and pursue proper care and solutions,’ Tim Walker describes, placing the relationship between music and activism as central to this part of the exhibition.
Another central room focuses on the Rebel Dykes, a post-punk collective whose members campaigned for nuclear disarmament, environmentalism, sex-positive feminism, and HIV solidarity. Inspired by Karlheinz Weinberger’s photographs of 1960s biker gangs, Walker creates large-scale group portraits accompanied by a short film in which the women reflect on their community and political work. Their presence brings a collective dimension to an exhibition otherwise built largely around individual sitters.
fashion, performance, and the freedom to become
The second half of Fairyland: Love and Legends explores fashion, makeup and drag as forms of self-expression and Tim Walker’s interest in fantasy takes on a more explicitly performative role. Its subjects include designers Jean Paul Gaultier and Michaela Stark; performers Paul O’Grady, David Hoyle, and Midgitte Bardot; television personalities Alan Carr and Sue Perkins; and actors Ncuti Gatwa, Hunter Schafer, Fiona Shaw, and Ben Whishaw. Musicians Björk, Lady Gaga, Frank Ocean, and Chappell Roan also appear. The exhibition ends with a series of erotic scenes that reimagine fairy tales and nursery rhymes from a Queer perspective, bringing together themes of sexuality, humor, and self-expression.
‘The Fairyland exhibition is me finally placing myself in the queer realm with confidence and greeting all the other friends who live here. Just as I learned from the queer artists who came before me, some of whom I’m lucky enough to have met and photographed here, Fairyland is me saying you are not alone. I want visitors to the exhibition to remember that your difference is your power. It is a precious and beautiful thing,’ Walker says, reflecting on the project.
project info:
name: Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends
photographer: Tim Walker | @timwalker
 curator: Susanna Brown
exhibition design: Shona Heath, with support from the National Portrait Gallery
location: National Portrait Gallery | @nationalportraitgallery, London, UK
dates: October 9th, 2026 – February 7th, 2027

09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the White House considers anyone who uses the term "artificial intelligence" instead of "super intelligence" an "enemy," reinforcing his administration's push to rebrand the technology.
"The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY! President DONALD J. TRUMP," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
Trump formalized the terminology change in an executive order on Sept. 29, directing federal departments and agencies to use "Super Intelligence" and "SI" instead of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents, to the extent permitted by law.
The order also directs the White House science and technology adviser to submit proposed legislative language establishing a federal definition within 60 days. The proposal must assess whether the new definition should modify, expand or supersede the existing statutory definition.
Separately, Trump established a Super Intelligence Force to coordinate the federal government's approach to the technology.
The group is led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and includes Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor.

South Africa scraps asylum directive after anti-immigrant violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:43:00 UTC
16:43:00 KST

South Africa’s government has withdrawn a directive requiring refugee reception offices to process more asylum applications after protests against the policy turned violent, leaving at least 24 vehicles burned, shops looted and public safety concerns mounting in Johannesburg and Durban.
The Home Affairs Department announced Friday that it was scrapping the directive after its implementation triggered overcrowding at refugee offices and intensified tensions between anti-immigration demonstrators and foreign nationals.
The department said the directive had led to “serious consequences,” with offices overwhelmed within days, officials placed at risk and threats to public safety and order emerging.
“The Department will embark on a fresh process,” it said.
The withdrawal followed violence Thursday in Johannesburg’s Soweto township and Durban, a coastal city in KwaZulu-Natal province, where protesters opposed the government’s handling of asylum applications following a Constitutional Court ruling.
Acting National Police Commissioner Lt. Gen. Puleng Dimpane said 10 vehicles were torched in Soweto and 14 in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in Durban in connection with an alleged assault on a South African protester.
“The right to raise concerns and to protest does not give anyone the right to commit crime,” Dimpane said, adding that police had reinforced public-order deployments in areas experiencing unrest.
In Soweto, violence broke out near a Home Affairs office in Orlando West, where several burned-out vehicles lined the streets. Metro police spokesperson Xolani Fihla said no injuries had been reported and officers were investigating whether additional vehicles had been set alight.
Fihla said police received reports of shots fired toward protesters, prompting retaliatory vehicle burnings. He did not identify who allegedly fired the shots or who owned the vehicles.
“The situation is a bit tense, but it has died down from the earlier violence that we did see during the day,” he said.
Community leader Tshepo Mposula said the demonstration began peacefully outside the Home Affairs office before some residents moved to close convenience stores owned by foreign nationals.
Mposula alleged that foreign nationals fired shots, angering protesters and prompting them to set vehicles ablaze. He said the demonstration was intended to remain peaceful.
“It was not supposed to escalate to this level. This was supposed to be a peaceful demonstration,” he said.
Fihla said police remained deployed as tensions continued and roads stayed closed. He acknowledged that officers initially monitoring the march lacked specialized public-order training and equipment.
“We couldn’t predict that this type of situation would happen,” he said.
In Durban, riot police were deployed to the city center as reports emerged of looting at shops owned by foreign nationals. The South African Broadcasting Corp. reported the looting, while smoke rose over parts of downtown as firefighters battled blazes, including a fire at a municipal building.
KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Col. Robert Netshiunda told SABC that three foreign nationals had been arrested on suspicion of attacking a South African protester and breaking the person’s neck. He said the incident may have triggered the unrest.
The violence followed months of demonstrations against undocumented immigration, with protesters demanding the deportation of foreigners living in South Africa illegally.
The unrest also reflects tensions surrounding a July ruling by the Constitutional Court, which struck down procedural barriers that had prevented some people from applying for asylum.
The restrictions affected people who entered South Africa irregularly, lacked asylum transit visas or missed deadlines for reporting to authorities. The court found that the barriers were unconstitutional, opening the way for more people to have their asylum claims considered.
Following the ruling, the Home Affairs Department instructed refugee reception offices to accept applications from people previously excluded by those procedures. Officials later acknowledged that they had been unprepared for the number of applicants who came forward.
The government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration held an urgent briefing Thursday to address overcrowding and the challenges facing refugee reception offices.
“We confirm that all refugee offices were overwhelmed by the numbers of those coming for applications,” the committee said after meeting Wednesday night.
Authorities had pledged to expand processing capacity, accelerate decisions and strengthen identity checks. They also stressed that the court ruling did not automatically grant refugee status or permanent residence. It allowed applicants to have their claims assessed.
The department’s decision to withdraw the directive signals a change in how the government intends to manage the influx of asylum applications, although it has not yet detailed the fresh process it plans to introduce.
South Africa, the continent’s largest economy, has long attracted migrants seeking employment and better opportunities. However, the country has experienced recurring outbreaks of xenophobic violence for nearly two decades, often fueled by allegations that foreign nationals compete with South Africans for jobs, housing and public services.
The tensions have intensified ahead of local government elections scheduled for Nov. 4, with unemployment exceeding 30% adding to public frustration.
At least four foreign nationals were killed in violence earlier this year, according to South African police, although some African governments reported higher death tolls.
The unrest has also prompted thousands of foreign nationals to leave the country. Zimbabweans and Malawians accounted for the largest numbers of departures, while nationals of Ghana, Kenya, Lesotho, Mozambique, Nigeria and Uganda also fled.
Some were repatriated by their governments, adding to diplomatic tensions with Pretoria.

You can lose access for insulting Claude - Anthropic introduces new rules
Kyiv • UNN
Starting November 12, 2026, Anthropic will prohibit prolonged abusive treatment of Claude. For violations, access may be restricted or terminated.
Anthropic updated Claude’s rules. Starting November 12, 2026, prolonged abusive treatment of the models may result in access being restricted or terminated. This is stated in the company’s official blog, UNN reports.
Anthropic has updated the rules for using its artificial intelligence models. The document will take effect on November 12, 2026. The company prohibits prolonged and unfounded abusive or cruel treatment of neural networks
If a user is suspected of violating the rules, they may receive a warning. The company also reserves the right to restrict, suspend, or completely terminate access. The document does not establish automatic blocking for every individual insult.
The rules cover users of Claude.ai and Claude Code, developers and businesses working through the API, as well as customers of third-party products with Claude integrated.
In addition to conduct toward the models, the document regulates other ways of using the services. In particular, the following are prohibited:
-  developing weapons and software for their use; 
-  organizing influence campaigns through fake accounts; 
-  monitoring people without their consent; 
-  circumventing blocks by using other accounts.

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- School closures due to worsening air quality from severe haze have been expanded to several states as well as the capital Kuala Lumpur and the administrative capital of Putrajaya on Friday.
Schools in areas that record air pollutant index (API) readings of more than 180 are to close starting Friday, while schools in areas that record APIs of more than 150 for three consecutive days will close from Oct. 12, the education ministry said in a statement late on Thursday.
According to the country's air quality rating, an API reading of zero to 50 is "good," 51 to 100 "moderate," 101 to 200 "unhealthy," 201 to 300 "very unhealthy," and 301 and above "hazardous."
Data from the country's Air Pollutant Index Management System showed most areas across Peninsular Malaysia recording unhealthy readings as of 1 p.m., with the states of Selangor, Johor and Negeri Sembilan along the west coast being particularly affected. ■

Across China: When terraces become stage, music brings new rhythm to tourism trends
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:40:48 CST
16:40:48 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- At first glance, dozens of curving terraces carved into a hillside in southwest China looked like farmland, but no crops were expected to grow there.
As night fell, more than 10,000 people filled the tiers, singing in the rain as music and bands of light swept across the hillside.
Held on Oct. 1, the first day of China's week-long National Day holiday, the open-air concert began at 7 p.m. in light rain at Shexiang Ancient Town, Dafang County, in southwest China's Guizhou Province. Guizhou-born singer Zhou Shen, a household name in China, performed alongside other musicians, drawing fans from across the country.
The unusual event has become a new tourism draw in a community originally built for relocated rural residents. There is no roof or enclosed auditorium, and the stage stands at the bottom of a bowl-shaped hillside. Landscaped terraces serve as seats, and the surrounding mountains and night sky form a natural backdrop.
Wang Lei, the concert's stage designer and chief director, said the guiding principle is to keep the design "down to earth," with the stage appearing as though it has "grown out of the earth."
Wang said the team has made use of an existing ornamental pool and drawn inspiration from Dafang's reputation for traditional bean products, shaping the stage like a traditional stone mill. With little elaborate decoration, the design is intended to blend into the landscape rather than compete with it.
Chen Hongjin, who traveled from Guiyang, the provincial capital, said the setting is part of the appeal.
"A concert in nature feels completely different from one in a stadium," Chen said. "You can hear the wind and the rustling leaves along with the music. It feels as if all your senses are heightened."
When the ancient town was developed as a relocation community in 2016, earth and rock excavated during construction were used to reshape a low-lying hollow into the curved tiers following the natural contours of the hillside. Flowers, shrubs and other ornamental plants were later added, creating a public space for residents.
Seen from above, the concentric curves resemble the ridges of a fingerprint, giving the site its name -- the "Fingerprint of Earth."
The town is now home to more than 12,000 people relocated from different parts of Dafang County. Before becoming a concert venue, the terraces hosted community cultural activities, including folk-song performances and traditional Torch Festival celebrations.
This summer, larger concerts brought the space to a much wider audience. Featuring popular singers, the concert series is designed as a long-term, community-oriented cultural program that combines artistic quality with free public access. Organizers have adapted the existing landscape rather than building a conventional venue, using the terraces as natural seating and lighting the curves of the hillside after dark.
The concerts have also brought a sharp rise in visitor numbers. According to local tourism authorities, the town recorded about 756,600 tourist visits between Aug. 1 and Oct. 1, up 154.74 percent year on year. Eight concerts held during this period attracted more than 296,000 visits.
On Oct. 1 alone, Dafang recorded about 99,800 tourist visits, while Shexiang Ancient Town received around 58,000 visits, more than six times the figure recorded a year earlier.
The concerts are free, though advance reservations are required. Economic benefits come largely from spending on food, accommodation, shopping and other tourism services.
In August, consumption in Shexiang Ancient Town and nearby areas exceeded 70 million yuan (about 10.4 million U.S. dollars).
Liu Hanxun, who runs a local barbecue restaurant, said his monthly revenue rose to more than 130,000 yuan in August, from around 40,000 to 50,000 yuan previously.
For the relocation community, the increase in visitors has also created more opportunities for residents to find jobs, run small businesses and raise income close to home.
Since 2022, local authorities have helped organize markets, performances and festival activities to encourage such opportunities, and the concerts have accelerated that trend.
The influx of visitors has also prompted improvements to walking routes, lighting, power supply, public toilets and medical service sites. During the National Day holiday, temporary parking and public transport services were expanded, while traffic management, security, food safety and medical support were strengthened.
Near the end of the concert on National Day, performers gathered in a circle on stage as the crowd joined them in singing the Chinese song My Motherland and Me. Fireworks rose above the valley.
Among the visitors was Wang Tingting, who traveled from Chengdu city in neighboring Sichuan Province after seeing the concert promoted on social media. A fan of Zhou Shen, she secured a reservation and made her first trip to Dafang.
"Sitting on the terraces and watching a concert was very different from being in a stadium," Wang said. "With the mountains and water around you, everything felt more natural and alive."
Wang said she came for the concert but planned to spend more time exploring the surrounding area and trying local food during the holiday.
"Music brings people here, but we hope their experience goes beyond the concert," said Huang Shan, deputy director of the county's culture, sports, radio, television and tourism bureau. "By linking performances with local scenery, food and other attractions, we want to turn visitor flows into broader tourism consumption." ■

NEW DELHI, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Indian government has imposed a 30 percent margin cap on the maximum retail price, amid complaints about exorbitant anti-cancer drug prices in the country over the years.
The cap would be imposed on non-scheduled cancer drugs. Essential cancer medicines included in the scheduled list were already subjected to strict government-set ceiling prices.
In an official statement issued by the Department of Pharmaceuticals in the Federal Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, the government claimed that the move would save cancer patients in the country around 25 billion Indian Rupees (approx. 258.7 million U.S. dollars) annually.
The ministry's statement further stated that an expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services will finalize the list of medicines to be covered, after which the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority would take a decision and issue a notification.
It was found that non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines carried an average price mark-up of approximately 170 percent, reaching 700 percent or more in some cases. The price rose sharply as the medicine moved through the supply chain before reaching the patients, the statement added. ■

China Focus: More than a factory floor: foreign companies expand innovation footprint in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:40:31 CST
16:40:31 KST

A staff member fine-tunes an intelligent device at the HP AI Innovation Center in Liangjiang New Area of southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, Jan. 27, 2026. (Photo by Zhang Yangyang/Xinhua)
CHONGQING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The AUDI Innovation & Technology Center (AITC), jointly established by Audi and Chinese automaker SAIC Motor, opened in Shanghai in early September -- a shift reflecting how multinationals are deepening their R&D roots in China.
With the AITC focusing on intelligent electrification and full vehicle development, the German luxury carmaker is treating China not simply as a place to build cars, but as a place to design them.
Audi and SAIC Motor have agreed to jointly develop four all-new AUDI models based on the ADP (Advanced Digitized Platform) 2.0, with the first model slated to launch in 2028.
The center is Audi's first R&D entity outside Germany to cover the entire value chain. It will not only lead the development of next-generation AUDI products but also channel Chinese innovations into Audi's global operations.
"We are combining German engineering precision with local innovation," said Johannes Roscheck, president of Audi China. "Our expanded R&D footprint will further elevate our competitiveness in China."
"Quite a few multinational companies are upgrading their manufacturing bases in China into innovation hubs, while their China R&D centers are evolving from local adaptation units into global innovation anchors," said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, at a press conference in April.
In 2025, foreign investment in China's scientific research and technical services sector accounted for nearly one-fifth of the country's total inbound foreign investment, a share that had risen steadily for seven consecutive years, 3.8 times its 2018 level.
The sector saw 14,000 new foreign-funded enterprises established last year, up 27.2 percent year on year. Beyond the numbers, a growing list of multinationals, including AstraZeneca, Philips, Porsche and Schneider Electric, have set up R&D centers in China in recent years.
Rapid market adoption and industrial coordination have become key drivers behind multinationals' accelerating R&D expansion in China. Jerome Dorlack, president and CEO of Adient, a global automotive seating supplier, said Chinese cities such as southwest China's Chongqing Municipality offer a world-class industrial ecosystem, where companies can find partners across the entire value chain, from customers to suppliers.
"Chinese consumers adopt new technologies very quickly -- typically within 12 to 14 months from launch to widespread adoption, whereas in some other markets the process can take three to four years," he said.
Adient has developed products such as the ProForce massage system in China, launching them first in the Chinese market before rolling them out globally. The company now operates 39 production bases and three global technology centers in the country. "Expanding our technology centers in China has been a great success," Dorlack added.
Han Jin-Kyu, president of the Asia-Pacific region for Germany's Vibracoustic, said the company, which specializes in automotive NVH (noise, vibration and harshness) solutions, operates plants in Chongqing and in the eastern Chinese cities of Wuxi and Yantai. Rather than simply supplying parts, it works closely with local automakers to jointly develop new products.
Han added that, with well-developed infrastructure, major cities such as Chongqing can foster joint development and innovation across sectors including AI, smart manufacturing, automobiles and semiconductors.
Talent and innovation capacity are another major draw. Michael Mertin, CEO of AT&S, a leading Austrian semiconductor materials company, said China has long made it a priority to train scientists and engineers, and that the new generation of Chinese engineers "not only possesses outstanding mathematical skills but is also increasingly creative."
Data shows that China produces more than 5 million STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) graduates each year, and that more than half of the world's top AI researchers, by undergraduate origin, come from Chinese universities.
Mertin said Chongqing is a key hub in the company's global network. The core technology of its signature product, the substrate, was first commercialized in the municipality and has since been refined and matured there.
"In today's digital age, no company, city or country can innovate in isolation," Mertin said. "High-tech progress depends on trusted global networks, cross-border collaboration, and the exchange of talent, expertise and ideas."
The same logic applies to other industries. This year, HP also opened an AI innovation center in Chongqing. The center has already rolled out its first product, an AI acoustic inspection machine. The device can accurately identify product defects and has been deployed in quality inspection across multiple manufacturing sectors.
"Chongqing's ability to attract and cultivate talent gives the city a strong competitive edge," said Jonathan Jennings, HP's chief procurement officer. "We are working with Chinese universities and local governments to build this hub, because we need to keep growing and stay on top of the latest innovations."
China is also stepping up policy support to bring more foreign innovation and technology into the country. Its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for more regional headquarters and R&D centers from foreign companies. A revised catalog of industries encouraged to attract foreign investment adds new entries in areas such as innovative drug development and digital creative technology, while foreign-funded R&D centers are eligible for tax breaks on imported research supplies.
He Yadong said the Ministry of Commerce will work with relevant departments to leverage China's "complete industrial system, high-quality talent pool and rich application scenarios" to draw more multinationals to base their R&D operations in China. ■

Experts urge heatwave plans to protect people with heart disease
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:40:18 CST
16:40:18 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Older adults with heart disease face up to seven times the risk of dying in a heatwave, prompting experts to call for tailored "heat plans" to protect vulnerable patients from extreme heat, a new report finds.
The report published in the European Heart Journal outlines measures to prevent heat-related deaths and hospitalizations, including preparing hospitals for surges in demand, monitoring patients at home and providing cooling resources such as fans, according to a statement published on the Australian Science Media Center website on Thursday.
"Extreme heat is not simply a matter of discomfort; it places considerable stress on the cardiovascular system and increases the risk of illness and death," said the report's co-author Georgia Chaseling from Australia's University of Sydney.
The report recommends identifying vulnerable patients before heatwaves and developing individual heat-management plans that consider their illnesses, medications, hydration needs and living circumstances.
Healthcare providers should also coordinate with emergency services, public health agencies and local authorities to reach socially isolated people and those with limited access to cooling, the report said.
The report called for extreme heat preparedness to become part of routine cardiovascular disease prevention and management as heat extremes become more frequent and intense. Endtiem

Feature: Reliving the Long March, 90 years on
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:40:05 CST
16:40:05 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- As firelight flickers across the walls and gunfire breaks the darkness, figures emerge from the smoke and move through the audience. These holographic images inside a theater recreate a battlefield from 90 years ago.
The spectators do not simply watch. They walk with the performers, finding themselves surrounded by scenes of retreat, pursuit and survival.
Through holographic projections, live-action performances and digital interaction, an immersive production called the "Red Ribbon" in Guiyang, capital of southwest China's Guizhou Province, is bringing the history of the Long March closer to today's audiences.
The Long March, a roughly 12,500-kilometer military odyssey that began in 1934, not only preserved the revolutionary forces, but also gave the Communist Party of China (CPC) a new foothold from which to grow the strength of the revolution, and a new starting point for carrying the revolution forward to victory. It has since become one of the defining chapters in the history of the CPC and a lasting symbol of the Long March spirit.
In the grueling journey, the Central Red Army set out with 86,000 soldiers, but only about 7,000 reached the revolutionary base in northwest China, meaning roughly one in 12 survived to witness the victory.
During the march, the Red Army crossed nearly 100 rivers, traversed vast grasslands once known as a "death trap," and climbed over more than 40 mountains, including more than 20 snow-capped mountains rising above 4,000 meters.
For generations, the Long March has lived not only in history books, but also in literature, on screen and on stage. More than two thousand books have been written about the Long March, including Edgar Snow's "Red Star Over China." Countless documentaries, films and television dramas have been made, and a growing number of immersive performances are bringing the audience into the epic journey.
As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March in October this year, these works of art are offering new generations different ways to approach a history that might otherwise seem distant -- turning names, dates and battles into sights, sounds and human stories.
During this year's summer holiday, Guiyang's "Red Ribbon" production increased performances from five to eight a day and added special evening shows, attracting more than 190,000 people. Since its opening in 2023, over 2.6 million people have participated in the immersive shows.
For some visitors, however, the Long March is not simply something to encounter. It is part of their own family history.
Ha Thi Tuong Thu, deputy editor-in-chief of Vietnam Pictorial, felt a particular connection to the journey. Her grandfather, Vietnamese general Nguyen Son (Chinese name Hong Shui), was among the few foreign soldiers who joined the Long March.
"My grandfather went through the entire Long March. What I'm seeing here at the performance is what he experienced. In the holographic show, a scene shows Chairman Mao Zedong calling on the Central Cadre Corps to come over. My grandfather must have been among them," she said during a visit to Guiyang in July.
Thu has long been fascinated by her grandfather's revolutionary life and plans to return with her children to retrace the Long March.
At the theater, one scene shows the Red Army crossing the Chishui River four times, repeatedly changing direction and outmaneuvering a much larger pursuing force. The river appears through digital images; troops advance, turn and disappear, evoking the twists and turns of one of the most celebrated maneuvers of the Long March.
Another aerial performance evokes the arduous trek across snow-covered mountains and grasslands -- landscapes that once tested the limits of human endurance.
"On stage, I can deeply feel the faith that carried them across the snow-capped mountains. When I see tears in the audience's eyes, I know that faith has found its way to people today," said Guo Hanxu, 24, who plays a female Red Army soldier in the "Red Ribbon" performance.
Productions about the Long March and the Red Army are not confined to the theater.
About a two-hour drive from Guiyang, another production is on at the foot of Loushan Pass, placing audiences amid the landscape where history unfolded. Over the past two months, it has drawn about 50,000 visitors.
Set against the actual mountain terrain, the large-scale outdoor performance "Victory at Loushan Pass" uses explosions, warhorses and billowing smoke to recreate the battle widely regarded as the Red Army's first major victory during the Long March.
Visitors follow the story from preparations before the battle to the final charge. Rather than watching from a distance, they move through the performance space at close range, hearing the gunfire and feeling the ground shake beneath them.
Guizhou Province was more than a stop along the Long March route. It was a place where the course of the journey changed, as the Red Army regrouped and turned military setbacks into strategic gains.
Today, across the province and along the wider Long March route, places once associated with those moments are searching for new ways to make the past tangible.
In Yudu, east China's Jiangxi Province, where the Long March began, a large-scale historical production, "The Long March's First Crossing," focuses not only on soldiers, but also on ordinary people whose lives became intertwined with the Red Army.
Among its characters is Yinggu, whose story is based on Duan Guixiu, a local woman and widow of a Red Army martyr. Duan passed away at the age of 108 in August this year.
Duan's husband, Wang Jinchang, joined the Red Army shortly after their marriage in 1932. He never returned and was later confirmed as a martyr. His absence shaped Duan's lifelong wait -- now part of a stage performance watched by people decades later.
In the play, Yinggu turns to the audience with an emotional appeal:
"Never forget: they were your family, your loved ones, the people to whom you owe a debt that can never be repaid."
The words transform history from something to be remembered into something inherited.
At the former site of the Zunyi Meeting in Guizhou, another immersive production takes visitors back to a pivotal moment in the Long March.
Through interactive performances, visitors can take the roles of residents, helping Red Army soldiers transport supplies, tend to the wounded, and guide soldiers through the terrain.
"We hope to make the spirit of the Long March tangible through these experiences," said Zhu Jingbo, head of a local culture and tourism bureau in Zunyi.
The approach seeks to breathe new life into revolutionary heritage, moving beyond the static displays traditionally found in museums and memorial halls. By inviting visitors to participate rather than simply observe, it also offers younger generations a more immediate way to encounter the past, while the approach itself contributes to local cultural tourism and development, Zhu said.
Along the route, memories of the journey have seeped into everyday life -- into place names, stories and local products.
In Zunyi, even pomelos carry a memory of the Red Army.
The local fruit is known as the "Red Army pomelo," a name linked to the story of Song Jiatong, a wounded Red Army soldier who stayed in the village to recuperate.
Today, the story lives alongside a 126.7-hectare orchard, which is expected to generate an output value of 1.2 million yuan (about 176,300 U.S. dollars) this year, turning a memory of wartime hardship into a source of livelihood.
Far to the northwest, in Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, traditional potato starch noodles are named "Red Army noodles," recalling techniques that the Red Army is said to have taught the locals.
The names have outlived the events that gave rise to them.
"One generation plants trees; the next enjoys the shade," said Belgian media professional Romuald Bronchart. "The true essence of the Long March lies in empowering people -- a vision China continues to fulfill through infrastructure building and inclusive development."
The journey is over, but the memory never stops moving.
For Dutch Sinologist and reporter Elsbeth van Paridon, the takeaway is simpler. "This is not forgotten history, but living heritage," she said. ■

Nobel Peace Prize 2026 set to be announced
