Explainer: Watches win, pharma waits as Swiss-India trade deal turns one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:18:34 UTC
16:18:34 KST

Explainer: Watches win, pharma waits as Swiss-India trade deal turns one
In October 2025, Switzerland, as a member state of EFTA, entered into what was billed as a historic free trade deal with India. One year on, Swiss pharma still wants more intellectual property protection.
The promise of zero tariffs on Swiss watches in India within the next five years fuelled high spirits at a mid-September gathering of Indian and Swiss entrepreneurs hosted by the Geneva Chamber of Commerce (CCIG). In 2025, Switzerland exported CHF295 million ($354 million) worth of watches to India, a figure up 35% since 2023. Switzerland paid 22% import duties on these last yearExternal link.
The event co-organised with the Swiss-Indian chamber of commerce (SICC) came ahead of the one-year anniversary of the trade deal between India and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). Switzerland is India’s most important trading partner among the group that also includes Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway.
“This is the most significant trade agreement worldwide”, said Vincent Subilia, the director of the CCIG.
TEPA came into force on October 1, 2025, after 16 years and 21 rounds of negotiations. Finalising the text was particularly arduous mainly due to disagreements between Switzerland and India over intellectual property rights. While Switzerland’s pharma industry is known for its innovative medicines, protected by strict intellectual property rights, India’s drug industry thrives on generic drugs that are marketed once those patents expire.
One of the biggest achievements for EFTA members was signing a deal with India before any other individual member states of the European Union, or the EU itself, and gaining preferential access to 1.46 billion inhabitants. The agreement covers key industries, such as machinery, watches and vaccine production, but leaves questions around pharmaceuticals unresolved.
In early October, on a trip to the Indian capital New Delhi to meet President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Guy Parmelin, who holds the rotating Swiss presidency this year, commenting on the deal declared “everything isn’t perfect”. The visit included negotiations on migration and professional youth exchanges. A bilateral agreement to protect Swiss company dividends and further discussions on intellectual property were also on the agenda. Swiss pharma giants Roche and Novartis took part in the trip.
What’s in the free trade agreement?
According to the agreement, 94.7% of Swiss exports will benefit from a reduction in tariffs, with industries either immediately becoming duty free, or gradually over the next five, seven or ten years. Gold and precious metals, dairy products, finished generics and cars coming into India from Switzerland are excluded from the agreement and will continue to be taxed.
Exports of machinery to manufacture semiconductors, high-purity chemical intermediates that are used in pharmaceutical production, vaccines, and aircraft components have all become duty free since the entry into force of the agreement.
For industries including Swiss watches, chocolate, auto components, and dental equipment, tariffs have already been reduced twice: once on October 1, 2025, and once at the start of 2026. These tariffs will continue to be lowered gradually (depending on the category), until they reach zero.
How have Swiss companies benefitted so far?
Swiss goods with an immediate reduction of customs duties have had a head start compared to European Union competitors, because to date the bloc has no trade deal with India. But EU negotiations were finalised this year and an agreement may come into force in 2027. This will narrow the gap between European companies and Swiss ones.
According to Philippe Reich, chairman of the SICC and an India specialist at Baker McKenzie, Switzerland’s multinational corporations have already expanded but small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) will also benefit in the long run.
Swiss-Swedish automation company ABB announced a $75 million (CHF62.3 million) investment to expand its manufacturing and R&D capacity in 2026, and Swiss engineering firm Sulzer opened a new hub in the Indian city of Pune a month after TEPA’s launch. These investments form part of a financial commitment that is spelled out in the agreement. EFTA signatories have committed to promoting their private enterprises and institutional funds to invest $100 billion in India over the next 15 years. According to the SICC, investments announced since TEPA have reached $29 billion in Switzerland alone.
Global geopolitical shifts, including tensions between the United States and China, have been decisive for SMEs that rely on foreign supply chains. Many have shifted investments from China to India to diversify risks.
“These companies may not necessarily leave China, but they are shifting their investments from China to India. India has become more important,” said Reich.
Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE), the country’s official organisation for export and investment promotion, has said it has seen signs of increased interest from Swiss companies in the Indian market but definitive conclusions will come once they finalise their analysis of Switzerland’s economic footprint in India.
Beyond larger and more experienced consultancies, the agreement has also led to the flourishing of smaller offices. In May 2026, entrepreneur Ruby Greber set up India Swiss Enterprise in Geneva, to cater to companies looking into expanding in India.
“We help Swiss companies to establish their business in India and vice versa,” Greber explained. The consultancy is still in discussion with potential clients.
What about Swiss pharma?
While part of the pharma industry was covered by the initial deal, others such as generics were excluded. Intellectual property rights remain a key touchpoint.
According to S-GE, no new pharmaceutical companies have moved to India following the agreement. Following the agreement, Roche announced it would invest about CHF1.7 billion in India. This amount will support its existing operations and the expansion of its hub in Hyderabad, in the state of Telangana in southern India, by 2030. But the company says it hasn’t yet observed tangible benefits for its imported drugs.
More
Patent battle in India tests Roche’s grip on rare disease market
Most of the company’s drugs, which range from oncology to antivirals, are imported into India as finished products and currently taxed at around 10%. Some drugs targeting rare diseases and cancer treatments have already become tax-free, but tariffs on most finished drugs will drop by 1% every year over a decade. Generics, insulin and antibiotics are excluded from the free-trade agreement and will continue to be taxed. The agreement will take longer to impact the price of these drugs.
Reich comments the real issue at stake for pharmaceutical companies isn’t so much tariffs but enhanced intellectual property rights protection, which is essential for greater pharma innovator investments in India.
India refused to grant pharmaceutical firms data exclusivity, meaning generic drugs are automatically approved based on the clinical trial data of the original drugs. The country also rejected broader intellectual property rights through which companies can extend patents beyond 20 years and conserve market exclusivity.
More
Why drugs are becoming more expensive to develop
Previously stalled bilateral talks on intellectual property rights between Switzerland and India picked up again in 2025, following the conclusion of the trade agreement. These talks continued during Parmelin’s visit and focused on patents and data protection during clinical trials. A spokesperson for Parmelin confirmed the exchanges were constructive and were due to continue.
“I’m absolutely convinced we will see pharmaceutical R&D in India but this is a work in progress. Companies will first need to feel comfortable about the regulatory environment from an intellectual property perspective to really go in a big way for it. But I think that’s a matter of time,” Reich said. He estimated a five-year timeline for pharmaceutical companies to seriously consider India as a research and production base.

Only one-third of Israelis want Netanyahu to remain in power, Hebrew University study reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:16:12 UTC
16:16:12 KST

Only about one-third of Israelis want Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to remain in office after the upcoming October 27 Knesset elections, according to a Hebrew University survey published on Wednesday.
Among the roughly two-thirds of interviewees who said they wanted an alternative candidate, about half pointed to Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot as their choice for the next prime minister, and the remainder were divided between former prime minister Naftali Bennett (B'Yachad party) and MK Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu).
Worry and uncertainty about the future of the State of Israel
The findings, according to researchers, point to a significant crisis of confidence in the state's future. When asked about their general feelings toward Israel's future, 36% of respondents reported feeling pessimistic, compared with 33% who reported feeling optimistic. Researchers noted that this represented a decline in both optimism and pessimism compared to previous years, indicating greater overall uncertainty.
Under 25% of Israelis believe that their children will live in a better reality than they do now, and less than half of those surveyed reported believing that Israel is safer today than it was before October 7, 2023. What is more, nearly one-third of respondents believe the country is less safe than it was before the war.
About 20% of interviewees said they were considering leaving Israel due to the current security situation and ongoing social issues.
Did Netanyahu achieve 'total victory'?
Asked about Netanyahu's stated objectives for the Israel-Hamas War, less than 20% reported believing that "total victory" was achieved. Approximately half of Israelis said that the government held the greatest responsibility for the security failures that enabled the October 7 massacre and subsequent war; about one-third laid the blame on the security establishment.
More than half of Israelis, both Jewish and Arab, reported believing that the war has increased divisions within Israeli society -- an increase from previous years -- while only about one-quarter believe the opposite, that the war has strengthened national unity.
The study was conducted by Dr. Nimrod Nir of the Agam Institute and Dr. Gayil Talshir of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on October 5–6, 2026. The sample included 2,437 respondents, all Israeli citizens.
The sample is representative of Israel’s adult population, age 17 and above, in terms of gender, age, religion, region of residence, voting in the 25th Knesset elections, level of religiosity, and ethnic background among Jewish citizens, who constitute 83% of the sample, as well as religious affiliation among Arab citizens, who constitute 17% of the weighted sample.
Data were collected online using the Polyeda platform. The Jewish sample was recruited through iPanel, while the Arab sample was collected through telephone sampling.
The sampling error is ±3.2% at a 99% confidence level.

Israelis unable to compete in FIDE amateur chess tournament taking place in Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:16:07 UTC
16:16:07 KST

The World Amateur Chess Championship, organized by the International Chess Federation (FIDE), is scheduled to take place from November 4 to 13 in Klang, in Malaysia's Selangor state, a country that prohibits Israeli citizens from entering its territory.
FIDE's official announcement states that "all FIDE member federations and all eligible players are invited to participate." However, Malaysia's entry restrictions effectively prevent Israelis from competing in the tournament.
Lior Eisenberg, who has campaigned against boycotts of Israel in sports and culture in recent years, told Walla: "I contacted the tournament organizer with an innocent question about participating, and immediately received a message saying he was sorry, but Israelis would not be able to play because of Malaysia's immigration policy. Right afterward, he deleted the message and added another saying they would get back to me. A place that does not accept Israelis or players from any other country should not be allowed to host a world championship."
The situation in Malaysia is not the only case raising questions about Israeli participation in international chess competitions.
In the Netherlands, controversy recently erupted over Israeli grandmaster Alexander (Aharon) Bagrationi, who was born in Ukraine, represents Israel, and lives in Germany. Bagrationi has previously played for several clubs, including Elitzur Elkana and Elitzur Samaria.
Organizers of the Amsterdam Chess Open contacted the Dutch organization The Rights Forum following allegations concerning Bagrationi's ties to clubs in Judea and Samaria. The organization recommended that he not be allowed to participate in the tournament.
Following the controversy, tournament organizers announced that, beginning in January 2027 and subject to legal review, they intend to bar players representing clubs located in territories that an international court has determined to be under illegal occupation.
Bagrationi rejected attempts to attach political significance to his membership in the clubs, saying they are recognized by both the Israeli chess system and FIDE. He argued that any objections to their recognition should be directed at the international federation.
He will ultimately not participate in this year's tournament but clarified that his decision was due to family commitments rather than the controversy.
The position communicated to Eisenberg by the tournament organizer is consistent with Malaysia's declared policy.
In July, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim reiterated that his country would continue to prohibit Israeli citizens from entering. Malaysia's Interior Ministry subsequently clarified that travel documents issued by Israel are not recognized for entry into the country. Anwar also said that any Israelis found in Malaysia would be deported.
FIDE regulations prohibit event held where Israelis cannot play
The policy also raises questions about FIDE's own regulations.
In 2019, the international federation publicly committed not to hold events in countries that refuse to issue visas or allow entry to all eligible players, regardless of nationality or citizenship. FIDE emphasized at the time that its events could only be held in locations where access was guaranteed to representatives of all member federations.
Israel is generally not considered one of the dominant nations in chess, unlike countries such as India, the United States, China, and Uzbekistan. Nevertheless, it has a significant chess tradition, with numerous grandmasters and players who regularly compete in Chess Olympiads, European championships, and international tournaments.
The central question, however, is not whether an Israeli player is likely to win the amateur championship in Malaysia, but whether an official world championship can effectively be closed to citizens of one of FIDE's member federations.
Eisenberg is now calling for pressure on FIDE to relocate the championship to another country.
"The biggest problem with boycotts and attempts to delegitimize Israel through sports is our complacency," he said.
"It doesn't matter whether a championship is held thousands of kilometers away and no Israelis are expected to attend, or whether it takes place close to home. The same rules should apply. These countries should no longer be allowed to host competitions without guaranteeing that Israelis can participate."
Eisenberg pointed to the 2019 dispute surrounding the World Para Swimming Championships, which had been scheduled to take place in Malaysia.
The International Paralympic Committee stripped Malaysia of its hosting rights after failing to receive guarantees that Israeli swimmers would be allowed to enter the country and compete. The championship was eventually moved to London.
Eisenberg was among those involved in the campaign at the time, and a petition on the issue gathered thousands of signatures.
"What applied in 2019 must also apply today, after the war," he said.
Pakistan refuses to play against Israel in Chess Olympiad
The controversies follow a series of unusual incidents in international chess.
Last month, Pakistan's national team refused to play against Israel at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. The president of the Pakistan Chess Federation said the decision was made in accordance with his country's policy and as an expression of solidarity with the Palestinians. Israel was awarded a win by default.
FIDE itself has previously taken a clear position against boycotts of Israeli players.
In September 2025, following an attempt at a tournament in Spain to prevent Israelis from competing under the Israeli flag, the federation announced that it "strongly condemns all forms of discrimination, including on the basis of nationality and flag."
FIDE also emphasized that the same rules apply to Israel as to all other member federations that are not subject to sanctions.
FIDE will now be called upon to explain how that position is consistent with its decision to hold an official world championship in a country that openly declares that Israeli citizens are not permitted to enter.

Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:15:15 UTC
16:15:15 KST

Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A new plan by care agencies and insurance companies aims to create 30 residential care zones in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area of Limburg, combining health services, activities and accessible living.
The plan, known as the Deltaplan Maastricht Heuvelland, aims to help older people live independently for longer and receive support and care closer to home, largely to tackle loneliness.
The initiative is a collaboration between municipalities, health insurers, residents, hospitals and elderly care advocacy agencies. Health insurers CZ and VGZ have provided €33.4 million for the project.
Nineteen of the 30 zones are currently under development, and organisers say the rest will be up and running next year.
“We have traditionally been accustomed to looking to nursing homes, but in this way, older people can continue living at home much longer, provided it is responsible,” Petra Lamberts, chair of Deltaplan, told regional news outlet L1.
The zones will also organise more activities, for example in a shared communal living room, to tackle loneliness. “Loneliness is a predictor of the need for care,” Lamberts told broadcaster NOS. “People notice minor ailments sooner when they are alone. When they take part in activities, they are distracted, and they are also encouraged to use their skills.”
Informal carers, such as family members, will also be able to hand over some of their tasks from time to time so they do not become overburdened.
A communal living room recently opened in Valkenburg, where local residents can take part in activities and meet for coffee.
The population of the region is ageing faster than the rest of the country. By 2030, one in four residents of South Limburg will be over 65.
According to Lamberts, a year of home care costs around €12,000, while a year in a nursing home costs more than €100,000.

US, Ukraine Set For Talks In Miami Amid Onslaught Of Russian Air Strikes

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:14:17 UTC
16:14:17 KST

WASHINGTON -- The United States and Ukraine will hold talks in Miami on October 9 to discuss proposals aimed at ending the Ukraine war, amid relentless Russian strikes on vital pieces of infrastructure in Kyiv and other cities ahead of winter.
The White House confirmed that envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would meet with Ukrainian representatives on October 9 to discuss a new joint proposal covering all aspects of the conflict and aimed at ending the war, now in its fifth year.
A senior US administration official told RFE/RL that the meeting would provide an opportunity to identify areas where the conflicting sides could cooperate, even where their positions remain different.
Previous engagements had produced practical results, including prisoner exchanges, the official said.
After the initial meeting, a broader session involving European allies, NATO, and the EU will take place.
Rubio Warning
The talks follow US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's warning that the conflict has reached a dangerous stalemate, with the risk of escalation beyond Ukraine's borders.
Rubio called the conflict "a very dangerous war" and warned that escalation could include Russian sabotage in neighboring NATO countries, a strike, or other actions that could rapidly widen the conflict.
That could "quickly turn what is a war between two countries to a much broader, far more dangerous regional conflict," he said.
"In the end, we do not believe that there will be military solutions.... We think this war needs to end, and the negotiated settlement is sooner and better."
US President Donald Trump said this week that he planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone soon.
Sources familiar with the plans said the Miami meeting would focus on proposals that US negotiators had begun developing with Russian and Ukrainian interlocutors during recent visits to the region.
The October 9 talks follow several rounds of negotiations held in Florida late last year, including discussions between US officials and Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev in October 2025 and subsequent meetings with Ukrainian officials in November and December that year.
Witkoff and Kushner also visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September as Washington renewed efforts to broker an end to the war. They met with Putin in Moscow before holding talks with Zelenskyy and Ukrainian officials in Kyiv.
Ukraine is expected to be represented by Kyrylo Budanov, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office; Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service and a former defense minister; David Arakhamia, parliamentary leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party; and Serhiy Kyslytsya, first deputy head of the presidential office.
Broader Meeting With NATO, EU
A broader meeting involving national-security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO, the EU, and US European Command, is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. local time. Talks are expected to resume later at 1:45 p.m.
Representatives of the White House National Security Council and the US Treasury Department are also expected to participate.
The agenda also includes a postwar prosperity and reconstruction plan for Ukraine and other aspects of a potential settlement, sources said.
Zelenskyy said on October 8 that Kyiv's negotiators had been briefed on the issues to raise with the American delegation, including strengthening Ukraine's air defenses.
"Yes, our negotiators have also been briefed on this for their talks with the American side. They know what to discuss and which pressing issues to raise with the American side," Zelenskyy told reporters via WhatsApp.
He added that Ukraine would separately discuss funding and air defense with European partners, including ways to secure financial support more quickly.
"Funding issues will be raised there as well -- the details of how to secure the funding sooner. This is very important. And air defense as well," he said.
Zelenskyy said he had also discussed the issues with European Council President Antonio Costa and expressed hope for a positive outcome.
John Herbst, who served as US ambassador to Ukraine under President George W. Bush and is now a senior director at the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL on October 8 that he expected there would be "a good-faith effort by the sides involved," adding he did not expect a major confrontation between Washington and Kyiv over the terms of a settlement.
Herbst said any serious disagreement between Washington and Kyiv would likely increase Europe's role in the negotiations, as European governments would be reluctant to see the United States put undue pressure on Ukraine to make concessions.
Herbst also said the Trump administration wanted to end the conflict and appeared to believe neither side was likely to achieve a decisive military victory.
He also cited remarks by Vice President JD Vance suggesting that Ukraine currently has a military advantage.
Attacks On Ukrainian Infrastructure
In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure.
Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service, obtained a copy of a Russian-language document from sources in Ukraine's defense forces outlining a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water.
Despite Russia's recent missile and drone attacks, Herbst argued, those strikes were not bringing Moscow closer to winning the war, while Ukrainian operations were making it harder for Russian forces to achieve their objectives.
Washington has maintained separate contacts with Russian officials. Russian presidential envoy Dmitriev recently visited Washington for discussions with American officials as diplomatic efforts to end the war continued.

What is the status of investigations into Hamas and Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:13:49 UTC
16:13:49 KST

What is the status of investigations into Hamas and Israel?
On October 7, 2023, Hamas’s terror attack on Israel triggered a devastating war in Gaza. Three years on, both Hamas and Israel are facing charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity before international courts. However, the proceedings are progressing slowly, and in some cases have been halted by the deaths of those accused.
On October 7, 2023, Hamas carried out the worst terrorist attacks ever suffered by Israel, killing nearly 1,200 people and triggering a spiral of violence in the Middle East. These attacks were immediately followed by a retaliatory war waged by Israel in the Gaza Strip. Since then, more than 70,000 Palestinians have died, according to figures from the Gaza Ministry of Health, which the UN considers reliable. The territory has been almost entirely razed to the ground.
These terrorist acts and the reprisals warrant their perpetrators – Hamas and Israel – being prosecuted under international law for war crimes and crimes against humanity. And that is without even considering the issue of internal investigations in Israel into what the government did or did not know prior to the attacks. Several legal proceedings are currently underway.
Hamas terror attack
On October 7, 2023 Hamas attacked military posts, Israeli villages and the Nova music festival. Some 1,200 people, two-thirds of whom were civilians, were killed, and 251 were taken hostage and taken to Gaza, where they endured months of captivity and abuse.
In May 2024, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) – a court that prosecutes individuals – requested arrest warrants for three Hamas leaders: Yahya Sinwar, Mohammed Deif and Ismail Haniyeh for war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence.
However, these three Hamas leaders were killed by the Israeli army in 2024. The requests for arrest warrants are withdrawn. They will therefore never be tried before the ICC, as it does not try the dead, as explained by Benjamin Fiorini, senior lecturer in criminal law at the University of Paris 8 and secretary-general of JURDI, an association of legal professionals promoting respect for international law.
“On the other hand, if the International Criminal Court identifies other individuals who, for example, may have ordered the October 7 attacks, it could open new investigations, provided, of course, that they are still alive,” he emphasised during an interview on Swiss public radio RTS.
However, Israel has assassinated the leaders of Hamas, as well as thousands of fighters, who can never be brought to justice, with the exception of 200 to 300 suspects accused of participating in the attacks, who are to be tried before an Israeli military court. This strategy of killing enemies — widely endorsed by the Israeli public, the families of victims and former hostages — responds more to a thirst for revenge than to a demand for justice under international law.
Legally speaking, capturing and trying people is preferable to executing them, continues Fiorini. War must respect international law.
“Whilst there may be individuals who were lawfully targeted, there are also people who have been victims of this conflict and who should not have been,” he says.
In Gaza, of the 70,000 dead, the majority are civilians (women and children), revealing disproportionate attacks, he emphasises. This justifies prosecutions for war crimes and crimes against humanity by the ICC, and even for genocide – in this case by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which prosecutes states rather than individuals.
Legal proceedings targeting Israeli leaders
There are legal proceedings targeting Israeli leaders since October 7, 2023. Firstly, there are the proceedings initiated by the ICC. In November 2024, it issued two arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes (the use of starvation as a method of warfare and attacks intentionally directed against the civilian population) and for crimes against humanity (murder, persecution and other inhumane acts in the Gaza Strip).
Other Israeli officials could also face prosecution by the ICC, according to Fiorini. He cites as an example the Israeli President, Isaac Herzog, “who went so far as to say that he intended to break the backbone of the Gazan population, and that he considered the existence of innocent Gazans to be a myth. This betrays a desire to inflict collective punishment”.
The ICC could issue further arrest warrants, but US sanctions targeting the court risk slowing down its efforts. Investigations are nevertheless continuing in secret to avoid pressure, he says.
>> Several independent UN experts have referred to a genocide in Gaza. Our article explains who decides, and on what basis:
More
When is a ‘genocide’ really genocide?
Proceedings against Israel before the International Court of Justice
In December 2023, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) was received a complaint lodged by South Africa against Israel for genocide in the Gaza Strip, supported by some 20 countries, including Iceland, the Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium and Spain.
The ICJ has recognised a plausible risk of genocide in Gaza and has asked Israel to implement provisional measures – three times in total over the past two years – explains Fiorini. But Israel has never complied with them. The proceedings are still ongoing, but are progressing slowly due to the complexity of the evidence and the sensitivity of the subject. Too slowly, given the situation in Gaza, Fiorini believes.
A trial could begin in 2028 before the ICJ. Until then, the Court’s 193 member states are obliged to do everything in their power to prevent genocide, for example by imposing trade sanctions against Israel or an arms embargo.

The Pentagon has drawn up plans for an intensive three-day military campaign against Iran, the New York Times reported on Thursday, even as President Donald Trump said Washington will not launch an attack before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Washington and Tehran were having "productive discussions."
The NYT also reported that Trump has repeatedly declined proposals in recent months to resume major combat operations against Iran, despite ordering the Pentagon to prepare new options.

UN report calls for urgent overhaul of global postal sector as economic shocks disrupt mail flows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:10:23 UTC
16:10:23 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The Universal Postal Union (UPU) called Friday for urgent structural changes to the global postal sector, warning that economic shocks, trade restrictions, and geopolitical conflicts are increasingly disrupting international mail flows.
In its State of the Postal Sector 2026 report, the UN agency said the industry's challenges are structural rather than temporary, requiring "immediate, radical transformation."
The report found that global postal revenue declined for a third consecutive year in real terms in 2024, falling 7% from its 2021 peak to $563.4 billion.
International letter volumes dropped to just 37% of their 2015 levels, with the decade’s losses deepest in Africa and in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Meanwhile, traditional postal operators held a median share of only 27% of domestic parcel markets.
The UPU warned that changes to customs rules had intensified pressure on international deliveries.
Following the US suspension of duty-free treatment for low-value imports in August 2025, inbound postal tonnage plunged 70.3% year-on-year in September, compared with an 8.9% decline in August.
The report also highlighted the impact of the Middle East conflict on global postal flows, pointing to oil price spikes, vessels avoiding transit near the Strait of Hormuz, and restrictions on Gulf airspace.
It added that disruptions to air transport capacity, transit routes, and insurance costs coincided with a 51.4% plunge in median postal tonnage from Arab region senders this March, while the number of active sender corridors fell from 784 to 504.
It warned that postal networks are becoming increasingly vulnerable to shocks despite improvements in delivery reliability, calling for faster decision-making, regulatory reforms, and greater international coordination.

Tests Find No Oil Products in Sea Near Bulgarian Coast After Ship Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:07:00 UTC
16:07:00 KST

No petroleum products have been detected in seawater near Cape Kaliakra, Byala and Sozopol following drone strikes on two merchant ships in Bulgaria’s Black Sea Exclusive Economic Zone, the Basin Directorate "Black Sea Region" reported after Environment and Water Minister Rositsa Karamfilova ordered an extraordinary inspection along the coast.
Specialists from the directorate in Varna collected and analyzed seawater samples from the three locations.
Yavor Dimitrov, director of the Basin Directorate "Black Sea Region," said samples had been collected on October 6 under an order from Karamfilova. Initial findings were available the following day, while results for additional substances were expected next week.
The analysis covered physicochemical indicators, including iron, copper, zinc, aluminum and polychlorinated biphenyls. No exceedances were found in any of these indicators in the Kaliakra area. At Byala, nitrogen levels exceeded the relevant threshold, while samples from Sozopol showed exceedances involving several nitrogen compounds and phosphorus.
Dimitrov said the findings could not be attributed to the October 6 vessel incident, as the elevated levels most likely reflected diffuse pollution from agricultural sources unrelated to the accident.
The samples were also tested for petroleum products. Inspectors did not observe the characteristic opalescence on the water’s surface associated with this type of pollution, and laboratory results confirmed the absence of petroleum products.
Dimitrov said the monitoring was launched immediately after the incident to establish the condition of the Black Sea waters as soon as possible.
"The goal was to monitor as early as possible, immediately after the incident, in order to have an idea of the quality of our Black Sea waters. This monitoring will continue in the coming days, and the points and indicators will be further specified, and will also depend on the hydrometeorological forecast," he said.

2026-10-09

The U.S. could leave more than 100,000 Ukrainians in "limbo" after temporary protection ends - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
TPS for Ukrainians in the U.S. expires on October 19. The program may not be extended, leaving automatic protection in place for another six months.
The Donald Trump administration is considering several options for Ukrainians to remain in the United States after temporary protection expires. One of them is not to officially extend the program, but not to cancel it either, which could give people another six months without the threat of immediate deportation. Politico reported this, citing sources familiar with the matter, UNN writes.
Details
The temporary protected status (TPS) program for Ukrainians expires on October 19. By that date, the White House must decide whether to extend it for more than 100,000 Ukrainian citizens who fled to the United States because of the war.
Some lawmakers from both parties support extending the protection. At the same time, Congress is also discussing a backup scenario: allowing the program to formally expire without a separate decision to terminate it. Under this approach, an automatic six-month extension mechanism could be triggered.
The U.S. administration has already applied a similar arrangement to citizens of El Salvador. However, problems then arose over determining their rights to work and study. Thus, although such an option could postpone the deportation of Ukrainians, it would not guarantee them complete legal certainty.
Politico's sources note that the administration must take into account the possible political consequences of the mass deportation of Ukrainians to a country where a war is ongoing. At the same time, ending the protection could meet the demands of supporters of a tougher immigration policy, who insist on tighter controls over migrants.
Washington's decision could also be influenced by relations between the United States and Ukraine. According to one of the publication's sources, Trump's team has pushed the war into the background, while no noticeable changes in its approach to Kyiv have occurred so far. The source believes that the simplest option for the administration would be to allow the program to expire.
The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services declined to comment on the possible decision. It only reported that it continues to review individual applications for reauthorization to remain in the country in accordance with current procedures.

You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:00:42 UTC
16:00:42 KST

In the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.
Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.
While there were slight variations among the three countries, larger patterns are clear. Among women who are under 50 in England, breast, bowel, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreatic and stomach cancers have increased. For men under 50 in England, there were increases in bowel, kidney, liver, pancreatic and prostate cancers. This is the opposite of what we would hope to achieve in public health – and no, it isn’t only because we have better diagnostic tools, or are doing more testing. While this explains some of the increase, it doesn’t account for it all. The data indicates that younger generations are experiencing a higher incidence of some cancers than previous generations at the same age. Put more simply: you have a higher chance of cancer at a younger age than your parents.
Scientists are now working to unpick what has changed between generations that might be driving this uptick, especially trying to find things people may have been exposed to during childhood or adolescence in the 1990s that they wouldn’t have been in the 1950s.
Here are some potential explanations: what we eat has changed significantly over the past 50 years, with the rise in ultra-processed and fast foods as well as sugary drinks. We also are more sedentary as a population. These changes are linked to rising levels of excess weight and obesity. Body fat, especially around the vital organs and waist, is a risk factor for chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction, all of which are linked to higher cancer incidence. Globally, obesity rates have more than doubled among adults and quadrupled among adolescents since 1990. Data collected in 2024 found that about 66% of adults in England were either overweight or living with obesity.
But diet, physical activity and excess body weight doesn’t fully explain the rise of certain cancers – such as breast cancer – in young people. Studies have shown that for women before menopause, a higher BMI is, in fact, linked to a slightly lower risk of cancer (which is in contrast to older women, where a higher BMI significantly increases risk of developing breast cancer.) Going further, scientists are looking at the health impact of sustained exposure to environmental toxins like air and water pollution, chemicals and plastics that have become widespread and almost impossible to avoid over the past 50 years.
It has been scientifically challenging to identify one toxin that explains the global increase in cancers. Cancer can develop long after exposure to a toxic chemical, and over our lives we encounter a range of chemicals and pollutants. Saying which one, or whether it was during childhood, in utero, or adulthood, is difficult to pin down.
On the positive side, one area that we have made progress with in young people is lung cancer, largely driven by anti-smoking campaigns and widespread awareness of the links between smoking and lung cancer. So not everything is getting worse.
None of the continuing research into risk factors for early onset cancer should mean attaching blame to patients. One of the first human impulses when getting a diagnosis is to think “what caused this?”, and even further, “what have I done?” – and this isn’t helpful. In addition, scientists estimate that only 40% of cancers at a population level are because of an “individually modifiable” behaviour like smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity, or weight. The other 60% is a mix of ageing, genetic susceptibility, infection, possible environmental factors, and sometimes just bad luck.
With the research and investment continuing into scientific research, we will eventually learn what’s driving the rise in cancer in younger people. But for now, that mystery is still to be uncovered.
- Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

Beneath Gaza’s rubble lie the missing – and possible evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Beneath Gaza’s rubble lie the missing – and possible evidence
Three years after the Hamas-led attack on Israel and the subsequent war, much of Gaza is still in ruins – and many families still haven’t found the buried bodies of their loved ones. Investigators from Geneva-based institutions are slowly documenting what lies beneath the rubble and pressing for its clearance to enable dignified burials and preserve evidence of possible war crimes.
More than two years after an explosion reduced his apartment building to rubble, Hamada Abu Hasira, a 29-year-old cook working for a charity in Gaza, is still searching for traces of his brother. Without the remains he cannot be assured his brother is truly dead and there is little chance those responsible will ever be held accountable.
He remembers that evening in March 2024 distinctly.
Night was falling over Deir Al-Hawa, the Gaza neighbourhood where he had lived, and the streets had largely emptied following Israeli evacuation orders. In the quiet, Abu Hasira could hear the rumble of tanks and military vehicles, punctuated by the voices of Israeli forces.
He and his family struggled to sleep. They had chosen the top floor deliberately. If the building was struck, they thought, being higher up might give rescuers a better chance of finding them.
And, the family thought, “if we are hit, we would rather be killed together”.
Then they heard movement around the entrance of the building. When the quiet returned, one of Hamada’s brothers went downstairs to check the family car and see whether they might still be able to leave, ignoring pleas from his family not to go because it was too dangerous.
Outside, he saw what looked like barrels of explosives. Inside the family’s car, a device was ticking. He ran back upstairs. His father decided that no one would go downstairs again. They would wait for daylight, then leave.
The blast came before dawn. The building collapsed over them. Abu Hasira spent more than 24 hours beneath the rubble before a neighbour heard his screams and helped pull him out. He and his mother Reem survived.
“I called my brother Ahmed. He answered me at first, but then his voice went quiet. That’s when I knew he was gone,” Abu Hasira, who works as a cook for a local organisation, told Swissinfo.
The bodies of his father Imran and brother Ahmed were recovered. His younger brother, Momen, is still missing. The absence of all three hurts him daily, more so as he prepared to celebrate his wedding.
The details of his account could not be independently verified and are based on the survivor’s recollection of events, as are all eyewitness accounts detailed in this story. Israel has barred international journalists from entering Gaza and has denied access to UN and other international investigative bodies, limiting documentation work and independent verification on the ground.
The accounts in this story were gathered by a Swissinfo correspondent in Gaza through interviews with survivors and neighbours. They echo cases documented by UN officials, who have briefed journalists in Geneva on efforts to recover remains from beneath the rubble.
Thousands still beneath the rubble
Across Gaza, entire families have been buried beneath collapsed buildings, many killed and countless others still missing in a landscape of shattered concrete. For families, the priority is to recover and bury their loved ones; for UN investigators, the same rubble may hold evidence of how they died. Gathering evidence in war zones is always challenging and can take years. In Gaza, it is complicated by the scale of destruction.
The war that followed the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023 has left much of Gaza in ruins. By June 2026, the United Nations estimated that 82% of all structures in Gaza had been damaged, including 134,422 which were assessed as destroyed.
Much of that rubble has yet to be cleared. “It is estimated that at least 8,000 bodies remain buried under the rubble across the Gaza Strip,” Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territory, told journalists in Geneva.
“At this pace, completing the recovery of the remaining bodies will take at least ten more years,” he said, speaking from Amman, Jordan.
Years without answers
For many families, the uncertainty has lasted for years.
In Gaza City’s Al-Zaytoun neighbourhood, an Israeli strike flattened the Abu Zour family home on December 4, 2023, according to neighbour Mohammed Al-Harazin. A 13-year-old girl was the sole survivor, he remembers. Around 50 relatives and displaced people were killed.
“The bodies of those who were killed remained under the rubble (until September) because the area was dangerous and it was difficult to carry out recovery efforts,” says Al-Harazin, an engineering student who had to relocate to Al-Mawasi in the southwestern Gaza Strip due to the war.
Amal Maqbel’s father, Ashraf, has been missing since an Israeli strike destroyed the family’s six-story building on December 6, 2023. “We did not know whether my father was still inside, whether he had managed to get out, or what had happened to him,” she said.
Recent findings reveal the scale of loss
Cases documented by the UN tell similar stories. Recent recoveries have begun to reveal the scale of what remains beneath Gaza’s ruins. More than 630 bodies and other human remains were recovered between November 2025 and September 2026, according to Palestinian Civil Defence figures cited by the UN.
“The remains recovered so far may only be the tip of the iceberg,” said UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan.
In September, the remains of 96 people from three Palestinian families were recovered from beneath the rubble in Gaza City, according to the UN human rights office, OHCHR. Around half were women and children.
Sunghay cited the case of the Malaka family, who lost 72 members in an Israeli airstrike on family homes in November 2023. Only three bodies were recovered at the time.
Remains believed to belong to 55 members of the family were among those recovered in September. The bodies of the remaining 14 are still missing beneath the rubble.
The scale of the destruction, Sunghay noted, is also making identification more difficult.
“The sheer explosive power of heavy munitions sometimes left no recoverable remains,” he said, speaking from Amman. “And it’s increasingly difficult to distinguish rubble from remains as the years pass.”
A recovery effort starved of resources
The recovery effort is hampered by acute shortages of machinery, fuel and personnel.
Sunghay said Palestinian Civil Defence teams had only one functioning excavator and were at times digging through rubble by hand because Israel restricts the entry of heavy equipment and trained recovery teams.
Israel says equipment entering Gaza is subject to security controls. COGAT, the Israeli military body that controls access to the territory, has justified restrictions on items it says could be used for a “terrorist build-up”. The Israeli military says Hamas used engineering vehicles to breach the barrier on October 7, 2023, and later to dig tunnels, plant explosives and retrieve weapons from rubble, calling them “a central component in Hamas’ ability to carry out terror operations.”
For some families, even reaching the ruins is impossible.
“Most of the territory of Gaza is now beyond the Yellow Line, inaccessible to Palestinians, including civil defence teams and families of missing persons,” Sunghay explained.
The Yellow Line is the shifting boundary separating areas of Gaza under Israeli military control from areas Palestinians can still access.
The October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas led to the return of all Israeli hostages and their remains. In return, Israel released nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees and returned Palestinian bodies it had been holding.
But key parts of the ceasefire remain incomplete. Hamas and other armed groups have not disarmed, Israel has not completed its planned withdrawal, and reconstruction (estimated by the UN and the World Bank to cost at least $71 billion, or CHF60 billion) has yet to begin at scale.
Preserving evidence
Clearing Gaza’s rubble is not only a question of reconstruction and recovering the missing. UN human rights officials say destroyed sites may also contain evidence relevant to investigations into alleged violations of international law.
“Recovering and burying the victims does not substitute for establishing the circumstances in which they were killed,” al-Kheetan told journalists in September.
UN satellite assessments do not attribute responsibility for each destroyed building. UN human rights bodies, however, have linked the overwhelming destruction of Gaza’s built environment to Israeli airstrikes, shelling and ground operations.
UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese has warned that rubble clearance could destroy both human remains and potential evidence. “Gaza’s rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes,” she said.
Albanese remains under controversial US sanctions over her outspoken criticism of Israel.
OHCHR has also warned that destroyed sites may contain evidence that needs preserving. Al-Kheetan said the office had grave concerns that Israel’s methods of warfare, including the use of wide-area explosive weapons in densely populated areas, “failed to ensure that they effectively distinguish between civilians and fighters.”
Israel insists its forces make these distinctions, in accordance with international humanitarian law and take precautions to minimise civilian harm, such as intelligence-based targeting and issuing evacuation orders. But it also argues those efforts are complicated by Hamas operating within civilian areas and infrastructure.
Now displaced and staying with relatives in central Gaza, Abu Hasira is still waiting for news of his younger brother, Momen. He fears the worst but wants at least to recover his body and give him a dignified burial. It is a wish shared by thousands of families across Gaza.
“They have a right to know the fates of their children, parents, siblings, cousins,” Sunghay said. “They have a right to mourn them with dignity, and they have a right to justice.”
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk has called on Israel to facilitate the recovery, identification and dignified burial of the dead “without delay”.
Danny Danon, Israel’s Ambassador to the United Nations in New York, said Türk had ignored Hamas abuses and jumped to accuse Israel before facts had been established.
Palestinian groups have asked the UN and relevant countries to set up a neutral body to recover the remains of the missing.
Hassan Herzallah is a Palestinian writer and translator based in Gaza

War in Gaza: the victims that no one talks about
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

War in Gaza: the victims that no one talks about
According to the United Nations, Gaza’s maternal and newborn healthcare system has been “decimated”.
In February, Nagham, a 29-year-old living in the Al-Mawasi camp, Khan Younis in southern Gaza Strip was rushed to hospital with bleeding and severe pain. That’s when she learnt she was pregnant.
She is now into her eighth month of pregnancy, which she has described overall as extremely “difficult”.
“The living conditions caused physical and emotional exhaustion, especially after the famine; the stress, the heat, the humidity, and the lack of hygiene,” she tells Swissinfo.
Nagham was unable to attend regular check-ups because the nearest hospital was two hours away and the journey cost more than she could afford. It was only this summer that a humanitarian organisation opened a clinic close to the camp where she could receive medical care. Finding essential vitamins and medication was likewise very difficult and costly.
Recently, she suffered from severe infections and needed antibiotics. Soaring temperatures – an average of 33°C in August in Gaza – combined with extreme humidity made breathing and sleeping difficult.
Nearly three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel and the start of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been reported killed according to OCHA, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
For pregnant and breastfeeding women in Gaza, the war has created particular risks. With much of the healthcare system decimated, access to care remains complicated and expensive. Hygiene conditions are minimal. Women often have no choice but give birth in tents or other makeshift conditions.
According to a study by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and Al-Quds University in Gaza City, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in June 2026, the mortality rate among women who were pregnant on 8 October 2023 was 948 deaths per 100,000 pregnancies. Most died from traumatic injuries.
More
After the ceasefire, survival still defines life in Gaza
Before the war, Gaza’s maternal mortality ratio stood at 30 deaths per 100,000 live births. That compares with 17.9 in the United States and five in Switzerland.
The study’s figures describe a population-level pattern and are not directly comparable with standard maternal mortality rates. They also do not establish the cause of every individual death.
A shattered health system
The broader deterioration of Gaza’s healthcare system has left pregnant women with fewer places to seek treatment.
According to the WHO Israeli attacks over the past three years have reportedly destroyed or damaged almost all hospitals, disrupted medical supplies, and, amid mass displacement and hunger, contributed to sharp increases in maternal mortality, miscarriages, and newborn deaths.
The UN stated in December 2025 that Gaza’s maternal and newborn healthcare system had been “decimated”.
“By the end of 2024, women in Gaza faced a threefold higher risk of dying during childbirth and a threefold higher risk of miscarriage compared with the period before the war,” the OHCHR reported.
Israel’s political and military leaders have consistently said its military’s operations in Gaza are conducted in self-defence, to defeat Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. They have also insisted that Israeli forces operate in accordance with international law and take all feasible measures to mitigate harm to civilians.
Israel has also said that Hamas is using hospitals in Gaza as shelters and operational bases for its fighters. A UN Commission of Inquiry said Israel had not provided evidence for its broader claim that more than 85% of Gaza’s major medical facilities had been used by Hamas. It did, however, confirm a tunnel and shaft at Al-Shifa hospital and evidence that armed-group members had entered the facility.
Where’s the focus on women?
Since the turn of the century, there has been growing international attention to the specific harms women experience in war. UN Security Council resolution 1325, adopted in 2000, put women’s protection in conflict and participation in peacemaking on the international agenda. International criminal law also addresses sexual violence in war.
Yet reproductive violence receives less global attention, even though international humanitarian law carves out specific protections for pregnant women and infants during armed conflict.
“The war in Gaza illustrates the extent to which violence directed at pregnant, labouring, and breastfeeding women, as well as women struggling to keep their newborn children alive, is completely absent from global political debates about the obligations of parties to armed conflict,” wrote Fionnuala Ní Aoláin, the former UN special rapporteur on counter-terrorism and human rights, in the online publication Just Security in February 2024.
Human rights and medical organisations have pushed to change that. Israel’s military campaign resulted in a 41% decline in births during the first half of 2025 compared with the same period in 2022, according to separate reports published in January 2026 by Physicians for Human Rights and Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (PHRI). The organisations also report significant increases in maternal mortality, miscarriages, neonatal deaths, and premature births.
“The severe and ongoing health and life-threatening risks faced by pregnant and breastfeeding women and their children are the logical consequence of the collapse of the healthcare system, the denial of basic living conditions, and an endless cycle of survival reduced to the absolute minimum necessary to endure,” said Lama Bakri, project leader at the Israeli human rights organisation PHRI.
More
The Board of Peace must address the basic needs of the Palestinian population
These organisations, along with the UN Independent Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, now accuse Israel of deliberately dismantling Gaza’s reproductive healthcare system.
UN investigators and human rights groups say the destruction of reproductive healthcare raises questions under international law. Some argue that violence against pregnant women and children in Gaza could amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity. Those are legal assessments made by the organisations concerned, not final judicial findings.
The UN Commission of Inquiry, for example, concluded in March 2025 that Israeli forces had systematically destroyed maternity wards and reproductive healthcare facilities and had intentionally attacked the Al-Basma fertility clinic in December 2023. These acts have been characterised as reproductive violence and obstetric violence by human rights groups and UN investigators.
In a report to the UN Human Rights Council, the independent UN experts stated that the destruction of maternity wards in Gaza and embryos stored at the fertility clinic could indicate a strategy aimed at preventing births within a particular population group. Under the Genocide Convention, that can constitute genocide if it is carried out with the intent to destroy the group.
Israel categorically rejects the suggestion that it is pursuing a policy intended to prevent Palestinian births and says that no such policy exists. Israel says its objective is to defeat Hamas rather than destroying Palestinians. Hamas led the October 7, 2023 attack that killed 1200 people and does not recognise Israel.
The same commission in September 2025 went further, and said there are reasonable ground to conclude that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. The commission’s findings were those of a UN investigative body, not a binding judgement by the court. Its findings do not establish genocide occurred. Israel rejected that conclusion.
The commission has not been granted access to Israel or the Palestinian Territories since it was established in 2021. Since the October 2023 attacks, Israel has imposed additional restrictions on the access and activities of other UN bodies and humanitarian personnel.
Deterioration despite ceasefire
Despite the ceasefire that has been in place since October 2025, reproductive health indicators in Gaza have continued to worsen.
Between January and June 2026, 3,958 miscarriages were recorded, according to the OCHA. This represented 208.5 miscarriages per 1,000 live births, a 3.3-fold increase compared with the second half of 2025.
The number of births also declined by 3.2% during the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier.
Nagham says she sees no change in her access over the past months. “We are still in the same place, in the same tents, under the same hygienic conditions.”
Even when women go to hospitals, they are told that other cases are more urgent.
“There is simply not enough care for pregnant women.”
The WHO reported in early August that there had been 45 attacks on healthcare facilities in Gaza since the beginning of this year.
More
Aid groups say Israeli restrictions leave Gaza without relief despite ceasefire

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,549,490 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:57:31 UTC
15:57:31 KST

Russia has lost around 1,549,490troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 9.
The number includes 1,710 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,402 tanks, 25,509 armored combat vehicles, 160,412 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,950 artillery systems, 2,199 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,693 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,908 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Bus firm Lux Ekspress raises fares as diesel prices climb

Unknown Publisher

Bus firm Lux Ekspress raises fares as diesel prices climb
Long-distance bus line Lux Ekspress is hiiking ticket prices on its Tallinn-Narva and Tallinn-Pärnu routes as diesel costs climb, its CEO has said.
Ingmar Roos, head of Lux Ekspress, said bus fuel now costs over 30 percent more than the company had forecast for this year, with further rises possible
The rise will add 50 cents to €1 to full-fare tickets on the Tallinn–Narva and Tallinn–Pärnu routes.
The cost of diesel has driven up expenses and inflation across many sectors. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kaubandus-tööstuskoda) has proposed to the government that fuel excise could be lowered in response, as many European countries, including Estonia's neighbors, have done.
"This does not compensate consumers and businesses for all the price growth there has been in fuel, and the reasons are known to everyone — they are not tax-related. But it would help to ease the situation to some extent. The costs that have grown in recent months are large, and in the millions, not insignificant numbers," said Mait Palts, director general of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
The world market price of diesel is double what it was a year ago; motor fuel is a significant cost for many business sectors.
"Our services have certainly become more expensive. And it is absolutely certain that for manufacturing and retail companies this is also an extremely important cost component. And where it used to be customary to account for the fuel factor once a month, in conditions of such volatility there is no other option — we have moved to weekly accounting. So changes in fuel prices change our expenditure prices weekly," said Alvar Tõruke, chairman of the board of DSV Eesti.
Lux Ekspress has already adjusted ticket prices. If fuel prices do not fall by November, bus lines face further increases, Roos noted.
"As a company operating solely on ticket revenues, we have to pass this cost on to passengers in some way. And if we avoided price rises in the spring, in an effort to attract more passengers against the background of the sharp fuel price increase, then today we really do have to raise ticket prices to some extent. Perhaps, understandably for bus passengers, the order of magnitude on the Tallinn-Narva and Tallinn-Pärnu routes for a full ticket will be around 50 cents to one euro," he said.
The government's assessment is that lowering excise is not viable.
"Such a reduction to the minimum level would be €210 million for a full year. That has to come from somewhere. On the one hand we understand businesses' concern, on the other we have to look at the overall competitiveness of the economy and the state of public finances," said Climate Minister Erkki Keldo.
The diesel price spike has mostly been driven by the war in the Middle East, which has disrupted supply. The G7 countries have released 100 million barrels of oil and diesel to be released from reserves in an effort to counter skyrocketing prices, following a threat by the Trump administration to impose an export ban on EU nations. Military ground vehicles also run primarily on diesel.

SpaceX strikes spectrum deal, paving way for Starlink to become major US mobile carrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:55:37 UTC
15:55:37 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
SpaceX announced on Thursday an agreement to acquire nationwide low-band spectrum licenses, advancing plans to turn Starlink Mobile into a major US mobile carrier through a network combining satellite and terrestrial services.
The agreement covers up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, the company said in a statement. The acquisition remains subject to final Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval.
SpaceX said the spectrum would address a key technical gap by allowing signals to penetrate obstacles such as walls, helping provide coverage inside buildings. Most existing mobile devices already support the band, it added.
The low-band frequencies would complement Starlink Mobile's global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum, which the company plans to use for high-bandwidth capacity in the US.
Once regulatory approval is secured, SpaceX plans to combine its satellite-to-mobile constellation with terrestrial infrastructure to provide connectivity indoors, outdoors and in areas without cellular coverage.
Separately, SpaceX said the FCC this week approved its next-generation Starlink Mobile constellation application, authorizing the launch of 15,000 satellites optimized for global operations using 2 GHz spectrum.
The company said its V2 Starlink Mobile satellites would deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of the current generation, supporting high-speed connections directly to unmodified mobile devices.
The FCC also authorized additional communications bands that would allow the satellites to use Starlink's existing ground gateway network, according to SpaceX.

Who is Dov Lando, the Israeli rabbi criticising Zionism?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:55:11 UTC
15:55:11 KST

Who is Dov Lando, the Israeli rabbi criticising Zionism?
The senior rabbi, whose party is in Netanyahu’s coalition, has caused uproar in Israel by calling Zionism disastrous.
One of Israel’s top ultra-Orthodox rabbis, Dov Lando, has become the centre of controversy in Israel after comments emerged in which he denigrated Zionism.
In a recently released video recording, the 96-year-old rabbi is heard saying the ideology of Zionism caused the Jewish people to suffer “disasters”, and that Jewish Israelis may have been better off without a state.
The remarks have drawn rebukes from Israeli politicians weeks before landmark legislative elections, in which the role of the country’s growing ultra-Orthodox community – particularly over military service – is a major issue. The political alignment of ultra-Orthodox parties could also prove crucial to the formation of the next government.
So, who is Lando and why are his comments significant?
Who is Dov Lando?
Dov Lando is a 96-year-old rabbi regarded as the leader of Israel’s Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community. Born in Poland and raised in the Lithuanian-style ultra-Orthodox tradition, Lando heads a yeshiva – a traditional Jewish academy – in the Israeli city of Bnei Brak.
He is a member of Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah, a council of senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis that offer religious guidance to the community, as well as the spiritual leader of Israel’s Degel HaTorah party. That party is part of the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance, which is a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition.
What has Lando said about Zionism?
Earlier this week, Israeli media released a video of Lando making year-old comments that harshly criticise Zionism, military service and secular Israelis.
Lando, who has made similarly critical remarks before, is heard in the video saying that Zionism “caused the Arabs to hate us” and brought physical as well as spiritual “disasters” on the Jewish people.
“It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state,” Lando said, adding that international or Palestinian rule would have been “the best situation” for Jews.
Lando went on to castigate soldiers who adhere to Religious Zionism – a strand of Orthodox Judaism that upholds Zionism – saying “they are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah.” Many military operations, he said, are carried out “not for saving lives, but for the honour of the state”.
The veteran rabbi also had harsh words for secular Israelis, who he said have “no connection to Judaism at all”. He described them as having built “a state of apostasy and heresy”.
What has been the reaction in Israel?
Lando’s remarks have drawn fierce criticism from numerous Israeli politicians, including all major figures that have joined an opposition alliance challenging Netanyahu.
Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party who is viewed as the opposition bloc’s most likely candidate for prime minister, said Lando’s “outrageous statements” were “the embodiment of anti-Zionism”.
Yair Lapid, the head of Israel’s opposition in the Knesset, called the comments “a disgrace to every Jew”.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance co-founded with Lapid, said Lando’s remarks are “anti-Semitic, anti-Zionist” and against the Israeli military.
Netanyahu has not commented on Lando’s latest reported remarks, but he publicly condemned earlier statements by the rabbi in July, when Lando accused the Religious Zionism movement of “incitement to murder” for its support for drafting religious seminary students into the military.
Could the controversy impact Israel’s upcoming elections?
Potentially.
Members of the anti-Netanyahu opposition bloc have called for the UTJ, which Lando’s party is part of, to be cast out of any future government, and criticised Netanyahu for staying aligned with the group.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, said Netanyahu is “silent because without Rabbi Lando and his emissaries, he has no government”.
Netanyahu’s “political survival is more important to him than Zionism, more than equality in service, and more than the blood of our soldiers”, Golan said.
But breaking with the UTJ would come at a huge political cost to Netanyahu, whose coalition is already in for a tough election battle on October 27 and is polling well below the 61-seat threshold needed for a majority.
UTJ is projected to win 8 seats in parliament, according to an October 5 poll by Israel’s Channel 12.
“If Netanyahu attacks Lando forcefully, he pays a price with the Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) he needs to form a government,” said Ehab Jabareen, a researcher on Israeli affairs. “If he stays silent, he hands his rivals material to tell right-wing voters that the man who speaks of Zionism and security depends on a religious leadership that doubts Zionism itself.”

How Kyiv’s “green” metro line operates - authorities provide an update

Kyiv’s “green” metro line operates on a special schedule during peak hours due to restrictions on the Southern Bridge. Some surface transport has been suspended.
In Kyiv, the "green" metro line is operating according to a special timetable during the morning and evening rush hours amid restrictions on the Southern Bridge. However, information about its suspension due to a power outage is not true. The Kyiv City State Administration explained this on October 9, UNN reports.
Has the "green" metro line in Kyiv been disconnected from power?
"Information about the suspension of the "green" metro line due to a power outage is not true. Ground electric public transport in certain districts of the city has temporarily suspended operations. Information circulating on social media about the alleged suspension of train services on the "green" metro line is not true," the Kyiv City State Administration said in a statement.
How the metro is operating
"Currently, the Syretsko-Pecherska line is operating according to a temporary special timetable during the morning and evening rush hours due to restrictions on the Southern Bridge: only one metro train may travel across it at a time. At other times, trains run as usual," the Kyiv City State Administration said.
How other public transport is operating
At the same time, due to a lack of power in the energy system, part of the public transport service in the Obolonskyi, Podilskyi and Sviatoshynskyi districts has reportedly been temporarily suspended.
According to Kyivpastrans, the funicular service has also been temporarily suspended due to a lack of electricity.

US sanctions 17 vessels linked to Iran’s ‘shadow fleet’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:52:40 UTC
15:52:40 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The US Treasury Department on Thursday imposed sanctions on 17 vessels linked to Iran’s “shadow fleet,” stepping up pressure on Tehran’s petroleum exports.
The department said the vessels had transported millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, petroleum and petrochemical products to South and East Asian markets.
The sanctions also targeted companies involved in the shipping network.
“No enabler of Iranian sanctions evasion is safe from the full force of Treasury’s authorities,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
Among the vessels targeted was the Vanuatu-flagged Tina 5, which Treasury said had transported more than 1.5 million barrels of Iranian crude oil in August.
The Comoros-flagged Sogl transported over 2 million barrels of Iranian propane and butane since September 2025, while the Cameroon-flagged Shenzen carried more than 3.5 million barrels of crude since November 2025, according to the department.
The action is part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched on Aug. 24 to restrict Iran’s access to international financial and commercial networks.
The campaign expanded sanctions exposure across several sectors, including shipping, aviation, technology, gold and digital assets. Treasury warned that entities facilitating sanctions evasion for Iran risk exclusion from the US financial system.
Separately, the department removed Hakuna Matata and Pinochio from its sanctions list after the vessels left the shadow fleet and were sold to operators not subject to sanctions.
