European Parliament Refuses to Recognize Russia’s New State Duma, Urges EU to Cut Contact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:52:26 UTC
15:52:26 KST

- Category
- World
European Parliament Refuses to Recognize Russia’s New State Duma, Urges EU to Cut Contact
The European Parliament has refused to recognize the State Duma formed after Russia’s September 2026 parliamentary elections, with 482 lawmakers voting in favor of the resolution, 41 against, and 39 abstaining, the European Parliament reported on October 8.
The resolution concludes that the elections were neither free nor fair and that the resulting State Duma cannot be considered a legitimate representative and legislative body of the Russian Federation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The vote followed elections held across Russia from September 18 to 20, which Parliament said took place without genuine political competition and amid systematic repression. Russia also organized voting in temporarily occupied Crimea and Sevastopol, as well as temporarily occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Independent analysis of Russia’s election results also raised questions about the scale of United Russia’s victory. While official results gave the ruling party nearly 58% of the vote, analysis of precincts without major statistical anomalies put its support at roughly 34%, while separate estimates placed actual turnout below 40%, compared with the official figure of more than 59%.
The resolution noted that Russia did not invite the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights to observe the elections. It also cited reports of ballot stuffing, statistical anomalies, vote transfers, and turnout spikes.
The document also stated that opposition politicians had been imprisoned, forced into exile, or barred from standing, while Yabloko candidates were excluded from the federal list.
Parliament separately condemned the voting organized in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories and said it does not recognize any legal or political consequences arising from them. It called for EU sanctions against those involved in organizing or standing as candidates in the illegal polls.
The European Parliament called on the Council of the EU and member states to adopt the same position of non-recognition toward the State Duma formed after the September elections.
Before the vote, Russian authorities sent mobile election teams to homes in temporarily occupied Donetsk alongside armed servicemen and police. Footage showed residents casting ballots outside their homes while armed personnel stood nearby.

Türksat and China Satcom have signed an agreement at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya to jointly develop and commercialize satellite technologies, expanding a partnership that began with capacity sharing.
The two satellite operators plan to develop drone communications systems, satellite-based internet of things technologies and smart border security systems.
The projects include hardware that would allow equipment used in energy, agriculture and logistics to be monitored and managed via satellite in remote areas without mobile networks.
Satellite monitoring systems would also provide real-time data transmission where terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable.
Türksat Deputy General Manager for Satellite Services Selman Demirel and China Satcom CEO Ma Haiquan signed the protocol at the Turkish company’s stand at the 77th edition of the congress.
Turkish and Chinese engineers will work together through each stage of development, from assessing market needs and building prototypes to testing, validation and commercialization.
The agreement builds on cooperation launched in 2025, when the companies began their capacity-sharing partnership.
Decisions reached at World Space Business Week in Paris expanded that cooperation into hardware and software development.
A joint steering committee with equal representation from both companies will oversee research and product development.
Progress will be reviewed every three months.

Nausėda: Lithuania struggles to spend defence funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:47:00 UTC
15:47:00 KST

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda has criticised the country’s defence system for struggling to spend its allocated funds, citing lengthy procurement processes, a lack of flexibility and difficulties in cooperating with Ukraine.
“The system is creaking under the strain and struggling to cope with the challenge of spending 5%, more than 5%, of our GDP on national defence,” Nausėda said in an interview published Friday on 15min.lt.
He noted that the Defence Ministry and the armed forces had spent less than half of the funding allocated for defence this year.
Lithuania’s defence budget for 2026 stands at 4.8 billion euros, equivalent to 5.38% of gross domestic product.
Nausėda said he was dissatisfied with the time it takes to move from planning a project to implementing it, warning that Lithuania could not afford delays of two to two-and-a-half years.
“We cannot afford the luxury of dragging this process out for two or two-and-a-half years. We certainly cannot explain to hostile countries that, you know, we need more time to prepare,” he said.
The president said both the military and government institutions were contributing to the delays, with the armed forces taking too long to clearly and quickly define their needs and institutions struggling to fulfil them.
He also expressed doubts about whether Lithuanian institutions were genuinely willing to learn from Ukraine’s wartime experience.
Nausėda said officials sometimes feared taking risks because they could face criminal liability if oversight bodies later identified serious violations. As a result, he said, they sought to avoid personal responsibility by hiding behind collective decision-making procedures, further slowing projects.
As an example, the president pointed to a stalled agreement between Lithuania and Ukraine on joint drone production.
While he initially suspected that Ukraine was reluctant to share its technology or issue the necessary export licenses, he said he increasingly believed that Lithuanian institutions were failing to offer terms that Kyiv would take seriously.
Nausėda said Lithuania had proposed purchasing 14 drones of one type and several of another, a proposal he suggested was too limited to justify joint production.
“Why should we discuss joint production with you if your needs are so small that there is no point in manufacturing them together? You can simply buy them from us, and that is where we draw the line,” he said, describing the Ukrainian position.
Lithuania and Ukraine signed a bilateral cooperation agreement in May covering joint drone production and the deployment of Ukrainian defence experts to Lithuania.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas has said Lithuania would manufacture unmanned aerial vehicles using technology purchased from Ukraine, a move he said would also stimulate Lithuania’s defence industry.

Bulgaria expects North Macedonia to fulfill the commitments agreed in 2022, including constitutional changes, and has set no additional conditions for its EU accession, Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said after meeting her North Macedonian counterpart Timco Mutsunski in Sofia.
Petrova described the bilateral talks as constructive, noting that North Macedonia had requested the meeting and she had agreed to it. She reiterated Bulgaria’s support for the country’s European perspective and said the requirements for progress remained unchanged since 2022.
"We expect that both the constitutional changes and all other elements of the agreed consensus will be implemented," Petrova emphasized.
She said she had asked Mutsunski to explain how Skopje viewed the deadlines for fulfilling its commitments.
"On their part, the view is that a sense of trust needs to be built. For me, the main way to build trust is to fulfill commitments. I hope to see positive steps in this direction," the foreign minister said.
Petrova noted that other Western Balkan countries, including Albania and Montenegro, had demonstrated the political will needed to advance toward EU membership. "I hope this will happen with North Macedonia," she added.
The minister stressed that Bulgaria was not imposing any new requirements on Skopje.
"We have no expectations other than those recorded in 2022, and we expect them to be met. The best guarantee is performance," Petrova said.
She explained that EU accession follows established rules and criteria, with member states making decisions within the agreed negotiating framework.
"No Member State can give guarantees to a candidate country for the continuation of the process. What it can give is a political willingness to stick to the commitments it has made. Bulgaria has shown this readiness," she said.
Petrova also raised the case of Iva Mihailova and her need for medical treatment during the meeting. She welcomed North Macedonia’s agreement to allow Bulgarian doctors to examine her, stressing the need to proceed quickly.
"For us, the readiness of North Macedonia to accept our doctors was positive news. It is important that this leads to treatment as quickly as possible. This is a humanitarian case that we must consider precisely through this prism," she emphasized.
No specific timetable has yet been established for the necessary examinations, Petrova said, adding that work with the medical teams was ongoing.
"The leading thing for all of us is that Iva gets quick access to adequate treatment. The end result should be one – she should be cured," the foreign minister said.
Petrova also addressed the return of the mortal remains of King Samuil, clarifying that the issue had not been discussed with Mutsunski.
"This is a great triumph for Bulgaria and something we can all be proud of. I see in this act a unifying function, not something that should be directed negatively towards North Macedonia," she said.
Petrova expressed hope that Skopje would take the necessary steps to implement the existing agreements and make use of the stronger momentum behind EU enlargement.

Tens of thousands march in Madrid to mourn pensioner whose eviction sparked housing protests
Tens of thousands of protesters joined a march in Madrid Thursday to mark the death of 87-year-old retiree Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her apartment in the Spanish capital in September sparked a wave of housing protests that prompted the government to call early elections.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Tens of thousands of mourners marched through Madrid on Thursday in tribute to a Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked national housing protests that culminated in the calling of early elections.
The death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal on Wednesday produced tears and anger in the Spanish capital's emblematic Puerta del Sol square, the epicentre of the movement where hundreds are camping in protest.
From Sol, where an improvised shrine of candles, flowers and placards lay on Thursday morning, demonstrators headed to Abascal's former home in the upmarket Retiro district around three kilometres (two miles) away.
"Maricarmen will be an icon of struggle. She has made us wake up and say 'enough'. We cannot put up with this situation any longer," Rosa Marin, a 48-year-old teacher, told AFP.
Abascal, who used a wheelchair, died in hospital two weeks after her eviction from the apartment where she had lived for 70 years.
Read moreEvicted pensioner Maricarmen Abascal, heart of Spain's housing protests, dies
Taken away on a stretcher after the real estate company that owned the flat drastically hiked the rent, she became the face of Spain's long-running housing crisis and the catalyst for nationwide protests.
Maricarmen "was the last straw, she was able to cause all this", said photography teacher Anton Alexander, referring to the camps and demonstrations that have placed housing at the heart of the November 29 election.
"Ultimately, Maricarmen is a symbol. I hope this is a turning point," added Alexander. "I know I'm not going to buy a house, it overwhelms me."
'Injustice'
People of all ages joined the march, chanting slogans such as "they aren't deaths, they are murders". A provisional estimate by the central government's delegation in the Madrid region put their number at 20,000.
Marisol Gallo, 82, attended in solidarity with the younger generations whose average salary falls far short of the astronomical rents and purchase prices demanded for a flat in Madrid.
"It's a disgrace, it's an injustice. This struggle will continue," Gallo told AFP, hoping the protests would "bring change" and make the authorities "get their act together".
Outside Maricarmen's former residence in Retiro, next to the popular UNESCO-listed park of the same name, the mourners applauded and left more flowers and candles before observing a silence.
A deal had been reached with the real estate firm allowing Abascal to return home at a lower rent, but she ultimately spent her final days in hospital.
Attempting to respond to the popular pressure, the left-wing government hastily agreed two decrees last week that included greater protections against evictions for vulnerable tenants and the automatic renewal of contracts.
But the conservative and far-right opposition voted down the minority coalition's measures in parliament, prompting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call the early vote on Monday.
Read moreSpanish PM Sanchez calls snap election as pressure mounts over housing crisis
'Inept' politicians
Whether Sanchez, who is trailing in most polls, can capitalise on the anger remains to be seen.
"We have a political class that is the most inept since the start of democracy," said 67-year-old retiree Manuel Martin, who joined the tribute to Abascal on Thursday evening.
"Housing is a structural issue that no party can solve alone. This is a national problem," he added.
For Juana Sotillos, a 68-year-old pensioner, no party can emerge from the episode with any credit.
Abascal "has been used as a political tool by one side and the other", she told AFP in Sol earlier on Thursday, criticising Sanchez for "doing nothing" on housing during his eight years in power.
Photography teacher Alexander said he wanted "a government that really takes responsibility for resolving this", warning that the Spanish welfare state was "collapsing".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Russia has requested the Netherlands to extradite nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials, who have been convicted in the country in absentia.
The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office said on Thursday it also sent requests to "a number of other countries" seeking the detention and extradition of the officials, including ICC President Tomoko Akane.
The Moscow City Court found the nine guilty in absentia in December 2025 of offenses including knowingly bringing an innocent person to criminal liability, unlawful detention and attacks on internationally protected persons or institutions. They received prison sentences ranging from three and a half to 15 years.
In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, the presidential commissioner for children's rights, for alleged war crimes in Ukraine.

Japan on Friday decried the Russian prosecutorial requests. Government spokesman Masanao Ozaki said the measures were "unjustified and unacceptable," according to Kyodo News.
The government intends to "respond appropriately, including by making further representations to Russia" and "maintaining communication with the ICC and other states parties," he added.
While Japan is a State Party to the Rome Statute, which established the court in 2002, Russia and the US are not.

China
Unknown Publisher

XI'AN, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- For the first time, Li Fuping traded his usual National Day in the fields for a new adventure. During the early October holiday, the grain farmer drove his wife and two children 300 km to Yan'an, a revolutionary base that draws millions of visitors every year.
"Ten years ago, this was the most unlikely time for us to travel," said Li, from Ganbei village in Pucheng County, northwest China's Shaanxi Province. Back then, farming families spent every day of the early-autumn holiday picking corn, clearing stalks and sunning grain, he recalled.
Modern farming has brought a new dimension to old practices. Land consolidation, water-saving irrigation and soil improvement have turned scattered plots into larger family farms, boosting yields by an average of 20 percent and more than doubling Li's annual income in recent years. With mechanized harvesters now completing the harvest in just days, Li has both the time and money to travel with his children, aged 13 and eight.
The trend is happening across the country. A China Tourism Academy survey found 81 percent of rural residents intended to travel in 2025, and in the first half of this year they made 869 million domestic trips, about a quarter of the national total.
At 59, Liu Shuyan took his first sightseeing tour last week to Beijing, and visited Tian'anmen Square and the Badaling section of the Great Wall. "In the past, we traveled mostly to visit relatives," said the farmer from the suburbs of Linfen in north China's Shanxi Province. "Now we travel for fun and to enjoy the landscape."
Xi'an-based tour operator Bai Fenglun said his agency has seen a marked rise in inquiries from rural customers, with many naming Yan'an as their top choice of destination.
Among them was a group of more than 40 villagers from Uqostang township in Kuqa, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. For Tursungul Abdugeli, 68, it was her first trip outside Xinjiang. "I'd only seen Yan'an and its history on TV, but now I've seen it with my own eyes," she said, shopping for souvenirs for her grandchildren and friends back home.
Wang Xiaoyong, an associate researcher at the Shaanxi Academy of Social Sciences, said he sees growing tourism demand from Chinese farmers, driven by higher incomes and lighter burden. More accessible high-speed rail and air routes and viral tourism videos have also brought faraway destinations within reach.
"Rural travelers are no longer content with short trips close to home," Wang said. "More people are willing to leave familiar ground to visit places that carry national memory, revolutionary heritage and natural beauty."
The surge has exposed gaps in how the industry serves these customers. Ma Yaofeng, a professor at Shaanxi Normal University's School of Geography and Tourism, suggests targeting the lulls in the farming calendar such as the breaks after the autumn harvest and around the Spring Festival, and promoting packages tailored to young migrant workers, middle-aged travelers and seniors.
"This way, more people will be able to broaden their horizons on the road, and feel closer to the country they call home," Ma said. ■

In addition to attending National Day events, the king will witness the signing of a bilateral criminal judicial assistance agreement, observe a joint air-ground military exercise, and tour the agriculture ministry’s Floriculture Research and Development Center in Tainan.
Other foreign dignitaries arriving in Taiwan for National Day included a delegation of 27 Japanese legislators led by Furuya Keiji, chair of the Japan-Taiwan Friendship Parliamentarians’ League, the foreign ministry said.

Study finds communication styles may affect judgments of suspects
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:44:15 CST
15:44:15 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Both autistic and non-autistic suspects may be judged more harshly when their behavior during police interviews differs from observers' expectations, a study led by Australia's Flinders University has found.
The study, published in the journal Law and Human Behavior, examined how autistic and non-autistic observers evaluated autistic and non-autistic suspects in mock police interviews involving accusations of computer hacking, according to a university statement released on Friday.
Participants rated suspects on suspiciousness, credibility, guilt and whether their behavior met expectations.
Researchers found no decisive evidence that autistic people were more likely to be judged harshly because of "unusual" behaviors associated with autism, or that people were better at interpreting the intentions of suspects who shared their diagnostic status.
The researchers said the findings suggested that how much a suspect's behavior violates expectations about how a suspect should act may influence judgments, regardless of whether the person is autistic.
The findings highlighted the need for police and courts to guard against assumptions of guilt based on suspects' communication styles and interpretations of suspects' responses, intentions and motivations.
The findings suggested that some autistic suspects may face particular credibility risks in investigative or legal contexts, but the same probably applies to some non-autistic suspects.
Co-author Flinders University clinical psychologist Alliyza Lim said communication behavior may affect perceived credibility without necessarily providing evidence about whether the person actually committed an offence. ■

EU faces a gas shortage as winter approaches - Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:43:37 EEST
15:43:37 KST

EU faces a gas shortage as winter approaches - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
The EU risks losing up to 14 billion cubic meters of gas this winter due to low storage levels and supply disruptions. This could drive up prices.
The EU is facing a gas shortfall this winter that could force it to try to replace lost energy supplies equivalent to the amount used by 12 million households. Politico reports this, citing relevant reports, writes UNN.
Details
The shortfall, it is noted, raises the prospect of higher electricity bills and forced energy-saving measures this winter if the bloc is unable to find sufficient supplies elsewhere.
"As the war with Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies, the EU faces an overall shortfall of up to 14 billion cubic meters of natural gas this winter, approximately 7% of the bloc's needs and enough to provide electricity to 10 to 12 million European households," according to a report by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S. energy think tank.
These findings, it is noted, are echoed in a key report by Europe's leading association of gas network operators, which was presented to national energy officials on Thursday, October 8.
Natural gas is widely used to heat Europe's buildings, power its industry, and generate electricity. But EU gas storage levels have fallen to their lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for use in the winter.
IEEFA found that gas prices are near a four-year high, while supplies are constrained by the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, leaving Europe with limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the previous one.
Although this does not necessarily mean that the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean that there could be 7 billion cubic meters less gas in storage available for use. This could force countries to purchase gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets or even require consumers to reduce demand if new supplies are unavailable.
Record-low EU storage levels leave the bloc "with a smaller buffer" against global supply disruptions, making it "vulnerable to price spikes." This was stated by Ana Yaller-Macariewicz, IEEFA's lead European energy analyst. If countries have to deplete this year's reserves, it will also create a need to replenish stocks next year, perpetuating the vicious cycle of low inventories and high prices, she added.
The same risks were outlined in the 2026–2027 winter supply outlook published on Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if liquefied natural gas imports are limited or even "optimal" during a cold winter, storage levels could fall to 11%, the baseline level required for strategic reserves that are not readily available for use.
If countries hope to restore their reserves to 30% by the end of winter—or face an increased risk of future cold spells—volumes equivalent to 7% of demand will have to be either cut or simply withheld from consumers, ENTSO-G warns.
Partly, the publication writes, this pressure stems from the upcoming ban on long-term contracts for Russian LNG supplies across the EU, which is due to take effect in January and, according to the IEEFA report, will reduce gas imports to Europe by a further 7 billion cubic meters. Russian gas was traditionally used to offset "demand fluctuations" during the winter, the report says. "Europe now depends on storage facilities to get through the winter," the report states.
Even worse, according to an IEEFA report, gas demand during the winter has risen sharply over the past two years, while imports into the bloc have remained flat. As a result, the EU relied more heavily on its reserves during the winter period, and net withdrawals from storage in January this year reached 22.6 billion cubic metres, compared with 18.8 billion cubic metres in January 2025 and 17.8 billion cubic metres in January 2024.
The alternative would have been to import new LNG, a seaborne fuel that the EU is increasingly purchasing from the United States. But at current prices, importing the volumes lost will cost Europeans an additional €3 billion, 12% more than the same volume would have cost last year, on top of already sky-high prices, according to the report. US LNG production is also operating at near-full capacity, meaning that these additional imports will further reduce supply, Yaller-Makarovych said.
For some, higher prices are more likely. Although ENTSO-G’s tight-market scenario envisages a "global shortfall," implying a 20% reduction in LNG imports to Europe, Laurent Ruseckas, a senior gas market analyst at S&P Global Energy, argues that storage levels may fall only to a certain point, "because a rapid drawdown at the beginning of winter will drive prices higher," prompting cargoes to flow to Europe from Asia.
"There is no large demand in Europe that could be destroyed," he added, noting that the war in Ukraine has already destroyed 20% of the bloc’s industrial demand. "And it has not recovered," he noted.

Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:40:54 UTC
15:40:54 KST

Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief.
For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities.
Retaining a constituency formerly held by your last leader, Keir Starmer, and which has been overwhelmingly Labour since it was created in 1983, is in normal political times not that notable an achievement, but these are not normal times.
A low turnout of 38.7% and Abdi-Wali’s numerically modest 3,364 majority that resulted might not appear the greatest endorsement of the government, but it is also likely to have been in part due to the widespread assumption that Labour would win.
And what of the Greens, and particularly Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England and Wales, who decided to go for the high-profile seat himself? Again, it may sound curious to think he would be happy with second place, but after the most challenging week of his political life, it could have been worse.
Polanski got just under 33% of the vote, well above anyone else apart from Abdi-Wali, a proportion which shows that in an another election, and up against a Labour party not enjoying a Burnham bounce, the Greens could still be highly competitive in seats like these.
When Polanski said he wanted to stand, the hope was for another wave of enthusiasm and publicity of the sort that propelled Hannah Spencer to victory in February in another supposedly safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton.
He will nonetheless be quietly pleased that the result does not seem to have shown much of a shedding of Green votes after criticisms of, and deep divisions in, the party since it adopted a highly controversial policy on Zionism and Israel last weekend.
The new policy, decided by members at the Greens’ annual conference, equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism, and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. It is publicly opposed by four of the party’s five MPs, with numerous councillors distancing themselves as well and a handful resigning.
Polanski’s decision to not take a side, and even to absent himself from Sunday’s debate so he could campaign in the byelection, has prompted deep unease among some Greens, who termed it a failure of leadership. It was notable that after the result, Polanski had to state that he intended to stay as Green leader. “Yes absolutely, that’s what leaders do,” he said.
While some in the Greens had questioned Polanski’s decision to contest a seat in north London, rather than east London, where he lives, his allies make the point that Nigel Farage took eight tries to become an MP.
Either way, the result has not made Polanski’s position any worse. Had the Green vote collapsed he would have been under very intense pressure. As it stands, he must try to reassure sceptics in the party before seeking re-election in a year from now, under the party’s policy of two-year terms for leaders.
And what of the others? The Conservatives will be quietly happy with beating Reform UK to take third place, their 7.1% being almost exactly the same proportion of votes as they took in 2024. This might not seem like much of an achievement, but the party’s national poll ratings remain stubbornly below 2024 levels, and thus stasis will most likely be claimed as more evidence of a Badenoch bounce.
Down in fifth place, the emotions are different. While they are byelection specialists, the Liberal Democrats were never going to win here, but they had put in at least some effort to boost their vote, with MPs going out this week to knock on doors. Coming behind Reform on just over 3% of the vote will be a disappointment.
Amid the noisy debates over the leadership of Labour, the Tories and Greens, it can be easy to overlook the disquiet among some of Ed Davey’s MPs that the Lib Dems do not appear to be cutting through. He will not be feeling relief this morning.

Malaysia shuts schools amid toxic haze from Indonesian fires
October 9, 2026
Malaysian authorities closed schools in the capital, Kuala Lumpur, and other parts of the country on Friday due to haze caused by forest fires in nearby Indonesia.
"I have instructed all state education departments and district education offices to continue monitoring the haze situation and take immediate action if conditions require it," Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said in a statement.
The minister announced which schools would be fully closed and which would continue operating partially in five states and two federal territories.
"Going forward, we will ensure that any decision to close schools is communicated in advance so that parents have enough time to prepare," Fadhlina added.
Deteriorating air quality
Air quality measurements in Kuala Lumpur remain at "unhealthy" levels, with Swiss air-quality monitor IQAir ranking the Malaysian capital among the most polluted cities in the world.
Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the issue on Thursday, saying schools should be closed whenever air-quality readings reach 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index (API).
API readings above 200 are considered very unhealthy, while levels above 300 are deemed hazardous. Readings exceeding 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.
Kuala Lumpur recorded an API reading of 170 on Friday.
The city lies about 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from Indonesia, where a wave of forest fires has affected millions of people since August. According to IQAir, Kuala Lumpur is currently the world's second most polluted city, behind only neighboring Singapore.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Thursday that Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto had agreed to take measures to tackle the haze, but did not provide more details.

Afghanistan’s emerald miners struggle with tools but attract global buyers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:36:48 UTC
15:36:48 KST

Afghanistan’s emerald miners struggle with tools but attract global buyers
Afghan miners endure harsh conditions, relying on basic tools to extract precious emeralds in Panjshir’s steep valleys.
Panjshir, Afghanistan — At a packed hall in the offices of the Panjshir provincial government, an auction is under way and the bidding is brisk.
The buyers, many from Kabul and some from overseas, have already closely examined the small piles of roughly cut green stones, shining their phone flashlights through them to check their quality.
Bidding for the best stones is competitive.
“Panjshir emeralds have many buyers around the world because of their very high quality,” gem merchant Ghulam Mustafa Habibi told Al Jazeera. “This is why their price is higher compared with other emeralds around the world.”
By the end of the auction, nearly 3,000 carats of the precious stones were sold – the 23rd sale of its kind so far this year. The value of emeralds sold to date in Afghanistan is estimated to be nearly 400m Afghanis ($6.12m), a steep rise compared with last year.
For a country impoverished by years of war and burdened by international sanctions, the trade in precious minerals is a valuable resource, especially in the remote corner of northeastern Afghanistan.
“Thankfully, more than 15,000 people are currently employed in Panjshir’s mining sector,” says Muhammad Aman Rezaii, a mining official responsible for overseeing the operation of many small artisanal mining operations dotting the Panjshir valley.
On the valley’s steep hillsides, miners toil for hours underground to make a living. In the otherwise barren and rocky landscape, which yields little, the precious stones are a lifeline.
“There are hardly any companies or manufacturing factories here. The main source of employment is the mining sector,” said Rezaii, adding that they have identified more than 2,000 other mining sites which could be developed.
Since taking power in 2021, the Taliban say they have signed deals with dozens of investors, mainly Chinese, Russian and Iranian, to mine gemstones and other valuable minerals.
According to the World Bank, state revenues rose 22 percent year-on-year in April and May, boosted by the auction of mines and other resources such as oil and precious minerals.
But Afghanistan’s gemstone mining sector is still lacking in international investment and expertise.
“There have been various proposals to establish an international market for Afghanistan’s precious minerals, particularly in Kabul,” Hafiz Muhammad Agha Hakim, the Governor of Panjshir province, told Al Jazeera.
“Processing machinery could be brought in so that these minerals can be processed and standardised here before being exported to markets around the world. At the moment, there is no standardised centre or proper processing facility.”
Back in the dusty confines of his mine, working in near-total darkness, miner Mahdi wields a crowbar while his friend beside him hits the surface with a hammer. He bemoans their lack of modern equipment.
“There are many challenges because we don’t have advanced equipment,” he says, taking a break from the digging. “We work only with basic tools such as shovels, pickaxes, drills and similar equipment.”
Rezaii said the miners need proper equipment that can make their work easier and safer, while also allowing the minerals to be extracted in a more professional manner. This would benefit the people of Afghanistan and particularly the miners,” he said.
“The area is vulnerable to landslides, avalanches, flooding and falling rocks. People here are working under extremely difficult and demanding conditions.”

Plans for a solar panel recycling plant in Tartu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:33:00 UTC
15:33:00 KST

Plans for a solar panel recycling plant in Tartu
Although volumes remain small, plans are underway to establish a solar panel recycling facility in Tartu. Epler & Lorenz has received nearly €500,000 in funding from the EU Cohesion Fund to develop the facility.
Most solar panels currently in use in Estonia will not need to be recycled for decades, but questions are already being raised about how to recover valuable metals from the panels in addition to glass. Producer responsibility also remains a major concern.
For more than a decade, solar power has been the fastest-growing renewable energy sector. According to Estonia's Register of Products of Concern, 60,000 tons of solar panels were placed on the Estonian market between 2018 and 2025. Piret Otsason, head of producer responsibility and hazardous waste at the Ministry of Climate, said solar panel waste is not yet a major problem.
"Waste management companies have estimated that Estonia could generate up to 1,000 tons of solar panel waste annually by 2027. The quantities are currently very small — for example, last year the figure was 100 tons," Otsason said.
Although solar panels have an average lifespan of 25 to 30 years and larger volumes of waste will not need to be dealt with for years, their disposal is already being discussed. According to Kaur Kuurme, head of electronics recycling organization Eesti Elektroonikaromu, panels are also replaced before the end of their useful lives.
"One reason is conventional mechanical damage, such as hailstorms that render some panels unusable. Another important reason is the opportunity to generate more electricity from the same surface area," Kuurme explained.
A typical silicon-based solar panel consists of approximately 80 percent glass, with the remainder made up of aluminum, polymers, silicon, copper and silver.
Harri Moora, a senior researcher at the Stockholm Environment Institute, said that while crushing and recycling glass is relatively straightforward, the challenge lies in recovering valuable metals.
"There are no really good technologies available yet and they are very expensive. As far as I know, Estonia does not yet have even a simpler version of such technology," Moora said.
However, a step in that direction has been taken. This year, waste management company Epler & Lorenz received nearly €500,000 in funding from the European Union's Cohesion Fund to establish a solar panel processing facility in Tartu.
Janis Lorenz, a member of the company's management board, said the project aims to develop the capacity to separate and recycle up to 1,600 tons of glass, aluminum, copper and silicon-based fine materials from solar panels annually.
According to estimates by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), global solar panel waste could reach 80 million tons by 2050. Although most solar panels come from China, EU directives require the waste generated here to be managed locally. Moora believes this raises a pressing question about producer responsibility.
"Companies operating today pay their fees, but the waste will only be generated 30 years from now. By then, those companies may no longer exist and neither may the money. The companies operating in the market at that time may be entirely different. This raises the question of where the funding for producer responsibility costs will come from in 30 years and who will cover the costs incurred by the waste management company, whether that is Epler & Lorenz or someone else," Moora said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mari Peegel

Lithuania reintroduces 50% train fare discount to alleviate fuel cost hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:31:00 UTC
15:31:00 KST

A 50% discount on domestic train tickets in Lithuania takes effect Friday for the second time this year, as the government seeks to ease the impact of exceptionally high fuel prices. The measure will remain in place until the end of the year.
LTG Link, the passenger transport company of the state-owned Lithuanian Railways group, is applying the discount to tickets already offered at reduced prices.
The company has urged passengers to plan their journeys in advance and said it would increase train capacity or add seats where possible to accommodate higher demand, particularly before holidays and long weekends.
The busiest routes are Vilnius-Kaunas, Vilnius-Klaipėda and Vilnius-Turmantas, according to a company representative.
New Swiss-made Stadler trains, each with 200 seats, are expected to enter service at the end of October.
A similar fare reduction in April and May attracted 5,800 more passengers than during the same period last year. The latest discount is expected to bring in about 45,000 additional passengers.
The government also plans to introduce the same 50% discount on intercity bus journeys from November 1 through the end of December. The exact start date will depend on when parliament adopts amendments to the Law on Public Passenger Transport Privileges.
Preliminary estimates put the cost of the train fare discount to the state at 2.8 million euros. The bus fare reduction is expected to cost about 3.15 million euros.

UN-Habitat has announced the five recipients of the 2026 Scroll of Honour Award, recognizing contributions to adequate housing and sustainable urban development in Brazil, Myanmar, Pakistan, Tunisia, and the United Kingdom. This year's winners include a housing organization working with communities affected by conflict and displacement, a researcher developing building materials from local and mining residues, an Indigenous village in Brazil, a public housing agency in Pakistan, and London Mayor Sadiq Khan. Selected from 101 nominations submitted across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas, the recipients represent a range of approaches to addressing housing and urban development challenges.
Launched in 1989, the UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour Award recognizes individuals and institutions whose work contributes to adequate housing, sustainable urbanization, and improved urban life. It also recognizes efforts supporting the New Urban Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The awards come as UN-Habitat continues to highlight the scale of the global housing challenge. According to the organization's World Cities Report 2026, up to 3.4 billion people lack adequate housing, while its SDG 11 Global Report 2026 reports that more than 1.1 billion people now live in informal settlements and slums, an increase of more than 130 million since 2015. The 2026 World Habitat Day theme, "Adequate Housing for All," similarly emphasized the role of housing as a foundation for inclusive, sustainable, and resilient cities.
Read on to discover the 2026 Scroll of Honour Award winners.
Related Article
On World Architecture Day 2026: A Call to Build Better, Build Differently, and Share Resources
Housing NOW / Bago, Myanmar
Housing NOW is a Myanmar-based bamboo construction organization developing affordable housing and community infrastructure for people affected by conflict, displacement, poverty, and disasters. Its construction system combines locally available bamboo, traditional knowledge, and prefabrication, with components prepared using portable guides and assembled on site. The organization has applied the approach to homes as well as schools, preschools, community centers, and medical facilities, including projects for communities affected by the 2025 earthquake. UN-Habitat also notes that Housing NOW employs members of the communities it serves and provides illustrated construction guides to support local builders.
Aldeia do Espraiado – Tekoa Ara Hovy / Maricá, Brazil
In Maricá, Aldeia do Espraiado – Tekoa Ara Hovy provides a permanent settlement for a Guarani Mbyá community and was recognized as Brazil's first Indigenous village established by a municipality. Thirteen families moved to the village in early 2025 after previously living within a state park without secure land tenure or access to several basic services. Developed with the participation of the community, the settlement includes traditional homes, a bilingual school, a health post, a cultural center, a community kitchen, water infrastructure, and solar lighting in shared areas. The initiative combines municipal investment with community participation and traditional building practices.
Punjab Housing and Town Planning Agency / Lahore, Pakistan
The Punjab Housing and Town Planning Agency is the government agency responsible for implementing the province's Apni Chhat Apna Ghar housing program, which supports low-income households that already own land but lack the resources to construct a home. Launched in 2024, the program aims to facilitate 100,000 affordable houses and apartments across Punjab, with eligible households receiving interest-free financing to build on their own plots. Applications and parts of the program's implementation are managed through digital systems, while the Bank of Punjab and partner microfinance institutions support the financing process. UN-Habitat recognized the agency for expanding access to safe and affordable housing among low-income households.
Abdelmalek Ghannem / Bizerte, Tunisia
Abdelmalek Ghannem, a sustainable construction specialist and founder of Société Industrielle de Blocs (SOIB), has developed building systems using locally available materials and industrial residues. Established in Bizerte in 2009, SOIB produces compressed stabilized earth blocks and interlocking construction systems that incorporate residues from quarries and mining. The blocks require less cement and mortar than conventional masonry, while their composition can contribute to thermal performance in hot climates. According to UN-Habitat, the approach has been used in more than 100 building projects across Tunisia, with the organization also providing training for architects, engineers, and builders.
Mayor Sadiq Khan / London, United Kingdom
Sadiq Khan was recognized for his work on affordable and sustainable housing and inclusive, climate-resilient urban development during his tenure as Mayor of London. His housing programs have included support for new council housing and affordable homes through City Hall funding, alongside policies targeting housing for key workers. In January 2026, Khan launched the Key Worker Living Rent initiative, with a target of starting at least 6,000 rent-controlled homes by 2030, with rents linked to the incomes of workers including nurses, teachers, carers, and bus drivers.
The 2026 Scroll of Honour Award comes amid a broader wave of initiatives addressing housing affordability and access. In Europe, the "Right to Housing! Now and Forever" European Citizens' Initiative launched its signature campaign in September, while the OBEL Award recognized the Balearic Social Housing Model for rethinking social housing administration. In the United States, the bipartisan ROAD to Housing Act became law in July, revising federal housing programs, financing, construction regulations, and community grants.

The White House has blocked Microsoft and several other technology companies from hiring professionals from other countries for permanent positions, the BBC reports.
On the 8th of October, US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft and other companies of abusing the H-1b (work) visa program and related processes that allow foreign workers to become permanent US residents. He claimed that Microsoft—one of the most valuable US companies—is replacing American employees with foreign contract workers. Microsoft responded by noting that the majority of H-1b visas requested during the previous fiscal year were for existing employees who earn the same wages as Americans.
Meanwhile, Vance insisted that no other company has exploited the visa system as unscrupulously as Microsoft. The Vice President leveled similar accusations against Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini. US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling stated that the US government would not process any new or pending work visa applications from Microsoft or the other seven companies.
He declared that companies like Microsoft, as well as universities, had become a "visa mill," flooding the US with foreign workers.
The annual cap for H-1b visas—which also serve as the first step toward obtaining permanent residency—is set at 85,000.

Klitschko Warns Kyiv Faces a Fight for Survival as Russian Strikes Threaten Winter Preparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:23:32 UTC
15:23:32 KST

Mounting Russian strikes that have pummelled the Ukrainian capital, hitting bridges and key infrastructure, have plunged Kyiv into survival mode ahead of the winter, the city’s mayor told AFP on Thursday.
In a tactical shift in recent weeks, Russia has expanded daytime missile and drone attacks against Kyiv, targeting key bridges and the city centre.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It has also resumed strikes on the energy grid, triggering power cuts that has Kyiv locals braced for a repeat of last winter, when heating and power were knocked out for days as temperatures hit -20C.
“Every day brings new reports of destroyed buildings, of people injured or tragically killed, as the shelling of our city intensifies,” Vitali Klitschko told AFP.
“Today the issue is survival,” added the mayor, a towering former world heavyweight champion boxer who has served as Kyiv mayor since 2014.
Russian troops advanced on the city in the first weeks of the 2022 invasion, but were pushed back in a matter of weeks.
The capital had since mostly been spared from the devastation in frontline regions, though missile and drone attacks on residential areas have still killed hundreds.
With the front line mostly static, Moscow has shifted its attention to long-range strikes on Kyiv, launching hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
- ‘Empty cities’ -
Russian attacks have killed at least 534 people since 2022, according to Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health data, obtained by AFP.
US, Ukrainian Delegations to Discuss Peace in Miami as Trump’s Envoys May Return to Moscow
Some 189 have died so far this year, surpassing the toll for all of 2025.
Klitschko said residents with friends or relatives outside Kyiv should consider temporarily relocating -- repeating a suggestion that had triggered a backlash last year.
He insisted he would never call for a full evacuation.
“That’s Putin’s goal... the best scenario for Putin is that we all leave and hand over our empty cities and our country to him,” he said.
Moscow has made life in the capital much harder.
It has repeatedly hit bridges across the Dnipro river, causing traffic to be suspended across the city.
“The connection between the left and right banks is one of the key factors in the city’s ability to function,” Klitschko said.
The city was developing alternative pontoon crossings to help ease the gridlock in a city with a daytime population -- including commuters -- of around 3.5 million.
The latest strikes have caused rolling power outages and left parts of Kyiv without water for several hours earlier this week.
Hours after the interview, service on the Kyiv metro was temporarily suspended due to power outages.
Klitschko also warned that disruption to Kyiv’s water infrastructure could cause a “quite large-scale” crisis.
- ‘Very difficult’ task -
To prepare for the winter, the city has been building backup heating systems and stockpiling fuel, food and drinking water.
“No matter how well we prepare, if air defence does not work, we could end up in a bad scenario,” Klitschko said.
He laid some of the blame for shortcomings on President Volodymyr Zelensky’s government, with which he has been perennially at odds.
In turn, the government has repeatedly accused Kyiv of lagging on its plans for winter.
Klitschko said the accusations were unfounded.
“Finding scapegoats won’t make people warmer,” he said.
The city authorities, he said, faced a “very difficult” task with “limited time, limited funding, a limited number of workers.”
Three people were killed in Russian strikes in Kyiv on Thursday.
In a sign of the near-constant threat the city now faces, an air raid alert rang out as Klitschko was speaking to AFP.
“When we hear an air‑raid alert, I pray to God -- and to our air defence, because the life of our city depends on them,” he said.

Interest in seaside homes in Spain is growing: what draws buyers to Dénia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:20:51 UTC
15:20:51 KST

Buyer priorities on the northern Costa Blanca are changing. International buyers are taking a closer look at construction quality, materials and the surroundings of their future homes. Increasingly, buying a property by the sea means planning to spend a substantial part of the year in Spain, alongside summer holidays.
Balticnews.com interviewed Māris Āboltiņš, Managing Director at MARA Holding, about Dénia’s property market and the MARA Residence development. The complex of 22 apartments and penthouses is under construction on Les Deveses beach, with an architectural design by Carles Faus Arquitectura. Completion is scheduled for 2027.
— According to idealista, property prices in Dénia rose by 17.4% between September 2024 and April 2026, reaching €3,361 per square metre. How do you explain this growth? What factors are shaping the market?
— Several factors are at work. Construction materials and labour have become more expensive in recent years. Higher fuel prices this year have also contributed to rising material costs. In some cases, suppliers and construction companies have had to revise their prices during the year.
There is also a local factor: the supply of new homes in Dénia is limited. For a time, new developments progressed more slowly, partly because developers were waiting for permits. Construction activity has now picked up, but high-quality new properties by the sea continue to attract considerable interest.
Dénia has traditionally been one of the more expensive locations on the Costa Blanca. Its location, port, natural surroundings and way of life all have their own appeal. Buyers pay attention to these qualities. However, I would not promise that prices will rise at the same rate every year: property values also depend on the wider economic situation.
— Who is interested in buying a home in this area today?
— We see interest comes from a wide range of buyers, including local Spanish buyers as well as buyers from Netherlands, Germany, the United Kingdom, and other countries. International buyers are particularly noticeable after the main summer season ends. In September, many holidaymakers return home, while people arrive for whom this is the start of a more appealing season: the weather remains warm, and the coast becomes quieter.
They include couples, retirees, people who can work remotely and those who want to spend extended periods here. For European buyers, being able to travel by car or motor home also matters. It allows them to use their home in Spain in a way that suits their lifestyle.
— What do these buyers look at first?
— Location is certainly important. But a beachfront position is not always the only deciding factor. Buyers ask detailed questions about construction quality, materials and how practical the apartment will be to use.
In our experience, many people buy primarily for their own use, rather than with an immediate intention to rent the property out. They imagine their everyday lives here: how they will spend time at home, what is nearby and how comfortable it will be to visit in different seasons. Price remains an important part of the decision, too. For example, buyers from the Netherlands, the price difference compared with their home country is particularly noticeable.
— What if a buyer is considering an apartment as an investment?
— A seaside property can serve different purposes: you can live in it, sell it later or rent it out. There is also demand for long-term rentals in Dénia, but any decision should take into account of the particular property and the buyer’s circumstances. For example, professionals who work on rotational schedules often look for long-term accommodation. There is little supply of this kind in new developments in Dénia.
Seaside homes in Dénia remain relatively easy to resell: supply is limited, while demand is steady. I would advise buyers to distinguish between opportunities and promises of guaranteed returns. The market depends on economic conditions, and rental requirements and procedures need to be checked separately. Buyers should understand in advance why they are purchasing an apartment and how they intend to use it.
— How did the concept for MARA Residence take shape?
— We wanted the development to feel like part of its setting. The beach, and natural landscape are close by. When choosing colours, textures, fittings and communal spaces, we therefore took inspiration from the surroundings. A dune with natural vegetation is being preserved directly in front of the development, with rice fields and orange groves nearby.
It was important to create a sense that life within the development extends naturally beyond the apartment into the garden, around the pool and along the path to the sea. For many people, nature and the climate are the reasons they choose this area. Another important factor is that Les Deveses beach has been restored through a government project: it has been widened, and breakwaters have been built to protect the shoreline from erosion.
— Why did you choose the Les Deveses area for the project?
— I like its combination of space and relative tranquillity. In summer, the central areas of the resort town attract large numbers of visitors. Here, you can enjoy greater privacy while remaining connected to Dénia and the surrounding towns.
We also considered everyday needs when choosing the location. It matters that residents can easily reach the main roads, access essential services and plan their lives here outside the tourist season. Outside the peak season, the main roads are five to ten minutes away. In summer, of course, traffic can increase journey times, and that needs to be taken into account. The area also remains active after the season ends, when many holiday destinations become almost empty. The area offers easy access to schools, golf course and a wide range of sports activities. There are also riding stables nearby for those who enjoy horse riding.
— Which features of the development will be particularly important to future owners?
— We have thought carefully about the communal spaces and how adults and children will use them. The development include a large shared swimming pool, a children’s playground area, a relaxation area for adults, a outdoor fitness area, landscaping gardens and access to the beach. We wanted the journey from the apartment to the sea to be convenient, and the grounds to be enjoyable even on days when residents do not feel like going to the beach. At the entrance, there will be foot showers and dog shower, as well as board racks, so owners do not have to bring their equipment into the apartment.
We are also paying particular attention to the building’s interior spaces and landscaping. The internal atrium will include planting to help keep it bright and welcoming outside the summer season. Plants, colours and textures should connect the development’s grounds with the coastal landscape. It is important that owners experience this in everyday life.
— Buying a home under construction in another country can raise many questions. How do you support international buyers?
— We have worked with buyers from different countries and understand how thoroughly the process needs to be explained. First, we help them choose an apartment. We then guide them through the sequence of the transaction and the documents required. We provide support with transferring funds and dealing with the bank, and assist them until the purchase is completed.
For matters that fall within the responsibilities of a lawyer, bank, notary or another specialist, we seek clarification from the relevant professional. Each stage of the transaction has its own rules and responsible parties. Our role is to stay in contact with the buyer and help them obtain clear answers.

Both sides of Brazil’s deeply polarised partisan divide have long accused each other of corruption and lawfare as political drama reaches a crescendo in the buildup to the October 25 runoff.
Lobbying the US
In March 2025, Eduardo Bolsonaro pledged he would move to the US full time to “focus 100 percent” of his energy on freeing his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The move cost him his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator.
The 42-year-old former lawmaker lives in Texas and is a green card holder.
He was convicted of lobbying to impose sanctions on members of the Brazilian government and to implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father.
Supreme Court justice
De Moraes, whom the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced in September 2025 to 27 years in prison for plotting to stage a coup.
The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his four-year sentence immediately.
“The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” de Moraes said.
De Moraes also cancelled Eduardo Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and instructed the country’s federal police to arrest him if he returns to Brazil.

Trump May Leave 100,000 Ukrainians in US Immigration Limbo Rather Than Renew Protections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:19:40 UTC
15:19:40 KST

More than 100,000 Ukrainians in the United States face an uncertain future as the Trump administration approaches an Oct. 19 deadline to decide whether to renew their temporary protected status (TPS).
Politico reported on Oct. 8 that some US lawmakers are considering allowing the protections to expire without formally canceling them, potentially triggering an automatic six-month extension that could delay deportations but leave Ukrainians in legal limbo.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The administration of US President Donald Trump must decide whether to extend or terminate the protections, which allow eligible Ukrainians who fled Russia’s full-scale invasion to remain in the US and work legally.
According to Politico, some lawmakers from both parties are urging the administration to renew the protections.
Others are discussing a less direct alternative: allowing the current designation to expire without formally terminating it, potentially triggering an automatic six-month extension.
The approach would give Ukrainians additional time in the US without resolving their longer-term immigration status, according to Politico.
A similar situation emerged in September when protections for Salvadoran migrants expired without a formal termination or renewal announcement. The resulting uncertainty left some recipients and employers unsure about their ability to work and study, the report added.
A congressional aide familiar with bipartisan discussions on Ukraine policy told Politico that the political backlash over deporting Ukrainians to a country still at war could make the fallback option attractive to the administration, despite its drawbacks.
Klitschko Warns Kyiv Faces a Fight for Survival as Russian Strikes Threaten Winter Preparations
“It’s flawed to keep them in a limbo status like El Salvador, but that might be a likely path for the admin,” the aide said.
Bipartisan push to extend protections
Lawmakers supporting an extension argue that Ukrainians should not be forced to return while Russia continues attacking Ukrainian cities and occupies parts of the country.
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat from New Hampshire and longtime supporter of Ukraine, said she was urging the administration to renew the protections but acknowledged that the current immigration policy made such a decision difficult to foresee.
A bipartisan group of senators, including Republicans Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine, also urged the administration to extend TPS for Ukrainians in a Sept. 22 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The senators argued that Ukrainian TPS recipients contribute to key US industries, including transportation, health care and construction. Ending their protections could remove experienced workers from the labor market and raise costs for American consumers, they warned.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Murkowski have also backed bipartisan legislation introduced by Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado that would extend TPS for Ukrainians through 2029.
Not all Republicans support extending the program. Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana has criticized TPS as a policy that places American workers at a disadvantage, while some immigration hardliners have called for ending the program more broadly.
The debate over Ukrainian TPS comes as the Trump administration faces pressure from immigration hardliners to restrict protections for migrants.
According to Politico, some lawmakers see allowing the protections to expire without formally canceling them as a way to balance those competing demands ahead of the US midterm elections.
The administration has also ended protections for migrants from several other countries, including Somalia, South Sudan and Yemen, as part of its broader effort to restrict immigration. In May, however, it extended protections for Lebanese migrants for another six months amid ongoing conflict involving Israel and Hezbollah.
The White House referred Politico to the Department of Homeland Security when asked about the future of Ukrainian TPS. US Citizenship and Immigration Services, which operates under DHS, declined to comment directly on the decision.
Ukraine’s future in US immigration policy remains uncertain
The debate over TPS is unfolding against a backdrop of strained US-Ukraine relations and disagreements over Washington’s continued support for Kyiv.
A person familiar with administration discussions told Politico that the broader relationship between the two countries was influencing the outlook for Ukrainian migrants, arguing that there was little incentive for the administration to take a step seen as favorable to Ukraine.
Trump previously considered ending a separate program that allowed Americans to sponsor Ukrainians seeking refuge in the US. His administration ultimately stopped accepting new applications for that program after facing bipartisan criticism.
Ukraine’s government has not publicly commented on the future of TPS for its citizens in the US, and the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington did not respond to Politico’s request for comment.

Musk received the award alongside Google cofounder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and AMD chief Lisa Su.
"I want to thank everybody for being here as we celebrate the exciting advance of science and technology in the golden age of America," Trump said in his opening remarks, before turning his attention to Musk, who he called an "industrial titan" and "our modern-day Thomas Edison."
"Few Americans in history have done more to advance America's national interest than Elon in one field after another. His genius and determination have made science fiction into reality," Trump said.
"Elon, I want to congratulate you. You're my friend and all of that, but you are a very, very special guy. Thank you very much and congratulations Elon," he added.
Despite his glowing words, Trump and Musk have navigated a rather volatile relationship in recent years.
Musk joined Trump in the latter stages of his presidential campaign and went on to take a much-publicised role as defacto leader of the White House's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) following Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, spearheading efforts to make the government leaner.
But the pair's relationship fractured after Musk criticised Trump's spending bill, the "One Big Beautiful Bill," prompting the start of a bitter and public feud.
However, Musk has found himself back in Trump world in recent weeks, with the Tesla CEO set to take on a role as co-director of "Project Meridian."
The project, commissioned by the Department of Defense, will study the future of warfare, helping identify the weapons and technologies the US military will need to build and master and proposing "actionable solutions to start developing, testing and fielding these capabilities."
A White House press release said Musk was awarded the National Medal of Science "for engineering achievements of extraordinary ambition and scale that have pushed the frontiers of space exploration, intelligent systems, communications, and beyond, renewing American technological leadership and opening a new chapter in American manufacturing."

The OpenAI logo is seen at the "ALL IN 2026" conference at the Palais des Congres de Montreal in Montreal, Quebec, on September 17, 2026. (AFP Photo)
OpenAI is bringing in about $20 billion less in annualized revenue than investors had been led to believe, the Financial Times reported, raising questions about the solidity of the AI business.
Citing documents shared with OpenAI's financial backers, the FT said the company put its annualized revenue at close to $50 billion as of the end of September.
Media reports late last month had pegged the figure at $70 billion based on information given to investors.
Investors track annualized revenue at OpenAI and Anthropic as the clearest signal of demand for artificial intelligence and the figures help justify enormous spending on data centers as well as the AI-fueled stock market rally.
The metric, which tech startups commonly use to signal their growth trajectory, is sometimes criticized as imprecise or even misleading, since it typically extrapolates a single month's sales across a full year.
In an apparent pushback, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the earlier number, which the network reported as $68 billion, counted gross revenue from OpenAI's partnerships with companies like chipmaker Nvidia.
That method was intended to make it easier for investors to measure the company against chief rival Anthropic.
The report lands as OpenAI negotiates a fresh private fundraising that could value it at roughly $1.4 trillion, according to the FT.
OpenAI, which confidentially submitted paperwork for an initial public offering in June, had been widely expected to go public this fall, but it has since pushed back the listing.
Archrival Anthropic is expected to list on the public markets next month.

Ukraine fortifies its filling stations against Russian attacks

Ukraine fortifies its filling stations against Russian attacks
KYIV, Oct 9 - Sand-filled blast barriers and concrete shelters are multiplying at filling stations in Ukraine in a push by retailers to fortify their networks as Russia attacks fuel infrastructure in major cities.
Russia has struck petrol stations in frontline areas since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, but in recent months it has broadened its air campaign to target fuel retailers in Kyiv, Dnipro and Kharkiv.
A senior executive at state-owned Ukrnafta, Ukraine's largest oil company, said it was taking steps to protect its facilities and the strikes would not cause shortages this winter despite an expected increase in demand of 10-15%.
Even when petrol stations are hit, operations are sometimes restored within days, said Lesya Zharska, director of Ukrnafta's station network.
"We will protect the facilities. We will restore the facilities. We are ready for the winter," she said in an interview at an Ukrnafta station on the outskirts of Kyiv. on the other side of the road, workers were rebuilding a station destroyed in a recent attack.
In recent weeks, at least six Ukrnafta filling stations have been hit in Kyiv. In total, Russia has destroyed more than 300 stations in the last six months, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said.
Moscow says it does not deliberately target Ukraine's civilian infrastructure but it has stepped up attacks on populated areas as its forces struggle to advance on the ground. Meanwhile, Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages in Russia, which has introduced an export ban.
MITIGATING RISKS
To mitigate the risks in population centres such as Kyiv, where it has three dozen of its 660 stations, Ukrnafta has put up blast barriers made of wire-mesh cubes - or gabions - filled with sand. The aim is to instal them in other cities soon.
"When there is a yellow or red air alarm, we stop operations and ask customers to leave, and staff head to shelters," Zharska said.
Russia is widely expected to intensify strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure once again as temperatures drop in winter.
Ukrnafta has already equipped stations across its network with back-up diesel generators and contracted sufficient fuel imports to prevent supply gaps, Zharska said, adding:
"We will carry out our work." REUTERS

Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: scientist’s soybean research pushes agricultural frontier
Lam Hon-ming’s groundbreaking work on soybean genetics and varieties has led to cultivation in mainland China, contributing to country’s food security
When Professor Lam Hon-ming returned to Hong Kong after completing postdoctoral work in the United States in 1997, he was fixated on one question: how can science help feed the country and the world?
He found that soybeans offered part of the answer. In addition to its nutritional value, the crop can fix nitrogen levels in the soil, reducing reliance on chemical fertiliser, and some varieties can be bred to tolerate drought and salinity.
Lam went on to spend almost three decades studying soybean genetics and developing varieties suited to marginal land.
“I wanted to work in agricultural research because it is important for everyone, although relatively few people were doing it,” said Lam, the director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s State Key Laboratory of Agrobiotechnology.
