Navi Pillay gets the news of her Nobel Peace Prize in Germany
The Nobel Peace Prize announcement is always eagerly anticpated, and this year the news had special resonance in one corner of Germany. That's because the laureate, Navi Pillay, received the news in the Bavarian city of Nuremberg.
The South African judge, and former UN human rights chief, is attending the Nuremberg Forum to discuss international law.
And the significance of the location was not lost on Pillay. Nuremberg is where Nazi war criminals went on trial after World War II.
Those trials helped lay the foundation of international law.
"Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me," she said to a standing ovation. "You know, you don’t want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this."
Germany to buy cruise missiles for mass deployment
Germany's army has decided to acquire large numbers of low-cost cruise missiles capable of striking targets up to 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) away.
Army chief Lieutenant General Christian Freuding announced the decision at a military gathering in Berlin, saying the weapons would be used to overwhelm enemy air defenses through sheer numbers.
The move reflects lessons from the war in Ukraine, where drones and missiles have been deployed in large numbers to exhaust air defenses. Launching numerous relatively cheap weapons simultaneously can force defenders to expend expensive interceptor missiles, potentially allowing more sophisticated weapons to reach their targets.
Germany plans to combine the cheaper missiles with more powerful weapons designed to strike strategically important targets, including US-made cruise missiles it intends to purchase.
Freuding said the army was considering two commercially available systems, although neither had yet been approved for use by the German armed forces. Initial deliveries could begin in 2027.
US defense company Covenant opened a cruise missile production facility in Leipzig earlier this week. It plans to manufacture 1,000 Anthem missiles in 2027 and 5,000 in 2028.
The company says each missile would cost a six-figure sum, below €860,000 ($1 million), compared with several million dollars for conventional cruise missiles.
Heart attack deaths down 15% since 2022
Deaths from heart attacks in Germany fell by more than 15% between 2022 and 2025, according to figures released by the Federal Statistical Office.
Deaths from cerebrovascular diseases, including strokes and brain hemorrhages, also declined by 6.3% over the same period.
However, deaths from respiratory diseases rose by around 8% in 2025 compared with the previous year, reaching 81,200.
Overall, Germany recorded around 1.01 million deaths in 2025, virtually unchanged from the previous year. The total was nevertheless 5.6% lower than in 2022.
Despite the decline in heart attack and stroke-related deaths, cardiovascular disease remained Germany's leading cause of death, accounting for 334,100 deaths in 2025.
Heart attack deaths fell among both men and women, with the sharpest decline, 30.6%, among people aged 80 to 85.
It is not clear what is behind the decline. Changes in population size and age structure may have contributed, as the statistics are not adjusted for age.
School leavers without diploma hit 20-year high
Nearly 65,000 young people left school in Germany without obtaining a basic school-leaving qualification in the 2024/2025 academic year, according to figures from the Federal Statistical Office.
The figure rose from 62,000 the previous year and 56,000 two years earlier, continuing an upward trend that has raised concerns about educational standards and Germany's shortage of skilled workers.
The proportion of students leaving school without at least a Hauptschulabschluss, Germany's basic secondary school qualification, reached 8.4% in 2024/2025.
That compares with 6.6% in 2018/2019 and around 5.5% in 2013/2014.
The latest rate is the highest recorded in 20 years, although it was even higher around the turn of the millennium.
The number of school leavers without qualifications has also risen substantially over the past decade, from around 47,400 in 2014/2015.
Numbers temporarily fell during the COVID-19 pandemic, potentially reflecting relaxed examination requirements, before beginning to climb again.
The figures were obtained by the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), a political party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht.
Police dig for woman missing since 2007
German police have begun excavating land in the southern state of Bavaria in a renewed search for a woman who disappeared without a trace almost two decades ago.
Investigators say new information suggests that the remains of Kerstin Lee Langley, missing since the summer of 2007, could be buried in a meadow and woodland near the village of Kadenzhofen, north of Neumarkt in der Oberpfalz.
Specialists from Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office and the Regensburg criminal police department are examining an area covering approximately 100 square meters (1,076 square feet).
An excavator is removing soil in layers, which investigators then examine for possible evidence.
Police spokesperson Corinna Wild told public broadcaster BR24 that investigators were following specific information suggesting Langley's body could be buried at the site.
Police told DW they had ruled out any connection between the search and a fatal shooting just a few kilometers away in the village of Berngau, where two local government employees were killed during a routine firearms inspection at around the same time on Thursday afternoon.
How was the Berngau suspect arrested?
Police said a man who opened fire on local government employees in the southern town of Berngau barricaded himself inside his home and contacted their operations center by telephone.
He admitted firing shots, said he had firearms in his possession and warned that he would not surrender without resistance.
Special police units, including a tactical response team with an armored vehicle, were deployed to the village. A police helicopter was also used, while residents were advised to stay indoors or avoid the cordoned-off area.
Negotiators spent hours trying to persuade the suspect to surrender peacefully.
"We always try to achieve a peaceful solution, and that generally happens through communication," a police spokesperson said.
However, at around 2:20 a.m. (0020 GMT/UTC) Friday, officers entered the building using explosives.
Police said officers fired shots during the operation, lightly wounding the suspect in the leg. He was subsequently given medical treatment.
Police have not yet established why the suspect allegedly opened fire on the two officials.
Investigators from the Regensburg criminal police department are expected to question the man in coordination with prosecutors in Nuremberg-Fürth.

NATO to hold major nuclear exercise amid escalating rhetoric with Russia
NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that its upcoming nuclear exercise in Italy is nothing to fear, despite heightened tensions between the alliance and Moscow.
Source: European Pravda, citing Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation Politico
Details: NATO announced on 8 October that 17 member states would take part in its annual Steadfast Noon exercise, which will run from 13 to 23 October. This year's drills come amid a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after the allies held an exercise near Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in August.
"We have been doing this every year and… this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry. This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate," said Nassima Barrows, Deputy Director of Nuclear Policy at NATO.
"Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability," she said.
Following a previous NATO exercise, Moscow sent the alliance a letter threatening to strike allied territory and referring to the possible use of its nuclear arsenal. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte publicly condemned the move last week.
Tensions are mounting as European countries are accusing Russia of carrying out sabotage and intensifying so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
"Our intention is to really keep things calm," a senior NATO official said. Russian officials "keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood", they added.
US Army Colonel David Bull, Chief of NATO's Nuclear Operations, said the exercise would involve a "similar" number of participants as in previous years. It would cover everything from "simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise", but "no live nuclear weapons".
Dual-capable aircraft and ground personnel will also take part to support the exercise and practise aircraft loading, refuelling and maintenance procedures, a senior NATO military official added.
Background:
- It was previously revealed that Russia had handed NATO a document stating the possibility of using its entire available arsenal, including nuclear weapons, in the event of an attempt by the Alliance to isolate Kaliningrad Oblast.
- NATO responded by emphasising the defensive nature of the Alliance and calling on Russia to stop its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.
- NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte emphasised that Russian leader Vladimir Putin knows he will never be able to defeat NATO.
- Lithuania described the new Russian threats regarding Kaliningrad as psychological pressure.

If the video is authentic, she said "the authorities will seek to establish how Mexicans, in this case individuals who may belong to a criminal group, became involved in an armed conflict taking place in Europe."
This marks the first time the Mexican government has openly addressed rumors of Mexican nationals linked to organized crime fighting in Ukraine as mercenaries. The institution provides performing arts education, and more than 500 music and dance performances open to the public each year. The first images of the design were released in 2022. The expansion triples the facilities currently dedicated to dance and will house Colburn's Trudl Zipper Dance Institute. The building, finished in a metallic pink coating, is located adjacent to Colburn's Grand Avenue campus in downtown Los Angeles and is expected to reach substantial completion in summer 2027.
Frank Gehry's design is composed of opaque and transparent interlocking volumes that step down with the contour of the site. The opaque volumes are covered with metal cladding in a pink paint finish called Pink Kandi, a fluoropolymer resin-based coating with aluminum flake, developed specifically for the building and inspired by automobile Kandy paint. A wide, light-filled entrance connects the building components and the gardens at street and rooftop level. The new building will complement Colburn's existing 428,137-square-foot facilities, which include administrative offices, a residence hall, the 430-seat Zipper Hall and the 189-seat Thayer Hall, as well as rehearsal areas, practice rooms and studios.
The building's 1,000-seat hall has an in-the-round design and features an orchestra pit and a stage large enough to accommodate large-scale works and orchestrations. The interior of the hall features natural light and adjustable acoustic elements in the shape of floating clouds, hovering above the performers. The space will be equipped for large-scale orchestra, dance, opera, jazz, and other productions, and will welcome both established and emerging performing arts organizations. For the acoustic design, Gehry collaborated with Yasuhisa Toyota of Nagata Acoustics, his collaborator on the Walt Disney Concert Hall, and with Michael Ferguson, who previously consulted on Gehry's New World Center in Miami Beach and the Fisher Center for the Performing Arts at Bard College.
In addition to the concert hall, the building integrates the Dance Center, the new home of Colburn's Trudl Zipper Dance Institute, which triples the space currently dedicated to dance at the school. It includes a 100-seat Studio Theater and four professional-sized studios, which will allow for expanded dance instruction, rehearsals, and performances. This area of the building is expected to open with the 2027-28 academic year, in August 2027. Programming for the hall and the Dance Center will be announced in spring 2026, including artist residencies, festivals and a mix of performances featuring students and faculty, guest artists and ensembles, and resident and rental organizations. Terri and Jerry Kohl Hall will become the permanent home of the Colburn Orchestra, the flagship ensemble of the Conservatory of Music.
The hall will be inaugurated with a gala concert on September 25, 2027, and a community celebration and ribbon-cutting ceremony will follow the next day. Free performances will be held throughout Colburn's campus, including inaugural performances at the Dance Center, and a grand finale concert will take place in Terri and Jerry Kohl Hall. The project adds to the recently announced opening of a new Gehry-designed Guggenheim Museum on Abu Dhabi's Saadiyat Island, expected on December 11, 2026. In late September, Los Angeles also saw the opening of MAD's Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, a 27,900-square-meter structure featuring galleries, two theaters, a retail store, a library, a café, a restaurant, and event spaces. Earlier this year, Peter Zumthor's LACMA David Geffen Galleries opened, offering a flexible art space that accommodates diverse curatorial projects as well as visitors' individual paths.

Hamas's leadership views its ability to withstand the IDF over the past three years as a form of "victory," despite Israel's control of approximately 70% of the Gaza Strip, according to Friday intelligence presented to Israel's senior political and defense leadership, including the prime minister and defense minister.
Hamas considers Israel's territorial control "temporary," according to the information presented to officials.
"They are convinced that US President Donald Trump's points-based plan for the Gaza Strip, which his son-in-law Kushner is advancing, including a plan for economic development involving tens of billions of dollars in investment, is a direct continuation of Sheik Ahmed Yassin's vision from 1999," a senior security official said. "They believe in it even if it is delayed."
The senior security official added: "They tell themselves, and we can see this, that by launching an attack with men wearing beards, jalabiyas, and flip-flops, and through their steadfast resistance against the IDF even after three years, they have not been defeated. They have not surrendered to an army that everyone says is the strongest in the Middle East. Something no other Arab army in the Middle East has managed to achieve."
According to the official, Hamas is therefore preparing for an IDF ground maneuver toward Gaza City, despite tensions between the terrorist organization's local leadership and Khalil al-Hayya in Qatar.
Hamas prepares for possible IDF ground offensive in Gaza City
"They are really working on this around the clock, in many ways: recruiting operatives, distributing weapons, digging defensive tunnels, manufacturing explosive devices, producing short-range projectiles, and preparing surprises," the official said.
Meanwhile, the IDF Southern Command, Military Intelligence Directorate, Israel Air Force, and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) have stepped up the pace of targeted killings of terrorists who participated in the October 7 attacks, as well as operatives preparing to carry out terrorist attacks or establish terrorist infrastructure.
The operations are intended to increase pressure on Hamas and disrupt efforts to rebuild its military wing.
The senior official further explained that because Hamas's leadership refuses to disarm or hand over control of the Gaza Strip to an alternative governing authority, the IDF is preparing for a scenario involving the mass movement of civilians and a ground maneuver into the heart of Gaza City.
The objective would be to dismantle terrorist infrastructure and destroy the battalions of Hamas's military wing that retain a high level of operational readiness.
The official assessed that a ground maneuver would ultimately be unavoidable.
According to an assessment within Israel's defense establishment, a decision on the issue will be made after the elections in Israel.
Ahmed Yassin's vision for Israel's destruction
Ahmed Yassin, the founder and leader of Hamas who was killed in an Israeli targeted strike in 2004, described Israel as "a temporary entity destined to disappear completely from the map and be replaced by an Islamic state throughout the entire Land of Israel."
In a 1999 interview with Al Jazeera, Yassin claimed that the State of Israel would cease to exist by 2027, or by 2028 at the latest.
His prediction was based on a theory of 40-year periods, which he divided into several stages.
The first was the generation of the Nakba, extending from 1948 until the 1980s. The second was the generation of resistance, which began the armed struggle against Israel.
The final generation, according to Yassin's vision, would bring about Hamas's victory, Israel's ultimate collapse, and the establishment of an Islamic state on its territory.

Nova security received warning of 'trouble on Sukkot' week before October 7, security chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:28:24 UTC
14:28:24 KST

Elkana Federman, who served as security chief for the Nova music festival and now leads the Tekuma party, said he received a recorded message about a week before the October 7 massacre warning of possible trouble along the Gaza border.
Speaking to Einat Meyron on the Maariv podcast, Federman said the message came from a security guard scheduled to work at the festival who was also serving as a soldier in the IDF’s Gaza Division. Sent on September 26, 2023, the recording referred to the possibility of “trouble” during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
In the recording, the guard can be heard saying: “I wanted to tell you something, so you know. I’m serving here in the Gaza Division, in Re’im, near where the Unity festival is. As the whole country knows, the situation in the Gaza sector isn’t great. Now I’ve also heard from the division’s chief warrant officer, who’s hinting to me that there’s going to be trouble during Sukkot.”
He continued: “I thought it would be better for you to know this too, so it doesn’t catch people there by surprise. That’s broadly what he told me, and the truth is, it might happen and it might not. So I’m telling you so you know.”
'I passed it on to those above me, and they told me everything was fine'
Federman said he forwarded the recording to those above him in the chain of responsibility.
“I listen to the recording, and I pass it on to those above me in the hierarchy,” he said. “They, I assume, checked it with the military and told me everything was fine.”
Although he had never believed Hamas was fully “deterred,” Federman said he had not imagined an attack on the scale of October 7.
“As far as I’m concerned, Hamas has never been deterred. As far as I’m concerned, the West Bank could erupt, Israeli Arabs could erupt, but I wasn’t prepared for anything like this,” he said.
He criticized the assumptions that shaped Israel’s approach before the massacre, saying the country had been “captive to a flawed conception.”
“Maybe we can do this or that with them and give them a good life. As though we’re, I don’t know, Gaza Disneyland,” he said.
Soldiers knew something was happening, Federman said
Federman stressed that, in his view, the recording did not prove there had been specific knowledge of the October 7 attack. Instead, he said, it reflected concerns among soldiers serving along the Gaza border.
“This recording isn’t actually a conspiracy,” he said. “Since I published it, this is what the soldiers were feeling on the ground. At the most basic level. What they felt on the ground, their conversations, and many others who talked about it.”
He said some soldiers had observed unusual Hamas activity before the attack.
“Look, Hamas is conducting exercises, Hamas is training, we’re about to face a different kind of event, and no one listened to them.”
Federman said his ability to respond as a civilian responsible for festival security had been limited.
“What could I do with a recording? I was a civilian,” he said. “On paper, we’re stewards, we’re not armed. What could I do? I did my duty, I passed it on.”
Had he understood the message to be a credible warning of a large-scale attack, he said, he would have acted very differently.
“If I had known, of course I would have passed it on to Ben-Gvir, stopped everything and at least prevented it. But there wasn’t... Who imagined it? Who knew?”
Federman added that, like many others, he realized something unusual was happening on the morning of October 7 only when rocket fire from the Gaza Strip began at around 6:29 a.m.

Photos: Gaza before and after – a city transformed by war

In Pictures
Photos: Gaza before and after – a city transformed by war
Archive and recent photos show how three years of war left Gaza’s streets, landmarks and public spaces unrecognisable.
Gaza City – More than 80 percent of Gaza’s buildings have been damaged or destroyed since Israel launched its war on the besieged enclave in October 2023, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, turning whole neighbourhoods into rubble and wiping out much of its infrastructure.
For generations, Gaza’s streets, markets, schools, hospitals and public spaces formed the backdrop to everyday life. They were places where people worked, studied, shopped, met friends and family, and built memories.
Many of the city’s familiar landmarks also carried a much longer history, reflecting Gaza’s thousands of years as a crossroads of different civilisations.
The war has also changed the face of Gaza by damaging or destroying many of those historic and recognisable landmarks.
UNESCO has verified damage to 164 cultural sites since October 2023, including 128 buildings of historical or artistic interest, 14 religious sites, nine monuments, eight archaeological sites, two museums and three depositories of movable cultural property.
Among them are the Great Omari Mosque, Gaza’s oldest mosque, Qasr al-Basha, the ancient Samaritan Bathhouse, al-Qissariya Market and the Church of Saint Porphyrius complex.
Some of these places have been reduced to ruins, while others remain standing but heavily damaged. The destruction has altered not only individual buildings but the streets and neighbourhoods around them, removing landmarks that once helped people recognise and navigate their city.
This photo series contrasts archive images of some of Gaza’s most recognisable streets, markets and public buildings with new photographs taken three years into the war, showing how these familiar places have changed after years of bombardment and destruction.

Estonian government approves several updates to primary healthcare rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:22:00 UTC
14:22:00 KST

Estonian government approves several updates to primary healthcare rules
Health centers in Estonia will have to provide up to three months' temporary coverage when a family doctor leaves a practice, among several new rules approved Thursday.
A bill of amendments the government greenlit Thursday will require health centers to find a replacement for a departing family doctor for up to three months, with the option to stay on longer by agreement.
If no permanent doctor is found to take over the previous doctor's practice list within that time, the Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) would step in.
A family doctor planning to leave a health center with their practice list would generally have to give six months' notice, although the doctor and center could arrange an earlier departure by agreement. The change is intended to give health centers time to reorganize.
Among other changes, the Health Board will be able to take over a doctor's practice list after 30 days, down from the current 60, if their patients have gone without family medical care.
Patient caps to be raised
The practice list cap will also be raised to 2,000 patients, or 2,400 if an additional doctor is available, although the bill still recommends a maximum of 1,600 patients.
Doctors with more than 1,600 patients will be able to turn away new patients if another family doctor in the area has fewer than 1,600. They will also have to direct patients to information on available practice lists.
The changes are intended to more evenly distribute patients among practices.
Pending Riigikogu approval, the amendments are set to take effect next March 1.
At the start of this year, 77 practice lists covering more than 132,000 patients across Estonia still lacked a permanent family doctor, with nearly one in 10 residents receiving primary care from temporary replacements.

"There were lots of comments on the RedNote account saying the service was good and reliable, so we trusted them," he told SBS Chinese.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
After paying a 10 per cent deposit, the pair received what appeared to be legitimate tickets. Confident the booking was genuine, Harding's housemate transferred the remaining balance — about US$2,500, or more than $3,500.
The booking appeared on Carnival's website. Their names were attached to it. They could log in, buy Wi-Fi packages and reserve restaurants.
"It just seemed legitimate," he said.
Then, less than a week before they were due to leave, everything disappeared.
"About six days before we were due to leave, we noticed the booking was gone," he said.
"From that point, they largely stopped responding to us and would just say things like, 'Please be patient'."
When Harding contacted Carnival, he says he was unable to get answers because the booking had been made using someone else's payment details.
"Because the travel agent had booked the tickets with a different credit card, the person on the hotline wouldn't give me any information for privacy reasons," he said.
"So even though it was our names and our passport numbers on the tickets, we couldn't actually do anything through Carnival."
The situation became even more complicated because the travel agent was based overseas.
"The travel agency was a Chinese travel agent and they booked the tickets through the American office of Carnival," he said.
"We're in Australia, so basically had no recourse because nobody here in Australia could help us."
Lured in by big discounts
Brisbane resident Lucy Liu says she had a similar experience.
She and three other passengers booked a five-day cruise after finding what appeared to be a heavily discounted fare through a Chinese travel agent.
The cabin was advertised for about $1,300, compared with around $1,800 on the cruise line's website.
"It was around a 30 per cent discount," Liu told SBS Chinese.
"They told us it was a last-minute promotional price, and that was what attracted us."
Like Harding, Liu believed the business appeared legitimate.
The RedNote account carried platform verification and displayed a business licence and company name.
"They had also displayed their business licence and company name on the account," she said.
But shortly before departure, Liu learned the booking had been cancelled.
When she sought an explanation, she received conflicting answers.
"At first they blamed us, saying we had entered our information incorrectly and that the cruise company couldn't contact us, which was why the booking was cancelled," she said.
"Then someone else said it was cancelled because we hadn't checked in."
According to Liu, the cruise line advised that the payment had been reversed and the money returned to the original account used to make the booking.
Liu says she later discovered information online showing the travel company's licence had reportedly been revoked by authorities in Beijing.
"The biggest difficulty, in my view, is probably related to cross-border consumer protection," she said.
"We weren't really sure which authority we should approach to resolve the issue."
How does this happen?
Melbourne-based cruise travel agent Snow Yu, who has worked in the industry for 14 years, says heavily discounted cruise fares can be a warning sign.
"They use very low advertised prices as a hook," she told SBS Chinese.
Yu says scammers have previously focused on highly sought-after Disney cruises before shifting their attention to brands including Royal Caribbean and Carnival.
She believes cases like these may involve fraudulent payment methods.
"It could be the result of credit card fraud," she said.
"After the cardholder discovers the transaction, they may report the card or transaction to the bank and recover the money."
"Once that payment is recovered, the cruise company has to cancel the booking.
"The problem isn't necessarily the booking itself, but the method of payment."
Carnival Cruise Line told SBS Chinese that travel scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated.
"Unfortunately, travel scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and we urge guests to exercise caution when purchasing a holiday through third parties," a spokesperson said.
"Guests should only book directly through Carnival Cruise Line or through reputable, accredited travel agents."
Melbourne commercial lawyer Tina Ji says consumers should be cautious if they're asked to transfer money directly or make advance payments outside established booking systems.
"Potential warning signs include requests for advance payment or requests to make private/direct transfers," she said.
Ji said people involved in disputes through platforms such as WeChat or RedNote should first consider reporting the matter through those platforms, noting that cross-border cases can raise jurisdictional challenges.
Yu recommends checking industry bodies such as the Australian Travel Industry Association and Cruise Lines International Association to help verify whether a travel agent is legitimate.
'Believe the official website'
Harding and his housemate eventually recovered their money after publicly challenging the travel agent online.
He says affected customers began comparing notes and found what appeared to be links between multiple accounts advertising cruise deals under different names.
"We knew that whoever was doing this was repeating the scam just under a different name," he said.
Harding posted comments warning other consumers and uploaded a video naming the travel agency.
"But in the end, because of all the pressure that we were placing on them, they did eventually refund us on the condition that we would remove the posts," he said.
"As of this day, I have not removed my post."
His advice to other travellers is simple.
"If somebody is offering you a ticket to something and it says it's sold out on the official website, believe the official website," he said.
"Don't believe the person who's trying to sell you something."
SBS Chinese contacted the travel agency involved for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: youth-led charity supports young cancer patients
Timothy Chan founded Youth Cancer Hong Kong so young patients can speak openly with others who understand what diagnosis and treatment mean at their age
Timothy Chan Chi-fung was 19 when a testicular tumour sent him into a Hong Kong hospital system largely designed for children or much older adults.
Neither door quite fitted. His experience eventually led him to found Youth Cancer Hong Kong, a contribution that has earned him a place as a finalist in the community category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards.
The awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, were launched in 2013 to recognise individuals and organisations whose work contributes to Hong Kong and its communities.
Chan was diagnosed in 2019 with a mixed germ cell tumour of the testis. He underwent surgery within two weeks of his diagnosis, followed by two cycles of chemotherapy. He lost his hair and his studies at university were interrupted. But he eventually recovered.

“My activism dates back to when I was 11”: Julie, a survivor and human rights champion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:15:05 UTC
14:15:05 KST

This blog contains descriptions of sexual abuse. We included this to stay true to survivors’ testimonies and their word.
Julie Gbanmeton, 26, is about to defend her master’s thesis in law at Parakou university, in northern Benin. Named a Human Rights Star by Amnesty International Benin in 2024, she leads her own organization – Femmes guerrières d’Afrique pour le développement (African Women Warriors for Development). With more than 50 members throughout Benin and Togo, its members conduct community outreach to promote women’s leadership and human rights.
“My activism dates back to when I was 11 years old because I experienced violence at that age. I was raped. And the first thing I did was speak out.
One weekend, I was left in the care of a man my parents knew. My father had something to do, so he asked the man to stay with me. Night fell, I went to bed to sleep, and while I was asleep, he committed his crime.
I screamed and screamed, but no one heard me; no one came to my rescue. After he was done, I went outside. It was 1 or 2 am. I didn’t have a phone, but I had a flashlight. I shone my flashlight on the path as I walked. Some customs officers were there. I wasn’t afraid, so I went up to them. I explained what had just happened, and that very night, they caught the man. The next day, he was taken into police custody. That’s when my father returned and found out what had happened. Legal proceedings began, the trial took place, and the man was sentenced to five years in prison.
That’s how my commitment to human rights began. After that, whenever I saw an injustice, I was shocked, and my sole concern was to grow up so I could put an end to it.
‘I decided I had to take on my responsibilities’
Today, I haven’t stopped fighting. Along the way, I’ve faced other challenges. When I was 17, I got pregnant. It happened because of ignorance! I was in high school, and I carried my pregnancy to term despite the prejudice. It wasn’t easy, but my parents supported me. If I were to give up the fight today, it would be as if I wanted my sisters to suffer the same violence and grow up in the same ignorance.
My daughter is nine years old. She was initially raised by her grandmother, but I fulfilled my role to her. I decided I had to take on my responsibilities as a mother.
Before, I didn’t talk about my story publicly because I saw it as a source of shame. But today, it’s a source of strength for me. Many people are encouraging me through this process. If I need to talk about my struggles and explain my mistakes to enlighten young girls in Benin, I’ll do so with pride. Serving others is part of my daily life. I know I have a long road ahead of me.
My family, my parents support me. My dad understands that I was born this way, that I’m against injustice. Before, I was seen as a rebellious child who did whatever she wanted. Today, my father can’t support me financially, but he encourages me.
From survivor to human rights defender
Before applying to the Human Rights Stars programme, I was very interested in Amnesty International’s work. I am interested in issues related to peace, international security, and social justice – not to mention human rights, which form the foundation of my commitment. After graduating from high school, I began studying law at the Parakou University.
I was active in a young lawyers’ organization, where I served as director in charge of project management. I also headed the International Women’s Rights Day organizing committee for three years. I learned a great deal.
Together with another human rights star from the Parakou region, we launched an awareness campaign in 2025 on gender-based violence and the prevention of early pregnancies in Djougou. We held awareness sessions at two middle schools. We also organized sessions on breast cancer and on gynaecological and obstetric violence – topics about which people lack sufficient knowledge.
Since 2023, I have also been leading an organization that promotes women’s leadership and the rights of women and children. Through this organization, I am currently doing a lot of work to empower women, combat gender-based violence, and promote the rights of women and children. We are about to celebrate International Day of the Girl Child, which is very important to us. It is a day for reflection and for celebrating the progress made in protecting and defending our rights; a day to take stock of our achievements, the challenges ahead, and the long-term outlook.
Paving the way for future generations
Through my organization, I set up a contest called “Children’s Voices, Voices of Hope”. It’s designed to help children learn about their rights and responsibilities in society and to express themselves in public. I had my daughter participate; she, too, will learn to fight. In this fight I’m waging, I won’t be alone. My daughter will also be a star that shines for others. I’m going to make this dream I see before me a reality.
I have a message to share. The time has come for us, the girls and women of Benin to shine, to know our rights and defend them, and to take responsibility. By doing this, we can contribute to social change. Our country cannot be built without us.”

Russia attacked Ukraine with 136 drones: 114 neutralized, including more than 80% of the jet-powered ones
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 136 drones at Ukraine, including 93 jet-powered ones. Air defense shot down or suppressed 114 unmanned aerial vehicles; the attack continued.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 136 drones during the night of October 9, 93 of them jet-powered. A total of 114 were shot down or suppressed, including 77 jet-powered drones, or 82.8%. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
From which directions and with what did Russia attack?
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 9 (from 18:00 on October 8), the enemy attacked with 136 Shahed-type attack UAVs (93 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How many were destroyed?
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 114 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (77 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by the enemy's air-attack weapons were recorded at 8 locations, as well as the crashes of downed targets (debris) at 7 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs remain in the airspace.

The Bangsamoro’s New Government Faces a Test of Public Trust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:12:00 UTC
14:12:00 KST

Last month’s parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines, the first ever, has settled one question but opened another.
The election results are now clear. The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) secured 31 seats across the party and district races, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) 30, and the BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) 15, with the remaining seats going to other parties and sectoral representatives. No party has the 41 votes needed to elect the chief minister. The 80 elected members of the first regular Parliament are set to assume office on October 30, marking the formal transition from the interim government to the first elected Bangsamoro government.
Most attention has understandably been directed at the question of which parties might come together to form the “Government of the Day”. But whatever its composition, the coalition that eventually emerges will offer an early indication of what kind of political order is taking shape in the Bangsamoro.
The September 14 election marked a transitional milestone from a negotiated peace settlement to elected government. The election results bring together political forces with different origins. BFP is composed of former combatants of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), including local political figures. The UBJP is associated with the MILF, while BGC brings together established political parties and clan-based political networks.
The poll also reflects the changing place of the Moro National Liberation Front, a Moro armed movement that signed a separate peace agreement with the Philippine government in 1996, in this political order. Its two political parties from its two major factions – the Mahardika and the Bangsamoro Party – did not secure seats as Sulu, where the MNLF has historically had a strong political presence, is no longer part of the BARMM electorate. But MNLF-linked voices have entered the new political order through other parties and individual representatives.
For the BFP, its coalition choice means defining what its break from the UBJP political camp means for the next phase of Bangsamoro politics. A BFP-UBJP alliance would bring together the two largest parties, potentially forming the “super majority”. The two share roots in the broader MILF political tradition but have since taken different political paths, particularly after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Abdulraof Macacua, then chief of staff of the MILF’s armed wing, the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces, as BARMM’s interim chief minister in 2025. Macacua later joined BFP and became its chair and president.
Such a coalition would test whether political differences within the former movement can be managed within the institutions created by the peace process. It could also allow BFP to broaden its political base through UBJP’s strong showing in the sectoral races, while bringing BFP’s relationship with Manila into a broader governing coalition.
For UBJP, a BFP coalition would likewise have significant implications. The party remains closely associated with the MILF and the peace agreement that produced the BARMM. An UBJP-BFP coalition could provide continuity with this political project within the new parliamentary system. BFP’s perceived close relationship with Malacañang could help move some of the remaining normalization commitments. At the same time, such a coalition would require UBJP to navigate the question of national government influence, which has contributed to political divisions within the MILF.
For a Bangsamoro public that has long been sensitive to Manila’s role in BARMM governance, the stakes would extend beyond securing a parliamentary majority. The two political strands that emerged from the MILF would have to work together without blurring the distinction between cooperation with the national government in implementing the peace process and preserving political autonomy for the Bangsamoro.
The BGC faces a different choice. With 15 seats, it has the numbers needed by either BFP or UBJP to form a majority. It has already indicated that it is open to working with either party, and its political forces bring established parties, local networks, and experience in governing into an arena increasingly shaped by MILF-linked politics. As such, it could bring familiarity with local government and the political relationships and practices that have shaped the region for decades. At the same time, its ranks include emerging political voices who may bring different priorities and forms of representation to the new Parliament. Depending on its choice, the BGC’s role in shaping the first elected government could either reinforce established ways of exercising political power or broaden what the new parliamentary system can represent.
BFP has since announced that it has secured enough support to form a majority, although coalition discussions among the parties are continuing. This makes the coalition combinations less hypothetical. A BFP-UBJP coalition signals an effort to reconcile competing strands of the MILF political project. A BFP-BGC or UBJP-BGC coalition would demonstrate how movement-linked politics and established political networks are negotiating power within the new parliamentary system. Much will depend on what the parties ask of one another in exchange for governing together and what they are prepared to commit to the Bangsamoro public. But the burden now falls more heavily on BFP to show what this majority is assembled around. Securing votes is one task; building a coalition with a shared governing agenda is another. A coalition can be politically viable without necessarily being ideologically coherent.
If the BGC and the established political networks aligned with it are central to the new government, that would not necessarily mean a reversal of the political transformation envisioned by the peace process. It could instead show that the new political order is becoming a negotiated space between movement-linked politics and longstanding sources of local political power.
However, the coalition question cannot be separated from the environment in which the new government will have to govern. As I noted before the polls, the challenge was not simply avoiding localized violence but ensuring that political disputes could still be contained through the institutions and relationships established by the peace process.
In Cotabato City, election-related violence before and on election day left several people dead and injured. Shortly after the election, localized fighting in BARMM’s Special Geographic Area prompted the deployment of joint Philippine government-MILF security mechanisms. These incidents exposed the complexity of the transition currently taking place in BARMM.
Another issue that may become more visible is the relationship between the new Bangsamoro government and Manila. With an elected government taking shape, the Bangsamoro public has stronger expectations that the BARMM should have greater political space to determine its leadership and governing arrangements. The issue will be how Manila’s involvement is perceived: as a support for Bangsamoro institutions or as an attempt to shape their political outcomes. If the latter perception takes hold, it could complicate the new government’s efforts to establish its own political authority.
For the incoming government, the mandate should extend beyond running the regional administration. It will also have to demonstrate a clear commitment to completing the remaining normalization commitments under the peace process, working closely with the MILF as a peace partner while maintaining a constructive relationship with the national government – while not becoming so closely identified with either that it loses the political space needed to govern in the interests of the Bangsamoro people.
The peace process in the southern Philippines sought to create institutions through which political authority could be acquired, exercised, and contested. The challenge for the new government will be to remain autonomous enough to govern in the interests of local people, but engaged enough to sustain the peace process.

New evidence gives family hope after death in Spain
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:11:46 BST
14:11:46 KST

New evidence gives family hope after death in Spain
- Published
Four years after watching his brother die in his arms, Maximilian White believes new evidence could help him get answers.
Tobias White-Sansom, a father-of-two from Nottingham, died in a Spanish hospital in July 2022, five days after a night out in Magaluf, and his family believes the way security and police officers handled him that night led to his death.
A blood spatter report and a court order received by the family this month have reignited their hopes that criminal proceedings could commence in the Spanish courts.
White told the BBC: "I won't stop until we get justice for Toby."
The 46-year-old medical cannabis entrepreneur said he found it difficult to talk about the way he lost his younger sibling, who was on a family holiday at the time.
White-Sansom was pinned down at a nightclub following a row over him removing his T-shirt because he was too hot, his family said.
They told the BBC the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was called and he was handcuffed, Tasered and injected with tranquilisers before going into cardiac arrest.
The family believe the blood spatter evidence - which forms part of an ongoing investigation that will see a court judge decide whether a criminal case is warranted - could suggest external force was used.
The report, which analysed White-Sansom's T-shirt, trainers and a sock, said several individual bloodstains were identified, which are compatible both with spatter stains caused through the application of an external force and with drip stains, produced by gravity.
An ambulance report, seen by the BBC, states White-Sansom had taken drugs and was agitated. He was administered a number of medications including fentanyl, the report added.
The Guardia Civil has not provided any further detail on the death.
At the time it issued a statement, saying: "Upon the arrival of the Guardia Civil police, this man was violent and police reduced him to be assisted by medical services.
"He was taken to the hospital for treatment. There, once while he was being assisted, he was arrested for a crime of injury."
Days later, White and the rest of the family were forced to make an agonising decision.
"The only thing keeping him alive was the life support machine," he recalled.
"And we discussed between our family members and we decided it was inhumane and we should let Toby die naturally.
"So then, my decision was to turn the machine off myself, and then my brother died in my arms.
"The doctors said he would slip away within five to six minutes, and Toby being the strong-willed person that he was, it took 11 minutes."
In the four years since, White said he had been trying to reach a resolution.
"The whole brutality of the situation caused my brother to pass," he said. "Someone needs to be accountable.
"It's accountability. And also, for his children to know that he was a good person, not a drunk tourist in Magaluf."
White said on the night in question, his teenage son wanted to go out but he did not want him to go by himself, so White-Sansom accompanied him along with his girlfriend.
"What never sat well with me was that my brother was not with a group of lads on a stag do," he said.
"It just didn't make sense. That's why I went so heavy in return, because I knew that's not how my brother lived and what he was about."
White spoke to the BBC days after receiving the evidence and a court order.
"The process is extremely gruesome because even when you're getting good news, it's bittersweet - my brother is still not here," he said.
"It's just the truth - fighting an uphill battle just to get the truth. At this point, it's a sweet picture but also bitter because Toby is not around."
An inquest into White-Sansom's death was also opened in the UK in 2022, and paused while investigations in Spain continued.
White believes the new evidence could significantly impact the process but if that fails, he says he will take the matter to the UK.
"The truth is out there, the evidence is there, we just need help putting it in front of the right people to get this justice for Toby that's needed," he said.
The family's lawyer in Spain told the BBC he had never seen a case like this before.
"I've never seen a case... with a whole package of circumstances and such a delay," said Jaime Campaner. "I've never seen it and I hope I never see it again."
He said he had been filing motion after motion to speed up the process, and said the Spanish Civil Guard - the Guardia Civil - was to blame for the delay.
The Guardia Civil told the BBC the case was before the court and it had no further comment to make.
"The Spanish investigation has been very slow," Campaner added. "And this is not common in a city like Palma, where investigations don't take so long."
He said the investigating judge in Spain would now consider the new evidence, and decide whether to proceed as a criminal case or shelve it.
"We believe this could be key evidence. We are not aware of the conclusions yet but it might end in results [for] this case," he said.
They are yet to be given a date for a court hearing but Campaner estimates the investigating stage would conclude by the end of the year, with a prospective court case starting next year.
"We all want to get this case closed and see some justice," said White.
"We're hoping that at some point in this chapter, we can close the door on this - and we can close the door on this pain."

Wealthy French quit failing state schools squeezed by pensions and austerity
PARIS, Oct 9 - Clemence Remy moved to the French city of Nantes in 2020 and enrolled her two girls in the local state school. The teachers were good, but she grew so exasperated by rolling staff strikes that she eventually put them in a private school.
Those concerns about state schools have helped fuel some of France's most violent protests in decades. They began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
France's public schools have long been held up as a crucible of the republican ideal, a place where children from rich and poor families alike can receive a top-notch education imbued with the values of "liberty, equality and fraternity".
But performance has been slipping for years, and the government is struggling to arrest the slide as gigantic pension outlays and a need to rein in public finances leave little room for manoeuvre.
Those issues have prompted a growing number of wealthier parents to abandon the public sector in favour of private schooling. Remy said the strikes at her daughters' school in Nantes, a left-leaning city in western France, were often last-minute, requiring repeated time off work with little notice.
"School is an institution we should be able to rely on," she said. "In the end, you realise you can't rely on the system."
STANDARDS FALL AS PENSIONS GOBBLE UP SHRINKING FUNDS
The maths and reading levels of French 15-year-olds have fallen drastically since 2003, reaching a record low well below the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average, according to the body's 2025 "PISA" results.
French state secondary schools were unable to staff nearly 10% of teaching hours - or almost half a day of teaching per week - in the 2024/25 school year, of which three-quarters is due to the non-replacement of absent teachers.
Between 10% and 20% of French school buildings are "in a significantly deteriorated condition", according to a 2025 report by Banque des Territoires, the investment arm of state-owned lender Caisse des Dépôts.
The government's inability to turn the tide on education is partly explained by a growing pensions bill that sucks resources away from other priorities, experts say.
France's 2027 education budget is €64 billion ($72 billion). Teachers' pensions add another 28% to the cost.
Total government spending on pensions, which is due to reach 436 billion euros or 14% of economic output next year, has grown faster than all other categories of public expenditure over the last two decades, while spending has slipped for education, according to Reuters calculations based on Eurostat data.
The steady growth in pension spending is due not only to an ageing population, but also to voters' resistance to increasing the retirement age or reducing what retirees get.
Economist Erwann Tison of the think tank Institut de l’Entreprise said pension spending "cannibalises" the education budget. That means France can only pay early-career teachers below-OECD-average salaries that contribute to frustration and strike action.
"France is effectively handing over large subsidies to older French at the expense of everyone else," Nobel-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote on his Substack on Thursday. "Mass national student demonstrations should come as no surprise."
WEALTHIER FAMILIES MIGRATE TO PRIVATE SCHOOLS
The vast majority of French private schools operate according to the "under-contract" model.
Almost entirely Catholic-run, such schools have greater control over staffing and admissions. Their teachers are paid by the state, with fees covering non-teaching costs. A larger pool of substitute teachers means they are less affected by strikes or absences.
Over 2 million children, or 17.6% of all pupils, attend one of France's more than 7,500 under-contract schools, according to a 2023 national audit office report.
Although this proportion rose modestly between 2011 and 2021, the percentage of children from wealthier families has grown at the expense of poorer children, the report found. It said some families had moved over to avoid local state schools, or had concerns about safety and teacher absences.
Pupils from "very advantaged" families accounted for 40.2% of the total in 2021 compared to just 26.4% in 2000, while over half of pupils at under-contract schools now come from "advantaged or very advantaged" backgrounds, compared with less than a third in state schools.
"Fifty years ago, ambitious families aimed for the public sector," said Louis Chauvel, a sociologist at the University of Luxembourg. "Today, private institutions are often seen as the better route if you want to maximise your kids' chances."
Virginie Durin, the president of Apel, France's main association representing parents of pupils in Catholic private schools, said not all were wealthy, and that many parents made great sacrifices to afford them.
But she acknowledged a growing concentration of wealthier students in certain neighbourhoods.
Nantes, where Remy lives, is a stronghold of under-contract schools in France, with 38% of pupils privately educated.
Remy, who pays €191 ($214) a month per child, recognised that private schools were not affordable for everyone, and were at risk of being colonised by the wealthy. But she had no regrets.
"I think it provides an environment where at least the children are encouraged to strive and do better." REUTERS

Graphene opens new way to detect brain damage after stroke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:03:29 UTC
14:03:29 KST

An international team of scientists involving Spain's CSIC has developed graphene sensors that pinpoint the brain regions most vulnerable after a stroke, tested in mice, opening the door to preventing further damage and improving treatment.
An international team of scientists has developed a graphene-based technology that makes it possible to monitor brain activity and identify the areas at greatest risk of sustaining additional damage after a stroke. The breakthrough, tested in mice, could help drive the development of more precise treatments for stroke.
The research, published in the scientific journal "Brain (source in Spanish)", involved the participation of Spain's National Research Council (CSIC), the University of Manchester, the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) and the German company Multi Channel Systems.
When a person suffers an ischaemic stroke, a blockage interrupts the blood flow to part of the brain. However, the lesions can continue to spread because of waves of disturbed electrical activity, known as spreading cortical depolarisations, which move through the affected brain tissue.
Until now, accurately detecting these signals has been a challenge, as conventional technologies struggle to record the extremely slow electrical changes that occur during this process.
Graphene helps identify the brain's most vulnerable areas
Using high-sensitivity graphene sensors placed on the brains of mice, the researchers succeeded in recording these electrical waves with an unprecedented level of detail. The results showed that the characteristics of the signals made it possible to distinguish between relatively healthy brain tissue, tissue at risk and tissue that had already suffered severe damage.
The scientists also found that these signals could anticipate the blood-flow response. While in healthier areas it increased to support recovery, in vulnerable regions it could fall even further, worsening the injury.
The team also discovered that a low dose of ketamine, a drug already used in medicine, reduced the duration of the harmful electrical waves, improved the blood-flow response and reduced the extent of brain damage in animal models. These findings point to a possible neuroprotective effect of ketamine after a stroke, although it has not yet been shown to offer the same benefits in humans.
A potential tool to improve treatments
"In broad terms, the study shows how cutting-edge technologies can not only improve the way brain activity is measured, but also reveal new and important information about how brain lesions develop and how they might be treated", explains Rob Wykes, a researcher at the University of Manchester.
For his part, Anton Guimerà-Brunet, a CSIC researcher at the Institute of Microelectronics of Barcelona, stresses that recording low-frequency brain activity is still a challenge for current technologies. "We have been developing our graphene-based technology for years, with our first results published in 2018, and the challenge has been to standardise and refine it for use in relevant preclinical studies", he says.
The breakthrough is part of a scientific collaboration launched years ago between institutions in Spain and the United Kingdom to develop graphene devices capable of recording brain signals.
Although the technology is still at the preclinical research stage, the scientists believe that in future it could make it possible to monitor in real time the condition of brain tissue during a stroke, identify patients at greatest risk of additional injury and contribute to the development of new treatments.

El Niño could weaken the polar vortex. Does a scorching summer mean a freezing winter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:02:41 UTC
14:02:41 KST

El Niño’s European weather impacts tend to be indirect and less severe than in the tropics. But experts warn it could weaken the polar vortex.
Experts have warned that this year’s El Niño event could be the “strongest in living memory” – increasing the likelihood of 2027 becoming the hottest year on record.
Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño events, and the weather phenomenon isn’t expected to peak until late autumn or early winter.
Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate that the extreme heat associated with El Niño could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths. The extra warming also paves the way for more extreme weather impacts, such as wildfires and floods.
South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.
But in Europe, El Niño’s weather impacts tend to be much more indirect and less severe. The natural phenomenon could increase the chances of more unsettled conditions later in the year, such as a milder, wetter and windier autumn and early winter.
So, why are fears growing that Europe will be cast into a deep freeze this winter?
What is a Sudden Stratospheric Warming event?
Every year in winter, strong westerly winds circle around the pole high up in the stratosphere – which extends from an altitude of about 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface.
This is referred to as the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and it circulates around cold air high over the Arctic.
However, following a peak in El Niño, the SPV can become weaker. This can increase the likelihood of a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event, which would subsequently increase the potential for cold weather.
A SSW is where temperatures rapidly increase (up to about 50C in just a couple of days) in the stratosphere. As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere.
“Typically this will form over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia,” the UK Met Office says.
“This means that northern Europe, including the UK is likely to get a long spell of dry, cold weather, whereas southern Europe will tend to be more mild, wet and windy. On the boundary of these areas, cold easterly winds develop and in some cases the drop in temperatures leads to snow.”
Will El Niño trigger a ‘deep freeze’ in Europe?
Multiple newspapers have recently warned of a “deep freeze” hitting Europe due to the risk of El Niño peaking and weakening the polar vortex.
However, winter weather across the UK and mainland Europe is influenced by a wide range of factors – including human-caused climate change. For example, a 2025 study from Newcastle University found the burning of fossil fuels is accelerating winter rainfall changes in the UK and Europe, almost 25 years sooner than expected.
Many of the factors that impact Europe’s weather cannot be predicted so far in advance. In fact, meteorologists can only reliably forecast individual SSW events about a week ahead.
“While there is a known teleconnection between El Niño and a colder end to the UK winter, this outcome is by no means guaranteed,” Grahame Madge, a Met Office climate spokesperson, tells Euronews Earth.
“There are many other drivers of UK winter weather including El Niño, and it is the balance of these drivers that determines the winter forecast rather than any single one.”

How the card surcharge ban could change our relationship with cash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:01:57 UTC
14:01:57 KST

How the card surcharge ban could change our relationship with cash
With the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) ban on card surcharges now in effect you might start seeing local businesses offering discounts if you pay in cash.
Cash payments in Australia are much less common than they were a decade ago, but the RBA's latest data showed a slight uptick in cash use in 2025.
How could the ban on card surcharges impact how cash is used in Australia?
How often do people use cash?
This graph from the RBA's 2025 Consumer Payments Survey tracks the percentage of Australians who use cash in a typical week.
As you can see, 2025's figure of 50 per cent is much lower than the 97 per cent in 2007.
But it's slightly higher than 2022's figure of 47 per cent.
Will we move back to cash?
John Hawkins, a senior economic lecturer at the University of Canberra, doesn't expect cash use to skyrocket.
"From January the government has required most grocery stores and petrol stations to accept cash, which may see some modest increase in its use," Dr Hawkins says.
"On the other hand, about 20 per cent of consumers say they used cash to avoid card surcharges.
"As these no longer apply we could see some drop in cash use."
Loading...
Angel Zhong, a finance professor at RMIT, says she would be surprised if the surcharge ban reverses the long-term trend of card payments.
"I expect a modest uptick [in cash use] mostly at the margins: the café, the barber or the tradie offering a few per cent off for cash," Professor Zhong says.
"Australians moved to cards and mobile wallets mainly because of convenience, speed and record keeping, not because of price.
"A small discount at a handful of businesses is unlikely to change entrenched habits for most people."
Data from the RBA's 2025 survey showed people aged 65 and older were the most likely to use cash.
Cash might also still be preferred by people in regional areas with limited bank access or poor internet signal, people managing tight budgets, and people who have privacy concerns.
Professor Zhong says the goal should be to continue offering people the choice of using cash or paying by card.
Why would cafés offer cash discounts?
Professor Zhong sees cash discounts as a sign of how much pressure small businesses are under.
"The RBA paired the ban with a cut to interchange fees, which was meant to soften the blow by lowering what businesses pay to accept cards," she says.
"But interchange is only one part of the cost.
"Small businesses typically pay their payment service provider a bundled rate, and there's no guarantee that the interchange savings flow through to that rate."
While big businesses could leverage their bargaining power to negotiate savings in their contracts, smaller businesses don't have that option.
And that means losing the ability to surcharge while missing out on a drop in costs.
"Against thin margins and rising operating costs, offering a discount for cash is one of the few ways a small business can steer customers toward a cheaper payment method," Professor Zhong says.
Are cash discounts legal?
Yes.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) says businesses can offer discounts to customers paying via particular means such as cash or PayID, but there are a few rules.
Discounts should be clearly disclosed before payment and they have to advertise the non-discounted price.
They're not allowed to display the discounted price more prominently than the full price.
Is it legal to hike prices to cover the surcharge ban?
Yes, but there are rules about how businesses label these price hikes.
"They must not mislead consumers about prices, including about the reasons for any price increases," the ACCC says.
An example of this might be a nursery that used to apply a 1 per cent credit card surcharge for its products.
To compensate for that cost, they might increase the cost of a $10 pot plant to $10.10.
But let's say the nursery owner decides that, while they're setting new figures, they'll increase the pot plant's price to $12 to cover the rise in their electricity and water bills.
That's totally legal too.
But they aren't allowed to say the price increase from $10 to $12 is because of the ban.
"This will be misleading because the price increase also reflects other business costs, not just the cost of accepting card payments," the ACCC says.

The fruit and vegetables to look out for this month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

The fresh fruit and vegetables to add to your shopping list in October
Asparagus is "absolutely sublime" at the moment, according to green grocer Jo Toscano.
Asparagus, snow peas and garden peas are increasingly prominent on shelves as spring sets in.
While no-one doubts the convenience of frozen peas, Effie Ramos from organic market garden Remi's Patch in Naarm/Melbourne says there's something special about the ritual of slowing down and popping the pods open yourself.
University of Newcastle nutrition professor Clare Collins says shopping seasonally can help us to introduce variety into our diets.
"If you eyeball all the veggies and fruit, look at what hasn't visited your trolley for a few weeks," she says.
What can you look for?
Vegetables:
- Asparagus
- Garden peas
- Snow peas
- Broad beans, including broad bean tips
- Broccoli
- Cauliflower
- Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli and bok choy
- Capsicum
- Beetroot
- Fresh garlic
- Celery
Fruit:
- Citrus, such as alfourer mandarins, navel and blood oranges
- Mangoes, as availability increases
Asparagus, peas and broad beans
Asparagus is expected to peak in mid-to-late October, Ms Toscano says.
People tend to avoid the thick asparagus spears, but she says they're "juicy and full of flavour".
White asparagus doesn't offer the "great value" of green asparagus, Ms Toscano says "it is divine". She recommends peeling it as the exterior can be "quite fibrous".
Dr Collins says asparagus works well in an omelette, quiche or with a simple cheese sauce.
Garden peas are also in season.
"Fresh peas sort of stay elevated in price but when they're good they're really good and it's worth it," Ms Toscano says.
When garden peas are fresh and young, she suggests using the pods (after they've been shelled) to flavour homemade vegetable stock or blitzing and sieving that mixture to make an intense pea-flavoured cooking liquid.
Broad beans are also "awesome" right now, Ms Toscano says.
Ms Ramos says the leafy green tip of the broad beans have been popular and are "really good, fresh in a salad".
Brassicas and Asian greens (again)
Broccoli and cauliflower "are pretty good value" and Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli are another good buy, Ms Toscano says.
Dr Collins says brassicas, including cauliflower, broccoli and cabbage, can be divisive because they can taste bitter to "super tasters" — people with a more sensitive sense of taste.
"But the good news, especially for parents, is that [through] repeated exposure you increase your tolerance," she says.
Avoid overcooking the produce and try roasting it or masking the flavour with something like a cheese sauce if someone you are cooking for finds it bitter, she suggests.
Seeing red (capsicum and beetroot)
Ms Toscano says lots of red capsicums are coming from Queensland and that there are "bargains to be had" over the next couple of weeks.
Dr Collins says you can use affordable capsicums and Asian greens in stir-fries.
Ms Ramos says it's a good time for beetroot, which can be added to salads, raw or cooked.
"A lot of people sort of underestimate the power of the leaves of the beets. You can have them raw, or I just blanch them with a little bit of olive oil," she says.
Ms Ramos expects an abundance of spring onions, coriander, parsley, which will decrease prices.
October fruit offerings
Grapes have started but they're still very expensive, Ms Toscano says, and the first stone fruit will begin appearing this month.
"With the confluence of WA and Queensland mango seasons in a few weeks, prices are expected to fall," she says.
Cathy Senn from Sensational Berries in Naarm/Melbourne says supplies of Victorian berries will increase as the month continues, adding to those coming from northern Australia.
"Starting with the strawberries and then we'll go on to raspberries and then later on we'll have the blueberries come on and then the strawberries, the blackberries after that," she says.
Citrus varieties are "diminishing", Ms Senn says, pointing to her "about finished" blood oranges, cara cara oranges and ruby grapefruits.
Dr Collins says at this time of year you can often buy bags of great value lemons and oranges. If she's got people coming over, she likes to cook her lemon-and-orange delicious.
"You use the rind, the more rind the better," she says.
Separating the egg white from the egg yolks is "the tricky bit", but it's also a good opportunity to teach kids or grandkids how to do it.

Russia slashes cancer care as defence spending hits post-Soviet record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

The federal cancer programme budget falls from 44.9 billion to 3.87 billion roubles in 2027 — a nearly 40-fold reduction against 2025 levels — as defence spending reaches 35% of all federal expenditure, the highest share since the Soviet Union collapsed.
Russia is cutting funding for its national cancer programme nearly twelvefold in 2027, from 44.9 billion roubles (€470.5m) to 3.87 billion roubles (€40.5m), according to the draft federal budget, as defence spending reaches its highest share since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The reduction is even sharper compared to last year: the programme received 148.5 billion roubles (€1.5bn) in 2025, meaning federal spending on cancer control would have fallen roughly 38-fold in two years if the budget passes as proposed.
Funding is projected to recover partially thereafter — rising to 5.76 billion roubles in 2028 and 12.78 billion in 2029 — but both figures remain far below current levels.
Since its launch, the federal cancer project has funded diagnostic equipment, cancer centres, and early screening programmes.
Under the new 2027-2029 budget, the remaining money is expected to go mainly to diagnostic and radiology equipment, while specialised units in smaller towns and rural areas face cuts, a distribution likely to deepen an already significant gap between cancer care in major federal centres and outlying regions.
Rerouting roubles
Officials have said some costs will be transferred to the compulsory health insurance system (OMS) and other budget lines rather than eliminated entirely.
Patient organisations and some experts have questioned whether the new mechanisms could fully offset the federal reduction, and noted that shifting costs to regional budgets and the OMS ties the quality of care more directly to the financial strength of individual regions.
The proposed cuts come as new data show Russian cancer patients are already bearing a growing share of treatment costs.
A study by the NGO Movement Against Cancer found that between 2019 and 2025, patients bought roughly one in every six or seven packs of cancer medicines out of pocket. In 2025 alone, household spending on anti-tumour drugs rose from 8.8 billion to 11.4 billion roubles, and the number of packs bought independently increased from five million to 5.8 million.
Around 94% of those drugs are on the list of essential medicines and should be provided free of charge.
The study's authors attribute the out-of-pocket spending not to patients choosing more expensive options — most purchases involved generics — but to supply disruptions and gaps in provision.
Russian law guarantees cancer patients free access to the medicines they need, but in practice, patients and doctors have long reported procurement delays and regional budget shortfalls.
State procurement remains substantial: official figures show the government bought 32.8 million packs of medicines worth 336 billion roubles through the OMS system in 2025. But the trajectory in out-of-pocket spending suggests the burden on patients is already rising ahead of the planned federal cuts.
Defence spending in the 2027 draft budget is set to reach 17.1 trillion roubles, or roughly 35% of all federal expenditure — a post-Soviet record.
More than four years of Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine have progressively shifted Russia's public spending, with civilian programmes including healthcare and medical infrastructure taking a backseat to continued expansion of defence outlays.
