Barcelona team develops AI that detects ageing in blood stem cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:01:05 UTC
13:01:05 KST

ChromAgeNet has decoded chromatin architecture, the 3D organisation of DNA in the nucleus, distinguishing young from aged blood stem cells and opening new paths for cell rejuvenation.
Ageing gradually undermines the body's ability to regenerate, severely affecting the production of blood cells. In this race against the biological clock, analysing changes in blood stem cells is crucial to opening the door to interventions that can slow their decline and restore their original function.
A scientific team in Barcelona has developed ChromAgeNet, an artificial intelligence tool that detects ageing in blood stem cells by analysing the three-dimensional structure of their DNA.
Published in the journal "Aging Cell", the research, led by Maria Carolina Florian (IDIBELL) and Paula Petrone (BSC-CNS/ISGlobal), shows that the organisation of chromatin contains information that makes it possible to distinguish cells from young and aged mice.
A bridge between biomedicine and supercomputing
To train the model, the researchers applied convolutional neural networks to 3D images of the nuclei of mouse stem cells (source in Spanish). ChromAgeNet uses neural networks to decipher how DNA ages. AI makes it possible to detect subtle structural variations that are imperceptible to the human eye.
One of the main concerns when using neural networks in biomedicine is not knowing what they base their decisions on. ChromAgeNet overcomes that barrier by offering an explainable AI (XAI) system.
The tool managed, on average, to correctly classify around 68% of cells as coming from young or aged mice using images obtained with DAPI, a standard, low-cost stain.
In addition, ChromAgeNet stands out as an explainable AI, allowing researchers to investigate which image features contribute to its predictions. These analyses highlighted, among other regions, changes at the periphery of the nucleus associated with ageing.
The analyses showed that chromatin is compact and organised at the edges of the nuclei of young cells, while in aged cells it appears dispersed. As a proof of concept, the tool assesses how certain epigenetic drugs (source in Spanish) induce changes in chromatin organisation that are consistent with patterns more akin to those observed in young cells. This showcases the potential of the tool for screening treatments that could regenerate blood tissue and strengthen the immune system. The code and the image database are already available to the international scientific community.
Collaboration with AI research teams
As for the practical applications of this research, Dr Maria Carolina Florian, principal investigator at the Bellvitge Biomedical Research Institute (IDIBELL), explains to Euronews: "Currently, we have developed a tool that works as a proof of concept in murine haematopoietic stem cells. We are now working to optimise it and adapt it to human stem cells, with the hope of using it to evaluate new drugs that can act on nuclear architecture and be used to rejuvenate aged stem cells."
Maria Carolina Florian tells Euronews that this work "has found the ideal ground to become a real tool thanks to the expertise of Dr Paula Petrone (BSC and ISGlobal). We plan to continue developing it and expand it for use with human stem cells. In addition, we are applying for further EU funding and seeking to establish links with other scientists in Europe who are interested in the practical application of our work."
For her part, Paula Petrone believes that this research "shows that a deep-learning algorithm can tell apart young and aged stem cells by analysing images of cell nuclei stained with a low-cost substance called DAPI."
3D maps and open code to rejuvenate cellular architecture
The internal map of the cell nucleus reveals a distinctive signature: in youth, chromatin is tightly entrenched at the edges of the nucleus; with age, that architecture falls apart. Identifying these patterns could help to study the decline of blood stem cells and to assess potential strategies capable of regenerating haematopoietic tissue and triggering changes throughout the body.
To demonstrate the practical potential of the algorithm, the team designed a proof of concept: they applied the tool to aged cells exposed to various epigenetic drugs. The goal was to determine whether the molecules were able to produce changes in chromatin organisation consistent with a more youthful state.
To accelerate new discoveries, the team has released the tool's code and a public database of 3D images of stem cells, with the aim of finding drugs that reinforce the immune system and quality of life in old age.
Numerous international studies underpin the evidence for the fundamental role of the immune system in the ageing of the body, as Maria Carolina Florian points out: "In our laboratory, we have contributed by demonstrating the possibility of stimulating and rejuvenating aged haematopoietic stem cells to improve not only immune system function, but also life expectancy and the health of the organism as a whole."
Long-term promise, caution for now: the science behind ChromAgeNet calls for prudence
The new ChromAgeNet tool will help to understand the basic molecular mechanisms involved in the ageing of haematopoietic stem cells, which could become targets for therapies to rejuvenate them. "We hope to deepen our knowledge, consolidate our findings and identify new tools and drugs to improve the function of aged haematopoietic stem cells," Florian concludes.
"In future, this technique could be used to screen new drugs with rejuvenating potential. By treating aged cells with different candidate compounds, AI could use image analysis to identify those that induce changes consistent with a more youthful state," Paula Petrone tells Euronews.
For Dr Petrone, "Extending life expectancy is not as important as extending healthy life expectancy. The discovery of new drugs with rejuvenating potential could help, for example, to improve ageing of the immune system and thereby support healthier ageing."
The researcher nevertheless stresses to Euronews the need for caution: "We must be very careful not to overestimate our results. These new technologies take years to be developed, validated and eventually reach the clinic. Our research is just one small contribution to the study of how we age and to the search for strategies that can support healthy ageing."

EU faces gas supply shortage as winter looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:01:00 UTC
13:01:00 KST

BRUSSELS — The EU is facing a winter gas shortage that could leave it scrambling to replace lost energy supplies equivalent to the power used by 12 million homes, according to new reports shared with POLITICO.
The shortfall raises the prospect of a winter of soaring power bills and forced energy saving measures if the bloc fails to find adequate supplies elsewhere.
As the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies, the EU faces an overall shortfall this winter of up to 14 billion cubic meters of natural gas — around 7% of the bloc's demand and enough to power between 10 and 12 million European households, according to a report by the Institution for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based energy think tank.
Advertisement
Those conclusions are echoed in a key report by a top European body of gas network operators that was presented to national energy officials on Thursday.
Natural gas is used widely to heat Europe's buildings, power its industry and generate its electricity. But the EU's gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level for the time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for later use in the winter.
With gas prices at near-four-year highs and supply constrained due to the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, Europe has limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the last, IEEFA found.
While that doesn't necessarily mean the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean there could be 7 billion fewer cubic meters of stored gas to draw upon. That could force countries to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets, or even require consumers to cut demand if fresh supplies are unavailable.
The EU's record-low reserves leave the bloc "with less of a buffer" against global supply disruptions, leaving it "vulnerable to price spikes," Ana Jaller-Makarewicz, IEEFA's lead European energy analyst, said in a statement. If countries are forced to exhaust stocks this year, that would also leave them with more to refill next year, continuing the feedback loop of low reserves and higher prices, she added.
The same risks were outlined in a 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if imports of liquefied natural gas are limited or even “optimal” in the context of a cold winter, storage levels could fall as low as 11%, a baseline needed for strategic reserves that can't be easily tapped into.
Advertisement
If countries hope to restore their reserves to 30% by the end of winter — or else face increased exposure to future cold spells — volumes equivalent to 7% of the demand will either have to be curtailed or simply withheld from consumers, ENTSO-G warns.
Part of that pressure comes from a looming EU-wide ban on long-term supply contracts for Russian LNG, due to take effect in January, which will reduce European gas imports by an additional 7 billion cubic meters, according to the IEEFA report. Russian gas has been historically used to offset "swings in demand" over the winter, it said. "Now Europe depends on storage to get through winter."
To make matters worse, the IEEFA report argues, gas demand over winter has crept up in the past two years, while imports to the bloc have flatlined. That's left the EU leaning harder on its reserves over the winter period, with net drawdowns rising to 22.6 billion cubic meters in January this year, up from 18.8 billion cubic meters in January 2025 and 17.8 billion cubic meters in January 2024.
The alternative would be to import fresh LNG, a seaborne fuel that the EU increasingly sources from the U.S. But at current prices, importing the lost volumes would cost Europeans an additional €3 billion, a 12% rise over what the same volume would have cost last year, on top of already sky-high prices, according to the report. U.S. LNG production is also near full capacity, meaning those additional imports would further squeeze supply, Jaller-Makarewicz told POLITICO.
To some, a rise in prices is more likely. While ENTSO-G's tight market scenario assumes a "global deficit" that sees available LNG imports into Europe reduced by 20%, Laurent Ruseckas, a senior gas market analyst at S&P Global Energy, argues that reserves can only ever fall so low, "since a rapid drawdown early in winter will drive up prices," drawing cargoes to Europe from Asia.
"There is not much demand to destroy in Europe," he added, pointing out that the war in Ukraine already destroyed 20% of the bloc's industrial demand. "And it didn't come back."

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:00:37 UTC
13:00:37 KST

A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.
But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.
Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.
Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.
Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.
However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.
He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.
Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.
They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.
“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.
“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”
The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.
Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.
“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.
Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”
The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.
Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”
The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.
Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens.

13:00:01 KST

STOCKHOLM, October 9. /TASS/. The Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday in Oslo.
Unlike other Nobel prizes, the award ceremony for the Nobel Peace Prize takes place in Oslo and not Stockholm, in accordance with the last will of renowned Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel. The document specifies that the prize should be awarded to a person, "who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses." In his will, the scientist also specified that the prize should be awarded by a committee of five members appointed by the Norwegian parliament. Traditionally, the committee includes retired Norwegian politicians and former party leaders.
Nowadays, the century-old wording is interpreted quite broadly, frequently drawing criticism toward the committee’s decisions. In recent years, the list of laureates included politicians, rights activists, political activists, and humanitarian organizations recognized for achievements across a wide range of fields.
The Nobel Peace Prize 2025 was awarded to Maria Corina Machado "for her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and for her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy".
Possible candidates
Traditionally, nominations for the prize can be made until January 31. After that, the right to nominate is reserved for committee members, who can exercise it at their first meeting, usually in February.
The full list of nominees is kept strictly confidential and may not be made public until after the 50th anniversary of the award. Each year, however, information about the nomination of certain candidates is leaked to the media by organizations or individuals with the right to nominate. These include former and current members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee and its advisors, previous Peace Prize laureates, members of national parliaments, university professors specializing in history, philosophy, law or theology.
The record number of contenders - 376 - was reported in 2016. A total of 287 candidates have been nominated for the 2025 edition of the prize: 208 individuals and 79 legal entities. According to media reports, US President Donald Trump was one of them. A number of public figures and political leaders spoke publicly about his nomination, including from Israel, Cambodia and Pakistan. A member of the House of Representatives of the US Congress, Anna Paulina Luna, also mentioned this.
Haakon Gjerlow, the head of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), which regularly publishes lists of potential contenders, named the Save the Children charitable foundation, Sudanese volunteer network Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), the International Space Station (ISS), the International Court of Justice of the United Nations, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) as possible laureates.
About the award
The Nobel Peace Prize was first awarded in 1901. There were years when no winner was announced, the last time being in 1972. The reasons for no award being given include World Wars I and II, disagreements among committee members, and a "lack of worthy candidates."
The award ceremony is in Oslo on December 10, on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death. This year’s monetary prize amounts to 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Nobel Week kicked off in the Swedish capital of Stockholm on October 6. Winners of the prizes in medicine, physics, chemistry and literature have already been announced.

Flat Land, Hidden Water: Architecture on Reclaimed Ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Reclaimed land is often presented as new ground: flat, available, and ready for architecture. It promises cities more space where space is scarce, allowing them to extend waterfronts and build cultural districts. Sometimes, these newly claimed lands may also develop into financial centers, create parks, and imagine futures beyond the limits of existing land. Yet reclaimed land is never simply land. It is an engineered surface, produced through fill, seawalls, drainage, and soil stabilization — a long-term negotiation with the water it claims to have displaced.
This makes reclamation one of architecture's most powerful and ambiguous spatial fantasies. On one hand, it offers freedom: a tabula rasa where streets and buildings can be planned almost from scratch. On the other, this apparent freedom conceals dependency. Made land must constantly prove itself as ground. It has to resist flooding, support foundations, grow trees, and hold public life above a terrain that did not previously exist.

Interview: China's exemplary development practices prove SDGs are attainable, says U.S. expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:58:44 CST
12:58:44 KST

by Xinhua writer Liu Yanan
NEW YORK, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China's practices in economic growth and poverty elimination are exemplary and have proven that the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are attainable, as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) helps achieve the goals, said an American expert.
China's economic success over the past two generations has offered valuable examples for other countries, said Lawrence Freeman, a U.S. political-economic analyst for Africa, who has been involved in economic development policies for Africa for over three decades.
The world faces enormous challenges in reaching the SDGs by 2030 with approximately 800 million people living in extreme poverty worldwide, Freeman said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
In Africa alone, approximately 440 million people live in extreme poverty, slightly less than one third of its population, while poverty continues to increase, said Freeman.
"However, the good news is that China, over the course of two generations, has completely transformed its economy, eliminated extreme rural poverty and leads the world in infrastructure-led physical economic growth. China has proven that it can be done," he said.
China, with its unwavering commitment to the development of the nation, and its mastery of effective economic governance, has proven to the world that the SDGs can be achieved, he noted.
The Global Development Initiative proposed by China in September 2021 articulates the most important essential concept of development to be understood by all nations, and the BRI and the growth of the BRICS have provided vital input and made on-the-ground contributions to achieving the SDGs, Freeman said.
China's key role in the Global South has been invaluable in driving the world forward in economic progress, he said. "We must recognize that the future of the planet lies in the development of the Global South."
The BRI has attracted needed investments in infrastructure throughout the developing sector, which the West has refused to offer, said Freeman.
In Africa, the BRI has been a primary contributor to the construction of hard infrastructure projects, particularly in the generation of electricity, railroads, ports and airports, he said.
Moreover, Freeman called for the creation of a new paradigm devoted to achieving economic progress in every country.
As part of the efforts, he proposed to eastablish a new international credit institution to provide sufficiently long-term, low-interest credit for investments in infrastructure.
The latest UN data show that only 36 percent of the SDG targets with available trend data are on track or making moderate progress, while 15 percent have regressed.
The UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was adopted in 2015, with 17 SDGs at its heart. ■

NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:56:28 UTC
12:56:28 KST

NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.
- Share:
After spending more than seven months aboard the International Space Station, NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have safely returned to Earth. Their spacecraft splashed down Thursday in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles, bringing an extraordinary mission to a close.
The four astronauts spent 237 days in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, and completed thousands of trips around Earth while carrying out scientific experiments that could help shape future missions to the Moon and Mars.
NASA will host a news conference at 3:30 p.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct. 15, at Johnson Space Center in Houston, where returning crew members will discuss their experiences and research accomplishments.
"Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey spent 237 days living and working in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, advanced important science, and returned safely home because of the extraordinary expertise and competence of thousands across NASA, SpaceX, and our international partners," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Building the capability, experience, and confidence to do this repeatedly is exactly what will allow us to go farther, and I am grateful to Crew-12 and their families for their service to humanity's greatest adventure."
NASA Astronauts Return After 237 Days and 100 Million Miles
The returning crew included NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
Their spacecraft touched down in the Pacific at 8:34 a.m. PDT. SpaceX recovery teams aboard specialized vessels reached the capsule shortly afterward and brought the astronauts and spacecraft aboard.
Following routine medical evaluations, the crew members will be transported to shore before traveling to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.
"NASA's activities supporting the International Space Station -- transporting crew, conducting impactful research, and maintaining critical national assets -- enable the science, engineering, and risk‑reduction needed for future missions across the solar system," said Dana Weigel, manager of NASA's Low Earth Orbit Program at the agency's Johnson Space Center. "We're grateful for the dedication across the human spaceflight team that makes this possible, and we're thrilled to welcome Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey home."
Over the course of their 237-day stay, the astronauts circled Earth more than 3,792 times, accumulating over 100 million miles of travel.
For Meir and Fedyaev, Crew-12 marked their second journey into space. Hathaway and Adenot, meanwhile, completed their first space missions.
The crew launched on Feb. 13 at 5:15 a.m. EST, reaching and docking with the International Space Station the following day.
Space Station Experiments Could Help Future Moon and Mars Missions
Beyond the remarkable distance traveled, Crew-12 devoted hundreds of hours to scientific investigations designed to support future human exploration and improve life on Earth.
One research project explored ways to produce stem cells in space for potential use in cell-based medical treatments. Another demonstrated technology capable of producing IV fluids on demand, an ability that could become especially valuable during long-duration missions far from Earth.
The astronauts also investigated how pneumonia-causing bacteria may contribute to lasting heart damage. Understanding this relationship could offer new insights into cardiovascular health.
Other experiments focused on nutrition in space and how individual physical characteristics may influence blood flow during spaceflight. These studies could help researchers better understand the health risks astronauts face during extended stays in microgravity.
Together, the investigations provide valuable information about keeping humans healthy beyond Earth while testing technologies that may eventually support crewed expeditions to the Moon and Mars.
Historic Spacewalks Mark Crew-12 Mission
The mission also included significant milestones outside the space station.
Meir carried out four spacewalks during Crew-12, raising her career total to seven. That achievement places her third among NASA women for the most career spacewalks, behind former astronauts Peggy Whitson and Suni Williams.
Adenot also reached a historic milestone by completing three spacewalks. In doing so, she became the first French woman to venture outside the International Space Station.
With Crew-12 safely back on Earth, NASA has completed another extended mission that combined scientific research, international cooperation, and human spaceflight experience. The knowledge gained will contribute to preparations for more ambitious journeys beyond Earth's orbit.

Wet and windy weekend ahead in Finland, with snow possible in the north
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:54:46 EEST
12:54:46 KST

Finland faces heavy rainfall, strong winds and possible snowfall as a low-pressure system moves across the country on Friday, 9 October, with the first measurable snow of the autumn expected in parts of the northeast by Saturday morning.
The Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI) said on Thursday that the weather system would bring widespread rain to southern and central Finland, with precipitation reaching 30–40 millimetres in some areas.
Rainfall totals will generally range between 5 and 25 millimetres, although parts of central Finland are forecast to receive up to 40 millimetres or more. Southern areas are expected to see between 5 and 20 millimetres.
The low-pressure system will also strengthen easterly and north-easterly winds, particularly across western sea areas and central Finland.
Weather warnings have been issued for Friday, with storm-force gusts expected at sea. Strong gusts on land risk causing local damage in Ostrobothnia, Central Ostrobothnia, North Ostrobothnia and Kainuu, according to a forecast published by Foreca meteorologist Joonas Koskela.
Heavy rainfall is also expected to raise river levels, particularly in western Finland.
In northern parts of the country, precipitation is forecast to turn into sleet or snow during Friday, especially in Kainuu and Koillismaa.
Driving conditions are expected to deteriorate in these areas on Friday evening as temperatures fall and roads become slippery.
By Saturday morning, parts of Koillismaa and Kainuu could record the first measurable snow of the season.
Under Finland's meteorological definition, the first snow is officially recorded when at least one centimetre of snow covers the ground at an observation station at 9am during daylight saving time.
"Statistically, the first half of October is a fairly typical time for the first snow in northern Finland," FMI meteorologist Jani Sorsa said in the institute's forecast.
The low-pressure system is expected to move eastwards by Saturday, allowing colder northern air to spread across much of Finland.
Daytime temperatures in Lapland will fall to just a few degrees above freezing, with some areas remaining below zero. In southern and central Finland, temperatures are forecast to range between 5 °C and 10 °C.
Lapland is expected to escape much of the rainfall as a high-pressure system keeps conditions calmer in the north.
Foreca reported that temperatures in Lapland on Friday morning might approach the lowest readings recorded so far this autumn. The season's lowest temperature to date was −6.6 °C, measured in Tulppio, Savukoski, in late August.
October has so far been several degrees warmer than average across Finland, according to the FMI.
Sorsa said temperatures were expected to rise again around the middle of next week as south-westerly winds strengthen, bringing milder and more unsettled conditions during the first week of the autumn school holidays.

Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said.
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+, citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said.
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

Prosecutors alleged that between January 2020 and March 2023, Zhang conspired with his son, a middleman, a shareholder of an estate developer in Dailian, Liaoning province, and others to accept bribes totalling HK$20 million from the shareholder in exchange for Greentown China acquiring equity interests in the developer’s project.

ICE agent shoots man in car with five-year-old child in New York: Mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:25:33 UTC
12:25:33 KST

ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests
Mayor Zohran Mamdani says immigration agents fire at car with child inside. DHS says man was an arrest target.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent has shot a man in New York City as he sat in a car with a child.
Citing an “unconscionable and incredibly serious situation”, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said early reports indicated that agents surrounded the man and a five-year-old in his car on Thursday in the Marble Hill neighbourhood before firing multiple rounds.
The child was believed to be physically unharmed, the mayor added as he said he has called United States President Donald Trump and would demand that he end all ICE enforcement actions in the city.
“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities,” Mamdani said.
Protests followed on Thursday evening with demonstrators saying the shooting illustrated the dangers of Trump’s immigration crackdown, and some scuffles with police broke out.
“We are heartbroken and enraged,” said City Council member Carmen De La Rosa, who represents the area.
Speaking at the scene in the evening, Mamdani said: “Today’s shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbours than they could ever have claimed to save.”
He demanded the agency “must be abolished”.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she spoke with Trump and US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night.
“I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York,” she said in a statement.
“I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public, so we can establish the facts and get to the truth.”
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said its officers were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” in the Bronx about 4pm to arrest a 28-year-old Dominican national with a criminal conviction identified as Oscar Belgal by city police.
It said an officer “discharged his weapon” and “the criminal illegal alien” was injured. The DHS added that the incident remains under investigation.
Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plain clothes approached with a gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn’t in uniform.
Belgal started to pull the car forward, and then at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear, Tisch said, confirming that the child was unharmed and was with a relative.
According to a statement by the New York Police Department, the man remained conscious and was receiving medical treatment at a nearby hospital.
ICE under scrutiny
The shooting took place after months of mounting criticism of the agency.
In January, federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens in Minneapolis: Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, killed by an ICE agent on January 7, and Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, shot by a US border agent.
After Good’s killing, Trump officials labelled her a “domestic terrorist” even as video of the shooting cast doubt on their claims she had tried to run over an agent.
The federal government removed local authorities from the investigation, rejected calls for a civil rights probe and sent hundreds more agents to Minnesota, bringing the total to 3,000, as protests against the killings and the immigration crackdown spread to hundreds of US cities.
Trump blamed the shift in US opinion about the immigration agency on unfair media coverage, urging DHS and ICE to publicise the “violent criminals” they arrest.
ICE has been tasked with deporting one million people a year.
The agency doubled in size in the first year of the second Trump administration to more than 22,000 agents by January and is now the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency with about $75bn allocated to it over four years under a tax bill Trump signed last year.

UK arrests two men for breaking into US intelligence hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:46 UTC
12:20:46 KST

UK arrests two men for breaking into US intelligence hub
British counterterrorism police have arrested two Latvian nationals accused of breaking into a military installation housing major US and NATO intelligence operations, just days after British authorities alleged an Iranian-linked terror plot at an airbase hosting American warplanes.
The two men, aged 32 and 36, were detained early Thursday inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire after security personnel discovered an abandoned vehicle and a breach in the base’s perimeter fence, according to police.
Both suspects reside in the UK and were initially detained on suspicion of trespassing and criminal damage. They were subsequently arrested under the National Security Act on suspicion of entering a prohibited site for a purpose prejudicial to Britain. Their identities and possible motives have not been disclosed.
RAF Molesworth, roughly 70 miles north of London, hosts US military intelligence operations covering Europe and Africa, as well as NATO’s Intelligence Fusion Centre. Although officially designated a Royal Air Force station, the facility is operated by the US military and does not function as an active airfield.
Counterterrorism investigators have taken over the case, but British authorities have not publicly presented evidence that the breach involved espionage, terrorism or a foreign government.
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites,” Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said. However, she acknowledged that “at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford.”
The latest incident follows a much-publicized security scare at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, where five men were arrested on September 27 after police discovered three suspicious vans near the base, which had been used by American bombers during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The arrests initially sparked allegations of a possible terrorist bombing or drone attack, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggesting there were “strong indications” of Iranian involvement. Tehran denied the accusations.
Police subsequently acknowledged that no explosive devices had been discovered, with the investigation finding only quantities of petrol in the vehicles. All five suspects were released on bail within days, prompting further questions about the initial assessment of the threat.
Two additional men, including a dual British-Iranian national, were subsequently arrested in connection with the alleged plot. Both have also been released on bail, bringing the total to seven suspects released without charges.
The Fairford scare also coincided with Washington’s abrupt withdrawal of its B-1 strategic bombers from the UK installation. US President Donald Trump linked the decision to security threats, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down a direct connection between the alleged plot and the redeployment.
In the latest Molesworth case, investigators also summoned explosives specialists to examine the abandoned vehicle, briefly imposing a security cordon around nearby roads. The restrictions were lifted after nothing suspicious was found.

From Ra’anana around the world and back: Edan Leshem takes a swing for Sharsheret - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:43 UTC
12:20:43 KST

For Edan Leshem, Friday’s Sharsheret tennis tournament in Ra’anana will bring him back to a place where his own tennis journey began.
More than two decades after he first picked up a racket at the Ra’anana tennis center as a five-year-old, Leshem will return to those courts in a very different role.
Rather than competing for himself, the former Israeli professional will be helping run the tournament, working alongside his longtime coach and colleague Ron Becker to make sure the players have the best experience possible.
For Leshem, now 29, it is a fitting way to give back to a sport that has been such a major part of his life.
“I feel it’s a great cause and that I really want to help,” Leshem said. “I’m just there to support the players and give them the best experience of the tournament.”
The inaugural Sharsheret Israel Tennis Tournament 2026, taking place this Friday at the Ra’anana Tennis Center, will bring together women from the community for a day of competitive tennis, social connection and support while raising awareness and funds for Sharsheret’s work supporting women and families affected by breast and ovarian cancer.
Sharsheret provides resources for Jewish women at risk of breast, ovarian cancer
Founded in 2001, Sharsheret provides personalized support, education and community programs for Jewish women and families dealing with breast and ovarian cancer, as well as for those facing hereditary cancer risk.
Its services include peer support, mental health and genetic counseling, educational programming and practical assistance throughout diagnosis, treatment and survivorship.
The organization launched an Israel initiative in 2024, expanding its support network and programs to women, men and families in Israel.
That includes connecting people with peers who have experienced cancer themselves, developing support groups and providing educational resources around breast and ovarian cancer and genetics.
That community component is particularly important to the Ra’anana tournament. The event is not simply about raising money or playing tennis.
It is designed to bring together women who may have shared experiences with cancer and give them an opportunity to connect in an environment centered around activity, friendship, and strength.
While all the players in Friday’s event will be female, the spectators will include women, men and children of all ages, cheering on their wives, moms, daughters, sisters, grandmothers, aunts, cousins and friends.
Leshem became involved after tournament co-chair Ariella Eltes approached him about helping organize the event. He quickly volunteered to take responsibility for the tournament structure, including organizing the groups and managing the competition.
He will be joined by Becker, the coach Leshem first worked with after moving to Ramat Hasharon at age seven.
A full-circle moment for Leshem
It is a remarkable full-circle moment for a player whose own relationship with tennis began almost by accident.
Leshem was an energetic five-year-old living near the Ra’anana tennis center when his grandfather, who played tennis himself, suggested the sport as a way to channel some of that energy.
What began as an activity to tire out a young boy eventually became a professional career.
By the time Leshem was seven, he had begun working with Becker and found himself surrounded by other young players who were competing seriously. He quickly discovered that he could hold his own.
“I realized I’m not that bad,” Leshem recalled. “I can play some tennis.”
The competition became addictive. He began playing national tournaments, then traveling internationally, and eventually established himself as one of Israel’s leading players of his generation.
Leshem reached the final of the Israeli national championships as a teenager, facing Israeli star Dudi Sela, and also trained with Amos Mansdorf, one of the most accomplished players in Israeli tennis history.
He joined Israel’s Davis Cup team at 17 and went on to represent his country on the international stage. His professional career included appearances in ATP events and extensive competition on the ITF and Challenger circuits.
His best period came in 2017, when he climbed into the world’s top 250, reaching a career-high No. 249 in the ATP singles rankings in December of that year. He also reached a career-high No. 349 in doubles in 2018.
Along the way, Leshem collected several ITF titles and competed against or practiced with players who would go on to become some of the biggest names in the sport, including Alexander Zverev, Andrey Rublev, Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz and Hubert Hurkacz. He also shared the court with players such as Kei Nishikori and Marcos Baghdatis.
One of his most memorable experiences came at an ATP event in Tel Aviv, where he competed in front of a home crowd. At the 2022 Tel Aviv Open, his home tournament, he qualified for the main draw having received a wildcard.
He defeated seventh seed Lorenzo Giustino and third seed Luca Nardi. He recorded his first ATP career win defeating compatriot, wildcard Yshai Oliel.
As a result, he climbed close to 70 positions up the rankings to No. 377 and became the No. 1 Israeli player in singles. He also won his first Davis Cup match in South Africa in 2018, another moment that remains particularly meaningful to him.
Those experiences gave Leshem a firsthand look at both the rewards and the enormous challenges involved in trying to make it as a professional tennis player.
His career also gave him an intimate understanding of the difficulties facing Israeli tennis players.
Leshem believes the country has plenty of talent, but not always the infrastructure necessary to develop it.
“When I was competing, we had a lot of players,” he said. “Everybody just wanted to play and compete and everybody was fighting. I think that’s what creates a lot of players.”
Today, he believes there is less of that healthy competition.
Tennis has become more social, he said, while competitive tennis has become increasingly expensive and difficult. Travel, coaching, training and education can all create obstacles, particularly for young Israeli players trying to compete internationally.
Leshem experienced those challenges himself.
While some of the players he competed against eventually reached the highest levels of the sport, traveling with coaches, physiotherapists and larger support teams, Leshem often traveled alone. The cost and logistics of competing internationally were significantly more difficult for an Israeli player who had to fly between tournaments.
He remembers looking at players who had far greater resources and wondering whether he could reach the same level without the same support.
Those experiences have helped shape what he wants to do now.
After a fall down a staircase on the way to a match resulted in a lower-back fracture and a disc injury, Leshem eventually realized that a comeback was no longer realistic. Instead, he began building a new career around the sport.
He started slowly, developing his coaching experience and building his own tennis club in Ra’anana.
The goal, he says, was never simply to produce professional players.
“I wanted to build a community of people who love the sport and want to enjoy it,” he said. “It gave me so much joy.”
That philosophy makes the Sharsheret tournament particularly meaningful to him.
Tennis, Leshem believes, offers far more than competition. It provides exercise, social connection, resilience and independence. Unlike team sports, there is nowhere to hide on a tennis court.
“If you have a bad day, it’s all on you,” he said. “So you have to be very resilient and very independent.”
That same quality can make the sport a valuable escape for people dealing with difficult circumstances.
For someone recovering from illness or cancer, Leshem said, tennis can provide a temporary break from everything happening outside the court.
“You go, you play tennis, you focus on the strokes, on the movement, you kind of forget everything around,” he said.
“Sometimes it’s just a nice way to get away from all those troubles.”
The Sharsheret tournament also provides something beyond the tennis itself: an opportunity for women who have shared difficult experiences to come together in a positive environment.
Leshem said many of the participants already know one another and have similar stories, making the tournament an opportunity to reconnect, share experiences and simply enjoy a sport they love.
“I think it’s a very nice way to connect them with each other, to share stories,” he said. “They get the chance to meet all their friends at the same place with something that they all enjoy doing, which is playing tennis and talk.”
That idea is central to Sharsheret’s broader work. Cancer can be an isolating experience, even when surrounded by family and friends. Sharsheret’s peer-to-peer model allows people to connect with others who understand the experience firsthand, while its educational and genetic counseling programs help families navigate issues that extend beyond the immediate medical treatment.
In Israel, where the organization is still expanding its presence, that network is becoming increasingly important.
Tournament raises awareness and creates a supportive environment
The tournament therefore serves two purposes at once. It raises funds and awareness for Sharsheret, while also creating precisely the kind of community environment that the organization seeks to foster: one in which women can talk, support one another, remain active and see themselves as more than their diagnosis.
For Leshem, that sense of community is ultimately what makes the event special.
The former professional has spent years experiencing tennis from the perspective of a player trying to win. He has also experienced the pressures, sacrifices, and limitations that come with attempting to reach the highest levels of the sport.
Now, back on the same Ra’anana courts where his journey began, he gets to see tennis from another perspective.
He gets to help other people enjoy it.
And on Friday, he hopes plenty of people will come out to join them.
“The more people who come, the event will get better and support the cause,” Leshem said. “If anybody watching this wasn’t planning on coming and wants to come, we will be happy to have them with us on Friday.”
For a player whose childhood introduction to tennis began with a grandfather looking for a way to keep an energetic five-year-old busy, it is another chapter in a relationship with the sport that has lasted more than 20 years.
This time, however, the goal is not to win a match.
It is to help make sure everyone who steps onto the court has a reason to feel like a winner.
Sharsheret hosts community sports events in the US and now in Israel to raise funds and support national breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and genetics programs. The upcoming Sharsheret Israel Tennis Tournament Benefit is scheduled for this Friday, October 9, 2026, at the Ra’anana Tennis Center. For more information, please visit sharsheret.org/israel-tennis

====================================================================================================

Top Jewish influencers say opting out is not an option when antisemitism is prevalent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:04 UTC
12:20:04 KST

Jonah Platt wants potential guests on his podcast to know that “private” solidarity is no solidarity at all.
Platt, a social media influencer and the host of “Being Jewish with Jonah Platt,” said in an interview with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that he is frustrated with the steady stream of personal messages and other signs of support from celebrities and thought leaders, both Jews and allies, who appreciate his program showcasing Jewish identity and pride - but then decline to come on it.
When declining, they tell him they are too scared for their safety or careers. They’re “afraid it will attract anti-Israel masses to their social media, afraid it will affect them commercially or afraid they’ll get death threats,” he explained.
The would-be guests often say they’ll support the Jewish community privately but not publicly. But to Platt that’s an empty offer. “Having private solidarity doesn’t move the needle when public spaces are being entirely surrendered to fear,” he said.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research survey released in July found that 4 in 10 Jews are less likely to wear anything identifying themselves as Jewish than they were before the deadly Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in just one sign of concerns about being Jewish publicly. In the three years since, a handful of Jewish influencers have tried to give Jews the support to come out and be proud.
”I think the more Jews speak about their own story, and the more we share it, the more we own it, the stronger we will be as a people and the more people will react positively,” said another influencer, Israeli activist Hen Mazzig, who interviews celebrities and pushes for Jews to express public pride in their heritage.
'Humanizing the Jewish experience' through social media
Despite the difficulties Platt and Mazzig encounter when encouraging people to speak out, they have still made a mark. On Instagram alone Hen Mazzig has 459,000 followers and Jonah Platt has 229,000. Mazzig’s show interviewing Jewish people about their identity, art and culture, “And They’re Jewish,” was just picked up by ChaiFlix, the Jewish and Israeli Netflix.
Platt’s podcast, meanwhile, is often the No. 1 ranked Jewish podcast on Apple podcasts. Views on YouTube for multiple episodes are above 50,0000, with nearly 1,000 comments on single episodes. And he has succeeded in attracting at least some high-profile guests - including Cindy Crawford, Jason Alexander and Mayim Bialik.
Platt developed his podcast in October 2024 as a safe space for Jewish and allied celebrities and thought leaders to share their stories around Jewish identity to help combat rising antisemitism and Jewish hate.
“It humanizes the Jewish experience for the audience, “ he said, especially when listeners can think, “Wow, this person whose movies I love is going through such a horrible time and is experiencing all this stuff, too. I had no idea.”
Platt said appearing on his podcast pays dividends. With only a tiny number of exceptions, according to Platt, everyone who’s been on his show has told him, “This has been so amazing. Everybody wherever I go is telling me how much they love this conversation.”
Platt said his guests find that the typical listener feedback is positive. Some of the responses they’ve received include: “It makes me feel seen. It makes me feel less alone. It makes me so proud to support you, and now I’m gonna buy tickets to every movie you’re ever in and have your back all the way!”
Positive impacts for guests on Platt's social media
A number of Platt’s interviews confirmed that they saw spikes in positive attention after appearing on his show.
“Not only is Jonah a fantastic host with whom I felt so safe, but after my episode aired, I have had so many people commenting online or coming up to me and thanking me for making them feel less alone,” Seth Rudetsky, SiriusXM’s Big Fat Broadway host and Jewish Broadway Alliance founder, wrote to JTA in an email.
Sarah Hurwitz, a former White House speechwriter, said that after her appearance on Platt’s podcast in February 2025, she saw sales of a book she published in 2019, “Here all Along,” go up.
“The fact that my sales were double, then triple what they were the week before the episode aired really does seem meaningful,” she said.
Platt said he’s heard of minimal negative pushback. “I can really only think of one instance where I heard back from a guest who said there’s some specific clips based on things they said that are getting them some hate online that they’re unhappy about it, but certainly didn’t regret appearing on the show,” said Platt. “They’re just like, I can’t keep promoting these clips anymore.”
That experience stands in stark contrast to what many other Jewish performers have found in other contexts, however. In recent weeks, Pink lost 100,000 followers overnight for airing her objections to Macklemore’s anti-Israel advocacy when he was opening for Ed Sheeran. (Stadium owners told Sheeran that Macklemore would not be welcome, and he dropped the rapper from his tour.) Jerry Seinfeld is still headlining the MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Portugal, but he’s facing boycott calls and several comedians have dropped out because of opposition to Seinfeld’s pro-Israel views.
But staying silent won’t change that reaction, according to Mazzig, co-founder of the Tel Aviv Institute think tank focusing on antisemitism.
“When Oct. 7 happened, a lot of people were hoping [increased Jewish hate] would be over in a few months,” Mazzig said. Three years later, it is evident that antisemitism is not diminishing, he said.
Mazzig, who is gay, likened the prescription for Jewish pride to the journey gays have undergone.
“It’s what Harvey Milk said about the gay community,” said Mazzig, referring to the trailblazing Jewish San Francisco city supervisor who was assassinated in 1978. Milk believed it’s important for gay individuals to come out to their friends, neighbors, and community, so they aren’t defined by what misconceptions others perceive about them. “And I think for us as Jews, we have to do the same thing,” said Mazzig.
Inspiring Jewish college students in the US
Hearing from proud Jews is especially important for college students, according to Andrew Pessin, a philosophy professor at Connecticut College and the founding director of the Institute for the Critical Study of Antizionism. As far as he can tell, his is the only classroom on campus where students can learn about Zionism in a positive way and have multi-sided discussions.
Pessin said that his Jewish students tell him his class is a safe haven. He said he’s heard things like, “Thank G-d for your class, because I am surrounded by hate on this campus,” and that there, “I realize I’m not alone, and this is actually a safe space for me.”
Avital Goldberg-Curran transferred from Connecticut College after experiences at New York University that left her feeling threatened. She was pleased to see Pessin’s name as a faculty member. “My rabbi would talk about him as a hero. A proud Jew,” she said.
“At NYU, there were days that I felt unsafe going to class because there were mass protesters in the lobby screaming death to Israel and Jewish people,” says Goldberg-Curran, an American history graduate of Connecticut College. “There were multiple times that I took a lap around the block and waited for the protests to be broken up by the police before I went inside because I didn’t know if there were weapons.”
Goldberg-Curran follows Platt and Mazzig and said their podcasts and writings remind her of the importance of being a proud Jew in difficult times.
“They very much inspired me while I was at NYU to lean more into Judaism and being observant,” she said. “I very much sought out observing Shabbos and visiting the Chabad house and surrounding myself with Jewish people.”
She added, “I think it’s been a very important takeaway that in times of struggle, we should be finding each other and leaning into them.”
Pessin believes being vocal on Jewish hate is important for his own self-worth. “If I don’t speak up, I’ll have changed myself,” he said. “If I see something, I have to speak up and say otherwise. If I don’t, it harms me on the inside.”
That feeling of being at peace with and connected to your inner self is part of what Platt guests get from being on his show.
“They feel good for having told their story authentically and being truthful to who they are, and in some cases, spoken about things in a setting where they feel comfortable to speak about things they don’t talk about elsewhere,” said Platt. “So for a lot of people, it’s been cathartic or healing to be on the show.”

Meta bans TikTok ads on its platforms in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:03 UTC
12:20:03 KST

Facebook and Instagram-owner Meta has banned advertisements by ByteDance, the Chinese parent of TikTok, on its platforms in the United States and a handful of other countries, a company spokesperson said on Thursday.
The move marks an escalation in the long-running rivalry between Meta and ByteDance, whose video-sharing app TikTok has emerged as one of Meta's most formidable competitors for user engagement, creators and advertising dollars.
Meta's ban takes effect immediately in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, and extends to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries, Meta said.
"We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta said. "Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience."
TikTok and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Meta's move.
TikTok's website shows that it does not support links that open or log users into other social media apps. However, users can still add links to their profiles that direct people to those platforms' websites.
Urge for Tiktok, Youtube to take on teen safety
Meta has been urging TikTok and YouTube to follow steps it agreed to take on teen safety in August following a settlement of up to $18 billion with US states over social media harms to children.
Meta in August agreed to impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.
TikTok has not publicly commented on Meta's campaign, but it reached a settlement with Alabama in September that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhance age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that it endangered children and misled consumers about its safety.
TikTok operates in the US as a majority American-owned joint venture after a deal aimed at safeguarding US user data and averting a US ban on an app used by more than 200 million users in the country.
Bloomberg News first reported Meta's ban earlier on Thursday.

Ukrainian Child Rescue Advocate Among Nobel Peace Prize Contenders as Trump Eyes Award

Ukrainian child rescue advocate Mykola Kuleba is among the names being discussed ahead of Friday’s Nobel Peace Prize announcement in Oslo, as US President Donald Trump continues his public campaign for the prestigious award.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee will reveal the 2026 laureate at 11 a.m. local time on Oct. 9, choosing from a field of 287 nominated individuals and organizations amid wars and humanitarian crises across the world.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kuleba, a former Ukrainian presidential commissioner for children’s rights, has campaigned for the return of Ukrainian children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred to Russia – an issue that has drawn international condemnation and become a central humanitarian concern during Moscow’s invasion.
His work places Ukraine among the causes being discussed by Nobel observers this year, alongside humanitarian responses to the war in Sudan, press freedom and international justice.
However, the Nobel Committee does not disclose the identities of nominees for 50 years, meaning publicly discussed candidates cannot be officially confirmed.
Ukraine’s abducted children in Nobel spotlight
Among the potential recipients mentioned by experts are Kuleba and the international charity Save the Children, both associated with protecting children affected by conflict.
Kuleba has played a prominent role in efforts to rescue and return Ukrainian children taken to Russia and Russian-occupied territories since Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Russia Launches Overnight Drone and Bomb Attacks Across Ukraine – Kyiv Among Areas Threatened
The issue has also drawn the attention of US First Lady Melania Trump, who has advocated for the reunification of children separated from their families by war.
Recognition of Kuleba’s efforts would put international attention on the fate of Ukrainian children and the continuing challenges of securing their return.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russian official Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
Russia denies that its transfers are unlawful, describing them as evacuations or humanitarian measures. Ukraine maintains that children were taken without proper consent and has demanded their return.
Trump seeks Nobel recognition despite unfinished wars
Much of the attention surrounding this year’s prize has focused on Trump, who has repeatedly claimed that he deserves the award for helping resolve international conflicts.
The US president has claimed credit for ending up to eight wars, although several of those conflicts have continued and his role in resolving others remains disputed.
His promise to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has also gone unfulfilled, with Russian attacks continuing despite months of US-led diplomatic efforts.
Speaking Wednesday, Oct. 7, Trump questioned whether the Nobel Committee would recognize his achievements.
“They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” he said, adding that denying him the award would be a “great discredit” to the committee.
Trump has previously criticized the Nobel selection process, maintaining that his diplomatic record deserves international recognition.
Nobel observers, however, have pointed to his administration’s military campaign against Iran, territorial ambitions involving Greenland and confrontational approach to multilateral institutions as factors weighing against his selection.
His response to Friday’s announcement has itself become a subject of discussion among Nobel experts.
Nobel Committee faces political pressure
The Norwegian Nobel Committee maintains that its decisions are independent of political pressure.
However, the selection comes amid questions about how Washington might react if Trump is overlooked.
Last year’s prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who subsequently presented her Nobel gold medal to Trump in recognition of his role in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
The gesture did not transfer the Nobel title, which remains with Machado.
The committee’s secretary, Kristian Berg Harpviken, said political considerations and possible reactions may be discussed, but maintained that such pressure does not determine the outcome.
The 2026 prize will be selected from 287 candidates – 208 individuals and 79 organizations – whose identities remain officially confidential, AFP reported.
The winner will receive a medal, diploma and monetary award at a ceremony in Oslo on Dec. 10.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index closed lower on Thursday as heavyweight stocks weighed on the broader market.

The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$161.36 trillion. For the week, the index gained 837.7 points, or 1.73%, marking its fourth consecutive weekly gain. The market will be closed on Friday for the National Day holiday.
Most of the index’s largest-weighted stocks ended lower. TSMC fell 1.35% to NT$2,550.
MediaTek lost 3% to NT$4,690, Foxconn declined 1.19% to NT$249, and Delta Electronics fell 1.26% to NT$1,965. In contrast, ASE gained 1.64% to NT$744, according to Anue.

Plastics stocks extended gains after Formosa Plastics Group President Wu Chia-chau (吳嘉昭) expressed optimism about the group’s operating outlook for next year. Formosa Plastics led the sector, rising 7.82% to NT$81.3, while Formosa Chemicals & Fiber, Usi, and Taiwan Styrene Monomer moved higher.
Among technology stocks, passive component makers continued to attract buying interest. Later Fine Ceramics, Taiwan Chinsan Electronic Industrial, Viking Tech, Max Echo Technology, and Ample Electronic Technology all reached daily limit-ups.

However, industry leader Yageo fell 1.85% despite reporting record monthly revenue in September. Walsin Technology, which had also performed strongly in recent sessions, retreated as investors took profits.
Advanced packaging and testing stocks also rose on demand for AI chips and application-specific chips. Advanced Wireless Semiconductor, Winstek Semiconductor, Chunghwa Precision Test Tech, and Taiwan-Asia Semiconductor hit limit-ups.
Senior analyst Chien Po-yi (簡伯儀) said investors had become more cautious as the TAIEX approached the psychologically significant 50,000-point level. The index fell on lower turnover on Thursday and closed below its five-day moving average, suggesting it could consolidate further in the short term, according to CTEE.
Chien identified the 10-day moving average, at around 48,700 points, as a key support level. He expects the market to consolidate before making another attempt at 50,000 points as selling eases and trading positions stabilize.
Looking ahead, Chien expects Taiwan’s corporate earnings to remain favorable next year, with AI-related industries continuing to offer investment opportunities. Areas to watch include AI servers, upgraded materials, power technologies, semiconductor materials and equipment, and high-dividend stocks.

Singapore, Mongolia to open applications for carbon credit projects
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:10:30 CST
12:10:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Singapore and Mongolia will open applications for carbon credit projects on Oct. 30 under a bilateral implementation agreement, Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and National Environment Agency said in a statement on Thursday.
The projects will generate carbon credits aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Under Singapore's International Carbon Credit Framework, the credits may qualify for use by Singapore-based companies liable for carbon tax to offset up to 5 percent of their taxable emissions.
Interested parties may apply for authorization of eligible carbon credit projects in Mongolia. The two governments will review applications jointly on a rolling basis.
The agreement is Singapore's sixth bilateral implementation agreement under which Singapore has opened applications for carbon credit projects, following similar agreements with Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda and Thailand. ■

New Zealand food, fiber exports hit record high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:10:12 CST
12:10:12 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's food and fiber exports reached a record 65.2 billion NZ dollars (36.6 billion U.S. dollars) in the year to June 30, up 8 percent from a year earlier, a senior official said Friday.
The result was 4.8 billion NZ dollars higher than the previous year and exceeded the Ministry for Primary Industries' June forecast of 64.3 billion NZ dollars, Agriculture and Forestry Minister Todd McClay said in a statement.
"The Middle East conflict and trade policies in some key markets have disrupted supply chains and pushed up inflation and input costs," McClay was quoted as saying.
Strong demand for New Zealand's food and fiber products, along with tight global supply, supported prices, McClay said.
Dairy export revenue rose 6 percent to 28.8 billion NZ dollars, while meat and wool exports increased 20 percent to 14.8 billion NZ dollars. Horticulture export revenue grew 5 percent to 9.3 billion NZ dollars, statistics showed.
In the year to June 30, food and fiber exports rose 20 percent to 5.3 billion NZ dollars to the European Union, 11 percent to 1.1 billion NZ dollars to the United Arab Emirates, and 24 percent to 541 million NZ dollars to India, ahead of a bilateral free trade agreement with India taking effect on Oct. 20, McClay said.
The government is targeting a doubling of the value of New Zealand's exports by 2034, he added. (1 NZ dollar equals 0.56 U.S. dollar) ■

Ukraine, Europe, US to meet in Miami for talks on ending war

Unknown Publisher

Ukraine, Europe, US officials to meet for talks to end war
October 9, 2026
Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.
Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.
More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.
What did Zelenskyy say about the Miami meeting?
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
Zelenskyy blames US for inaction
Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
Ukraine president rejects Rubio claim that war is deadlocked
Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.
Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.

Nava Koster, an Israeli stranded in Dubai since Tuesday, told Walla on Wednesday that the alternative flight she had booked for Thursday had also been canceled. “The flight we bought tickets for tomorrow has also been canceled. All the rescue flights have been canceled,” she said.
Despite reports of efforts to bring stranded Israelis home from the United Arab Emirates, Koster said she and the other members of her tour group still do not know how they will return to Israel.

The group was scheduled to return from Sri Lanka on October 6 via Dubai, with a connecting flydubai flight to Tel Aviv. That flight was canceled amid disruptions following the incident aboard a flydubai flight to Israel and the suspension of service on the route.
