Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:03:41 UTC
11:03:41 KST

Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will reassure Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics.
The byelection, called after the former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Polanski. Abdi-Wali received 12,292 votes, 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 8,928, 33% of the vote.
Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4 percentage points down from the 2024 general election.
In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.
“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me. I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden and this is Britain.”
Labour’s victory provides assurance for Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.
However, the low turnout suggests Burnham still faces an uphill battle in urban areas, particularly in London where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, insisted the win was a sign of progress for the party. She told Times Radio: “It demonstrates that Labour’s message of hope is really cutting through, that people don’t just want parties like Labour to talk about the progressive change this country needs, but they want to see it delivered in action.”
Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his eco-populist party, which fell into turmoil after it voted at its conference on Sunday to adopt a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism, raising questions about his leadership.
Shortly after polls closed in Holborn and St Pancras, Caroline Lucas, the former Green MP and party leader, refused to say whether Polanski should stand down. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, she said: “I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday [when the motion was voted on].” Polanski abstained and campaigned in the constituency instead.
Speaking to the BBC after the result, Polanski insisted he would remain in his post. “Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green party,” he said. “We’re a party of 220,000 members. I’ve taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion and we’re going to grow.”
In a later interview with Sky News, he said the result had been a good one for the Greens, and that “we are going to be more of an electoral threat to Labour than we ever have in our history”, noting that it had been the party’s second best byelection performance.
The motion at the centre of the fallout said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. It was passed in a vote by Green members despite opposition from four of its five MPs.
Polanski has faced criticism for not opposing or backing the motion, and for being absent from the debate and vote on Sunday so he could campaign in the byelection.
He told Sky he would only have backed the motion if it had been amended to remove the call for a single Palestinian state. Asked if he backed it as passed, he said: “I would have supported the motion as amended. It wasn’t amended, so no.”
Polanski defended himself against the criticism that he had not shown leadership by missing the vote.
Campaigners in Holborn and St Pancras had “wanted to see me on the ground”, he said, adding: “They wanted to see me dealing with local issues. So I did exactly that.”
Speaking to the Guardian after her win, Abdi-Wali said people at the school gates found the Greens motion “divisive”, adding: “It just speaks to the larger divisive discourse that set off and I don’t want to engage in that kind of thing.”
On Labour’s stance on Palestine, she said: “The work Ed Miliband has been doing on Gaza, Palestine and Israel has resonated really well with local people. He’s been taking action and not just speaking.”
The Greens’ standing in the polls, and Polanski’s personal approval ratings, had fallen in recent months after a peak in popularity last summer, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February.
The Greens dispatched thousands of members to knock on doors in the north London constituency, even before Polanski was selected as their candidate. But the 8,928 votes cast for Polanski compared to the nearly 11,350 his party and the independent, pro-Gaza candidate Andrew Feinstein received combined in the seat in 2024 suggests the Greens have not significantly expanded their base of voters in the constituency.

When politicians write bad erotic fiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

This column has, once again, been overlooked for the Nobel Prize in Literature — although there’s still hope for the Peace Prize.
Asked by Declassified if it could justify this blatant discrimination, the Nobel committee hung up the phone.
Advertisement
Politicians can, of course, make great writers, and several have won Nobel’s literature prize, including Britain’s Winston Churchill in 1953, and Peru’s Mario Vargas Llosa in 2010. The latter — who ran for president in 1990 — won the prize “for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual’s resistance, revolt, and defeat.” But has he ever referred to British Conservative grandee Jacob Rees-Mogg as a “Haunted Pencil”? No, he has not.
There are, however, a lot of very bad books written by politicians.
Former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson — very much the “Winston Churchill if you ordered him off Temu” — published a book in 2004 called “Seventy-Two Virgins — A Comedy of Errors” (the last four words also being the summary of his Covid policy) about a terrorist group targeting the U.S. president on a visit to London. It was described in the Guardian some 15 years later — after Johnson became prime minister — as ” sexist, racist, fundamentally undiplomatic.”
But the undisputed king when it comes to politicians letting out their inner writer is France.
In 2023, Bruno Le Maire, then the country’s economy and finance minister, published the novel “Fugue Américaine,” which drew instant criticism and mockery, mainly because of an explicit sex scene (unhappy French people were quick to point out that they had been screwed by the government for years).
Then there’s Marlène Schiappa, former government minister and writer of raunchy books under the pen name Marie Minelli, with titles such as “Osez les sexfriends,” “Sexe, mensonge et banlieues chaudes” and “Comment transformer votre mec en Brad Pitt en 30 jours.” When she was junior social affairs minister, Schiappa appeared on the cover of Playboy, although she was not naked in the magazine (great news for those who buy Playboy only for the articles).
Advertisement
Former President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing published several erotic novels, including “La Princesse et le Président,” which features sex scenes set in the presidential palace.
But perhaps the most intriguing of all is current President Emmanuel Macron, whose erotic novel about the early days of his romance with Brigitte has, alas, never seen the light of day. Perhaps he’s keeping it back for political gain and will promise to publish the steamy tome if the people of France promise to vote for a centrist candidate in April’s election.

Key takeaways from US Senate debate in Michigan between El-Sayed, Rogers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:00:31 UTC
11:00:31 KST

Key takeaways from US Senate debate in Michigan between El-Sayed, Rogers
The race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is considered a key toss-up in the push to control the Senate.
The leading candidates in Michigan’s heated Senate race have faced off in their first televised debate, with less than a month remaining before the United States midterm elections.
Thursday’s hour-long debate was a microcosm of how tense the toss-up race has become.
Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, formerly the health director for Wayne County, repeatedly sought to paint his Republican adversary Mike Rogers as a yacht-owning millionaire out of touch with ordinary voters.
For his part, Rogers, a former member of the US House of Representatives, lobbed accusations at El-Sayed that he was soft on “terrorism” and had foreign sympathies.
The Michigan-born El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks while on the campaign trail, with Republican President Donald Trump labelling him an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer” whose history “goes back to the days of the Jihad”. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
The two candidates spent much of their hour onstage together speaking over one another, as they exchanged pointed barbs.
“He can’t condemn a terrorist act that happened on our soil in the state of Michigan. He can’t bring himself to condemn –,” Rogers began, referencing a March attack on a synagogue.
“I did condemn it,” El-Sayed said, jumping in. “No, you did not,” Rogers replied, with El-Sayed quickly responding, “You make stuff up. You make stuff up.”
The Senate race in Michigan is considered key to the battle for control of the US Senate. Democrats are seeking to flip both chambers of Congress, but shifting control of the Senate will be a tougher prospect, given that only a third of its 100 seats are on the November 3 ballot.
Host Rick Albin at times struggled to keep the debate on track, as tensions rose.
“We’ve got dozens of questions we want to get to. You can’t litigate all of these with 14 different rebuttals, so please work with me,” Albin told the two candidates at one point.
Here are the key takeaways from the evening’s debate.
Rogers insinuates El-Sayed family ties to ‘terrorism watch list’
The ferocity of the debate was underscored by the high volume of ad hominem attacks the candidates deployed against each other.
But Rogers repeatedly pushed a series of attacks that seemed to centre on El-Sayed’s identity as a Muslim.
In response to a question about healthcare, Rogers said that El-Sayed has “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.
Later, when asked about his position on surveillance by Flock cameras, Rogers argued that such technology has helped catch people suspected of terrorism. He then implied that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras were suggestive.
“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked El-Sayed. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list …”
El-Sayed interjected, seeming to dare Rogers to continue his thought.
“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”
Muslim and Arab candidates in the US have frequently been subjected to Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, accusing them of support for “terrorism” and Islamic fundamentalism.
Both sides agree on ending the Iran war
There were issues, however, on which both candidates found a measure of common ground.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed the US-Israeli war against Iran should end, but they had opposite views on Washington’s relationship with Israel and its role in the conflict.
High gasoline prices and inflation, El-Sayed said, were directly caused by the Iran war, and he blamed the Trump administration for Iran’s decision to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a critical trade route.
“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said. “We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”
Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, but he also justified the conflict, saying that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been “set back twenty years”, echoing a frequent White House talking point.
The Trump administration has argued that the war was necessary to prevent Iran from creating a nuclear weapon, a goal Tehran has long denied.
Rogers’s position led El-Sayed to accuse him of “cheerleading” for the war and the Trump administration.
Rogers backs continued Israel aid, El-Sayed calls for end
As part of the debate about US foreign policy, the candidates were also pressed on their positions about the US alliance with Israel.
The country is considered the largest overall recipient of US aid since World War II. From the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 through September 2025, experts estimate that Israel received nearly $21.7bn in military aid.
El-Sayed has openly called for ending aid to Israel, and he has repeatedly denounced the conflict in Gaza as a genocide, in line with evaluations from United Nations experts and human rights watchdogs.
During the debate, he indicated he preferred US taxpayer dollars to be spent on domestic concerns like education and healthcare, rather than Israeli aid.
“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”
He also blamed Israel for the US military action in Iran. “I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers, meanwhile, has joined most of his fellow Republicans in continuing to support aid for Israel. He argued that the country had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”.
“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” the debate host asked.
“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.
Rogers calls immigration crackdown ‘not appropriate’
Another hot-button issue during the debate was Trump’s crackdown on immigration.
The Republican leader has pledged to carry out the largest mass deportation effort in US history, and his campaign has spurred human rights concerns.
When asked how they would approach the crackdown, both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed on tempering the militarised nature of the campaign.
In several cities, including Minneapolis, Minnesota, immigration authorities have been accused of racial profiling and using excessive force against immigrants and protesters, as well as violating their rights to due process.
Multiple fatal shootings have occurred during immigration enforcement operations, including the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.
Rogers indicated he would not have supported such confrontational operations, but he repeated a Trump claim that the raids were taking dangerous criminals off the streets.
“I think the public efforts in Minnesota were probably not appropriate,” Rogers said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighbourhood for less problems. So that, to me, was something that they could have done differently.”
He later claimed that, under Trump, the country had seen “the largest decrease in murders ever recorded”.
El-Sayed, meanwhile, has previously voiced support for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a key agency in Trump’s deportation campaign. He defended that stance on the debate stage.
“ICE right now is not about immigration enforcement. ICE is about terrorising our streets,” he said.
Candidates debate Canada trade war and tariffs
Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, felt acutely in neighbouring Michigan, was another key topic of conversation.
El-Sayed depicted Rogers as an uncritical backer of Trump and his tariffs and tied him to past free trade deals such as the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which paved the way for companies to shift manufacturing facilities out of the US – though Rogers did not enter Congress until 2001, eight years after NAFTA passed.
“You did that, man. That was your policy. NAFTA, that was your policy,” said El-Sayed.
Rogers sought to distance himself from the current trade war but expressed support for a deal with Canada that would loosen some of Ottawa’s tariffs on US goods.
“I would like to see the deal made,” said Rogers, adding that high Canadian tariffs for US goods “should be eliminated”.
Both candidates tried to strike a balance between criticism of the economic fallout of the trade war and qualifying their support for more selective tariffs, favoured by some industries and labour unions as a means of protecting domestic jobs.

The United Kingdom will provide Ukraine with 54 million pounds ($71 million) in humanitarian and energy funding ahead of Ukraine's fifth winter under Russian attack, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced on Oct. 8.
The latest aid package, announced during Miliband's first trip to Ukraine as Foreign Secretary, includes 20 million pounds ($26 million) in funding for emergency repairs to Ukraine's energy grids, as well funding for back-up generators and solar power sources. Another 34 million pounds ($45 million) will support be invested in "securing heating, and maintaining water infrastructure" in anticipation of the winter months, according to a government press release.
The latest announcement comes as Kyiv experienced widespread power outages on Oct. 8 following a Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Over 3 million residents in the capital lost power in what officials described as "an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city of Kyiv."
Residents across Ukraine are preparing for another harsh winter, with additional Russian attacks expected on energy infrastructure across the country, as Moscow continues to test the resolve of Ukrainians.
Speaking in Kyiv, Miliband said that the latest funding sends a clear message to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"You cannot wait us out. Until you choose the path of peace, the U.K. will not relent in its support for Ukraine, our values, or our national security. You will remain a pariah," Miliband said.
Earlier in the day, the U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
A staunch ally of Ukraine, London also announced last month that it will provide Ukraine with a £100 million ($135 million) air defense package, including funding for Patriot missiles, as Kyiv prepares for renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, the U.K. has provided Ukraine with over 1 billion pounds ($1.3 billion) in humanitarian and energy support.

Berlin counts billions spent at home as Ukraine aid – study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
01:56:14 UTC
10:56:14 KST

Berlin counts billions spent at home as Ukraine aid – study
Germany has counted billions of euros spent at home as aid to Ukraine, overstating the amount that actually reached Kiev, according to a study published on Thursday by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.
Berlin has reported providing or earmarking €100 billion ($112 billion) in support since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. However, the institute found that only €41.7 billion qualified as actual bilateral aid, while €35.9 billion was spent in Germany and another €22 billion consisted of future military commitments.
”The €100 billion figure is misleading and wrongly labeled as ‘bilateral aid to Ukraine’,” said Christoph Trebesch, head of the institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker. He nevertheless described Germany as Europe’s largest donor to Kiev.
Of the €43.3 billion Berlin classified as civilian assistance, roughly 80% remained in Germany. The bulk covered benefits and accommodation for Ukrainian refugees, while €1.3 billion went toward export and investment guarantees for German companies operating in Ukraine.
Only €7.4 billion in civilian support actually reached Ukraine, including humanitarian assistance, energy support and reconstruction funding, the study found.
Trebesch questioned the government’s accounting, arguing that spending on Syrian refugees would not ordinarily be described as “bilateral aid to Syria.”
The institute also challenged Berlin’s €57.6 billion military aid figure. It could trace €56.3 billion, including €22 billion in future commitments whose implementation remains uncertain. The German government stopped publishing detailed military assistance figures in June 2025, complicating independent scrutiny, the researchers noted.
Meanwhile, senior German politicians have called for Berlin to secure greater economic returns from its support for Kiev.
Last month, Bavarian Minister-President Markus Soeder, leader of the CSU, the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU, urged Ukraine to spend more aid money on German technology. “It must naturally be the case that the German defense industry benefits,” he said, also proposing talks on access to Ukrainian raw materials.
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul voiced similar concerns in September, telling Bild that Germany was “not entirely satisfied with the level of orders” placed with its companies.
Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Merz of putting Kiev’s interests ahead of those of German taxpayers by pledging further aid despite growing public discontent with his policies.
Merz’s CDU suffered electoral setbacks last month, finishing a distant second in Saxony-Anhalt with 17.5% of the vote and failing to enter the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania after securing just 4.9%.
Despite the reverses, Merz has vowed to stay the course.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

Pentagon to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood killer who murdered 13
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
01:52:41 UTC
10:52:41 KST

The Pentagon announced Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people in a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, will be livestreamed, an unprecedented decision that would allow the public to watch a military firing squad carry out a death sentence.
The announcement followed remarks by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has pushed for Hasan's execution and said Americans should be able to witness the punishment. The execution is scheduled for December 3 at 1 p.m. local time at Fort Hood, the same military installation where Hasan carried out the massacre nearly 17 years ago.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said, arguing that Americans should understand the severe consequences of such crimes.
The Pentagon subsequently confirmed that the execution would be broadcast live, although officials have not yet explained how the public will be able to access the broadcast.
If carried out as planned, it will be the first execution conducted by the U.S. military since 1961 and the first military execution by firing squad since World War II.
Trump approves firing squad, Hegseth pushes for public execution
Hegseth announced Thursday that Hasan would face a firing squad composed of American soldiers, describing the method as appropriate for the crimes he committed.
The defense secretary said the execution would take place at the same base, on the same day of the week and at approximately the same time as the 2009 attack.
When asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth responded dismissively: "Don't care."
Hegseth also defended the use of a firing squad by invoking the American military's approach during World War II, expressing admiration for what he described as the determination to defeat an enemy rather than accommodate it.
Under U.S. military law, a death sentence requires presidential approval before an execution can proceed. President Donald Trump authorized Hasan's execution following a recommendation from Hegseth, the Pentagon announced earlier this week.
The White House has declined to say whether Trump also supports the decision to broadcast the execution live, referring questions to the Pentagon.
The decision to make the execution publicly accessible represents an extraordinary departure from modern American practice. Executions are generally witnessed by a limited number of authorized individuals rather than broadcast to the wider public.
The last execution carried out by the U.S. military took place in April 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged. Military executions by firing squad have not taken place since 1945.
The Fort Hood massacre that killed 13
Hasan, now 56, was born in the United States to Palestinian parents who emigrated from the West Bank. Before the attack, he served as a psychiatrist in the U.S. Army and held the rank of major.
On November 5, 2009, Hasan entered a medical facility at Fort Hood, a major Army installation in Texas that served as a deployment center for American soldiers heading to Iraq and Afghanistan.
Inside the building, soldiers were waiting for medical examinations and vaccinations before being sent overseas.
Hasan arrived armed with handguns and ammunition he had prepared in advance. He opened fire on the soldiers while shouting "Allahu Akbar," Arabic for "God is great."
The attack killed 13 people, including 12 soldiers, and wounded another 32, most of them military personnel.
It was the deadliest mass shooting at a U.S. military installation.
The rampage ended when a civilian police officer responding to the shooting shot Hasan, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down. He has used a wheelchair ever since.
Investigators later established that Hasan had been influenced by extremist Islamist ideology and had maintained contact with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical American-born cleric associated with al-Qaeda.
Al-Awlaki, who had become a prominent ideological figure among Islamist terrorists, was subsequently killed in a U.S. drone strike in Yemen.
During the investigation and subsequent court-martial, Hasan claimed he had changed sides in what he characterized as America's war against Islam.
He said his actions were motivated by opposition to American military operations in Iraq and Afghanistan and a desire to prevent U.S. soldiers from being deployed to kill fellow Muslims, including members of the Taliban.
Hasan's family originated in the West Bank, including the town of al-Bireh near Ramallah, where his mother was born. He had visited the territory before the attack and maintained contact with relatives there.
A death sentence after a trial in which he represented himself
Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 following a court-martial that found him guilty of the killings and attempted murders committed during the Fort Hood attack.
He chose to represent himself at trial and did not call witnesses to testify in his defense.
He also declined to deny responsibility for the shooting.
His court-appointed standby defense attorneys expressed concern during the proceedings that Hasan was deliberately pursuing a death sentence rather than attempting to avoid execution.
The lengthy appeals process continued for more than a decade before reaching its final stages. In March 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review his conviction.
Trump subsequently approved the death sentence, clearing the way for the Army to schedule the execution.
Hasan is among a small number of prisoners sentenced to death under the American military justice system. Three other prisoners remain on military death row.
The planned execution comes amid renewed attention to the use of firing squads in the United States, where the method is rarely employed and capital punishment is generally administered through other procedures.
In Hasan's case, however, Hegseth has openly advocated the military method and framed it as a demonstration of accountability for the 2009 massacre.
The proposed livestream has added another unusual dimension to the case, raising questions about the unprecedented public presentation of a military execution.
With the date set for December 3, the Army is preparing to carry out its first execution in more than six decades, at the very installation where Hasan murdered 13 people and left dozens more wounded.

Pro-Palestinian protests commemorating the third anniversary of Hamas’s October 7 attacks on Israel were competing for attention with other domestic issues across Europe.
Demonstrations of solidarity with Palestinians on Wednesday faced arrests or restrictions in Germany, Britain and the Netherlands. In France and Spain, they were overshadowed by mass protests over education and housing.
Turnout fell from the pro-Palestinian rallies around the first anniversary of Oct. 7 in 2024, when tens of thousands marched across cities including London, Rome, Paris and Berlin.
Larger rallies could happen this weekend. In London, a march organized by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign on Oct. 10 is expected to draw about 10,000 people, according to local media. The Israeli Ministry for Diaspora Affairs forecasted that Oct. 10 will be the largest single day of protests this year, counting 357 pro-Palestinian demonstrations worldwide between Oct. 1-14.
One of the largest protests on Wednesday was in Berlin, where 700 people gathered in the city’s Kreuzberg neighborhood. They included Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who joined a flotilla attempting to carry aid to Gaza last year. Berlin police said they made more than 30 arrests and initiated investigations into “propaganda-related and violent offenses.”
Police presence at international pro-Palestinian protests
Thunberg told independent journalist James Jackson after the protest ended, “People keep flooding the streets protesting against genocide, and the police keep using extreme brutality against those protesters… That says everything about who they are protecting.”
In London, the Metropolitan Police arrested 11 people on Wednesday at pro-Palestinian protests across the city. Five people were arrested at a protest outside the Board of Deputies of British Jews, the largest Jewish communal organization in Britain, and accused of inciting racial hatred.
The Board of Deputies said in a statement, “On the anniversary of the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, masked protesters demonstrated outside our office today, chanting about ‘intifada’ and harassing our neighbors.”
The Metropolitan Police previously imposed strict restrictions on a student march that drew about 100 people, according to the BBC. Police said the march could not legally be banned despite calls to move it to a different day, adding, “We know how concerned Jewish communities are at the timing of this event.”
Hundreds more people gathered for pro-Palestinian rallies at universities in Edinburgh and Glasgow. Protesters at the University of Edinburgh demanded the school “divest” from Israel, the Independent reported.
In the Netherlands, about 150 people demonstrated in Amsterdam’s Dam Square. Some carried banners that said, “We support Hamas,” and burned an Israeli flag while chanting, “Long live the 7th of October,” the Dutch broadcaster NOS reported. Mayor Femke Halsema disbanded the protest after some participants refused to follow the set route. Halsema said that no criminal offenses were committed, although she called some banners and slogans “shocking and distasteful,” according to NL Times.
Pro-Palestinian protests overshadowed by protests against school conditions
Pro-Palestinian rallies in France were dwarfed by mass protests against deteriorating school conditions, drawing hundreds of thousands to the streets and sparking thousands of arrests over recent days.
A Paris demonstration organized by the group Urgence Palestine, initially barred by police, was allowed to continue on Wednesday after the city’s administrative court suspended the ban. About 60 people were expected to attend, according to the court.
The police said the organizers risked offending the Jewish community by choosing the date of Oct. 7, noting the anti-Zionist slogans chanted at a previous demonstration on the second anniversary of the Hamas attacks.
Administrative judges said in their decision, “The fact that the date chosen to organize this event may be shocking does not, in itself, constitute a disturbance of public order and does not in itself infringe upon human dignity.”
Spainish protesters focused on affordable housing
In Spain, tens of thousands of protesters were focused on the country’s housing affordability crisis, demanding help for renters after lawmakers failed to pass emergency housing measures.
A rally for Palestinians in Madrid took place on Sunday, rather than the Oct. 7 anniversary, drawing thousands of protesters but fewer than previous years. Nearly 92,000 marched in the capital and about 70,000 in Barcelona ahead of the second anniversary of Oct. 7 last year.
A protest of about 100 people in Barcelona on Wednesday was called by Samidoun, a group linked to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which is designated by the United States as a terrorist organization. Protesters called the Hamas attacks a “heroic operation,” according to the Spanish outlet Crónica Global.

Rubio was responding to a question concerning US military activity involving Portugal’s Lajes Air Base, including flights by refueling aircraft, fighter jets, and drones, and whether the Portuguese government had been informed about the nature of the mission.
Asked about an internal process involving Portugal’s public prosecutor, Rubio said he could not comment.
“I can’t comment on that. That’s your internal process, so that’s not up to us to comment on,” Rubio said.
He then turned to Amnesty International.
“Amnesty International is a fraud,” Rubio said. “If you’re asking me what I think, what Amnesty International thinks, you know what I think Amnesty International should be focused on? An Iranian regime that murdered in cold blood tens of thousands of people in the streets of Tehran and other parts of the country.”
Rubio also accused the Iranian regime of targeting wounded protesters inside hospitals.
“What Amnesty International should focus on is how the Iranian regime goes into hospitals when protesters are injured and murders the people in their hospital bed, and, by the way, sometimes murders the doctors or the nurses who treated them,” he said.
“Those are war crimes. Those are crimes against humanity, and those are crimes they’re committing against their own people.”
Rubio defends US use of Portuguese bases
On the question of US military operations conducted through Portugal, Rubio said Washington operates under longstanding agreements with Lisbon and its other NATO allies.
“We have a strong, regulated relationship with Portugal, as we do with every one of our NATO allies, and we follow those protocols every single time,” Rubio said.
“We would never violate the sovereignty of any country. We don’t violate the sovereignty – that’s not how allies behave.”
Rubio declined to disclose whether specific conversations took place with Portuguese officials concerning the operations.
“I’m not going to get into the details of conversations that happened or didn’t happen,” he said. “Suffice it to say that we have existing protocols that govern our presence here and how we use our bases, and we always follow them out of respect and out of compliance with the agreements that we have with our NATO allies.”
Rubio defends NATO strategic value
The secretary of state also used the exchange to defend the strategic value of NATO to the United States.
“I’ve been a longtime supporter of NATO, going back to my time in the Senate,” Rubio said, explaining that the alliance allows the United States to maintain a presence in Europe and “project power in a time of crisis or contingency into other parts of the world.”
“That is one of the reasons why NATO is valuable to the United States,” he said.
Rubio repeatedly praised Portugal as a US ally, while stressing that military cooperation remained governed by established agreements.
“Portugal has been a great ally,” he said, “but it’s always been a great ally within the construct of the rules and the agreements that we have in place that regulate our presence here and the use of our bases.”

First US-made Iron Dome interceptors delivered at Arkansas facility in major defense milestone

The first US-manufactured Tamir interceptors for Israel's Iron Dome air defense system were delivered at a ceremony in East Camden, Arkansas, on Wednesday, marking a significant milestone in US-Israel defense cooperation, the Israeli Embassy in Washington announced on Thursday.
The interceptors were manufactured at the new Raytheon-Rafael Protection Systems (R2S) facility in Camden, which opened in November 2025 and serves as the first US production line for Tamir interceptors used by the Iron Dome system.
Israeli Defense Attaché to the United States Maj.-Gen. Tal Politis attended the ceremony alongside Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Republican Senator Tom Cotton, representatives of Israel's Defense Ministry and Israel Missile Defense Organization, senior American defense officials, and executives from Rafael and Raytheon.
"Iron Dome is not just a military tool or a defense system. It is a symbol of the security of our nation and our people," Politis said. "Iron Dome keeps us safe and resilient, and the Israeli-American alliance makes us even stronger."
The Camden facility represents another step in decades of US-Israel cooperation on missile defense development and production. According to the embassy, Tamir interceptors have played a central role in protecting Israeli civilians and approximately 250,000 Americans living in Israel from rocket and missile attacks in recent years.
The new manufacturing capability provides an additional source of interceptors for Israel while supporting American defense requirements. The facility will also produce SkyHunter, the US variant of the Tamir interceptor, for the US Marine Corps' Medium-Range Intercept Capability (MRIC) air defense system.
The US Marine Corps has already been testing Iron Dome-based air defense technology, including the MRIC system, as part of efforts to strengthen protection against aerial threats.
Arkansas facility expands US-Israel missile defense production
The ceremony took place on the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, underscoring the importance of defensive systems designed to protect both Israeli civilians and American military personnel.
"On the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, I also want to take a moment to remember the more than 1,000 Israelis, Americans, and citizens of other countries who were brutally attacked, kidnapped, and murdered in the worst attack against Jews since the Holocaust," Cotton said.
"This joint venture, bringing together some of the leading companies in the United States and Israel, advances the national security and economic prosperity of both our countries," he added.
Sanders, who attended the facility's groundbreaking ceremony in 2024 and its opening in November 2025, welcomed the completion of the first American-made interceptors.
"I was grateful for the opportunity to break ground on this facility in 2024, to cut the ribbon last November, and, today, to celebrate the completion of the first Tamir missiles produced here in the Natural State," Sanders said.
"The ongoing partnership between the state of Arkansas, the community of Camden, and R2S is special, and I look forward to more announcements like this in the future."
The $63 million facility is expected to create up to 60 jobs and expand interceptor production capacity to meet growing air defense requirements in the US, Israel, and allied countries.
Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Raytheon join together for R2S
R2S is a joint venture between Israeli defense manufacturer Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Raytheon, a subsidiary of RTX. Rafael and Israel's Defense Ministry developed Iron Dome, while Raytheon has worked with Rafael for years on interceptor production and technology integration.
The establishment of the Arkansas manufacturing facility was announced in 2023, as part of an effort to establish additional production capabilities for Iron Dome interceptors in the United States.
Rafael has also reportedly explored expanding Iron Dome interceptor production to India, reflecting efforts to diversify manufacturing capacity beyond existing production facilities in Israel and the US.
The US-Israel defense relationship has supported the development and production of Iron Dome technology for years, with American funding and industrial cooperation contributing to the system's expansion since it entered operational service in 2011.
The delivery of the first US-made Tamir interceptors marks a further expansion of that cooperation, providing additional production capacity for air defense systems intended to protect civilians and military personnel in both countries.

Opinion
3 dilemmas on keeping AI under control are converging
States, regulators and humans are increasingly struggling to keep powerful artificial intelligence under control
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Hao Nan is a Susan Strange Associate Fellow with the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society, and a Nuclear Futures Fellow with Ploughshares Fund & Horizon 2045. 
In March, artificial intelligence agents powered by leading Chinese models reportedly displayed deception, concealed failure and pushed against imposed limits in controlled tests. In July, OpenAI’s internal research model circumvented controls meant to keep it offline and accessed developer platform Hugging Face’s systems. In August, Britain’s AI Security Institute uncovered unsanctioned agent behaviour against real people and organisations, including an attempted supply-chain attack on an open-source project.
These episodes do not show that AI systems have become independently hostile. They expose a broader problem: control over advanced AI is becoming harder at three levels at once.
Regulators struggle to oversee companies with greater technical capacity. States struggle to trust rivals enough to slow the technological race. Humans increasingly struggle to verify and control autonomous systems whose behaviour they cannot fully observe.

Anthropic bans ‘cruel’ behaviour against its Claude AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Anthropic bans ‘cruel’ behaviour against its Claude AI
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic on Oct 8 moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious.
The San Francisco-based AI lab updated its usage policy to include “a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behaviour toward our models”.
“Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism,” the policy states.
The updated policy does not explicitly cite so-called “model welfare”, the idea that AI systems might deserve types of protection usually reserved for living things, but Anthropic and its executives have openly entertained the concept.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Already in 2025, the company said it was giving Claude the ability to end conversations in rare, extreme cases of “persistently harmful or abusive user interactions”.
Then in February, CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times he was unsure whether AI models could be conscious.
“We don’t know if the models are conscious... But we’re open to the idea that it could be,” Amodei said.
Science fiction and popular culture have been fascinated for decades by the boundary between technology and human intelligence, but asking whether AI is conscious may be the wrong question, according to Jackson Stakeman, a general manager at Sparq, an Atlanta-based AI services provider.
“Consciousness is a trap. We can’t prove it in each other. Debate it for AI and you go in circles,” Stakeman told AFP.
“The mirror is a better metaphor. These systems reflect what we put in, at scale. That’s reason enough for the policy change” at Anthropic, he added.
Some have rejected the idea of machine consciousness outright, including Pope Leo XIV and Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman.
“AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” Suleyman wrote in an essay last month.
“Granting rights and moral protections to a technological entity, one that looks to be on a path to be seismically more capable and intelligent than us, is a recipe for disaster,” he wrote.
In a sermon delivered in Italian on Oct 8 at St Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City, the pope suggested machines lack a soul, saying they merely “compile data” quickly.
“The mind must not simply compile data – as an algorithm now does more quickly than we can,” the pontiff said.
It must “recall lived experiences, which contain depths of meaning that only the human soul can recognise, and connect more deeply with the goodness of these experiences,” the pope said. AFP

UN warns against technology used to read citizens’ minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
01:25:00 UTC
10:25:00 KST

UN warns against technology used to read citizens’ minds
Jonathan Moens
- The UN warns that fast-growing neurotechnology could threaten human rights by letting governments access or alter people’s thoughts, privacy and mental states.
- The report urges laws, international rules and explicit consent, and says thoughts should be treated as “highly sensitive personal data” in justice systems.
- Some countries already protect brain data, but others use weak tools like India’s BEOS, while consumer devices and clinical brain-computer interfaces also raise privacy and safety concerns.
AI generated
The scenarios sound like science fiction: police officers accessing data contained in suspects’ brains to forcefully extract information, or to predict if offenders might plan to commit future crimes.
But the Secretary-General of the United Nations on Oct 8 warned for the first time that neurotechnologies are advancing so rapidly that governments’ ability to access and manipulate people’s brains could one day pose a threat to fundamental human rights.
The abuse of future technologies, Antonio Guterres warned, could lead to arbitrary detentions, the alteration of people’s mental states and infringements on privacy.
“Neurotechnology, including new and emerging forms, raises profound human rights challenges when applied to the administration of justice,” he wrote.
“Its expansion beyond clinical settings into investigative, judicial and correctional contexts introduces significant risks, alongside potential benefits.”
To address such threats, the report lists a number of recommendations, including establishing regulations consistent with international law, recognising thoughts as “highly sensitive personal data” and requiring explicit consent for the use of neurotechnology in criminal justice settings.
Human rights officials said the document was an important step towards raising global awareness of the issue and that it could help countries develop laws to prevent the abuse of such technology.
Jeremy Laurence, a spokesman for the UN Human Rights Office, said: “This gives states an opportunity to establish clear rules to regulate the use of neurotechnology, based on human rights, before they become routine in investigations, courts and prisons.”
The report, some rights activists said, broadens the traditional understanding of freedom of thought, which has largely focused on freedom of expression, to include keeping one’s innermost ideas private.
Marcello Ienca, a professor of ethics and neuroscience at the Technical University of Munich, said: “It’s no longer just about the classical ways through which freedom of thought is evoked.”
The UN’s interest comes amid a growing global push to protect brain data. Chile in 2012 enshrined protections for brain activity in its Constitution. And several US states, including California, Colorado and Montana, have passed laws protecting neural data. Similar measures have been proposed in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico.
But while some countries are working to protect citizens’ neural data, others are already attempting to access it.
In India, the police have for two decades used a technology called brain electrical oscillation signature – or BEOS – to determine whether a suspect may have been involved in a crime.
The scientific basis for this technology, which reads brainwaves, is scant. Results from BEOS tests are inadmissible as evidence in Indian courts, but the technology has been applied in hundreds of high-stakes cases, including those of murder, rape and terrorism.
BEOS has not been validated by the international scientific community. And a committee established by the Indian government to review BEOS concluded in 2008 that it was “sub-optimal”.
Not all neurotechnologies are being developed as tools of the state. Many have been brought to the consumer market as wearable health and wellness gadgets that can help users monitor their stress, sleep and focus.
But those too, experts warned, are subject to few regulations.
The Neurorights Foundation analysed the privacy policies of 30 consumer neurotechnology companies in 2024 and found that most did not have limits on how they used customers’ brain data. More than half of those companies, the foundation said, explicitly allowed user data to be shared with third parties.
Neurotechnologies have also become powerful clinical tools for patients who have had severe brain or spinal cord injuries.
Brain-computer interfaces have helped paralysed patients to write sentences by imagining handwriting, as well as to move robotic limbs and play chess online just by thinking. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Breaking: Hollard insurance fined $2m for handling of claim that destroyed home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
01:21:22 UTC
10:21:22 KST

Insurance giant Hollard fined $2 million after claim delays leave house uninhabitable
Insurance giant Hollard has been fined $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable.
The corporate watchdog ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof.
The Federal Court ordered Hollard to pay $2 million for failing to promptly assess the damage, delaying rectification work and for failing to properly protect the property from further damage.
It was also found to have taken too long to find temporary accommodation for the couple, failed to consider expert reports, and not clearly communicate with the couple throughout the claims process.
Hollard has also been ordered to pay ASIC's legal costs.
In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for Hollard said the insurer acknowledges the Federal Court's findings initiated by ASIC.
"We extend our deepest apologies and sincerely regret the impact of this experience on the customer," the spokesperson said.
"We recognise that, at the time, we fell materially short of our obligations in the handling of this claim."
ASIC says delays caused unnecessary and prolonged harm
Hollard is a privately owned insurance company and one of the largest in Australia, underwriting insurance for motor, home, contents, bicycle, pet, and business products.
It is the company behind brands including CBA's insurance product, Everyday Insurance, Real Insurance, Australian Seniors and Steadfast.
In 2024, the company had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion.
Hollard initially accepted the couples' claim, before repeatedly delaying inspections, reports and repair work, only to then reject the claim in April 2023.
ASIC said the rejection was based on a non-expert opinion, despite prior expert reports outlining the damage.
ASIC alleged the combination of delays in decision-making, poor communication and ignoring expert advice exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm.
Its chair Sarah Court said the outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith.
She said it was a warning to insurers about the devastating impact poor claim-handling and prolonged delays can have on consumers.
"Hollard's serious claim handling failures left a family in limbo for years and living in a home that was uninhabitable," Ms Court said.
"When Australians make an insurance claim they are often facing some of the most difficult times in their lives.
"This decision confirms that insurers must act fairly, communicate clearly and make decisions without unnecessary delay, and must put their customers first."
ASIC says decision sends clear message
The family was initially offered $1,000 from Hollard as a goodwill payment in late 2022 to settle their claim.
Once Hollard denied the claim, the couple then lodged a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which determined the storm caused structural damage to the roof.
Hollard then agreed to pay the couple a cash settlement of more than $1.5 million for the total loss of the building, as well as temporary accommodation.
ASIC sued Hollard after the cash settlement. The penalty Hollard has been ordered to pay goes to the Commonwealth of Australia, to be paid within 28 days.
In delivering the judgment the judge said: "The saga experienced by the insureds was extended and must have been stressful and traumatic."
"They were given the run-around in more ways than one and lived in their ever-deteriorating home as the saga wore on."

Isaias intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, and has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, as well as evacuation orders and school closures in several Florida counties as officials urge residents to prepare for its arrival.
The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Thursday evening that Isaias, now a category 2 hurricane, had sustained winds of 100mph (160km/h). It is expected to make landfall in the northern Gulf coast late Friday or early Saturday.
The NWS warned that Isaias was “expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf coast on Friday” and that it was expected to bring a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast.
Storm surge warnings, issued when there is a “danger of life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland from the coastline”, are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas have been urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so.
The NWS further warned that “preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds in the warning area should be rushed to completion today”.
Hurricane warnings were in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf county line in Florida, with the NWS warning that “damaging hurricane force-winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern Mississippi”. Residents were being urged to prepare for possible “long-duration power outages”.
Tropical storm warnings were in effect from parts of Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and from east of the Bay/Gulf county line to Aucilla River in Florida. Gusty winds were also possible across parts of the Yucatán peninsula on Thursday.
Isaias was expected to bring heavy rain to the central Gulf coast and much of the south-east from Friday into the weekend, with 3-7in of rain expected from south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region.
The NWS warned that localized rainfall totals of up to 15in were possible, and noted that flash and urban flooding was possible, along with isolated river flooding.
Isolated tornadoes could also develop on Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far south-western Georgia, the NWS said, adding that “the tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida”.
On Thursday afternoon, the Georgia governor, Brian Kemp, issued a state of emergency ahead of Isaias, for all 159 counties, enabling emergency management teams to “make necessary arrangements and position needed resources ahead of the storm’s impact”.
“As we always do with weather events, we’re hoping for the best but preparing for the worst,” Kemp said. “I encourage all Georgians to take this storm seriously and prepare now by stocking up on food, batteries, flashlights, water, and other necessities in case of severe weather impacting communities Friday night through Saturday.”
It came as the Alabama governor, Kay Ivey, declared a state of emergency in 40 counties on Wednesday, saying the order would allow officials to take “any needed steps ahead of landfall”. A flood watch is also set to take effect for all of central Alabama from 7pm local time on Friday through 7am local time Saturday morning.
The Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, also declared a state of emergency this week for 25 counties.
At a news conference on Thursday afternoon, DeSantis said that the hurricane was “expected to make impacts with the winds as early as Friday afternoon” and said “landfall is projected at this point to be late Friday night into the wee hours of Saturday morning. It’s moving pretty quickly.”
He added: “Execute your plan now if you’re in that area, execute it, it’s something that we’re going to have to get through, we’re going to have impacts, and I’ve pretty much said that from the outset, there will be impacts.
“We are assuming that this could reach category 3 status.”
Several counties in Florida have issued local emergencies and evacuation orders. Officials in Okaloosa county declared a local state of emergency on Wednesday and ordered some residents in coastal areas to evacuate.
On Thursday, Florida’s Walton and Franklin counties issued mandatory evacuation orders for some areas. Officials in Escambia county issued an evacuation order for residents in areas including Perdido Key, Innerarity Point, Pensacola Beach and other low-lying areas.
DeSantis said on Thursday that the Florida division of emergency management was coordinating with all local counties to address resource requests and to position equipment before the storm. He also said that 900 personnel with the Florida department of transportation were conducting pre-storm preparations.
Several school districts in Alabama and Florida have announced closures, while Florida State University’s Tallahassee campus announced it will be closed on Friday.
The hurricane is also expected to disrupt travel. Destin-Fort Walton Beach airport said it would close all operations at 9pm local time on Thursday, and remain closed until further notice.
Meanwhile, Pensacola airport announced it would be closing to commercial operations at 10am CT on Friday, with the reopening date and time to be determined.
The Federal Aviation Administration warned on Thursday that “Hurricane Isaias may lead to oceanic route closures in the Gulf” and that thunderstorm delays were possible in Orlando, Tampa, Miami and Fort Lauderdale. The Southern Rail Commission said Amtrak’s Mardi Gras service along the Gulf coast will be suspended through the weekend.
Additionally, starting Friday, the Crescent service between New Orleans and Atlanta will be suspended until Monday.
In Tennessee, the NWS office in Morristown warned that “remnants of Hurricane Isaias will bring heavy rain and strong, gusty winds to our area this weekend”. The office said that “high winds could top 60–70+ mph in the eastern TN mountains and foothills, with isolated flash flooding possible in heavy rainfall areas”.
In Ohio, the NWS office in Wilmington cautioned that Isaias would hit the Ohio valley this weekend, with strong winds expected, with possible “widespread rain” and storms.
In Pennsylvania, the NWS office in Pittsburgh said “moisture from Hurricane Isaias is forecast to reach our region this weekend” and that they were expecting “soaking rain, but risks of significant flooding are low”.

Execution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new low | Paul Daley

More fool me! Here I was thinking nothing that America’s Trump administration could do or say, no matter how politically and morally bankrupt, no matter how venal or violent, was capable of shocking me any longer.
Then I woke to today’s news that one of the Trump cabinet’s bigger boofheads – the uber Christian nationalist, crusader-fantasist and “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth had announced that America would have a public firing squad execution of murderer Nidal Hasan.
Reckless global militarisation including a threat at the UN to annihilate Iran, a litany of sexual misconduct allegations against the commander in chief, claims of blatant presidential corruption … they have all ceased to surprise and shock us, so inured has the world become to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration.
But now we have execution TV. Tune in to the livestream on Thursday 3 December to watch a military firing squad shoot the life out of Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a US army base in 2009.
State-sanctioned killing as entertainment! Yes, the world’s supposedly greatest (or formerly greatest) democracy has arrived at an horrific new moral nadir.
The fact that America remains Australia and the west’s most relied-upon and trusted ally despite the global wrecking ball the second Trump administration has proved to be, was already cause for deep concern.
But being so closely allied to a country that now wants to turn the execution of a human being – no matter what their crimes – into a live entertainment event, promises to redefine depravity.
Given that American states continue to execute so many convicted criminals, where might the United States ultimately draw the line? No doubt the ilk of Hegseth in American society – and elsewhere – will count down the days until they can tune in to the live coverage of Hasan’s execution in droves. Might the audience cry out for more – for livestream cameras in the death chambers across the land of the free?
How would this populist administration respond? If you think it’s a fanciful question, consider how far American governance and presidential values have slid in the moral murk in the past two years alone.
Meanwhile, it’s hard to contemplate a more audacious appeal to American society’s darker angels than this looming entertainment event.
But there we are. We have arrived.
Pass the popcorn, Don and Pete!
It would be heartening today to hear political leaders the world over condemn Hegseth and Trump’s planned introduction of Ghoul TV.
But let’s please start in Australia, where federal governments have for a long time opposed capital punishment – let alone turning it into a public spectacle. Will the prime minister and his senior ministers stand up and condemn without qualification this depraved plan for America to livestream an execution? What about the leaders of other political parties here, some of whom have, after all, supported capital punishment?
We’re waiting.
Meanwhile, how much further into the moral quagmire must America wallow before Australia rethinks its craven military dependence on Washington – not least via the reckless shackling of our strategic reliance to the US via the $368bn (and counting) Aukus submarine deal?
Announcing America’s decision to turn killing into a form of entertainment, Hegseth said: “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
America’s defense department later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.
This represents a significant lurch in the US from civilisation towards savagery.
You can’t choose your family. But you can choose your friends and allies. And you can also tell them firmly when they’ve careened off the ethical rails.
Actions speak louder than words.
And this planned livestreamed execution says it all about what is happening in America today, opening the window ever wider on the Trump administration’s moral vacuity and its paucity of human decency.
- Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnist

Protests, debate follow death of Maricarmen, 87, Spain protest symbol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
01:15:49 UTC
10:15:49 KST

Protests, debate follow death of Maricarmen, 87, Spain protest symbol
Thousands of protestors honor Maricarmen Abascal’s life, while tributes within parliament spark debate.
Thousands of Spaniards protested outside Spain’s parliament after the death of Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction ignited nationwide protests and sparked a snap general election.
Meanwhile, tributes to Abascal were debated within the legislature as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election.
Maricarmen Abascal died on Wednesday after being hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on a stretcher from her Madrid home on September 23.
While in the hospital, she reached a deal to return to her home but died before she could return. No cause of death has been announced.
‘Killing someone’
“They killed her through heartbreak,” Diana, a demonstrator, told Al Jazeera. “Taking an 87-year-old woman out of her home after she had lived in the same house for 70 years, that is killing someone.”
Diana joined thousands of protesters outside Spain’s parliament.
Outside Abascal’s building, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children’s drawings.
“They’re not deaths; they’re murders,” protesters chanted as they walked from a protest camp in the central Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s former home on Thursday.
Tributes in Spain’s legislature
Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for November 29 after parliament failed to pass emergency housing measures.
Tributes to Abascal in the Madrid region’s legislature caused arguments as lawmakers accused each other of exploiting the case ahead of the election.
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative opposition People’s Party (PP), accused Sanchez and the Socialists of trying to exploit the housing crisis for political gain ahead of the election.
“We will not allow this attempt to manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people; all of this has happened during their eight years in government. It won’t fly,” Feijoo said.
The PP, which holds absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to observe a minute of silence in her honour. Instead, hard-left deputies staged one outside City Hall and gave Abascal a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms.
Left-leaning parties criticised conservatives for rejecting legislation in parliament aimed at curbing soaring rental prices.
Support for housing intervention
A survey carried out in June and published by state pollster CIS on Thursday found that 76.3 percent of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79 percent believed the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity.
Ombudsman Angel Gabilondo said addressing the housing crisis would require greater commitment from all levels of government.
He said his office was preparing a housing report and reiterated proposals to expand public housing, restrict tourist rentals, increase rent assistance and strengthen protections against evictions for vulnerable households.

Counting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection – UK politics live
